a new SUXIIII us, e it a new Gc71, a new toy, or a new person. Approach  
responses are positive, whether displayed by mood expression (smil- 
ing, verbalizations, and the like) or motor activity (swallowing a new  
food, reaching for a new toy, active play, and so on). Withdrawal  
reactions are negative, whether displayed by mood expression (crying,  
fussing, grimacing, verbalizations, or the like) or motor activity (mov- 
ing away, spitting new food out, pushing new toy away, and so forth). Statements showing high approach inZfart "He always smiles  
at a stranger," "She loves new toys," or "He is interested in tasting  
anything new we give him." High withdrawal would be illustrated by,  
"He ignores a new toy until it has been around for several days," and  
"When I introduce a new food, her first reaction is to spit it out."
In the toddler period, a statement illustrating high approach  
would be, "We went to her new play group yesterday; as always she  
plunged right in." High withdrawal in the same situation might be  
shown by, "We started a new play group 2 weeks ago.

best friend." Low adaptability in infancy would be illustrated by,

we are outside—and that has been going on for 3 months."

got her first tricycle and couldn't master it, called it 'stupid.' But then I  
noticed her practicing on it everyday and by a week she was out  
pedaling happily with her friends." A statement illustrating low adap- 
tability would be, "It took him all fall to go contentedly to nursery  
school and each time he gets a cold and is out for several days, he  
becomes reluctant to go again."
In middle childhood, a statement of high adaptability might be,  
"He went to a tennis camp this summer.

section_title: Welcome and Introduction of Dr. Michael Kerr
text:
[Welcome and Introduction of Dr. Michael Kerr]

**Speaker 1:** Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, welcome to our public lecture making a difference in self family. I am Peggy Chen of international social service Hong Kong branch. This is the first event of a series of programs conducted by Dr Michael Kerr we are greatly honored to have Dr Michael Kerr being with us to enlighten us on the Bowen theory. Dr Kerr is the director of the Bowen Center for the Study of the family and Georgetown Family Center. Dr Kerr has a 20 year association with Dr Murray Bowen, founder of the Bowen theory. Dr Kerr is the co author with Dr Bowen of the book Family Evaluation an approach based on Bowen theory. This book has become the authoritative text for anyone wanting to study Bowen theory. Dr Kerr has devoted his professional life to the understanding application and extension of the Bowen theory. Under his leadership, the Bowen theory has developed to greater depths and heights. He speaks frequently to medical schools, universities and professional meetings on the Bowen theory in the United States as well as different parts of the world. He has conducted workshops on the Bowen theory in Japan and Korea, and the workshops were very well received. He's familiar with the concerns and questions we have about applying the Bowen theory in the Asian culture. So let's welcome Dr Kerr.

section_title: Historical Overview: Griesinger, Darwin, and Freud
text:
[Historical Overview: Griesinger, Darwin, and Freud]

**Mike Kerr:** And I'm going to try in this talk, just to present the basic ideas in the theory that Bowen developed, and something about its application. In many ways, it's a very simple, very straightforward theory, but different than any other theory that's come along. I'm not saying it's better, just different, and appreciating that difference is what I hope to accomplish while I'm here. So I'm going to begin with a very brief historical perspective.

So I go back to Wilhelm Griesinger, a German psychiatrist in the 19th century, and he's one of many who viewed madness as a manifestation of a brain disease. Physically, there's something wrong with the brain and that causes the madness that was the dominant viewpoint in the 19th century. He also had an interesting idea called unitary psychosis. He did not differentiate between things like schizophrenia, manic depression, depression, paranoia, saw it as all on a continuum, and in some respects, that's more consistent with Bowen theory.

Another key figure historically that is important to understand is, of course, Charles Darwin, expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals. 1872 the book was summarized by one person how animals and humans Express and signal to others their emotions. Animals and humans Express and signal their emotions. A second point about Darwin that many aspects of human behavior, in his view, exist on a continuum with other species, including morality, which he began to try to think through in the Descent of Man. So as you'll see a little bit later, why I consider Darwin important, because Bowen theory has a critically important evolutionary base to help important to understand.

Freud made many contributions. He also made errors in certain ways. But perhaps one of the most important contributions is that rather than consider madness, in his case, the psychoses and the neuroses. Disease as the result of physical diseases of the brain, some structural or anatomical disturbance, put forth the idea that it could be a functional disturbance in the brain. There's nothing wrong with the brain, structurally or anatomically, the symptoms of the individual reflect a disturbance in functioning. And that idea has carried over into Bowen theory. And that doesn't rule out the role of things like genetics and other biological factors, and I hope we can appreciate that as we go along.

section_title: Kraepelin, Selye, and Stress Response in Bowen Theory
text:
[Kraepelin, Selye, and Stress Response in Bowen Theory]

**Mike Kerr:** A dominant point of view in psychiatry, at least in the United States, and I think globally, is represented by this man, Emil Kraepelin, German psychiatrist, turn of the century. He considered dementia praecox, manic depression and other psychiatric disorders, distinct clinical entities, and that was different from Griesinger, who put them on a continuum, distinct clinical entities that have different underlying brain pathologies, anatomical defects, and therefore different etiologies. To this day, that is the dominant view in psychiatry. Freud was kind of shoved aside, as I'm sure most of you know, and this idea has resurfaced in a way that's hard to explain easily. Bowen theory bridges this dichotomy between functional and structural and sees their inner relationship.

Selye is so important, that's why I put him up more than anyone else, Selye demonstrated the role of emotional responses in causing or combating, combating much of the wear and tear experienced by human beings throughout their lives. This idea is critically important in Bowen theory that activation of the stress response too much and too often over time, leads to a wide range of clinical conditions. The important question is, what is the stress that activates the stress response? Bowen theory's major contribution to that is that it's all about human relationships, primarily about human relationships, and they reach their greatest level of intensity in the family setting.

section_title: Attachment Theory Compared to Bowen Theory
text:
[Attachment Theory Compared to Bowen Theory]

**Mike Kerr:** I say this because I know this is a probably, today, the most influential developmental theory globally. It certainly is in the United States, and I know there's been a lot of understanding of it developing here. And Bowen theory and attachment theory are very different and different in a very specific way. But I would say this about attachment theory and John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, two very fine contributors to our understanding of human behavior, but different. In contrast to Freud, they did define attachment as an instinctually based process. You didn't have to make it happen. It happened. It's rooted in instinct. It's not just something that's learned, but like Freud, they viewed inadequate mothering packaged in a number of different delightful and less than delightful ways as a primary cause of human emotional problems, and I will strike a sharp contrast with that in Bowen theory, an unavailable or unresponsive mother can result in the insecure attachment of the offspring. Those of you that know attachment theory know that statement, so I'll be presenting a different idea.

section_title: Paul MacLean, Mammalian Family Behaviors, and Symbiosis
text:
[Paul MacLean, Mammalian Family Behaviors, and Symbiosis]

**Mike Kerr:** And this is another important scientist whose work was developed in parallel with Bowen's work. They worked in the same place, the National Institutes of Mental Health in Washington, DC. They kind of knew each other, but didn't really know each other's work that well back in the 1950s that came later, but Paul MacLean came up with this idea, first of all, that he viewed the family as coming into existence with the evolution of the mammals, and by family, meaning a sort of long term relationship bond. Long term can range from up to weaning and then severed all the way into adult life, but much longer term than previously in evolution, largely because of the development of nursing. The mammalian female nursed the young, along with the rest of maternal care. So as I would see it, the mother became suddenly extremely important, more important to the well being and survival of the young because of this nursing relationship. And not surprisingly, the young developed ways of communicating with the mother to let them know when they're hungry and in distress. In other ways, audio vocal communication for maintaining the mother offspring relationship.

Additionally, play behavior. So McLean called these the triad of family behaviors, and you see them in all mammalian species, although the overall social structure of mammalian species can vary enormously. But number one and number two, nursing, combined with a communication system that keeps the mother and the offspring in contact, are basically what Bowen theory would define as the symbiotic relationship that's normal in early life. Without it, the infant's going to die, and particularly the human infant, who's so altricial at birth, so helpless without the care and protection and feeding of the mother he's gone, and for all mammals, that's true in terms of nursing. So that is a backdrop on which Bowen's ideas eventually would be anchored.

doc_name: 2011 04 Making a Difference in Self and Family Public Lecture - Michael Kerr - 2011-04-23
section_title: Family as Emotional Unit and Bowen's Early Research
text:
[Family as Emotional Unit and Bowen's Early Research]

**Mike Kerr:** So now we're going to talk about Bowen family systems theory and the family as an emotional unit. In the 1960s 50s and 60s, many of the family researchers began to see the family as a unit in its own right. Referred to it as an organism, an entity in its own right. This was new. We're not talking about trying just to understand individuals. We're trying to understand individuals in the context of the family, that the family is regulating the individual as much as the individual is regulating the family. What's different about Bowen is emotional unit, and by emotional I take it back to Darwin, that it's driven by a process that we human beings have in common with other mammals, other primates, other mammals, other forms of life.

Where did the idea come from? I'd like to walk you through that very briefly. Dr Bowen began his research after World War Two, when he got out of the army in training at the Menninger clinic in Topeka, Kansas, where he was from 1946 to 1954 first in training, then on staff, and then in 1954 moved to Washington, DC, to the National Institute of Mental Health to continue his research. And I will give you a little background on that in a minute. But when he was at Menninger's, many of the people he saw carried these diagnoses, and they were severe cases, essential alcoholism, meaning pretty severe stuff, severe depression, enough for long term hospitalization and hard core schizophrenia. These were people who were very unstable, in and out of hospitals, eventually would come to Menninger. So these were the patients that he was seeing.

He was among those, and there weren't a huge number, but he wasn't the only one who took an interest in the family members who came to visit the patient. In this case, I symbolize the mother. She comes to visit the patient. He sits down and he talks with the mother. How do you think about this? I like to say what made Bowen theory possible is he sat down and asked the mother a question and listened to her answer, trying to see it from her point of view. What is she up against? What has she been trying to do? What is she like? And then also had opportunity to watch the patient interact with the mother, and I'm sure most of you have seen this and other family members, but the mother, particularly the patient, would change around the mother. And the mother would change around the patient. They had some kind of effect on each other that suddenly these are almost two different people. A mother could be calm, cool and collected till the patient entered the room, and then she might say, straighten that shirt, please. It's the tail is out, and the kid, who's been not oppositional for a certain amount of time is now resistant and sullen. That kind of impact bringing the two into proximity can have on each.

So Bowen got interested in this. It seemed to him, at that point that these two were still in a symbiotic attachment, which is normal early for the survival of the young, but by the time you're 22 years old and trying to lift off, it's supposed to be over and you're supposed to be moving on and separating. And it didn't appear that that was happening. So he got intrigued by that and referred to it as the symbiosis. But it wasn't long because, well, when he came to that was at Menninger, and when he came to NIMH, he realized how intense that connection could be, particularly studied at NIH which was hard core. The adult offspring was diagnosed with hard core schizophrenia, the most severe, unstable kind of schizophrenia, and he just recognized and appreciated better. This thing is really intense, and neither person really seems all that interested in giving it up. It's a very, very tight, symbiotic, like connection.

section_title: Multi-Generational Process and Differentiation
text:
[Multi-Generational Process and Differentiation]

**Mike Kerr:** So also the idea, and I'm making this broad overview, and leaving out a lot of detail to convey impressions, but that it's a multi generational thing. How do families become intensely interdependent? This would be a family, let's say that's vulnerable to producing pretty severe clinical problems, but also may have one youngster who comes out of it doing unusually well. Always in families, you have things moving in both directions, but that is a product of a multi generational process, a family doesn't get here overnight. Bowen at NIMH talked about a minimum of three generations again, and this would at the same time those original ancestors can spawn offspring that produce families that are unusually adaptive people are connected at the same time they're distinct individuals in that connection. Differentiation is the word Bowen theory use is not about being distant or disconnected, it's being an individual in the togetherness in the interdependence, present and accounted for.

Again, this is covering a lot of ground, but that continuum that I just showed on the last slide then renders the families more or less adaptive to life challenge. So ironically, in a sense, the families that are most interdependent, most intensely connected, most reactive to each other, compared to the families in which there is more, as Kahlil Gibran called it, spaces in the togetherness. These are the families that are most vulnerable to being overwhelmed by challenge in ways I will describe in a little bit more detail later, and becoming symptomatic, and here I'm showing an escalation of anxiety in the family system that reflects the difficulty the family system is having adapting to a life challenge, whereas the average level of tension and anxiety in this family over time is going to be less the families just deal with challenge. Challenges like the birth of a kid, the death of a parent, move, geographic moves, financial upheavals. Just deal with it more effectively generate less of what Selye described as the stress response, and consequently, overall, fewer human problems.

But when people can think about their families in these multi generational terms, there's a level of neutrality in that that's incredible. I don't know how else to get it. How do you get beyond blaming the family or blaming yourself for how things go in life. It requires a broader understanding of what it's all about. How do things come to be the way they are? What is my part in that? And how do you define your own part without slipping over into blame and self blame. I've got a part. The others have got a part. There's a neutrality in seeing that, but particularly in seeing it multi generationally. You know, this kid here might be pretty hung up. Say this one, he's more caught in the family problem, blaming his parents for how things have gone in his life. But if he starts to examine, you know, what's the family his father came from? What was he up against? You see what I'm getting at. There's an objectivity in that that comes from acquiring new information that gets beyond just the way you felt about things.

section_title: Emotional System, Darwin, and the Relationship System
text:
[Emotional System, Darwin, and the Relationship System]

**Mike Kerr:** So to come back to this idea of the emotional system, Darwin's book, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals was influential in Bowen's development of theory. He believed to move toward a science of human behavior, theory must be anchored in our understanding of human beings as an outcome of the evolutionary process that we're part of nature. Families follow the same natural laws that other species follow. So the emotional system is the force that motivates. Emotion means force, what movement? Movement motivate. The emotional system in human beings is the force that motivates and you see it play out in the relationship system. So instead of, when you watch a family interact in ways that seem hard to understand and bizarre and destructive, instead of this is a pathological bunch, this one's this way. This one's that way. You can diagnose everybody in it, if you want to, but if you step back, this is an intense, anxiety driven emotional process. This family is not that different from other families. It's just that the volume is turned way up. It's become fragmented and chaotic and difficult rooted in people's underlying dependence on one another, and consequently, how much their well being is tied up in how each other acts.

So it doesn't mean everything's emotional. Of course, feelings are the way it's expressed within the individual. We can, we can track our emotionality through the feeling system, which is extremely important to be aware of. It's very important information. But we also have an intellectual system that allows us to think about it, to reflect on it, not only reflect on it as it plays out within ourselves, but reflect on it as it plays out within the system as a whole. And that's huge in the therapy part, getting outside just one's own internal state and seeing really seeing how it's linked to the external set of relationships, and not only how those relationships affect you, but how you affect other people, which is often harder to see without, you know, getting into guilt and denial, but just seeing it for what it is.

I bring Luther on board to show how fragile the intellect is. What the heart desires, the will chooses and the mind justifies. How many people have done this in the last 60 seconds? I mean, we do it all the time, we use our cognitive, higher brain to justify our emotionality that drives actions. And often call it rational. I'm being rational. You're being emotional. But the one who's accusing the other, as Bowen liked to say, the one who accuses the other of rejection is usually doing more rejecting than the one they're accusing.

section_title: Clinical Vignette: Marion F and Unresolved Symbiosis
text:
[Clinical Vignette: Marion F and Unresolved Symbiosis]

**Mike Kerr:** Okay, so now I'm going to go to a clinical vignette to illustrate emotional fusion, unresolved symbiosis. And again, there are different degrees of this, he saw it initially in the extreme, and then it realized that there are just many, many different levels of the attached, original, caretaker offspring, attachment not being resolved. That's another way of saying it is unresolved emotional attachment. Part of the problem in using this word is people often do equate Bowen theory with attachment theory because it uses the same word. Okay?

This is the case of Marion F. This goes way back. Let me tell you how long I've been around - to August 1967 I was a first year psychiatric resident at Georgetown, working at the city hospital psychiatry section. And this patient, Marion F, who lived in the DC area, 27 years old, presented with increasing depression over about six months. The mother, and her younger brother brought her to the emergency room. I was the resident on call, and I saw her that evening. The father had died three years earlier. I won't go into the rest of the family. It's not necessary for telling this basic story.

So we hospitalized Marion F and I Dr K became her primary therapist and had a supervisor, typical training model. We also placed her on medication, and I was seeing her twice a week in psychotherapy. She did very, very well. She was hospitalized for about six weeks, and we did it longer in those days, but she had marked improvement. The Depression pretty much cleared. And then the plan was to discharge and I would continue with Marion F in twice a week outpatient therapy under supervision. Everybody was happy. Marion F was happy. I was happy. My supervisor was happy.

At the end of six months of therapy, the patient continues to do well, but I'm starting to get phone calls and cards from the patient. More phone calls than I expected, wanting to talk things out between appointments. I'm a pretty inexperienced therapist. How well aware I was of my unease, I don't know, but I show it in my expression. I looked in the mirror carefully in the morning, maybe I would have figured it out. But as far as my supervisor is concerned, everything is going great. And according to Marion F, everything is going great.

So at the end of my first year of residency, the patient continues to do well, but there are even more phone calls and more of these cards, and she's very positive about the therapy. And as you can see, this is getting to me. I don't know how well I communicated this to my supervisor, because I don't know how aware I was. At that point about all this, but at the end of my first year of residency, then I moved from the city hospital up to the university, and I was supposed to set up an appointment for Marion F and continue with her in outpatient therapy up at Georgetown during my second year of residency. And I fully intended to do that, but for some reason, I delayed, avoided setting up a new appointment schedule for her. So as you can see, she was becoming unhappy. I was I don't know what, and my and my supervisor didn't really know much about this yet, until she made a suicide attempt. I think more a gesture than an attempt, but she made one.

So I report this to my supervisor, and his response is, she never got the good mothering she needed. Assure her that you will be there for her and you can provide the corrective emotional experience, that in the therapeutic relationship, she can be healed. And this was his advice. He was a psychoanalyst, and a darn good one. So I had you know, was pulling away and distancing from the patient out of my own discomfort with her neediness and expectations and rising anxiety, and that triggered this. So we were operating really on the maternal deprivation hypothesis she had never gotten her needs adequately met from an unavailable, cold, aloof mother, and that was her problem, and she was seeking healing from that, and the therapist can provide this if handled skillfully and fix this problem.

As you can see, I was somewhat ambivalent about my supervisor at that point, but followed his directions. He was my supervisor for gosh sakes, and the patient perked up, and off we went on that hypothesis. And over the next six months, things continued, pretty much as they had always been, cards and phone calls, and she is doing very well. But as you can see, my unease is significant again. So much to learn. I don't know how aware I was of my own emotional functioning in that, again, I find reasons to see her less often, a second suicide attempt, she never got the good mothering she needed. Assure her you will be there for her and you provide the corrective emotional experience. So I suck it up. I want to graduate. This is getting very intense, very intense, and over the next two months, I return to the old approach, but again, begin to wonder about my supervisor's assessment in some way.

But at that point I started, I'd just begun supervision with Murray Bowen. It was the end of my second year of residency, and I sought him out in May 1969, now 41 years ago for supervision as part of the family therapy program, which was the way it was set up at Georgetown then. And so I presented the case. Probably wasn't supposed to do that, but I did it, and he drew the above diagram on the board showing this intense, symbiotic, unresolved attachment between mother and daughter, the father in the outside position, and this being the freer sibling, and now she had cut off from here. And now look who mother is, and then Dr Bowen says, always sympathetic. It's not maternal deprivation, but the unresolved symbiotic attachment her mother was overly involved with her she has cut off from her mother and replicated that. In relationship with you. Good luck. Bowen. Had a way of turning the problem over to you, but still being there. Essence of differentiation. How do you turn the problem back to the other but still be there? That's differentiation. You don't lose contact, but you are a self.

So it helped that at that time my first supervisor was ending, so I didn't have him to worry about. Bowen suggested I stop seeing Marion F individually and pressed to have sessions that would include her mother, detriangle from her mother. We'll go into that more later. That was Bowen's advice. It did not make a hit with Marion F. Marion F was not interested in having her mother come and soon stopped the sessions with me. I handled it very awkwardly. I do know that she did not make a suicide attempt that time, and continued to work at her job. I wanted to keep seeing her, but in this new way, but now I was trying to work my way out of this intense symbiotic attachment to me. I was not distancing this time, but suggesting a new direction. It was not a direction that she wanted to go. I did hear about her a number of years later, simply to know that she survived it, but I never had direct contact or correspondence with her again, but obviously this was a very, very important lesson for me.

section_title: Chronic Anxiety, Adaptation Failure, and the Triangle
text:
[Chronic Anxiety, Adaptation Failure, and the Triangle]

**Mike Kerr:** Now I'm going to talk about Bowen family systems theory in relationship to chronic anxiety, and this shift from a family system that's health promoting through the calming and supportive sense of a comfortable emotional connection with others, one of the most powerful forces in nature, I believe, into illness promoting. And again, what I'll be describing, I don't think is lost on any of you, but here I show a family system of six members, and I make these relationships black and dotted to say that they're comfortably relaxed people in reasonably good contact, but now some potentially stressful circumstance occurs. Maybe the job, the husband's job, is threatened, or the wife's maybe the wife's mother has been diagnosed with a terminal cancer. Maybe they've just moved across country or from Hong Kong to Vancouver, and also the wife's mother has been diagnosed with cancer. A series of potentially stressful circumstances has arisen that this system now has to succeed in adapting to. So what I'm going to be talking about is a failure and adaptation.

So let's say one or more individuals in the system react to these events. They're more personal to them. I call it anticipatory anxiety, in the sense that so these two or three individuals, but it may just be one, you know, begin to think worst case scenario, or, Oh, my God, the sky is falling. Begin to worry about it, chew on it like a bone, and begin to get anxious themselves about the event that in itself, is not a huge problem, and potentially, the relationships the person has with others can help in calming that problem through talking it out, expressing themselves freely others, not overreacting to that, etc. What I'm showing here is that instead of being just handled within self, it's being acted out in behavior. And by that, I mean the person may develop the attitude I'm anxious and the other should do something about it. Have some kind of unrealistic expectation of what the other is supposed to do about their upset, and the other may get anxious in response, feeling on the one hand that they're supposed to fix it, they're supposed to do something about it. And on the other hand, not wanting to get incredibly entangled in trying to solve a problem they don't know how to solve, so that the relationship now becomes infected with anxiety. The way that people are dealing with each other has changed that's not caused by the challenge. It has to do with the way these individuals are dealing with the challenge and the way it gets played out in their relationship.

And these are what I call social cues, the most common things all of us react to, the perception that not enough attention is being paid to self or sensitivity to the accusation that you're not paying enough attention to the other, approval, disapproval, expectations you have of yourself, expectations you have of others that aren't met and reacting to upset in one another. These are not about psychiatric diagnoses, just things that are part of all human beings. And as we'll talk about, the less self people have, the more these things can take over and dominate. Because part of the problem is the inability to reflect on what's happening, to keep the higher brain in gear and have this emotional process take over, and then it can spread to another member of the system, and spreads even further as anxiety escalates through the system, and eventually everybody's caught up in it, mother, father, kids, grandparents, whoever those symbolize the spread is complete. This is a failure in adaptation.

And as anxiety mounts, one way it's dealt with is through the activation of, say, or intensification of the triangle. By the triangle, I mean that, say, these two people that were over here sort of cohere with the parents, the one that was over here sort of come together in a oneness with the parents and begin to see the problem the way the parents see it and behave as if that's true, and begin to focus on this one as the cause of the family's upset, so that the these members of the family, their anxiety that I showed going up, is now being managed or cope with through an attitude that blames the other and actions that go along with that, for example, and they support focusing on one member as the cause of family anxiety. I hope everybody knows this goes on when a family is anxious, people start looking at one another, blaming one. If only you weren't acting the way you are, this family wouldn't be so upset. And that's said, of course, in an upset way, as if that doesn't count.

So the triangle is one way the system manages anxiety, and that can result in this one. Let's say it's a teenager, in this case, absorbs the system, generated anxiety, begins to feel isolated, misunderstood, out of control, treated unfairly, what have you. And literally, the system is ganging up on that one, but that one is playing an equal part in the problem. In families with a good prognosis, I'll get up at the board and say, 1/3 of the problem is here, 1/3 of the problem is here, and 1/3 of the problem is there. In families with a poor prognosis, the father or the mother will get up and say, No, you're close. 1/6 is here, 1/6 is here, and two thirds is there. As long as people are thinking that way, all the effort is mobilizing to change that person. And of course, that person is either going to give in to it or fight it. But that build up of anxiety that's absorbed from the system then becomes the fuel in Bowen theory for symptom development, cellular stress response can play out in physical health, play out in what we call psychiatric symptoms, or it can play out in aberrant behavior.

And my point here is that this is a universal emotional process. I know you have triangles here in Hong Kong. I've been in them already. I'm an active participant. They've been pretty mild. People have been very nice, but trying. Triangles are everywhere, and they're in Washington, DC, and they're global. The point of this theory is that this is trans cultural, that certain fundamental processes, like patterns of emotional functioning, like the triangle, and we'll come to some others, the build up of anxiety, emotional attachment, multi generational process. These things are universal. Culture colors it. But underneath the culture is an emotional process, according to Bowen theory, common to us all and that we have to some extent with other forms of life.

And I just put this in, just to keep some perspective. It's it's fueled by blame and self blame, but often carried out with the best of intentions. I'm focusing on you and trying to regulate you because I'm trying to do good for you. Best of intentions only the other can then give up more and more responsibility for their own functioning, it can also get quite nasty, but a peaceful, agreeable family can be just as toxic, where everybody puts a premium on getting along can still have powerful emotional undercurrents as families that are overtly conflictual and nasty, two sides of the same coin.

Two, it's not just about this person or that this group is going kind of crazy, and so this person tries to think it through for themselves, to think, feel and then act for self, instead of being so entangled and regulated by the environment that's all differentiation means it doesn't mean being distant. Means being present and accounted for, but hanging on to yourself instead of being defined by the system in very basic ways. The beauty of it is, if that happens, it can calm the whole system. It can happen in a workplace. It can happen if you're important enough to the workplace, but it can happen in the family, particularly if the parents take responsibility when say it's an adolescent problem, you can't expect the adolescent to do it. He just he's too dependent on the system.

[Personal Example: Kerr Family 1974–1976 and Anxiety Escalation]

**Mike Kerr:** So I'm going to show you a clinical vignette to illustrate this escalation of chronic anxiety in a family system in an effort towards increased differentiation. I won't go into a lot of details on this, but this is the family I grew up in. Whoops, I'm here. I was, believe it or not, I was once 34 married at that point, two kids. This goes back to the period between 1974 and 1976 as you can see, I had an older brother, 37 this is a girl that died at 10 days. This brother had committed suicide. I'll talk more about him tomorrow morning, particularly. But he was diagnosed as schizophrenic and committed suicide in 1969 and it was one of the ways I learned about getting beyond thinking of schizophrenia as a disease to see what's underneath it. And I'll talk about that tomorrow. And an older brother, a half brother, actually, who also lived in Pennsylvania. So this was North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Washington, DC. My father died in 62 and my mother's first husband was already dead. My dad had one surviving sister. He was from Minnesota. He was the youngest. This boy died young, so he was basically the youngest boy with two older sisters and a much older half brother. But she lived in Washington with her husband, and we had a lot of contact with those that family. My mother, from Western Pennsylvania, only one sibling was still surviving at that point.

Well, the event that happened was that my uncle Ben died was not totally unexpected, but more unexpected than not. And as you might expect, my aunt Marie's reaction was intense. They had no children. section_title: Triangle, Fusion, and Two Counter-Balancing Life Forces
text:
[Triangle, Fusion, and Two Counter-Balancing Life Forces]

**Mike Kerr:** All right, we're getting there. Bowen family systems theory, the triangle reduced to its simplest level, my theory explains how two people can be very close early in their relationship but become distant over time. Now to understand that idea, what he just said up there, begins with understanding that relationship systems, two person and beyond, function as if they are governed by two counter balancing life forces, one for emotional attachment or fusion, and one for emotional separateness or differentiation.

Now you may figure it out. I put this in because I was coming here, because I think, in a way, it comes close to it. I wanted to get across the idea that differentiation is not about being disconnected. It's about being present and accounted for, but still being an individual. You're not rebelling against the other, and you're not trying to change the other. You're there, and you can think for yourself, but you're part of the group, and you're working with the group all the time. That's why I put that yin yang thing in because I thought it did, in many ways, convey that.

So here's the idea that people predictably gravitate to intimate adult relationships that replicate the emotional intensity of the process in which they grew up. The more intense the unresolved attachment to family, the more intense the attachment you gravitate to. This means that relationships will vary in how much they're fused. The kid who's more caught with the parents will leave home and fuse more intensely and replicate that. The kid who's less caught will leave home and form a relationship that's a little less interdependent. So this just symbolizes the investment of emotional energy each has in the other. Bowen theory calls this fusion, and that's the overlap, fusion means the degree to which a person's sense of emotional well being and functioning depends on what the other does or doesn't do. And you're never going to not have fusion. It's always going to be there. It's instinctive, but it varies based on different developmental experiences, so that on the one side, you have differentiation, which includes the ability to think for self, a certain autonomy to feel for self, because people's feelings can be totally governed by what's going on around them, and act for self in the presence of others, whereas the fusion part of it has to do with the sensitivity to these things like attention, approval, expectations and distress.

To quote Bowen, people don't have to worry about having enough togetherness in a relationship. It's instinctive, and it will always be there. The hard part is maintaining enough differentiation. The default mode is fusion. When anxiety goes up, people push for oneness, sameness and agreement. And it's that pushing and needing and pressing that begins to heat up the molecules and makes it difficult for people to be together and again. So there's a heightened reactivity in the fusion. It's intensified. And these are the things people are reacting to, whether you're obsessive, compulsive or histrionic person, or you're tend to be paranoid, whatever. Fundamentally, these are the things people are reacting to in each other. It's not about diagnoses, but it's about the ability to be a self in a relationship or not, and how much harder it is when anxiety goes up.

And then emotional distance is the most common way anxiety is managed, people begin to pull away from each other because they find it hard to deal with each other, and the more the fusion, the more likely this is going to happen. So in that sense, the anxiety gets bound in the emotional distance. But unfortunately, typically, the distance is more calming for one person than for the other. And let's say, in this case, this person begins to put that emotional energy into the workplace. And now that leaves, let's say the mother in a more anxious spot, but that can be managed through involvement with a kid. That's the basic idea, emotional attachment, anxiety and the way anxiety is managed. And that triangle can be stable for a time, but it's not to the child's benefit.

text:
Chapter 1 
Bowen Theory in Perspective 
Human behavior, viewed from a broad perspective, has been remarkably 
constant since Homo sapiens first appeared on the planet. Man repro­
duces, raises offspring, attends to needs for shelter and sustenance, and 
seeks to establish and defend a home range or territory as have his 
ancestors across the millennia. Like all other life-forms, man is a product 
of the earth and is intimately connected to it. How the human has approached and managed the dual biological 
mandates of self-preservation and reproduction is seemingly unique in 
the history of life on Earth. Equipped with his marvelous brain, man has 
a range of flexibility apparently unmatched by his animate cousins. That 
brain and its variety of responses have made it extremely difficult for 
humankind to study itself. The incredible manifestations of human 
behavior contain thousands of alluring byways and dead ends that 
captivate attention and absorb research energy. One can become 
fascinated with the display and miss the underlying function of behavior 
in the process of life. Yet people have also been aware of or at least believed in an 
orderliness to life even in the face of chaos. At some point the early 
human intelligence became capable of observing the tides, the patterns 
of the stars, and the cycle of the seasons. Life forms have long 
responded to such phenomena. But to observe and reflect upon them 
added a new dimension.

observable, can be defined as emotion (MacLean, 1970). MacLean 
defines three types of affect. Basic affects are information of bodily 
needs recognized as hunger, thirst, and the various feeling manifesta­
tions of bodily processes. Specific affects occur with the activation of a 
particular sensory system as when feeling pain after a noxious stimulus. General affects are feelings which pertain to situations, individuals, and 
groups and concern self-preservation and preservation of the species. Although the limbic system receives both internal and external 
sensory input, MacLean's research suggests that internal signals have 

8 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
the overriding influence on neuronal discharge. In other words, the 
lirhbic-based behavior of an individual occurs to the beat of an internal 
drummer. Feeling and the sense of conviction can be completely internal and 
have no relationship to, or even contradict, external reality. Under the 
guidance of the limbic system the individual may react to external 
stimuli on the basis of an internally guided perception of reality 
(MacLean, 1970). The evolution from reptiles to mammals is marked by three 
behavioral advances: (1) nursing, (2) parental care, and (3) a warm­
blooded condition (MacLean, 1982a).

The evolution from reptiles to mammals is marked by three 
behavioral advances: (1) nursing, (2) parental care, and (3) a warm­
blooded condition (MacLean, 1982a). In a series of experiments with 
Syrian golden hamsters {Mesocricetus auratus), MacLean and his col­
leagues demonstrated the role of the limbic system in these behaviors 
and in a fourth mammalian development, play (Murphy, MacLean, & 
Hamilton, 1981). Within the first 48 hours after the animal's birth, the 
neocortex was removed. Those animals without the neocortex were 
then simply observed as they grew. The experimental animals grew at 
a normal rate and with the typical developmental timing of the species. In subsequent trials, the neocortex and the midline limbic structures (the 
cingulate convolution and the underlying dorsal sections of the 
hippocampus) were destroyed. These animals retained many species-
typical behaviors but displayed no play during development and 
showed major deficits in maternal behavior. The research demonstrated 
that "in a rodent ...the striatal complex and limbic system, with the 
remaining neuraxis, are sufficient for giving expression to a wide range 
of unlearned forms of species-typical behavior and that the midline 
limbic structures are required for the expression of play, behavior and 
integrated performance of maternal behavior" (Murphy et al, 1981, 
p. 461). The limbic cortex can be divided into three main divisions.

461). The limbic cortex can be divided into three main divisions. Two of 
the three are associated with the olfactory apparatus and are involved in 
self-preservation and self-protection. The third section, within the upper 
part of the limbic convolution, MacLean refers to as the great arc 
(MacLean, 1982b). Not only is the great arc implicated in play and 
maternal behavior, but additional research indicates that the rostral end 
of the arc is required for the spontaneous production of the isolation call, 
the most fundamental and elemental of all mammalian vocalizations. This evidence, along with the connections between the great arc and the 
frontal lobes, lead MacLean to the following observation: "Indeed, one 
might say that the history of the evolution of mammals is to a large 
extent the history of the evolution of the family" (MacLean, 1982b, 
p. 304). Bowen Theory in Perspective 9 
MacLean's work on the function of the R-complex and limbic 
system in emotional expression and behavior points toward the 
definition of an emotional system that is similar in a general way to that 
proposed by Bowen. It suggests the neural machinery that might 
underlie such an emotional component within an individual. It suggests, 
further, that much of human behavior may be automatic and outside of 
human awareness, let alone control. More importantly, it fits the 
development of the human family into evolution and places the human 
brain alongside all of its evolutionary forebears.

development of the human family into evolution and places the human 
brain alongside all of its evolutionary forebears. Such a view of the 
human family is rooted in biology and points in the same direction as 
Bowen Theory, which assumes the basic commonality of all living 
things. John B. Calhoun's journey from a Tennessee childhood to the 
position of major researcher is a fascinating story (Calhoun, 1977). He 
reports, in retrospect, that three related ideas guided his research: 
(1) population, (2) environmental design, and (3) social consciousness, 
mental health, and human evolution. Those ideas led him initially to 
academia and eventually to the National Institute of Mental Health 
(NIMH), where for several years he pursued these themes in major 
experiments involving population density and environmental designs. Working generally with populations of laboratory mice and rats, 
Calhoun studied the effects of population density on animals within a 
specially constructed habitat or "universe." There are many points of 
interest to the family theorist in Calhoun's work. In general they concern 
the effect of other animals upon an individual in a stable environment. In his experimental habitats or universes, Calhoun essentially allowed 
populations to grow without the usual environmental restraints. The 
result was increasing population density within the universes.

"The growth rate of a population will be 
inhibited in the absence of predation and in the presence of an excess of 
food and harborage. This inhibition arises through the social interaction 
among the members of the population with respect to the distribution 
of goals and barriers through the environment" (Calhoun, 1963, p. 2). Calhoun's "backyard" project continued for 27 months. The rat 
population increased as predicted and then leveled off. Early in the 
history of the project the more dominant animals tended to occupy a 
particular area within the pen (the southeastern half). This territorial 
structure was maintained for the entire study (Calhoun, 1963). As the 
population grew, competition between animals increased, driving some 
rats from the early and higher ranking colonies in the southeastern 
portion of the pen. The migrating animals were primarily male and of 
lower social status. Such migration led to increasing social interaction 
among animals of the newer, socially lower ranking colonies. With time there came to be an excess of males in the northwestern 
sector of the pen (Calhoun, 1963). Within this area no male was able to 
clearly establish a territory. Females within this area, when in estrus, 
tended to be pursued by packs of males. Often a female would be 
mounted frequently (Calhoun estimates as much as a thousand times in 
one night), and her behavior indicated that she was experiencing 
substantial stress.

mounted frequently (Calhoun estimates as much as a thousand times in 
one night), and her behavior indicated that she was experiencing 
substantial stress. Such females tended to have reduced conceptions and 
were able to raise young only with great difficulty. Normal maternal 
behaviors, essential to the successful raising of the litter, were greatly 
inhibited or completely lacking. In contrast, in the southeastern sector of 
the enclosure, males were able to establish territories around several 
high-ranking females. Such females were not hounded by other males 
and were highly successful in conceiving and rearing young. Several other interesting observations were made from the Balti­
more project. While socially higher ranking rats were able to maintain 
a bimodal nocturnal rhythm in visiting the food pen, lower ranking 
individuals tended to feed only when higher ranking animals were 
absent. The effect was to make lower ranking individuals more active in 
the dawn and dusk time periods rather than the nighttime periods 
preferred by the more dominant rats. A second observation was that 
individuals bom into lower ranking groups (primarily in the northwest-
em sector) experienced greater inhibition of growth than animals from 
higher ranking groups. Bowen Theory in Perspective 11

From this original research environment Calhoun's thinking moved 
to more controlled and observable settings. He moved first to Walter 
Reed Army Medical Center and then to the NIMH. With the move to 
the NIMH came access to the space needed to conduct further research. In a barn made available to the project, Calhoun constructed the 
research environments or "universes." Each was essentially a square 
enclosure of a specific size. Along the vertical walls were constructed 
sources for food and water as well as boxes for nesting. Ample nesting 
materials were available at all times. Into such prepared environments 
Calhoun introduced a breeding pair of mice or rats. The populations 
were allowed to develop essentially unchecked. As density increased, so 
did general pathology, defined as the inability to adjust to changing 
conditions (Calhoun, 1971). The observations of such populations led to the development of 
several important concepts. Of particular interest is the concept of social 
velocity. In the laboratory, social velocity was defined as "a measure of 
the amount of time an individual spends in that portion of its home 
range or field of action where it is maximally exposed to contacting 
associates and then becoming involved in social interaction" (Calhoun, 
1967, p. 28). Calhoun's studies indicated a predictable curve of social 
velocity in a group of mice.

velocity in a group of mice. The dominant male and female had the 
highest rankings, and the less dominant individuals fell into place as the 
curve descended. Individuals with high social velocity showed appropriate territorial 
behaviors. As social velocity declined, however, animals showed 
behaviors that appeared to deviate increasingly from those considered 
optimally "mouselike." On the lower end of the curve, animals tended 
to avoid contact with others and to be ignored by the more dominant 
individuals altogether. As environmental stress increased (due to 
population density), fewer and fewer individuals were able to maintain 
a high social velocity and ever greater numbers of animals exhibited 
behaviors common to the lowest end of the curve. Although the curve 
and the differences between individuals tended to be intensified under 
environmental stress, Calhoun concluded that even under optimal 
environmental conditions the social velocity curve, with attendant 
alterations in behavior, will develop. It is simply a predictable outcome 
of group living (Calhoun, 1971). Calhoun's explanation of this apparently fixed outcome concerns 
the type of contact between individuals. He reasoned that contact can 
be gratifying, frustrating, or neutral. Each gratifying contact leads to a 
refractory period during which the gratified individual will not respond 
appropriately to meet the social need of another.

Each gratifying contact leads to a 
refractory period during which the gratified individual will not respond 
appropriately to meet the social need of another. The result of such a 

12 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
nongratifying contact is a state of frustration for the unfulfilled 
individual. In the natural course of group interaction, some individuals 
will benefit from gratifying contact much of the time and others will 
arrive at varying degrees of frustration. In this manner the social 
velocity curve develops. The inappropriate response to a needy other, 
whether due to gratification or frustration, Calhoun defines as aggres­
sion (Calhoun, 1971). Calhoun goes yet a step further to suggest that through evolution 
a species develops a genetic constitution compatible with adjustment to 
the physiological consequences of frustration. This in essence implies 
that there is a genetically determined balance of gratification and 
frustration for an individual. When an individual has too many 
gratifying encounters, it will actively seek encounters in which the other 
will respond aggressively in order to maintain the physiology required 
by the genetic basis of the individual, that is, a balance of gratification 
and frustration (Calhoun, 1971). Yet another factor in theoretical gratification - frustration basis of 
social velocity concerns the intensity of interaction.

Yet another factor in theoretical gratification - frustration basis of 
social velocity concerns the intensity of interaction. The length of the 
refractory period following contact will be proportional to the intensity 
of contact/interaction. "It is this accommodation of intensity of inter­
action to the dynamics of life in a particular sized group which leads to 
the origin of basic group size" (Calhoun, 1967, p. 26). The effect of 
increased population density is to force contact beyond that determined 
by optimal group size leading to alterations in the behavior of all 
individuals. The intensity of contact or interaction can be influenced by the 
heredity and past history of the individuals involved. In a different 
experiment, Calhoun selected two strains of the same species, the house 
mouse. The strains differed from one another in the area of physiological 
stability (Calhoun, 1956). The research objective was to determine the 
extent to which heredity might modify social behavior. Introducing a 
pregnant female of each strain into an identical environment initiated the 
colonies. As population density in the colonies increased, Calhoun found 
deterioration of social interaction occurred rapidly among the less stable 
strain. These mice fought more frequently, and dispersed groups were 
less successful in reproducing beyond the initial litter and died off more 
rapidly at higher population densities.

rapidly at higher population densities. Calhoun also found that if 
population density increased sufficiently, even the stable strain of mice 
developed similar behavioral changes. The more stable strain, however, 
was able to function with less intense interaction in conditions that had 
produced extreme behavior in the less stable strain. Bowen Theory in Perspective 13 
Calhoun, as noted previously, defined pathological behavior as the 
inability to adjust to ongoing or changing conditions. Generally the 
individual relies on both heredity and learning to cope with such 
alterations. Any set of circumstances producing conditions with which 
the individual is unable to cope can be called an ecological trap. As an 
example, Calhoun cites the lemming (Calhoun, 1967). Every three to 
four years the population of lemmings in arctic tundra regions becomes 
extremely dense. Often the crisis is solved by the sudden death of large 
numbers of animals. In some circumstances, however, vast migrations of 
the small animals occur. Over most arctic regions such migrations lead 
to eventual dispersal of population and individual death. In Scandinavia, 
however, the tundra is marked by long valleys extending to the sea.

Over most arctic regions such migrations lead 
to eventual dispersal of population and individual death. In Scandinavia, 
however, the tundra is marked by long valleys extending to the sea. In 
these regions the migrations of the lemmings can take the form of huge 
aggregates of individuals that appear to have lost all behavioral 
restraints. The masses move continuously crossing everything in the 
path up to the sea itself. The water is no barrier, however, as the animals 
swim out into the sea until eventually all drown. Such migrations into the sea cannot be explained solely by 
heredity. After all, the only survivors are the ones who do not exhibit 
the trait. Over time, therefore, one could presume natural selection 
would have removed the trait if it were hereditary. Calhoun believes 
that the particular configuration of the Scandinavian tundra forces the 
movement of the lemmings into a constant directionality reinforced in 
effect by the movement from high to low population density and 
requiring a long extinction period. Upon reaching the sea, the strongly 
implanted necessity to move ahead forces the animals into the water and 
on to their deaths. In a carefully reasoned manner, Calhoun sought to subject his idea 
to experimental conditions. Focusing on a population of wild mice in a 
natural habitat, the experimenters sought to induce the movement of 
mice away from their established territories. In essence all the mice in a 
central area were removed by trapping.

In essence all the mice in a 
central area were removed by trapping. The belief was that mice on the 
perimeter of the central trapping area would become aware of the void 
and would automatically move into it to equalize the intensity of stimuli 
impinging from all sides. In effect, the experimenters would create an 
implosion of the mouse population, the opposite of the lemmings 
migration but based on the same principles. The experimenters caused 
four waves of mice to move into the central area, each more numerous 
than the preceding (Calhoun, 1967). The mice were caught in a set of 
circumstances to which they could not adjust; they were in an ecological 
trap. 14 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
The crowded universes also produced ecological traps. One of 
these, the behavioral sink, arose from observations of behavior as 
density increased. As used by Calhoun, the term behavioral sink refers to 
the process by which a population spread fairly evenly or uniformly 
across the space accessible to it becomes transformed into localized 
aggregates that far exceed optimal group size (Calhoun, 1967). As 
population rose, it happened that more than one animal would attempt 
to feed at the same time. Eating, therefore, came to be associated with 
the presence of another animal. Over time the animals tended to return 
to the same hopper, since the chance of encountering another increased.

the presence of another animal. Over time the animals tended to return 
to the same hopper, since the chance of encountering another increased. As population reached about three times the optimal, ever larger 
aggregates came to feed at the same hoppers, even though others were 
well-stocked and virtually ignored. The extreme crowding at the 
preferred hoppers led to levels and intensity of contact that resulted in 
impaired behavior in some animals. In general sexual and maternal 
behaviors deteriorated and aggressive behaviors increased. Over time as 
density continued to increase, individuals in great numbers became 
either very withdrawn or turned into what Calhoun called "the beautiful 
ones," mice who appeared to be in excellent health with fine pelage. These animals did not reproduce (Calhoun, 1962). Much of Calhoun's work with crowding is based on a calculation 
of optimal group size, which for mammals varies by species from twelve 
to eighteen individuals. In general, twelve adults in a social group 
comprises the general tendency of mammalian evolution (Calhoun, 
1977). Optimum group size is a product of heredity, experiential 
history, and environmental setting. When population density forces a 
degree of contact twice that of the optimum, the group will split into 
two. When density increases even further, pathology will appear.

would permit each individual to associate with approximately twelve 
adults. Calhoun attributes the ability of the human to move beyond the 
constraints of group size to the development of conceptual space or 
area. "Conceptual area amounts simply to the acquisition of values and 
codes which permit role differentiation to the extent that, even in a 
double-sized group in the original physical area, meaningful social 
contacts would continue at the rate necessary to maximize gratification" 
(Calhoun, 1971, p. 358). Calhoun believes conceptual space has in­
creased as human population has increased. Calhoun and MacLean are studying the mechanisms and outcomes 
of the "dance of life," the emotional system that governs much of 
animate life. That such an emotional system plays a role in human 

Bowen Theory in Perspective 15 
behavior appears indisputable, and it is only in the context of an 
emotional system, a dance of life, that Bowen Theory can be under­
stood. Calhoun and MacLean make clear the dilemma such automatic 
behavior produces.

Calhoun and MacLean make clear the dilemma such automatic 
behavior produces. What originated in evolution as an adaptive 
mechanism to provide greater response and flexibility to the early 
mammal can limit adaptive capacity if pressed by too great a pressure 
to cope with a changing environment. Calhoun's notion of the 
ecological trap addresses this dilemma. If, to this view of the emotional system, one adds the idea of 
individual variation in the ability to manage and retain adaptive 
flexibility, one arrives at a perspective analogous to the concept of 
differentiation, the cornerstone of Bowen Theory. The basic notion is 
that different organisms have differing ranges of tolerance to the 
demand to adapt. Such differences are a product of heredity and history. Once the tolerance level is surpassed, response becomes increasingly 
rigid and intense. If this state continues for an extended period of time, 
stress-induced changes can become irreversible. In a sense Bowen Theory addresses the interplay of different levels 
of brain development as expressed in the behavior of the individual. The 
limbic functions, presumably an evolutionary development providing 
greater adaptive response and flexibility to the early mammal, can 
inhibit the functioning of a later evolutionary development, the 
neocortex. A key variable is the level of demand to adapt to a changing 
environment.

A key variable is the level of demand to adapt to a changing 
environment. The more the pressure to adapt, the greater the likelihood 
of the operation of automatic behaviors or mechanisms that hinder the 
full potential of neocortical functioning. To see the dance of life, however, does not imply understanding. Yet unless one can see it, Bowen Family Systems Theory makes little 
sense. At the heart of Bowen Theory is the concept of the system. The 
remainder of this volume will essentially be concerned with defining and 
explaining this concept. Specific systems are known to science. Astronomers refer to 
various systems of planets and stars. Medicine knows the cardiovascular 
system and other bodily systems. Yet the mind balks at the effort to 
comprehend systems. Words like interdependence, mutual influence, and so 
on are often used to catch the flavor of systems. Such terminology is 
inadequate, however, to convey more than a glimpse of the concept. Systems can best be observed with a broad focus. Bowen once likened 
it to looking at a football game from the roof of the stadium rather than 
from a seat on the fifty-yard line. 16 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
A significant element in that broad focus involves the continued 
effort to see the operation of natural systems. Systems operating 
principles are contained as much within the seed of a flower as within 
the vast herds of wildebeest on the African plain.

principles are contained as much within the seed of a flower as within 
the vast herds of wildebeest on the African plain. Among the most 
important natural science research within which the nature of systems 
can be observed is the work of field biologists like George Schaller or 
Jane Goodall and of sociobiologists, most prominently E. O. Wilson. The system of an insect society or a lion pride is not the same as a 
human system. The point is to learn to recognize the characteristics of 
natural systems. In the effort to study man, one can focus on human uniqueness, on 
how man differs from all other living things. Any effort that essentially 
takes as its object the productions of the human brain concerns itself 
with how humans are different from other life-forms. A second option, 
however, is to concern oneself with how man is like other living things. Biology is the study of life and living things, and the recognition of the 
similarity of life-forms was and is an important step in the process that 
produced the theory of evolution. In a 1976 paper, Bowen highlighted a principal assumption that 
guided his work. "The theoretical assumption considers emotional 
illness to be a disorder of the emotional system, an intimate part of man's 
phylogenetic past which he shares with all lower forms of life, and which 
is governed by the same laws that govern all living things" (Bowen, 
1976, pp. 59-60).

in the urge to survive and to engage in sexual activity leading to 
reproduction. In a static environment any organism could simply 
employ particular strategies to assure its own survival and reproduction, 
and there would be no need to evolve. There is, however, no such thing 
as a static environment. With the evolution of multicellular life-forms, 
the interplay of organisms became more complex, and greater adaptive 
flexibility was required. Each organism that has ever lived possesses some sort of guidance 
system governing its efforts to survive and reproduce. Early forms 
obviously did not rely on anything like a brain or central nervous 
system. Simple chemical or electrical mechanisms may have served early 
living things much as they do many modern forms. Within a particular environment each guidance system fits with 
every other. This is most clear in the predator-prey attachment or in 
mating behavior within a species. In a sense every organism is 
dependent on every other, even its enemies, to assure the efficient 
performance of its own guidance mechanisms. Should either predator or

prey, for example, attain a new response it has a potential advantage if 
the new response furthers its own efforts to survive and reproduce.

In 
short, every organism influences and is influenced by its environment 
and such interplay is necessary for the evolutionarily programmed 
behavior of the organism. Organism and environment evolve together. Although this is a simple point, some examples may help illustrate 
the interplay of guidance systems in nature. Certain parasites of the 
phylum Acanthocephala (thorny-headed worms) have evolved a fasci­
nating strategy that alters the guidance system of another organism 
(Moore, 1984). These worms infect an intermediary host, in this case the 
common pill bug, and alter the behavior of the bug in such a manner 
that it becomes an easy meal for the definitive prey, various birds in 
whose innards the parasite finally lodges. Normally a secretive creature eschewing unsheltered and dry areas, 
the pill bug, when infected, appears to ignore available shelter and tends 
to be less averse to dry, light-colored areas than noninfected insects. Without shelter and exposed on a light background, the pill bug 
becomes an easy prey for scavenging birds. Moore also reports on the 
activity of another sort of parasite that affects the behavior of organisms 
in water, causing them to expose themselves to predation by various 
types of water fowl, thereby conveying the parasite to the definitive 
host. A different sort of example comes from two dinosaur nesting sites 
in Montana (Homer, 1984).

A different sort of example comes from two dinosaur nesting sites 
in Montana (Homer, 1984). At these sites fossilized nests have been 
discovered with eggs and the remains of young dinosaurs still in place. These remains suggest that 80 million years ago certain herbivorous 
dinosaurs were evolving toward some sort of adult interaction with 
offspring. Among the dinosaur nests the investigators also found eggs 
laid in a straight line, quite unlike the circular, clearly constructed nests 
of the herbivores. These are the eggs of carnivorous dinosaurs, who are 
believed to have hatched within the nesting grounds where they could 
prey upon the young vegetarians. The interplay of the two dinosaur 
species presumably was shaping the instinctual behavior of each, the one 
toward parental care and the other toward enhanced predation. Homer's 
paper points to early evidence for the development of bonds between 
parent and offspring, an early harbinger of what has come to be called 
family. With mammals, however, the development reached its greatest 
complexity. Modem man (Homo sapiens sapiens) is only the most recent 
version of a long evolutionary line. Modem man appeared on the planet 
between forty and fifty thousand years ago, quickly replacing his 
immediate predecessor, Homo sapiens neanderthalenis (Pilbeam, 1984).

Modem man appeared on the planet 
between forty and fifty thousand years ago, quickly replacing his 
immediate predecessor, Homo sapiens neanderthalenis (Pilbeam, 1984). 18 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
With slight exceptions the evolution of homonoids and hominids has 
been marked by increasing brain size and, presumably, increasingly 
complex behavior. Kinship bonds within the living group, that is, family, 
has been a part of that evolution. To state that family is a biological phenomenon is merely to note 
the obvious. It is as much a product of evolution as the migrations of the 
whales, the waggle dance of the honeybee, and the newborn calf's 
lurching steps toward the mother's nipple during the earliest moments 
of life. The roots of the family are very old indeed, perhaps as much as 
250 million years to the evolution of the therapsids or mammal-like 
reptiles. The family is one manifestation of the human guidance system 
at work, and the family as a unit is a natural system. Whether humankind has the ability to study and understand its 
own functioning remains to be seen. A major stumbling block is the 
tendency for each person to exclude self from the web of interconnec-
tedness and automatic response that forms the dance of life. Human 
subjectivity defines self as different from all others.

The Family as a Unit 
Earth's great oceans, atmosphere, and land have always formed an 
interactive whole. (The planet is believed to be about 4 billion years 
old.) When life emerged to become a fourth major component is not 
certain, but modem research has pushed the date backwards to a 
moment at least 3 billion years ago. Contemporary investigators use the 
term biosphere to refer to all living things on Earth and their environ­
ment. The biosphere is flexible and fluid. Its components shift and move, 
adapting, adjusting, and responding to one another. The earth is never 
at rest, and the biosphere is never static. The atmosphere moves and 
changes. Its component gases shift and blend in ever-new and mostly 
consistent and stable ways. The land and the waters display similar 
fluctuations, again mostly within a stable and consistent range. Living 
things, too, are mostly consistent and stable. From this perspective Earth is a system. A shift in any of its 
elements produces a response in others. The shift-response cycle can be 
minimal, affecting only a few things within a small area. It can also be 
global, altering the nature of the biosphere itself. As a result, the modern 
planet is different from the swirling amalgam of gas and molten metal 
that emerged from the formation of the solar system four or five billion 
years ago. It is different, too, from the planet that produced living things 
three to four billion years ago.

It is different, too, from the planet that produced living things 
three to four billion years ago. Living things have always had the capacity to influence their 
environment. The earliest atmosphere had little oxygen, which was 
toxic to the microbial life occupying Earth's niches (Margulis & Sagan, 
1986). These living forms, essentially cells without nuclei, developed 
mechanisms to harness light and elements in the air and water to 
produce nutrients for themselves. In the process, prokaryotic cells, as 
modern scientists classify these organisms, released waste products. Among them was oxygen in sufficient quantities to change the basic 
21 

22 Bowen Family Systems Theory 
composition of the atmosphere. Other microbes developed the ability to 
utilize these wastes. Clearly the interdependence of living things was 
established early in life's development. Microbes remain the most abundant of living things. They occur in 
all environments known on Earth and are essential for the proper 
functioning of other living creatures. They live independently and in 
conjunction with other forms of life. Such cohabitation is sometimes 
peaceful and sometimes deadly. Between one and one-half and two 
billion years ago life took a second turn. A new kind of creature 
emerged that was radically different from the microbe. This new 
phenomenon was the nucleated cell or eukaryote.

A new kind of creature 
emerged that was radically different from the microbe. This new 
phenomenon was the nucleated cell or eukaryote. So great is the gulf between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells that 
some have called it the most important evolutionary development of all 
time (Margulis & Sagan, 1986). No one knows for sure how this 
development came about. One line of thinking suggests that the 
nucleated cell was produced when certain prokaryotic cells altered their 
predator-prey relationship and formed a cooperative alliance. Instead of 
destroying the prey, the predator became incorporated into it. The 
enemies merged and became interdependent. Each maintained some of 
its original capabilities and assumed a function necessary for the other. Such thought suggests that cooperation was at least as important as 
competition in the process of evolution. The nucleated cell is the basis 
of all complex organisms. All living things other than the microbes are 
formed from arrangements of nucleated cells cooperating with one 
another. Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells are naturally occurring systems. Like the biosphere of which it is a part, the cell is flexibly fluid. Its parts 
are functionally interdependent. Without each part of the cell fulfilling 
its function, the survival of the cell is jeopardized. A shift in the 
functioning of one part produces shifts in the functioning of other parts.

Without each part of the cell fulfilling 
its function, the survival of the cell is jeopardized. A shift in the 
functioning of one part produces shifts in the functioning of other parts. Each element of the living cell has the capacity to influence the whole 
and to respond to the influence of elements outside itself. The shifting fluidity of the cell's interior results in certain processes 
or behaviors that are recognizable when one focuses on the cell as a 
whole. For example, food is imported and by-products exported from 
the cell. A free-standing cell may move, altering is shape and its position 
relative to other parts of its environment. Reproduction occurs, replac­
ing one cell with two identical ones, and so forth. Although the cell is shifting fluidly in response to a myriad of 
internal and external cues, at any given moment its components have a 
particular interactional configuration or condition. This condition can be 
thought of as the functional state of the cell. The cell's capabilities for 

The Family as a Unit 23 
maintaining itself and for behavior are determined by its functional state. The notion of health is really one of functional state. A healthy cell has 
certain capabilities and options for behavior open to it which differ from 
those of a less healthy cell. A healthy cell behaves differently from an 
unhealthy one.
