Because Bowen Family Systems Theory is a theory about the 
human and human functioning, a member of the faculty is expected not 
only to talk about theory but to embody it. At the heart of Bowen 
Family Systems Theory lies the concept of differentiation of self. A 
faculty member can never address him- or herself sufficiently to the 
concept of differentiation, not only in what he or she says but in how 
he or she functions. On a broad level differentiation takes up the manner 
in which organisms differ from one another in terms of sensitivity and 
automatic or instinctual response to the environment. An important 
direction in training involves the effort to learn about one's own 
sensitivity and automatic responsiveness. The learner also aims to 
develop a degree of control over the automatic nature of the response. Frequently the task of learning about differentiation is framed in 
terms of the distinction between the emotional and the intellectual or 
cognitive systems of the individual. The term emotional system has a 
specific connotation. The emotional system incorporates the processes 
generally called feelings but is believed to be much broader and more 
fundamental than feelings. The emotional system is identical to the 
instinctual system, the automatic internal guidance system of the 
organism. All life-forms have some sort of emotional system.

they involve mental processes. One could also address differentiation in terms of subjectivity and

world outside the skull. Nevertheless one can distinguish between the 
self-centeredness of subjectivity and a broader, more balanced perspec­
tive called objectivity. In a subjective mode the human defines self as 
different from all others, is acutely aware of the impact of others on self, 
and operates as if one were the center of the universe and the judge of 
all that occurs. Objectivity appreciates the similarity of living forms, is 
mindful of the influence of self on another, and is aware of one's 
dependency on all other living things and on the earth itself. Each person's understanding of differentiation of self tends to differ 
somewhat from that of another. Although a great deal can be learned 
from the families one sees professionally, the clinician's own family is a 
most productive teacher. Faculty members, therefore, are expected to 
spend time learning about their families and their own sensitivity to 
important family members. Here formulas for observation, objectivity, 
and fact are forged and tested. Basic lessons in respect for family 
emotional process are brought home unforgettably. The learning from 
such efforts becomes an important element in a faculty member's effort 
to represent differentiation of self.

to represent differentiation of self. In addition to representing differentiation of self, a faculty member 
is expected to be familiar with and to apply what is called systems 
thinking. The preceding chapters, in essence, have attempted to describe 
some of the details of systems thinking. In general, however, it is 
characterized by a broad rather than a narrow perspective. Instead of 
breaking phenomena into parts for analysis, the systems thinker 
attempts to see the operation of wholes and how pieces fit with one 
another. Secondly, a systems thinker is always aware of and interested 
in the effect he has on the phenomenon observed. The observer 
becomes a part of the system. The instructor's effort in training resembles the work with clinical 
families. Any individual, as a representative of a family, presents an 
opportunity to learn more about the human. The goal for the instructor 
is to be in contact with the thinking of the learner without responding 
emotionally to it. The goal for the learner is to move toward greater 
differentiation of self. In this process, both parties are in fact learning. Each challenges the other to think for him- or herself. It is difficult to assess an individual's level of differentiation of self 
on a short-term basis. Work and experience in training represent only a

on a short-term basis. Work and experience in training represent only a 
beginning. What can be reasonably expected, however, is that the 
learner will have developed a working understanding of the concept 
that allows him or her to continue the effort toward differentiation on

into the future. One can also expect that the learner will have developed 
a way to recognize his or her own undifferentiation in the family of 
origin, the family in which he or she lives, and in the families seen in 
clinical practice. A necessary quality in both teacher and learner is a curiosity about 
the nature of human behavior and the problems families face. Although 
one can broadly generalize about families and problems, each family 
sees itself as unique. And to a degree each family is different, and each 
problem is an opportunity for the clinician to learn. To see that 
opportunity in any family is a challenge to both the experienced as well 
as the inexperienced therapist. An important question can frequently act as the catalyst to 
thinking and ultimately seeing. Good questions beg solutions and lead 
to appreciation of complexity and sophistication in understanding. What is an important question? It must, in the first place, be a serious 
question. It must touch upon the unknown — both to learner and 
faculty and to science itself.

What is an important question? It must, in the first place, be a serious 
question. It must touch upon the unknown — both to learner and 
faculty and to science itself. Secondly it must be a question that can be 
worked upon and that work has the potential to contribute both to the 
individual and to knowledge. In a sense, all good questions are 
essentially the same — how does one see what one has never seen 
before, even though one may have looked a thousand times? The 
distinctions between faculty and trainee blur when addressing such a 
question. Both become investigators. Each has the potential to help the 
other move further and understand more than either could have 
accomplished alone. Good questions are not always easily formulated, 
and the interactional process between instructor and learner can be a 
delicate balance. A great deal depends upon the abilities of the 
instructor. The clinician is continually tempted to fit observations of a family 
to a preconceived set of notions about the nature of family behavior. Yet the effort to fit the facts to one's own view is the heart of 
subjectivity and obscures an accurate, broader viewpoint. In a similar 
fashion, the learner is tempted to build a way of thinking about a family 
on a single observation or insight. The mind makes connections and 
interpretations that have no factual basis. The resulting vision of a 
family rests more on imagination than on fact.

An important and basic question for teacher 
and learner alike concerns objectivity. How does one observe a family 
objectively? What is the difference between a subjective and an 
objective observation? How does one work toward becoming a more 
objective observer of the world. In many ways training in Family Systems Theory is about the 
process of thinking. How a one thinks — rather than what one thinks 
— assumes basic importance. Systems thinking is based in a broad 
perspective rather than a narrow one. It also involves recognizing and 
challenging firmly held assumptions about human nature and behavior. It places a high premium on identifying facts of human behavior, 
particularly as they occur within the family network. The effort to 
expand perspective, challenge assumptions, and note facts becomes 
central to the effort to see the world differently, to apprehend that 
which one has never recognized before. The focus on objectivity goes hand-in-hand with questions about 
thinking. Trainer and trainee alike grapple with what is factual about a 
family. What is the difference between a fact, an opinion, a belief, and 
a conviction? What is the difference between a family and a group or a 
family and an organization? Is there any? How does one know? Is the 
evidence factual or does it represent someone's opinion? These ques­
tions, and dozens of others like them, lie at the heart of training in 
Bowen Family Systems Theory.

How does one know? Is the 
evidence factual or does it represent someone's opinion? These ques­
tions, and dozens of others like them, lie at the heart of training in 
Bowen Family Systems Theory. Even simple questions like what is factual about a family require 
careful consideration. Vital statistics, such as births, deaths, changes in 
location, and changes in health, are generally verifiable. A different level 
of thinking and observation is required when one attempts to make 
factual statements about a family as a unit. What happens, how, when, 
where it happens, and who is involved can be observed and generally 
verified. With such information it is possible to make factual statements 
about difficult concepts or abstractions. What people say is generally 
less important than what they do or how they react when they are 

Training in Theory, Thought, and Therapy 105 
talking about a difficult idea or subject. The feelings and thoughts are 
not observable. Their effects, expressed in relationship, are. Discrepan­
cies between how one thinks about a family and what one observes are 
important to note. Each such deviation from what one expects has the 
potential to expand one's understanding of a particular family and of 
families in general. It is often more efficient to look for what does not 
fit one's notions than to look for evidence to support them. People do not find it easy to think about familiar things in new 
ways.

It is often more efficient to look for what does not 
fit one's notions than to look for evidence to support them. People do not find it easy to think about familiar things in new 
ways. The process of apprehending something differently seems to 
require many efforts with a mixture of failures and partial successes. The 
task is lengthy, although with diligent effort most seem able to broaden 
perspective, loosen conditioned ways of thinking and understanding, 
and "see" in ways never before possible. Consequently training in Bowen Family Systems Theory is con­
sidered a long-term process, not easily measured in terms of time spent 
in a particular training program. Time spent in a training program does 
not necessarily produce learning and competency. People learn differ­
ently. A beginner intuitively and naturally may think with greater 
breadth and clarity than an advanced student with several years training.' 
Some understand an idea or concept at first meeting, and others never 
grasp it no matter how long they try. The situation is further 
complicated by different levels of understanding. One can have some 
understanding of ideas without seeing how they apply to the world or 
to oneself. For this reason the Family Center has avoided offering 
short-term training. Each training segment lasts one year, and several 
segments are believed necessary for an adequate beginning.

While such instructional tapes are used in training, only rarely are tapes 
of clinical sessions shown. There seems to be a tendency for viewers to 
lose sight of theory and focus intently on techniques when watching 
these tapes. Such a focus works against the direction of training at the 
Family Center. Consequently the library of faculty tapes remains an 
archive for future research only. Supervisory sessions involve a small number of people (three to 
six) meeting with a faculty member. Participants present current clinical 
work, report on their thinking about and efforts with their own families, 
and raise questions of interest to them. With beginning trainees, the 
faculty member may spend part of the time illustrating and clarifying 
basic concepts. Participants may present videotapes or audiotapes of 
their own clinical work. A simple principle operates in the conduct of many supervisory 
and didactic sessions in the training program. The presenter or 
supervisor attempts to define his or her thinking as clearly as possible 
and to engage the thinking, reflective capacity of the other. The effort 
is to define self and broaden thinking, not to change the beliefs or 
thinking of the other. The point is simply to keep the interaction 
between instructor and learner as thoughtful as possible, to respect the 
differences in the way people think about the world and at the same 
time to expand perspective where possible.

Foreword 
Family therapy began in the 1950s when therapists in various parts of 
the United States began to study the interaction of family members. Instead of focusing on the individual as the "problem," they shifted the 
focus to the family unit as the problem. This shift was not simply 
another way of looking at the family, but represented a new model or 
paradigm through which the family is viewed. These early pioneers 
were creating new ways of seeing family process and were not simply 
searching for techniques. Among these leaders was Murray Bowen, one of the first 
psychiatrists to put whole families in the hospital in order to observe 
their interaction. From these observations, Bowen began to hypothesize 
that schizophrenia is a three-generational, evolutionary process. This 
close contact with families allowed him to postulate the concept of 
differentiation of self, which became one of the building blocks of his 
theory. Michael Kerr, in his foreword that follows, gives a more detailed 
description of this process. Most of the early pioneers in the field have moved into other areas 
of research, but Dr. Bowen has continued to develop and refine his 
theory. One cannot begin to study the field of family therapy without 
studying Murray Bowen. He is to the field what Immanuel Kant is to the 
history of modem philosophy: the one person who is the starting point 
on the journey of knowledge.

Foreword 
It is difficult to say when anyone "begins" a career of discovery. The 
capacity to look at the same things others have looked at and to see 
things no one has seen before is probably part of an orientation to the 
world that is evident in childhood. Murray Bowen's "formal" career of 
discovery in psychiatry began in 1946 at the Menninger Clinic in 
Topeka, Kansas. Bowen had served as a general medical officer in the 
Army from 1941-1945, and his wartime experiences significantly 
influenced his decision to specialize in psychiatry. Psychiatric casualties 
were very common during the war, and many young physicians became 
interested in developing more understanding of such problems. The 
Menninger Clinic was a premier institution for training in this exciting 
and rapidly growing specialty.

text:
The 
Menninger Clinic was a premier institution for training in this exciting 
and rapidly growing specialty. Bowen was not in psychiatry very long before he began to 
question the soundness of the field's basic theoretical foundations, 
foundations that rested in the formulations of Sigmund Freud. The 
Menninger Clinic had a strong psychoanalytic orientation, and Bowen 
was being trained accordingly. He was an avid student. Yet while 
considering many of Freud's contributions to be enormously important 
and valuable, Bowen gradually came to believe that many of Freud's 
most influential theoretical ideas were subjective and that the amount of 
subjectivity effectively precluded Freudian theory from ever becoming 
an accepted science. Freud had striven toward a scientific base for his 
formulations about human behavior, but too many of his central 
concepts had no basis in the life sciences. For example, the Oedipus 
complex came from literature, not from science. Bowen has argued that 
Freud was aware of the uncertain base of many of his theoretical ideas, 
but that many students of Freud treated those ideas as if they were facts. Perhaps like Freud, Bowen came to believe early in his career that 
human behavior could become an accepted science. This belief has 
shaped his professional life course for more than forty years.

Bowen's first steps toward exploring the possibilities for a scientific 
theory of human behavior was to read extensively in the sciences, 
particularly in biology and evolutionary theory. What human beings 
imagine the world to be is one thing; what the world is is something else. Imagination is part of human subjectivity. Verifiable facts about the 
planets, the earth, and all living things are part of science. Man's effort 
to make his thinking more consistent with the factual world is part of 
human objectivity. Bowen attempted to make his thinking about human 
emotional functioning and behavior as consistent as possible with this 
factual world. An important effort was that concepts about human 
behavior should be grounded in the ways that human beings are similar 
to all life rather than the ways that human beings are a unique species.

An important effort was that concepts about human 
behavior should be grounded in the ways that human beings are similar 
to all life rather than the ways that human beings are a unique species. Bowen's reading in the natural sciences coupled with his extensive 
research and clinical experience with families of patients who had a wide 
range of psychiatric and other diagnoses led to his developing a new 
theory of human emotional functioning and behavior, family systems 
theory. The theory conceptualizes the family as a naturally occurring 
system that exhibits patterns of emotional functioning that are related to 
patterns observed in subhuman species. The clinical dysfunctions 
(physical, emotional, and social) are linked to these emotionally 
governed patterns that man has in common with the lower forms. Furthermore, Bowen theorized that differences in the emotional func­
tioning of families are quantitative rather than qualitative in nature. The conceptualization of the family as an emotionally governed 
system or unit (emotion is synonymous with instinct, not feeling) was 
a radical departure from accepted psychiatric theory of the time and led 
almost automatically to an equally radical new form of therapy, therapy 
directed at the family unit. If this conceptualization is accurate, then 
therapy directed at any family member, not just the symptomatic 
member, can modify the whole unit.

family. It is therapy based on a way of thinking that conceptualizes a 
reciprocity in functioning between family members. Bowen left the Menninger Clinic in 1954 and organized a family 
research project at the National Institute of Mental Health in Rockville, 
Maryland. The project, which lasted until 1959, involved having entire

important developments in theory and therapy have occurred during his 
tenure at Georgetown. One of these makes this book by Dr. Daniel 
Papero especially important. To place this development in context, 
however, it is necessary to go back to the beginning of the family 
movement. The family movement surfaced in the mental health world at the 
American Orthopsychiatric and American Psychiatric Association meet­
ings in the spring of 1957. Prior to 1957, a number of investigators were 
studying the family, but with little knowledge of one another's work. The shared vision of those pioneering family researchers was that the 
study of the family had the potential to alter drastically our understand­
ing of the forces that govern individual development and behavior. Several of these researchers envisioned that individual theory would 
eventually be replaced by a theory based on an understanding of the 
family as a unit. However, family therapy, not family theory, captured 
the interest and enthusiasm of the mental health world. The potential of 
the family movement for radically altering man's view of himself, and 
for moving toward a science of human behavior, was lost. By the mid 
1970s, the emphasis on therapeutic techniques had resulted in the 
development of numerous "schools" of family therapy. Distinctions 
between major leaders in the family field were made largely on the basis 
of how they were perceived to conduct therapy.

problems generated by being involved with it. There is an alternative

change oneself in relationship to it. A focus on the extended family has 
some distinct advantages over an exclusive focus on the nuclear family.

Once this new therapeutic approach had been presented nationally by 
Bowen and then others who worked with him, mental-health professionals

origin. It was an important, exciting, and radical development in psychother­
apy. As was the case in 1957, in the minds of many people the importance of 
sound theoretical understanding to the success of a therapeutic effort was 
lost. Many people did and still do attempt to pry themselves loose from their 
unresolved attachments to their families by using a base in individual theory. Because individual theory does not conceptualize the complex family rela­
tionship system, it is not an adequate theoretical base for guiding an effort in 
the family of origin. Without an understanding of the relationship system as 
a whole, people are highly vulnerable to falling into the same old emotional 
patterns, Failing to get a balanced view, they blame the family too much or 
they blame themselves too much. Other groups around the country soon became interested in some ver­
sion of therapy that focused on the extended or multigenerational family. Most of the approaches developed by these groups bore little resemblance to

Preface 
Murray Bowen's influence on the study of the human family is 
immeasurable. Hardly a paper or article is presented today without some 
reference to his work. Any original thinker and researcher attracts 
followers. That is both a help and a hindrance. In fortunate circum­
stances the learner can carry a trailblazer's work forward into new areas 
of exploration. When followers become proselytizers of a new "truth," 
the outcome is far different. The opportunity to write about the ideas of a pioneer in the area 
of family study does not come often, at least in the format of this series. I have experienced it as a thrill and a challenge. The act of writing 
combines the effects of an Xray and a Rorschach administered to the self. In fine, sometimes painful, detail one sees the truncated skeleton of one's 
knowledge and the fantasies of understanding the pacesetting work of 
another. Every concept, and in fact every sentence, must be as accurate 
as possible, yet complete accuracy is ever elusive. The written paragraph 
never quite captures the point to be made. In the end I have come to 
realize what should have been obvious at the onset. The following 
volume represents more of my thinking about the human family than it 
captures that of Dr. Bowen. Caveat lector! My special thanks go to Dr. Murray Bowen, whose work and 
endless questions have stimulated my thinking and productivity far 
beyond my expectations. Dr.

text:
[Family Systems Theory and Emotional Regression Concept]

The emotional regression concept is part of family systems theory, a theory that has guided my psychiatric practice for five decades. Heightened chronic anxiety in families is what drives periods of emotional regression, heightened and sustained. The anxieties in reaction to real and imagined threats within and external to the family. Regression renders family members vulnerable to replacing rational decision-making and a long-term view with intense feeling reactions, subjective thinking, and a short-term view. Anxiety is the polarizing force, not the specific content of polarized issues. That's a very important distinction, I think. And as one family member said it in a tape Murray Bowen did with a couple in Pittsburgh years ago, she said it's not what her insight was. It's not what we're fighting about, but it's that we are fighting. And that's the difference between thinking content and process. And systems helps you toward process. Next one, please.

text:
Having laid the foundation of the basic ideas that guide his 
thinking in the first ten pages of The Rational Optimist, Ridley 
takes the reader through 50,000 years of human cultural and 
economic development, describing the development of exchange 
and specialization, the accompanying development of rules to 
manage the increasing complexity of trade, the advent of agricul
ture, urbanization, industrialization, and the age of technology. Under the heading, “A better today,” (11) Ridley marshals 
evidence that the vast majority of people alive today are sub
stantially better fed, sheltered, protected against disease, and 
much more likely to live to old age than their ancestors had ever 
been. “Since 1800, the population of the world has multiplied six 
times, yet average life expectancy has more than doubled and 
real income has risen more than nine times.” (14) Time saved is 
the key to prosperity: “The true measure of something’s worth 
is the hours it takes to acquire it.” (22) In contrast to the prosper
ous life, Ridley defines self-sufficiency as a condition in which 
“every day you must get up in the morning and supply yourself 
entirely from your own resources.” (33) Clearly, self-sufficiency 
does not lead to prosperity; it is interdependence through trade 
that makes modern life as sustainable as it is.

The cumulative accretion of knowledge by specialists

How collective intelligence evolves
Ridley summarizes early hominid evolution, a period of a 
million and a half years, as yielding little economic progress. The hand axe represents the level of technology achieved. Its 
design was perfected around 600,000 years ago, coinciding with 
emergence of Homo heidelbergensis. There was no sign of cultural 
take-off or progress in technology until a new kind of hominid 
appeared. Data from anthropology and archaeology show the 
earliest indicators of new technology in Africa beginning around 
200,000 years ago. Ridley proposes that the explanation “must be 
something that gathers pace by feeding upon itself, something 
that is auto-catalytic.” (56)
That “something” was the invention of exchange, a new way 
of humans relating to one another that began to build a collec
tive intelligence. Ridley makes a distinction between reciprocity 
and exchange. Reciprocity or cooperating for mutual benefit is 
common in primates and highly developed in humans. Exchange 
(or barter or trade) is a different, and uniquely human, order of 
interaction.

How exchange leads to virtue 
Ridley asks, “But is trade made possible by the milk of 
human kindness, or the acid of human self-interest?”(93) He 
turns to Adam Smith for the answer. In The Wealth of Nations 
(1776), Smith proposed the principle of enlightened self-interest 
as the basis for trade between strangers: “In turning strangers 
into honorary friends, exchange can transmute base self-interest 
into general benevolence.” (104)
For exchange to work, there must be trust. A history of 
building trust is behind the success of a product or service. A 
reputation is at stake in every transaction. Ridley takes eBay as 
an example of what it takes to build trust between anonymous 
strangers. They simply asked their customers for feedback after 
each transaction and posted the comments. In other words, 
transparency is basic to trust, a lesson important in all human 
relationships.

He also stresses the need for 
institutions and rules such as the golden rule, the rule of law, 
respect for private property, democratic government, impartial 
courts, credit, consumer protection, a free press, and customs 
and conventions in order to create the conditions that support 
commerce and economic growth. However, these institutions 
are effective only when they emerge bottom-up in society in a 
co-evolutionary process between inventing new tools and new 
rules. When imposed top-down by authorities, rules and insti
tutions tend to become obstructions to progress. How the earth can support the nine billion 
The human population is expected to reach nine billion by 
2050. In 1798, Robert Malthus predicted that population growth 
would outpace food supply because the productivity of the land 
was finite. Ridley notes that Malthus was wrong, but that “it was 
no easy matter. ...famine was never far away.” (139) Tracing the 
history of agriculture from its origins around 10,000 years ago, 
he sees trade as developing before agriculture and providing 
the incentive to generate surplus food that could be exchanged 
for many other goods. The synergy between agriculture, an 
expanding population, and exchange brought a succession of 
discoveries and technologies. Ridley sees intensive farming as the way to increase food 
production while reducing the area of land under cultivation.

Ridley sees intensive farming as the way to increase food 
production while reducing the area of land under cultivation. He offers a dizzying array of facts and statistics to show how 
agriculture is currently supporting more people on less land 
and how it can go much further in this direction. He details the 
technologies and practices that could make it possible to double 
agricultural production and thus feed nine billion people in 
2050. Especially important will be the role of genetically modi
fied crops, “...one of the most rapid and successful adoptions of 
a new technology in the history of farming.” (154)
How trade builds cities and fosters prosperity
The majority of the world’s people now live in cities, and that 
is a good thing in Ridley’s view—more than half the population 
“can leave subsistence and seek the possibilities of a life based 
on the collective brain instead.” (189) It is good for the planet

because “city dwellers take up less space, use less energy and have 
less impact on natural ecosystems than country dwellers.” (190) 
As with agriculture, urbanization was long preceded by 
trade.

Ridley traces the history of cities, from their origin in large 
settlements that emerged about seven thousand years ago (the 
oldest in Mesopotamia, now Iraq), through centuries in which 
cities, economies, and empires rose and fell at different times in 
various parts of the world. It is a challenge to follow the multiple 
interlocking variables that he weaves into the story. A few of the 
elements are the emergence of the middleman, or merchant, as 
a facilitator (and at times an exploiter) of trade, the maritime 
revolution that allowed the crossing of seas that connected mar
kets, countless innovations that, although improving productiv
ity, also contributed to obstacles and setbacks to trade such as 
plague, war, politics, and piracy. There are many examples of 
countries sinking back to self-sufficiency for decades or longer, 
but Ridley believes that “inexorably, gains from trade could be 
rediscovered,” (179) and economic vitality would take off again. According to Ridley, trade works as a bottom-up process: 
“Trade emerged from the interactions of individuals. It evolved. No one was in charge.” (165) However, once established, a free 
trade area lends itself to exploitation and control of wealth 
by rulers. Ridley sees government as a mixed blessing, more 
negative than positive.

Ridley sees government as a mixed blessing, more 
negative than positive. Government can be helpful to trade and 
growth when it provides central services and removes impedi
ments to trade and specialization; but more often it operates as 
a monopoly bringing inefficiency and stagnation to most things 
it runs, stifling free enterprise with taxes and regulation. How humans have escaped the Malthusian trap
As with all animals, human populations rise and fall with 
cycles of abundance and scarcity. What is different in humans 
is the accompanying cycle of rising and falling specialization. Specialization increases along with density in times of plenty 
and reverts back toward self-sufficiency in times of shortage. Ridley provides this important analysis: 
Instead of dying from famine and pestilence when too 
numerous for their food supply, people can increase 
their specialization, which allows more to subsist on 


 182

                     2014
the available resources. On the other hand, if exchange 
becomes harder, they will reduce their specialization, 
which can lead to a population crisis even without an 
increase in population. (193) 
 
In short, decreasing specialization, not population growth, is the 
problem. The unique propensity to specialize gives humans a 
way of escaping the trap of Malthusian population limitation.

Oil, coal, and gas are finite, but Ridley defends their use 
with mathematics by showing that fossil fuels have spared 
land from industrialization by replacing the acres that would 
be needed by other energy sources such as solar panels, wind 
farms, woodland, hayfields, and hydroelectric dams. Always 
optimistic, he concludes that oil, coal, and gas “will last decades, 
perhaps centuries, and people will find alternatives long before 
they run out.” (238)
Ideas are the ultimate renewable resource
Ridley’s next subject is the history of the growth of knowledge 
and invention. In his view, knowledge is the one thing you can 
give away and still keep. He compares innovation to a bush fire 
that flares, sputters and dies only to flare up elsewhere. It leaps 
from one technology to another, from one industry to another. Ridley contests Francis Bacon’s proposition that “science is the 
father of invention.” (255) He sees it more the other way around. Invention is frequently a bumbling, tinkering, trial-and-error 
bottom-up phenomenon, and science comes along afterwards 
to explain it. He also does not see money, government, or intel
lectual property rights as drivers of invention, so, if none of 
these, then what? Exchange! Ever-increasing exchange of ideas 
begets the modern world’s ever-increasing rate of innovation.

problems is massive breakdown in human relationships at the 
societal level: alienation, struggles for dominance, and fierce 
competition for resources. In his writing on emotional process 
in society, Murray Bowen saw major disruptions in human-to-
human relationships as rooted in “man’s disharmony with his 
environment, a long-term evolutionary process.” (Bowen 1978, 
450) From a broad, natural systems perspective, economic devel
opment, trade, and technology are one part of this evolutionary 
process. If one were to write a natural systems balance sheet, 
social costs and environmental costs must be counted along with 
the benefits that economic growth has brought. From the perspective of Bowen theory, what is missing from 
The Rational Optimist is the understanding of emotional process 
in human life. Ridley’s thinking encompasses the ebb and flow 
of history, the triumphs and the downfalls of civilization, virtue 
and corruption, progress and regression, but he does not have 
a theoretical framework for seeing the whole of it as a unified 
process. Collective intelligence develops in human families and 
societies alongside collective emotion. Bowen described human 
emotional functioning as based on a counterbalance between 
the deep, instinctual emotional system and the more recently 
evolved intellectual system. He also described it in terms of 
the counterbalance between the force for individuality and the 
force for togetherness.

but conceptualize it differently. For Ridley, societies regress

was manifested in decision-making that was based more on short-

in the markets and a major disruption to the economy. Bowen 
theory would see that phenomenon as an example of regression, 
the intellectual system becoming dominated by, and working in 
the service of, the emotional system at a societal level.

Ann Jones RN, PhD
The shift away from genetic determinism in the 1990s was 
followed by research exploring gene-environment interactions. The mechanism at play appears to begin with the organism’s 
perception of the environment capable of triggering patterns 
of genome-wide transcription factors. Evolutionary preserved 
responses to the environment turn on and off immune system 
genes capable of preparing the organism for conflict as well as 
increasing the risk for disease. The almost minute-to-minute 
response of the genome to its environment and the transmission 
of these patterns across generations lend support to Bowen 
theory concepts of level of differentiation of self, psychological 
oneness, and the multigenerational transmission process. The 
role of perception and anxiety level highlight the nexus of social 
genomics and Bowen theory. Key words: epigenetics, social genomics, Bowen theory, 
family system, emotional system, differentiation of self, 
multigenerational transmission process
In April 2014, The Bowen Center for the Study of the Family 
hosted a conference entitled, Generation to Generation: The Inter
play of Genes and Family Process.

MURRAY BOWEN AND SCIENCE
Bowen theory, developed by Murray Bowen, MD (1913–
1990), provides a framework for viewing human behavior based 
on scientific principles. Throughout his life, from his boyhood 
days growing up on a self-sustaining Tennessee farm, through 
medical school, his service in World War II to soldiers with 
emotional problems, his years at the Menninger Clinic learn
ing psychoanalysis and practicing psychiatry, and his research 
at NIMH, Bowen showed an interest in the natural world and 
the part humans played in nature. These experiences may have 
shaped his later view of the human as a product of evolution.

forces as yeast, honey bees, and chimpanzees. Bowen theory is 
unique among theories of human behavior in its effort to sepa

...the human is as scientific as the other forms of life on 
the planet, that it will finally be possible to construct a 
total human theory from scientific facts alone, and that 
the feeling elements of human existence will be handled 
in relationship with other human beings. ...I fashioned a 
natural systems theory, designed to fit precisely with the 
principles of evolution and the human as an evolutionary 
being. (Kerr and Bowen 1988, 360)
Bowen’s leadership style, teaching, writing, and clinical pres
ence all reflected his emphasis on scientific knowledge and the 
importance of critical thinking. Over the decades, Bowen invited 
scientists to be the featured lecturer at the Annual Symposium. He 
also featured them at the Thursday Lecture Series and in many 
topic-oriented conferences, and challenged faculty and trainees 
to read in the sciences.

the molecular level. Murray Bowen stood mostly alone when he 
sought to “conceptualize emotional illness as a product of that 
part of man he shares with the lower forms of life.” (Bowen 1978, 
xiv) Based on progress in thinking about the human genome it 
may now be possible to test this hypothesis using advances in 
scientific technologies. Possibilities for Bowen theorists to collabo
rate and share knowledge with the sciences continue to expand. GENETICS
Genetics is the science of heredity and variation in living 
organisms. It has long been recognized that living things inherit 
traits from previous generations. This knowledge led to efforts 
to improve crops and animals through selective breeding. It 
was not, however, until Gregor Mendel presented a paper in 
1865 that the process of inheritance, based on specific laws and 
discrete units of inheritance called genes, began to be under
stood. Later research identified the molecular basis for genes as 
deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), long chains of nucleotides where 
genes reside. These chains of coded instructions form the pro
teins necessary to build and maintain an organism’s cells and 
pass genetic traits to offspring.

Until recently, genetics has been viewed as an unalterable 
process (except by random mutations and natural selection) with 
traits from a parent passing to their offspring. Children whose 
parents and grandparents had high blood pressure, dementia, 
or cancer assumed they were likely to “inherit” these conditions 
based on their genetic heritage. In the 1990s, the Human Genome 
Project found that humans, in all their complexity, really have 
only about 22,000 genes, slightly more than a worm and slightly 
fewer then a mouse. This finding, coupled with the discovery 
that one gene can code for many proteins or for none, challenged 
genetic determinism, which was the dogma of the day. Genetic 
determinism, as the name implies, taught that one gene codes for 
one protein in a unidirectional process that always begins with 
the gene and ends with the protein. Research collaborators on 
the Human Genome Project hoped that, by mapping the human 
genome, individual genes responsible for specific disease states 
could be identified and then lead to specific treatments for condi
tions such as cancer, heart disease, and asthma. The completed 
map of the human genome failed to support this view, instead 
revealing a more complex and dynamic process.

inherited set of genetic instructions. Although monozygotic twins 
are sometimes called “identical twins,” they exhibit differences 
in what is referred to as their phenotype. Phenotype is an organism’s observable characteristics or traits

as well as the influence of environmental factors and the inter

be taller, have asthma, a higher IQ, or be more athletic than the 
other. Studies of specific diseases in monozygotic twins show 
discordant rates for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder (Franga et 
al. 2005) and Parkinson’s disease (Factor and Weiner 2008). The nature-nurture debate has long been an arena for teasing 
out the effects of genes versus environment in human development

text:
A specialty of genetics called epigenetics has 
garnered attention with its focus on how the environment can 
influence gene expression from plants to humans. Thinking and 
research efforts have shifted away from gene and environment 
as independent forces. Epigenetics is the study of changes in the phenotype, or gene 
expression, which occur without changes in the underlying DNA 
sequence of the gene. Epi comes from the Greek word meaning 
over or above and thus refers to effects that are in addition to 
genetics (Callinan and Feinberg 2006). The epigenome acts like 
a second code on top of the DNA. The molecular basis of epi
genetics is complex, involving modification in the activation of 


110	
	
  	
          Family Systems	
	
                     2014
genes without changing the basic structure of the DNA. When 
the cell divides, these modifications are preserved and can be 
maintained both within the life span of the organism and across 
generations (Whitelaw and Whitelaw 2006). Epigenetic research 
has looked at the effects of nutrients, toxins, stress, and mothering 
style in an attempt to understand how these external factors act 
to silence or activate gene expression. Researchers have discov
ered an array of environmental exposures capable of triggering 
chemical changes in the body or brain, leading to silencing or 
activation of certain genes (Kuehn 2008). An early area of study in epigenetics was nutrition. Nutri
tion affects the phenotype of an organism.

text:
An early area of study in epigenetics was nutrition. Nutri
tion affects the phenotype of an organism. Experiments in mice 
demonstrate the importance of a mother’s diet in the phenotype 
of her offspring. Mice with the agouti gene can occur in two 
forms. If the gene is unmethylated (meaning no methyl group 
has been attached at that specific gene location) the mouse will 
have a yellow coat, be obese, and prone to diabetes and cancer. When the agouti gene is methylated (as it is in normal mice) 
the coat is brown and the mouse has a low risk for disease. Fat 
yellow mice and skinny brown mice are genetically identical. A pregnant fat yellow mouse fed an enriched diet causing the 
agouti gene to become methylated will produce skinny brown 
pups showing that the prenatal diet of the mother affects their 
offspring (Dolinoy 2008). Studies of the 1944–45 Dutch famine 
found that children of pregnant women exposed to the famine 
were more susceptible to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular dis
ease, and other health problems. These children were smaller at 
birth and, as adults, also produced children who were smaller 
than average, even though this next generation of pregnant 
women had a normal caloric intake. The famine is believed to 
have resulted in epigenetic changes affecting phenotypic expres
sion that was passed down to the next generation (Roseboom et 
al. 2001).

of the environment through the senses. We may sense danger, see 
a shadowy figure, or hear a cry for help. This perception alerts 
the central nervous system to begin pumping out signals via the 
endocrine and sympathetic nervous systems. These signals are 
picked up by receptors on the surface of cells and transmitted to 
the cell nucleus where strands of DNA reside. DNA sits quietly 
in the nucleus of a cell waiting for basal transcription factors to 
bind to promoters on the DNA, thus beginning the process of 
replication. DNA is known as the double helix and looks like a 
twisted ladder. The process of replication begins by unzipping 
the DNA so a copy can be made and used for the next step. This step is called transcription and results in the formation of 
mRNA. Finally, mRNA is translated into amino acid sequences 
that form proteins capable of influencing health and behavior. An animated version of the description above can be found on

text:
Recent research from the field 
of human social genomics finds evidence that our “molecular 
selves” (Slavich and Cole 2013) are not fixed and static, as once 
believed, but are fluid and permeable in our physical and social 
environments. This research suggests that the social environment 
acts to affect gene expression by turning certain genes on and off 
based on different social and environmental conditions. Slavich 
and Cole (2013) think our genome has the ability to create a wide 


112	
	
  	
          Family Systems	
	
                     2014
variety of “potential biological selves.” Over our life span, the 
social conditions we encounter determine which biological self 
emerges. Environmental factors could act almost like a dimmer 
switch, sending signals to our genes to turn them up and down 
(Dobbs 2013). An elegant bee study offers a window into how this pro
cess works. Gene Robinson (Zayed and Robinson 2012) and his 
research group studied European honeybees and African killer 
bees to understand how the environment shapes gene expres
sion in these two subspecies. Robinson and others knew that 
the environment could affect gene expression in select genes, 
resulting in some behavioral changes. He wanted to test the 
conventional wisdom that the environment causes fairly lim
ited changes in gene expression by brightening or dimming the 
activity of only a few genes at a time.

activity of only a few genes at a time. Robinson hypothesized 
that the environment had a more significant impact on behavior 
by changing the expression of large sectors of genes across the

infant African killer bees and put them in the hives of the mild 
mannered European honey bees. At the same time they moved 
infant European honey bees into the hives of aggressive African 
killer bees. Each week researchers removed a few of the foster 
bees from each hive, instantly chilling them to capture their 
gene activity at that moment. The brains of the bees were then 
ground up and run through a micro assay machine to see which 
genes were active at the moment of capture. The team found

Bowen theory’s concept of differentiation of self is a nuanced, 
multilevel term. He described it as the cornerstone of his theory 
(Bowen 1978, 362). It grew out of his ability to see the family as 
a system and to see symptoms in an individual as a reflection of 
an active process involving every member of the family (Bowen 
1978). In his writings, Bowen often referred to the “stuck togeth
erness” he observed in families as the “undifferentiated family 
ego mass.” All families have some degree of stuck togetherness 
or psychological oneness as Bowen called it in the 1950s (Butler 
2013, 106). Bowen postulated that this psychological oneness 
reflected fusion of the intellectual and emotional systems in 
all members of the family. When the two systems overlap to a 
significant degree, individuals and families have difficulty pro
cessing information accurately. A young adult’s desire to move 
to another city for a job is interpreted by the mother as a rejec
tion of the family, and she develops symptoms of depression. Faced with his wife’s depression, the husband begins drinking 
heavily and risks losing his job. An attempt by one member of 
the family to take an action for self leads to increased anxiety 
in others. In a fusion it is difficult to act for self based on one’s 
own principles. Family members react by blaming the other or 
by blaming themselves, neither of which is accurate and both of 
which come out of the emotional system.

BOWEN THEORY’S ROLE IN SCIENCE
Research in epigenetics and social genomics can inform 
the concepts of Bowen theory and move it closer to a science of 
human behavior. The research on the adopted bees shows how 
bees with a certain set of genes function differently according to 
the hive they are placed in, and that this shift in behavior and 
gene pattern activity can be passed on to the next generation of 
bees. Cross-fostered rhesus macaque infants grow up and dem
onstrate the mothering characteristics of their adopted mother, 
not their biological one. These findings appear to offer support 
to the concept of multigenerational transmission process. What 
would it take to test this idea further? Bowen coined the term family emotional system to describe 
the unique relationship he saw among family members. He 
stressed the idea of the family as a system, with the behavior 
of one member capable of influencing the functioning of others 
in the family. The family emotional system is more intense and 
has a greater capacity to shape behavior than the larger social 
system. Bowen recognized the unique property of the family, call
ing it the undifferentiated family ego mass. He saw an individual’s 
functioning in the social system as shaped by experiences in the 
family of origin. In a 2010 article, Michael Meaney challenged the psychologi
cal sciences to develop a conceptual framework that meaningfully 
integrates research on brain development and function.

the interplay between gene and environment in defining 
individual differences at the level of complex traits. (Meany 2010, 42) 
Meaney is searching for a theoretical framework broad 
enough to account for the research advances in epigenetics and 
social genomics. Without that framework the data and findings

emotional illness as a product of that part of man he shares with 
lower forms of life, and its conceptualization of the family as a 
system, provides a broad-based theoretical framework. Bowen’s 
observational research on families is now being confirmed by 
findings in epigenetics and social genomics at the biological and 
cellular level. Research documenting neural-hormonal responses

to the environment that endure for several generations provide 
evidence for the concept of multigenerational transmission pro

awareness of the family as an emotional system. This lead to his 
development of treatment strategies that moved away from the 
idea of symptoms residing within the individual and toward a 
theory that addressed the family as a system. Research in epi
genetics and social genomics demonstrates the effect of the social 
environment on individual genomic expression and supports 
the view of the family as a system. It is time for Bowen theory 
to share new knowledge with the accepted sciences, move into 
the future with the other sciences, and establish a science of 
human behavior. ❉

HOSPITAL LEADERSHIP AND THE CHRONICALLY 
SUICIDAL ADULT
Erik Thompson, MA
Chronic suicidality is one of the most taxing problems in the 
mental health care field. Leading researchers have noted that the 
standard treatment for acute suicidality is counterproductive in 
cases of chronic suicidality, which calls for a different approach 
toward hospital admission and discharge criteria. The issue of 
who takes responsibility for another’s safety is at the heart of 
this policy discussion. In this single-subject case experiment, 
Bowen theory guided the modification of hospital admission 
and discharge criteria for one chronically suicidal individual, 
allowing the patient access to the hospital for any reason but 
clarifying the hospital’s accountability in order to heighten 
the patient’s own responsibility for her safety. Measured in 
terms of crisis-bed days, responsibility increased with decreased 
crisis-bed usage. Bowen theory predicts that a shift in the 
level of self-definition of a significant party in a relationship 
system will evoke a “change back” move. Events consistent 
with this prediction emerged during the experiment, involving 
behavior that appeared dangerous but was instead revealed to 
be a deceptive display.

A SELF WITH ONE’S SPOUSE
 
JOAN JURKOWSKI, MS 
This presentation is used to illustrate the challenge of “lending 
a hand” to a person who is working to reduce symptoms without 
addressing the underlying relationship factors that contribute to 
the symptom. Consultation with a coach can result in decreased 
anxiety and improved thinking and is often associated with

solid change. This is a presentation of a client who worked to 
improve his relationship with his spouse, got a job, and stopped

Bowen theory, family therapy, solid change

with me for thirteen sessions over four months, then he missed

ALLOPARENTING: THE WORKS OF 
SARAH BLAFFER HRDY
Merry Muraskin, PhD
This article is a personal review of three books by anthropologist 
Sarah Blaffer Hrdy: The Woman That Never Evolved (1981), 
Mother Nature: Maternal Instincts and How They Shape 
the Human Species (1999), and Mothers and Others: The 
Evolutionary Origins of Mutual Understanding (2009). Rather 
than write a typical book review, I have chosen to relate how 
her works, together with my understanding of family systems 
theory, have led me to fresh perspectives on my life and on of 
my extended family and have also led me to new insights into 
my previous study of a group of male gorillas. Keywords: alloparent, gorillas, evolution, cooperative breeding, 
sibling position, family systems theory
I was born into troubled times. In July 1942, six months after 
the United States entered World War II, my mother gave birth to 
a sickly, low-weight baby girl who grew up to be me. According 
to my mother I barely missed being put in an incubator. I spent 
the first several months of my life seized by bouts of projectile 
vomiting.

text:
When I was about four months old, my mother decided to 
return to eastern Tennessee where she was born. She always 
described this journey with dramatic flair. It was wartime. Every
thing was rationed. It was difficult to get anywhere. She desper
ately searched for a ride back to her family. For the final lap over 
the Appalachians down into Chattanooga she managed to wangle 
a ride from some policemen who, despite the bad weather, were 
willing to take us on the nighttime trip over the mountains. She 
made it sound like a dangerous escape from behind enemy lines. A relative who would drive her north to the small town of her 
birth, greeted her in Chattanooga with the remark, “You’re the 
closest thing to a walking corpse I’ve ever seen.” 
My mother told me that soon after our arrival at my grand
parents’ house, many neighbors came to visit us. She was flat
tered by all the attention until she learned that they had come to 
pay their last respects to her dying baby. At the time I was still 
a scrawny infant, unable to put on much weight and doing my 
best to throw up anything that landed in my stomach. My mother settled into her familiar home, living with her 
mother, her father, and her youngest sister, then sixteen. I stopped 
vomiting and finally began to put on weight. My father was 
soon shipped overseas, and my mother and I remained with 
my grandparents until my father returned from Europe when 
I was two years old, whereupon my parents and I headed back 
to Colorado.

This is the narrative of my beginnings as my mother told it 
to me, a story I heard many times as I was growing up. This tale 
later fleshed itself out when I spent many years studying Bowen 
family systems theory. Vol. 10, No. 2   	      Alloparenting: The Works Of Sarah Blaffer Hrdy             147
MY PARENTS’ RELATIONSHIP 
Before my exposure to Bowen’s understanding of families, 
I had thought of my mother as a dud and my father as a genius. He made all the decisions; she went along. My mother told me 
an anecdote that summed it all up. When they married she voted 
Republican; he voted Democratic. The first time elections rolled 
around after they were together, my father told my mother that 
if she voted the way she usually did, she would cancel out his 
vote. Thereafter she voted with him as a matter of course. As I learned about family systems, I thought of my parents’ 
relationship more as “he overfunctioned; she underfunctioned.” 
Two of my cousins helped me make that shift. One cousin, the 
daughter of my mother’s second oldest brother, told me how 
impressed she was that my mother had made several trips to 
Missouri to see her brother and his family. That brother was very 
cut off from his family, and my mother was bridging a very large 
gap. My cousin’s family enjoyed my mother’s liveliness, intel
ligence, and sense of humor.

Another relative, a second cousin, the daughter of my moth

because she was so impressed with my mother (not my father). My mother was the first in her family to go to college, the 
first woman in her family to have what was then a high status 
job, teaching school. (My grandmother, her mother, was an occa

teaching probably had negative status.) One of the ways that my 
mother worked her way through college was by selling maga

in the late 1930s. Even though my view of my parents’ relationship changed 
greatly when I took up the study of family systems, it took many 
years before I could see the family patterns that had been estab
lished from my infancy.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The first meeting of the editorial board of Family Systems was 
held on September 19, 1990. At this meeting the Board selected 
Michael Kerr as its editor. When Volume 1.1 of Family Systems 
was published in 1994, Dr. Kerr, writing his first “From the Edi
tor” article, described the contribution the journal could make 
to the future development of Bowen theory:
 
Bowen wrote in detail about all the major components 
of his theory and therapy. Over the years, however, he 
repeatedly emphasized that the theory was incomplete, 
not fixed in stone; it could be modified, amplified, and 
extended by new facts. Death ended Bowen’s work on the 
theory, but this journal is dedicated to the future of the 
theory and its many applications. It seems apt that Bowen 
suggested the journal’s title, Family Systems. (Kerr 1994, 3)
By fostering viable contact with the accepted sciences 
Family Systems is intended to contribute to the development of 
the theory. Kerr wrote:
A natural systems theory can transcend the various 
compartments of knowledge concerned with human 
functioning. A steady influx of factual knowledge and 
ideas from these various compartments or academic 
disciplines is critical for shaping the future of Bowen 
theory. This journal is not trying to create a new discipline, 
but to provide a forum for exchange between existing 
disciplines.

In discussing his research observations at NIMH more than 
half a century ago, Bowen described how the change in his think
ing developed into a systems perspective: 
Once it was possible to focus on the family as a unit, it 
was like shifting a microscope from the oil immersion to 
the low power lens, or like moving from the playing field 
to the top of the stadium to watch a football game. Broad 
patterns of form and movement that had been obscured in 
the close-up view became clear. The close-up view could 
then become more meaningful once the distant view was 
also possible. (Bowen [1960] 1978, 50)

This observation and the subsequent theory of the family he 
developed represented a genuine paradigm change in viewing 
human behavior. However, while the change toward a clinical 
approach involving the family initially met with widespread 
interest, the principal individual paradigm still predominates in 
psychiatry, psychology, and the broader field of mental health. Individual and gene centered perspectives have also remained 
predominant in the sciences. From a very broad view of the his
tory of ideas this development is not entirely surprising. At times 
Bowen stated that it may take a century or more for his systems 
paradigm to be accepted given the extent to which the individual 
paradigm is entrenched in society, in science, and in medicine.

I have wondered at the absence of a discussion of the fam
ily unit as a central element in shaping human behavior and in 
shaping the variation in adaptiveness of individuals over their 
life course. In the recent development of social neuroscience, for 
example, the family as a factor in brain functioning and develop
ment is largely omitted. One reason for this omission may be that 
most of the studies on neuroendocrine factors involved in social 
relationships are with nonhuman animals in laboratory environ
ments. And, in those studies that look at both neuroendocrine 
functioning and complex social behavior in natural settings, the 
focus remains largely on mammals and their interactions in the 
social environment. A second factor may be that the relationship studies are gen
erally based on attachment theory and thus are focused on dyads, 
principally mother-offspring dyads. While greatly contributing 
to knowledge of how such dyadic interactions influence devel
opment, the influence of the family system on the functioning 
of the dyad and how the dyad is deeply embedded in the larger 
system is missing. It also appears that many investigators see the family as sub
sumed under the category of social groups. In contrast, Bowen 
theory postulates that the family emotional system is distinctly 
involved in regulating behavior both in the present and over 
multiple generations.

Title: Hospital Leadership and the Chronically Suicidal Adult
Author: Thompson

129
HOSPITAL LEADERSHIP AND THE CHRONICALLY 
SUICIDAL ADULT
Erik Thompson, MA
Chronic suicidality is one of the most taxing problems in the 
mental health care field. Leading researchers have noted that the 
standard treatment for acute suicidality is counterproductive in 
cases of chronic suicidality, which calls for a different approach 
toward hospital admission and discharge criteria. The issue of 
who takes responsibility for another’s safety is at the heart of 
this policy discussion. In this single-subject case experiment, 
Bowen theory guided the modification of hospital admission 
and discharge criteria for one chronically suicidal individual, 
allowing the patient access to the hospital for any reason but 
clarifying the hospital’s accountability in order to heighten 
the patient’s own responsibility for her safety. Measured in 
terms of crisis-bed days, responsibility increased with decreased 
crisis-bed usage. Bowen theory predicts that a shift in the 
level of self-definition of a significant party in a relationship 
system will evoke a “change back” move. Events consistent 
with this prediction emerged during the experiment, involving 
behavior that appeared dangerous but was instead revealed to 
be a deceptive display.

Although I am not neutral 
about suicide, I acknowledged that I did not know what it was 
like to live in their skin. Differentiating a self with my clients also meant defining 
myself clearly. In this effort I looked to the four patterns described 
in the concept of nuclear family emotional process in Bowen theory, 
which explores the emotional interplay between parties in the 
family. Resting on the central concept of differentiation of self, 
it identifies four patterns of interaction: (1) distance, (2) conflict, 
(3) triangles (the process by which immaturity is transferred from 
the parents to a child), and (4) overfunctioning/underfunctioning 
reciprocity, also referred to as overresponsible/underresponsible 
reciprocity (Bowen 1978). Behavior is conventionally viewed on a continuum, with high 
functioning on one end and dysfunction on the other. The notion 
that one end helps shape the other is typically absent from this 
viewpoint. Over years of working with families whose members 
exhibited extreme behavioral issues, Murray Bowen observed 
that “dysfunctioning and overfunctioning exist together” (1978, 
155) in a symbiotic relationship. Bowen’s theory links social, 
physical, and emotional dysfunction in a family member to func
tional positions in an interconnected network of relationships.

DEFINING RESPONSIBILITY FOR SAFETY
Bowen theory helped me carefully think through my level 
of responsibility for my patients’ safety, and I made sure they 
understood my position that I did not believe I was responsible 
for keeping them alive and would not go to irrational lengths to 
do so. I viewed repeated hospitalizations in response to self-harm 
behavior as irrational. My position was often tested. I will never 
forget the phone call from one of my patients telling me she was 
about to overdose in a nearby city. This patient had engaged in 
alarm-stimulating suicidal behavior some twenty-five times in 
the previous six months. Now she said she had the pills in hand. As was my practice, I talked to her about her best thinking about 
the situation and considered how to define myself. I learned that 
she was with a friend in a changing room at a clothing store and 
that the friend (whom I knew well) was watching her carefully. The number of pills she had in her hand was not large. After a 
sincere and respectful exchange, I informed my patient that I 
did not believe in taking action to protect her. I expressed my 
sincere hope that I would see her at our scheduled appointment 
in a few days, and that I would truly miss her if she decided to 
complete suicide. Vol. 10, No. 2   	 Hospital Leadership and the Chronically Suicidal Adult          135
She found her way to the emergency room that night but was 
discharged without being admitted, a rare occurrence.

In more differentiated groups, individu
als are more thoughtful about what they can and can’t control in 
the other and are less driven to manage their own lives by con
trolling others’ actions. In institutional dealings with chronically 
suicidal adults, efforts to get others to change tend to concentrate 
on partner organizations as well. For example, hospitals blame 
the local mental health organization for not preventing hospi
talization, and the outpatient team blames the local hospital for 
chronically admitting them. I often heard clinicians say that as 
stressful as treating chronic suicidality was, being blamed for 
the problem by one’s peers was worse. The more extreme the 
suicidal behavior, the more regular were the calls for large, multi-
organizational meetings to see if everyone could get on the same 
page. At their worst, these became finger-pointing sessions. An 
advantage of Bowen theory is that a change in leadership does 
not require that everyone in a system be in agreement. Bowen 
theory asserts that anyone who is well connected to the symp
tomatic party and to the key players in the system can make 
progress by managing self. As my individual work progressed, I came to think I should 
assume leadership in the larger treatment system surrounding 
our highly symptomatic patients. My principles of operation in 
that group were an extension of those I defined for my patients.

EXTENDED FAMILY RELATIONSHIPS: A COMPARISON OF 
HIGH AND LOW SYMPTOM FAMILIES
Phillip Klever, MSW
Bowen theory contends that viable emotional contact with 
the multigenerational family contributes to a more orderly, 
asymptomatic life. This article describes a fifteen-year research 
study that tested this hypothesis. The study examined extended 
family relationships of five low symptom nuclear families and 
five high symptom nuclear families. The study found that 
participants with low symptom nuclear families, as compared 
to high symptom nuclear families, had extended family 
relationships with more frequent contact, a lower percentage of 
cutoff, and a higher percentage of open relationships with the 
extended family. In addition, the low symptom participants 
had less geographic distance from their extended families. They also had more of their extended family members at 
their weddings, and they attended more of the funerals of 
their extended family members. Three themes emerged in 
the qualitative analysis of the interviews: a continuum of 
emotional contact to cutoff, shifts in involvement due to 
life events and anxiety, and parental influence on extended 
family relationships.

text:
Bowen theory hypothesizes that reduction in family anxiety 
may reduce the symptomatology of the family. But the theory 
posits that other variables, in addition to anxiety, also influ
ence variation in functioning. Differentiation of self, one of 
the central concepts in Bowen theory, is another key variable 
that influences a family’s functioning. The interaction of the 
spouses’ levels of differentiation and the anxiety in the family 
are hypothesized to influence the degree of symptomatology in 
the family. Bowen theory’s concept of nuclear family emotional 
process describes the different pathways for undifferentiation 
and anxiety to manifest itself within the unit—marital distance 
and conflict, reciprocal functioning between the spouses, and 
projection onto one or more children. These relationship pro
cesses are thought to contribute to physical, psychiatric, social, 
and/or marital symptoms. It is as if there is a quantitative amount of undifferen
tiation to be absorbed, and it may be focused largely 
in one area or mostly in one area and less in others or 
distributed evenly in all three areas. (Bowen 1978, 203)  
The overall level of symptomatology of the unit could 
potentially be an indirect measure of the mix of undifferentia
tion and family anxiety. More symptomatic families would 
reflect lower levels of differentiation and/or higher levels of 
anxiety. Less symptomatic families would reflect higher levels 
of differentiation and/or lower levels of anxiety.

text:
DISCUSSION
This study supports Bowen’s assertion that some kind of 
viable emotional contact between the generations contributes 
to a less symptomatic life. A previously reported quantitative 
analysis of the whole study sample (Klever 2015) supported 


125	
	
  	
        Family Systems	
	
                     2016
this hypothesis by finding an association between less symp
tomatic functioning and open relationships with the extended 
family, contact with cousins, and knowledge of family facts. The study reported here builds on the quantitative study by 
doing a more in-depth analysis using a small group comparison 
of the extended family relationships of the most symptomatic 
nuclear families and the least symptomatic nuclear families. The results of the analysis revealed that low symptom families, 
as compared to high symptom families, had more contact with 
their extended family members, especially aunts and uncles, 
fewer cutoff relationships, more open relationships with the 
extended family, and more geographic closeness with their 
aunts, uncles, and grandparents. They also had more multi
generational family members at their weddings and attended 
more funerals of their extended family members. While the 
sample was small, the findings created a cumulative effect 
with each measure of viable emotional contact corresponding 
with higher functioning.

to-one, personal relationships with members of the multigen
erational family. It suggests that such an effort over time has 
the potential to improve personal and family functioning. To 
establish “some kind of viable emotional contact” or to bridge 
some of the cutoff in the family usually requires commitment, 
knowledge about the family system and one’s part in the fam
ily, and application of this knowledge in family relationships. In addition, the effort is made possible with some degree of

THE FAMILY PROJECTION PROCESS WHEN 
THE FATHER IS THE PRIMARY CAREGIVER
Mariana Martinez, PsyD 
The family projection process describes the triangle formed by 
mother, father, and child, the underlying fusion among them, 
and the anxiety that emerges from the undifferentiation. The 
original formulation of the family projection process points to 
the intense mother-child fusion with the support of the father 
on the outside angle. This presentation describes two families 
with symptomatic children that illustrates this phenomenon. In both families the mother is the primary breadwinner and the 
father is the primary caregiver. The question posed is whether 
or not the reversal of traditional parenting roles plays a role 
in  the way the family projection process manifests itself. An 
analysis of the cases supports the notion that, regardless of 
this family arrangement for care giving of the children, the 
most intense fusion remains between mother and child, with 
the father participating by focusing primarily on his wife. Keywords: family projection process, primary caregiver, 
parental roles, primary triangle, fusion, symptoms in children
Dr. Martinez is a faculty member and administrator of the Family Center Clinic at 
the Bowen Center.

FACULTY CASE CONFERENCE
The faculty case conference is held monthly at the Bowen Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference 
from their clinical practices. The conference is not intended 
as supervision or as a meeting to arrive at a consensus about 
how to manage a specific case. It is intended as a learning 
experience for the faculty and to keep them aware of one 
another’s general approach to clinical problems. 166

                     2016
The question I would like to raise today relates to the con
cept of the family projection process, the triangle formed by 
mother, father, and child, the underlying fusion among them, 
and the anxiety that emerges. The family projection process is 
a powerful concept for understanding how symptoms develop 
in children. Dr. Bowen’s observations in his NIMH research 
project indicated that the mother and the schizophrenic daugh
ter had an intense fusion, and that this position in the fusion 
was supported by the father. Later, he and other clinicians 
observed this configuration is also typical in families with less 
symptomatic children.

Later, he and other clinicians 
observed this configuration is also typical in families with less 
symptomatic children. One explanation for what is involved in the formation of 
the intense mother-child fusion with the father on the outside 
angle could be twofold—one biological and the other social. The first factor would have to do with the activation of the 
biologically driven system of attachment between mother and 
offspring, between mother and father, and father and offspring. The second would be the socially learned role of mothers and 
fathers in relation to the child. This typically includes mother 
spending more time with the child and having more respon
sibilities for daily activities, while father supports her efforts 
with work outside the home and has fewer activities with 
the child. With new family arrangements and the changes in 
gender roles in our society, the question that arises is whether 
the projection process can shift. I wonder if the increased 
involvement of fathers in child rearing responsibilities and the 
increased involvement of mothers working outside the home 
has an impact on the way the family process unfolds. In this clinical presentation I will describe two families 
with symptomatic children in which, presumably, the projec
tion process is a key factor. In both families the father is the 
primary caregiver and the mother the primary breadwinner.

Elizabeth Kolbert’s book, The Sixth Extinction, is an explo

the disappearance of species in the present day. This powerful 
book lends credence to Bowen’s prediction of man being “on 
a collision course with his environment.”(Bowen 1978, 272) 
In the 600 million year history of living species, mass 
extinctions have only occurred five times, triggered by natural 
catastrophes. Rather than a background hum of species vanish
ing while others evolve, mass extinctions eliminate significant 
proportions of the world’s species in a rapid amount of time. In those periods, conditions change so drastically that evolu
tion, operating through the survival of the fittest, is no longer 
the primary ingredient of survival. In these catastrophic, but 
rare, periods, large groups of living creatures are eliminated, 
never to reappear. Making the case that our present era is one of 
these times, she cites as evidence that one-third of reef-building 
corals, a third of all fresh-water mollusks, a third of sharks 
and rays, a quarter of all mammals, a fifth of all reptiles, and 
a sixth of all birds are headed toward extinction (16). For the 
first time, extinction is triggered by a living species—mankind. Extinction, as a term, was coined near the end of the 18th 
century by Georges Cuvier, after doing a careful study of fossil 
bones at the Paris Museum of Natural History.

Extinction, as a term, was coined near the end of the 18th 
century by Georges Cuvier, after doing a careful study of fossil 
bones at the Paris Museum of Natural History. Prior to that 
time, the general belief was that all animals were created fully 
formed and immutable. Cuvier first examined the remains of 
a giant mastodon that had been found in Ohio. After study
ing several other species, he concluded that the collection of 
bones was from another era in which the animals had died 
out. He proposed a new concept of lost species, a group of spe
cies that had existed previously and then became extinct. He 
gave a groundbreaking lecture on “the species of elephants, 


 185	
	
  	
        Family Systems	
	
                     2016
both living and fossil” (33) in which he succeeded in estab
lishing extinction as a fact. Fossils dug up in the countryside 
flooded his museum, allowing many other extinct species to 
be identified. Cuvier was not a believer in evolution. Instead, 
he thought the creatures he was identifying were wiped out 
by a catastrophe of a scale unknown in his time (33-46). Charles Lyell, a young geologist at the time Cuvier was 
developing his theories on extinction based on catastrophic 
events, came up with quite a different explanation.
