text:
Charles Lyell, a young geologist at the time Cuvier was 
developing his theories on extinction based on catastrophic 
events, came up with quite a different explanation. Observing 
his native England and volcanic islands near Naples, he con
cluded that changes in the landscape were based on gradual 
changes, such as erosion, volcanic activity, or sedimentation 
that could be observed in the present. He also believed that 
changes in species came about gradually. His book, Principles 
of Geology, became one of the primary reference books for 
Charles Darwin on his five-year voyage on the HMS Beagle. Darwin believed that his observations of the natural world 
during the voyage confirmed Lyell’s ideas of gradualism (48-
51). One biographer claimed,  “Without Lyell there would have 
been no Darwin.” (53)
Yet Lyell, like Cuvier, drew a distinction between gradual 
changes in geologic properties and those in living species, 
adamantly opposing the concept of transmutation in which 
species changed to better adapt to their environment. Dar
win began to document that living creatures, like geologic 
formations, slowly changed over time. His theory of natural 
selection spoke to how species were created as well as to how 
they died out. Darwin wrote: “The appearance of new forms 
and the disappearance of old forms were bound together.” 
(54)  Speaking from the gradualist framework, he maintained 
that the disappearance of a species was so slow that it was 
unobservable.

text:
Darwin’s view that extinctions were gradual was proved 
wrong during his lifetime when the last of the great auks per
ished. This bird, once ranging from Norway to Newfoundland 
and numbering in the millions, was particularly vulnerable to 
human hunting. While it could swim at great speed, it nested 
on shore, allowing it to be easily slaughtered by seaman look
ing for provisions on long voyages. The last auk was killed 
in 1844. However, Darwin, viewing mankind as one of the 


 186	
	
  	
        Family Systems	
	
                     2016
competitors in natural selection, saw this sudden extinction 
of a species as an aspect of the survival of the fittest (Darwin 
[1859] 1964, 65-69). Cuvier’s proposal that cataclysmic events were responsible 
for mass extinctions received verification when the abrupt 
changes in life at the end of the Cretaceous period (also known 
as the K-T extinction) sixty-five million years ago were better 
understood. In the geologic record, the K-T event is marked 
by a thin layer of sediment that can be found throughout the 
world in marine and terrestrial rocks. This layer of clay shows 
high levels of the metal, iridium , which is rare in the Earth’s 
crust but abundant in asteroids. Proposed by a team of scien
tists led by Luis Alvarez,  the K–T extinction is now believed 
to have been triggered by a massive comet/asteroid impact 
and its catastrophic effects on the global environment.

periods of gradual change, interrupted by sudden extinctions 
of species created by extreme natural events. At the end of the 
Ordovician period, 444 million years ago, the oceans receded 
and eighty-five percent of marine species vanished. The cur
rent theory is that this extinction was created by glaciations, 
resulting in CO2 levels dropping, temperatures falling, and 
the ocean’s chemistry changing. (102) What triggered these 
changes still remains a mystery. The Permian extinction (252 million years ago) also seems 
to have been ushered in by a change in climate produced by a 
massive release of carbon into the atmosphere. Temperatures 
soared. The seas warmed as much as eighteen degrees and 
became acidified for perhaps 200,000 years. This period was 
so devastating that it killed off all the creatures in the oceans 
and most of the creatures on land (103). What then of our current epoch of extinction which humans 
have ushered in since the last Ice Age twelve thousand years

What then of our current epoch of extinction which humans 
have ushered in since the last Ice Age twelve thousand years 
ago? Named the Anthropocene by Paul Crutzen, a Dutch  chemist 


 187

                     2016
and Nobel laureate, this is a geological epoch dominated by the 
impact of human activity on the planet, including deforesta
tion, the extinction of species, the changes in the atmosphere, 
and  the acidification of the oceans (107-109). The rest of Kolbert’s book documents how human activ
ity is profoundly and forever altering the composition of liv
ing species on Earth. One example is the acidification of the 
oceans. When water and air come into contact in the oceans, 
which cover seventy percent of the Earth’s surface, gases from 
the air are absorbed by the water and gases from the ocean 
are released into the atmosphere. As human activity such as 
factory pollution have changed the atmosphere’s composition 
through greenhouse gases and CO2, more carbon is absorbed 
by the oceans, which become acidified, resulting in the oceans 
becoming thirty percent more acidified than in 1800. Acidifi
cation alters the availability of key nutrients such as iron and 
nitrogen and changes the amount of light that passes through 
the water. Highly tolerant organisms such as tiny plankton will 
become abundant, while overall diversity in ocean life will be 
lost.

become abundant, while overall diversity in ocean life will be

seven pounds of carbon into the sea.” (114) Although some sea 
creatures thrive with this change, others do not. Acidification 
of the ocean played a key role in two of the five major extinc

impact on coral reefs. Corals, which are composed of billions 
of polyps belonging to a hundred different species, engage in 
vast communal building over generations by adding to the 
exoskeleton of the reef. Thousands of species have coevolved 
over millions of years around the reefs. These elaborate eco
logical niches are sensitive to the warming and acidification of 
the oceans. Scientists predict that “reefs will be the first major 
ecosystem to become ecologically extinct.” (130)
Another example is global warming. Although global 
warming is often thought to have a great impact on Arctic 
environments, it may have a greater impact on the tropics. As 
one travels across the ecosystems from the poles to the equator, 
the number of species exponentially increases as the climate 
warms (150).

manipulate the environment in ways the Neanderthals never

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The term paradigm has come to be used more loosely than 
it was in Thomas Kuhn’s influential book, The Structure of Sci
entific Revolutions, first published in 1962. I think, however, that 
it has been useful in understanding the gap that exists between 
what has been described as an individual paradigm and a 
natural systems paradigm in the study of human behavior. Kuhn used the term to describe the communities of scien
tists or practitioners attracted to transformative ideas which led 
them away from the predominant modes of scientific under
standing and inquiry of the time. New paradigms generally 
emerge when a sufficient number of discrepancies or anomalies 
arise which cannot be explained within the predominant para
digm. He added that the new paradigm “was sufficiently open 
ended to leave all sorts of problems for the redefined group of 
practitioners to resolve.” (2012, 11) New paradigms, then, are 
seen as opening up and defining new arenas for practice and 
research. Though Kuhn principally referred to the physical 
sciences, his view of the normal process of science has been 
applied to the social and life sciences as well. Fifty years ago the first publication of the family systems 
theory developed by Murray Bowen was published (Bowen 
1966).

I don’t believe it is an exaggeration to say that the “fam
ily movement” represented a change in paradigms from the 
conventional individual perspective. While Bowen was interested in the clinical application of 
a new way of thinking, he was principally interested in the 
potential the observation of the family had in moving toward 
a science of human behavior (Kerr 1997). He studied psycho
analytic theory in the hopes it could move toward science, but 
he came to the conclusion that the underlying assumptions in 
psychoanalytic theory would not allow it. Among the many 
assumptions he questioned were that emotional illness resulted 
from maternal deprivation, or that emotional illness was unique 
to the human and a product of socialization processes. The facts 
that the same mothers raised well-functioning children or that 
emotional illness could be found in all cultures and in other 
species raised more questions for him. His NIMH study led to 
his observation that the family functions as a unit and laid the 
groundwork for a new theory of human behavior.

paradigm in the mental health field, but it has remained a part 
of the broader individual paradigm. Biological psychiatry prin

the medical model and cause and effect thinking. The broader 
individual paradigm may also include psychoanalytic theory 
and its derivative formulations, such as attachment theory, as 
well as a rich confluence of other perspectives. It would seem that Bowen theory represents a paradigm 
in the formal sense of the term. A theory and a paradigm are 
not the same. A new paradigm may be based on a new theory, 
as the theory itself may represent a new way of thinking. One 
way of describing this is that the paradigm based on Bowen 
theory represents a natural systems view of human behavior 
and that Bowen theory is a formal theory of one natural sys
tem, the human family. Kuhn wrote that paradigms consist of 
communities of scholars, investigators, and practitioners who 
attend the same conferences, share papers, define the problems 
to be addressed, and train future practitioners. Bowen theory 
can be seen as representing a paradigm, but theories of other 
natural systems might also develop within this paradigm. Though knowledge can be shared across paradigms, there 
are inevitable “translation problems” in a new way of think

translate the new way of thinking. The same behavior is viewed 
through different “lenses.” A central aspect of paradigms is 
that they entail unquestioned belief systems and assumptions 
which guide the research and its interpretations (Hand 2015; 
Kuhn 2012). The belief systems become institutionalized and 
determine training, hiring, research, and funding. Interdisci
plinary work is commonplace in the broader fields of science, 
though it generally occurs within particular paradigms. The proposition, for example, that the family functions as 
an emotional unit is accepted by practitioners seeing families 
using a Bowen theory perspective. To one grounded in an 
individual paradigm, however, the family is generally seen as 
a social or cultural group—a collection of individuals. Shared 
underlying assumptions and beliefs about behavior make the 
translation to a family unit way of thinking difficult to grasp. The institutionalization of beliefs in a shared paradigm creates 
obstacles to the exploration of a newer paradigm.

obstacles to the exploration of a newer paradigm. Kuhn referred 
to this as the “incommensurability” that can exist between 
proponents of different paradigms. This does not mean that 
knowledge or thinking cannot be shared across paradigms. The recognition of different ways of thinking, however, is 
important to the discussion. According to Kuhn, paradigms are vital to the process of 
science. They provide a structured vehicle for the exploration 
of complex phenomena and a certain unity of perspective 
necessary for a community of scholars, researchers, and prac
titioners to function within. Newer paradigms emerge when 
the limits of a predominant paradigm become apparent. This 
occurred in the middle of the twentieth century with respect 
to psychoanalytic theory when increasing questions about 
whether it was scientific arose. The family systems theory developed by Murray Bowen 
represents a transformative view of human behavior and an 
open ended conceptual framework offering a wide horizon of 
phenomena to be explored, both of which qualify the theory as 
a new paradigm. A community of scholars and practitioners has 
slowly developed, witnessed by professional meetings, training 
programs, and publications. As its subtitle suggests, the journal

ing and knowledge relevant to a natural systems paradigm.

LEARNING FROM THE NURSES’ NOTES FOR 
BOWEN’S 1954-1959 NIMH PROJECT:  
A WINDOW INTO THE DEVELOPMENT OF THEORY
Catherine M. Rakow, MSW
From 1954 to 1959, the nurses in ward 3E—of the NIMH 
Clinical Center building, in Bethesda, MD—kept detailed 
notes of psychiatric patient behavior based on twenty-four 
hour observations. These ward nurses played an integral 
role in Dr. Murray Bowen’s research into human family 
behavior. Their notes are now archived in the National 
Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD.1 This paper analyzes 
the notes for August 1955, offering a unique window into 
the nurses’ practices of objective observation and disciplined 
psychiatric care, while also showing us their contribution to 
Bowen’s process of developing what would eventually become 
his theory of the family as an emotional system. Key words: Bowen NIMH research, Bowen theory, family 
emotional system, reciprocal functioning, concept of the 
triangle, family psychotherapy, milieu therapy, psychiatric 
nurses’ observations, emotional neutrality
INTRODUCTION
Dr. Murray Bowen’s seminal research at NIMH, from 1954 
to 1959, was an effort to test clinically the theory of human 
family functioning he had begun developing during his ten 
prior years of study and research at the Menninger Foundation 
in Topeka, Kansas.

The difference on this project was the application of 
these nursing practices to multiple family members. In this paper’s analysis of the nurses’ detailed notes the 
reader has the opportunity, figuratively speaking, to be on the 
ward with those nurses, seeing what they saw at NIMH as 
they participated in this historic development of a new theory 
about the human family. It also allows present day nurses to 
reclaim the historically significant contribution made by the 
nursing profession to Bowen family systems theory. Early Research at Menninger 
From 1946 until 1954, Dr. Murray Bowen was first a psychi
atric resident then a staff member at the Menninger Foundation. While there, he pursued his own interest in making Freudian 
theory more scientific, designed investigations to further this 
quest, gathered clinical observations, and studied the literature 
from numerous fields of science and human inquiry. One out
come of these explorations was the recognition that Freudian 
theory did not account well for what he was observing clini
cally and  what he was learning from the other sciences. This 
left Bowen with a dilemma: Should he try to make the facts 
fit the existing psychoanalytic theory, or should he step into 
the unknown with the facts? Choosing the latter, he began to 
formulate concepts and hypotheses about human functioning 
that eventually formed the basis of his natural systems theory.

During these studies, one process that Bowen and his team 
noted was the patient’s intense focus on the therapist. This 
focus on the other appeared to interfere with the patient’s abil
ity to attend to her or his own goals, or what is called “self.” 
In prior presentations of my research over the years, I have 
referred to this phenomenon—which Bowen himself never 
named—as “eyes on the other.”
Another observation made by the nursing staff at Men
ninger—from their mothering position in relation to the 
patient—was what Bowen eventually called “forcing mother
ing,” including its effects on the patient’s capacity to recover 
(Bowen 1995, 26). Bowen observed that no progress could 
be made if he or the nurses (as the parent substitutes) moved 
toward the patient by encouraging him or her to grow up; nor 
could progress be made if they, as the parental figures, moved 
away, withdrawing emotional support and threatening the 
loss of the relationship. That is, even when patients were able 
to resolve or “regressed below” their symptoms, psychosis 
would return if the nursing staff either moved toward their 
patients with over-helpful urging or enthusiasm, or withdrew 
emotionally (Bowen 1995, 25-26). This observation led to the 
principle that attention and treatment would be made avail
able but not carried out until the patient explicitly asked for 
it. In other words, some forms of being helpful turned out to 
be unhelpful.

be unhelpful. To ameliorate the tendency for “eyes on the other” and

condition whereby the patient found it possible to attend to 
his or her own goals for growth. The difficulties nurses had

This 
differed from the then current understanding of the mother, 
especially maternal deprivation, as the cause of the schizo
phrenia. Bowen’s observations and investigations supported 
his contention that it was excessive love, not deprivation of 
love, that kept mother and child intensely focused on each 
other. Though such maternal love was certainly appropriate 
at particular, earlier developmental stages, it was insufficient 
and counterproductive for independent functioning of either 
mother or child into adulthood (Bowen, 1995, 32). And nei
ther mother nor child knew how to extricate self. In short, 
schizophrenia could be seen as a manifestation of an intense 
interdependent relationship. Based on this view, Bowen’s NIMH project in December 
1954 was initially titled, “Influence of the Early Mother-Child 
Relationship in the Later Development of Schizophrenia.” 
(Bowen, 1954, 1). Bowen stated that the project’s goal was to 
“check the belief that [the] presence of the mother is beneficial 
to the treatment of schizophrenia.” (Bowen 1954, 1). Four months into the project, Bowen’s developing view 
of schizophrenia was
...not [as] a clinical entity unto itself, but rather one of the 
more severe symptom complexes in a long continuum, 
and one that encompasses almost every experience in 
human living, [and that] when we have understood 
schizophrenia, we will have understood mankind.

By the end of 1955, a hypothesis change is evident in the 
year-end summary report where Bowen notes that he now 
sees schizophrenia as a symptom of a disturbed family that is 
concentrated in one member (Bowen 1955b). To study his initial hypothesis, Bowen decided to hospital
ize not just the identified patient but also the primary caregiver 
or parent. While he might have considered different parent/
offspring configurations, he initially chose mother/daughter 
pairs because they could be accommodated by the available 
ward space (Bowen 1972). For his NIMH project, that was the 
all-female ward, 3E, in the Clinical Center building that was 
part of the NIMH campus located in Bethesda, MD. From 
March 1955 on, with rare exceptions, the project used the entire 
ward. Nurses were crucial to the collection of data that led to 
the essential observation—in the first year—that the family 
is an emotional unit, thus supplying the missing element for 
the new theory. In the first year, the mother-daughter pairs were not hospi
talized in the usual, more restricted sense, but rather mothers 
agreed to spend as much time on the ward as possible. It was 
not the intensity of schizophrenic symptoms that was selected 
for but a positive symbiosis (Bowen et al. 1957). Positive indi
cated that parent and child could weather prolonged contact 
with one another.

It was expected that if the environment could provide these 
necessary conditions, the natural growth process that exists in 
all humans would kick in and that such change from within 
the family would be longer lasting. This initial hypothesis was 
operationalized for the NIMH project and became an integral 
part of the NIMH ward environment. The Key Roles of Nursing Observation and Provision of Care 
As co-contributors in Bowen’s NIMH research project, 
the ward nurses were asked to function in ways that were 
consistent with their professional training and orientation, yet 
with an emphasis on that key quality of neutrality that Bowen 
identified at Menninger. That is, Bowen modified the nursing 
practices of observation, managing self, and patient care with 
the desired outcome of improved functioning within the family. Observation and objectivity are generally considered 
essential for nursing practice. The difference for the NIMH 
project was that the unit of study was the family, not the indi
vidual, and this required a paradigm shift in what and how 


139	
	
  	
          Family Systems	
	
                     2016
the nurses observed. In addition, the project staff, including 
nurses, was not to use psychiatric jargon to interpret perceived 
behavior. Rather, observers were simply to record what could 
be seen and heard in the behavior of the family members as 
they interacted with one another and with staff. Even staff 
attitudes were of particular importance.

Even staff 
attitudes were of particular importance. For example, though 
the intense attachment in the mother-child relationship was 
seen as an arrest in the ordinary course of development, the 
milieu was designed so that the attachment would resolve and 
move to mature growth. Seeing that attachment as pathologi
cal, rather than as a necessary developmental stage, would 
have established a different, counterproductive emotional 
atmosphere. All of these elements were considered essential 
for valid observational data collection. This research project 
has not yet been integrated into nursing history. To draw from a 1963 definition of nursing practice that 
would have been current at the time of the NIMH project, 
nursing’s 
...distinctive function is to give close and individual 
service to the patient, performing for him what he 
cannot do for himself, giving supportive care, physical 
and emotional, to bring him through dependence to 
self-directed activity, towards his own health.” (Reiter 
and Kakosh 1974, 15) 
In Bowen’s research, the nurses were asked to function 
with the usual goal of promoting health yet not to be the fam
ily’s caretakers, per se, but to assist the family in solving its 
own problems and challenges. In particular, Bowen asked that 
nurses leave to each family any nursing functions that family 
members could perform themselves.

By 1957, a nascent understanding beyond 
NIMH of the potential benefits of studying families is given 
by Lidz,3 Hotchkiss and Greenblatt. Relatives are thus often regarded as a serious problem 
to contend with, rather than a welcome opportunity 
to extend the orbit of the hospital’s usefulness deeper 
into the family structure, and an opportunity to observe 
intrafamilial influences that require modification or 
correction. (Lidz, Hotchkiss, and Greenblatt 1957, 537)
The expectation of the nurses’ working on their own 
functioning and being participant observers was unique to 
Bowen’s project and in contrast to his peers’ view of nursing. Jordan Scher4 defined the functions of a nurse as meeting the 
patient’s needs and improving patient functioning/commu
nication and social participation. Scher says the relationship 
between patient and nurse goes through the specific activity 
requested rather than direct nurse-patient relating of self, one 
to another, in contrast to the doctor whose efforts go toward 
increasing this capacity of the patient while maintaining that 
capacity for self (Scher 1955, 309). The nurses did not passively go along with Bowen’s 
wishes and do as they were told. There were on-going, daily, 
discussions of responsibility regarding ward management 
and practices. The nurses were part of the decision making for 
ward operations.

Out of five years’ worth of archival materials generated 
by Dr. Bowen’s NIMH research project, I chose August 1955

into the project and the idea of the family as a unit, while not 
yet explicitly hypothesized, was emerging. And it was in this 
month that the family/staff meeting was established, which I 
will describe later in this paper. In August, there were two mother-daughter pairs being 
observed on Bowen’s research ward: the B family and the C 
family. (The A family was on leave from the hospital for the 
summer.) While an analysis of both the B and C family was 
done for this month, I decided to focus primarily on the nurses’ 
notes for the B family to further narrow the scope of analysis 
for this paper. The C family was a local family; the mother 
had younger children at home, and there was a transit strike 
that impeded her ability to spend extensive time on the ward.

(Nursing Unit Report August 18, 1955) She no longer carried

The behaviors and interactions observed during August 
1955 were not unique to the B family. Similar dynamics were 
seen with the other two families. At times, all three daughters 
appeared more mature than their mothers did, but none could 
sustain that level of functioning. It was only sustained when 
their mothers’ functioning had declined. By August 1955, Bowen was referring to the family unit as 
the object of study. And just four months after these nurses’ 
notes, he began to implement this extension of his hypothesis to 
include father, mother, and impaired offspring. On December 
28, 1955, Mrs. D and Daughter D arrived, and on December 
30, 1955, Mr. D came as a transfer from another psychiatric 
hospital where he had been treated for depression. From that 
point on, all parents were required to live on the ward. The 
subsequent families all showed the same patterns seen in the 
first three mother/daughter pairs but having the fathers living 
on the ward made it possible to see the intensity more clearly 
within the nuclear family, with less transfer of upset to staff, 
further substantiating the first year’s findings. The Genesis of Family Psychotherapy
During this same period of time, August 1955 to January 
1956, Bowen introduced the family-staff group meeting. He 
implemented this in response to the degree of anxiety and 
discord being transferred from family to staff.

I started my NIMH research in 1954 after having worked 
with psychotherapy and families a number of yrs. in 
Topeka. By 1955 I had conceptualized the family as an 
“emotional unit,” following which it was conceptually 
accurate to do psychotherapy with the entire family. At 
the time I had never heard of family therapy. (Bowen 
1986, 1)
Bowen used the term family psychotherapy to describe the 
research ward meetings, and he may be the first professional 
to use this term publicly (Bowen, 1956b, 6). It was in March 
1957 at the Annual Meeting of the American Orthopsychiat
ric Association in Chicago, that researchers from around the 
country openly discussed family therapy. ...the first national meeting for psychiatrists doing 
family research. It was a section meeting at the annual 
meeting of the American Orthopsychiatric Association... All the papers were on family research. ...I believe this 
was the first time (family therapy) was discussed as a 
definite method at a national meeting. That was the 
beginning of family therapy on a national level. (Bowen 
1978, 287-288) 
With the admission of the first father, mother, multiple 
offspring family in January 1956, the nurses now were charged 
with keeping notes on mother, father, impaired offspring, and 
sibling. Over time the nurses’ notes align with the conceptual 
framework giving evidence of implementation in staff.

Here I have only skimmed the surface of 
support for concepts such as triangles, differentiation, anxiety 
transfer, and reciprocal functioning and have given indica
tions of the shift underway to the seminal understanding of 
the family as a unit. The organism of the family unit, in ever 
changing interaction with its self and its environment, resides 
in these notes. The incipient idea of the father’s involvement 
and the systemic elements of the living family can be seen in 
only one month’s data. The pulse of the challenges to the staff 
to think differently is there. August 1955 is ten months into Dr. Bowen’s research effort, and only one month of the fifty months 
the project continued. The richness in these notes reveals Dr. Bowen’s foresight in believing that the human can be a sci
entific being. That idea, along with the mingling of human 
behavior with other animals, is still considered radical. The 
paradigm shift required to think that the human is a part of 
the process of evolution is outside the accepted beliefs within 
psychiatry. For now, the observations that the family system 
influences autonomy and interdependence remains a softening 
barrier to questioning and acceptance of Bowen theory by other 
researchers in the sciences. From the edges of the universe 
to the living systems within the human body, solid evidence 
exists about the dependence on functioning systems for the 
continuance of all existence.

macro level going back to the work of Copernicus and Darwin, 
and interactive systems are found at the micro level of biolo

Family Systems Journal Vol. 12.1
Title: Bonding and Babies: The Evolution Of Biparental
Author: Donley
Pages: 7-26

7
BONDING AND BABIES:
THE EVOLUTION OF BIPARENTAL CARE
AND THE PRIMARY TRIANGLE
Margaret G. Donley, MSW
In a broad sense, the human family is less a product of culture 
and more a product of forces that led to the development of 
pair bonds and biparental care. The co-occurrence of pair 
bonding and biparental care evolved under conditions in 
which additional parental involvement was required to 
ensure successful rearing of young. Although the female brain has deeply embedded maternal 
circuits to prepare females to care for infants, paternal 
behavior evolved through different mechanisms. More 
recent research suggests that male care of the young is often 
motivated through mating and cohabitation with a female. This has led to questioning the “paternity investment 
hypothesis” in favor of a perspective that examines male-
female interaction as a key ingredient to understanding 
paternal care. The involvement of the father in the care of 
the young sets the stage for the establishment of the mother-
father-child triangle, often referred to in Bowen theory as 
the primary triangle. The evolutionary roots of the primary 
triangle are based in the way pair bonding and biparental 
care are interconnected.

The triangle between self and parents is the most

a person develops the triangle relationship patterns 
that remain relatively fixed in all relationships. (Bowen 
1978, 531)
Understanding the evolutionary underpinnings of the 
human family can be daunting to family therapists who have 
spent their careers immersed in the social sciences. The prob
lems presented in clinical sessions often seem removed from 
the neurobiological aspects that live beneath the surface of 
what binds people together.

The prob

the neurobiological aspects that live beneath the surface of 
what binds people together. Yet nothing could be further 
from the truth. Indeed, the research coming from the natu
ral sciences can offer clinicians a useful perspective on how

love, to have children, and to live in family units. This paper

and children form the essential architecture of the human 
family.1 Although the human family may be more complex, 
we are by no means unique in our ability to form long-lasting 
pair bonds and to raise offspring in a family unit. Nonhuman 
mammals that form monogamous pair bonds demonstrate 
equally intense selective attachments, exhibit biparental 
care, and live in family units. Undoubtedly, the mechanisms 
underlying the emotional dimensions of parenting have

However, 
when the tension mounts between two individuals and cannot 
be contained, others become involved through triangles to 
manage the mounting anxiety. The concept of the triangle 
is based on the observation that a relationship between two 
individuals is inherently unstable and easily disturbed by 
the forces within and outside of it (Bowen 1978). This basic 
concept in Bowen theory provides a broad theoretical guide 
to understanding how anxiety is managed within a living 
system—from a group of cells to a troupe of primates. When 
the triangling process occurs within the nuclear family it is 
often referred to as the primary triangle. The connection of pair 
bonding and biparental care sets the stage for uncovering the 
evolutionary roots of the primary triangle in the family. For 
example, if the equilibrium in the parental pair bond can no 
longer sustain both people’s comfort, a disturbance emerges 
that creates a relationship shift. Disruptions in the balance of 
a relationship can trigger anxiety, leading one person to seek 
more togetherness to restore comfort. If the togetherness pull 
becomes too constraining or demanding, the other person will 
automatically react by distancing and moving towards another 
person to ease the relationship pressure. Pulling in a third 
person to manage the tension and anxiety in a relationship 
helps stabilize the system (Kerr and Bowen 1988).

bond can become strained and infrequent. Not surprisingly, 
male and female sexualities are organized differently in the 
brain (Panksepp 1998). Oxytocin, an important neuropeptide 
that influences receptivity in women, is built on affiliation 
and bonding, which is in short supply as anxiety and tension 
increase in a marriage. As men become frustrated and upset 
by their wives’ lack of affection, they are more likely to become 
angry, resentful, and withdrawn. In this state, men are less 
likely to provide what women need most—emotional support 
and help with childrearing—and women are less likely to be 
affectionate and show an interest in their husbands. More
over, sexual activity that helps promote pair bonding and male 
investment (Panksepp 1998) all too often diminishes, leading 
to a further disruption in the relationship. Research suggests 
that married women who are stressed are less interested in 
sex compared to married men who are stressed (Bodenmann

to cooperate and be a resource to each other, tend to propel

overinvolved at work, using substances, and/or having affairs. His emotional disengagement is an important component in 
the problem. Another way the primary triangle can unfold is if the 
father works to avoid any conflict with the wife by going 
along with and supporting her focus on the child. He adopts 
a “peace at any price” posture and compromises his beliefs 
to relieve the anxiety of the moment. (Bowen 1978, 63) The 
father is careful not to voice disagreement and tries to “help” 
his wife by being compliant. His need to keep her happy and 
not upset her enables him to be calmer. The primary trian
gle still operates with the father focused on the wife to keep 
harmony, while the mother is focused on the child. All the 
while, through pathways in the primary triangle, the anxiety 
shifts around within the system, thus preventing any one rela
tionship from overheating (Kerr and Bowen 1988). The primary triangle affects parenting so automatically 
it is often hard to see it in action. More often than not, the 
mother is the gatekeeper to the children and thus has subtle 
ways of promoting or constraining the father’s involvement 
with the children.

More often than not, the 
mother is the gatekeeper to the children and thus has subtle 
ways of promoting or constraining the father’s involvement 
with the children. The most consistent predictor of a father’s 
engagement with their children is the quality of the marriage 
(Belsky et al. 1984, Feldman et al. 1983), and marital conflict 
frequently results in men withdrawing from their children and 
their spouses (Christensen and Heavey 1990). The impact of 
the marriage on a father’s involvement with his children (De 
Luccie 1995) sets the stage for the way fathers respond to their 
children based on the emotional state of the marriage and/or 
the cues they receive from their wives. Mothers who have a 
positive view of their marriage tend to see their husbands as 
involved fathers, further highlighting the way that the pair 
bond influences parenting. How this triangling process operates in families can be 
simply illustrated through the following scenario. A father 
comes home from work and finds his wife upset with the 
children. His sensitivity to his wife’s unhappiness with the 
children impels him to immediately punish them for upsetting

between maternal and paternal care. However, how intense 
this pattern becomes is based on the level of differentiation 
of self and the degree to which relationships govern the 
emotional functioning of the parents. Understanding the evolution of the primary triangle has 
far-reaching implications for how a clinician thinks about the 
problems that couples present in therapy. Couples that seek 
therapy all too often define themselves as having “problem
atic communication and lack of emotional affection.” (Doss 
et al. 2004, 410) What is often missed is an understanding of 
how the primary triangle is influencing the marital relation
ship. More often than not, the children (his, hers, or theirs) are 
part of the equation in subtle yet substantial ways in what, 
at first glance, appears to be a “marital problem.” The focus 
that women direct toward their children often comes at the 
expense of the marriage, and the focus that men direct toward 
their wives often comes at the expense of paternal involve
ment. The problems that develop in marriages are not driven 
by these gender differences and they exist in most families to 
some degree.

psychological and social mechanisms underlying parent

paternal care evolved reflects the differences between males 
and females and suggests predictable ways that the primary

FACULTY CASE CONFERENCE
The faculty case conference is held monthly at the Bowen 
Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference 
from their clinical practices. The conference is not intended 
as supervision or as a meeting to arrive at a consensus about 
how to manage a specific case. It is intended as a learning 
experience for the faculty and to keep them aware of one 
another’s general approach to clinical problems. DEFINING A SELF IN MULTIPLE RELATIONSHIPS
Randall T. Frost, MDiv
This case provides evidence that the way a young woman 
has functioned with several partners, friends, and at work, 
duplicated her position in relatively fixed patterns of 
functioning in the primary triangle with her parents and in 
several interlocking triangles in her family. Over a four-year 
period, as the young woman was gradually able to define more 
of a self in the triangles of her family, she began to modify her 
functioning in these other important relationships as well. The woman got more clarity about a career path, enrolled in 
a challenging postsecondary program, and actively pursued 
other goals important to her. Changes in the functioning of 
her parents and paternal grandmother also took place over 
the four-year period. Her younger brother came in for four 
individual sessions during her first year of counseling.

BRAINWASHED: THE SEDUCTIVE APPEAL
OF MINDLESS NEUROSCIENCE
By Sally Satel and Scott O. Lilienfeld
reviewed by Roberta Gilbert , MD
Brainwashed, the Seductive Appeal of Mindless Neuroscience, 
has been named a finalist for the Los Angeles Times Book 
Prize. And well it should. Here we have an understandable 
review of what brain science is and what it is capable of. As well—and refreshingly—we see many of its limitations. This book balances much of the superficial enthusiasm for 
neuroscience and brain imaging reported in the press, litera
ture, medical writing, and even the courtroom, with a more 
thoughtful approach.

The book begins with an overview of fMRI, explaining 
how the brain works and is researched. This explanation gives 
the reader an appreciation for the awesome complexity of the 
brain and its functions. At the same time, we begin to see how 
thoughts, motivation, and emotional content can scarcely be 
inferred from imaging alone, although many will tell you it’s 
possible. Neuromarketers claim they can discern what people really 
think about products and advertisements more accurately 
from these images than from verbal reports. The authors cast 
a great deal of doubt on this. Those in the field of addiction have used neuroimaging to 
“prove” that addiction is a “brain disease.” Satel and Lilienfeld, 
however, point out that there are many factors contributing to 
addictive behavior and plead for a much broader understand
ing of the issue. They note that “if the brain were the core of 
the problem, it would need to be part of the solution...” 
Clinically, the reality is just the opposite. Dr. Satel—with 
her many years in the field of addiction—states firmly that 
the most effective interventions aim not at the brain but at 
the person and their story of how the addiction developed, 
how and why it continued, and how they managed to stop 
the cycle.

predetermine human behavior? Can it shed light on design
ing social policy? Can the human be said to have free will? These and many other intriguing questions are considered in 
Brainwashed, but the authors predict that, in the end, no matter 
how dazzling the fruits of inquiry or how clever the means 
by which they are obtained, it is our values that will guide us 
in implementing them for good or for bad. The danger lies in 
muddling those values under the pretense of following where 
neuroscience supposedly leads us. To some neuroscientists and philosophers you may be 
nothing more than your brain. ...But to you, you are a 
“self,” and to others you are a person—a person whose 
brain affords, at once, the capacity for decisions, the 
ability to study how decisions happen, and the wisdom 
to weigh the responsibilities and freedoms that these 
decisions make possible. (154)

roadmap for the beginnings of a new science of the self, show

BOOK REVIEW
 DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF:
BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS PERSPECTIVES
Peter Titelman, Editor
Reviewed by David S. Hargrove, PhD
It could be said that differentiation of self is the driving force 
in the application of Bowen family systems theory. It is criti
cally important in attempts to put the theory into practice. It is 
also at the heart of Bowen’s theoretical formulations because it 
defines the all-important relationship between the individual 
self and the systems of which the individual is a part. The enormous contribution Murray Bowen made was to 
define the system of relationships as the determining factor 
in the functioning of the human. Humans function within 
systems of relationships like most other species. This postula
tion is in contrast to the traditional view that human behavior 
is motivated by internal forces, either physiological or psycho
logical. Freud’s theoretical concept of the ego, id, and superego is 
one example of internal processes that have long been thought 
to be the primary determinants of behavior.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
One of the more interesting and challenging questions 
raised in the neurosciences is how to account for the emer
gence of consciousness. And with regards to what may be 
unique to the human, how did an awareness of conscious
ness emerge? The longstanding mind/body dichotomy has 
gradually been dissolving under the weight of evidence, but 
nailing down the neurophysiological processes accounting for 
self-awareness continues to be explored. There is increasing 
acceptance that consciousness and the awareness of conscious
ness are based in the physical brain and body, but can the 
awareness of being conscious develop apart from a social 
context? This last question may not be possible to answer, 
but it does raise the question about the extent to which our 
social brains require interactions with others for the elaborate 
ability to observe self develops. Knowledge regarding how much of human behavior and 
decision making occurs outside the realm of awareness has 
also been one of the great areas of discovery. This effort is not 
new, of course. For millennia, humans have sought to under
stand both the dark and heroic behavior of individuals and 
also what might contribute to health and illness. Unseen forces 
from the gods to chemicals were believed to account for the 
behavior of individuals.

Title: Family, Self, and the Intermix of Emotional
Author: Noone
Pages: 27-50

27
FAMILY, SELF, AND THE INTERMIX OF EMOTIONAL 
AND INTELLECTUAL FUNCTIONING
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The capacity to observe to some degree one’s feelings and 
emotional functioning and to consciously use reasoning 
and logic in managing one’s life is a recent evolutionary 
development. While the evolution of the cerebral cortex has 
been central to this function, the degree to which it can be 
utilized is reliant on the maturation of a self that is embedded 
in complex interactional processes occurring in automatic, 
subcortical, bodily, and family functioning over the course 
of development. The evolution of the cerebral cortex in the 
mammalian line occurred in the context of increasingly 
prolonged and engaged parental care and, in the human, 
involved the co-evolution of the reproductive unit of the 
family emotional system. Bowen theory posits that the family 
emotional system shapes individual development. This is seen 
as principally manifested in the degree to which individuals 
develop the capacity to use higher cortical functions in 
regulating the automatic emotional system or what Bowen 
referred to as the intermix of one’s emotional and intellectual 
functioning.

And, as Edelman suggests, an understanding of the 
brain and its functioning in relation to behavior requires an 
understanding of its evolution and individual development. The family systems theory developed by Murray Bowen 
(1978) posits that the family is the principal context for shap
ing development and generating individual differences in 
basic adaptiveness. Family interactions influence the degree 
to which offspring mature or emotionally separate from their 
parental caretakers. The concept of differentiation of self was 
developed by Bowen to account for how individuals vary in 
the level of emotional autonomy they attain by adulthood and 
entails what he described as the differentiation of the intel
lectual system. It is a developmental process which optimally 
allows the human to utilize higher cortical functions in regu
lating self and directing one’s life course. This process occurs 
in the context of the family emotional system over the course 
of development and over multiple generations, resulting in 
variation in the intermix of emotional and intellectual functioning 
found among individuals. Since the original development of Bowen theory, a wide 
body of research has emerged which is shedding light on 
higher brain functions which contribute to the capacity of 
individuals to effectively manage self in responding to life 
challenges.

The Human Brain and Self-Regulation
Basic to all life is the challenge of maintaining a stable 
internal environment in relation to an ever-changing exter

and brains, the earliest forms of life required the ability to 
sense their environment in order to adapt and survive in a 
changing environment. Bacterial colonies, for example, can 
be observed to sense the environment and pick up chemical 
signals through receptors which allow them to move toward 
sources of nutrition and avoid toxins (Ben-Jacob et al. 2011). Although unaided by a nervous system, they nevertheless 
have the ability to integrate information about the environ
ment, store it, and respond adaptively. The evolution of life on earth involves a history of increas
ingly complex forms of life and ever more complex means 
of self-regulation. In multicellular organisms the differentia
tion of cells and organ systems evolved to allow for greater 
efficiency and flexibility in interacting with the environ
ment.

to self-regulate. In all brained animals, from invertebrates to 
humans, these functions are largely automatic and result

interactions with the environment during development and

Genetic and developmental processes specify the

stable internal temperature in the face of environmental shifts 
in temperature is metabolically expensive and required an

allowed for a wider range of responsiveness to the environment, 
it also involved an increased ability to regulate an organism’s 
multiple internal systems. As Antonio Damasio points out in 
discussing neurons:
...neurons exist for the benefit of all the other cells in the 
body. Neurons are not essential for the basic life process, 
as all those living creatures that have no neurons at all 
easily demonstrate. But in complicated creatures with 
many cells, neurons assist the multicellular body proper 
with the management of life. (2010, 38)
At a very basic level, then, brains can be said to have 
evolved to assist in the management of life. The brain is contin
uously encoding information it is receiving about the internal

text:
The brain, of course, is a part of the body and not sepa
rate. Its processing of information does not occur in isolation, 
but is colored by the host of body and subcortical systems 
with which it is highly integrated. And the brain is not only 
physically embodied, it is intricately embedded in the environ
ment in which it develops and interacts. Damasio beautifully 
captures this process:
Life and the conditions that are integral to it—the 
irrepressible mandate to survive and the complicated 
business of managing survival in an organism, with 
one cell or with trillions—were the root cause of the 
emergence and evolution of brains, the most elaborate 
management devices assembled by evolution, as well 
as the root cause of everything that followed from the 
development of ever more elaborate brains, inside ever 
more elaborate bodies, living in ever more complex 
environments. (2010, 60)
The emergence and evolution of ever more complex 
management devices led to increasing levels of plasticity in 
the capacity of organisms to self-regulate and respond to envi
ronmental stimuli. These automatic processes long preceded 
consciousness and are amazingly elaborate. Still conserved by 
natural selection, they continue to underlie the most sophis
ticated manifestations of human existence, shaping our lives 
and behavior more extensively than we are generally aware of.

The later evolved heightened capacity for cognition, enabled 
by the expanded neocortex and its elaborate prefrontal cortex 
(PFC), remains intricately embedded in the earlier evolved 
emotional systems. One of the clearest examples of the degree to which higher 
cortical systems such as the PFC remain embedded in older 
and more automatic regulatory systems is that of the stress 
response system. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) and 
the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system (HPA) are acti
vated in response to perceived internal or external threats and 


32

designed to upregulate and downregulate the physiological 
systems needed to respond (fight, flight, or freeze). Given 
the primacy of survival, these evolutionarily older systems 
take precedence in the face of threat. Jaak Panksepp describes 
this priority:
...our higher brain areas are not immune to the 
subcortical influences we share with other creatures. Of course, the interchange between cognitive and 
emotional processes is one of reciprocal control, but 
the flow of traffic remains balanced only in nonstressful 
circumstances. In emotional turmoil, the upward 
influences of subcortical emotional circuits on the 
higher reaches of the brain are stronger than the top 
down controls.

and in limbic systems such as the thalamus and amygdala. Further, these systems don’t simply relay information; their 
processing is influenced by previous experience and by the 
hormonal and autonomic nervous systems to which they 
are connected. Though the PFC may not sit as a detached execu

the potential for some cognitive influence over a large 
variety of cortical and subcortical systems (Arnsten 
2009, Fuster 2013). The prefrontal cortex—which
sits at the front of the neocortex and makes up almost a third 
of the cortex (Elston 2003)—represents the area of greatest 
expansion in hominid evolution. And not only did the size of 
this area increase dramatically, the complexity of the neurons 
and their synaptic connections did as well (Elston 2003).

The human brain retains from evolution, as a matter of

human brain, in addition, has become pre-adaptive. (2013, 24)
While remaining integrated with and influenced by the

an individual the ability to reflect on one’s self-in-the-envi

and making projections into the future—and to have some 
choice in behaviorally responding to one’s context. Being 
conscious of our consciousness may be a uniquely human 
characteristic. But, while the evolution of the neocortex has 
endowed the human with an increased capacity to regulate 
one’s functioning, the principal evolutionary context in which 
it evolved—the family—also entailed an increase in the degree 
to which the thinking, feeling, and behavior of individuals can 
be co-regulated. As John Cacioppo and William Patrick write:
The primary task of every organism in nature is to

The rapid expansion of the brain found in Homo sapiens

able. With over 30 billion neurons in our neocortex alone and 
more than a million billion interactive connections between 
these cells (Edelman 2006), it represents a quantum leap in 
complexity from that of our nearest living primate relative, 
the chimpanzee. A number of factors have been cited as to how the human 
brain evolved in such a brief evolutionary period. For the 
human, the social environment is central. It has been suggested 
that the rapid expansion of the neocortex during evolution was 
selected for the advantage it provided in adapting to the social 
complexity within and between large clans (Dunbar 2002). The 
development of the brain occurs during a prolonged period of 
dependency within the family. For most of human evolution, 
this development took place in large extended families and 
involved multiple caretakers for infants and a wide range of 
social interactions for the developing child.

The co-evolution of the family and the 
brain, building on the maternal/offspring attachments of our 
mammalian ancestors, involved profound adaptations in the 
hominid biology (Flinn, Ward, and Noone 2005). Neuroscien

regulation” (2011, 281) between caregiver and infant, states:
The caregiver becomes part of a complex feedback 
system supporting the biological and behavioral needs 
of the infant. Within this model of symbiotic regulation, 
the caregiver is not solely giving to the infant. The 
behaviors of the infant also trigger specific physiological 
processes (e.g., neural and endocrine feedback circuits) 
that help establish strong bonds, provide emotional 
comfort for the caretaker, stimulate neural pathways, 
and support the health of the caregiver. (281)
Over the course of hominid evolution, neuroendo
crine processes regulating mother-infant involvement were 
expanded to other relationships to include the interdepen
dent attachments observable in the human family. The increase 
in responsiveness among family members to one another 
increased the influence the family unit had on development 
and the functioning of its members. Heightened interde
pendence observed in the family includes not only higher 
cortical systems but other neuroendocrine systems as well.

systems can vary in the level of their integration and the degree 
to which regulatory processes are centralized. Such processes 
are generally bi-directional and the components reciprocally 
influential. The human brain would be an example of neural 
systems influencing each other, with no one system directing 
brain functioning. Likewise, an ant colony regulates the func
tioning of its members, but it is the interactions of individuals, 
not any top/down controls, which determine the functioning 
and morphology of its members (Gordon 2010). From this perspective, the family and brain development

nid evolution and are central to the capacity of individuals to 
successfully navigate through the social complexity of human 
life.

their environment.

of the human family as a highly integrated, self-regulating 
system and the principal environment that influences brain 
development and behavior. Its evolution represents a new 
level of complexity that shapes variability in “the intermix of 
emotional and intellectual functioning” among offspring and 
their basic adaptiveness in life. Individuals can be observed to vary in their capacity to 
respond to stressful situations effectively over their lifetimes. The brain and its development are key factors in determin
ing this capacity. Bowen theory posits that the family is 
central in shaping differentiation of self which affects the 
degree to which offspring emotionally separate from the 
family unit and the differentiation of the individual’s intel
lectual system. Over the course of multiple generations, this 
process leads to significant variation in the basic adaptiveness
of individuals.❉

Title: Marriage Preparation Programs and Bowen Family Systems Theory
Author: Riordan

69
BRIEF REPORT
MARRIAGE PREPARATION PROGRAMS
AND BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY
Kathleen F. Riordan, MSW
This article provides background information on marriage 
preparation programs and describes a unique interview 
format with engaged couples guided by Bowen family 
systems theory alongside traditional marriage preparation 
inventories. The unique format includes a review of 
individual and family functional facts and family emotional 
process. It also presents an opportunity for the pair to 
look beyond the courtship to early marriage. The author 
finds this combined methodology significantly broadens 
and enhances the more typical approach used in marriage 
preparation programs. BACKGROUND
For many years now churches, synagogues, and other faith 
based organizations have sponsored marriage preparation 
programs. One of the earliest examples of church sponsored 
programs would be the Catholic Church’s Pre Cana program. The program name is a reference from the biblical story in John 
2: 1-12 of the wedding at Cana. More about this program can 
be found at foryourmarriage.org. 1975 saw the enactment of the Family Law Act (FLA) 
and no-fault divorce. Both made it easier to obtain a divorce, 
resulting in a subsequent uptick in the frequency of divorce.

PREPARATION PROGRAMS
Many traditional marriage preparation programs 
sponsored by faith-based organizations utilize marriage 
preparation inventories to identify potential problem areas 
in engaged couple relationships. Two of the more commonly 
used instruments are PREPARE (Pre-Marital Preparation and 
Relationship Enhancements) and FOCCUS (Facilitating Open 
Couple Communication, Understanding, and Study). In the 
FOCCUS Facilitator Manual, this instrument is described as
...a self-diagnostic inventory designed to help couples 
learn more about themselves and their unique 
relationship...not as a test nor as a predictor of success 
or failure in marriage but as a tool to help couples name 
and work through issues before marriage. (1997)
Responses to the inventory are calculated according to matches 
and differences. This results in a percent of agreement in each 
category between the two individuals. Low agreement in any 
category is viewed as potentially problematic and points to 
the need for further discussion with a facilitator.

Over the past twenty years the author, a Bowen family 
systems therapist, has interviewed hundreds of engaged 
couples as part of a church sponsored marriage preparation 
program. In the early steps of the prescribed ten-step program, 
couples complete the required marriage preparation inventory 
and schedule two consultations with the therapist. The therapist is aware that the individuals being inter
viewed are presenting at a particular time and developmental 
stage. The courtship stage has predictable steps such as meet
ing, becoming attracted, dating exclusively, possibly living 
together, becoming engaged, and planning marriage. Individ
uals arrive at each of these stages following the earlier years 
of development in their families. That earlier developmental 
period ultimately goes toward shaping an individual’s way 
of functioning, and the way they automatically relate in the 
present. The participating couples—mostly in their twenties 
and thirties—have often completed formal education and may 
have realized or still may be clarifying a specific career path. At the time of their engagement, they may have accumulated 
significant personal or educational debt, been underwritten 
by family, or built more adequate financial resources allow
ing them an associated degree of independence.

In the two required interviews, the therapist focuses on 
three tasks: (1) developing a family diagram to learn functional 
facts and clarifying the emotional process of each individual 
and their family system, (2) reviewing the responses to the 
marriage preparation inventory items and, (3) putting together 
feedback for the church marriage preparation coordinator. At the first interview, three-generational family diagrams 
are drawn. The family diagram is a way to learn about the 
functional facts of individuals and families. Functional facts 
include birthdate, education, health, and professional work 
history. For this population the therapist also includes what 
the individuals enjoy when not working and facts about earlier 
serious relationships. Constructing the family diagram with 
each individual in the pair brings forward a broad picture of 
the two family systems. This exercise highlights the context 
each individual grew up in through their respective years of 
relating with parents and family members. The process of 
constructing the diagrams provides evidence of how knowl
edgeable individuals are regarding their families. The exercise 
also hints at how familiar or not the partner is with the facts 
of the other’s family.

CONCLUSION
Murray Bowen writes “The beginning of a nuclear 
family...is a marriage. ...The two spouses begin a marriage 
with lifestyle patterns and levels of differentiation develope
din their families of origin. (1978, 376) Bowen held that people 
marry individuals at their same level of differentiation and 
Bowen theory’s way of accounting for this is based on the 
variation in levels of differentiation and chronic anxiety. Michael Kerr writes, “People select mates at the same level 
of differentiation.” (1988,171) Bowen theory does not say indi
viduals select partners with same level of chronic anxiety. But 
it does hold that higher levels of differentiation are accompa
nied by lower levels of chronic anxiety and convesely lower 
levels of differentiation reflect higher levels of chronic anxiety. (1988, 115-117)

often repeat through generations. This brief report reflects the author’s work in progress

FROM THE ARCHIVES
A special feature of Family Systems is a previously unpublished 
manuscript by Murray Bowen and other researchers in the 
family field. Since the manuscripts reflect the thinking of the 
authors at the time they were written, they are introduced 
with comments to place them in historical context. Dr. Bowen’s 
manuscripts have been selected from a large archive of written 
records that are preserved at the National Library of Medicine. FROM THE ARCHIVES
A LETTER FROM MURRAY BOWEN
ABOUT LEWIS HILL
Murray Bowen, MD
Introduction by Ruth Riley Sagar, MA
This 1972 letter from Dr. Bowen to a person he was supervising 
sheds light on the importance of funerals in the life of a 
family. In this letter he talks about Dr. Lewis Hill, the last 
of three “father figures” who had a profound influence on 
his professional development after they both arrived at the 
National Institute of Mental Health in 1954. With the 
letter, Dr. Bowen also enclosed the funeral address by Dr. Sarah Tower, a moving tribute to Lewis Hill as a person, 
as a teacher, and as a pioneer in building psychoanalysis 
in the Baltimore-Washington area. A striking feature of the 
eulogy was the deep respect and affection she conveyed for 
her analyst and also the pervasive influence of psychoanalysis 
as Dr. Bowen began the final year of his five-year historic 
Family Study Project.

Dear BC:
I liked your obituary for Arlie. Just to really “be there” for the 
whole funeral and preparations for it, was an act that will be much 
appreciated by the family. To get the courage to “talk” puts you in 
a class by yourself. Also found an extra copy of the funeral address by Dr. Sarah 
Tower for Lewis Hill. Sometime I will tell you the story of how 
Lewis Hill was my last “father figure.” There are many details. I did a “cutoff” with my own father and then, in psychiatry, had 
two great “father figures.” The first was Karl Menninger, which 
still holds to a degree. That was terminated in a tearful parting in 
the Spring of 1954 before I moved to NIMH (National Institute 
of Mental Health). Lewis Hill, the exact age of Dr. Karl, was the 
analyst emeritus of the Washington-Baltimore area. He was trying 
to cut down on the hard work, and began a consultantship at NIMH 
to begin to “learn something again” and to do something different. He arrived in July 1954, at the same time I did, and he became my 
consultant.

and listened. He knew everything and everybody in psychoanaly
sis, and at that time I was still crusading for PSA1. He’d been 
President of the American PSA Association back in the late 1930s 
and was the only living person who held membership in BOTH 
the Washington and Baltimore PSA Societies. Lewis somehow 
gave me the courage of my convictions. I’d get a new idea, but I 
would be reluctant to “buck the tide of professional opinion” that 
would oppose. Lewis somehow could ask the questions that would 
cause me to dare to do what seemed so difficult. When I would hit 
a crossroads of decision making, I’d call Lewis to “talk.” Then I 
would hit the trail to Sheppard Pratt and we’d sit in his study in the 
big house on campus now occupied by Larry Kubie. Lewis never 
gave advice or did a direct suggestion about what to do. Often his 
most powerful question would come as I was leaving.

Reba Hill and Lewis, his son, have asked me to speak at 
these services, for myself, about what Lewis meant to me. This I 
am glad to do. But I wish less to speak about what Lewis meant to 
me than about how he came to have meaning. I remember vividly, 
with the quality of the morning light, the hour towards the end of 
the first year of analysis when the notion of the analyst as catalyst 
came to me, as it has come, I am sure, to thousands of analysands 
in many rooms. There is a fallacy in that analogy, but from it has 
come, in time, the concept of analysis as process, which I now 
teach, and the concept of teaching as process which I now prac
tice. I speak of the process of enablement. Whether as therapist or 
teacher, it is, I believe, as enabler that Lewis Hill is chiefly being 
remembered by us here today. One of his colleagues at the Na
tional Institute of Mental Health described it last evening: “Lewis 
didn’t often answer your questions. It was his questions that count
ed. And especially the questions he put in the last few moments as 
he was going out the door.” This struck me. 154	
	
  	
          Family Systems	
	
                     2017
	
I had, of course, been meditating on endings. This one, 
with death, but also the ending of an analysis. After the abatement 
of hate, the renunciation of revenge, the enablement of grievings 
long overdue, the setting free from the past, then the enablement of 
grief for the separation in process.

of hate, the renunciation of revenge, the enablement of grievings 
long overdue, the setting free from the past, then the enablement of 
grief for the separation in process. The acceptance of the real and 
present loss of the analyst, and the turning elsewhere. I had been 
considering, also the sequence of weanings, which is life. The way 
growth weans our children from their infancy and we, their moth
ers and fathers, with them. The painful longing for just one more 
baby to stave off that weaning. And birth, as it closes one phase 
and opens another for two persons. And so on to death which we 
are now faced with, and the painful longing for a few more mo
ments, the looking back. It is understandable that people may 
expect that the one who has died is now entering a new life, though 
for many of us here our reason tells us that this is not necessarily 
so. What is clear is what we are here for. To look back, to consider 
our loss and mourn, and so to accept the separation in due course 
to turn elsewhere. Our challenge is to use this separation as Lewis 
would have used it, for enablement, to enlarge our perceptions, to 
reflect on the uses and limitations of reason, to enjoy the conta
gious excitement of an idea, and even to play with it with the gift 
of words and the illumination of humor. And to put some questions 
going out the door. Vol. 12, No.

The faculty case conference is held monthly at the Bowen 
Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference

Joan Jurkowski, MS
This clinical case was presented at a faculty case conference 
in May 2017. Identifying data have been altered to ensure 
confidentiality. The case is a description of how anxiety is 
managed in a nuclear family after a series of difficult life 
events. The theory posits that under increased anxiety, spouses 
manage tension in one of several ways. These are: conflict 
in the marriage, projection onto a child, and distance and/or 
dysfunction in a spouse.

WITHIN-FAMILY VARIABILITY:
THE FAMILY PROJECTION PROCESS 
IN AN ADOPTED FAMILY
Laura Brooks, MSW
The Adoptive Family Study (AFS) is a longitudinal, 
qualitative, prospective study of eight adoptive families. This 
paper uses a long-term case study design of one participant 
family composed of a mother, father, and their four children, 
two by adoption and two by birth. The family was recruited 
from a private adoption organization. Observations of the 
family were made over the first thirteen years of the study, 
with data collected in annual interviews with the couple in 
their home. Annual updates of changes in the three generation 
family included discussion of each child’s adjustment. Transcripts of the interviews were coded from the perspective 
of the family projection process, a key concept in Bowen family 
systems theory that describes the process in which parents 
project their anxiety onto a child. This process contributes to 
a child’s vulnerability to anxiety and dysfunction. Keywords: within-family variability, adoptive families, 
family projection process, adoption, Bowen theory, 
multigenerational emotional process
INTRODUCTION
Although exhaustive research has been done on why chil
dren in the same family turn out differently, little is known 
about within-family variability from a systems perspective.

text:
In contrast to the prevailing individual viewpoint of exist
ing research, Bowen theory broadens the lens to a view of the 
family as a system of relationships that has regulatory effects 
on the functioning of the offspring (Bowen 1978). The effect 
varies depending on the intensity of the family projection 
process—the degree to which the parents project their anxi
eties onto the children. In this process, the mother or father 
may be more tuned into one of their children. The child’s 
gender and birth order, the level of anxiety in the marriage, 
the extended family relationships at the time of the child’s 
birth, or a view of the child as special in some way, all may 
contribute to a mother’s heightened sensitivity to one of her 
children. This child focus may inhibit the child’s development 
towards higher levels of emotional autonomy and responsible 
functioning (Bowen 1978 and Kerr 2008). From this systems 
viewpoint, the Adoptive Family Study (AFS) explores how the 
family projection process—an indicator of emotional involve
ment driven more by parental anxiety than the reality needs 
of the child—contributes to differences in the functioning of 
children, whether by adoption or birth, in the same family. LITERATURE REVIEW

in how children in the same family experience shared family

Environmental Influences
In 1987, a seminal and comprehensive review of studies 
that used quantitative behavioral genetic methods, non-genetic 
influences such as differential parenting, extra-familial expe
riences, and possibly luck, were synthesized, resulting in a 
conclusion that two children in the same family can be as 
different from one another as are pairs of children selected 
randomly from the population (Plomin and Daniels 1987 and 
Plomin et al. 2001). In other words, family influences are not 
determined by the family environment, but by each specific 
child’s experience of the environment (Plomin and Daniels 
1987). Studies of twins, adopted children, and birth children 
were included in the review. Plomin challenged researchers to 
identify the relevant family experiences specific to each child 
in the family that contributed to differential outcomes (2001). Conley (2004) examined three national sets of social and 
economic data and conducted in-depth interviews with 175 
individuals from 68 families longitudinally.

He hospital
ized several families with a psychotic adult child for up to 
three years, observing the differences in how parents variably 
projected their immaturities onto their children. In this way, 
children in the same family had different experiences. The more the adults in the family projected their anxi
ety onto a child, the more anxiety that child absorbed. This 
affected their capacity to self-regulate or, as Bowen described it, 
to “differentiate a self.” (1978, 366) Bowen called this phenom
enon the family projection process that resulted in some children 
becoming more vulnerable to social, physiological, and psycho
logical symptoms than other children in the same family. Family projection exists in all families to some degree and 
represents one way that anxiety is managed. Parental anxiety 
takes many forms, but most commonly it can be observed in a 
preoccupation with a child, or being overly solicitous towards 
a child, doing things for the child that they can do themselves, 
and over-reacting to a child rather than responding realistically 
or objectively. In all forms, the anxiety begins with the mother 
and/or father and the child reciprocates as a full participant. To the extent that an individual absorbs the anxiety of 
others—that is, to the extent the individual is regulated by the 
expectations and reactions of others—that person will have 
less capacity to think and act autonomously for self.

overinvolvement, an additional stress in the mother’s life, for

level of differentiation than a child who receives less parental 
anxiety.

This 
study contributes a conceptual bridge to existing research 
conclusions that adoptive and birth parents make a difference 
in the life adjustment of their children. However, by moving 
from an analysis of the individual to the family system, the 
impact of the family projection process accounts for within-
family variability. It also establishes that, while being adopted 
is an important fact of a child’s history, the anxiety that flows 
from the parents to the child has more impact on the child’s 
development. To the degree that parents anxiously focus on a 
child, the child is vulnerable to dysfunction. Further studies will examine each parent’s parental trian
gles and how anxiety travels through a multigenerational 
emotional process that affects the nuclear family. Expanding 
the research to include extended family may further elucidate 
the relationship processes that shaped the parents’ responses 
to each other and to their children. Insights from this family 
may also assist in the development of programs to support 
adoptive families and meet the permanency needs of the 
adopted children. Limitations

alized to other families. However, it does afford a view of the 
persistence of family relationship patterns over time and how

BOOK REVIEW
MINDSET: THE NEW PSYCHOLOGY OF SUCCESS
by Carol S. Dweck
Reviewed by Margaret G. Donley, MSW
At first glance, the book Mindset by Carol Dweck appears 
to be a typical self-help book among the many that are avail
able in any bookstore. As is often the case with self-help books, 
Mindset puts an interesting spin on a subject that is far from 
nove—mainly that people vary in their ability to embrace 
challenges and to essentially turn lemons into lemonade. The 
author effectively explores this variation between people by 
focusing on the idea of “mindset,” which, she argues, often 
determines how a person approaches challenges and failures. She identifies two basic mindsets, the “growth mindset,” 
which enables a person to move toward challenges and to 
embrace failure as an opportunity for growth, and the “fixed 
mindset,” which leads a person to avoid challenges out of a 
fear of making a mistake and failing. Given her arguments, 
it is not hard to see that the former contributes to a focus on 
effort and learning, whereas a fixed mindset is more driven 
by the fear of how one is seen by others. Although the book is 
a bit redundant at times, the author does a nice job of weav
ing in a vast amount of research from a number of different 
areas, including parenting, business, leadership, school, and 
relationships.

An equally intriguing aspect of her research relates to 
motivation. A growth mindset tends to fuel motivation, in 
contrast to a fixed mindset where constant praise and encour
agement are required to maintain motivation. It is not hard to 
see how the central differences in these two mindsets relate to 
Bowen’s postulation of solid self versus pseudo self (Bowen 
1978). Like those with a fixed mindset, for example, people 
with less solid self have less energy for goal-directed activity, 
are more easily molded by others, and tend to lose motivation 
when they become uncomfortable (Kerr and Bowen 1988). Before reading this book, I had given little thought to how 
a child’s mindset could be a marker of the way anxiety in the 
parents gets projected onto their children (albeit to varying 
degrees depending on the child who receives the most focus). However, after finishing the book, I could not stop thinking 
about how a child’s mindset is clearly shaped by the family 
emotional process. Implicit in Dweck’s idea of fixed mindset 
is the way the child is emotionally constrained and especially 
sensitive to the expectations of the parents. As I reflected on 
this process, both in my own family and in my clinical work, 
it became increasing clear that a more fixed mindset in a child 
is the product of the way the parents’ chronic anxiety and 
emotional immaturity is projected onto the next generation 
and takes root in the brains of their children.
