and scientific grounding of Murray Bowen’s theory of human 
emotional functioning. Dr. Bowen never strayed from science 
and evolutionary theory as he built his theory and refined 
his clinical practice. During his lifetime he met with and 
talked to hundreds of scientists, but rarely found one willing 
to look beyond the individual to see the emotional system 


Vol. 12, No. 2                                    Book Review                                               183
and its phylogenetic origins. Dr. Noone and Dr. Papero have 
identified scientists whose research transcends the individ
ual view and looks more broadly at the interplay among 
individuals as they shape one another’s behavior within an 
emotional system. The Family Emotional System demonstrates Bowen theory as 
a cohesive whole, weaving together the concept of the family 
emotional system proposed by Bowen and then offering scien
tific research with a range of animal models documenting how 
emotional systems exist among animals and shape behavior. It 
moves Bowen theory closer to the accepted sciences and builds 
a bridge for future collaboration and research. ❉

BOOK REVIEW
MINDSET: THE NEW PSYCHOLOGY OF SUCCESS
by Carol S. Dweck
Reviewed by Margaret G. Donley, MSW
At first glance, the book Mindset by Carol Dweck appears 
to be a typical self-help book among the many that are avail
able in any bookstore. As is often the case with self-help books, 
Mindset puts an interesting spin on a subject that is far from 
nove—mainly that people vary in their ability to embrace 
challenges and to essentially turn lemons into lemonade. The 
author effectively explores this variation between people by 
focusing on the idea of “mindset,” which, she argues, often 
determines how a person approaches challenges and failures. She identifies two basic mindsets, the “growth mindset,” 
which enables a person to move toward challenges and to 
embrace failure as an opportunity for growth, and the “fixed 
mindset,” which leads a person to avoid challenges out of a 
fear of making a mistake and failing. Given her arguments, 
it is not hard to see that the former contributes to a focus on 
effort and learning, whereas a fixed mindset is more driven 
by the fear of how one is seen by others. Although the book is 
a bit redundant at times, the author does a nice job of weav
ing in a vast amount of research from a number of different 
areas, including parenting, business, leadership, school, and 
relationships.

FACULTY CASE CONFERENCE
The faculty case conference is held monthly at the Bowen 
Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference 
from their clinical practices. The conference is not intended 
as supervision or as a meeting to arrive at a consensus about 
how to manage a specific case. It is intended as a learning 
experience for the faculty and to keep them aware of one 
another’s general approach to clinical problems. ANXIETY AND THE NUCLEAR FAMILY SYSTEM
Joan Jurkowski, MS
This clinical case was presented at a faculty case conference 
in May 2017. Identifying data have been altered to ensure 
confidentiality. The case is a description of how anxiety is 
managed in a nuclear family after a series of difficult life 
events. The theory posits that under increased anxiety, spouses 
manage tension in one of several ways. These are: conflict 
in the marriage, projection onto a child, and distance and/or 
dysfunction in a spouse. The presenter describes how all these 
mechanisms played out in this case study, with the exception 
of marital conflict. The family’s functioning has stabilized over a four-year period. Anxiety decreased and relationships are more thoughtful. However, the focus of anxiety shifted to extended family 
members.

the nuclear family emotional system. In his book, Family Therapy in Clinical Practice, Dr. Bowen 
describes how anxiety in a family is managed:
Most spouses can have the closest and most open 
relationships in their adult lives during courtship. The fusion of the two pseudo-selfs into a common self 
occurs at the time they commit themselves to each other 
permanently... (1978, 377)
I have thought about how once people marry it is much 
more difficult to manage themselves with each other. Bowen 
discusses how one person becomes the dominant decision 
maker, and the other adapts. The dominant one gains self, and 
the adaptive one loses self. The problem is the fusion between 
the two that can cause anxiety. In a family, anxiety is managed 
in one of four ways: conflict, distance, dysfunction in a spouse, 
and projection onto a child. This family has a high level of 
tension, but the marriage seems so comfortable. BACKGROUND SUMMARY

I first saw him, he came in for symptoms of anxiety. He was 
also grieving for his father, who had died about six months 
before I met him. And his son had moved away a few months 
before I met him.

Title: FROM THE EDITOR
Author: Noone

99
FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The effort to understand the severe impairment of individ
uals led Murray Bowen to study the mother-child relationship 
in his research project at NIMH. The study, which lasted from 
1954 to 1959, initially involved mothers and adult daughters or 
sons living on the research ward. (Bowen 2013) Early on in the 
study, the intense, intertwined relationships between mothers 
and their adult children diagnosed with schizophrenia could 
be observed. This intensity was seen as a reciprocal process in 
which each could be seen as “living and acting and being for 
each other.” (Bowen 1978, 10) When it became clear that the 
process involved more than the mother-child dyad, fathers 
and siblings were invited to participate. Once the focus of study shifted from the individual to 
the family, a new order of observations not previously seen 
was possible. Most significant was the reciprocal influence 
the members had on the behavior of one another. An interac
tional focus in the study led to a shift from a view of behavior 
as intrapsychically driven to one of response patterns at play 
among family members. Bowen’s observation that the family functioned as a 
unit led to the discovery of stable and predictable patterns 
of behavior which operated outside the awareness of family 
members.

The title and subtitle of this journal reflect this perspec
tive. It is interesting to note that over recent decades “systems 
thinking” has developed in the study of natural systems at 
many levels, but that the study of the family as a natural 
system has been largely neglected. A systems view emerged 
in biology and other life sciences when it became evident that 
bi-directional processes are at play at all levels of complexity, 
from genes to cells to organ systems to social systems. Genes have been found to bi-directionally interact with 
the cellular and other environmental contexts.

Genes have been found to bi-directionally interact with 
the cellular and other environmental contexts. Knowledge 
of the degree to which cortical and subcortical systems are 
continuously interacting and influencing each other has been 
rapidly developing. The nervous, endocrine, and immune 
systems, once thought to be autonomous regulatory systems, 
are now known to be highly integrated and reciprocally influ
ential. Discoveries of the interactional processes of the stress 
response systems with higher cortical systems and the entire 
body, along with their implications for health and illness, have 
been astonishing. The effort to understand the complexity of social interac
tions among individuals has also resulted in the use of systems 
thinking. Complexity theory developed out of chaos theory 
with the objective of understanding complex systems. Initially 
it was principally comprised of investigators from the fields 
of mathematics, cybernetics, and economics. The effort to 
understand living systems led to the inclusion of evolution
ary theory which gave rise to development of the concept of 
complex adaptive systems, with a focus on understanding all 
natural systems. Complex systems are seen as having emerged 
through the increasing interdependence of their interacting 
components. It is based on the assumption that the functioning 
of wholes cannot be accounted for by simply understanding 
their parts and their interactions.

All of these rich areas of investigation, and others, utilize 
systems thinking and are contributing to a science of human 
behavior. And yet, given the universal centrality of the human 
family in the development of individuals, the focus on the 
family as a level of biological organiz ation is largely absent. While systems thinking is applied to levels of organization 
from genes to societies, the family as a unit is overlooked. The family as a natural system has yet to become a focus of 
study or even to be considered a focus of study in the life 
sciences. It would appear that in the study of natural systems, 
a leap from the individual to social groups occurs in all of the 
above mentioned fields of study. Family may be cited as an 
environmental or cultural factor influencing individual devel
opment or behavior, or the mother-child dyad may be a focus 
of study, but the functioning of the family system is generally 
overlooked. The question that arises, of course, is what contributes 
to this “blind spot” in the study of natural systems? Several 
factors come to mind as possible obstacles to viewing the 
family as a highly integrated, self-regulating system. One is 
simply its automaticity and proximity to experience.

determine whether or not there is support for this theory but, 
for the level of complexity involved in observing the family, 
a systems theory seems required. And finally, it is not surprising that the family systems 
theory developed by Bowen has been principally utilized in 
the clinical world. For those who have integrated this theory 
into their clinical work, the multigenerational family is the 
unit of study. It allows for the acquisition of data pertaining

knowledge related to the context of symptom development as

functioning and that of their families. For most, the appli
cation of the theory has involved an ongoing study of their 
own families. With a few exceptions, the use of Bowen theory has not

At a time when the study of emotion was largely neglected, Dr. Panksepp’s research focused on the brain mechanisms of emotional 
experience and motivational processes. He coined the term affective 
neuroscience, and his 1998 book of that title remains a central text in what 
is now the accepted study of emotion in humans and other mammals. He received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Pittsburgh and 
a master’s degree and doctorate from the University of Massachusetts. Dr. Panksepp joined the faculty at Bowling Green State University in 
1972, and his early research involved the study of how the brain influ
ences the desire for food, drink, and sleep. He later was recognized for 
work on autism and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder. At the time of his death, Dr. Panksepp was a Professor for the College 
of Veterinary Medicine at Washington State University in the Veterinary 
and Comparative Anatomy and Pharmacology and Physiology Depart
ment. Prior to his work at Washington State University, Dr. Panksepp 
taught at Bowling Green State University where he was a neuroscientist 
in the Psychology Department retiring in 1998. Dr. Panksepp was an important influence for many interested in the 
study of the family and Bowen theory. He participated in several confer
ences sponsored by the Bowen Center for the Study of the Family in 
Washington, DC as well as Bowen theory meetings in Chicago and 
Vancouver.

EMOTIONAL PROCESS IN SOCIETY:
A REVIEW AND EXPANSION OF THE CONCEPT
Katharine Gratwick Baker, PhD
Murray Bowen began thinking about human functioning 
in large nonfamily systems in the 1940s. Over the next 
thirty years, he returned many times to this subject in 
papers and presentations and, in 1974, he introduced the 
eighth concept—Emotional Process in Society (EPS)—in 
his family systems theory. Although Dr. Bowen did not 
fully flesh out the concept during his lifetime, others have 
continued to explore and expand it, relating it to the other 
concepts in the theory and to a broader understanding of 
large human social units. This article reviews Bowen’s 
original writing on EPS and offers specific examples of its 
interface with differentiation, triangles, projection, cutoff, 
and multigenerational family process. Key words: Bowen theory, progression and regression 
in societal process, differentiation, triangles, projection 
process, cutoff, multigenerational transmission process
INTRODUCTION
With the eighth concept in his theory, Murray Bowen 
began to develop a theory of human society as an emotional 
system. This concept, emotional process in society, led Bowen to 
observe and explore patterns in human social groups larger 
than the family as well as patterns in the human’s relationship 
to the larger natural environment over time.

In 1972, Bowen was invited by the newly formed Environ
mental Protection Agency to present a paper for a symposium 
on the environmental crisis of that period. Preparation for 
the symposium led him to develop a new concept that he 
first referred to as “societal regression” and later modified to 
become “emotional process in society.” With this concept, and 
through the application of systems thinking, Bowen began 
to develop a logical bridge between what he had described 
as “emotional process” in the human family and the same 
phenomenon in larger human social systems. Vol.13, No. 1             	
  Emotional Process in Society  	
	
         11
This author believes that the concept can best be described 
as an arena beyond the family, in which the other seven 
concepts from Bowen theory can also be observed. At the 
societal level Bowen observed differentiation—a continuum of 
variation in functioning—that is driven by anxiety, emotional 
triangles operating between and within social groups, emotional 
projection as an example of intense triangling, functioning 
position (a broader societal analogy to sibling position in fami
lies), a multigenerational, or historical, transmission process, 
and emotional cutoff between and within social groups. The 
nuclear family emotional process at the societal level could be 
described as patterns of overfunctioning and underfunction
ing, as well as closeness and distance, between and within 
social groups.

In 1973, Murray Bowen delivered a presentation enti
tled “Societal Regression” at the Annual Georgetown Family 
Symposium. Two years later, in 1975, he published a paper in 
a Symposium collection based on his 1973 presentation enti
tled “Emotional Process in Society.” Versions of this paper 
are included in his book of collected papers, Family Therapy in 
Clinical Practice (1978, Chapters 13 and 18). In these two chap
ters, Bowen articulated his primary definition and description 
of the eighth concept in his family systems theory. In Chapter 13 of Family Therapy in Clinical Practice (269-
282), “Societal Regression as Viewed Through Family Systems 
Theory,” Bowen reported on a presentation he delivered at 
the Nathan W. Ackerman Memorial Conference in Venezuela 
in February 1974. The major points in the chapter include a 
description of his early interest, beginning in the 1940s, in soci
etal issues and his slow extension of concepts about the family 
into larger social systems during the 1950s.

the other. As an example, he again noted that the triangling process 
in a family can parallel a similar process in society, with 
emotional tension spreading outward and interlocking with 
emotionally vulnerable others.

At the higher end of a societal scale of differentiation 
change is orderly and gradual; the generations are able 
to maintain some kind of viable emotional contact, 
working together to create continuities that are in the 
best interest of the society; this end of the scale reflects a 
balance of the forces of togetherness and individuality. At the lower end of scale, change is disruptive or 
violent; both generations can manifest distancing 
behaviors, such as blaming, separation, and denying 
the importance of the past; at this end of the scale 
distancing and cutoff behaviors occur in response to 
an intense togetherness force. (Baker 2003, 388)
The author also hypothesizes that “societies that have 
significant long-term cutoff between generations are vulner
able to a wide variety of health, social, and environmental 
problems.” (388-89) This hypothesis is confirmed in her single-
case study of Russia and the Soviet Union in the twentieth 
century (Baker 2003). There are multiple examples of cutoff and its emotional 
consequences in large social systems (See Gottlieb’s 2003 study 
of Holocaust survivors) as well as in smaller, less complex 
social systems, such as communities, schools, religious insti
tutions, and the workplace.

FROM THE ARCHIVES
A special feature of Family Systems is a previously unpublished 
manuscript by Murray Bowen and other researchers in the 
family field. Since the manuscripts reflect the thinking of the 
authors at the time they were written, they are introduced 
with comments to place them in historical context. Dr. Bowen’s 
manuscripts have been selected from a large archive of written 
records that are preserved at the National Library of Medicine. FROM THE ARCHIVES
A SYSTEMS VIEW OF THE AGING PROCESS
Murray Bowen, MD
Introduction by Ruth Riley Sagar, MA 
On October 14, 1976, the Georgetown University Family 
Center, under the auspices of the Department of Psychiatry, 
sponsored its first Conference on Aging within the Family 
and Society. It focused on the value of intergenerational 
contact and continuity across generations. The elderly person 
exists within the multigenerational family unit, and this unit 
exists within society. The speakers addressed the problem of the elderly person 
within the multigenerational family unit and the forces that 
promote cutoff between the generations—resulting in the 
disruption of individual and family functioning. Dr. Bowen 
was the first of several speakers who addressed aspects of the 
aging process in the context of the multigenerational family 
and the society of which it is a part.

The Bowen family systems theory is made up of eight 
separate theoretical concepts that have been presented in 
detail in other publications. All the concepts are important in 
understanding the details of the theory. Some are more impor
tant than others in understanding the broad aspects of the 
aging process. The following is a list of all the concepts with 
special emphasis on those most important in later life. 1. Differentiation of self
This concept provides a single dimension for understand

of human functioning. People have the quality of “fusing 
with,” or “being like” those about them.

People have the quality of “fusing 
with,” or “being like” those about them. Those with the most 
separateness of self, and who predictably operate with this 
separateness under all the varying degrees of stress and 
emotional tension, are said to be the most “differentiated.” 
Those with the least separateness of self who either fuse into 
the emotional environment about them, or who bristle and 
fight the emotional environment are the most “undifferenti
ated.” The most differentiated people who know what they 
believe and who they are, and who predictably stand on their 


50

convictions under emotional stress, are the most successful in 
life. They live orderly lives, they are the most productive at 
whatever they do, and they are remarkably free of physical, 
emotional, and social illness. The most undifferentiated people 
have the capacity of getting along in a simple, brief interper
sonal situation, but this automatic tendency to compromise 
self to relieve the anxiety of the moment results in long-term 
complications. People with the lowest levels of differentiation 
emerge as the liabilities of society, either being taken advan
tage of or taking advantage of others. A high percentage of the 
total human problem comes from a relatively small spectrum 
of people with the lowest levels of differentiation of self.

human problems include chronic physical illness, emotional 
illness, and the full spectrum of social illness such as misbe

their families and for society are those with lower levels of 
differentiation of self. Better differentiated elderly people 
have led orderly lives since childhood. When they are old 
they adapt to their increasing infirmities and they are able 
to remain as self supporting contributors to their families as 
long as they live. It is impossible to offer more than a brief overall descrip
tion of this concept in this presentation. The concept is so 
consistent from generation to generation, and within a genera
tion, that I originally presented it as the differentiation of self 
“scale” with broad outlines for comparing people with varying 
levels of differentiation of self. Professional people missed the 
functional variables involved in the concept and they began 
a narrow, concretistic effort to apply it in specific clinical 
situations. They were missing the degree to which a poorly 
differentiated person can “pretend” to be more or less differ
entiated than they really are.

8. Emotional Process in Society 
The same emotional process in a family is also present in 
the total of society. In stress, a family can regress from a 
more adaptive to a less adaptive form of adjustment or, in 
periods of calm, it can progress from a less adaptive to a 
more adaptive level. When society regresses, it influences the 
behavior and life style of a high percentage of families. It is 
the least differentiated who are most responsive to societal 
change. Since the early to mid 1960s, societal adaptation has 
had minor upswings with an overall course into a sizeable 
regression. Manifestations of the regression are an increase in 
segregation between the generations, the sexual revolution, 
the increase in crime, the inability of society to deal with 
crime, an increase in divorce, alcoholism and drug abuse, 
and increasing immorality in business and government.

emotional problems which is now being used in an increas
ing number of other family centers. The initial effort is directed 
at helping the cutoff family to work on establishing emotional 
contact with families of origin. Success at this depends on 
the family configuration, the intensity of the cutoff, and the 
emotional reactiveness of the generations to each other. In 
some, the families are so fragmented and isolated and the 
available family members so allergic to each other, that it is

produces tremendous yield for elderly people. It brings them 
into closer personal contact with their children, grandchil

physical disabilities, and the elderly are able to adapt to and 
live with their disabilities better than ever before. Once one 
segment of the family is seriously working toward a better 
personal relationship with the elderly, then other segments 
of the family begin to do the same thing. Even if the older 
person is in an institution, the increased personal contact 
with the family provides them with a new lease on life. There 
is even a dividend for the confused “senile” elderly person

decreases the confusion and provides more normal periods 
in which a personal relationship is possible and confusion is 
not as necessary as it formerly was. The biggest yield comes 
in families who otherwise would proceed to put the elderly 
into institutions and nursing homes. As the ability for personal 
relationships develops, there is often one child in the family 
who is willing to take the elderly person into their home or 
work out other living relationships that facilitate a better level 
of personal closeness.

Title: Women After All: Sex, Evolution, and the End of Male Supremacy
Author: Ferrera

BOOK REVIEW
WOMEN AFTER ALL: SEX, EVOLUTION, AND THE
END OF MALE SUPREMACY
Melvin Konner
Reviewed by Stephanie J. Ferrera, MSW
As the title of this book suggests, Melvin Konner has a 
point to make. He introduces it in his opening statement: “This 
is a book with a very simple argument: women are not equal 
to men; they are superior in many ways, and in most ways 
that will count in the future.” (3) Ways in which women are 
superior to men include being more pragmatic, caring, trust
worthy, reliable, and fair, being freer from distracting sexual 
impulses, and being less bigoted and violent than men. (4-5)
Citing Elizabeth Cady Stanton’s 1869 speech, Konner 
underscores her two basic points: that man and woman are 
different and that they complement each other. To this he adds 
a third point: that the ways in which women are different from 
and superior to men are the prime characteristics needed in 
positions of responsibility and leadership in today’s world. His use of generalizations in attributing certain character
istics to women and others to men is sure to spark reactions, 
but the reader who can put controversy aside and focus on the 
crux of Konner’s case will learn a great deal from this book.

Bowen focused on the human family, the foundation on which 
communities and societies are built. Men and women have always been equal in fundamental 
ways. They are equal in being half of the population, equal in 
intelligence, equal as human beings, and, Konner notes, were, 
for the most part, equal in social status in the hunter-gatherer 
era which is “most of human history.” (15) Yet, in the transition 
to the agrarian way of life, human relationships, including the 
relationship between the sexes, changed dramatically in the 
direction of increasing violence, stratification, and inequal
ity. How to account for this change is a central question. Both 
Konner and Bowen offer important perspectives. 92

                     2017
Focusing on the family, Bowen noted the natural comple
mentarity between male and female. The mother’s central 
role in reproduction and childrearing tend to make her the 
“emotional nucleus” around which the father and the family 
organize. While biologists have focused on the differences in 
reproductive roles and attendant conflicts of interest between 
the sexes, Bowen theory takes these differences as givens and 
focuses on the functional question: How do men and women 
live with and work out these differences? The answer encompasses the range of human emotional 
functioning, from anxious reactivity to thoughtful collabora
tion.

are mature enough to leave the den. Each parent finds a new 
mate the following year. The researchers initially chose twelve out of one hundred 
wild foxes that lived in individual cages on a fox farm to

aggressive as the others. The researchers were careful to avoid 
inbreeding. Within three generations, some of the pups were a little

ened by them. Considerable variation on a continuum, from 
tamer to aggressive, existed in this third generation, with the 
majority being aggressive. That ratio changed markedly over 
the next thirty to thirty-five generations of breeding for tame

As the title of this book suggests, Melvin Konner has a 
point to make. He introduces it in his opening statement: “This 
is a book with a very simple argument: women are not equal 
to men; they are superior in many ways, and in most ways 
that will count in the future.” (3) Ways in which women are 
superior to men include being more pragmatic, caring, trust
worthy, reliable, and fair, being freer from distracting sexual 
impulses, and being less bigoted and violent than men. (4-5)
Citing Elizabeth Cady Stanton’s 1869 speech, Konner 
underscores her two basic points: that man and woman are 
different and that they complement each other. To this he adds 
a third point: that the ways in which women are different from 
and superior to men are the prime characteristics needed in 
positions of responsibility and leadership in today’s world.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The effort to understand the severe impairment of individ
uals led Murray Bowen to study the mother-child relationship 
in his research project at NIMH. The study, which lasted from 
1954 to 1959, initially involved mothers and adult daughters or 
sons living on the research ward. (Bowen 2013) Early on in the 
study, the intense, intertwined relationships between mothers 
and their adult children diagnosed with schizophrenia could 
be observed. This intensity was seen as a reciprocal process in 
which each could be seen as “living and acting and being for 
each other.” (Bowen 1978, 10) When it became clear that the 
process involved more than the mother-child dyad, fathers 
and siblings were invited to participate. Once the focus of study shifted from the individual to 
the family, a new order of observations not previously seen 
was possible. Most significant was the reciprocal influence 
the members had on the behavior of one another. An interac
tional focus in the study led to a shift from a view of behavior 
as intrapsychically driven to one of response patterns at play 
among family members. Bowen’s observation that the family functioned as a 
unit led to the discovery of stable and predictable patterns 
of behavior which operated outside the awareness of family 
members.

How does one conceptualize an intra-family 
psyche? In 1955-56 we used a term for it that was later dropped 
because it was not completely satisfactory. Recently I have 
come back to it as a term that conveys, on a descriptive level, 
a fairly accurate notion of the concept. From the Archives | 149
It is the term UNDIFFERENTIATED FAMILY EGO MASS. According to the concept, certain children differentiate them
selves almost completely from the “family ego mass” with 
each developing a well-defined autonomous “self.” This is 
synonymous with our familiar concept of a “mature person” 
or a person with a strong ego. Especially important is their 
ability to function as contained emotional units. This person 
would marry a spouse with an equal level of ego development. They could be emotionally close without either one losing self 
or without the obliteration of ego boundaries between them
selves. Children who later become psychotic are examples 
of those who achieve the least differentiation of self. They 
function as extensions of the family ego mass. They might 
separate themselves from the family and function as depen
dent attachments to others who will guide and direct them. They might have so little “self” that they collapse in psychosis 
when they attempt to function autonomously. Children who 
later become parents of psychotic children are among those 
who achieve poor levels of differentiation of self.

Children who 
later become parents of psychotic children are among those 
who achieve poor levels of differentiation of self. They do 
not “grow away” from the “family ego mass.” Instead, after 
reaching physical maturation, they “tear” themselves away, 
maintaining a kind of pseudo-separateness from the family by 
means of angry rebellion or distant indifferent positivity. They 
function satisfactorily in business and intellectual pursuits, but 
when such a person marries a spouse with equally poor ego

because it is the theoretical basis from which the psychother

by the way the therapist views man and his struggles, and 
particularly by the therapist’s theoretical concept of the nature 
of the problem he is treating. For instance, a therapist who 
views the problem as a product of early maternal depriva
tion will think, be, and act differently than a therapist who 
sees the problem in another way. Whether this concept proves 
valid or profitable as a way of viewing family problems, it 
has been used as a thinking model for this method of family

intra-family psyche, or the “undifferentiated family ego mass” 
is an undifferentiated amalgamation of emotional selfs that 
occurs when these people with poorly defined ego boundaries

they are separate physical beings with some autonomy and

Now to a brief summary of family psychotherapy with a 
psychotic offspring. Functionally this child is “welded” into 
the ego gap between the parents and he functions there, as 
an ego “nothing,” to permit the parents to be an ego “some
thing” until the passing years and his own growth make this 
into an untenable resolution. As I see it, the phenomenon 
is no one’s fault and there is no malevolence or chicanery 
involved. Given this particular situation between the parents 
and a child, consciously or unconsciously conceived to fill this 
gap, the triadic union is consummated just as automatically 
as the force that causes the sunflower to always keep its face 
to the sun. It occurs in spite of conscious forces to oppose it, 
just as the alcoholic gets another drink in spite of conscious 


154 | Family Systems 13:2 2018

tioning of the triad is disrupted. There are powerful forces to 
restore triadic equilibrium as well as growth forces toward 
differentiation and separation. An example was a family 
with a withdrawn, psychotic daughter. After a year of family 
psychotherapy, the daughter became a vigorous aggressive 
participant in family life. This seemed to be a hopeful change 
but the change caused anxiety in the parents. They had her 
institutionalized and tranquilized.

FACULTY CASE CONFERENCE
The faculty case conference is held bi-monthly at the Bowen 
Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference 
from their clinical practices. The conference is not intended 
as supervision or as a meeting to arrive at a consensus about 
how to manage a specific case. It is intended as a learning 
experience for the faculty and to keep them aware of one 
another’s general approach to clinical problems. THE DIFFERENCE BOWEN THEORY MAKES IN CLINICAL 
PRACTICE: CHALLENGES AND CHOICES
Victoria Harrison, MA
This clinical case was presented at a faculty case conference 
in October 2017 after two months of family systems 
psychotherapy with a couple. It is an example of the difference 
it makes for a therapist to draw upon Bowen family systems 
theory to define for herself decisions and directions involved 
in the challenges of therapy practice. This presentation illustrates ways that family history 
and a family diagram help to understand and interrupt 
a common emotional process that persists in individual 
therapy—focus on the other as the problem. Defining the 
focus of therapy as “working on self” offers an alternative 
perspective that facilitates a shift from blaming each other 
toward understanding patterns of reacting that each brings to 
problems in the marriage.

tration of what Murray Bowen described so well in the GAP 
Report1 that compared the premises and practices of therapy 
based in psychoanalytic theory with those of family systems 
theory. Conventional therapy defines techniques based upon 
whether the symptoms occur in individuals or in relationships. One family of four, for example, might see six therapists. Each 
parent and each child might have an individual therapist. The 
couple might also see a therapist as a couple and the whole 
family might meet together with another therapist. Training 
in individual therapy would emphasize the importance of 
seeing one individual in the family and referring others to 
other therapists. Bowen family systems psychotherapy is based upon a 
radically different view. The family is an emotional unit that 
governs the biology and behavior of each member. Everyone 
plays a part when symptoms occur for any family member. Any symptom is a function of common factors. Levels of differ
entiation of self and degrees of chronic anxiety are central to 
development of symptoms in individuals and in relationship 
problems.

relationship, how those dilemmas are a product of their own 
reactivity, and what people can do to change those reactions. 1

STUDY OF WEIGHT LOSS AS A MODEL FOR CLINICAL 
RESEARCH: SHIFTS IN THE FAMILY SYSTEM, THE
SUBJECT’S FUNCTIONING, AND THE 
COURSE OF CLINICAL SYMPTOMS
Laura Havstad, PhD and 
Kathleen J. Sheffield, MS, MA, RD
Clinical sciences have not yet systematically tested the 
potential of Bowen family systems theory to understand and 
predict the course of a wide range of clinical symptoms. This 
is a progress report on the development and application of 
a reliable method to document the emotional impact of the 
family system on clinical subjects and the course of their 
symptoms over time. A systematic method of analyzing 
data from family evaluation interviews has been developed 
to track shifts in the family emotional system associated 
with weight loss in overweight and obese individuals. The 
method produces a timeline of shifts in the family system, 
shifts in the functioning and anxiety levels of subjects, and 
changes in subjects’ weight. Four studies are described that 
illustrate and support the development and use of the method. It is hoped that this framework will encourage the practice 
of tracking the family system as a variable in mainstream 
clinical research, especially in studies of the course of 
symptoms and treatment outcomes over time and across a 
broad range of clinical disorders.

After having spent thousands of hours sitting with 
families, it became increasingly impossible to see a 
single person without “seeing” his total family sitting 
like phantoms alongside him. (Bowen 1978, 152)
“Family system shifting in the background
Unobserved, its impact
Ubiquitous.”
—Laura Havstad, PhD
Clinical psychological science has not yet systematically 
tested the potential of Bowen family systems theory to under
stand and ultimately predict the course of a wide range of 
clinical symptoms in individual family members (Bowen 
1978). Neither has clinical science thought to systematically 
control for always-present family system effects in evaluating 
treatment outcomes.

Neither has clinical science thought to systematically 
control for always-present family system effects in evaluating 
treatment outcomes. Among the reasons for this may be the 
lack of a reliable and valid research method that satisfies the 
conventional criteria of scientific method to assess the family 
emotional system and its many variables as an integrated unit. This is a progress report on such a research method, which is 
being developed in a study of married women whose symp
toms of overweight and obesity went into remission as they 
successfully lost their excess weight. The method uses a family evaluation interview adapted 
to gather data about the impact of the family emotional 
system on the emotional functioning of the clinical subject 
and their weight change over time, focusing on the shifts that 
preceded successful weight loss and achievement of their 
goal weight. The analysis of the data from the family evalu
ation interview tracks the relationship in time between shifts 
in the family system, shifts in the research subjects’ anxiety and 
functioning levels—also known as functional levels of self—and 
shifts in the course of their symptom of overweight. This group of 
variables summarizes the complexity of how Bowen theory, 
when utilized in a framework for clinical research, captures how 
the emotional state of a family member and their symptoms 
shift together with variables of the relationship system.

the dynamic interdependence between family relationships 
and the subjects’ emotional functioning with the direction of 
change in their symptoms. Shift in the Family System and Change in Symptoms
The recognition of the concept of shift goes back to Murray 
Bowen’s early observations of the family emotional system in 
his landmark research from 1954 to 1959 at the National Insti
tute of Mental Health (NIMH). Bowen studied families with an 
adult schizophrenic child who lived in the hospital for round 
the clock observations. (Bowen 1978). While the term shift 
is not anywhere indexed in Bowen’s 1978 book of collected 
papers (Family Therapy and Clinical Practice), a search of the 
kindle edition of the book turns up 161 instances of the term 
shift. Bowen’s observation of anxiety shifting between family 
members, and how the patient’s symptoms changed as the 
anxiety shifted off the patient onto another family member, 
was basic to recognizing the family as an emotional unit. As 
the NIMH study project went on, it became possible to define 
how anxiety shifts among family members in nonrandom 
ways. Anxiety shifted from one to another in the family as a 
function of the automatic ways the family managed emotional 
discomfort. Automatic responses resulted in repetitive rela
tionship patterns between family members.

family member had more, the patient’s symptoms moderated. These observations formed the basis for family psychotherapy,

be regulated to a significant degree by the family emotional 
system. This will be referred to here as the clinical hypothesis 
from Bowen theory.

who had dieted all the way to their goal (Havstad 1979). The 
research method and framework proposed here for studying 
the family system variable and its relationship to the course 
of clinical symptoms has been developed using the data

The question at the start of this study was whether family 
system shifts before the decision to seek surgery are related to 
postsurgical weight loss outcomes. Bariatric surgery guaran
tees initial weight loss, but long-term outcomes vary greatly 
with identical procedures, and weight loss maintenance is 
variable. The clinical field of bariatric surgery recognizes 
suboptimal weight loss outcomes as attributable largely to 
psychological and behavioral factors, while also recogniz
ing the absence of predictive variables. The finding from the 
retrospective pilot study that an emotional shift occurred in 
all subjects who had dieted to goal weight suggests that a 
reliably identifiable emotional shift prior to bariatric surgery 
may be a predictive variable for weight change after surgery. Early evidence presented here suggests that it is—to some 
degree. An additional hypothesis for later stages of this study 
is that, with time, the shift that occurred in the individual is 
changeable as shifts in the family continue to occur. Presence 
or absence of family system shifts may also have predictive 
value in explaining or predicting weight relapse over time in 
the years after the surgery. Patients seeking bariatric surgery during 2011-2013 were 
evaluated for whether or not shifts in the family system had 
occurred and affected their anxiety level, approximately four 
to twelve weeks prior to pursuing bariatric surgery.

A Method of Documenting Shifts and the Clinical Hypothesis 
of Bowen Theory
Four studies have been described that are the basis for the 
development and beginning of testing the method of docu
menting shifts in the family system that is the subject of this 
paper. First, results of a pilot investigation supported the clini
cal hypothesis of Bowen theory that changes in symptoms 
follow changes in the family system. The evidence of the pilot 
study strongly pointed to the hypothesis that successful diet
ing to goal weight reflects a shift in emotional functioning of 
subjects in the family system. In a study to test whether the observations from the 
pilot study could be replicated, a method was constructed to 
document shifts by analyzing the text of family evaluation 
interviews that focus on changes in the subjects’ weight and 
shifts in their family system. Shifts in the family system and 
associated changes in subjects’ anxiety level, functioning level, 
and weight are organized in a single timeline to clarify how 
shifts in the variables follow one upon the other.

may be an effective strategy for retrospective research on

system. The study of shift and bariatric surgery outcomes is a 
first effort to do a prospective study of shifts in the emotional 
system and treatment outcomes. The theoretical framework that underlies the clinical 
hypothesis based on Bowen theory can also be operational
ized in any number of ways that make it possible to document 
shifts in the family system as they affect the course of many 
clinical disorders. The method developed here, based on the 
family evaluation interview, is apparently effective for captur

different clinical populations. The focus on shifts in active family relationships makes it 
possible to observe and document the dynamic family system 
variable as it affects the emotional functioning of family 
members in its wake. Associated shifts in two main variables

symptoms. The association of these variables is a result of the 
family system which functions as an emotional unit.

Experimental studies suggest that self-regulatory capacity 
is a limited resource, and that variation in situational demands 
on attentional and cognitive resources affect self-regulation in 
favor of automatic responsiveness to the environment. Taxing the

attention of dieters with distracting tasks increases vulner
ability to temptations in the environment at the expense of 
self-regulatory goals (Mann and Ward 2007). This is consis
tent with theory and clinical observation that in daily life the 
emotional load generated by family relationships can run 
down the attentional and cognitive resources for self-regula
tion of its members. Reducing the emotional load of the family 
emotional system through relationship shifts that reduce anxi
ety and/or enable functioning up for self may be significant 
preconditions to access the self-regulatory resources for the 
behavioral changes needed for significant weight loss. The family system distributes chronic anxiety among its 
members, and this leads to variation in levels of self within 
the family. Increased anxiety for a family member means that 
more effort is required to remain self–regulated. Bringing the 
family system into view reveals the context of self-regulation 
capacity that resides in the family system.

that the family system is a necessary but not sufficient vari
able in the development of clinical symptoms. For a hurricane 
to occur, it requires the activity of multiple variables, each 
variable alone being insufficient to produce the hurricane, but 
each essential. The observations of dieting to goal weight and 
results of bariatric surgery are consistent with the hypothesis 
that the family process is one important and maybe neces
sary factor in symptom remission. This is hidden from view 
for most individuals. Few spontaneously cite changes in their 
primary relationships as reasons for their dieting success. Training Clinical Researchers to See and Document the Family

observe and document family process so that other researchers 
can follow and evaluate the evidence. It is a long-term process 
to train clinicians to see the family system. Likewise, with

in the family system require experience not easily communi

FROM THE EDITOR

BOOK REVIEW
Book reviews are a significant way to address and discuss ideas 
relevant to Bowen family systems theory. The journal will select 
reviews of books, chosen at a reviewer’s discretion, which 
critically engage the ideas presented in the text and address 
their significance to the ideas contained in natural systems 
thinking. Texts chosen for review should represent relevant 
scientific ideas that extend theoretical understanding of the 
natural world. Appropriate areas of inquiry include, but are 
not limited to, biology, sociology, sociobiology, anthropology, 
psychology, psychiatry, and medicine. THE ISLAND OF KNOWLEDGE 
by Marcelo Gleiser
Reviewed by: Anne S. McKnight, EdD, MSW
What is needed is no less than a unified concept of man, 
a frame of reference that will enable us to understand 
the necessary connections between cell and psyche, 
and perhaps psyche and the entity we know as soul. (Bowen 1978, 46)
Murray Bowen spent a lifetime working to develop a 
science of human behavior as connected to other forms of 
life that have evolved on Earth over the millennia. He stud
ied the facts of human behavior as a basis for creating the 
eight concepts of Bowen theory which form a framework for 
understanding an individual’s behavior within the family and 
larger relationship systems.

Gleiser writes about the 
history of scientific discovery with clarity and conciseness. He 
traces how the search for knowledge about the physical world 
ranged from the use of reason by the Greek philosophers to 
explain the world, to Galileo’s astronomical explorations of the 
heavens, and to the complexities of modern quantum physics 
in modern times. He describes the way scientists studied the 
unknown on Earth and in the cosmos, revealing the mysteries 
layer by layer. He also articulates what science does not know 
and cannot explain—the seas of the unknown which surround 
this island of knowledge. Gleiser begins: “How much can we know of the world? Can we know everything? Or are there fundamental limits to 
what extent we can understand the nature of physical reality?” 
(xiii) What we can see of the world is only a sliver of what is 
out there. So much is invisible to the eye, even with the most 
sophisticated technology. He continues engaging the tension 
of the two inconsistent realities, the one we can “know” and 
measure through the scientific method and the intangible 
which is traditionally related to religious belief. His book 
creates an interesting intersection with Bowen’s ninth concept. Gleiser describes different beliefs about the origins of 
creation in religion and philosophy that emerged in early 
cultures.

Gleiser describes different beliefs about the origins of 
creation in religion and philosophy that emerged in early 
cultures. Humans, facing threats to survival from Earth and 
the skies, invented stories of powerful gods to explain their 
helplessness in confronting the unknown. Ancient cultures 
created myths and monuments to form a connection between 
the human and the cosmos. With the advent of the Abrahamic 
faiths, time became linear, with a beginning and an end, from 
which emerged the concept of a single lifetime. For Chris
tians and Muslims, the belief in life after death created a dual 


Book Review | 187
role for time, linear in life and without dimension in Para
dise. According to Gleiser, “The urge to know our origins and 
our place in the cosmos is a defining part of our humanity.” 
(13) This urge is not so different between humans who spun 
creation myths and scientists who today probe the mysteries 
of the universe through telescopes. The challenge is to under
stand the reach of rational explanations and where they end 
in the inexplicable and unknown. Chapters in the book form a chronology of discovery by 
examining the beginnings of scientific inquiry up to the pres
ent probes of the universe and examination of the smallest 
particles of the atom. The Greeks sought to understand reality 
through logic and conjecture, placing tremendous faith in the 
power of reason to address the questions of existence.

The Greeks sought to understand reality 
through logic and conjecture, placing tremendous faith in the 
power of reason to address the questions of existence. Their 
work began redefining “the human’s relation to the unknown 
from a passive reliance on fate and the supernatural to an 
active approach to knowledge and personal freedom.”(15) 
These Western philosophers were pushing the boundaries of 
rational explanations the way that reason and science bump 
up against the unexplained and the unknown. Plato synthesized the thinking of the early Greeks, 
embracing geometrical notions as the bridge between the 
human mind and the world of pure thought—a reach for the 
rational in a time of political unrest in Greece. Through his 
observations of the heavens, Copernicus proposed that the 
Earth revolved around the sun which reflected and reinforced 
the earlier views of Aristotle and Maimonides. He believed 
that the cosmos, centered around the sun, was built on the 
idea of beauty and harmony with little input from astronomi
cal observations. By the 1660s in the Kingdom of Denmark, King Frederick 
II awarded Tycho Brahe an island and a grant to support his 
creation of never before seen measuring instruments. These 
instruments allowed him to measure planetary positions 
with unprecedented accuracy and to discover a new star—an 
impossibility in the previously mathematically determined 
universe.

astronomy through the physics of cause and effect. He hypoth

well, with the two bodies attracting one another. The move
ments of these bodies in the heavens resulted from magnetic 
force. This was the cornerstone of Newton’s theory of gravita
tion developed in the 17th century. A year after Kepler’s publication of his theory, Galileo 
published a book which changed the way we look at the 
universe. Based on his development of the telescope, he could 
see the complex beauty of the heavens farther and clearer than 
anyone before. He discovered the pitted surface of the moon, 
the millions of stars in the Milky Way, and the four moons of 
Saturn, upsetting the Catholic dogma of the time. The most 
spectacular of Galileo’s discoveries pertains to the nature of 
gravity. Contrary to logic, all objects fall to the ground at the 
same rate.

The most 
spectacular of Galileo’s discoveries pertains to the nature of 
gravity. Contrary to logic, all objects fall to the ground at the 
same rate. Thus nature became amenable to rational explora
tion, through the combination of mathematical calculations 
and gathering of data. Newton emerged as a unifier of Kepler’s and Galileo’s 
work with the law of universal gravity. He concluded that 
Galileo’s law of free fall and Kepler’s laws of planetary motion 
were, in effect, describing the same phenomenon. The laws of 
the cosmos applied equally to the motions of both the planets 
and the falling apple. He also theorized that the nature of light 
was a rainbow of colors ranging between violet and red which 
were not visible to the eye. His new theory that explained 
celestial movements through the invisible forces of gravity 
swept the scientific and theological worlds. Newton believed 
that only the Creator could be responsible for so great a feat. God and the Universe were one and the same. Science became nature’s grand narrative, ready to uncover 
the cosmic blueprint armed with mathematics, intuition, 
and carefully measured data. The scientific method became 
increasingly tool driven, through exacting observations of 
nature expressed in mathematical laws. What the human 
could discover exploded in the next century.

The scientific method became 
increasingly tool driven, through exacting observations of 
nature expressed in mathematical laws. What the human 
could discover exploded in the next century. However, as the 
tools for discovery expanded, they also exposed how much 
was not known, particularly what was revealed in the tiny 
life forms discovered through the microscope. Increasingly 
the human could describe and create a narrative about natu
ral forces such as gravity, but could not offer explanations of 
how these forces exist or what they are. Book Review | 189
Einstein’s theory of relativity offered a revolutionary view 
of the nature of gravity by suggesting that its universal attrac
tive effect is due to the curvature of space around a massive 
body. He tested this hypothesis by measuring the curvature 
of light around the sun during an eclipse. Space became elas
tic. Not just space, but also time responded to the presence 
of matter. Einstein showed how space and time should not 
be viewed as absolute quantities, but formed a “space-time 
continuum” in which time is considered a fourth dimension. The special theory of relativity lets observers account for the 
way nature operates based on the assumption that the speed of 
light is always constant, and that it is the fastest speed within 
which signals can be communicated. What the human sees 
as “real” is viewed through our human senses, below which 
operate the forces of space, time, and matter in the universe.

What the human sees 
as “real” is viewed through our human senses, below which 
operate the forces of space, time, and matter in the universe. Einstein assumed that his theory, which he first applied 
to the solar system, would apply throughout the universe—
that matter was distributed the same way everywhere. He 
believed that since matter was based on the geometry of space, 
that it had to correspond to the simplest shape possible—the 
sphere. This viewpoint was shattered in 1929 when Edwin 
Hubble published his observations of distant galaxies, show
ing that they were receding from the Milky Way with velocities 
proportional to their distance. That is, a galaxy twice as far 
away moved at twice the speed. This “Hubble flow” means 
that the cosmos is expanding and carrying along galaxies. In the years following Hubble’s work, powerful new think
ing triggered further revolutions in our understanding of the 
universe. Einstein’s theory was correct in its prediction that 
space expands in relation to the matter within it. However, if 
one looks backwards in time, galaxies, rather than expanding, 
had to recede until they were so close together that they were 
a point in the universe. This point is called a singularity. Stephen Hawking and Roger Penrose showed that an 
expanding universe had to have a singularity in the past. This 
cosmic singularity pointed to a need for a new physics beyond 
what Einstein’s theory of relativity provided.

of quantum physics—the marriage of the general theory of 
relativity with the study of the tiniest bits of quantum matter. Gleiser outlines more scientific discoveries that will 
intrigue the reader of The Island of Knowledge. Humans are

surround us. We don’t possess the night vision of owls, the 
acute vision of eagles, or the sonar hearing of dolphins. Infor
mation from any object takes time to reach us. We each have a 
different processing time and a different perception of reality. Each one of us is an island of perception which becomes our 
“sphere of now.” Gleiser writes that “Now” is a cognitive illu
sion related to how we define space and time quantitatively. What does exist is memory of the past and expectations about 
the future. The human is only capable of “seeing” a small part 
of what makes up our actual reality. Gleiser celebrates these leaps in scientific advancement. He sees science as an open-ended pursuit, confronting theories 
with data but never leading to complete knowledge. Uncer
tainty allows horizons to be explored and understood. The 
more we know, the more we realize how great is our igno
rance.

Uncer
tainty allows horizons to be explored and understood. The 
more we know, the more we realize how great is our igno
rance. Searching for meaning and purpose within the scientific 
framework must always be the task of science. However, to 
believe that the search has an end, and that the unknown has 
boundaries that science can chart reflects a human arrogance. How does The Island of Knowledge relate to Bowen’s ninth 
concept of the supernatural? It elucidates that—even with all 
our striving for the known through the scientific method—
we come pitifully short of understanding the complexity of 
the world and the cosmos we live in. Our theories of time, 
matter, energy, and the expanding universe only highlight 
how finite our perceptions are. So how open are we to explore 
what is above (super) and what we can know in our reality? Gleiser’s book does not delineate what the supernatural looks 
like. He does lay the groundwork for respecting the possibili
ties it holds. ❖

99
FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The title of this journal was well-chosen, as it conveys both 
the uniqueness of the journal and of Bowen theory. In describ
ing the journal as one of “natural systems thinking,” it places 
the human family system in the broader context of all natural 
systems. Natural systems thinking represents an assumption 
that there are interrelated processes at play in nature of which 
the human is a part. From this perspective, science ultimately 
seeks a unity of knowledge of all natural systems. Murray Bowen’s early effort to determine if psychoan
alytic theory could become the basis for moving toward a 
science of human behavior resulted in his decision that it was 
not possible. He came to believe that psychoanalytic theory’s 
grounding in human subjectivity would not allow it to take 
its place among the sciences. The exchange of knowledge 
among the natural sciences would be necessary to the ongoing 
development of a science of human behavior and, while such 
knowledge could inform and enrich psychoanalytic theory, it 
could not be integrated with it. Dr. Bowen made a significant effort to clarify what distin
guished science from nonscience. He made a disciplined effort 
to define his understanding of science and the basic elements 
of the scientific process.

he later described as a natural systems theory of the family. In defining the family as an emotional system, Bowen 
grounded his theory in evolution. He saw the family as a natu

conceptualization of the family as a natural system provided 
a framework for making connections with all of the natural 
sciences. In a previous issue of Family Systems, I wrote that I

interrelatedness of all life on Earth, including the human. It

represented a form of natural systems thinking. There is elegance to natural systems thinking which reso
nates at an emotional level. Charles Darwin captured this in 
his famous closing paragraph in The Origin of Species:
There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several 
powers, having been originally breathed into a few 
forms or into one; and that whilst this planet has gone 
cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so 
simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and 
most wonderful, have been, and are being, evolved. (Darwin 1859, 490)
The appreciation of an underlying unity in nature is not 
limited to scientific discovery. It can be found in the world’s 
great religions and philosophies, though they can lead to a 
more subjective rather than a less subjective view of nature. From the Editor | 101
The task of science is to distinguish between the two and to 
move toward establishing the workings of nature which exist 
independently of human subjectivity. Nevertheless, the aesthetic appreciation of life’s under
lying unity appears for many to be one of the motivational 
elements in the scientific endeavor. E. O. Wilson entitled 
the first chapter of his book Consilience (1998) “The Ionian 
Enchantment.” In it he described, as a sophomore in college, 
his own sudden grasp of a unified process at play in nature.

categories of organisms gave way to a new sense of an under

theoretical structure to natural history for Wilson. Wilson described this as his own “Ionian Enchantment, 
“a term he borrowed from Gerald Holton (1995) who used it 
to describe a deep conviction that there is an order to life and 
the cosmos and a potential unity of knowledge in the sciences. The term referred to the 6th century B.C. philosopher, Thales of 
Ionia, who had developed his own view of the unity of nature. The emotional component of such a conviction can be 
based in observations of natural phenomena and lead to an 
intuitive vision of a “whole” and what might be involved in 
the structure and functioning of a system, be it a cell, an ant 
colony, or the brain.

In a letter to a friend, Einstein captured this 
rewarding experience: “It is a wonderful feeling to recognize 
the unity of a complex of phenomena that to direct observation 
appear to be quite separate things.” (Wilson 1998, 5)
The observation of the unity of a natural system can be 
exciting, but science requires further observations, the repe
tition of patterns, the development of concepts attempting 
to account for the phenomena, and ultimately the develop
ment of a theory which represents an effort to integrate facts, 
assumptions, and hypotheses into a unified, coherent whole. Such a theory then leads to further observations and testing. A natural systems paradigm reflects a view that there is 
a unity in nature. A natural systems theory, such as Bowen 
family systems theory, must be consistent with existing facts 
in the natural sciences. As Bowen wrote,


102 | Family Systems 13:2 2018	
                   
On a strict level, I have not considered a theory to be 
valid unless it can somehow be synonymous with 
the universe, the earth, the tides, the seasons, the 
predictable cycles of life and man as a reproductive, 
evolving form of life. (2013, 103) 
This quote, I think, reflects a view of an underlying unity in 
nature and an ultimate objective in science of attaining a unity 
of knowledge. The development of Bowen theory involves the 
ongoing effort to integrate knowledge from science.

toward a science of human behavior, though it is certainly a 
motivating element. There is a grandeur in the view of the 
family as a natural system and the interrelatedness of the 
human experience and human behavior with all of life. ❖

STUDY OF WEIGHT LOSS AS A MODEL FOR CLINICAL 
RESEARCH: SHIFTS IN THE FAMILY SYSTEM, THE
SUBJECT’S FUNCTIONING, AND THE 
COURSE OF CLINICAL SYMPTOMS
Laura Havstad, PhD and 
Kathleen J. Sheffield, MS, MA, RD
Clinical sciences have not yet systematically tested the 
potential of Bowen family systems theory to understand and 
predict the course of a wide range of clinical symptoms. This 
is a progress report on the development and application of 
a reliable method to document the emotional impact of the 
family system on clinical subjects and the course of their 
symptoms over time. A systematic method of analyzing 
data from family evaluation interviews has been developed 
to track shifts in the family emotional system associated 
with weight loss in overweight and obese individuals. The 
method produces a timeline of shifts in the family system, 
shifts in the functioning and anxiety levels of subjects, and 
changes in subjects’ weight. Four studies are described that 
illustrate and support the development and use of the method.

129
DEVELOPING A SYSTEMS MODEL
FOR FAMILY ASSESSMENT
Daniel V. Papero, PhD, MSSW
In personal conversations, Murray Bowen often floated 
the idea of a system of family diagnosis or assessment. He 
believed that it would be possible to create a family diagnostic 
system that could be used alongside or even in place of 
the DSM. In the book Family Evaluation, Michael Kerr 
proposed a general schema for such an assessment. Although 
several attempts have been made to informally follow the Kerr 
proposal, none has been extensively tested and validated. In 2011-2012, the NIMH began development of the Research 
Domain Criteria (RDoC), “...a research framework designed 
for studying the full range of human behavior from normal to 
abnormal based on biology, behavior, and context.” (NIMH 
RDoC Publications accessed September 28, 2017) The RDoC 
moves away from the categorical classification model of the

of all members for affection, security, and growth are again 
being met in a satisfying fashion.” (1949, 97) McCubbin and 
Patterson indicate that good adaptation involves
...(a) the maintenance or strengthening of family 
integrity (a term used to refer to the degree of 
connection and affection in the family unit), (b) the 
continued promotion of both member development 
and family unit development, and (c) the maintenance 
of family independence and its sense of control over 
environmental influences. (1983, 20)
Indicators of poor adaptation include prolonged tension in 
the family and emotional impairment of one or more family 
members (Hill 1949), deterioration of family integrity, a 
decline in the health and development of one or more family 
members, a decline in the well-being of the family unit, and 
curtailment of family independence and autonomy (McCubbin 
and Patterson 1983). One can infer, therefore, that the term systemic dysfunc
tion refers to a deterioration in the processes of coping with 
adversity that promote the maintenance of the family’s ability 
to meet the needs of its members.

He 
proposed that the family become the unit of treatment rather 
than the individual, and that the therapy be directed at the 
family helplessness. Bowen’s research led him to view the family “...as a fluid, 
ever-changing, functional system...” (Bowen 1978, 159) The 
term fluid captures the many-sided reciprocal interactions of 
the family system as people respond to one another continu
ously. It also includes the range of shifts in the emotional tone 
of the family in its interpretation of the challenge faced and 
the shifting emotional ground upon which the behavior of the 
family rests. The term functional suggests that the family has a 
task to perform or a purpose to accomplish. He added that the 
human family system is a natural system subject to the laws 
of other natural systems. (Bowen 1978, 151). If one views the 
family as a functional natural system, then a number of tasks 
can be inferred. The family unit must respond to the condi
tions of its environment in a manner that allows the family 
to meet the biological needs of its family members. It must 
extract resources from the environment— such as food, shel
ter, and other critical resources—to sustain life. In this sense, 
then, the family has an economic function. In addition, it must 
provide a context for reproduction and the development of 
succeeding generations. It has, therefore, a regenerative or 
growth function.

Bowen’s work with the family led him to focus on what 
he called “systems thinking” which he contrasted to what 
he called “individual thinking” or “conventional thinking” 
(Bowen 1978). The primary elements of conventional thinking, 
as Bowen used the term, include simple cause-and-effect asso
ciations and a preoccupation with the individual and his or 
her internal make up. Systems thinking begins with a focus on 
facts (Bowen 1978). Factual information about the history of 
the family takes on importance. How did people function in 
their lives? What are the facts about education, employment, 
health and general functioning of family members across time? Where has the family lived, where has it moved, and what 
led to move? What’s been the degree of connection between 
family members? Who have been the family leaders across 
time, and how well have they functioned. Specific family 
events and happenings can be examined with a view toward 
factual accounting. Who, what, where, and when become 
important questions for the individual and the family. Who is 
involved, what happened, when did it happen, and where did 
it happen. A further question—how did it happen—requires

ment framework with Bowen theory as its foundation. Most 
proposed efforts, while broadly informative, have proved 
cumbersome and difficult to use clinically. A different 
approach, one that utilizes Bowen’s identification of the family 
as a dynamic functional system, may ultimately provide a 
more user-friendly framework for assessing the functioning 
of the family unit.

By extrapolating from Bowen’s descriptions of individual 
characteristics of differentiation of self, of systems thinking, 
of the role of leadership in the family, and of the effects of 
anxiety, stress, and tension on the dynamically shifting family 
system, it becomes possible to sketch out a dimensional or 
continuum-based framework for assessing family unit or 
system functioning. The creation of a dimensional model may 
allow the expansion of the NIMH’s RDoC model to include the 
functioning of the family as an element in the context of the 
emotional well-being of a person. It may also permit accurate 
conceptualizations of the complex interplay between indi
vidual and family unit developmentally across the individual 
lifetime, between generations within the family system, and 
between the individual, the family system, and the broader 
social network in which all participate. The following five dimensions or continua represent a 
beginning effort to construct a dimensional model of family 
system functioning. The five dimensions, (1) resourcefulness, 
(2) family connectedness and integration, (3) tension manage
ment, (4) systems thinking, and (5) presence of goal structures, 
will be described below. Resourcefulness

Using systems thinking, it is possible to conceptualize two 
categories of goals: achievement goals and process goals. One 
can describe achievement goals fairly easily. A person can aim 
to attain a particular career, to live in a particular part of town, 
to attain a certain social position, and so forth. Process goals 
reflect the individual’s ability to understand the functioning 
of relationship networks. Process goals may include tension 
management, reducing cutoff, and the activity Bowen called 
de-triangling (Kerr 1988, 145-146). The idea of goals for a family unit has not been explored 
within the context of Bowen theory. It is possible to concep
tualize a set of family goals broadly. These goals reflect the 
evolutionarily based functions of the family unit—to repro
duce and raise offspring to the point of sexual maturity and to 
locate and extract from the environment resources to support 
life and the reproductive function. From these most funda
mental functions of the family unit, one can identify more 
complex goals related to the basic needs of family members. In 
a general sense the need-based goals involve (1) basic support 
for the development of children, (2) provisioning of resources 
to sustain life, (3) a defensive function when the family unit is 
faced with threat, and (4) a maintenance function of the mech
anisms that underlie the previous three goals.

 HOW EMOTIONS ARE MADE:  
IMPLICATIONS FOR BOWEN THEORY
Dave Galloway
Lisa Barrett’s book, “How Emotions are Made,” describes her 
decades long work in the field of emotion research and presents 
her theory of constructed emotion. Bowen theory places 
particular importance on the role emotions and feelings play  
in human functioning. The theory of constructed emotion 
posits that if one changes their concepts about a subject that 
this would lead to constructing different emotions/feelings 
regarding that subject. Bowen theory provides an individual 
with a rich set of new concepts for how one can think about 
their relationships and their own functioning. Barrett’s 
theory offers an explanation of how these new concepts can 
create new emotional (feeling) responses. The implication is 
that the value of “thinking systems” is that it will create new 
emotional responses that will support improved functioning. Key words: emotions, constructed emotions, Bowen theory, 
family systems, differentiation of self, feelings
INTRODUCTION
The concept of the emotional system is one of the 
most important in family systems theory. (Kerr and 
Bowen 1988, 26)
Those interested in Bowen theory may find Lisa Barrett’s 
theory of constructed emotion (ToCE) a useful way to think 
about emotions and feelings. Dr. Barrett’s book, How Emotions 
are Made , (2017) references decades of research to support 
a detailed explanation of how emotions are created.

concepts of emotion and feeling. Stimuli, Simulations, and Prediction Loops
The ToCE builds on the idea that the brain uses simula -
tions and prediction loops to construct a mental representation 
of the world. The brain creates a simulation using informa -
tion the senses provide; for example, photons hitting the eyes. Humans, like other species, evolved to predict what action 
should be performed as quickly as possible, so the simulation 
with the lowest prediction error that supports one’s goals is 
used until further stimuli warrant a different simulation. The 
brain is using as little information as it can, getting a good 
enough match so that it can react to the incoming stimuli as 
quickly as possible. If the goal is to eat, the brain creates differ -
ent simulations and predictions than if the goal is to mate, 
fight, or flee. Reflexively trying to catch something versus 
trying to avoid something is an example of this process: the 
brain predicts where the hand needs to be (via simulations) 
based on the trajectory (sensory inputs and more simulations) 
of the object in order to catch the object (the goal).

Another 
aspect of ToCE is that, to make the process more efficient, 
humans developed the use of concepts to more quickly catego -

How emotion S are made | 131
rize stimuli and more accurately predict actions to be taken. Concepts and categories support the process of recognizing 
something with very little information in order to act quickly. To continue the example, very little sensory information is 
required for the concept of “cup” to be used by the brain, 
which is then used in the process, unless the prediction error 
gets too high. The ToCE posits that concepts are a key part of 
how we simulate and predict. In milliseconds, working with 
incomplete information, we use concepts to decide what we 
are experiencing and begin to execute an action plan that 
aligns with our goal. We then create the emotion/feeling that 
fits with the situation. The ToCE core idea is that emotions/
feelings are created to fit the simulation that was predicted 
to be the best choice based on the goal. One person catching 
a falling cup could experience pride while another experi -
ences relief, while another embarrassment. It all depends on 
the sensory input, their concepts, goals, and “body budget.1”
In short, the ToCE process begins with the biology of 
sensory input and processing, followed immediately by the 
use of psychological constructs of learned concepts and goals 
to “construct” a particular instance of an emotion, consciously 
experienced as a feeling.

INTEROCEPTION AND THE BODY BUDGETS:  
WHAT I FEEL, I BELIEVE
A significant source of sensory input is from our “intero -
ceptive” system. Interoception is the process that senses the 
energy state of the body and its readiness to perform actions. If the body can’t sense itself in space and time, how can it 
reflexively catch, avoid, or pursue something? If it can’t sense 
its energy level, how can it correctly activate the body to react? Sensing place and energy is the function of the interoceptive 
network which includes areas of the brain associated with 
emotions. It generates valence, which is “felt” as affect and 
arousal. This system evolved to ensure that our energy budget 
is monitored and kept in balance, such that predicted energy 
1 The body budget concept includes parts of the internal interoceptive network that 
senses and maintains our energy expenditures and needs. In order to react to our 
environment the body has to predict its energy needs in seconds. 132 | F amily SyStemS 14:2 2020

in, and influences, simulations and predictive loops being 
used with the other senses. If you have been cold, hungry, 
tired, scared, or flu-stricken, you have experienced your 
interoceptive system influencing your “feelings.” According 
to the ToCE, the interoceptive systems contributes to creating 
emotions/feelings and sometimes these created emotions/
feelings are inappropriate.
