For example, according to the 
ToCE, I may get angry at someone because I’m just hungry or 
tired, not because they are being mean to me. My simulation 
includes my sensing discomfort and linking it to you. I then 
simulate and categorize this unpleasant feeling of discomfort 
as “you are being unpleasant,” thus inappropriately creating 
an instance of a feeling I call “angry.”
While the interoceptive network includes brain areas asso -
ciated with emotion, it evolved not for us to “feel” but for 
our body budget to stay balanced, based on predictions being 
made about what our body will need in order to respond to 
the situation. Nature doesn’t care what we feel, but it does try 
to keep us alive (Barrett 2017, Kindle location 1403). Construction of Emotions
The ToCE posits that emotions are constructed using 
multiple inputs. It is a process, working as a system, where 
everything is influencing everything else. The inputs are 
from one’s external senses, the interoceptive system, and a 
collection of concepts and goals. The affective state influences 
how the inputs of external stimuli are processed. For exam -
ple, it influences how the sensory systems prioritize stimuli 
(Akrami et al. 2018). Because the brain is a signal processor 
(audio, visual, tactile, etc.), it works to predict what these raw 
signals are and what they mean by creating simulations and 
running predictions using previously established concepts. For example, “dog” is a concept.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
This author believes that the ToCE offers important 
considerations for clinical work, starting with one’s ability to 
read a client’s emotions. Reading Emotions
 Barrett is clear that given our poor ability to interpret 
facial expressions one needs to be careful when reading facial 
expressions and body language to assess the emotions of 
others. There is a very good chance that the outcome will be 
wrong. In addition, one’s affective state and recent events can 
bias the evaluation. A client’s ability to read the therapist’s 
emotional state will be affected by the level of stress or anxiety 
they have during a session as will their concepts about coun -
seling and counselors. Asking process-oriented questions to gather functional 
facts can help the therapist avoid an incorrect reading of a 
client’s emotional state. Barrett’s work makes it clear that 
understanding what and how a client is thinking about a situ -
ation is more useful than attempting to interpret the client’s 
emotional state through visual impressions. 136 | F amily SyStemS 14:2 2020                     
The expression a client believes they see on the therapist’s 
face may also not be what the therapist means to convey. This 
supports the idea that working to be neutral with clients is 
important since they are likely to misinterpret the therapist’s 
facial expressions and emotional state.

 Barrett recommends that individuals learn to be more 
specific when labeling an emotion/feeling and calls this 
“emotional granularity” (Pond et al. 2012). By being more 
specific, one builds up a larger, more accurate set of emotional/
feeling concepts which is useful for creating the emotion/feel -
ing in the future (Kashdan, Barrett, and McKnight 2015). For 
the clinician, inviting a client to think  about a feeling and to 
create a specific label for that feeling could help the client to 
become more specific about the emotional process that led 
to that feeling. This should help them recognize and manage 
their emotional process in the future. This labeling, also called 
“affective labeling,” has been shown to be more effective for 
emotional regulation than cognitive reappraisal or distraction 
(Kircanski, Lieberman, and Craske 2012). Bowen describes the 
example of a husband becoming enraged just from the “look” 
his wife gave him. Once the husband understood the details 
of this particular emotional experience, he was better able to 
control his response (Bowen 1978). This understanding led to 
changing his goal, which meant his simulations and prediction 
loops changed to calculate the appropriate response using the 
new goal.

FROM THE ARCHIVES
A special feature of Family Systems is a previously unpublished 
manuscript by Murray Bowen and other researchers in the 
family field. Since the manuscripts reflect the thinking of the 
authors at the time they were written, they are introduced 
with comments to place them in historical context. Dr. Bowen’s 
manuscripts have been selected from a large archive of written 
records that are preserved at the National Library of Medicine. THE INTEGRATION OF KNOWLEDGE
Murray Bowen, MD
Introduction by Robert J. Noone, PhD
It is now fifty-five years since Murray Bowen’s formal 
theory of the family was first published in Comprehensive 
Psychiatry. The 1966 paper, “The Use of Family Theory in 
Clinical Practice” represented an important milestone in 
psychiatry and was the product of Bowen’s effort over the 
preceding two decades to develop a more scientific view of 
human behavior. At the time, the popularity of family therapy 
was accelerating in the field of mental health, and Bowen 
was widely recognized as a principal pioneer in the field. The 
awareness that a radically new theory of human behavior was 
being introduced, however, was not widespread. The interest 
in the therapy with families predominated.

Throughout history there has been a lag time between 
the time a scientific idea is introduced and the time it is 
finally accepted by society. The lag time is universal. It has 
extended itself for centuries, or it may be compressed into a 
few decades. The reasons behind this are difficult to define. There are differences about the nature of science, and what 
qualifies as a science, and the way generally accepted facts are 
finally accepted into what is known as science. To get beyond the endless debates, I will talk mostly about 
the lag time in the integration of knowledge.

text:
To get beyond the endless debates, I will talk mostly about 
the lag time in the integration of knowledge. It appears to 
be related to long held impressions and subjective ideas that 
are in conflict with newly defined facts. One way of think
ing would say that lag time was greater in former centuries 
because of poor communication. Another way of thinking 
would say that the instant communication of the twentieth 
century disseminates facts quickly, but that it also generates 
feelings and reactivity which produce a lag within itself. This 
brief column will be devoted to a few examples of lag time, 
ending with issues that have involved Freud, psychiatry, and 
psychotherapy. The longest lag time in history may have occurred with 
systems ideas. Carl Sagan has indicated that systems ideas 
first surfaced for a time around 500 B.C. The ideas may 
have reappeared briefly in building projects in the centuries 
that followed, but final acceptance of systems thinking did 
not return for some 2,000 years, until after the Dark Ages 
in Europe. Some scholars have suggested that the original 
systems ideas were in conflict with religious ideas about the 
early gods and goddesses. Systems thinking finally reappeared 
with astronomy, physics and chemistry, all related to aspects 
of the nonliving worlds. Over the centuries that followed, 
systems ideas were used with plants and animals in the living 
world.

Title: Emotional Process when a Spouse Changes Gender
Author: Brooks

157
FACULTY CASE CONFERENCE
The faculty case conference is held monthly at the Bowen 
Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case conference 
from their clinical practices. The conference is not intended 
as supervision or as a meeting to arrive at a consensus about 
how to manage a specific case. It is intended as a learning 
experience for the faculty and to keep them aware of one 
another’s general approach to clinical problems. EMOTIONAL PROCESS WHEN
A SPOUSE CHANGES GENDER
Laura R. Brooks, MSW
What is the emotional process in a marriage when one of 
the spouses transitions to the other gender? Is the process 
unique? Is a spouse’s decision to transition to the other 
gender a symptom, an adaptation, or an effort to define self? In this family, the adaptive patterns in the marriage were 
apparent since the couple’s courtship and persist throughout 
the transition of the husband to the female gender. After years 
of opting for harmony by going along with her husband, 
the wife uses the crisis to define herself more clearly in 
the relationship. Keywords: transgender, emotional process, differentiation, 
adaptation, chronic anxiety, Bowen theory, multigenera
tional family system
Ms. Brooks is a clinical social worker in private practice in Ellicott City, 
Maryland and is on the faculty of the Bowen Center.

CHILD PORNOGRAPHY OFFENDERS: OVERVIEW 
AND PERSPECTIVES OF BOWEN THEORY
John F. Butler, PhD
We often learn of people arrested, prosecuted, and imprisoned 
for child pornography. This report surveys a standard 
individual risk assessment specific to child pornography 
offenders, the Risk Matrix 2000, and emerging methods 
such as the Child Pornography Offense Risk Tool and 
Correlates of Admission to Sexual Interest in Children. Other psychosexual risk assessments are highlighted, such 
as physiological measures, The Abel Assessment of Sexual 
Interest (AASI), polygraphs, and specialized psychosexual 
testing. Also reviewed are the applications of the concepts 
of Bowen family system theory in this clinical area. Bowen theory shifts the focus from the individual to the 
multigenerational family using theory for assessment and 
treatment. Last, using Bowen theory, several clinical cases 
are presented. Keywords: child pornography, risk assessments, applications 
to Bowen family systems theory
INTRODUCTION
The internet creates the possibility of wide distribution of 
pornographic images and makes private viewing relatively 
easy. Child pornography, the visual depiction of sexually 
explicit conduct involving a minor, is a growing problem.

FAMILY VARIABLES AND CHILD PORNOGRAPHY
Some research exists about the interaction of family vari
ables and men drawn to child pornography. For example, 
Babchishin et al. (2010) completed a meta-analytic review 
revealing online sex offenders have higher rates of physi
cal and sexual abuse in childhood compared to the general 
population. Wollert, Waggoner and Smith (2012) report federal 
internet pornography offenders having a history of social 
isolation and problematic social relationships related to their 
offenses. Interpersonal skill deficits are seen by Henshaw et 
al. (2015) as important focuses for treatment. Lastly, in their 
review article, Babchishin et al. (2018) summarize examples 
of various treatment regimens. They identify poor social skills 
as an essential treatment area. There is recent research on early family risk markers 
for pedophilia that evaluates possible associations between 
parental characteristics and pregnancy factors which might 
predict child pornography offenses (Babchishin et al. 2019). This study of 655 males convicted of child pornography in 
Sweden used an unselected sample with matched controls. The study is atypical because few studies mention family 
variables. There were two main findings.

Cause and Effect Thinking
One significant difference between the individual perspec
tive and systems thinking is the focus on reciprocal emotional 
processes among the family (Kerr 2019). In noting obstacles to 
thinking systems, Kerr (2019, 5) cites the area of physical abuse 


Child Pornography Offenders | 137
and the challenge of not viewing one person as the victim and 
the other as an abuser or perpetrator. It is essential to understand this reciprocal process 
to address this problem adequately. The ability of 
someone in the family to make this shift is the primary 
determinant for the success of the family. Kerr’s comments on physical abuse applies to sexual 
abuse and child pornography offenses. The outcome of family 
psychotherapy depends on the ability of the therapist to make 
this shift and to see the offender more neutrally. The Family as an Emotional Unit
Bowen’s concept of the family as an emotional unit in 
the NIMH Family Study Project is the cornerstone of family 
systems theory (Bowen 2013). In the first year of the project, 
Bowen focused on mother-daughter dyads. During the last 
three years of the project, his attention shifted to the family 
unit—the parent(s) and siblings. Bowen came to realize that 
the emotionality within the mother-daughter dyads involved 
other essential members of the family, notably fathers and 
siblings. He viewed schizophrenia as a family process rather 
than something just in the patient (Bowen 2013).

Kerr (2019) defines triangles as the building block of 
families. He includes impairment of children and the child 
projection process within the core concept of triangles. 138 | Family Systems 15:2 2021	
 
Triangles are one of the core concepts in Bowen theory indi

“conceptualize a pattern of emotional functioning in relation

family can become emotionally unstable, and another person 
becomes involved to help manage the anxiety. Triangles 
accommodate more tension than a two-person system. This core concept is often present with men charged with 
child pornography and their families.

This concept describes emotional connections 
between generations. The life pattern of cutoffs is determined by the way 
people handle their unresolved emotional attachments 
to their parents...The degree of unresolved emotional 
attachment to the parents is equivalent to the degree 
of undifferentiation that must somehow be handled 
in the person’s own life and future generations

to note the type, extent, and nature of contacts that family

offenses, it is useful to determine who and how often family 
members visit, call, or write the person incarcerated. Along 
the same line, who contributes money to their commissary 
account? Men released from prison must have a physical 
address for release, and most often, it’s with a family member

Family Diagrams
Family diagrams remain a staple of family assessment 
with Bowen family systems theory. The major publications on 
Bowen theory acknowledges this (see Bowen 1978, Kerr and 
Bowen 1988, and Kerr 2019). Recently, Harrison (2018) devoted 
an entire book to the family diagram as a guide to address 
the differentiation of self in a person’s family of origin. Many 
works on Bowen family systems theory and its applications 
highlight the importance of family diagrams and suggest stan
dard symbols to use in constructing family diagrams. Family 
diagrams remain a cornerstone of Bowen family systems 
theory for over sixty-five years and will continue to be so 
in the future. The use of multigenerational family diagrams with men 
convicted of child pornography offenses is indispensable. There is general agreement on the basic symbols used in draw
ing family diagrams (see McGoldrick et al. 2008, McGoldrick 
2016, and Harrison 2018). The diagrams provide information 
on relationship and reproductive history, sibling position, 
and the facts of functioning in health, education, occupations, 
and legal history. Family diagrams highlight the functioning 
position of the patient which influences their vulnerabil
ity to symptoms.

 The amount of anxiety in the probation system is often 
underestimated. Some probation officers assume all offenders 
released from prison for child pornography are at high risk 
to re-offend. To clarify, we are talking about men convicted 
for the possession of child pornography, not those who have 
contact offenses with children or who are travelers, men who 
travel to other localities to meet with what they assume are 
underage children. Scores on risk assessments determine the 
risk for re-offending, which is more accurate than an educated 
guess. However, parole/probation officers are on the front 
lines, and they are directly responsible for people under their 
supervision. They work in a very anxious system and are more 
likely than not to take a negative view of the parolee. 140 | Family Systems 15:2 2021	
 
The probation system is not the only area with an anxious 
focus. Child pornography is a topic where society is far from 
neutral. The requirements of public registration of sex offend
ers, residential restrictions, annotations on driver’s licenses, 
and the isolation of offenders on Halloween are all signs of 
significant societal anxiety. The teaching point is to be aware 
of societal anxiety in the area of child pornography and how 
this impacts clinicians and probation or parole officers.

view shows there is a biology and psychology to individuals 
on probation or parole for child pornography offenses. Bowen theory highlights the influence of change within the 
family relationship system and suggests that it can influence 
the emergence of behavior, such as viewing child pornogra
phy. Also, Bowen theory considers the unresolved emotional 
attachment to parents. Rather than emphasizing a particu
lar stage of development, such as adolescence, Bowen theory 
proposes a theory of emotional development where differen
tiation of the child from the parents is key. Lack of parent-child 
emotional separation impacts the social and emotional devel
opment of the child (Kerr 2019). Bowen theory concepts offer 
a broader lens for treatment of offenders, emphasizing the 
family as an emotional unit and providing theoretical concepts 
useful for both assessment and treatment. The topic of child pornography offenders offers numer
ous opportunities for quantitative, qualitative, and clinical 
research. With the foundation for risk assessments estab
lished, perhaps the coming decade will witness increased 
focus on understanding family system variables related to 
child pornography offenses and stimulate new thinking on 
treatment options. ❖

It is now fifty-five years since Murray Bowen’s formal

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
BOOK REVIEW
Book reviews are a significant way to address and discuss ideas 
relevant to Bowen family systems theory. The journal will select 
reviews of books, chosen at a reviewer’s discretion, which 
critically engage the ideas presented in the text and address 
their significance to the ideas contained in natural systems 
thinking. Texts chosen for review should represent relevant 
scientific ideas that extend theoretical understanding of the 
natural world. Appropriate areas of inquiry include, but are 
not limited to, biology, sociology, sociobiology, anthropology, 
psychology, psychiatry, and medicine. HIDDEN VALLEY ROAD:
INSIDE THE MIND OF AN AMERICAN FAMILY
Robert Kolker
Reviewed by Michael E. Kerr, MD 
For many years, I have recommended Shot in The Heart 
by Mikal Gilmore as the go-to book to read that illustrates 
most of the concepts described by Bowen theory. Robert 
Kolker’s carefully researched book about the Galvin family 
of Colorado, a family with six out of ten male siblings diag
nosed with schizophrenia, drops Gilmore’s book into second 
place. A quote by Kolker describing his assessment of the 
family’s youngest sibling, Mary Lindsey, summarizes the 
overall message of the book, one entirely consistent with 
Bowen theory: 
Lindsey understood now more than ever that we are 
more than just our genes.

can be summarized by the word “avolition,” a term used to 
describe the lack of motivation or ability to do tasks or activi

because no medication exists that can increase a person’s 
basic level of “self,” which Bowen theory views as the basis 
of negative symptoms. Conventional psychiatry has no way 
of explaining what drives negative symptoms. Mary Lindsey, described above by Kolker, is the youngest 
of the twelve Galvin family siblings and, by my estimation, the 
most differentiated of the siblings. I assess her brother Donald, 
the oldest sibling, to be the most poorly differentiated of the

than five points on the continuum of differentiation. In the family, ten male children were born in succes

descriptions of Donald’s life experiences make clear that 
Donald’s lack of “self” severely impairs his ability to success

responsibility and navigating an intimate relationship.

asked to complete the sentence “When I was a child” Donald 
finished with “I still am” (82). Donald despaired about not 
meeting the expectations he had of himself and obsessed about 
being the man his parents thought he could be. In Bowen’s five 
classes of stressors that can trigger enough anxiety to push a 
schizophrenic patient into psychosis, one of the classes is not 
meeting the expectations that one has for oneself and another 
class is not meeting the perceived expectations of others. In his early twenties, Donald married Jean. The marriage 
was rocky throughout the three years it lasted, its ups and

trouble expressing affect. The doctor did not describe Donald 
as having lost in the marriage whatever pseudo self he could 
muster, but Bowen theory describes it as just that.

theory is in being able to conceptualize the relationship 
processes in these schizophrenic-level match-ups. As Bowen 
observed at NIMH, in relationships with this much emotional

One hospital psychiatrist who treated 
Donald suggested that he periodically seemed to “choose” to 
become psychotic, which Bowen theory suggests is preferable 
to experiencing the full depth of the anguish associated with 
a relationship disruption. An unfortunate fact about this book is that Kolker appar
ently never heard of Bowen family system theory and its 
conceptualization of symbiosis and unresolved emotional 
attachment. He did read about Ted Lidz, a member of the 
family movement during the 1960s and 1970s. Seemingly 
still steeped in psychoanalytic thinking, Lidz theorized that a 
child’s problematic experiences during the first few years of 
life could render a schizophrenic level of vulnerability later 
in life. It remains an enigma to me why symbiosis and unre
solved emotional attachment have still barely penetrated the 
public consciousness. Even the family movement never under
stood or embraced it. Speaking of symbiosis, Bowen theorists would want to 
know how Kolker describes Donald’s relationship with his 
mother, Mimi, and the parental triangle in which Donald was 
embedded. There are an assortment of clues consistent with 
the strongly unresolved attachment between them. On the 
one hand, she was a no nonsense, “It’s my way or the high
way,” type person. On the other hand, Donald lived with his 
parents for long periods after hospitalizations. His mother 
was not going to give up on any of her schizophrenic sons.

age ninety-three, looked after her schizophrenic siblings in a 
more mature way than her parents did. She was one of the two 
siblings that married successfully and did not get divorced. They had two children. She carried her own level of chronic 
anxiety, but it was less than her mother’s and she was better at 
acknowledging and managing it. Mary’s nuclear family had its 
own version of the family projection process, but less intense 
than her family of origin. Mary placed Donald, now in his 
middle seventies, into an assisted living facility in Colorado 
Springs where he will likely live out his life. Mary drives him 
to medical appointments, shopping expeditions, and other 
errands. She has not abandoned any of her schizophrenic 
siblings. In fact, her contact with them has been an important 
factor in their stability. In my judgment, her efforts with her 
siblings are based more on principle than they are dictated by 
her own anxiety. Kolker has a chapter in the book about each of the other 
siblings, schizophrenic and not schizophrenic. I am not going

a conflict for Bowen theory. The theory does not say that the

and others were saying about schizophrenia helps to support a 
schism in psychiatry about the value of drugs versus therapy. Families with schizophrenia in their history are four times 
more likely than the rest of the population to pass along the 
condition to future generations. However, this is not evidence 
to support opposing the role of nurture. Many of the research

continues to search the brain for causes of schizophrenia. In 
my reading, not much progress had been made. It reminded 
me of the work of Robert Weinberg, who discovered the first

DIVERGENT SPOUSE FUNCTIONING
Phillip Klever, MSW
Bowen theory explains how tension and undifferentiation 
influence individual and family functioning through 
emotional relationship processes within the family unit. This article examines one of those nuclear family emotional 
processes—the dysfunctional spouse process or divergent 
functioning in the marriage. Over fifteen years the study 
found variation within the sample in divergent spouse 
functioning ranging from absence to persistence in 
frequency of the pattern, from mild to severe symptoms, 
and from fluctuation to rigidity in who was the more and 
less symptomatic spouse. Three variables were tested for 
their association with divergent spouse functioning. These 
were husband-wife differences in self-direction and goal 
effectiveness, multigenerational family functioning, and 
divergent spouse functioning of participant parents. This 
study found statistically significant correlations between 
these independent variables and the degree of difference 
between husband-wife symptomatology.

What contributes to one spouse becoming more or less 
symptomatic than the other? This introduction addresses this 
question by drawing from three areas of study. These are:

ronment shapes the functioning of the male and female, 
particularly reproduction and parenting behavior. One 
factor in the social environment is the animal’s position in 
the group hierarchy which can inhibit reproductive behav
ior (McClintock 1987, Sapolsky 1987) and compromise 
physiological functioning. A second social factor that affects 
reproductive functioning in some species is social density and 
isolation (McClintock 1987).

Human research has shown that greater emotional reactiv

and poorer health outcomes. Also, marital instability or dissat

health and psychological problems for couples (Kiecolt-Glaser

physical and mental health trajectories through their interde

a converging influence on each other’s health, sometimes the 
influence is divergent. Researchers have studied gender and 
dominance-submission as possible factors that contribute to 
this divergent functioning. Marriage research findings related to gender are mixed as 
to whether the husband or the wife is more affected by marital 
instability. Married women, as compared to married men, have 
shown a stronger association between inflammation, health 
problems, and marital distress (Derry et al. 2015, Keicolt-

hormone, a stress hormone (Loving et al. 2004). The Contribution of Bowen Theory
Bowen theory provides another explanation for diver
gent functioning between spouses. This theory sees that the 
dysfunctional spouse process is usually influenced less by 
gender or dominance–submission and more by the emotion
ally driven relationship processes within the family unit. These processes have a biological root from our evolution
ary inheritance. Natural systems research has explored some 
of these biological influences. Bowen theory goes a step 
further by providing a unique framework to understand the 
family as a natural system. Nuclear family emotional process, a 
concept in Bowen theory, describes four relationship processes 
that unequally distribute the family’s undifferentiation or 
emotional immaturity and anxiety—the response to perceived 
threat—to various parts of the family.

(2) marital conflict, (3) projection onto a child, and (4) dysfunc
tion in a spouse (Bowen 1978, Kerr and Bowen 1988). The 
family’s level of differentiation and anxiety influence the 
chronicity and intensity of these nuclear family emotional 
processes. These processes are hypothesized to be both auto
matic as a part of our evolutionary heritage and learned or 
shaped by experience. These processes contribute to mari
tal, physical, psychiatric, and social symptomatology within 
the family unit. This study focused on the fourth pattern, the 
dysfunctional spouse process or divergent spouse functioning. Bowen theory hypothesizes that people marry at the same 
basic level of differentiation, but that their functional level 
may vary considerably. This is due to uneven distribution of 
anxiety or tension between the spouses and within the family. Several relationship processes contribute to this disparity. First 
is the borrowing and trading of self within the marriage. This 
is characterized by one spouse losing self-direction or defini
tion and absorbing the tension from his or her partner and

family relationships, while the other spouse has more room to 
pursue his or her direction and therefore absorbs less anxiety 
from the marriage and family. This is a reciprocal process with 
each affecting the other.

each affecting the other. The spouse who absorbs the tension 
and loses purposeful self-direction and goal effectiveness is 
hypothesized to be less able to moderate the physiological 
arousal of the stress response (Ishida and Okada, 2006, Ishida 
et al. 2011) and is more susceptible to becoming symptomatic 
(Klever 2018, 2009b), while the one who gains “self” tends 
to have less tension and be less symptomatic. Kerr (2019, 47) 
stated, “The capacity to maintain a ‘self’ in relationships is a 
very powerful anxiety reducer.” 
The style of functioning, dominating-submitting, lead
ing-following, or overfunctioning-underfunctioning, does not 
predict who will be the more or less symptomatic spouse. For example, either the dominant or submissive spouse may 
absorb more tension than the other due to the family emotional 
processes. The dominant one’s contribution to becoming more 
symptomatic may be to not think about his or her needs, 
principles, or goals while being consumed with the burden 
of keeping the family running smoothly and compensating 
for the submissive one’s lack of initiative or responsibility. In contrast, the submissive spouse’s contribution to becom
ing more symptomatic may be by losing “self” and absorbing 
more of the family tension and by becoming increasingly 
overwhelmed or unmotivated and feeling lost, helpless, disor
ganized, or left out.

spouses absorbing more or less anxiety is triangling, which 
involves two or more members projecting the tension onto a 
third party, who absorbs it. With divergent spouse function
ing, the more dysfunctional spouse is usually the third party. For instance, the dominant spouse becomes the focus in the 
triangle when his/her partner joins with the children, family 
of origin, and/or friends in criticizing the dominant spouse 
(“You’re too controlling or bossy.” “You’re no fun.”), prais

you.”), or distancing. In contrast, the triangles transfer tension 


Divergent Spouse Functioning | 109

family of origin helping too much, being critical of his or her 
underfunctioning, feeling sorry for him or her, treating the 
underresponsible one as someone who needs to be taken care 
of, and/or leaving him/her out of interaction. Absorbing the 
anxiety from the triangling process makes it more difficult to 
sustain self-direction, and, in turn, loss of self-direction makes 
one more susceptible to absorbing the anxiety from triangling.

her family of origin. Some spouses have a slightly higher level 
of differentiation, some the same, and some lower. Therefore, 
a husband and wife may have multigenerational families 
with different levels of symptomatology and instability. So,

explored the following four questions:

frequency, from mild to severe symptoms, and from alternat

question tested these descriptions in Bowen theory with this 
sample. This researcher defined divergent spouse function

in which the emotional relationship processes contributed 
to differences in overall physical, psychiatric, and/or social 
symptomatology between the husband and wife. 2. Did discrepancy in goal effectiveness and self-
direction between the spouses contribute to divergent 
spouse functioning?

with fifty-one couples. Information about the independent and 
dependent variables was collected annually through struc

Bowen theory describes how the family operates as an 
emotional unit as it experiences the family’s undifferentia
tion and anxiety. The triangles within the family unevenly 
distribute the family tension and emotional immaturity so 


Divergent Spouse Functioning | 121
that the functioning of some are enhanced and the functioning 
of others are compromised. This study focused on the family 
emotional processes enhancing the functioning of one spouse 
and diminishing the functioning of the other. The first study question explored variation in frequency 
of divergent functioning, severity of symptoms, and rigidity 
versus flexibility regarding who was the more or less symp
tomatic spouse. Spouses appeared to influence each other’s 
functioning with either converging or diverging symptomatic 
outcomes. This study found that the husband and wife’s levels 
of symptomatology were more frequently convergent than 
divergent. When divergence occurred, it ranged from infre
quent to persistent, from mild to severe symptomatology, and 
from stuck in one spouse to alternating between the spouses. Lower functioning couples tended to have more frequent 
divergent functioning with more severe symptoms, while 
higher functioning couples usually had divergent functioning 
that was absent or infrequent with milder symptoms.

The vari
ation described in this sample was consistent with Dr. Bowen’s 
observations of the occurrence of the dysfunctional spouse 
pattern as one of the nuclear family emotional processes and 
of its variation in frequency, intensity, and rigidity. Divergent functioning at times showed flexibility by alter
nating between the husband and wife. At other times the 
pattern was more rigid with the same spouses being more and 
less symptomatic. When the dysfunctional spouse pattern did 
not alternate between the spouses, the wives were frequently 
the more dysfunctional spouse (eighteen wives: six husbands). At first glance this seemed to support the idea in some of 
the marriage research (Keicolt-Glaser and Wilson 2017) that 
wives were more likely to absorb marital tension. But when 
the number of years was counted that husbands versus wives 
were the more dysfunctional spouse, the genders were equal. This suggested that both men and women were similarly 
affected by the emotional processes in the family. One possible explanation for these three variations in 
divergent spouse functioning was variation in levels of 
differentiation. Bowen theory predicts that at lower levels of 
differentiation the dysfunctional spouse process would tend 
to be more persistent, intense, and rigid. At higher levels of 


122  Family Systems 2021 | 15.2	
                   
differentiation, divergent functioning would tend to be short 
term with milder symptoms and more flexibility.

term with milder symptoms and more flexibility. Another 
explanation for variation is the fluctuation in family tension. As family tensions ebbed and flowed, divergent spouse func
tioning may have responded in kind. Another factor that 
probably contributed to the variation in divergent function
ing was the variation in mechanisms the family units used to 
manage the tension and emotional immaturity. For instance, 
some family units more frequently manifested distance, mari
tal conflict, and/or child projection and less projection onto a 
spouse. Each family unit had its own pathways for distribut
ing family emotional immaturity and tension that may or may 
not have included divergent functioning. The second study question examined the association 
between spousal disparity in goal effectiveness and self-direc
tion with divergent functioning. This was an indirect test of the 
effect of the borrowing and trading of self within a marriage, 
a key component of divergent spouse functioning. The results 
found that the spouse who had less goal effectiveness and 
mature self-direction was more susceptible to becoming 
symptomatic, while the spouse with more goal effectiveness 
and self-direction tended to be less so.

Measuring the differences in 
goal effectiveness and self-direction were an indirect, partial 
measure of the borrowing and trading of self in the marriage. The other limitation in a correlation analysis was that it was 
unclear whether lack of goal effectiveness influenced more 
symptomatology or whether more symptomatology influ
enced less goal effectiveness. A systems perspective would 
propose that the two variables probably influenced each other. Natural systems research describes the effects of the social 
environment on the functioning of the pair bond. Bowen theory 
sees the multigenerational family as a central component of 
the pair bond’s social environment. This study examined 
two aspects of the multigenerational family—multigenera
tional family functioning and divergent spouse functioning 
in the family of origin. Spousal differences in multigenera
tional family functioning had the strongest association with 
the dysfunctional spouse process. This supported the idea that 
a possible risk factor for becoming the more dysfunctional 
spouse was being a part of a more symptomatic multigenera
tional family than one’s partner’s multigenerational family. In contrast, more stability and less symptomatology in one’s 
multigenerational family may have been a protective factor 
for the less symptomatic partner.

and/or a stressor for each participant and his/her developing

came from a multigenerational family with more dysfunction. Her parents divorced in part due to her father’s alcoholism 
and his physical aggression directed at her mother. He died 
in his fifties from alcohol abuse. Her sister also had problems 
functioning related to her alcohol abuse. Ms. Smith did well 
in her work, her marriage, and as a mother, but worried often 
about her sister and multigenerational family. She gener

or social symptoms and the lowest level of symptomatology 
in the study. One of the processes for managing tension in a nuclear 
family is to project blame, worry, or tension onto one’s chil
dren and/or spouse. In the dysfunctional spouse process, the 
spouse who projects blame shifts some of his or her tension to 
the partner who absorbs the anxiety. This tendency is thought 
in part to be learned through experience in one’s family of 
origin and extended family. The last study question explored 
whether the dysfunctional spouse process in the multigen
erational family, specifically in the marriage of participants’ 
parents, was associated with the same pattern between the 
participant and his or her partner. The results of the bivariate 
correlation and HLM individual analyses confirmed this asso
ciation. If divergent functioning was absent in the marriage 
of one of the spouse’s parents, that participant appeared to be 
less susceptible to becoming the dysfunctional spouse.

programming or automatic ways of perceiving, feeling, and 
behaving from his or her experience in the multigenerational 
family into his or her nuclear family, such as projecting versus 
absorbing tension in the triangle. This variable was left out 
of the two HLM group models probably because parental 
divergent functioning was associated with divergent multi
generational symptomatology, .231, p=.001. Perhaps parental 
divergent functioning occurred more frequently in more 
symptomatic multigenerational families. FUTURE DIRECTIONS

nuclear family emotional process and the functioning of the 
family as a unit. Future directions are to do a quantitative and

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
On July 30, 2020, the next landing craft to roam over the 
surface of Mars was launched. After travelling 300 million 
miles over almost seven months, the Perseverance rover 
touched down on the red planet’s surface. I watched in awe 
and with some suspense the last twenty minutes of the space
craft’s entry into the Martian atmosphere and the flawless 
landing on its surface on February 18, 2021. I was emotion
ally moved by this amazing accomplishment and could not 
help thinking about what it must have entailed in terms of the 
years of dedicated work and cooperation by so many engi
neers and scientists. I thought of the high level of systems thinking that had 
gone into planning this endeavor over the past ten years since 
the previous landing and the number of generations that 
had developed the accumulated knowledge required. I am 
sure I was not alone in thinking about what it would take 
for the human to accomplish the same level of cooperation 
and systems thinking to address the most urgent problems 
we face so much closer to home. Systems thinking is obvi
ously required to adapt to the impact of the human’s rapid 
population growth and technological advances which contrib
ute to the disruption of the ecological environment necessary 
to sustain human life.

Title: The Growing Picture of “Intuition” and Possible Implications for Bowen Theory
Author: East

31
THE GROWING PICTURE OF “INTUITION” AND 
POSSIBLE IMPLICATIONS FOR BOWEN THEORY
Chris East, PsyD
Over the past two decades intensive research has been 
conducted on the implicit learning system in general, and 
the phenomena we refer to as “intuition.” The import of 
this research suggests that intuition is not an extraordinary 
mechanism in the hands of a few gifted persons, but a 
universal neural mechanism with an evolutionary history 
based in social adaptation. Research further suggests that 
intuition is not only highly effective in shaping positive 
responses, but also quite common in human behavior. Such 
speculation naturally leads to significant implications in all 
learning theory, and Bowen theory in particular. Keywords: Implicit learning system, intuition, dual 
process theory, Von Economo neurons,moral behavior, 
Bowen theory, differentiation of self, chronic anxiety, 
multigenerational transmission
One need not search too hard to find relative skepticism 
in professional circles around the subject of intuition. Like the 
larger culture, the phenomenon of intuition is often relegated 
to the genre of parapsychology, having been left outside the 
domain of serious scientific thought. Nevertheless, many of us 
have encountered real life situations that cannot be so easily 
dismissed.

been conducted by Gerard Hodgkinson in an article entitled

Sciences” (2008). Hodgkinson traces the evolving definitions 
and conceptions around dual-process theory; the cognitive, 
affective, and somatic mechanisms underpinning intuition; 
and finally, the expansive interest in the accuracy of intuition. Dane and Pratt define intuition as a process,

System 1 is neither purely cognitive nor purely affective; it 
is a fusion of both (Claxton 2000, Damasio 2000). System 1 is 
defined as a neural process that can “cut through” details and 
quickly arrive at a conclusion in socially complex settings. In contrast, System 2 is slow, conscious, effortful, detail 
oriented, mentally taxing, verbal and declarative, affectively 
neutral, nonabsolute and nonjudgmental, hypothetical, diag
nostic, and limited in scope. System 2 has the appearance of 
“pure” cognition but is also driven by affective substrates. System 2 follows certain rules in inquiry and is most effec
tive when time restraints are minimal. While research firmly 
posit these two distinct systems, there is consensus that these 
systems operate in tandem as a check and balance—chal
lenging and/or supporting one another. The most effective 
human behavior, in terms of making a “right” decision, is 
often understood as resulting from the cooperative interplay 
of these two systems. The study of intuition, which represents a major focus 
of recent research, has led to certain phrases that also define 
this neural process. Intuition has been referred to as social 
intelligence, practical intelligence, cultural capital, fluid intel
ligence, and decoding behavior.

Jonathan Haidt comes out 
of a larger school of moral psychology that has relied heavily 
on cognitive psychology for understanding human behav
ior. However, during his graduate work, Haidt was heavily 
influenced by three books that are typically outside the field 
of cognitive psychology. They were E. O. Wilson’s Sociobiol
ogy: The New Synthesis (1975), Antonio Damasio’s Descartes’ 
Error (1994), and Frans de Waal’s Good Natured: The Origins 
of Right and Wrong in Humans and Other Animals (1996). These 
texts confirmed for Haidt the importance of understanding 
evolutionary biology (Wilson), the nonconscious emotional 
process that is related to intuition (Damasio), and the build
ing blocks of human moral behavior which could be found 
in other primates (de Waal). Haidt’s seminal work, The Righ
teous Mind: Why Good People Are Divided by Politics and Religion 
(2012), represents his research on moral development as a 
function of intuition. We may think that moral decisions are 
shaped by careful, deliberate exercises whereby we debate 
with one another over what is “right and wrong.” Yet, accord
ing to Haidt, this is simply not the case. In fact, like other high 
encephalization quotient (EQ) mammals, critical social behav
iors are chosen quite quickly, drawing on an inner reservoir of 
social learning that has been unfolding over a lifetime, as well 
as previous generations.

The tendency to distrust—even deplore—emotion has been 
aggravated by the rise of professions with their insistence on 
detachment, distance, cool appraisal and systematic proce
dures (Noddings 1996, 435). THE IMPLICATIONS OF INTUITION 
FOR BOWEN THEORY
Bowen theory posits two key variables shaping human 
behavior, which largely determine the effectiveness of social 
adaptation. The first has to do with the presence of chronic 
anxiety that is active in both the individual and the larger social 
systems. Early in his observations Murray Bowen utilized 
the phrase undifferentiated ego mass to describe the level of 
emotional reactivity, or stuck togetherness, that is active, in vary
ing degrees, in all family systems. As chronic anxiety is more 
prominent in any system, there is a measure of automaticity in 
human behavior generating greater emotional reactivity, and, 
therefore, greater overall problems in human functioning. As 
human behavior becomes more driven by emotional reactivity, 
there develops a need to bind anxiety; that is, for individu
als and/or social units to select largely automatic moves to 
prevent anxiety from rising too high. Bowen noted that within 
the nuclear family, we might observe (a) a surge in conflict, 
(b) relationship reciprocity, (c) social or emotional distancing, 
and/or (d) a relationship change in important triangles—
especially a projection process with children.

objective in the field of psychology, this raises the question 
“How do we employ the scientific method to study that which 
is not observable?” 
On the American scene, during the first half of the twen
tieth century, Watson and Skinner supported a new school 
of behaviorism in which psychology would become more of a 
science by focusing completely on observable behavior. Mental 
functioning, after all, ultimately leads to behavior. Why focus 
on feelings, emotions, and the state of an “inner mind” that is 
unobservable, when study can focus on behavior as a marker 
of the mental state? The resulting school of behaviorism could 
become more of a hard science, focused objectively on the way 
people think, learn, and, especially, make choices.

As a college student 
in the 1970s, I myself became a “lab rat” of many strange 
research projects. Into this split, Murray Bowen began to develop a theory 
of human behavior that would not exclude deep emotional 
process, which is so influential in human evolution. With the 
larger lens of systems thinking, close observation of human 
behavior could inform and guide us to understand the deep 
workings of the human mind. Bowen wrote, 
I conceive of one brain center that controls emotions 
and another that controls intellectual functions. The 
fusion suggests centers that are side by side with 
some degree of fusion, or grown togetherness. ...The 
more the separateness between the centers, the more 
the intellectual center is able to block, or screen out, a 
spectrum of stimuli from the emotional center, and to 
function autonomously. (Bowen [1976] 1978, 372) 
 
Bowen was commenting here on the dynamic interplay 
between the emotional and intellectual life of the human 
brain, and how we manage a modest but important opportu
nity to understand the fusion of emotion and cognition that 
dominates neural functioning. It is difficult, if not impossi
ble, to take an fMRI of a neurosis. We cannot simply observe 
an unresolved transference in subcortical pathways that are 
creating havoc in key relationships, but we can see, in situ, 
specific behavioral patterns where excess emotionality damp
ens intellect such that a greater measure of chaos enters the 
family system.

CONCLUSION
Bowen theory suggests that the development of emotional 
objectivity is important in order to enhance differentiation 
of self. Emotional objectivity is operative, as the measure 
of fusion between the emotional and intellectual systems is 
well-managed. Differentiation of self, which is in place to enhance 
objectivity, is often presented as a deliberate effort whereby 
principled thinking directs our mental process and choices. The thesis presented in this paper suggests that while 
deliberative thinking (System 2) is of service in terms of under
standing the world and making calculated choices, intuition 
(System 1) is largely underrated as a dominant force in human 
behavior. Intuition, properly understood, does not fall in the 
domain of parapsychology, where some people are thought 
to be “gifted” with an almost magical ability to see and act in 
astonishing ways. Rather, it is a product of evolution, espe
cially assisting high EQ mammals with the ability to cohabitate 
and cooperate according to learned behavior. Implicit learning 
was selected naturally and has been employed by the family 
and other social units to understand the natural world such 
that important, immediate decisions are being made routinely. This means that emotional feedback, learned through the 
generations, is more critical than previously understood.

FROM THE EDITOR

BOOK REVIEW
Book reviews are a significant way to address and discuss ideas 
relevant to Bowen family systems theory. The journal will select 
reviews of books, chosen at a reviewer’s discretion, which 
critically engage the ideas presented in the text and address 
their significance to the ideas contained in natural systems 
thinking. Texts chosen for review should represent relevant 
scientific ideas that extend theoretical understanding of the 
natural world. Appropriate areas of inquiry include, but are 
not limited to, biology, sociology, sociobiology, anthropology, 
psychology, psychiatry, and medicine. FAMILY AND SELF: BOWEN THEORY AND 
THE SHAPING OF ADAPTIVE CAPACITY
Robert J. Noone 
Reviewed by Stephanie J. Ferrera MSW 
Murray Bowen described his life’s work as “an odys
sey toward science” (1988, 339). Drawing from knowledge 
of evolution, biology, and the natural sciences, he studied 
the human family and created an original theory that signifi
cantly advances the science of human behavior. Those who 
have studied Bowen theory, and have gained some command 
of “systems thinking,” have found that it opens up a broader 
and more complex understanding of oneself, of others, and of 
the world of human relationships.

five decades of study, research, teaching and clinical practice. Noone introduces the book with an account of his early

was underway in the mental health field, and there was a shift 
toward expanding the lens of understanding human behav
ior from the individual to the family. Working as a member 
of a crisis intervention team based in a state mental hospi
tal, Noone had the golden opportunity to visit symptomatic 
psychiatric patients in their own homes, to see them in the 
context of family interaction, to see the potential of families 
to calm down and mobilize resources, and, in many cases to 
avert a hospitalization. He writes: “I was hooked. A novel and 
exciting way of viewing human behavior was underway” (6). Chapter One 
“Family and Adaptive Capacity” begins with an elegant 
description of the development of the individual. It is a 
multilevel, orderly process of adapting within the physical 
and social environment while “maintaining a stable internal 
homeostasis” (9). Noone defines adaptive capacity as the abil
ity “to adjust to environmental threats or challenges and take 
advantage of its resources.” He notes that “variation in adap
tive capacity has, of course, been central to natural selection 
and the diversity of species” (15).

their ability to adapt to life’s requirements. Noone suggests

drawn between the individual paradigm and a “natural 
systems paradigm” (21), between a psychological concept 
and one based in biology, between viewing the family in the 
context of culture and viewing it in an evolutionary context. With this first chapter, Noone gives a preview of the breadth 
of thinking and discovery that will be encompassed in the 
following nine chapters. Chapter Two
“Toward Emotional Objectivity” notes the obstacles that 
humans face in looking at our own behavior. Historically, 
philosophical and scientific efforts to see human behavior 
objectively focused on the individual. “Observational blind
ness” keeps us from seeing the extent to which we depend 
upon and are shaped by the family. With the shift in focus 
from the individual to the family, Bowen’s research opened a 
new world.

Chapter Ten
Essential to the learning of Bowen theory is seeing its rele
vance to one’s own family and life. Readers who have had 
their curiosity stirred and are motivated to go deeper into the 
study of their own families will find a treasure of guidance in 
Chapter Ten: “Family as Pathway toward Enhancing Adaptive 
Capacity.” Noone brings his decades of clinical experience as 
a therapist and coach together with his own dedicated effort 
toward becoming a more mature self in his own family to this 
chapter. He traces the development of forms of psychotherapy 
that accompanied the development of the theory. He offers a 
nuanced map of the myriad steps one can take, and missteps 
one would do well to avoid, on the path toward a higher level 
of differentiation of self. It is clearly an effort by the self and 
for the self, one that can be greatly aided by a coach who has 
travelled the path himself. Book Review | 87
In the closing pages of the book, Noone offers astute 
perspectives on where we are as a species and where science 
is in the ability to use systems thinking toward integrating 
knowledge from different disciplines. He situates Bowen 
theory within the world of science, noting that it is a relatively 
new theory, and that the family as a distinct natural system has 
not been recognized by many disciplines in science. Stating 
that “much about the theory remains to be fully and rigorously 
explored,” he puts forth a set of questions for further research.

In Family and Self, Robert Noone situates Homo sapiens 
within the natural world, noting the remarkable ingenu
ity and accomplishments, as well as the “expansionary and 
acquisitional nature” that have brought us to a position of 
ecological dominance. As we face a host of environmental and 
humanitarian crises that have come with our dominant posi
tion, “the adaptive capacity of the human is being tested as 
never before” (200). Looking for a way to characterize this book, the title of 
Edward O. Wilson’s book, Consilience: The Unity of Knowl
edge (1998), comes to mind. One important way that science 
is advanced is through the process of connecting areas of 
knowledge and proving the consistency between them. I see 
Family and Self as an important milestone in Noone’s long 
effort to follow this principle in the service of building a 
science of human behavior. He has integrated thinking from 
diverse sources while maintaining the distinctions and has 
provided extensive references to research from many areas of 
science. The book will serve as a catalyst and inspiration for 
further research. For this reviewer, the book leaves no doubt 
that a solid theory of the family will be the keystone in build
ing the broad conceptual framework needed to understand 
human behavior. ❖

Family Systems Journal Vol. 17.1
Title: The Emotional Side of Socioeconomic Status
Author: Lassiter
Pages: 9-30

9
THE EMOTIONAL SIDE OF 
SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS
Laurie Lassiter, PhD
Can Murray Bowen’s observations about the health and 
illness consequences of one’s position in the family be extended 
to an understanding of the significant effects of socioeconomic 
status on health and well-being? Research shows that 
negative health effects are linked to low socioeconomic status, 
even when people live in a safe neighborhood and have access 
to healthy food, good medical care, and transportation. Feeling rejected and not part of the larger society is linked to 
increased inflammation and poor health. Individuals who live 
in poverty but attend religious organizations and feel part of 
a community are more likely to avoid the ill health associated 
with low income. The Whitehall research of stratified British 
civil servants revealed that health follows rank, even in 
situations in which a person’s occupation, such as physician, 
is high status outside of the civil service rank order. The 
human version of primate hierarchy, socioeconomic status, 
is generally stressful, as even those of high status and income 
compare themselves to others. Bowen theory offers a way 
to understand the instinctive/emotional forces that regulate 
people outside of their awareness in their reactions to status 
or lack of status.

Human life and labor 
became more stratified with the beginning of socioeconomic 
status as we know it. Robert Sapolsky (2017) states that even given the stressful 
social hierarchies of primates in general, the shift from hunter-
and-gatherer society to control over agriculture and livestock 
created extreme stresses unknown in the other primate groups. The ability to accumulate wealth led to a subjugation of those 
at the bottom. “Humans committed themselves to a unique 
trajectory when we invented socioeconomic status. In terms 
of its caustic, scarring impact on minds and bodies nothing in 
the history of animals...comes within light-years of our inven
tion of poverty” (Sapolsky 2017, 476). Primate Social Rank
According to Sapolsky, primate societies in general pose 
a greater stress on individuals than the stresses of the physi
cal environment. In other words, the pressures of finding 
food, shelter, and safety from predators are not as great as 
the demands of managing one’s position in the group. The 
stressful hierarchies of primates have adrenocortical, cardio
vascular, reproductive, immunological, and neurobiological 
effects on individuals. He adds that these consequences of 
social position apply to the human as a preeminent social 
species (Sapolsky 2005). Subordinate status in humans, as well as other primates, 
is linked to inflammation and a range of chronic illnesses.

Subordinate status in humans, as well as other primates, 
is linked to inflammation and a range of chronic illnesses. Numerous studies using experimental animal models have 
shown that gene expression leading to inflammation can be 
induced by repeated social defeat or threat of it (Powell et al. 2013), unstable social hierarchies (Cole 2012), as well as shifts 
to low social status (Tung et al. 2012). The animals’ physiology 
changes in response to the stimulus of social defeat perceived 
by the nervous system (Cole 2012). Rhesus macaques have been studied as a model for under
standing the effects of social status in people, including the 
effects of socioeconomic status on health and well-being (Barr 
2004, Newman et al. 2005, Sapolsky 2004). Jenny Tung exper
imented with shifting the social positions of female rhesus 
macaques to examine how social position affects physiol
ogy and health at a molecular level (Tung et al. 2012). She

believed that she could learn about the effects of social posi
tion in humans by studying its equivalent, social status, in 
these nonhuman primates. Would shifting their social status 
change their physiology, with its attendant health effects? Tung experimentally controlled the social status of female 
macaques by altering their social groupings. She found that the 
genetic expression1 of several hundred genes would change 
when the animal’s social status changed.

She found that the 
genetic expression1 of several hundred genes would change 
when the animal’s social status changed. Shifts in genetic 
expression were linked to significant positive or negative 
health effects. The more subordinate the animal’s position, the 
greater the increase was in inflammation and poor health. If 
she analyzed an animal’s genetic expression, she could predict 
its social position eighty percent of the time (Tung et al. 2012). One of the main discoveries she made was that gene expres
sion is surprisingly fluid, shifting whenever social position 
changes. A conclusion reached from her research is that it is 
not one’s genetic expression but one’s position in the group 
that is difficult to change.2
Since it was possible to predict changing genetic expres
sion by shifting social status, Tung concluded that one’s social 
rank is a determinant of one’s gene expression, rather than the 
other way around (Tung et al. 2012). Her discoveries support 
an increasingly acknowledged link between the nervous 
system and hormonal and immune function in human and 
nonhuman primates (Tung et al. 2012, Irwin and Cole 2011). Once the nervous system receives a stimulus of social defeat, 
there is a coordinated, even at times massive, stress response 
that affects the endocrine and immune systems, increasing 
inflammation, even in the absence of conscious awareness of 
the original social insult (Irwin and Cole 2011).

Given the complexity of 
human families and social systems, ending harmful social 
stress over time would require a change in human nature itself 
(Lassiter 2020). There is reciprocity between the social environment at 
one end and physiology and behavior on the other, as each 
affects and is influenced by the other (Bowen 1978, Irwin and 
Cole 2011). Social rejection is perceived through the nervous 
system, which stimulates a stress response, which changes 
genetic expression, thus increasing inflammation and prompt
ing changes in behavior. The individual may be unaware—or 
dimly aware—of the process. With the increase in inflam
mation, an individual may withdraw socially or lash out in 
reaction—sometimes without understanding why—leading to 
a lowering of their position in the social environment, which 
then increases their reactivity (Tung et al. 2012, Irwin and Cole 
2011). The individual may then react further to the increasing 
stress of the lower status, getting into a deeper hole in the 
family or other social system. How can individuals, families, and other groups manage 
the effects of cycles of debilitating social stress? Both human 
and nonhuman primate subordinates alleviate the effects of 
social stress by having close family relationships and friend
ships within the group (Abbott et al. 2003).

and nonhuman primate subordinates alleviate the effects of 
social stress by having close family relationships and friend

the poverty level may mitigate the health symptoms linked to 
poverty if they have close kinship, attend church or other reli
gious organizations, and feel part of a community (McClintock 
et al. 2005). Bowen observed that those individuals who can 
manage their emotional reactions and automatic behaviors, 
even in stressful family and other social environments, can 
reduce physiological and behavioral reactions to rejection and 
blame. Bowen theory provides guidance in gradually learning 
to see social interactions neutrally without feeling threatened 
or taking insults personally. This learning allows motivated 
individuals who may initially feel under attack to take slow 
steps to improve their position in the group (Bowen 1978). 14 | Family Systems 2022 17.1	
                   
Bowen theory also describes the obstacles that anyone 
faces in an effort toward significant change and does not 
sugar-coat the process. It is not only our struggles with our 
own emotions and habits that hold us back, but also the reac
tivity to change in our families, friendships, and even in the 
socioeconomic group of which we are a part.

The film, The 
Town, by Ben Affleck, is an entertaining crime thriller on the 
surface but also illustrates the multilevel social forces that 
keep people stuck. The town, a blue-collar neighborhood in 
Boston, symbolizes the social environment in which people 
are embedded through kinship, friendship, and a shared 
socioeconomic group, all of which are intertwined and tied to 
attitudes and values that keep people in place. As anyone who 
has attempted to change oneself knows, each step forward is 
blocked. In his efforts toward differentiation of self in his own 
family and with others, Bowen eventually discovered a way 
through this puzzle, based on a deep understanding of how 
families and other social groups operate (Bowen 1978). Socioeconomic Status (SES) and Comparisons with Others
Health, illness, and longevity are linked to socioeco
nomic status, or class rank, based on income, occupation, and 
education. The health problems associated with low socio
economic status have been found to result from more than 
a lack of resources on SES may have chronic health effects 
even if one is unaware of the accumulating costs to health 
(Fredrickson 2015). In a study of the influence of neighborhood-level socioeco
nomic status on mortality, researchers found that individuals 
of low SES determined by income and education level who 
lived in higher SES neighborhoods had a higher mortality rate.

Response to Adversity 
Low socioeconomic status is associated with an ancient 
epigenetic response, the conserved transcriptional response to 
adversity, or CTRA, mediated by chronic social stress (Powell 
et al. 2013, Chen 2009, Miller et al. 2009, Cole 2013). When 
CTRA is triggered, there is an up-regulated expression of 
genes involved in inflammation and a down-regulated expres
sion of genes involved in Type I interferon responses, which 
provides protection from viruses.

an orchestrated increase in inflammation. Inflammation is a 
nonspecific reaction to attack that occurs immediately before 
there is time to discern the nature of the attack or what kind 
of immunity is needed (Powell et al. 2013). While CTRA is an automatic program of genetic expression 
in response to any serious threat, it is more often activated—
especially in developed nations— by social attack or the fear 
of an impending social attack. In the early evolution of Homo 
sapiens, CTRA functioned in response to life-threatening acci
dents, war, or infection. Inflammation, a nonspecific response 
to any harmful stimuli, can be life-saving. Increased swelling,

repair injured tissue (Cole 2014). Humans evolved during alternating periods of peace and 
war, as well as periods of social upheaval within a tribe (Wilson 
2012). Evidence suggests that warring tribes and individuals 
within tribes presented life-threatening challenges (Wilson 
2012). Social conditions were decisive in the early develop
ment of the human immune system. Those who feel rejected 
and despised have an immune system that prepares them

In societies free of the effects of war or physical catastro
phe, CTRA is most often precipitated by situations common 
among low SES: social isolation, the threat of rejection, or lack 
of confidence in being accepted, when the increase in inflam
mation has no life-saving function (Cacioppo and Patrick 
2008, Cole 2010). CTRA is mounted in response not only to a 
specific social insult but also to a belief that the social world 
is generally unwelcoming (Cacioppo et al. 2009). Variation in 
stress response to real or imagined social threat, as described 
by Bowen, depends not only on social position but also on 


18 | Family Systems 2022 17.1	
 
the degree of sensitivity to being regulated by social ups and 
downs (Bowen 1978, Cacioppo et al. 2009, Cole 2014, Fredrick
son et al. 2013, Fredrickson et al. 2015). Individuals who take 
social affronts more personally are more likely to be provoked 
by them to reactivity that gives rise to inflammatory genetic 
expression (Cacioppo et al. 2009, Cole 2014). It is the sensitivity 
to social cues rather than the external social conditions them
selves that releases neural and endocrine responses that allow 
for social signals to regulate gene expression (Irwin and Cole, 
2011, McEwen and Gianaros 2010, Slavich et al. 2010). Accord
ing to Bruce McEwen, “subjective social status,” a person’s 
sense of relative standing in a social hierarchy, affects one 
sense of value as a social being and is often directly related to

Through these methods, they were able to assess how 
perceived discrimination affected the pathways involved in 
CTRA (Thames et al. 2019). Relative to White Americans, Black Americans showed 
increased activity of two key pro-inflammatory transcription 
control pathways and two major stress-response signaling 
pathways. Results suggested that differences in experiences of 
racial discrimination could potentially account for more than 
fifty percent of the total race-related difference in pro-inflam
matory transcription factor activity (Thames et al. 2019). They 
conclude that exposure to racial discrimination contributes to 
racial disparities in health outcomes. The mechanism for the 
emotional aspect of racism is the activation of the social threat-
related molecular programs that change genetic expression, 
stimulate inflammation, and contribute to an increased risk 
of chronic illnesses. The study demonstrates a likely biologi
cal mechanism, leukocyte genetic expression, through which 
racial discrimination influences health outcomes. Although 
there are multiple possible causes of the health effects of 
racism, the emotional effects that can lead to a massive social 
stress response and inflammation cannot be overlooked as 
potentially important. The researchers conclude that racial discrimination may 
be accurately viewed as a health risk factor similar in nega
tive effects to those of smoking, obesity, high blood pressure, 
and substance abuse.

In the following story, Iris Origo observed how identifi
cation with a particular underclass can affect perception of 
reality (Origo 2017). Emotional reactions can occur at the level 
of a group or larger society, and individuals who identify with 
the group are drawn into a coordinated emotional reaction. Belonging to a group can mean people are vulnerable to a

contagion of distrust and resentment. Can these group-level 
emotions, triggered through nervous system reactions to feel
ing socially put down or inferior as a group, or a nation, affect 
major political actions? As an upper-class English woman who married an Italian 
landowner, Iris Origo was in a position to observe the feeling 
state of Italy during the late 1930s when fascism was taking 
root. She had broad access to London diplomats, to other Ital
ian landowners, and to laborers who worked on her husband’s 
estate and provided services in the town. Mussolini was decid
ing whether to resist Hitler or to join in a fascist, nationalistic 
alliance with him.

by membership in socioeconomic groups. Although DNA 
remains stable throughout life, which genes are expressed is 
surprisingly fluid and affected by the environment, including 
the social environment and social position (Tung 2012). That 
the social groups we participate in, from the family to socio
economic groups, regulate individuals at the molecular level 
of genetic expression supports Bowen’s (1978) observations 
that individual development and life course are determined 
in part by the larger systems in which they live. Cole (2014) 
suggests that the characteristics of belonging to a particular 
socioeconomic group may be contagious, affecting all those 
who identify with the group.

Barbara Fredrickson and colleagues wondered how 
people could alter the effects of CTRA based on how they 
lived their lives (Fredrickson et al. 2013). They identified the 
genetic expression linked to different kinds of happiness that 
were associated with different ways of functioning socially. A 
hedonic form of happiness would be generated by the pursuit 
of self-gratification, while a eudaimonic form would stem from 
devoting one’s efforts to a noble cause or purpose beyond 
oneself. Fredrickson and colleagues found that high levels 
of eudaimonic well-being were associated with significantly 
lower levels of CTRA-related gene expression, while people 
who showed high levels of hedonic well-being relative to 
eudaimonic well-being showed significantly elevated CTRA 
gene expression (Fredrickson et al. 2013).

Socioeconomic Status and Differentiation of Self
People from all walks of life can be categorized according 
to socioeconomic status. Research shows that health is affected 
by one’s social standing, independent of the factors that would 


	
       The Emotional Side of Socioeconomic Status |  23 
seem to directly affect health: neighborhood safety, food secu
rity and access, quality health care, and transportation (House 
et al. 1988, Marmot 2006, Cohen et al. 2006, Cohen et al. 2012, 
Chen 2009). Socioeconomic status as an elaboration of primate 
hierarchy is hard-wired in all people. To a degree, everyone is 
susceptible to being stressed by it through its emotional effects 
on people. People view themselves in a ranked relationship to 
others, perceiving how they are valued compared to others. Regardless of one’s values and beliefs about the importance 
of socioeconomic status, it is a major way that people rank 
themselves and each other, occurring to a degree outside of 
awareness while nonetheless having an emotional and health 
impact (Marmot 2006). Although the greater size and complexity of society allows 
for more factors to influence functioning, the emotional pres
sures of ranking oneself compared to others may increase 
or decrease functioning in a similar way as occurs in the 
multigenerational emotional process of a family.

have and some don’t have, and with knowledge and practice

less taking things personally, resenting others, blaming others, 
and taking sides with some against others. There is an ability 
to assess a situation with less emotional reactivity clouding 
judgment, accompanied by actions for a positive outcome for 
oneself and one’s group as a whole. Self-regulation, a concept in the scientific literature, is 
being studied in the context of the stress of low socioeconomic 
status, isolation, rejection, and inflammation (Shields et al. 2017, Baumeister et al. 2005, Cacioppo et al. 2009, Wagner and 
Heatherton 2013). Self-regulation is described by researchers

in order to get along (Baumeister et al. 2005). Evidence 
suggests that self-regulation is impaired by the inflammation 
that accompanies reactivity to isolation and chronic social 
rejection (Shields et al. 2017). At the same time, greater self-
regulation leads to less regulation by social pressures and 
less inflammation.

indicate that being in a lower status job compared to others 
leads to increased illness and mortality, even when a person 
makes a good living and has a profession like a physician 
that in another context would be admired (Marmot 2004). The 
surprising discovery that each small change in position in 
the hierarchy was accompanied by a matching shift in health 
and longevity was at first hard to explain. One of the keys 
to understanding the phenomenon was seen in an exception 
that Robert Sapolsky points out in the National Geographic 
film, Stress: Portrait of a Killer (2008). One of the workers in 
the Whitehall research who was of a lower rank had excellent 
health. The outlier was a star baseball player on a community 
team. The ill effects of low status can be ameliorated by find
ing high status in another arena of life. Michael Marmot, who led the original Whitehall study that 
showed that stratified British civil servants experience health 
or illness depending on their rank, describes his surprise at the 
findings that even small differences in social rank shift health 
and longevity outcomes. The remarkable finding is that among all of these 
people, the higher the status in the pecking order, the 
healthier they are likely to be. In other words, health 
follows a social gradient.

a slightly bigger house, though not crucial in and of them
selves, are markers for what is crucial in health and longevity: 
autonomy and degree of social engagement, how much we 
are a part of things. 26 | Family Systems 2022 17.1	
                   
This is really rather surprising, astonishing even. Why 
should educated people with good stable jobs have a 
higher risk of dropping dead than people with a bit 
more education or slightly higher status jobs? Is living 
in a five-bedroom house with three bathrooms better 
for your health than “crowding” the spouse and two 
children into a four-bedroom house with only two? (Marmot 2006, 2)
After a lifetime of study and over twenty-five years of 
research, he concludes:
Autonomy—how much control you have over your 
life—and the opportunities you have for full social 
engagement and participation are crucial for health, 
well-being, and longevity. It is inequality in these that 
plays a big part in producing the social gradient in 
health. Degrees of control and participation underlie 
the status syndrome.

I believe that Bowen theory can be extended and applied 
to health in the larger society, supporting efforts toward both 
autonomy and social integration. Gradually learning to see 
social interactions neutrally without feeling threatened or 
taking insults personally can be applied to the stress of socio
economic status. Bowen theory’s view of one’s position in the 
family, which can be more or less favorable, can be extrapo
lated to one’s social position. Individuals lack awareness of 
the health effects of stress associated with SES, just as indi
viduals are unaware of the health effects of family emotional 
process. Bowen has shown that people can become more 
aware (Bowen 1978). Successful life functioning is linked to 
one’s level of sensitivity to social regulation, and that sensi
tivity can be modified. Low socioeconomic status is less of a 
determining factor when there is a path forward to manage 
oneself to increase responsible functioning (Bowen 1978, Cole 
2014). Bowen theory has a place in understanding the stress 
of socioeconomic status, as well as in guiding people in find
ing meaning and well-being in their lives, in their families, 
and in the larger society.
