BOOK REVIEW
MAMA’S LAST HUG: ANIMAL EMOTIONS AND WHAT 
THEY TELL US ABOUT OURSELVES
Frans de Waal
Reviewed by Anne S. McKnight, MSW, EdD
Since the publication of Chimpanzee Politics in 1982, Frans 
de Waal has written many books about the social behavior of 
animals in ways that illuminate the evolutionary development 
of human social interactions. In Chimpanzee Politics, de Waal 
described the intricate political machinations of males who 
formed alliances to gain the alpha position in the troop. The 
leadership position in the group was based less on the physi
cal strength of the male than on his support by both males and 
female allies. Often a male would strategize how to navigate 
both his close allies and his opponents based on knowing their 
relationships with others in the troop. Aggression between 
males was frequently brokered by a third individual, often 
a female, to achieve reconciliation without violence erupt
ing that would disturb the group’s stability.

the capacity to define self within important relationships, as

The family unit is essential 
for survival but is also threatened by tension from within the 
group. As in human societies, Mama’s capacity to manage self 
in tense situations while staying connected with competing 
males allows the troop more functional flexibility. Is Mama’s 
functioning in the chimpanzee troop an evolutionary step
pingstone to differentiation in the human? The meat of the book is in de Waal’s summary of differ
ent viewpoints about the origin and function of emotion. For 
much of the last century, animal behaviorists believed that 
animal emotion was a response to stimuli from the environ
ment and that animal behavior was based on learning from 
experience. They saw human emotion as unique and differ
ent from the rest of the animal species. The behaviorist line 
of thinking about animal emotions contrasted with psycholo
gists who were beginning to highlight mental process and to 
explore consciousness and thinking while studying humans. De Waal, a scientist who has spent his career researching 
emotion in animal species, summarizes simply and clearly 
some of the divergent points of view among researchers, 
particularly the different viewpoints of Jan Panksepp and 


92 | Family Systems 2022 17.1	
                   
Lisa Feldman Barrett on the nature of emotion. Panksepp situ
ates emotion in the subcortical brain areas shared across all 
vertebrate species.

text:
Panksepp situ
ates emotion in the subcortical brain areas shared across all 
vertebrate species. Emotions such as fear, play, and maternal 
connection are shared by both animals and humans, although 
filtered through the expanded cerebral cortex of the human. He 
believed that emotions are universal across human cultures. Barrett, on the other hand, considers emotions to be 
mental constructs which vary with language and culture. Instead of being hardwired, they emerge from experience 
and judgments of reality. They are private experiences that 
differ between individuals. In the debate between these two 
theorists, de Waal points out that Panksepp is referring to 
emotion hardwired in the brain and Barrett is describing feel
ing, the human’s subjective interpretation of an experience 
(256). In this debate, he sides with Panksepp in understanding 
the foundation of emotion in the brain as hardwired early in 
species in the evolutionary tree of life. Early in his career, Bowen conceptualized the human 
family as an emotional unit that evolved from other species 
that preceded its formation. He thought that the human 
possessed both an “emotional system” inherited from the 
evolutionary tree of life and an “intellectual system” unique 
in the human’s expanded cortex. De Waal’s viewpoint that 
emotion exists in animals in similar ways to the human is theo
retically supportive of Bowen’s view of the emotional system.

De Waal’s viewpoint that 
emotion exists in animals in similar ways to the human is theo
retically supportive of Bowen’s view of the emotional system. In further chapters, de Waal discusses sentience, which is 
widely debated in the sphere of science, particularly in rela
tion to the animal world. After summarizing different ideas 
on sentience, he concludes that it has three levels. The first 
level is self-preserving sentience, which can be unconscious 
and automatic. It’s present in every living organism in order 
to maintain homeostasis and safeguard existence. The second 
level is the capacity to relate to experiences of pleasure, pain, 
and other sensations to the point they can be remembered. This level, which is present in every animal with a brain 
regardless of size or complexity, permits learning and modi
fication of behavior. The third level is consciousness, in which 
internal and external states are not just remembered but also 
analyzed, judged, and connected to serve both feelings and 
problem solving (p. 255). Book Review | 93
Consciousness spans the human and the animal world. For de Waal, a recognition of this commonality is a stepping
stone to the book’s final chapters in which he advocates that 
animals should be acknowledged as sentient beings. He joins 
Jane Goodall and Temple Grandin, both activists for more 
humane treatment of animal species, in acknowledging that 
animals have complex and recognizable emotions.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The development of the family systems theory by Murray 
Bowen included several significant discoveries not previously 
observed. The history of science provides an overview of the 
wide range of time involved between the initial introduction 
of new discoveries and their general acceptance. The range 
extends from immediate acceptance to one taking decades. Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution is an interesting 
example of the lag time taking place following a novel discov
ery. According to evolutionary biologist Ernst Mayr (2004), 
the majority of biologists accepted evolution within a couple 
of decades after Darwin first published his theory. Thinking 
about evolution had been “in the air” among biologists for 
some time, so its acceptance was not a major leap. It took more 
than eighty years, however, for the acceptance of Darwin’s 
concept of natural selection—central to his theory—to be 
accepted by most biologists. Mayr believed that two of the major obstacles in the 
acceptance of natural selection were: (1) the universality of 
typological or essentialistic thinking which had predominated 
since the pre-Socratic era, and (2) the lack of knowledge at that 
time about what contributed to the variation on which natural 
selection acted. It is interesting to consider the same two factors in relation 
to Bowen theory.

In his search for how individuals varied in their basic 
adaptive capacity, Bowen hypothesized that this could be 
observed in the degree to which individuals varied in their 
ability to distinguish between their thinking and their feelings. This hypothesis is explicated in his concept of differentiation 
of self (Bowen 1978). Bowen’s observations regarding how individuals vary 
in their basic adaptiveness was based on two discoveries. He observed (1) that the family generates nonrandom varia
tion in the maturation attained by offspring over the course 
of development, and (2) that over multiple generations this 
process leads to greater variation in maturity among individu
als in the broader population. The variation in maturation he 
observed entailed the differentiation of what Bowen defined as 
the intellectual system, the function that provides the potential 
“to think, reason, and reflect, and enables man to govern his 
life, in certain areas, according to logic, intellect, and reason” 
(Bowen [1976] 1978, 356). Darwin observed individual variation in all of life’s many 
forms. Bowen’s observation of the multigenerational trans
mission process was not simply an extension of the variation 
Darwin had described.

Bowen’s observation of the multigenerational trans
mission process was not simply an extension of the variation 
Darwin had described. If Bowen theory is accurate, the nonran
dom variation in maturity or differentiation of self found in 
the human population is generated by the functioning of the 
family unit and the differential emotional involvement of the 
parental caretakers with their offspring. Environmental factors 
influence this process, but the process itself is hypothesized to 
exist across environments. As I have come to think about it, the course of Hominin 
evolution led to the emergence of a new level of biological orga
nization, the highly integrated human family (Noone 2021). From the Editor | 5
The evolution of a more complex brain along with lengthy 
period required for its development entailed prolonged paren
tal care and the cooperative breeding found in the extended 
family or clan. Bowen theory is not a theory about how the human 
family evolved, but how it functions. But variation in the basic 
adaptive capacity found in the human population may well 
have been the product of the co-evolution of the family and 
the brain, the emergent property of a new level of biologi
cal complexity. The concept of the multigenerational transmission process 
describes a phenomenon not previously observed. The human 
family as a source of nonrandom phenotypic variation, if accu
rate, entails a radically new view of human behavior.

family as a source of nonrandom phenotypic variation, if accu

this concept nor the theory have yet been significantly consid
ered in mainstream biology or even psychology. Bowen theory 
scholars have made extensive contact with scientists and with 
knowledge developing in the sciences but, to date, the effort 
has been largely one-way. The observation of the multigenerational family process 
requires knowledge of the other concepts in Bowen theory. It is 
also a concept not easily tested even though Bowen’s research 
methodology was similar to that used by Darwin. The concept 
cannot be tested by experiments but requires gathering facts of 
multigenerational families over lengthy periods and determin
ing whether those facts are consistent with the concept or not. Much remains to be learned about the multigenerational 
transmission process. Bowen described it as his least devel
oped concept. At this point it has been studied for more than 
five decades by countless individuals who have researched 
their own multigenerational families or clinical families. While 
several longitudinal studies are underway, the concept has not 
yet been rigorously researched.

Research shows that 
negative health effects are linked to low socioeconomic status, 
even when people live in a safe neighborhood and have access 
to healthy food, good medical care, and transportation. Feeling rejected and not part of the larger society is linked to 
increased inflammation and poor health. Individuals who live 
in poverty but attend religious organizations and feel part of 
a community are more likely to avoid the ill health associated 
with low income. The Whitehall research of stratified British 
civil servants revealed that health follows rank, even in 
situations in which a person’s occupation, such as physician, 
is high status outside of the civil service rank order. The 
human version of primate hierarchy, socioeconomic status, 
is generally stressful, as even those of high status and income 
compare themselves to others. Bowen theory offers a way 
to understand the instinctive/emotional forces that regulate 
people outside of their awareness in their reactions to status 
or lack of status. Keywords: socioeconomic status, health, gene expression, 
primate hierarchy, inflammation, immune system

Murray Bowen described his life’s work as “an odys
sey toward science” (1988, 339). Drawing from knowledge 
of evolution, biology, and the natural sciences, he studied 
the human family and created an original theory that signifi
cantly advances the science of human behavior. Those who 
have studied Bowen theory, and have gained some command 
of “systems thinking,” have found that it opens up a broader 
and more complex understanding of oneself, of others, and of 
the world of human relationships. This, in turn, opens up a 
new level of awareness and previously unrecognized options 
for adapting to life. Bowen trained a generation of psychiatrists and students 
of human behavior. A number of them went on to create what

OBSERVATIONS OF CHANGE WHILE 
WORKING ON DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF: 
A CASE STUDY BASED IN BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS 
THEORY AND THERAPY
Victoria Harrison, MA, LMFT
ABSTRACT
This Observations of Change case study describes and 
documents changes in symptoms and functioning that 
occurred over a three-year period for an individual, her 
spouse, and children while she was enrolled in the Bowen 
Center’s Postgraduate Training Program and learning 
Bowen family systems theory and practicing its application 
in her family. Careful records about symptom occurrence and 
intensity,  nodal events, and family work, combined with 
quarterly physiological measures of sympathetic nervous 
system activity, cortisol and brain wave activity provide a 
framework for evaluating the difference that one person’s 
work on differentiation of self can make for the nuclear family. The qualitative and quantitative design of this study allows 
for correlation of changes with nodal events in the family 
as well as with various activities involved in working on 
differentiation of self.

Training in Bowen family systems psychotherapy requires 
working on differentiation of self with a coach or therapist 
who has extensive experience in the process. Therapy is 
based on using the concepts of Bowen theory to (1) observe 
emotional process in important relationships, (2) recognize 
the part one plays in patterns associated with symptoms, 
and (3) make changes in one’s own functioning. Progress in 
therapy is indicated not only by changes in symptoms but 
also by increased ability to distinguish facts from feelings, 
to distinguish between emotional reactions and thoughtful 
action, and to represent one’s self in word and deed with 
important relationships. Bowen wrote that (therapy) 
...is designed to help one or more family members to 
become aware of the part self plays in the automatic 
emotional responsiveness, to control the part that self 
plays, and to avoid participation in the triangle moves. When one person in the triangle can control self while 
remaining in emotional contact with the other two, the 
tension between the other two subsides... The therapy 
also involves a slow process of differentiation between 
emotional and intellectual functioning and slowly 
increasing intellectual control over automatic emotional 
processes. (Bowen [1975] 1978, 307) 
A summary of steps that are described and illustrated in 
Bowen’s work include:

CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
This Observations of Change case study is rich with quan
titative measures and qualitative descriptions that use Bowen 
family systems theory to expand the perspective on changes 
in symptoms and functioning that occur for the person who is 
working on differentiation of self and for family members. The 
following recommendations would strengthen this protocol 
in future studies. This study of factors that affect the process and outcome 
of learning Bowen theory and working on differentiation of 
self in one’s own family failed to take into account the family 
and functioning of the coach or therapist. Bowen observed and 
taught that a therapist’s own family is central to psychother
apy practice and outcome. Future studies would be enriched 
if therapists used this same protocol to describe and document 
their own family work while working with clients. The participant’s careful recording of dates and descrip
tions of symptoms and functioning for her spouse and 
children did provide a more accurate picture of a changes that 
occurred within the family system based upon one person’s 
work on differentiation of self. This expanded view of the 
family system afforded examples of shifts in symptoms and 
functioning both around nodal events in the family as well as 
around steps that Ms. A took to become a more responsible 
and thoughtful family member.

SIMILARITY IN SPOUSE FUNCTIONING
Phillip Klever, MSW
Bowen theory describes how a couple’s functioning is 
influenced by the emotional processes between the couple 
and within the family. Through this lens this study examined 
similarity in the levels of husband-wife symptomology. In the 
study sample, higher functioning families more frequently 
had spouses with similar, lower levels of symptomology which 
were steady over time. In lower functioning families there 
was less frequent spouse similarity in functioning, higher 
levels of spouse symptomology, more year-to-year fluctuation 
in husband-wife symptomology, and more divergent spouse 
functioning.

INTRODUCTION
What contributes to human pair bonded partners often 
functioning similarly? This question came out of a fifteen-
year study of divergent spouse functioning (Klever 2021). The 
study found that while couples sometimes manifested diver
gent spouse functioning or the dysfunctional spouse pattern, 
more frequently the spouses had similar levels of function
ing or symptomology. This article explores the literature that 
examined the factors that contribute to partner similarity in 
nonhumans and humans.

text:
This article explores the literature that 
examined the factors that contribute to partner similarity in 
nonhumans and humans. These factors are assortative mating, 
convergent partner functioning, and partner coregulation 
through behavioral and physiological synchrony. Next, couple 
similarity is examined through the lens of Bowen theory, the 
theoretical foundation for this study. The author then presents 
the research questions, the methods for measuring husband-
wife similarity, nuclear family symptomology, year-to-year 
steadiness versus fluctuation of spouse symptomology, and 
the results. In the discussion section the author elaborates on 
the findings and proposes that husband-wife similarity in 
symptomology is influenced by spouses marrying at the same 
level of differentiation, by the effects of the couple’s level of 
differentiation, and by the emotional processes that manage 
the couple’s oneness. These emotional processes contribute to 
convergent spouse symptomology. Assortative Mating
Mate choice is one of the many factors in nature that influ
ences similarity of mating partners. Biologists have found 
that animal mate selection is generally nonrandom, and that 
animals often pick a partner with phenotypic similarities, 
which is known as assortative mating (Jiang et al. 2013). The 
phenotypic similarities that are most strongly associated with 
assortative mating in nature are size, age, visual signals, and 
structural characteristics.

that husbands and wives tended to select partners who were 
similar in height, arm span, and length of left forearms (Pear
son 1903). Since that study male and female partners have 
been shown to select a mate with a wide range of similarities. Age was one of the strongest similarities (Schwartz and Graf 
2009). Others were race, ethnicity and religion, though the 
frequency of these similarities in mate choice has declined over 
the last century in the United States and Western countries 
(Kalmijn 1991, Salzano and Bortolini, 2002). Partner similari

are level of education and socioeconomic status (George et 
al. 2015, Hur 2016, Sweeney and Cancian 2004, van Leeuwen 
et al. 2008). Pair bonded partners also tended to select each 
other based on the following shared factors: risk tolerance 
(Bacon et al. 2014), cooperation and altruism (Tognetti et al. 2014), antisocial behavior (Knight 2011), alcohol dependence 
(Grant et al. 2007), emotional intelligence (Smieja and Stolar

1994), personality and intelligence (Conroy-Beam et al. 2019, 
Escorial and Martin-Buro 2012), psychiatric disorders (Nords
letten et al. 2016), health (Guner et al. 2018) and gene similarity 
(Nishi et al. 2019).

only by the initial impact of assortative mating, but also by

and shared life experiences have on their similarities to each 
other over time. Biologists have shown how pair bonded part

as vocalizations (Hile et al. 2000), scent signaling (Greene and 
Drea 2014), affiliation (Rieger et al.2021, Snowden et al. 2010)

tendency toward pair bond convergence related to happi

hypertension, hay fever, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, 
asthma, arthritis, and self-directedness (Cobb et al. 2015, Di

mutual sensitivities manifest is in physiological synchrony or 
linkage. This is expressed in co-regulation or co-dysregula

cardiovascular, and endocrine systems.

Bowen theory describes three factors that contribute to 
spouse similarity. One is spouses marrying at the same basic 
level of differentiation. A second is the effect of the couple’s 
level of differentiation over time. A third is the emotional 
processes within the family. This theory hypothesizes that 
couples select a partner at the same basic level of differentia
tion of self or emotional maturity (Bowen 1978, 91-92). This 
similarity often gives the spouses a similar ability/inability to 
adapt to anxiety and life’s stressors and challenges. Anxiety is 
the response of the organism to real or perceived threat.

levels of differentiation. This difference is understood through 
variation in the degree of the couple’s emotional oneness. Bowen described the couple’s emotional fusion, oneness, or 
undifferentiation as a couple begins their relationship. They [the new husband-wife] fuse together into a “new

and incorporation of the two “pseudo-selfs” into a 
“common self.” ([1966] 1978, 166)
The amount of oneness that drives a couple varies accord

less oneness and lower levels having more.

self involves integrating one’s intellect with one’s emotional 
guidance system (Bowen 1978, 362) and sustaining one’s indi

differentiation the partners and their families of procre

and goal effectiveness while relating maturely with others,

to be a resource to others as well as responsibly engage the 
resources of their multigenerational family and social relation

and family stress response (Noone 2020). This moderation at 
higher levels of differentiation reduces the dominance of the 
oneness (Bowen 1978, 91), reduces the effects of anxiety, and 
provides stability that reinforces the similarity in husband-
wife emotional maturity. The researcher conceptualizes the 
levels of individual and family symptomology as one indi
cator of individual and family functioning for this study 
and this article. At lower levels of basic differentiation the family members 
have less self-definition with more unsteady, absent, and/or 
immature self-direction and goal effectiveness, and less objec

The spouses’ functioning is 
driven more by their oneness or sensitivity to each other and 
less by their internal self-definition. The researcher proposes 
that behavioral synchrony and physiological coregulation 
may be one manifestation of the marital oneness. Another 
characteristic of families with less differentiation is more 
emotional cutoff with the extended family and less ability 
to access its resources. All of these aspects of undifferentia
tion tend to intensify family reactivity, leaves members more 
susceptible to the effects of anxiety, and contributes to more 
instability, rigidity, and/or fluctuation in functioning and 
more chronic and limiting marital, physical, psychiatric, and/
or social symptomology. The third factor that influences similarity in spouse func
tioning is the emotional processes within the family. With 
more emotional oneness the intensity of the couple’s sensitiv
ity to each other can be difficult to manage (Bowen [1966] 1978, 
166) and add to less adaptability in coping with stress. Bowen 
theory’s concept of nuclear family emotional process describes 
the relationship processes a couple uses to cope with the undif
ferentiation and anxiety. These are distance, conflict, triangling 
(two projecting onto a third), and borrowing and trading of self 
(Bowen 1978, Kerr and Bowen 1988, Kerr 2019, Noone 2021).

child focus, the spouses’ borrowing and trading of self, and/

symptoms. The symptoms are an indirect measure of the

instrument as the DSFA (Klever 2021) that was used to assess 
divergent functioning. The DSFA has been renamed the SFA 
to reflect that this instrument measured the continuum from 
divergence to similarity of husband-wife functioning.

Birds of a feather do seem to flock together. One of the 
characteristics in human and nonhuman families, especially 
with pair-bonds, is that partners are often similar to each other, 
which appears to be due in part to the original assortative 
mating and the influence of pair bond interaction or part
ner convergence. The automatic processes of behavioral and 
physiological coregulation between the partners also affects a 
component of their similarity. This study added the perspec
tive of Bowen theory which sees couple similarity influenced 
primarily by the emotional processes in the family system. This study assessed similarity of the overall functioning 
or symptomology of the individual partners. Using the overall 
composite of physical, psychiatric, and social symptoms, this 
study was able to compare the degree of overall individual 
and family function-dysfunction rather than just a particular 
characteristic, illness, or difficulty. This approach is consis
tent with Kerr’s description of the unidisease concept, which 
describes the universal, underlying relationship processes 
driven by chronic anxiety which interacts with the biologi
cal processes in physical, mental, and behavioral problems 
(Kerr 2019).

self-regulation and their family interactions included more 
thoughtfulness to manage emotional reactivity, more self-
defined communication while respecting the other, and less 
distance, conflict, and projection of tension on to others. These types of interactions likely promoted more year-to-year 
steady similarity. Study families with less differentiation had less self-regu
lation and appeared to rely more on the family relationship 
processes of distance, conflict, triangling (two projecting onto a 
third), and/or the loss and gain of self to handle stress, imma
turity, and the family oneness. The evidence for this increased 
reliance was higher symptomology in the marriages, the chil
dren, and/or more frequent divergent spouse functioning. In addition, spouses in these families also often demon
strated convergent functioning with year-to-year fluctuating 
symptomology. The author hypothesizes that the oneness of 
the couple and family contributed to the husband and wife 
mutually binding anxiety in their physical, psychiatric, and/
or social symptoms along with the convergent emotional 
processes of mutual loss of self, mutual projection of tension 
or immaturity onto another and/or distance.

in lower levels of marital distance and conflict, lower levels

to moderate the family stress response and enhance steadiness. Changing levels of stress also may have contributed to 
the fluctuation of spouse convergence and/or divergence in 
higher symptom families. The Smiths, a high symptom family, 
demonstrated these shifts in stress, in nuclear family patterns, 
and in mutual fluctuation of husband-wife symptomology 
responding in tandem. Over the first three years Mr. and Ms. Smith each had a mutual decrease in individual and marital 
symptomology. The marital pattern of over-underfunction
ing appeared to be adaptive in the short run with the more

and the over-underfunctioning pattern seemed to be insuffi
cient to manage the family challenges and even added to each 
spouse’s tension. Their mutual positive focus onto the children 
seemed to stabilize the couple from the first through third year. Then they were overwhelmed with the increase in one son’s 
problem in the third year. In addition, they had a significant 
increase in marital distance and conflict from the third to fifth 
year. These tensions and family symptoms increased as the 
resources of the marriage were less available, the focus on the 
problem child increased, and their individual symptomology 
increased. While the over-underresponsible pattern is often 
associated with divergent functioning, this couple demon
strated how both spouses lost self, and each bound anxiety in 
their individual symptoms. In contrast, the Taylors demonstrated how lower symp
tom families with their higher differentiation and access to 
multigenerational family resources seemed to moderate the 
intensity of the family stress reactions. This didn’t mean that 
the Taylors were above the nuclear family emotional processes.

the Taylors were above the nuclear family emotional processes. For example, they had an increase in individual symptomol
ogy as stress increased from year four to five, but the increase 
was minor or below the standard deviation. Bowen theory 
describes how nuclear family processes are in all families, but 
that the frequency, chronicity, and intensity may vary signifi
cantly from higher to lower functioning families. The Jones family is another case example of how the 
third factor, family emotional process, played a primary role 
in spouse similarity. They were a mid-range family on the 


158 | Family Systems 2023 17.2	
 
NFFS and had similar spouse symptomology for eleven of 
the fifteen years. During each of those years their high level 
of husband-wife symptomology was steady and seemed to 
be influenced by persistent patterns of projecting and bind
ing anxiety. They appeared to triangle by projecting anxiety 
through their steady, anxious focus on psychiatric problems in 
one child and on troubles with the husband’s ex-wife. These 
were common topics of conversation between them, which 
was reported in the annual interviews and questionnaires. Their detailed focus on their own health problems each year 
appeared to be part of a process of absorbing or binding family 
anxiety. In contrast, their marriage scored as one of the most 
open and low-conflict marriages in the sample for most of the 
fifteen years.

In contrast, their marriage scored as one of the most 
open and low-conflict marriages in the sample for most of the 
fifteen years. Over the fifteen years their rather high family 
stress appeared to be absorbed steadily in their high degree 
of individual physical symptoms and projected onto the child 
and ex-spouse, while the marriage remained calm. CONCLUSION
Bowen theory sees the family operating as an emotional 
unit with its members reciprocally influencing each other in 
varying degrees. This study focused on one aspect of family 
unit functioning, similarity in spouse functioning. The study 
found that higher-functioning families more frequently had 
steady similarity in husband-wife symptomology. Lower-func
tioning families had higher spouse symptomology that was 
less frequently similar, more intense or severe, more unsteady 
or fluctuating, and more frequently divergent. When these 
spouses had convergent symptomology, it often increased or 
decreased in tandem. The author proposes that similarity in spouse function
ing was due in part to spouses marrying at the same level of 
differentiation of self. Higher levels of differentiation helped 
to moderate the family stress response and to provide stability 
in adapting to the challenges of life. This promoted steadier 
similar spouse functioning.

distance and conflict, child dysfunction, and divergent spouse 
functioning. In addition to these family emotional processes 
and symptomatic outcomes this study found that spouses 
sometimes functioned in a convergent way as a result of the 
couple mutually binding anxiety in physical, psychiatric, and/
or social symptoms, mutually losing self, mutually project
ing immaturity and tension onto a child and/or other family 
member, and/or distancing.❖

text:
FAULT LINES: FRACTURED FAMILIES AND HOW TO 
MEND THEM
By Karl Pillemer
Review by Anne S. McKnight, EdD, LCSW
Fault Lines, written by Karl Pillemer, a sociologist and 
professor at Weill Cornell Medical College, is the outcome of 
research interviews over a five-year period with 1,600 families 
who experienced estrangement. In the process of his research, 
Dr. Pillemer became aware of the concept of cutoff, one of 
the eight core concepts of Bowen theory. He traveled to the 
Bowen Center to learn more about cutoff, interviewed faculty 
members, and then was invited to speak about his research at 
the Bowen Center’s 56th Annual Symposium. Although Fault Lines does not attempt to explain Bowen 
theory, Pillemer’s research and clinical observations are one of 
the clearest examples of how field research can illuminate and 


186 | Family Systems 2023 17.2	
                   
amplify a concept in Bowen theory. The concepts of Bowen 
theory, including cutoff, emerged from Murray Bowen’s 
research with a clinical population. Pillemer’s research 
supported Bowen’s premises on cutoff through a broad cohort 
from the general population who cited estrangement as a 
family dilemma. The concept of cutoff, formulated by Bowen in 1975, is 
the seventh of eight concepts of Bowen theory.

doc_name: FSJ 17.2 McKnight Fault Lines Fractured Families
text:
The concept of cutoff, formulated by Bowen in 1975, is 
the seventh of eight concepts of Bowen theory. The other 
concepts are differentiation of self, nuclear family emotional 
process, family projection process, multigenerational transmis
sion process, emotional cutoff, sibling position, and societal 
emotional process. Although distance as a mechanism to 
manage anxiety in the family was initially included within 
the rubric of the nuclear family emotional process, he later 
formulated cutoff as a separate concept to highlight its impor
tance in describing the emotional process through which a 
child separates from his or her family. Cutoff, as a concept, is 
interwoven within the eight concepts. In Bowen’s view, cutoff 
is a mechanism to manage an intense attachment, or fusion, 
between children and their parents. The fusion between the 
generations is fueled by a family projection process in which 
anxiety focused by the parents onto a child prevents the child 
from developing sufficient autonomy to separate successfully 
from the family. He termed this process “unresolved emotional 
attachment” in which the child does not develop enough “self” 
or individuality to emerge as a functioning adult. All individu
als carry some unresolved emotional attachment into their 
adulthood, reflecting the imprint of family patterns and func
tioning on adult lives. However, if fusion is intense enough 
between the generations, the child struggles to separate from 
the parents.

doc_name: FSJ 17.2 McKnight Fault Lines Fractured Families
text:
However, if fusion is intense enough 
between the generations, the child struggles to separate from 
the parents. There are several ways to manage this recipro
cal fusion between parents and children. They are: remaining 
dependent on each other, cutting off contact, or the child sepa
rates by rebelling. Bowen also described cutoff as a more internal mechanism 
through which a person has superficial, dutiful visits to family 
without genuine connection or communication. Cutoff is often 
a family pattern through which a family manages tension 
across generations. What is important about the concept is that 
cutoff is a reaction to emotionality in an intensely connected 
family unit and reflects the overall level of differentiation of 
a family. This is different from how estrangement is often 


Book Review | 187
portrayed as being a difference in values, a reaction to an 
abusive upbringing, or a generational divide. Cutoff can be 
approached and negotiated through thoughtful and principled 
self-regulation in a relationship system, an indication of higher 
differentiation in a family. Although Pillemer does not address this framework 
for understanding the emotional process underlying cutoff, 
his research goes a long way to describe and elucidate the 
viewpoints of those who cut off and the ways that people 
manage to reconcile.

text:
What is especially interesting is that his 
wide-ranging interviews are a statistical sample, which he 
states reflects one-fifth of American adults (44 million). Across 
every race and socioeconomic class, individuals experienced 
estrangement—and at times reconciliation—without knowl
edge of Bowen theory. (27). Through his interviews, Pillemer 
found individuals cited six triggers to cutoff: (1) a legacy of 
family patterns of cutoff, (2) the impact of divorce and siding 
with one parent, (3) the problematic in-law, (4) money and 
inheritance, (5) unmet expectations between both parents and 
children, and (6) values and lifestyle differences. An interest
ing sociological fact is that more children cut off from their 
parents than parents from children. He explains this as the 
parents being more dependent on their children for fulfillment 
than the children are on their parents. The rest of Fault Lines is focused on the impact of cutoff 
on families and what influences successful efforts to recon
cile. Through his interviews, Pillemer learned that people 
who are estranged from a family experience deep sadness, 
long for reconciliation, and wish to turn back the clock to 
prevent the rift. (56) He states: “Human nature is such that our 
happiness depends on reliable, secure, and predictable social 
relationships, and without them we feel lost.”(57) Estrange
ment threatens human health and happiness in several ways.

text:
First, it fulfills the criteria of chronic stress through a set of 
challenging circumstances that persist over a long period 
of time. In estrangement, individuals experience a negative 
emotional state that results from a difficult, unfixable family 
situation. Second, there is a broken attachment with family 
members which leads to grief and loss. Third, those who are 
estranged experience social rejection from their estranged 
family member, an especially powerful emotion as human 
beings have a fundamental drive toward social inclusion and 


188 | Family Systems 2023 17.2	
                   
belonging. According to the interviewees, the impact of rejec
tion exceeds that of other losses. Finally, they cited the perils 
of uncertainty about a relationship, or a prolonged state of 
ambiguity, which is a mix of both hope and disappointment. Pillemer also discusses the collateral damage of a cutoff. Those who are estranged lose “social capital,” the support 
and pooled resources of a connected family. This can reflect 
and continue a history of cutoff, a process repeated across 
generations, leaving the family without the history as well 
as the relationship resources from the past. These rifts ripple 
into future generations as well, leaving children and grand
children without knowledge of and connection to extended 
family relationships. Part two of Fault Lines, which is the heart of this book, 
addresses the road to reconciliation.

doc_name: FSJ 17.2 McKnight Fault Lines Fractured Families
text:
Part two of Fault Lines, which is the heart of this book, 
addresses the road to reconciliation. Pillemer was particularly 
interested in interviewing the one hundred people from his 
sample who were estranged and then reconciled with a family 
member. The benefits of reconciliation, according to Pillemer’s 
research, are many. Reconcilers, as he identifies them, recon
nected with an estranged family member and neither they nor 
their family member regretted the reconciliation. The recon
ciled interviewees had useful perspectives and advice about 
the process of bridging a cutoff. They advised people to “do 
it for yourself.” Carrying the burden of an estrangement was 
a weight of anxiety, uncertainty, rumination, and guilt which, 
for them, was alleviated by reconciling. Avoiding future regret 
of never reconnecting was powerful for many. Getting back 
into the fold of the family who were affected and reacted to the 
estrangement made a difference. Access to the shared capital of 
the family’s resources and support created immense rewards. Finally, many experienced a shared lifetime of connection that 
gave them a sense of a renewed future. The advice Pillemer collected from the reconcilers who 
bridged estrangement is remarkably similar to the thinking 
that Bowen theorists bring to families who experience cutoff. These include:
•	 Examine the event which precipitated the estrangement.

text:
These include:
•	 Examine the event which precipitated the estrangement. Look at the history of the relationship and not simply 
the “volcanic moment” that blew it up. How does one 
understand the underlying tension that has simmered 


Book Review | 189
in the relationship over time? What is the deeper 
meaning of the event? He recommends to those who 
are contemplating reconciliation to address the situa
tion and not let the tension fester over time and to be 
aware of a moment in time when one can step back and 
think about reconciliation. Reflection and perspective 
are important ingredients of the reconnection process. •	 Let go of the past. One of the most challenging dilem
mas confronting estranged relatives is the extent to 
which people have different versions of past events. A static version of what happened develops. A 
barrier to reconciliation is the effort to agree upon 
past histories. Acceptance that the views of the past 
will not align is important in reconnecting. Aban
doning the apology is also useful. Moving forward 
in the present does not need to involve reviewing 
the past. Building a shared future in the relation
ship is a more productive way to move forward. •	 Take responsibility. Essential to a reconciliation is 
the willingness to take responsibility for one’s part 
and to end blaming the other for the rift. Estrange
ment is rarely one person’s fault.

doc_name: FSJ 17.2 McKnight Fault Lines Fractured Families
text:
•	 Take responsibility. Essential to a reconciliation is 
the willingness to take responsibility for one’s part 
and to end blaming the other for the rift. Estrange
ment is rarely one person’s fault. Often people 
exhibit a defensive ignorance as to why the sepa
ration occurred, ignoring events and tensions that 
they contributed to. The reconcilers worked on 
gaining perspective, seeing the situation from the 
other’s point of view. They often gained perspective 
through writing or by engaging a neutral point of 
view through a friend, therapist, or spiritual leader. •	 Change expectations. Often people have expectations 
about how a parent, a child, a sibling, or other rela
tive should behave or what they are owed in the 
relationship. Examining expectations allows one 
to determine what one can live with to maintain 
a relationship and the benefits that come with it. •	 Set boundaries. A central component of estrangement 
that emerged in Pillemer’s interviews was the fear of 


190 | Family Systems 2023 17.2	
                   
being overwhelmed by the emotion that triggered the 
separation. Individuals are afraid to make themselves 
vulnerable to unwanted demands, fights, criticism, and 
disapproval. Setting clear boundaries for interactions 
was important for reconnection. Pillemer found that 
reconciliation was most successful when parameters 
were clear about how to reengage—moving beyond 
old patterns and behaviors.

text:
Pillemer found that 
reconciliation was most successful when parameters 
were clear about how to reengage—moving beyond 
old patterns and behaviors. Persistence in setting 
limits is important, as old patterns of interactions can 
easily reappear. Bowen theorists would approach these guidelines from a 
different framework based on an individual’s efforts toward 
differentiation of self. Nevertheless, Pillemer’s research 
describing how reconcilers overcame estrangement provides 
a helpful description of the qualities of the efforts necessary 
to change an emotionally charged process in family life. Gain
ing perspective, taking responsibility for one’s part, letting 
go of expectations of what the other will offer, reentering the 
relationship without trying to settle the issues of the past, and 
developing clarity on managing self, are all aspects that Bowen 
trained clinicians engage when coaching individuals and fami
lies to bridge cutoff. For this reason, this book may be a useful 
read for coaches and their clients who are tackling the hard 
work of reengaging cutoff in the family. In thinking about the 100 reconcilers of the 1,600 estranged 
individuals interviewed in the cohort, questions I pondered 
included: How could one think about the variation in the level 
of functioning in these families? In detailing a family history 
and thinking about the range in the level of differentiation, 
could a researcher predict which families were more likely to 
reconcile?

FROM THE EDITOR

In 2004, at the age of 100, Ernst Mayr, one of the most 
eminent evolutionary biologists of the 20th century, wrote 
his last book. In What Makes Biology Unique? Mayr presents 
his view on the science of life and gives two brief defini
tions of science:
Science is the human endeavor to achieve a better 
understanding of the world by observation, 
comparison, experiment, analysis, synthesis, and 
conceptualization. (11)
And
Science is a body of facts (‘knowledge’) and the concepts 
that permit explaining these facts. (11)
Mayr saw the science of Galileo, Descartes, and Newton 
as based in mechanics and mathematics. This view was 
held to be the basis of all science. While describing some of 
the similarities in the science of physics and biology, Mayr 
argues that the science of biology is not simply a branch of the 
science of physics. Unlike physics, a science of the living world 
cannot be reduced to universal laws. According to Mayr, laws 
in physics are equivalent to concepts in biology. He cites a 
number of characteristics of living systems which obviate the 
existence of universal laws in biology, such as the probabi
listic nature of living systems or that reductionism by itself 
cannot explain them. In a major work, The Growth of Biological Thought: Diversity, 
Evolution, and Inheritance (1982), which defined the place of

based on Bowen theory has remained limited. To date, the 
theory has largely remained in the realms of application (clini

theory are presented. In a three-year case study of partici

framework for evaluating the difference that one person’s

text:
The research article by Phillip Klever is based on a fifteen-
year longitudinal study of couples and their families. The 
author examines couples in which there has been similar
ity in the development of symptoms over the course of the 
study. The author concludes that the study’s results support 
the hypothesis in Bowen theory that individuals tend to select 
mates at similar levels of differentiation of self, resulting in 
a husband and wife having similar capacities in adapting to 
life’s challenges. Each of these studies entails hypotheses derived from 
Bowen theory and involve a variety of methods for testing 
them. One of the challenges involved in testing Bowen theory 
is the importance of researchers having an adequate grounding 


102 | Family Systems 2023 17.2	
                   
in this complex theory of the family. The investigators in both 
studies demonstrate such a grounding. Ernst Mayr captured some of the uniqueness of biology 
in his study of complex living systems. Central to this process 
is the development of concepts and their testing through a

spouse, and children while she was enrolled in the Bowen 
Center’s Postgraduate Training Program and learning 
Bowen family systems theory and practicing its application 
in her family. Careful records about symptom occurrence and 
intensity,  nodal events, and family work, combined with 
quarterly physiological measures of sympathetic nervous 
system activity, cortisol and brain wave activity provide a 
framework for evaluating the difference that one person’s 
work on differentiation of self can make for the nuclear family. The qualitative and quantitative design of this study allows 
for correlation of changes with nodal events in the family 
as well as with various activities involved in working on 
differentiation of self.

text:
Among 
the several characteristics of the nuclear family, Bowen 
describes emotional stuck-togetherness or fusion and its 
variation according to a person’s degree of differentiation 
of self. He describes the mechanisms utilized in the system 
to manage emotional tension—marital conflict, dysfunction 
in a spouse, and the transfer of the problem to a child. He 
discusses the implication of the mix and intensity of these 
mechanisms for the success of the therapeutic effort. His 
original drawings illustrate the discussion. In the second section of the manuscript Bowen discusses 
the concept of the family projection process. He describes 
a number of factors or mechanisms that lead to the 
development of the process. Although either parent can lead 
the process with the other in support, Bowen asserts that the 
mother generally leads the process. Her involvement with 
the earliest life of the child as primary care provider and her 
deep emotional sensitivity to the child combine to facilitate 
her role in the process. Her fantasies and fears about the 
child’s well-being lead her to attend to perceived defects 
in the child. The father generally supports the lead of the 
mother. The child reinforces this focus as he or she reacts 
to the parents’ attention. Bowen describes how the parent’s 
worries lead the family to the medical community. There 
the child eventually receives a diagnosis, confirming the 
parental perception, cementing the process in place.

Bowen’s shift from psychoanalysis to systems thinking. The 


From the Archives | 101
descriptive language retains its psychoanalytic flavor, but 
the concept stretches into the new world of systems. In the 
half century since Bowen prepared this lecture, a research 
literature has developed focused on what is called differential 
parenting. The process is seen as transactional, and the 
literature investigates how parents respond differently to 
their various children and the effects of that process.1 Welch 
and colleagues argue that mother and child co-regulate the 
autonomic function of each. Dysregulation of this process 
can produce physiological and behavioral disturbance.2 The 
burgeoning literature on epigenetic and polymorphic effects 
linked to interactional processes adds depth to the idea that 
a child’s functioning is linked to the context of development. Although such research does not utilize Bowen’s theoretical 
formulation of the family projection process, the findings 
are consistent with Bowen’s theoretical formulation that 
a process between parents and child can result in an 
impairment in the child.

Family Systems Journal Vol. 18.2
Title: It Didn’t Start with You: How Inherited Family
Author: Cauley
Pages: 145-148

145
BOOK REVIEW
IT DIDN'T START WITH YOU: HOW INHERITED FAMILY 
TRAUMA SHAPES WHO WE ARE 
AND HOW TO END THE CYCLE
Mark Wolynn
Reviewed by Kathleen Cotter Cauley, MEd, LMFT
Mark Wolynn is the founder and director of the Family 
Constellation Institute, and a prominent expert in what is often 
referred to in his field as family intergenerational trauma. This review will highlight a key component of Bowen theory. There is not an assumption that events are seen as traumatic 
in a family, nor that these events are transmitted directly to 
individuals. As a young man, Wolynn lost his vision and embarked 
on a path to understand his future. Twice he met with experts 
who advised him to return home and to connect with his 
parents. After following this advice, his life evolved to his 
professional focus. It Didn't Start with You covers current research in 
epigenetics and neuroscience. His focus is largely on individ
ual symptoms, family history, and language. He draws the 
reader in for a deep dive into family stories and memories. Wolynn references the research of Rachel Yehuda, who shows 
“how descendants of trauma survivors carry the physical and 
emotional symptoms of traumas they have not directly expe
rienced” (20).

the same right to belong in a family system, and that 
no one can be excluded for any reason whatsoever. This includes the alcoholic grandfather who left our 
grandmother impoverished, the stillborn brother 
whose death broke our mother’s heart, and even the 
neighbor child our father accidentally killed as he 
backed out of the driveway. The criminal uncle, our 
mother’s older half-sister, the baby aborted- they all 
belong in our family. (45)

The idea that we relive family traumas may well be at 
the core of what psychiatrist Norman Doidge alludes 
to in his breakthrough book The Brain that Changes 
Itself, when he writes, “Psychotherapy is often about 
turning our ghosts into ancestors. (49)
 
Although Wolynn’s writing is primarily focused on an 
individual perspective, it is intriguing to read with a Bowen 
theory lens. The eight concepts can unfold in the mind of the 
reader, most notably nuclear family emotional process, family 
projection process, multigenerational transmission process, 
and emotional cutoff. However, any evidence of a suggested 
rigorous and long-term effort that is part of differentiation of 
self, the hallmark of Bowen theory, is absent. A principle in Bowen theory is that the individual and 
the family are the experts, and the consultant provides ques
tions with a research attitude.

A principle in Bowen theory is that the individual and 
the family are the experts, and the consultant provides ques
tions with a research attitude. The facts of the family often 
include challenging events, but only the individual can report 
whether these events are viewed as traumatic. Individu
als in the same family can view events very differently, and 
there can be variation in the functioning of family members 
in the same family as well as across generations. A curious 


Book Review | 147
consultant does not make assumptions or interpret these 
stories but can guide the individual to their own discoveries. Wolynn focuses on the ideas of core traumas and core 
language discoveries. The vehicle for this journey is language, the buried 
language of our worries and fears. It’s likely that this 
language has lived inside us our whole lives. It may 
have originated with our parents, or even generations 
ago with our great-grandparents. Our core language 
insists on being heard. When we follow where it 
leads and hear its story, it has the power to defuse our 
deepest fears.” (11)
Kerr states:
Bowen theory views the family as not just the outcome 
of millions of years of evolution that led to our 
particular species, Homo sapiens, but also of the several 
billion years of phylogenesis that led to the emergence 
of the genus Homo.

A Bowen theory view includes an awareness of the 
impact of chronic anxiety and the multigenerational trans
mission process in terms of how and what is transmitted. The level of differentiation of self—maturity—impacts how 
people view challenging events. When symptoms become 
apparent, Bowen theorists have learned to look for broader 
patterns of family emotional process,  including the impact 
of chronic anxiety, automatic reactivity, emotional maturity, 
level of differentiation and shifting relationships on the emer
gence of symptoms. As Kerr says, 
Bowen theory assigns a very important role to 
heightened and sustained levels of anxiety in the 
development of clinical symptoms of all types, whether 


148 | Family Systems 2024 18.2	
                   
they manifest in mental illness, physical illness, or 
social illness. (2019, 118)
Throughout the book Wolynn poses questions a reader 
can ask, when faced with a symptom, to redirect their focus 
from the symptom to the broader multigenerational family 
emotional context. His questions provide new angles of entry 
into exploration of the family, and pique a reader’s curios
ity. A person trained in Bowen theory can easily discover 
applications to the work on self and be met with surprises 
along the way. ❖

with key milestones shaping our understanding of life at 
its most fundamental level. From the initial observations of

whose shoulders modern cell biologists stand. The narrative 
skillfully interweaves the latest findings with a respectful 
nod to the pioneers who laid the groundwork for our current 
understanding of cellular biology. By contextualizing his narrative within this histori
cal framework, Mukherjee invites readers to appreciate the 
evolutionary nature of scientific inquiry.

Multicellularity is a fascinating saga

cooperative interactions among individual cells, leading to

connecting the dots between the origins of multicellularity 
and its implications for our current understanding of diseases. The transition to multicellularity is not only a testament to 
the adaptability and resilience of life but also a critical factor 
in the emergence of diseases as we know them today. One of the book’s remarkable achievements is its abil
ity to bridge the gap between complex biological research

family systems and each individual’s health within that

tangible implications for medical practice that go beyond 
reductionist thinking and (in my opinion) approaches

text:
Among the many mechanisms Mukherjee examines, 
one of the most important is the differences between innate 
and adaptive immunity. Innate and adaptive immunity are 
two crucial components of the immune system, working 
in harmony to defend the body against pathogens. Innate 
immunity is the first line of defense, providing immediate 
and non-specific protection against a wide range of invad
ers. This includes physical barriers like the skin and mucous 
membranes, as well as cellular components such as macro
phages and neutrophils that quickly respond to any foreign 


142 | Family Systems 2024 18.2	
                   
threat. Innate immunity is evolutionarily conserved and does 
not require prior exposure to a specific pathogen. On the other hand, adaptive immunity is a more 
specialized and precise defense mechanism. It involves the 
production of antibodies and the activation of T cells, which 
are tailored to recognize and eliminate specific pathogens. Adaptive immunity has memory, meaning that once exposed 
to a particular pathogen, the immune system “remembers” 
it, providing a quicker and more targeted response upon 
subsequent encounters. Unlike innate immunity, adaptive 
immunity takes time to develop but offers a long-lasting and 
highly effective defense against specific threats.

the molecular underpinnings of various cancers and other 
diseases. The research interwoven into the narrative paints 
a vivid picture of the relentless pursuit of knowledge in the 
quest to understand and conquer one of humanity’s most 
formidable foes.

BOWLBY’S ATTACHMENT THEORY AND 
BOWEN’S FAMILY SYSTEM THEORY: 
THEIR DIFFERENCES AND THE IMPLICATIONS 
FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
Anne S. McKnight, EdD, LCSW
Murray Bowen, MD and John Bowlby, MD have 
many characteristics in common. Both were trained in 
psychoanalysis, were interested in the evolutionary origins of 
the human, and studied human relationships in the present. Bowlby’s research on mother-infant bonding profoundly 
influenced the mental health world in the twentieth century. He proposed that the mother who nurtured her infant with 
“secure attachment” ensured the mental health of the adult, 
while other styles of maternal care were the foundation of 
later psychiatric problems. His research was amplified by 
Mary Ainsworth, who identified and diagnosed other types 
of maladaptive mothering. His focus was on the dyadic 
relationship between the mother and child and continued to 
be grounded in Freudian theory. Bowen, on the other hand, based his theory in the framework 
of the family as an emotional unit. He believed that the 
family system, as dynamic and interactive, is adaptive to 
the stressors from the environment. The family system 
includes the relationship system with the father and the 
extended family, rather than simply the interactions 
between the mother and child in infancy, as important in the 
developmental growth of the child.

INTRODUCTION
John Bowlby (1907–1990) and Murray Bowen (1913–1990) 
were contemporary pioneers who departed from traditional 
psychoanalytic thinking that dominated psychiatry in the 
years after World War II. Both were trained as physicians and 
psychoanalysts, and each served in WWII and studied the 
impact of war on soldiers who fought. Psychoanalysis—founded by Sigmund Freud (1856–
1939), an Austrian neurologist, and disseminated through 
his followers, Karl Jung and Anna Freud—was the predomi
nant psychological paradigm of the first half of the twentieth 
century. Freud developed a clinical method for treating psycho
pathology that revolutionized the treatment of mental illness 
through “talk therapy” with a patient.

doc_name: FSJ 18.2 McKnight Bowlbys Attachment Theory and Bowens
text:
Freud developed a clinical method for treating psycho
pathology that revolutionized the treatment of mental illness 
through “talk therapy” with a patient. His methodology was 
based on an analyst listening to and interpreting the free 
associations of a patient’s memories of childhood and of his 
or her dreams. Freudian ideas influenced art, literature, and 
the general culture in such a way that a common view of a 
misspoken work is still a “Freudian slip.” 
Based on their observations in clinical work, Bowlby 
and Bowen questioned the scientific foundation of Freudian 
theory and both turned to the natural sciences and evolution
ary theory to understand human behavior. In contrast to the 
Freudian approach of dream analysis and free association, 
Bowlby and Bowen were each interested in the developmen
tal history of the human based in the relationship processes 
of the family. As they developed their theories, Bowlby and Bowen 
came to conceptualize human relationships from distinctly 
different viewpoints. Bowlby’s model was grounded on the 
observations of mother/infant attachments as the basis for 
successful adult maturation, while Bowen concluded that 
the multigenerational family system was the foundation of 
adult functioning. Attachment theory and family systems 
theory are often confused and conflated but are distinct and 
different theoretically, based on differing viewpoints about 
human behavior. Bowen and Bowlby met once on March 13, 1958.

Bowen and Bowlby met once on March 13, 1958. The

The ‘I–Thou’ philososphic notion is fine, but I had 
already been into the Bowlby (from Tavistock) thing 
while I was still at NIMH and I did not want any more 
of the two person relationship. (Bowen 1986) 
What is the importance of understanding the differences 
in the two theories? Attachment theory is a predominant 
set of theoretical premises in mental health treatment that 
posits that deficits in mother/child interactions are the basis 
of mental health pathology and the development of physical 
and social symptoms in adulthood. It influences the field of 
trauma theories and fosters a focus on the importance of a 
nurturing and ever-attentive mother on childhood develop
ment and adult functioning. Bowen theory, on the other hand, considers a broader 
view of the family system in the development of the child 
into adulthood. This view includes the importance of the 
father and his relationship with his partner and the child, as 
well as the functioning of the family systems of the father and 
the mother, and the levels of both connection and anxiety in 
those systems in relating to the nuclear family.

He worked as a physician during 
World War II and continued as the Deputy Director of the 
Tavistock Clinic. At the Child Guidance Clinic in London, he 
began to explore issues related to maladapted children and 
was particularly interested in orphans who were separated 
from their parents during the war. During this period, he also 
published a book, Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves: Their Characters 
and Home Life (1947), based on his study of delinquent boys 
and their families. The Development of Attachment Theory
Bowlby examined how childhood attachment to a 
mother/caregiver affected the development of a child into 
adulthood. He proposed that a child’s healthy emotional 
development depends on a safe and functional relationship 
with a mother/caregiver that begins in infancy. He sought 
new understanding about maternal/child interactions from 
such fields as evolutionary biology, ethology, developmen
tal psychology, cognitive science, and control systems theory 
and drew upon them to formulate the innovative proposition 
that the mechanisms underlying an infant’s tie to its mother 
emerged as a result of evolutionary pressure (Cassidy 1999). As he looked at studies of Lorenz on imprinting, of 
Harlow on maternal care, and on natural studies of human 
attachment, Bowlby came to believe that attachment behav
iors were inherent survival mechanisms to protect an infant 
from predators.

He was influenced by leading European 
ethologists, particularly Robert Hinde and Julian Huxley, 
who introduced him to the work of Tinbergen, including his 
book The Study of Instinct ([1951] 1991). Studying ethology 
extensively, he wanted to rewrite psychoanalysis to reflect 
the empirical method that psychoanalysis lacked (Van der 
Horst 2011). Bowlby wrote a trilogy on attachment and loss: Attach
ment, Volume I (1969), Separation: Anxiety and Loss, Volume II 
(1973), and Loss: Sadness and Depression (1980). In this trilogy 
he writes about attachment in infants as reflecting a process 
of proximity seeking to an attachment figure in situations 
of distress for the purpose of survival. When the mother is 


 
       Bowlby’s and Bowen’s Theories | 85
not attentive, the child reacts in fear, or anger, regulating the 
distance between the mother and child in a dynamic equilib
rium. This first relationship is the basis of an internal working 
model for the child, influencing his thoughts and expectations 
in subsequent relationships. As the child grows, a “secure 
attachment” develops, an ideal attachment between mother 
and child that forms the basis for future relationships, a sense 
of stranger wariness, and reunion behaviors. The alternative 
to a nurturing and attentive caregiver created an “insecure 
attachment,” resulting in a child growing up with psycho
logical insecurities and neuroses. In 1988, Bowlby published A Secure Base.

The concept of the importance of the nurturing mother 
became the predominant ideology of childrearing of the 
time, popularized by pediatrician Benjamin Spock’s widely 
read book, Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946; 
6th ed., 1992), which influenced generations of parents and 
made his name a household word. The belief that the baby 
should regulate her sleeping and eating schedule, with the 
mother being responsive to the child’s cues, replaced more 
regimented thinking about child care of an earlier time. The Clinical Implications of Attachment Theory
Bowlby had a revolutionary impact on clinical practice 
in the years after World War II. Attachment theory, which 
maintained that maternal deprivation is central to adult 
psychopathology, became one of the predominant influences 
on practitioners in the mental health community. Bowlby 
wrote in Attachment (1986):

the seasons and farm animals. His family moved to Waverly, 
a small town (population 1,000) in western Tennessee, where 
they ran a funeral parlor. He graduated from the University 
of Tennessee, with a BS in 1934 and an MD in 1937. Following 
time as a rural physician and as a resident in New York City, 
he joined the Army as a medical officer for five years, includ

the psychological traumas of World War II soldiers led him to 
change his specialty in medicine from surgery to psychiatry. He chose to become a resident at the Menninger Institute in 
Topeka, Kansas, one of the foremost psychoanalytic hospitals 
at the time, where he became deeply engaged in the psycho
analytic treatment of schizophrenics.

During the years at NIMH, Bowen developed the view
point that the family is an emotional unit in which tension 
is managed and absorbed differentially by various family 
members. Through his research with whole families who 
were hospitalized and, later, in an outpatient practice, he 
developed six concepts describing the emotional function
ing of a family system. These included the nuclear family 
emotional process, triangles, multigenerational transmis
sion process, the family projection process, sibling position, 
and the scale of differentiation to capture the variation in the 
maturity of families. He observed that in the nuclear family 
emotional process, tension was managed in triangles, in over/
under functioning reciprocity between spouses, in conflict or 
distance, and through worry, reactivity toward, or focus on a 
child (Kerr and Bowen 1988). Bowen added the concepts of cutoff and societal emotional 
process in 1975.

Bowen added the concepts of cutoff and societal emotional 
process in 1975. By including cutoff in his theory, he sought 
to distinguish the emotional process of severing contact 
between parents and a child from the concept of distance as 
a mechanism to manage tension in the emotional oneness 
of the family. Cutoff as a process specifically addressed the 
“unresolved emotional attachment” or residual dependency 
between the generations (1978). As he read widely in the natural sciences and ethnology, 
Bowen concluded that the human family was a developmen
tal outcome of evolutionary forces over time and shared a 
biological and behavioral history with other living species 
(Bowen 1978). The instinct to defend the family group, to 
rear offspring, to share resources, and to work collectively 
as a unit for survival is shared with a long line of other 
species, although varying in how particular living organisms 
are organized for survival. The origin of the human family 
in evolution led Bowen to formulate his ideas of a natural 
systems theory and to look to science for a broader under
standing of human behavior (Kerr and Bowen 1988). Bowlby’s and Bowen’s Theories | 91
Differentiation of Self 
What is unique about Bowen theory is the placement of 
the functioning of the family unit on a continuum of maturity 
or differentiation. The concept of differentiation is a corner
stone of Bowen theory and central to understanding the 
family as an emotional unit.

The concept of differentiation is a corner
stone of Bowen theory and central to understanding the 
family as an emotional unit. Bowen created a scale of differentiation with the observa
tion that some families function more flexibly, tolerating and 
benefiting from the individual differences of the members to 
adapt to the challenges they face as a unit. Tension exists in 
every family between the amount of energy that individuals 
expend responding to the group’s needs and to each other 
and the momentum for their own autonomy. Bowen (1978) 
called this interplay the balance in the forces for individuality 
and togetherness. Individuals in families with more flexibility are able 
to access their intellectual systems, the capacity for think
ing, reflecting, analyzing, and strategizing in order to work 
cooperatively together to adapt to the challenges they face. Families at the higher end of the continuum have more 
capacity to use the problem-solving prefrontal cortex of the 
brain, to reflect and self-regulate, and to stay connected with 
other family members while operating based on principles 
and values they had embraced to chart their own life courses 
(Bowen 1978). This variation among families includes those in a middle 
section who have some ability to manage emotion and work 
cooperatively together.

of anxiety generated as it adapts to the challenges it faces. 92 | Family Systems 2024 18.2

unemployment, illness, or a climatic change disaster. A family 
with a higher level of differentiation carries less weight of 
emotion from the past and will be less affected by an anxiety-

The concept of cutoff was an effort by Bowen to define 
and describe the process of separation between a child and 
their parents. In separating from the fusion or family oneness 
of the family system, an individual retains an “unresolved 
emotional attachment” to the previous generation. Bowen’s 
use of the term “unresolved emotional attachment” is often 
conflated with attachment theory, but has a distinctly differ
ent meaning in Bowen theory. Based on the level of differentiation of the family and 
their position in the family, young adults have varying capac
ities to transition to adulthood as self-sustaining, responsible 
people. The more differentiated the family, the smoother 
the transition of the child to adulthood. When fusion in the 
family is intense or anxiety is high, the young person will 
have more difficulty in establishing a platform for adult life, 
taking one of three stances: rebelling, remaining dependent, 
or cutting off. These reactions reflect an intense interdepen
dency that constricts the adult child’s ability to establish 
agency, autonomy, and capacity to function outside the 
family. Bowen wrote: 
The person who runs away from his family of origin is 
as emotionally dependent as the one who never leaves 
home.

Bridging cutoff, or reconnection with family members—
both those who are estranged and those previously unknown 
in the extended family—allows a person to appreciate ways 
that “unresolved emotional attachment” to the parental 
generation is present. The work of differentiation in defin
ing self in the family is the effort to self-regulate while

staying connected within that interdependency. It is a step
pingstone toward managing self with more maturity and 
self-direction based on thoughtful principles rather than the 
automatic patterns of reactivity inherited from past genera
tions (Bowen 1978). When a child grows up without knowing grandpar
ents, aunts, uncles, or extended family, not only are these 
relationships not resources, but the child observes and inter
nalizes that tension is best handled with distance, superficial 
contact, or cutoff. The Family as a Multigenerational Emotional Unit
Bowen conceptualizes the emotional life of a family as 
a part of the multigenerational process in which powerful 
emotional forces and patterns flow from one generation to 
the next. Distance and cutoff, over/under functioning reci
procity, and the projection process are patterns transmitted 
in triangles across generations.

The implications for how a professional engages clini
cally with families through the lens of Bowen theory are 
wide-ranging. An important premise is that a clinician has 
worked on differentiation of self in their own family. This 
includes coaching with a Bowen professional to observe the 
emotional patterns, the triangles, and the multigenerational 
process in their family. Over time the clinician works to define 
themselves in important relationships in their family, based 
on thought-out principles. Theoretically, the clinician who 
has worked on differentiation is better equipped to manage 
self clinically within the emotionality and undifferentiation 
of families they are consulting with. Since the level of differentiation and the level of anxiety

is experiencing, the effort of family members to self-regu

Bowlby’s belief—that attachment was an evolutionary 
survival mechanism of the maternal/child bond that ensures 
the protection and safety of an infant—challenged traditional 
Freudian thinking. By promoting the viewpoint of the impor
tance of a secure attachment of a child with the mother, he 
stimulated a shift in thinking about child development in 
the twentieth century. This thinking permeated the mental 
health world in which clinicians came to believe that maternal 
deprivation was a major source of psychopathology as well 
as physical and social symptoms in adulthood. Bowlby had 
a tremendous impact on the concept of childhood trauma. Although he departed from Freudian theory in many ways, 
he never broke from the viewpoint that neurosis and trauma 
were a pathology within the psyche of an individual. Ther
apy consists of a warm and supportive relationship with a 
therapist who “corrects” the damage of early deprivation. Profoundly influenced by his work at Menninger’s with 
schizophrenic patients and by research with in-patient fami
lies at NIMH, Bowen developed a broad viewpoint on the 
functioning and interactive dynamics of whole families, 
rather than a focus limited to maternal/child attachment. He 
viewed the family as an emotional unit that regulates and is 
regulated by the interactions of family members. Over time, 
he developed the concepts of differentiation, triangles, and 
reciprocal emotional patterns to describe those interactions.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
One of the interesting elements in the development of 
a natural systems theory of the human family by Murray 
Bowen was the expansion of his observations to increasing 
levels of complexity during his research. Clues at each level 
led to new areas of exploration and new hypotheses to be 
tested. The principal period of his investigations primarily 
occurred from 1946 to 1975. Recently published books based 
on archival research have shed new light on the early years of 
his research (Butler 2013; Rakow 2022). The theory was first 
published in 1966 and expanded in 1975 with the addition of 
two concepts to the original six concepts in the theory. What I find remarkable was the expansion of the field 
of observation beginning with a focus on the individual, 
moving to the observation of the mother-child dyad, which 
led to the observation of the triangle, to the family as an inte
grated unit, to the multigenerational family, to the family as 
an evolutionary system. Bowen’s investigation led him to a 
natural systems theory involving multiple levels of complex
ity entailed in human behavior. The Individual

The Triangle
Another level of complexity observed by Bowen was the 
triangle. Rakow (2023) described Bowen’s early awareness 
of three-person emotional processes while he was in Kansas 
and reports that he initially used the term “triangle” in 1953, 
though he used the term “triad” in some later writings. At 
Menninger and at NIMH Bowen had observed the impact 
fathers had on the mother-daughter dyads when visiting, and 
later, during the NIMH study, he observed the research staff 
being drawn into the dyads when they became more intense. Bowen’s observations and conceptualization of the triangle 
was central to the theory. In completing his manuscript for 
the first publication of the theory Bowen wrote: 
Several years went into the integration of the separate 
concepts. ...Somehow there had to be a basic force 
that held the concepts together. The idea of ‘triangles’ 
appeared to be that force, but it was elusive. (Bowen 1988, 378) 
He described the importance of the concept of triangles 
in completing the final draft of the 1966 theory paper: “The 
idea of triangles was the cement that integrated the concepts 
into a single theory” (1988, 379). The Family as a Unit

The first seven months of the project (at NIMH) showed
