The Multigenerational Family
The exploration of the multigenerational family process 
marked another broadening of the observational lens. After 
originally being curious about whether schizophrenia 
developed over a number of generations, Bowen under
took a detailed study of multiple generations of families, 
including his own. Thousands of hours went into a microscopic study of a 
few families, in which I went back as far as 200 or 300 
years, and I traced the histories of numerous families 
back a hundred years or more. All families seemed to 
have the same basic patterns. (Bowen, 491)
The Family as a Natural System
Early in his investigations at Menninger, Bowen came to 
the view that if the study of the human were to become scien
tific, it required placing the human as a part of all life, as a 
product of evolution. It remained a part of his background 
thinking as he explored the more detailed aspects of indi
vidual and family behavior.

Now the theory was well developed in Kansas, down

saw ....I conceptualized family as an evolutionary 
form of life. (Bowen 1987a, 18)
This represented, I believe, a shift from considering 
the human as a product of evolution to actually seeing the 
family as a natural system among natural systems. This was 
a remarkable conceptual shift. It highlighted the evolution

step to a more objective view of human behavior. Bowen’s development of family systems theory entailed 
an ongoing progression with clues observed at one level of 
functioning leading to observations of broader processes 
involved in the family emotional system. At present, my own 
view is that the theory has led an increasing number of indi
viduals to an ongoing effort to engage knowledge developing 
in the sciences.

Anne S. McKnight, EdD, LCSW
Murray Bowen, MD and John Bowlby, MD have 
many characteristics in common. Both were trained in 
psychoanalysis, were interested in the evolutionary origins of 
the human, and studied human relationships in the present. Bowlby’s research on mother-infant bonding profoundly 
influenced the mental health world in the twentieth century. He proposed that the mother who nurtured her infant with 
“secure attachment” ensured the mental health of the adult, 
while other styles of maternal care were the foundation of 
later psychiatric problems.

text:
FAMILY PROCESS AND VARIABILITY
IN HUMAN AGING

Laura R. Brooks, MSW

Conventional human aging research has established that everyone
ages and that the process is unique for every individual. An explora-
tion of the individual on social and psychological levels, however, has
not yielded clear explanations for variability in individual adjust-
ment in the later years, Family systems theory views the individual
in the context of instinctual processes in the relationship system
that govern social, physiological, and psychological functioning. This perspective contributes to understanding the differences among
individuals as they adjust to the challenges of growing old. INTRODUCTION

Researchers on human aging agree about two fundamental
facts: aging occurs automatically and there are important differences
between individuals in how it takes place. Aging is defined as intrin-
sic, universal changes in psychological and physiological processes
that begin to occur at reproductive maturity with gradual deleterious
consequences for the individual in structural and functional capaci-
ties (Arking 1991). This paper focuses on variability in adaptiveness
during the individual's post-reproductive years. Conventional human research has treated aging more as a
problem than as a fact of nature. It views the human as unique from
other species. In fact, aging is a natural phenomenon, the last stage
of the life cycle that occurs in every kingdom of living organisms.

When considering the functioning of the individual in the group,
however, similarities between the human and other social species
are more difficult to observe and study than biological processes. Some research of other social species tends toward a view of the
individual as inseparable from the relationship system of which it
is a part. For example, in a colony of vervet monkeys, the presence
of a grandmother contributes to her adult daughter's reproductive
success as well as the quality of the daughter's relationship with
her infant. (Fairbanks 1988, Fairbanks and McGuire 1986). Studies
of this multigenerational process are difficult to find in the human
aging literature. Although less prevalent in human research, observations of
the individual in the context of the relationship system accelerated
in the early 1950s with the family movement. One of a group of
innovative family researchers, Murray Bowen, developed a natural
systems theory of human emotional functioning. Study of inpatient
and outpatient families during the 1950s and 1960s led to observa-
tions that the mother-child relationship, his original unit of study,
was only a fragment of a much larger network of relationships. After
including other family members in the study, it became clear that the
family operates as a system in that a change in any one part automati-
cally evokes changes in other parts of the system (Bowen 1978).

and is affected by the thinking, feeling, and behavior of the others in
the family as they relate to him and also to each other. For instance,
a man experiences a chronic mild depression and psychosomatic
complaints in part related to the extent to which he accommodates his
wife’s demands. Soon after her death, however, a new relationship
with another woman contributes to an improved mood, more active
engagement in life, and stable health. Hisnew found vigor challenges
his children to either attempt to maintain the status quo or treat him
as a competent adult. A shift in one relationship in a family system
has consequences for all the others. For example, with their father’s

pursue their own goals. This shift, then, affects their relationships
with their own spouses and children. Vor. 4, No. 2 Famity Process AND VARIABILITY IN: HumMAN AGING

explain adaptiveness. THE INDIVIDUAL MODEL AND RELATIONSHIP MODEL

Cross-sectional and prospective longitudinal studies of ag-
ing in the human species are often inconclusive and contradictory. However, they do consistently demonstrate that some individuals
show decreases in social, psychological, and physiological function-
ing while others continue to show increases or at least to maintain a
high level of functioning even into advanced age (Busse et al. 1985,
Palmore 1974, Schaie 1983, Shock et al. 1984, Vaillant 1977). Most research defines adaptiveness and “successful aging” as
being satisfied with one’s life. In a review of thirty years of research
on the well-being of older Americans, Larson (1978) summarizes the
effect of numerous variables but concludes that the greatest propor-
tion of variance in scores of well-being is left unexplained. More
recently, successful aging has been specifically defined as avoiding
disease, actively engaging in life, and maintaining high cognitive
and physica! functioning (Rowe and Kahn 1997), The authors sug-
gest the concept of resilience to account for an individual’s ability
to recover from stressful events, and note the paucity of research to
explain differences between people in this regard.

functioning and without impinging on the functioning of significant
others. Individual adaptiveness subsumes life satisfaction, well-being,
health, level of activity, and mental capacity amongst many other
variables. Itis measured by the facts of functioning of important others
as well as self on social, psychological, and physiological levels. Conventional research explores three main arenas to explain
variation in individual adjustment to later life events, such as retire-
ment, widowhood, and a change in health status. These include the
effects of socioeconomic and personality characteristics, percep-
tion of self and one’s circumstances, and social interactions—more
specifically variables such as education or income level, subjective

110 Famiuy Systems 1998

evaluation of one’s health, and perceived support from others. These studies, however, are bereft of theoretical underpinnings
to explain and integrate the findings. In a review of 645 articles in
eight majorjournals on aging, seventy-two percent of those reviewed
failed to cite any theory in the interpretations of their findings
(Bengston et al. 1997).

eight majorjournals on aging, seventy-two percent of those reviewed

formulated, however, since the 1950s and 1960s that focus on how
individual behavior creates meaning and social structure or how social
and economic structures affect individual behavior (Bengston et al. 1997). None specifically attempts to explain individual variability in
response to events in later life such as retirement, widowhood, and
change in health status. Human aging research views the individual as a thinking,
rational, and self-directed entity immune to the influence of attach-
ments and instinctual forces that are common to all life. Relationships
are seen as static and perception of self and one’s circumstances as
solely an internal process. On the other hand, the relationship model considers the fact that
the human is an instinctual or “emotional”! animal whose behavior
reflects in part its position in a social network. As they attempt to
survive and reproduce, all life forms exhibit emotionally driven be-
haviors such as foraging, mating, nesting, territoriality, and rearing
the young. This instinctual life process accounts for the predictable
patterns of behavior and fundamental similarities between species.

Physiological Research

Even ona biological level, researchers have begun to recognize
that aging of some tissues (that is ovary, adrenal cortex, kidney, and
thymus) is at least partly regulated by the broader physiological
system to which they belong (Arking 1991). Old mice ovaries trans-
planted to young hosts generally begin to cycle again. And research
onnonfunctional thymuses indicates that transplantation toa younger
animal revives the capacity to function normally. The long-lasting effects of the individual's early family relation-
ships on an individual's physiology across the life span have been
reviewed by Henry and Sapolsky in their respective articles on the
development of hypertension in the later years and neuronal death
in the aging brain (Henry 1976; Sapolsky 1992). In his summary of
the research on the early pathophysiology of essential hypertension,
Henry states that the symptoms that bring

the patient to the physician with the development of the final
kidney, heart, or cerebrovascular breakdown are only the last
phase ina complex chain of events whose origin lies buried in

112 Faminy Systems 1998

the early experience of the individual and his genetically and
culturally determined patterns of response to the social group
in which he lives (author’s emphasis) (Henry 1976, 71). Likewise, Sapolsky hypothesizes that prolonged exposure to glu-
cocorticoids (central to the stress response) over the lifetime can
accelerate aspects of brain aging.

Research on nonhuman social species also yields powerful
insights into the degree to which individual functioning is regulated
by the relationship with the broader system. For instance, aged
nonreproductive male orangutans appear to be extremely solitary
animals, avoiding even their own kind. However, upon closer obser-
vation, it becomes apparent that they aggressively protect the area
that contains their adult offspring to contribute to their offspring’s
survival and reproductive success (MacKinnon 1979). The influence
of the relationship system has been demonstrated in research on the
differences in the functioning of vervet monkeys whose mothers
are alive compared to those whose mothers have died. Monkeys
with living mothers produce significantly more surviving offspring. They also have a fifty percent lower rate of infant mortality and are
more likely to challenge the rank of others (Fairbanks and McGuire,
1986).

and access to food. Members of the group thus benefit from the older
individual's store of knowledge about such things as location of food
or prey, In the orca whales, the need to catch prey and protect against
predators is compromised in the effort to prolong longevity of the
oldest members. This is done by providing food and assisting in
flotation (Gormiey 1982). In another example, the interdependence
between an aged matriarchal elephant and the group is highlighted
when she dies suddenly. The survivors mill around her body in panic,
seemingly unable to reorganize to protect themselves (Moss 1988). This occurs among the closest relatives of humans as well. An
old female chimpanzee can act as a stabilizing influence. She can dif-

nonhuman species than in our own. Human Aging Research

The results of conventional aging research also lend support
to the concept of emotional interdependence between family mem-
bers. For example, commonly the mental and physical health of a
formerly healthy and psychologically stable spouse deteriorates
during widowhood (Clayton et al. 1973, Gerber et al. 1975, Mad-
dison and Voila 1968). Furthermore, many spouses of patients with
a myocardial infarction suffered persistent distress and major life
adjustments (Mayou et al. 1978). Many studies have demonstrated a higher morbidity and mortal-
ity in the recently widowed (Clayton 1979). Another study of mortality
among bereaved close relatives looks beyond the marital unit to the
broader family system. Bereaved relatives, including spouse, child,
parent and sibling, had a sevenfold increase in mortality during a
six-year period. (Rees and Lutkins 1967). Again, it would appear that
this level of interdependence operates in the broader system and at
a level more basic than the psychological since the responses were
physical symptoms and death. Researchers would attribute these responses to psychological
stress. Individual variation, however, remains unexplained.

including old age, is governed by the system of which the individual
is a part. This is seen as the most important variable influencing
adaptation to old age. ADAPTATION OVER THE LIFE SPAN

Relationship process appears to be shaped in large part by the
interplay of two biologically rooted counterbalancing forces (Kerr
and Bowen 1988). One force towards individuality, the drive to be
distinct and autonomous, is in constant tension with the other force
towards togetherness or the drive to be attached. The balance be-
tween the two is evidentin fish that travel in schools but are precisely
spaced apart from one another, or in a young chimp that insists on
exploring on its own but panics when it loses eye contact with its
mother, or humans who unite for a common cause but eventually

events such as retirement, the death of a spouse, or the development
of a health problem challenge the established balance of individual-
ity and togetherness. Anxiety increases and individuals either feel
or act as if threatened by the other.

self (Bowen 1978). The concept of differentiation represents a single
continuum on which the functioning of all people can be described
and reflects the degree to which the emotional attachment to the
original caretaker, usually the mother, has been resolved. Immature
resolutions of attachment are manifested in a person's continued
dependence on others for a sense of self and well-being. Bowen

early in life, individuals who were impaired in their earlier years
usually experience difficulties in functioning in their later years

Generally, greater responsiveness to others reflects a lower
level of differentiation and a higher average level of chronic anxiety. Chronic anxiety is a characteristic of all living organisms as they in-
teract with the environment and respond to real or imagined threats. The level of chronic anxiety, although to some degree a reflection of
current stressors, reflects to a larger extent a person’s level of undif-
ferentiation. The more differentiated or self-directed a person, the
lower their level of chronic anxiety about managing “what is” and
the calmer they are about what might happen in the future or what
has happened in the past. On the other hand, acute anxiety often
occurs in response to life events such as the death of a spouse or a
life-threatening illness. Acute anxiety, however, is time-limited and
requires adjustments on the part of the person. To account for variation in an individual's and family’s response
to the same event, therefore, one must look to the individual's level
of differentiation more than to the acuteness of the event itself to
understand the intensity and duration of the response. For instance,
in the case of a more differentiated couple, a calmer adjustment to
retirement is predicated on a pre-existing ability to function rela-
tively independently of each other on an emotional level. There is
less anxiety about having more contact while staying in charge of
one’s life.

A significant increase in human life expectancy over the last
century has resulted in the presence of commonly three, and some-
times as many as five, generations of a family at one time. This
multigenerational family has the opportunity to profoundly affect,
positively or negatively, the emotional well-being of all its genera-

generations in a family could be much more positive if aging were
viewed as a natural phenomenon in the continuum of life. This
broader perspective lends to a more objective view of aging as a part

degree to which they are influenced by others and the degree to
which they are self-directed on social, physiological, and psychological
levels. The level of interdependence in the relationship system has
an emotional basis that humans share with all life forms, Viewing
individual functioning in the context of emotional interdependence
contributes to a clearer understanding of variability in adaptiveness
during the course of aging. REFERENCES

text:
BIOLOGY AND RELATIONSHIPS:
ADAPTATION IN NATURE

David Crews, PhD

A useful concept in evolutionary biology is that traits that are
common are ancient and fundamental, whereas less common traits
are more recently evolved. The fact that (1) behavioral facilitation
of reproduction occurs in all kinds of organisms, ranging from
blue-green algae to mammals, and (2) the diversity of organisms
exhibiting behavioral facilitation is greater than the diversity of
organisms exhibiting sexual reproduction (meiosis), suggests that
behavioral facilitation is more fundamental, or more ancient, than
is sexual reproduction. Since behavioral facilitation is an interac-
tive process, this means that relationships and reactivity to these
relationships is absolutely fundamental to biological systems. Because we are evolved beings and subject to the same pro-
cesses and principles as other organisms, appreciation of the origin
and diversity of relationships in natural systems has importance for
better understanding the role reactivity to relationships plays in hu-
man healthand illness, Indeed, inhis natural systems theory Murray
Bowen considered biology and behavior as having great impact on
relationships in the family and society as well as influencing how the
individual can control and modify his or her own functioning. The
relationship process is basic to the adaptation of life, and reactivity
to relationships is built into the biology and behavior of all species.

The
relationship process is basic to the adaptation of life, and reactivity
to relationships is built into the biology and behavior of all species. The humancondition, both inits positive and negative aspects, hasits
biological foundations in the aggressive, sexual, and parental bonds
that have evolved in response to environmental challenges. Evolution is a process predicated on reproductive success. Reproductive success can be defined as the production of young that
themselves reproduce. In evolutionary terms it is not sufficient for
the individual to produce young—for those young may not reproduce
themselves, thereby ending the genetic contribution of the original
individual to future generations. In other words, if the individual

ogy and Neuroscience, The University of Texas at Austin, Texas. © Georgetown Family Center, 1998 99

is to have an impact at least two generations must follow. To most people reproduction is equated with sex, and one of
the great questions in evolutionary biology is Why does sex exist? To
an evolutionary biologist sex means meiosis or the recombination of
genes following fertilization or when the chromosomes pair. Recent
work suggests that recombination is a way to get rid of deleterious
genes, But to most, sex means males and females. It is widely ac-
cepted that biparental reproduction developed very early in the
origin of life.

doc_name: FSJ 4.2 Crews Biology and Relationships Adaptation
text:
It is widely ac-
cepted that biparental reproduction developed very early in the
origin of life. That is, offspring were produced from the union of
two gametes at some stage of the life cycle. Initially, biparentalism may have involved the union of equal-
sized gametes (isogamy), asis the case in some unicellular organisms
today. But by far the more common pattern is the union of gametes
of unequal size, with small gametes uniting with larger ones (an-
isogamy). This represents sperm and eggs or, in essence, males and
females. The origin of males and females then generated a new set
of phenomena such as sexual dimorphisms, sexual selection, the
mating system, competition both between and within the sexes, and

BOWEN THEORY AND EVOLUTIONARY THEORY

Michael E. Kerr, MD

Darwin's theory ofevolution by natural selection explains how highly
integrated social systems evolve. Bowen's family systems theory
describes how relationship systems function. This article reviews
the contributions of Darwin and others to the theory of natural
selection, describes basic concepts in Bowen theory, applies Bowen
theory to naked mole-rat colonies, and discusses ideas in Bowen
theory that might expand evolutionary theory's understanding of
living systems. These ideas include multigenerational emotional
programming, emotional regression, and an individuality-together-
ness balance in relationship systems. The article does not attempt
to integrate the two theories or to explain one theory in the context
of the other, but to delineate their different perspectives on the same
life processes,

ory of evolution by natural selection and to explore Bowen theory's
potential contributions to the understanding of all living systems. The article does not attempt to apply the theory of natural selection
to the human family. Family systems theory was developed by psychiatrist, Mur-
ray Bowen (1978). The theory conceptualizes the human family as
an emotional unit.

Family systems theory was developed by psychiatrist, Mur-
ray Bowen (1978). The theory conceptualizes the human family as
an emotional unit. The term “emotional” means that there are basic
forces and patterns operating in families that have evolved over
several billion years. Man’s large brain has spawned language, a
complex psychology, and an elaborate culture but, as important as
these developments have been, the most fundamental forces and
patterns governing family functioning appear to have evolved long
before the human neocortex evolved. The term “unit” means that a
family is a well-organized system of interlocking relationships. This

act as much as internal forces affect how they act; each individual's
behavior functions to maintain patterns of interaction in the family
system, and patterns of interaction in the system function to regulate
each individual's behavior. Families differ in the intensity to which
the relationship system pressures individuals to function in certain
ways, and individuals differ in how much choice they have about

text:
Bowen theory and Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by
natural selection (1859) are distinct in that the former describes how a
system functions and the latter describes how a system evolves, Bowen
theory describes the functioning of the human family emotional
system. Natural selection describes the interplay of forces that lead
to the evolution of, for example, the social system of a hive bee or
the anatomy of a giraffe. The myriad observations on which natu-
ral selection rests include detailed studies of the organization and
functioning of the social systems of many species, but the theory
itself is not about how these systems function. Natural selection ex-
plains how individual traits, both anatomical and behavioral, and
types of social organization function in the service of survival and
reproduction. Evolutionary biologists distinguish between proximate cau-
sation and ultimate causation. Proximate causation describes how
certain stimuli in an organism’s environment and processes operat-
ing within the organism trigger ways of reacting and functioning
that the organism has evolved. For example, a seasonal decrease in
daylight hours triggers migratory behavior in birds. Ultimate causa-
tion, in contrast, attempts to explain why an organism has evolved
its particular morphology and ways of functioning.

Living organisms
continually change as their structures and instincts undergo slight
variations. Some variations are heritable, thus can accumulate in
descendants over generations and spread slowly through a popula-
tion. After many generations, an accumulation of slight variations
may modify the structures and instincts of the individuals in a popu-
lation sufficiently to endow its members with enough distinguishing
traits to demarcate the population as a new species. The heritable variations that spread through a population are
those that render an organism and its descendants more adaptive,
more able to survive and reproduce. Nature “selects” the organ-
isms that have the adaptive traits in the sense that these individu-
als will gradually monopolize a niche’s life-sustaining resources,
consequently making it difficult for their less adapted competitors
to survive. If a new trait enables an organism to access a new life-
sustaining resource in a niche, this reduces competition and allows
both the variant and original populations to co-exist. This leads to
an increase in the diversity of life forms in a niche. Survival in an environmental niche depends on an organism's
abilities to cope with the physical environment and to manage in-
teractions successfully with members of its own and other species.

in colonies of overlapping generations, one or a few individuals
produce all the offspring, and all other individuals are functionally
sterile, helping to rear the young and protect the colony, Altruism,
along with cohesion and cooperation are key properties of social
existence according to Edward O. Wilson (1975). The hypothesis of family selection answers the question of
how sterile altruists can evolve by natural selection, but it does not
answer other important questions about the evolution of complex
social systems. For example, the hypothesis does not explain why
exaggerated forms of altruism and other features of eusociality have
evolved in certain taxonomic groups and not in others (Alexander

This type of formulation is also referred to as kin
selection. The basic idea is that the greater the degree of genetic re-
latedness among individuals in a community, the stronger their ten-
dency to evolve social behaviors such as altruism. In other words, a
close genetic relationship is the primary incentive for social evolution. The reason for this link between the evolution of social behavior and
genetic relatedness is that if an individual behaves altruistically to-
wards a close relative, even though his actions may jeopardize his
individual fitness (his number of surviving offspring), the actions
may still raise his inclusive or genetic fitness (his number of surviv-
ing genes). In this model of social evolution, the survival of one’s
genes is more critical than the survival of one’s offspring. An action can raise inclusive fitness even though it may lower
individual fitness because one’s relatives have at least some genes
identical to one’s own; the closer the relative, the higher the percent-
age of identical genes. If the beneficiary of an altruist’s action is suffi-
ciently closely related to him, and if the altruism sufficiently raises
the beneficiary's individual fitness, it can compensate for any loss
the action causes in the altruist’s individual fitness.

plains why so many species that have evolved eusociality belong to

all hymenopteran species have a closer genetic relationship with

species. This does not result from inbreeding, but from an unusual
system of geneticinheritance. Therefore, a sterile worker ant tending
her colony’s larval brood is aiding the survival of sisters who have

in the habitat. (3) It increases their use of an extremely localized re-
source, such as a safe sleeping site or suitable breeding site. In other

In their model, the evolution of a colony begins when changes
in selection pressure (resulting from members of a species mov-

favor individuals that belong to a characteristically solitary species
developing more social tolerance. The increased social tolerance,
which Lin and Michener suggest may be genetically based, makes
it possible for adult females of the same generation to found nests
together. Field observations suggest that these nest founders are
often not closely related genetically. Once a nest has formed, a divi-
sion of labor emerges. The mechanisms for establishing the divi-
sion of labor vary depending on the species. The division of labor
is characterized by one individual functioning as the principal egg
layer (the queen) and the other individuals functioning as partially
or completely sterile helpers (the auxiliaries). This is referred to as
a semisocial colony. Aqueen gains fitness in asemisocial colony because she benefits
from defensive and foraging activities carried out by the auxiliaries. An auxiliary female can gain fitness in several ways. One way is for
her to bide her time in the safety of the nest until the queen leaves
or dies, then take over as the new queen. Another way is for her to
lay her own eggs surreptitiously in the nest.

The concept of reciprocal altruism was formulated by Robert Triv-
ers (1971) to explain how cooperation between unrelated individuals
of the same or different species can evolve by natural selection. The
concept is similar to mutualistic social behavior. Reciprocal altruism
occurs in the following way: an individual behaves altruistically
towards an unrelated individual; the action induces the unrelated
individual to behave altruistically in return (immediately or later);
the reciprocated altruism produces a net gain in individual fitness
for the individual who first acted altruistically (the help he receives
increases his fitness more than the help he gave decreased it); thus,
natural selection preserves the genes encoding for altruism in the first
individual. The evolution of reciprocal altruism requires repeated
interactions between the cooperating individuals.

Having reviewed some basic ideas about how social systems
evolve by natural selection, the discussion will now shift to Bowen
theory's description of how family systems function. One distinction
between the theory of natural selection and Bowen theory is that
while both theories address the phenomena of complex biological
systems, Bowen theory's vantage point is the system as a whole and
natural selection theory looks at the system through the “eyes” of
its individual members. Bowen theory concentrates on how indi-
vidual behaviors function to maintain patterns of interaction in a
relationship system and on how the patterns regulate individual
behaviors; evolutionary theory concentrates on how an organism's
behavior functions to enhance its genetic fitness. The two perspec-
tives on behavior can overlap because an organism's behavior can
enhance its genetic fitness by maintaining a pattern of interaction
in a relationship system. BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY

There are many definitions of what constitutes a family, Bowen
(1985) defined a family as the total number of individuals attached to
an emotional nucleus. By this definition, an individual is part of a
family if the forces and patterns operating in the family unit affect
his emotional functioning and his emotional functioning affects
the forces and patterns in the unit.

The theory distinguishes between an emotional system, a feeling

system “includes the force that biology defines as instinct, reproduc-

system, subjective emotional and feeling states, and the forces that

tional system is not necessarily identical to the emotional systems
of other species, but it has evolved gradually during the long line
of species ancestral to Homo sapiens. This makes it likely that some
common denominators exist between the human emotional system
and the emotional systems of other species. Bowen writes:

The theory postulates that far more human activity is gov-

to admit, and there is far more similarity than dissimilarity
between the “dance of life” in lower forms and the “dance
of life” in human forms. (1978, 305)

The intellectual system is a function of the cerebral cortex, the
most recently evolved part of the human brain. This system enables
human beings to think, reason, and reflect, and to use those abilities
to govern certain areas of their lives. The ability to discriminate be-
tween intellectual and emotional functioning enables people to exert
some conscious control over their automatic emotional reactivity.

that generate chronic anxiety. Comfortable relationships can calm

poorly differentiated people to relationship disturbances. For exam-
ple, the lower a person’s level of differentiation, the more reactive
he is to real or imagined shifts in distance from or involvement with
important others. People sometimes express these reactions as feel-
ing “too isolated” or “too crowded” in their relationships. Relationships can generate chronic anxiety, and anxiety can
affect the character of relationships. For example, one individual
may be anxious, but become even more anxious in reaction to others’

matic response is to attempt to reduce anxiety in themselves. (A
more thoughtful response might be to tolerate the anxiety.) An
automatic response when people feel isolated or unsupported is to
make more emotional contact with others; an automatic response
when people feel crowded or adversely affected by others is to get
more distance. Because everyone in an anxious system is attempting
to get comfortable, the system is unstable. However, all relationship
systems have patterns of emotional functioning that help stabilize the
system by “binding” anxiety in certain parts of it. Family theory describes four patterns of emotional functioning:
emotional distance, emotional conflict, reciprocal functioning, and triangles. The patterns reduce individual anxiety by binding or integrating it

withdrawal or internal mechanisms) reduces anxiety generated by
too much contact. Emotional conflict (verbal or nonverbal) reduces
anxiety generated by too much contact or too much distance.

Symptoms tend to impair the functioning
of a relationship system. A decline in system functioning is termed
an emotional regression. Usually one of two scenarios unfolds after clinical symptoms
develop in a relationship system. In one scenario, a family gets
highly focused on the symptoms and symptomatic member, and
the symptomatic member becomes (to varying degrees) chronically
dysfunctional and dependent on the family. This type of “caretaker-
patient” interaction can bind family anxiety and thus allow a system
to regain stability. The stability occurs, however, at the expense of
the group becoming preoccupied with its internal problems and hav-
ing a chronically ill member. In another scenario, the symptoms so
threaten a family that they generate even more anxiety and intensify
the regression. As the regression deepens, symptoms may appear in
multiple people. In contrast to these scenarios, symptoms sometimes
serve as a stimulus for a system to pull out of a regression. A multigenerational transmission process determines the
levels of differentiation of self of the members of a family unit and
the consequent vulnerability of the unit to regressions in emotional
functioning. The information determining level of differentiation
is transmitted through genes, intrauterine effects (Noone 1995), be-
havior, and the communication of attitudes, values, and beliefs.

The purpose of describing this species in such detail is to illus-

families operate ina distantly related mammalian species. The forces
and patterns could have evolved independently in the phylogenetic
lines leading to human beings and naked mole-rats, but it is more
likely that both species exhibit them because they evolved before
the phylogenetic lines split. If this is true, it supports the idea that
fundamental and highly influential aspects of human emotional
functioning evolved long before the human neocortex evolved, long
before the emergence ofa complex psychology, elaborate culture, and
language. The far more complex brain of Homo sapiens adds myriad
details to human behavior that make human beings different from
naked mole-rats in important ways, but the similarities between the
two species are as important for understanding human behavior as
the differences. Ecology

Naked mole-rats are subterranean-dwelling rodents that inhabit
the semiarid and desert regions of the horn of Africa. Their fossil
record there extends back three million years (Van Couvering 1980). They are hairless creatures small enough to fit into the palm of a
human hand. Colonies range in size from 25-295 members, with an
average being seventy to eighty members (Brett 1991a). Naked mole-rats have two large protruding incisors they use
for digging, feeding, and fighting.

Naked mole-rats have two large protruding incisors they use
for digging, feeding, and fighting. They excavate extensive burrow
systems by forming digging teams composed of a long line of ani-
mals. The lead animal in a line digs to extend a tunnel, then pushes
the excavated dirt under itself to the animal behind it. The next in
line pushes the dirt under itself to the one behind it, and so on down
the line until reaching the last animal, who kicks it onto the surface. Burrow systems consist mainly of shallow foraging tunnels running
below ground at the depth of a colony’s food sources; the rest of the
system is deeper and includes nests, toilet areas, and food storage
areas (Jarvis and Bennett 1991). Naked mole-rats feed on widely
spaced and patchily distributed underground roots, tubers, and
bulbs. The food is difficult to locate, but a colony can survive on it
because many individuals search for the food and then transport it
to the nest and storage areas for all to consume. Vor. 4, No. 2 Bowen Theory Ano Evouutionary THEORY 137

It appears the inhospitable environment that is home to naked
mole-rats has been a key selective force for their evolving to live in
groups and cooperate extensively (Alexander 1991, Brett 1991b), An
observation supporting this hypothesis is that members of different
species of mole-rats that inhabit regions with plentiful rainfall usually
live solitary existences (Jarvis and Bennett 1991).

Anaked mole-rat colony has only one breeding female and one
to three breeding males. They are the reproductive specialists for a

defend the colony against intruders and smaller animals tend to do
maintenance work (Jarvis et al, 1991). This correlation is complex
in that an animal may perform one task when it is young and small
and a different task when fully grown.

Strong pair-bonding exists between a breeding female and
each of the breeding males, and an especially strong bond typically
exists with one male. These relationships persist outside as well as
during the mating period (Jarvis and Bennett 1991), The breeding
female and her primary consort are usually in proximity. If she
leaves the nest to roam the burrows, he soon follows her. The bond
between a breeding female and a breeding male also manifests in

side by side in the naso-anal position, rousing periodically to smell
or rub the partner's genital area (Jarvis 1991), Ano-genital nuzzling
sometimes occurs between a breeder and a nonbreeding animal (of

nonbreeders unless there is colony strife.

Nonbreeding animals in a colony do not pair-bond, but they
do interact and communicate almost continuously. Interactions
range from harmonious to highly conflictual. The most common
vocalization in a colony is a “soft chirp.” Soft chirping accompanies
harmonious interactions, and may serve as a contact or cohesion call
among colony members (Pepper et al. 1991), Aggressive interactions
are accompanied by loud chirps. In general, an animal reacts ag-
gressively if a colony mate interferes with his getting something he
wants or tries to take something he has. For example, if an animal
is behind another in a tunnel and wants to pass, the lead animal
may block him, triggering both animals to emit loud chirps. After
a brief vocal exchange, the lead animal may squat down and let the
rear one pass over him, particularly if the rear one is bigger than he
is. Sometimes the lead animal will turn, gape its jaws, and threaten
the rear one with its incisors. A bout of “incisor fencing” and biting
may then ensue. Though momentarily fierce, the conflict is typically
short-lived and resolves without serious injury. The breeding female is the most dominant animal in a colony,

(Reeve and Sherman 1991), To avoid such treatment by a breeding

of a colony, but the animals spend a majority of their time huddling
together peacefully in the nest area. Pressing against and lying on
top of one another reduces the energy demand of a colony (Brett
1991b), This is because the physical contact helps the animals control
evaporative water loss and body temperature (Jarvis and Bennett
1991). In other words, naked mole-rats have evolved to use external
processes such as relationships to help regulate certain internal func-
tions. Presumably, such adaptations have evolved because they are
more efficient for this species in this environmental niche than other
types of water and temperature control (Alexander 1991). Relationships and Physiology

Relationships affect the physiology of naked mole-rats in other
important ways. One way is that the number of animals living ina
colony constrains the physical growth of the colony’s members.

Once a male or female naked mole-rat becomes a breeder in a

Group Agonistic Interactions

Another aspect of life in a naked mole-rat colony is coordinated
group attacks on predators, on foreign naked mole-rats, and even
on colony mates. If a poisonous snake enters a colony in search of
prey, the individuals that discover the snake hiss and bite at it, sound
alarm grunts, and often push dirt into the tunnel to block its further
entry (Lacey et al. 1991). The alarm calls rapidly summon large
nonbreeding colony members to the site. The defenders may stalk

bites from their incisors (Alexander 1991). Naked mole-rats are highly xenophobic (Brett 1991a). One

hours after parturition (Lacey et al. 1991). In colonies where most

a pup sheltered within the curve of their bodies, gently nudging
and grooming it. In sharp contrast, in colonies where a low litter
survival rate can be predicted, tunnel-born pups may never make it
to the nest. They often die from physical trauma inflicted by highly
energetic subadult animals sweeping and kicking them through
the tunnels. Pups that are in the nest are not retrieved if they fall
out, and nonbreeding adults may even drag or kick them out. The
pups are placed at further risk by the breeding female nursing them
irregularly. In some poorly functioning colonies, adult animals
cannibalize newborn pups.

emotional conflict are easily observed in naked mole-rats because

between the breeding female and another colony member, and her
excited behavior and vocalizations trigger other colony members to

TIONARY BIOLOGY

Having reviewed some of the central ideas in both evolution-
ary theory and Bowen theory, and having applied Bowen theory
to naked mole-rats, the next question to address is whether Bowen
theory describes importantaspects about the functioning ofemotional
systems that current evolutionary theory either does not address
or does not address adequately. The thesis to be developed here is
that Bowen theory, particularly with its emphasis on relationship
processes, addresses phenomena that are not presently emphasized
by evolutionary theory but that can contribute to evolutionary
theory. Furthermore, the complexity of the phenomena may offer
a challenge to evolutionary theorists to explain their evolution by
natural selection.*

Three phenomena or emotional processes described by Bowen
theory will be discussed. The first process is emotional programming. Emotional programming is an important process to consider for
understanding the transmission of information across generations
and it may also provide a link between role differentiation and level
of differentiation. The second process, emotional regression, will be
described in considerable detail because, of the three processcs, it
has the most obvious potential for extension to nonhuman species.

individual development and behavior by a relationship system, are
easily incorporated into Bowen theory. However, Bowen theory’s
concept of a multigenerational transmission process is broader than
what biologists generally mean by behavioral transmission. The
multigenerational transmission process includes the emotional pro-
gramming of one generation by the generations preceding it. The

transmission and emotional programming both involve learning

content of the information transmitted across generations (such as a
specific skill or belief) and emotional programming refers to a process
between the generations.

Emotional Programming in Human Families

Emotional programming occurs through the ongoing interac-
tions parents and other family members have with a child during
his developmental years. Some programming may occur during in-
trauterine development. Emotional programming appears to affect
a child’s biochemical, physiological, psychological, and relationship
functioning. Differences in the intensity of family triangles result
in siblings being programmed differently. In other words, parents
typically focus more on one child than on the other(s). Chronic anx-
iety drives the more intense focus, not the reality needs of the child. Parents commonly say they are more involved with or worry more
about one child because that child has more problems or needs but
miss how they unwittingly program the child to need more of their
energy and attention. Their unrealistic needs for and expectations
of the child program him to have unrealistic needs for and expecta-
tions of them. The process is anchored in the emotional system but
includes complex feeling and psychological components. The more focused-on child develops more of a “relationship ori-
entation” than his sibling(s). This means his functionin g and ability
to maintain a feeling of well-being (and accompanying physiological
equilibrium) are more dependent on the approval, acceptance, and
reinforcement of others than is the case with his sibling(s).

The description that follows of prairie voles and montane voles

behavior except during the postpartum period. Adults live in iso-

they do often and indiscriminately. Mothers nurse and care for their
pups, but lose interest in the pups after weaning and abandon them. Males never see their offspring. Pups show little distress in reaction

Application of the Individuality-Togetherness Concept to the Voles

The contrasting social organizations of prairie voles and mon-
tane voles can be used to address the question of whether the concept
of an individuality-togetherness balance in relationship systems is
relevant for explaining the evolution of differences between species
in their social organizations, Human relationship systems operate as
ifthey are governed by two counterbalancing life forces: the individ-
uality force promotes separateness, distinctness, and autonomy; the
togetherness force promotes closeness, agreement, and dependency. The forces function reciprocally in that the more energy individuals
invest in a relationship system, the less energy they have for autono-
mous pursuits. Human beings react to threats to individuality and
togetherness, with the reactivity to both threats increasing as basic
level of differentiation decreases. Prairie voles react strongly to threats to emotional contact (social
isolation). The reaction is reflected in the marked distress displayed
by pups separated from the nest, by the lengthy time pair-bonded
adults sit side-by-side, by pair-bonded adults routinely attacking
unfamiliar adult intruders, and by the mere fact that prairie voles
live in groups. The seemingly high level of social tolerance of prairie
voles suggests that they may react less strongly to threats to emotion-
al distance (social proximity) than to emotional contact.

text:
FROM THE EDITOR

Bowen theory distinguishes between the emotional system
and the relationship system. The human emotional system is a
product of several billion years of evolution and is the driving force
of the family and other relationship systems. The emotional system
accounts for the activity of the patterns of interaction and ways of
functioning in a relationship system. The definition of the emotional system in Bowen theory is quite
broad or general. The emotional system can be defined as that part of
man he has in common with other forms of life. The definition does
not necessarily imply that the human emotional system is identical
to the emotional systems of even closely related primate species such
as the chimpanzee, but it appears that human emotional functioning
has much in common with the other primates. Furthermore, some
aspects of the human emotional system are probably the legacy of
processes that evolved far back in the history of life. Murray Bowen may have defined the emotional system broadly
so that the concept could encompass all that would eventually be
learned about the emotional functioning of Homo sapiens and other
species. This issue of Family Systems not only contains much infor-
mation about the emotional functioning of human and nonhuman
species, but, insome instances, the authors also examine the informa-
tion from the perspective of Bowen theory, from the perspective of
natural selection, or from both perspectives.

BRIEF REPORT

INSTINCTS OF REPRODUCTION

Barbara J. Meagher, BSN

This brief report presents the author's belief that the comfortable,
good feeling experienced by a couple, that they come to call love,
is really the relationship climate necessary for reproduction. The
type of “climate” needed will vary. The reproductive instincts will
drive and guide the maintenance of that climate while remaining
largely out of the individual's awareness and control. A\n instinct can be defined as in inborn tendency to act,
feel or think in a certain way under certain circumstances. Darwin
wrote that the very essence of an instinct is that it is followed inde-
pendently of reason. Easily-recognized instincts would be the desire to eat when
one feels hungry, the need to drink when one feels thirsty and the
drive to get back to a comfortable body temperature when one feels
either too hot or too cold. All of these instincts seem to operate in a similar manner. The
person feels uncomfortable (hungry, thirsty, cold or hot). The feeling
triggers an action, The action relieves the discomfort. But that is not
the primary purpose of the action. The primary purpose of the action
is to get the human physiology back into equilibrium. One need not
have any comprehension of the physiological process behind the
feeling of discomfort. The uncomfortable feeling itself is enough to
trigger the appropriate action.

text:
BRIEF REPORT

STEPHEN EMLEN:
THE BIOLOGICAL BASIS OF THE FAMILY

Daniel V. Papero, PhD

Stephen T. Emlen, the Jacob Gould Schurman Professor of
Behavioral Ecology in the Division of Biological Sciences at Cornell
University, sets out in a series of articles to develop a conceptual
framework rooted in Darwinian thinking that might contribute toa
better understanding of human behavior. The absence of a general
evolutionary theory of the family, he reports, has contributed to
the slow progress in integrating evolutionary theory into the social
sciences. First he develops an evolutionary framework for under-
standing the development of the family in nature. Emlen proposes
a general evolutionary context for the family based upon the inte-
gration of three areas of behavioral ecology: ecological constraints
theory, kin selection theory, and reproductive skew theory. From
these ingredients he develops fifteen predictions about family living
in the areas of family formation and stability, family dynamics, and
family structure. In the most recent paper he turns his attention to
the human family by drawing comparisons to animal species that
live in social contexts of multigenerational family groups in an effort
to glimpse and describe genetically rooted behavioral predisposi-
tions in human behavior.

and to express those behavioral variants that maximize their
fitness. . . (1995),

Most animals display a broad range of behaviors in their
interactions with others, and what behaviors an animal presents in
any given set of conditions can significantly affect its survival and
reproduction. Individuals able to assess the conditions they face
accurately and to select or choose behaviors appropriately gain an
advantage over those who are less able to do so. Natural selection,

works from behavioral ecology, it is possible to determine at least
some of the rules for decision-making that affect behavior and make

contact and continue to interact into adulthood with their parents,
and he restricts the definition of family to this group. He further
divides the family units into simple or extended based upon whether
breeding is shared among several or monopolized by a single breed-
ing pair. In simple families, only one male and one female breed,
and in extended families two or more group members of one or both
sexes reproduce. In addition, the presence or absence of the breed-
ing male makes a further distinction possible—biparental families
(where the breeding male is present) and matrilineal. Finally, Emlen
distinguishes between intact families, where the original breeding
pair is still active, and replacement families, where a breeder has
been replaced (1994, 1995, 1997b),

Cooperative breeding systems, where adults provide care to
young that are not their own, appear to be relatively rare, occurring
in about three percent of bird and mammal species (1997a). Units
formed of grown offspring assisting their parents to raisc additional
siblings comprised the most common form of cooperative breeding. Yet those individuals who remain with their parents appear to pay
a cost in terms of their own reproduction.

Yet those individuals who remain with their parents appear to pay
a cost in terms of their own reproduction. What prompts offspring
to remain with their parents to form family systems? Emlen argues
that “The key to understanding the evolution of families is under-
standing the causes of delayed dispersal.” (1995)

Two schools of thought have attempted to answer the ques-
tions posed by delayed dispersal: ecological constraints model and
benefits-of-philopatry model. The former sug gests thatreproductive
vacancies for maturing offspring are scarce, and that early efforts
to reproduce without assistance often meet with failure. The poor
chances associated with leaving, therefore, press the individuals to
remain with their parents. The latter suggests that benefits accrue to
individuals who remain with their parents. These include increased

outside the family, more ability to compete when these chances
materialize, and the possibility of inheriting the parental breeding
Position itself (1994, 1995). Citing the work of Koenig et al., Emlen suggests that these two
perspectives are actually complementary. Poor prospects for breed-
ing enhance the value of staying at home, and the home situation
becomes a standard against which other opportunities are assessed
(1994).

Poor prospects for breed-

(1994). Emlen proposes a generalized economic model of family
formation:

(i) Delayed breeding occurs when the production of mature
offspring exceeds the availability of acceptable opportuni-
ties for their independent reproduction. (ii) Under such
circumstances, some offspring must wait until acceptable
reproductive vacancies arise and then compete to fill them. (iii) Families form when such waiting is best done at home,
when remaining on the natal territory and/or associating
with one’s family somehow augments the offspring’s inclu-
sive fitness. (1995)

On the basis of this formulation, Emlen derives two predictions
regarding the formation and stability of families (1995). He presents
supportive evidence from a number of studies for each prediction. The first predicts that the stability of families will be related to the
relative availability of other reproductive opportunities for offspring. When such opportunities are limited, offspring will remain with
their parents and, when opportunities improve, family grou ps will
dissolve, The second predicts that families that control high quality
resources will be more stable than those that control poorer ones.

Differentiation of self refers to a person's ability to be aware of the
degree to which important life choices are influenced by automatic
emotional process or by deliberate appraisal. Emotional process
describes the predictable ways that social groups, including families,
both generate and manage the chronic anxiety they have inherited
from past generations, as well as the acute anxiety born of efforts to
adapt to life in the present. Both differentiation of self and automatic emotional process
are important ingredients in regressive or progressive functioning in
individuals, families and societies. Some key factors associated with
regressed functioning include: (1) an increase in chronic anxiety; (2)
an increase in acute anxiety; (3) a corresponding decrease in people's
ability to manage their automatic reactivity; (4) an increase in vulner-
ability to emotional swings in others; and (5) a decrease in the ability
to deal with life's stressors in a thoughtful, intentional way. In his study of the human family, Bowen discovered that an
increase in anxiety and reactivity could activate any of several au-
tomatic relationship-oriented responses to mitigate the effects of
anxiety and help maintain functioning. Later, he found that society
used thesee same responses as well. Whilc.. the short-term effects of
these processes did maintain functioning, their use over time tended
to increase overall levels of anxiety.

or society. Feeling dominates thinking; automatic behavior governs
important life choices; togetherness solutions proliferate, insisting

replaced by an increasingly narrow focus. In this context, changes in the thinking of vulnerable individu-
als can include increased symptom focus, a tendency toward "group
think.,," polarization of the problem, scapegoat ing of self or others,
and an attraction to short-term solutions. Changes in feelings can
include increased irritability, anger, and rancor. Changes in behav-
ior reflect increased dependence on traditional antidotes to anxiety. These include dependence on drugs and alcohol to maintain func-

on togetherness, and irresponsible, impulsive actions that increase

THE PERSPECTIVE OF BOWEN THEORY 
To be in the presence of human need and affliction evokes a 
deep emotional response. Sympathy and the desire to help one's 
fellow in distress are instinctual responses, so basic that Darwin saw 
them as part of the "social instinct" that the human has in common 
with many other animals (Darwin [1871]. Ng). Animals express 
the soda' in 
 in seeking and taking comfort in one another's 
company, nurturing and protecting one another, joining in mutual 
aid to defend against threats, and at times risking and sac king 
their own safety or lives for kin or group mates. Certainly all of this 
is evident in humans. Emotional responses at the other end of the 
spectrum are also evoked, such as fear that the needs of others will 
encroach on one's resources or freedom, anger at others for having 
the problems they have, and despair at the seeming magnitude of 
the problem, 
Bowen described human functioning in terms of three sys-
tems that operate in varying kinds of balance with one another the 
emotional system, the feeling system, and the intellectual system. The emotional system griverns Ono aIttornatic, instinctual aspects of 
human behavior and relationships including the basic survival and 
reproductive functions that humans have i n common with all forms 
of life.

individual variation (Robinson 1988). When a rat is given a single
injection of amphetamine, cocaine, morphine, or corticosterone, it
will respond with a good bit of motor activity. Some rats will be
immediately sensitized; that is, if after a long period of time, the rat
is given another injection, the "sensitized" ones will respond with
quite unexpectedly large amounts of motor activity, more than after
the first injection (Antelnian 1988). On the other hand, many rats
can tolerate quite large doses in the first injection and not become. sensitized. 34 FAMILY SYSTEMS SPECIAL ISSUE ON H65.1.174 CAR.E

in their reaction. Some will have heightened motor reactions to the
first doses and will subsequently self-administer the drug at accel-

studied rats in a shock-induced aggression paradigm. Put two rats

begin a kind of ritualized, defensiveboxing with each other; pushing,
shoving, but not really hurting each other. Premedicate both with
mescaline, turn on the shock, and they both become " pathologically
aggressive," severely wounding each other, sometimes to the point
of death. Premedicate one and not the other, turn on the shock, and
the unmedicated one becomes pathologically aggressive. The medi-
cated one does not. The authors speculated that the altered motor
behavior of the medicated individual acted as a cue triggering the
extremely aggressive behavior of the unmedicated rat. BO EN THEORY FRAMEWORK

quality of functioning, including symptoms, is often associated with
the intensity of chronic anxiety in a relationship system. When any
relationship system is subjected to pressure for long enough and
lives with the associated intense anxiety long enough, symptoms
will begin to appear in that relationship system. Less differenti-
ated systems will experience the symptoms sooner and with more
intensity than more differentiated systems (Bowen 1978, Kerr and
Bowen 1988, and Paper® 1990). If intensity and duration of anxiety is associated with more
symptoms, one might ask what are possible sources of variation
in anxiety in the situation of prescribing psychoactive medication. blot. 5, No, 1 VAFtrAIION TN RESPONSE TO PSYCHOACTIVE MEDICATION 35

Possible candidates for proximate sources of anxiety include the in-
dividual, his or her relationship system, the prescriber, and his or her
rel ationship system. Anything that could be done to lower anxiety
in the family system and in the professional's relationship system
might enhance the apparent effects of medication in the individual
and his family. Conversely, intensifying anxiety in any of these sys-
tems could potentially blunt the apparent effects of medication. If
the occasion of prescribing medication coincided with any transfer
of anxiety away from the symptomatic one to some other part of
the family or professional system, the apparent medication effects
would be enhanced.

Variations in Present and Past Anxiety

Stern and Hartmann (1972) studied amphetamine lethality
in rats. Acute stress increased lethality over the baseline; chronic
stress decreased it. Repeated tail pinch, a challenge to a rat known
to produce the physiological reactions of anxiety, has been associ-
ated with subsequent differences in intensity of motor reaction to
amphetamine (Piazza et a L 1990). Restraining the movement of a rat
for a significant period of time had the effect of intensifying the rat's
motor reactions to both amphetamine injections and also morphine
injections (Deroche et al. 1992). Antelrnan and colleagues found that a "lower intensitystressoe
would enhance a rat's responsiveness to haloperidol; whereas a
"higher intensity stressor" decreased the rat's responsiveness (1991). As noted earlier, animals vary in the extent to which they become
sensitized after a given dose of a stimulant, opioid, or glucocorticoid. The phenomenon of sensitization inherently includes one influence on
indivi dual variation: the extent to which an anim al's history includes
sensitizing experiences. That is by definition, animals who have
had sensitizing experiences in the past will have larger reactions to
future injections or to threat experiences (Antelman 1988).

The reviewed studies consistently illustrate wide variation in
the effects of medication, and show that aspects of social-emotional
functioning are associated with that variation. How one understands
these effects is another matter.. To date, the literature offers only
limited explanations_ Bowen thanry offors Ll] way of thinking about
variation in response which provides a coherent theoretical direction
to pursue in understanding these effects. Qualitative variation in human functioning often involves a
substantial portion of variation in the chronic anxiety and differen-
tiation of the individual and relationship system (Bowen 1978, Kerr
and Bowen 1988, Paper® 1990). Variation in response to medication
is merely one kind of qualitative variation in human functioning. Most of the studies involved aspects of functioning known to be
associated with variation in anxiety. Position in a dominance hierar -
chy is often found to be inversely related to physiological measures
thought to reflect aspects of chronic anxiety (Jones 1994). When a
social animal is isolated, it tends to react as if it is threatened and
will overreact to new perceived threats; this is reflected in measures
of its physiology (Stanton, Patterson, and Levine 1985). The studies

IMPLICATIONS

The context of medication use in human beings is the relation-
ship system of the individual receiving the medication and the work
systems and family systems of the professionals involved in the
prescribing. The original speculation was that variation in response
would be influenced by the quality of functioning of the relationship
systems around the medication transactions. If these thoughts have
any merit, theory might suggest the following: Better functioning
eliont gysterna and professional sTatems not only would get befter
results but would tend to view the medication more realistically,
indulging in less magical thinking about the power of medication
and more accurately seeing broader influences in the system. A
poorer functioning client system and /or a poorer functioning pro-
fessional system could result even in a worsening of the person's
symptoms with medication. A well functioning professional system
might facilitate an average patient system to use the medication
productively. A poorly functioning professional system could over-
ride the opportunity which medication might offer to some people. A particularly well functioning system of the client could counter a
poorly functioning professional system.

The emotional system describes
how a relationship system, or group of individuals who have regular
contact wi th one another, develops emotional interdependencies and
functions as an emotional unit over time_ Governed by the emotional
system, relationship systems exist in a constantly fluctuating state
of balance between natural life forces of individuality and together-
ness (Kerr 1998). Individuality refers to the instinct to be a separate
and indepencl ent person, while togetherness is the drive to join with
others and be accepted by them. The way these forces are played
out in a group is determined by the levels of " self’ in its members. Emoti onal reactions wi thin a. group will move around the individuals
in predictable patterns. Conflict, distance, cutoff, overfunctioning-
underfunctioning reciprocity, and triangles are examples of these
emotional reactions or patterns_

Bowen (1978) observed that these basic patterns in work and
social relationships are identical to those in the family but are less
intense. The degree of intensity in the organization is inversely
related to the level of differentiation of self in its members. Bowen
described differentiation of self as the degree of fusion between
emotional and intellectual functioning. People who have lower
levels of differentiation of self are less flexible, less adaptable, and
more emotionally dependent on those around them.

force in humans, drives the individual toward being an emotionally

In contrast, a strong influence of the togetherness force can result

function in ways that allow this to happen and that allow individuals

Book reviews are a significant way to address and discuss ideas 
relevant to Bowen family systems theory. The journal will select 
reviews of books, chosen at a reviewer’s discretion, which critically 
engage the ideas presented in the text and address their significance 
to the ideas contained in natural systems thinking. Texts chosen 
for review should represent relevant scientific ideas that extend 
theoretical understanding of the natural world. Appropriate areas 
of inquiry include, but are not limited to, biology, sociology, socio
biology, anthropology, psychology, psychiatry, and medicine. OUR SON, KEN
 Sarah E. Lorenz
reviewed by
John F. Butler, PhD
This small paperback book, published in 1963, is the story of 
the author, her husband and their oldest child, Ken, described as 
“emotionally disturbed.”(9) It is the story of a very child-focused 
family who, like families of the past and present, are desperate to 
help their child. The author, a writer, chronicled the family’s course 
through many way stations in the inpatient and outpatient psychi
atric world of the late 1950s and early 1960s. And one of these stops 
was in Bowen’s NIMH Family Study Project. In fact, about half of 
her book is devoted to her reactions and impressions of her family 
while in the project.

The author and her husband, Cleve, married when she was in

offering us evidence? . . .Had we missed the warning signs?” (19)

The writing in the book is emotional. The author had some de

Project was not singled out for special consideration. Her search 
primarily for “the right place” is a journey that continues for many 
families today. I had expected a positive review of the Family Project, 
and a “happy ending.” However, in my coaching of child focused 
families, especially ones where the child has had multiple inpatient 
admissions, I know these families are very challenging, and there 
are no “happy endings.”
Throughout the book I noted the tremendous pressure on parents 
generated by placing the problem back into the family. Attempting 
to “stay out of the transference,” as Bowen called it, is never easy 
(Bowen 1978). I can empathize with the frustrations of the parents 
and also see the clinical challenges of maintaining constant detach
ment from families on an inpatient unit for extended periods of time. In his second annual update about the project, Bowen (1956) 
wrote about how his approach of “staying out of immature attach

n his introduction to Stoner, acclaimed Irish writer John McGahern 
includes a quote from John Williams characterizing the book as “an 
escape into reality.” Indeed, it is a “beautiful” escape, an adjective 
that Murray Bowen often used when people described frustrating 
and seemingly unsolvable relationship dilemmas that illustrated 
his theory unusually well. Hearing Bowen exclaim, “Beautiful, 
beautiful!” did not always amuse people but they responded 
positively to the smile with which he delivered the comment. The 
life of William Stoner, though fictional, is indeed a beautiful escape 
into reality because it fits so exceptionally well with Bowen theory. McGahern summarizes the basic plot of the book briefly as 
follows:
The novel then details the outwardly undistinguished career 
of an assistant professor of English within the walls of the 
university: his teaching, his reading and his writing, his 
friendships, his falling in love with an idealized woman, his 
slow and bitter discovery of that person once they marry, 
and how their gentle, pliable daughter becomes the wife’s 
chosen battleground. Outside the marriage, Stoner’s affair 
with a young teacher becomes entwined in bitter, vindictive 
university politics.

Family Systems Journal Vol. 9.1
Title: Triangles, Togetherness, and the Challenge to Forgive
Author: East
Pages: 45-68

45
TRIANGLES, TOGETHERNESS, 
AND THE CHALLENGE TO FORGIVE
Christopher F. East, PsyD
The emotional process known as “forgiveness” is so subjective in 
nature that it is quite difficult to talk about this process objectively. Beyond the difficulty of developing an objective definition, there is 
considerable confusion about how a state of forgiveness is achieved. This dilemma is particularly pertinent in the clinical setting where 
so many clients are deeply interested in achieving a new level of 
forgiveness, but find themselves quite “stuck” in achieving this 
desired emotional state. T
his dilemma can be addressed by approaching it through the 
larger lens of systems thinking and recognizing how ubiquitous 
triangles manage chronic anxiety in every family and social system. As members of a family or social system begin to perceive that 
togetherness levels are under threat, they make certain automatic 
moves within the interlocking triangles to lend and borrow self. The 
individual or group that is caught in this pattern of lending self will 
be vulnerable to a condition referred to as unable-to-forgive.

text:
What does it say about our culture that achieving forgiveness is so 
problematic? How can one forgive a person or a group that does 
not offer any genuine apology or restitution? As a clergyman and a psychotherapist I have been challenged to 
become more objective in understanding how it is that we become 
so emotionally intense in our behavior on the subject of forgive
ness. Why are some people able to ”move on,” while others cannot? Theologians and psychoanalytic theorists struggle to speak coher
ently about this subject. At the core of this dilemma seems to be an 
inability to see this phenomenon as a systems process rather than 
an individual problem. A linear, causal view depicts a perpetrator who inflicts harm on 
a victim. There is an assumption that until the perpetrator makes 
proper restitution, the victim is going to remain resentful. When 
no restitution is forthcoming, the victim will enlist the support of 
third parties. A view derived from Bowen theory takes a step back 
to gain a broader view of what is unfolding in the system. In par
ticular, Bowen theory describes fluctuations in the togetherness force 
within the relationship system and how these fluctuations influence 
the more or less automatic moves in various triangles. Triangles 
function to bring stability to the relationship system in response to 
a perceived loss of togetherness for an individual or relationship.

doc_name: FSJ 9.1 East Triangles, Togetherness, and the Challenge
text:
Triangles 
function to bring stability to the relationship system in response to 
a perceived loss of togetherness for an individual or relationship. By understanding the automatic moves within triangles as binding 
mechanisms that control the level of anxiety, we can better under
stand the condition of unable-to-forgive and establish a treatment 


 Vol. 9, No. 1         Triangles, Togetherness, and the Challenge to Forgive	           47
plan that is based on a more objective understanding of life. Family systems theory, as developed by Murray Bowen, speaks 
to this emotional condition. The emotional process of a family or 
work system can focus on one member of the system such that this 
person will become symptomatic. One expression of this is when an 
individual or group finds itself unable-to-forgive. When one is able to 
see this process as a function of the system, then it becomes possible 
to understand that what is at play is not an individual weakness, 
but stress in the unit that is finally absorbed by one member of 
that unit. Being unable-to-forgive has more to do with how different 
positions develop in the unit, and how changing just one of these 
positions can change the outcome. Resolving this condition is not so much about correcting a 
neurosis in the mind of the one person who feels troubled, but in 
effecting a change in the part that one is playing in the relationship 
system.

This requires understanding how triangles stabilize the 
system, and how certain triangles and togetherness forces can lead 
to symptoms in a family member who gets stuck in an especially 
frustrating position. Beyond the need to be able to recognize triangles 
and togetherness forces in the family or social system, there is a 
need to learn how to alter one’s position in the interlocking triangles 
while remaining emotionally engaged in the relationship system. THINKING SYSTEMS
Murray Bowen (1978) observed that two-person relationships 
are not stable and gain stability by triangling in a third person. Initially this third person is in the outside position of the triangle, 
appearing to have less emotional contact. Nonetheless this third is 
no less concerned about his or her need for acceptance, approval, or 
need to meet the needs and expectations of the relationship system. As tension builds in the two-person relationship, one person 
will increase emotional contact with the third by looking for some 
measure of acceptance, approval, or attention. According to Bowen 
(1978), a more anxious person will seek togetherness with this third. This togetherness compensates for the unresolved anxiety in the 
primary relationship. This search for togetherness does not resolve the disagreement 
in the primary relationship, but it does alleviate some of the im
mediate anxiety.

an individual one. This is not to suggest that individual binding 
mechanisms are insignificant, only that the most potent way to bind 
anxiety is in a relationship process within the relationship system. An individual may be emotionally aroused by difficulties, but this 
arousal is always heightened by the emotional challenges in the 
relationship system. The relationship system needs mechanisms to

outside position is less desirable. Anxiety may well float around the 
relationship system as different individuals move in and out of the 
inside position within the family unit.
