doc_name: FSJ 9.1 East Triangles, Togetherness, and the Challenge
text:
Anxiety may well float around the 
relationship system as different individuals move in and out of the 
inside position within the family unit. Chronic anxiety is defined in Bowen theory as the response of 
a person to a real or imagined threat (Bowen 1978). Chronic anxiety 
emerges as a persistent emotional state that is perceived as irresolv
able. Chronic anxiety emanates from a fusion between the intel
lectual and emotional centers of the brain leading to an inability to 
think about various ways to address the challenge. When a person 
or system is under the influence of chronic anxiety, the goal is not 
so much to resolve the anxiety but to bind the anxiety so that there 
will be no further harm or damage to the individual or relationship 
system. All individuals and relationship systems function with dif
ferent levels of susceptibility to chronic anxiety. The level of chronic 
anxiety, and how it is managed, is a key factor in determining how 
well humans function. Bowen theory describes this vulnerability as 
emotional fusion or unresolved emotional attachment. A person’s level of differentiation has a great deal to do with 
how anxiety is managed in the family of origin. In a family where 
parents manage their own chronic anxiety well, their children will 
learn to do the same. These children will mature into adults who 
are a bit less susceptible to emotional reactivity in their adult years.

text:
When 
the level of anxiety increases in the relationship system, being in 
the inside position is no longer the preferable position. At higher 
levels of anxiety, interpersonal contact begins to take the form of 
active conflict between those in the inside position. The conflict may 
be in the form of both people engaging in some active or passive 
aggression or in the form of reciprocal functioning in which each 
one is making emotional moves and countermoves to contain the 
anxiety within the relationship. What follows, then, is a vying for the 
outside position. A teenager, for instance, who is under the anxious 
introspection of parents, seeks the outside position and leaves the 
parents dueling with each other in the inside position. A husband, 
observing the immaturity of his child and the provocative behavior 
of his wife, may try hard to stay on the outside, leaving his wife 
and child dueling on the inside. At this heightened stage of anxious activity, the triangle finds a 
way to stabilize itself, but only at the cost of heightened emotional 
reactivity. An “ideal” situation may be a pattern where each person in 
the triangle gets a break in the outside position, while the other two 
are dueling. However, the triangle may not bind the existing anxiety 
equitably. For instance, a woman may be fighting with her child in an 
anxious inside position and then do the same with her husband. As 
a result, the woman is fighting on two fronts.

anxiety is being contained predominantly in the wife. In this scenario, 
she is “carrying the load” for the entire family. When automatic movements into the inside and outside posi
tion do not adequately bind the chronic anxiety within the family 
system, one family member may work to reinforce an interlocking 
triangle. For example, the wife may choose to engage a third party 
such as a best friend, school official, or therapist to assist her with 
either her “recalcitrant child” or her “irresponsible husband.” Inter
locking triangles can bring some stability to the original triangle, but

text:
Her anxiety may be temporarily satiated, but no new 
life course will appear on the horizon. The interlocking triangles 
serve to disperse the chronic anxiety of the family to other parties, 
thus bringing temporary stability to the original family system. The 
original problem in the marriage is now lost in the process. What happens if the interlocking triangles do not adequately 
bind the chronic anxiety in the family? Under exceptional anxiety 
one member of the triangle may feel pushed or pulled into giving 
up self in the service of stabilizing the triangle. From a Bowen theory 
perspective triangles are the smallest social molecule designed to 
provide stability to the family unit. However, this does not mean 
that triangles will always be effective. When triangles are not man
aging the chronic anxiety of the system, then one person—in this 
case, the wife—may be inclined to give up self and thereby bring 
stability to the system. Giving up or lending self, through choices 
often made outside of personal awareness, occurs when a person 
is acting inconsistently with his or her best thinking or core values. Lending self brings a measure of peace to the relationship system. Going along with, tolerating, or not challenging what is viewed as 
less mature behavior in others will bind anxiety, but there is also a 
loss of self. This can result in social, physical or emotional disability.

There is a large group of marriages in which differences are 
settled by one spouse who reluctantly “gives in” after a brief 
period of contesting rights. ... This spouse volunteers to 
“give in” and to become a “no-self” to strengthen the self of 
the other, on whom he [or she] is dependent. A spouse who 
habitually “gives in,” either reluctantly or voluntarily, can 
reach a state of sufficient “no-self” to become incapacitated 
with (1) physical illness, (2) an emotional illness, or (3) a 
social dysfunction ... (Bowen 1978, 111)
This pattern is apparent, to some degree, in the behavior of all 
individuals and all relationships. However, this pattern can become 
more fixed and more intense in certain individuals and certain rela

volitional process. Bowen is speaking here of an emotional process

function to contain the chronic anxiety within the family system. When the discomfort of functioning to contain the chronic anxiety 
for the family unit exceeds the discomfort of changing self, then the 
person who is lending self may begin to redefine his or her position 
in the family unit. All people have an emotional dependency on triangles to bind 
the anxiety that otherwise would disrupt individual functioning 
and the functioning of the family system. However, when a person 
chooses to assume a position in which he or she is constantly giving 
up self for the sake of the relationship system, then their mental 
or physical health will be jeopardized. Unfortunately others in the 
family system tend to be oblivious to the level of anxiety that is 
being contained in the person who is giving up self. The exhausted 
wife, for example, may find that all her giving of self gets her are

text:
Resolution 
has to do with understanding family emotional process and in 
changing one’s own part in the relationship system. In other words, 
resolution has to do with a person understanding how he or she 
began to de-self self and then make appropriate life adjustments that 
are egosyntonic. De-selfing self is not a common phrase in Bowen 
theory. It represents an attempt to articulate the distinctive pattern 
in which a person makes consistent behavioral choices which un
dermine their own essential life values. Being unable-to-forgive is an emotional condition that unfolds 
as people allow themselves: (1) to be pulled into vulnerable inside 
positions whereby some of their most primitive unresolved attach
ment are awakened and managed by the triangle, (2) to be pulled 
into conflict in the inside position as a way of managing chronic 
anxiety in the family system, (3) to engage in expanding interlock
ing triangles to further manage the emotional process in the family 
system, and, finally, (4) to de-self self or give up self to establish a 
measure of togetherness in the family system, but at the cost of 
depleting one’s own physical or mental health. THINKING BRAIN FUNCTION
While the strength of Bowen theory lies in the intentional effort 
to base theory on observational data and functional facts, today 
there is also an interest in correlating findings in the behavioral 
sciences and neuroscience with Bowen theory.

While the study of 
neural processing of primates is arguably still in its infancy, there 
is some consensus that significant data is beginning to emerge from 
research that offers insight to those in the behavioral sciences who 
are working to refine and further develop Bowen theory. Bowen was cautious in the development of theory. Nonetheless, 
Bowen seemed to be clear enough regarding brain function that he 
was able to intuit the following general scheme of brain activity:
  
I conceive of one brain center that controls emotions and 
another that controls intellectual functions. The fusion 
suggests centers that are side by side with some degree of 
fusion, or grown togetherness. ... The more the separateness 
between the centers, the more the intellectual center is able to 


 Vol. 9, No. 1         Triangles, Togetherness, and the Challenge to Forgive	           53
block, or screen out, a spectrum of stimuli from the emotional 
center, and to function autonomously. ... The emotional 
center controls the autonomic nervous system and all other 
automatic functions. The intellectual center is the seat of 
intellect and reasoning. ... The intellectual center is either 
appended to, or directed by, the emotional center. In the 
various psychotic and neurotic states, the intellect is either 
obliterated or distorted by emotionality.

text:
The intellectual center is either 
appended to, or directed by, the emotional center. In the 
various psychotic and neurotic states, the intellect is either 
obliterated or distorted by emotionality. (Bowen 1978, 372) 
Bowen had a deep appreciation for the dynamic interplay 
between the highly interactive emotional and intellectual neural 
processes. There was a time when some theorists suggested that 
the dominant neural process was in the cognitive domain centered 
in the neocortex, which makes up the bulk of brain mass. However, 
the work of Paul MacLean (1990) in identifying the triune brain 
brought into sharp relief the critical and pervasive role of the limbic 
system in shaping the behavior of all mammals. Emotional process
ing contains the capacity to quickly dominate as survival instincts 
are stimulated. Such emotional excitation suggests a fusion between 
these two processes. There is a unique reciprocal relationship between a slower, 
more deliberate and thoughtful neural process (which Bowen called 
intellect) and a more rapid and immediate neural process (which 
Bowen referred to as emotion). Optimally these two processes work 
tangentially to co-create an outcome which is the result of a balanced 
functionality as opposed to a more fused process in which emotion 
dominates. Bowen theory refers to this more optimal process as 
differentiation.

Bowen theory refers to this more optimal process as 
differentiation. In less optimal circumstances these two processes 
function in a more chronically fused state, which practically de
mands that the emotional center dominate, leading to a more reac
tive relationship with the external world. If this general schematic 
is accurate, then over time research will confirm it. While this article does not review the research, I will highlight a 
few interesting conclusions of Joseph LeDoux (1996) in his research 
on what he terms the “emotional brain.”  LeDoux’s research has 
focused on neural processes in relation to emotional processes in the 
brain. In terms of evolutionary development, LeDoux has identified 
one of our earlier brain structures, the amygdala, as functioning in 
a reciprocal relationship with the more “advanced” executive func
tion of the prefrontal cortex. Appreciating this reciprocity seems to 
be quite relevant to understanding more chronic emotional states 


 54

                     2012
such as the unable-to-forgive position. LeDoux writes:
... this work suggests that the prefrontal cortex and amygdala 
are reciprocally related. That is, in order for the amygdala 
to respond to fear reactions, the prefrontal region has to be 
shut down. By the same logic, when the prefrontal region is 
active, the amygdala is inhibited, making it harder to express 
fear.

text:
By the same logic, when the prefrontal region is 
active, the amygdala is inhibited, making it harder to express 
fear. Pathological fear, then, may occur when the amygdala 
is unchecked by the prefrontal cortex, and treatment of 
pathologic fear may require that the patient learn to increase 
activity in the prefrontal region so that the amygdala is less 
free to express fear. (LeDoux 2002, 217)
This organic reciprocity is also described in LeDoux’s exploration 
of the two different avenues in which the amygdala communicates 
its own emotional state. Again, there is a slower, more deliberate 
pathway of communication to the neocortex, which may or may not 
sustain the heightened activity of the amygdala as it moves into its 
co-creative function. There is also a quicker, more automatic process, 
in which the amygdala bypasses cortical processing. LeDoux writes: 
 
The path from the thalamus through the cortex to the 
amygdala, the so-called high road, allows complex 
information about objects and experiences to initiate fear 
reactions. But the amygdala also can be activated directly

patterns of de-selfing self in my family of origin and in my nuclear

of healing would have a great deal to do with taking responsibility 
to develop some new thinking and move into a stronger functioning

look like to function as more of a self within the system. While all 
people enjoy gaining the approval and acceptance of others, there 
is a clear demarcation where one begins to absorb the anxiety of the 
system as a cost for securing this approval and acceptance. In all 
likelihood leaders in faith communities are especially susceptible 
to this process as theology can be misconstrued to support lending 
self such that “one suffers for the sake of the whole.”

of self, might be juxtaposed with a more functional position in the 
family or social system in which differentiation of self is pursued. Defining a self balances inevitable short-term costs with greater long-

position. As this position is sustained, the entire system is likely 
to calm down to some degree. While this change may be ever so 
slight, it nonetheless should have lasting value. As an individual discovers the ways in which he or she has 
been participating in the chronic anxiety that is within the family 
or work system, especially the ways in which he or she has lost self 
in the relationship system, and as this individual learns new ways 
to function with less of an emotional need to avoid or overcome 
the perpetrators, then something substantial has taken place within 
this person. They have defined a new way of relating to the larger 
world.

Title: FROM THE EDITOR
Author: Kerr
Pages: 3-8

3
FROM THE EDITOR
From its earliest planning stages in the late 1980s, the editorial 
board of Family Systems has been dedicated to representing Bowen 
family systems theory and its many applications as accurately as 
possible. This mission leaves room for publishing differences of 
opinion about theory and its applications, but not for eclecticism. Wikipedia defines eclecticism as:
A conceptual approach that does not hold rigidly to a single 
paradigm or set of assumptions, but instead draws upon 
multiple theories, styles, or ideas to gain complementary 
insights into a subject, or applies different theories in
particular cases. A 
multicausal model is commonly invoked as a rationale for an 
eclectic approach to clinical problems. The idea is that more 
than one cause can be involved in the development of a clinical 
problem, and thus more than one type of treatment is needed to 
address the problem adequately. For example, a clinical assessment 
of a young adult female’s depression might include three areas of 
focus:  psychological traumas in her childhood, tensions in her marital 
relationship, and a biologically based tendency for depression. The 
therapy, therefore, might include individual therapy for the trauma 
issues, conjoint therapy for the marital issues, and psychoactive 
medication for the biological issues.

The

issues, conjoint therapy for the marital issues, and psychoactive 
medication for the biological issues. This approach is based on the 
assumption that the causes of the woman’s symptoms operate fairly 
independently of one another. The difference between multicausal thinking and systems think
ing is important for Bowen theorists to understand because they 
are vulnerable to mixing the two and often do it unwittingly. If a 
therapist mixes cause and effect thinking with systems thinking, it 
is not a Bowen theory based therapy. Bowen theory “purists” as
sume that if the functioning of the relationship system improves, 
clinical problems will resolve. In contrast, therapists who mix the 
models assume that changes in the relationships alone are insuf
ficient for clinical problems to resolve. If a therapist’s thinking flips 
back and forth between systems and cause and effect, it makes it

much harder for the family in treatment to think systems. Systems 
thinking leads to questions that focus on a system’s process; while 
cause and effect thinking leads to questions that focus on an indi
vidual process. Mixing models implies that there are two separate 
problems, individually based ones and relationship based ones.

Mixing models implies that there are two separate 
problems, individually based ones and relationship based ones. In a systems model, many factors are seen to be at play in a 
clinical problem, but none of the factors cause the problem. The 
relationship system that links the factors is what is important to 
understand. Factors A, B, C, and D continuously interact with each 
other, not necessarily directly, through a systems process. The fac
tors powerfully regulate each other, and the systems process they 
generate powerfully regulates each factor. Consequently, a cause 
for what is transpiring does not reside within any factor. Bowen 
theory describes variation between family systems in the degree of 
this regulatory process, but the fact that some degree of regulatory 
process operates in all families makes cause and effect thinking an 
inaccurate explanatory model. A clinical example will illustrate 
this idea. One day a mother, father, older teenage daughter, and younger 
teenage son are together, relating fairly calmly and openly. The 
next day the daughter and her boyfriend get into a horrible fight 
and break up. She returns home in a tearful state. This triggers an 
intense flow of emotional reactions among family members that 
leads to everyone becoming increasingly anxious and reactive.

retreats to his room and slams the door, and the daughter becomes 
deeply distraught and begins cutting herself. Based on how family 
members are dealing with each other, the daughter’s level of distress 
has gotten magnified far beyond anything related to the breakup. Thoughts, feelings, and emotional reactions are operating within 
each individual, but a cause for the internal processes does not reside 
within each individual. The process of the family system regulates 
the internal processes of family members which, in turn, regulate

on his wife. This can lead to increased marital tension and, con

and the relationship with his mother.

and the relationship with his mother. In other words, triangles can 
stabilize a family system for a long time, but those who live by the 
triangle—as if anyone escapes it—become vulnerable if members 
of the triangle become unavailable. A concept in Bowen theory where people commonly mix sys
tems thinking with multicausal thinking is the multigenerational 
transmission process. The mixing occurs in reference to what exactly 
is transmitted across generations. Bowen theory is highly specific 
about an individual’s basic level of differentiation being the result 
of a relationship process that operates between the generations. The 
development of a child’s basic level is promoted or constrained by the 
degree of emotional fusion that exists between parents and child and 
the associated emotional programming that occurs within the fusion. The amount of “self” a child has developed by the time he leaves 
home is the outcome of a multigenerational transmission process. The theory is less specific about whether chronic anxiety and 
patterns of emotional functioning are transmitted across generations. Many Bowen theorists believe they are.

The theory is less specific about whether chronic anxiety and 
patterns of emotional functioning are transmitted across generations. Many Bowen theorists believe they are. This belief may have gained 
some support from a number of non human animal studies showing 
that stressed mothers, either as the result of epigenetic, intrauterine, 
or nurturing effects, can have offspring and even grand offspring 
that exhibit a highly reactive stress response when exposed to a 
novel stimulus. Demonstration of a heightened stress response to 
a novel stimulus in an adult mouse, however, is not equivalent to 
the phenomenon of chronic anxiety as described by Bowen theory. 6

                     2012
The transmission of chronic anxiety across generations also gains 
support from a common observation that highly anxious people 
often have or had highly anxious parents. Different opinions among Bowen theorists about what is trans
mitted multigenerationally may stem from failing to keep in mind 
the nature of the relationship between the two main variables in 
Bowen theory: (1) the degree of anxiety, and (2) the degree of integration 
of self. Differing opinions may also stem from failing to keep in mind 
the distinction between basic and functional level of differentiation. The two main variables are distinct, but closely interconnected.

Differing opinions may also stem from failing to keep in mind 
the distinction between basic and functional level of differentiation. The two main variables are distinct, but closely interconnected. In the earlier clinical vignette of the family of four, the infectious 
spread and escalation of anxiety was related to the degree of un
differentiation in the family unit. Basic level of differentiation (the 
degree of integration of self) is a property of individuals that is 
transmitted across generations, but chronic anxiety is a property of 
the family emotional system or field and can fluctuate considerably 
depending on prevailing conditions in the field. The conditions 
vary depending on the degree of stressors on the family unit and 
the unit’s capacity to deal with them without marked and sustained 
escalations of chronic anxiety. Therefore, basic level of differentiation 
is transmitted across generations, but it is only the vulnerability to 
chronic anxiety that is transmitted across generations, not chronic 
anxiety itself. Assuming that chronic anxiety itself is transmitted across genera
tions is multicausal thinking. It implies a non existent independence 
between the two main variables in Bowen theory. It implies a similar 
non existent independence between basic and functional levels of 
differentiation.

It implies a non existent independence 
between the two main variables in Bowen theory. It implies a similar 
non existent independence between basic and functional levels of 
differentiation. If a therapist loses sight of the tight interconnection 
between level of “self” and vulnerability to chronic anxiety, he is 
more likely to steer people towards techniques to control anxiety 
rather than keeping the focus on the difficulty of maintaining a 
“self” in relationship systems. Lack of “self” fosters a buildup of 
chronic anxiety in a system, anxiety that is then absorbed by one 
person. It is tempting to opt for new and better ways to cope with 
anxiety rather than taking on the more difficult task of trying to 
develop more “self.”
Patterns of emotional functioning, such as distance or reciprocal 
functioning, are also properties of an emotional field, not properties 
of individuals. Overfunctioning, for example, is not a fixed per
sonality trait, but a way of functioning that is context dependent. As is the case with chronic anxiety, which drives the patterns of 
emotional functioning, it is the vulnerability to overfunction that

in reciprocal relationship to the underfunctioning of others in an 
emotional field.

Additionally, a person’s basic level of differentia
tion strongly influences the magnitude of whatever overfunction
ing/underfunctioning reciprocity he or she helps to co-create—or 
tri-create, since the degree of anxiety-driven reciprocal functioning 
in a dyad is always influenced by the triangle (and interlocking 
triangles) in which it is embedded. Murray Bowen once said, “There are two ways to deal with 
anxiety: one is with drugs, the other is with self—self is better!” 
Human relationships are sufficiently anxiety provoking that most 
people are in a fairly continuous search for ways to manage it. Anxiety is not easy to control, but people are at an advantage if 
they do not view anxiety and its associated reactivity as a distinct 
system that has been programmed out of the past, but view it as a 
system intimately linked to the capacity to be a self. ❉

for trainees in Bowen theory. The marriage between William Stoner 
and Edith is central to the story and tugs powerfully on the reader 
to take sides. Most will side with William, feeling the background 
sadness that he feels, but also experiencing him as a kind of hero as 
he soldiers on through myriad difficult challenges, in the marriage 
and in his academic career. Edith is easy to diagnose. She seems to 
have few redeeming features. She makes childish demands, rejects 
William, and fitfully attempts to mold their daughter into the person 
Edith thinks she needs to be. The end result is disastrous. The reader schooled in Bowen theory may be usefully reminded 
of Murray Bowen’s caution to his research staff at the NIMH. When 
exposed to the emotional intensity of a schizophrenic family, it is 
easy to slide down the slippery slope of identifying with the victim, 
applauding the hero, and hating the villain. Fortunately, the author 
develops the complexity of William and Edith and their interactions 
so richly that it becomes possible for the reader to focus less on 
their personalities and bring into focus a core relationship process: 
a highly emotionally fused pattern of interaction in which passiveness 
(William) and aggressiveness (Edith) are reciprocal functions of each other.

the patterns of interaction, thus helping the observer get beyond 
cause and effect thinking that blames one person for the actions of 
another person. The interactions between William, Edith, and their daughter 
Grace are also difficult to view objectively. John McGahern used the 
term “pliable” in reference to Grace, which is one way of describing 
her painful lack of “self.” It is truly hard to watch. Fortunately, this 
is fiction, but, of course, it is not fiction. This is exactly the way a 
developing child fails to find enough emotional space in an intense 
triangle to develop some semblance of being an individual. It is 
again easy to blame Edith, but the discerning reader can see the

Stoner’s nearly year-long affair with Katherine Driscoll, a young 
fellow teacher in the English department, had powerful influences 
that are quite familiar to experienced therapists. John Williams de
scribes the impact of becoming romantically involved with Katherine 
on Stoner himself in the exquisite prose that is a hallmark of the 
book: “He felt lift away from him the waves of despair.” If Murray 
Bowen heard Professor Stoner say this, he would likely smile and 
say, “Beautiful, beautiful.” Another somewhat less familiar effect 
was that Stoner’s relationships with Edith and Grace improved for 
a time, even though Edith knew about the affair. She told him she 
knew about it, she demanded nothing, and she never broached the 
subject again. The death knell for the affair was it becoming public 
knowledge on campus. The consequence was that Katherine was 
soon forced to leave the university. Stoner thought about leaving 
too, but ultimately chose not to. He was not concerned about leaving 
Edith and Grace but told Katherine he would not leave because, “It 
would destroy both of us as human beings.” Stoner’s first serious 
illness occurred the summer following Katherine’s departure. He 
survived the illness and continued on at the university for more 
than two decades. The marriage between William and Edith is central to the 
story, but almost as central is the relationship system of Stoner’s 
academic community.

The marriage between William and Edith is central to the 
story, but almost as central is the relationship system of Stoner’s 
academic community. Murray Bowen would exclaim from time 
to time, “People can be so nasty!” Stoner’s academic community 
could be very nasty. There, too, the triangles were often malignant 
in their toxic effects. Any doubts people have about the applicability 
of the concept of triangles to work systems will be easily cast aside 
upon reading about the impact on Stoner’s career of the death of his 
mentor and English Department chairman, Sloan, his fierce clashes 
with the new department chairman, Lomax, and his ability to take 
an important stand with Lomax thanks to the backing of Stoner’s 
longtime friend, who was the Dean of the School of Arts and Sci
ences. Stoner stood firm and on principle with Lomax, the kind of 
stand he could not muster in his family. However, he minimized 
its significance, characterizing it as “a victory won out of boredom 
and indifference.”
Ultimately, Stoner’s emotional dependence on his academic 
life, dependence reinforced by a deep and abiding love of English 
literature, played a key part in his demise.

The depth of Stoner’s 
emotional overinvestment in his work is captured in the following 
description of Stoner in the later years of his life: “He hoped that he 


 92

                     2012
was at last defined by what he did.” The overinvestment was clearly 
an attempt to counterbalance feelings related to the disintegration 
of his family and the absence of other meaningful relationships. It 
rendered him hopelessly vulnerable when Lomax led the charge to 
force him to retire. He lived less than a year after retirement. The period when Stoner was dying provides additional impor
tant insights. As is frequently the case in “real” life, tensions eased 
greatly between William and Edith after the cancer was diagnosed 
and he was increasingly bedridden. John Williams writes the fol
lowing about Stoner’s reflections as Edith cares for him. They reveal 
a side of her that had been largely hidden under all the turmoil in 
their family: “He felt Edith’s hands on him, moving him, bathing

seemingly unalterable; his dysfunctional only child had cut off from

Bowen theory, however, provides an important addition to the fac
tors governing a particular individual’s emotional state, namely, that 
the ups and downs of an individual’s key relationships, especially 
within the family, can have a powerful impact on his or her emo
tions, for better and for worse. The emotions of each member of a 
family system affect the system and the flow of emotions through 
the system affects each member’s emotions. This book captures a particularly important aspect of the in
terplay between the emotions of the individual and the emotional 
system of the family, which is that the individual, the family, and 
the interplay between them change over time. People may cope suf
ficiently at one point but not at another point. For years, Edith and 
William distanced emotionally to reduce tension and conflict. The 
parental triangle with Grace “bound” tension until it came time 
for Grace to lift off. Edith coped by using withdrawal mechanisms 
that sometimes bordered on the psychotic, and William coped by 
linking his emotional well being to his professional life.

Edith coped by using withdrawal mechanisms 
that sometimes bordered on the psychotic, and William coped by 
linking his emotional well being to his professional life. Thanks to 
the coping mechanisms, the system stayed reasonably balanced 
for many years, with leaks around the edges, but the consistent 
failure to address relationship problems reduced the flexibility of 
the system over time. Stoner’s retirement was a “tipping point” 
that finally overloaded the system’s ability to adapt, and a serious 
symptom was not far behind. John Williams’ “escape into reality” in telling the story of 
Stoner is indeed a gift to all who don’t recoil from seeing life as it 
really is. The lament over “what might have been” in relationships 
is familiar to students of Bowen theory when they gain objectivity 
from careful study of the past, present, and future generations of 
their families. Such study enables people to comprehend the power
ful impact of the way people deal with each other on their health, 
functioning, and well-being. It is an interesting paradox that people 
are both humbled and calmed by appreciating the constraints that 
relationships exert on emotional autonomy.

Conference in October 2011. Identifying data including family 
surnames have been altered to insure confidentiality. This presentation was selected to illustrate how Bowen theory offered 
a young woman a framework for getting beyond blame and anger

case illustrates the heightened emotional reactivity that is triggered 
through a nodal event in a family and an individual’s efforts to 
beome more thoughtful and objective in managing herself in the 
emotionality. Concepts in Bowen theory such as differentiation of 
self, triangles, cutoff, and multigenerational process are explored

Family Systems Journal Vol. 9.1
Title: Self-Harm and Bowen Theory
Author: Thompson
Pages: 31-44

31
SELF-HARM AND BOWEN THEORY
By Erik Thompson, MA
In this report I examine self-harm through the lens of Bowen theory. Observations from clinical interviews suggest that self-harm 
regularly occurs in response to perceived social separation, but it 
may be better explained by the level of reactivity to separation, not 
the intensity of the separation itself. The concept of differentiation 
of self accounts nicely for a variation in reactivity to separation 
experiences and its role in self-harm. Family interviews point to a 
link between the development of self-harm and an environment of 
energetic protection. The concept of the family projection process is 
consistent with this finding. Clinical practice guided by these two 
theoretical concepts is useful in establishing meaningful contact with 
individuals who engage in self-harm as well as their family members. It can prevent helpers from becoming emotionally entangled within 
the paradox of those who seek help and refuse it at the same time. The productive cause of suicide naturally escapes the observer 
of individuals only; for it lies outside of individuals. —Emile Durkheim, Le Suicide, 1897

text:
In my clinical experience, I was struck by the relationship be
tween self-harm and social separation experiences. Humans who 
engage in self-harm are consistently responding to a disruption 
in a family or family-like relationship. Other observers, too, have 
remarked on this link. Rosen and colleagues (1990) found that self-
harm increased in the days preceding the loss of important relation
ships in an adolescent residential program. Richman (1981) noted 
that a disruption of an enmeshed relationship between adolescents 
and their parents was a common precursor to self-harm. Prisoners, 
separated from their family networks, engage in self-harm at higher 
rates than the general population (Puisis 2005). More than a century ago, French sociologist Emile Durkheim 
recognized separation as a social context for self-harm. In his 1897 
book on suicide, Durkheim wrote: “A young girl, daughter of 
healthy parents, having spent her childhood in the country, has to 
leave at about the age of fourteen to finish her education. From 
that moment she contracts an extreme disgust, a definite desire for 
solitude and soon an invincible desire to die.” (Durkheim [1897], 
64) Three case examples from my practice illustrate the relationship 


34

                     2012
between self-harm and social separation.

Like self-harm, such distress vocalizations arouse the attention and 
care-giving motivations of bonded adults, who have specific loca
tions in their auditory physiology that are highly tuned to receive 
this particular communication (Buchwald et al. 1988). SCALE OF DIFFERENTIATION
In Bowen theory, a relationship between self-harm and high 
responsiveness (or reactivity) to social separation is consistent 
with the concept of the scale of differentiation (Bowen 1978, Kerr 
and Bowen 1988), which asserts that individuals achieve varying 
degrees of emotional separation from their families of origin. The 
term differentiation comes from biology, its association with cell 
differentiation suggesting a separation process deeply rooted in 
nature, developing over evolutionary time. Differentiation is not 
the same as physical or emotional distance, nor is it a reptilian 
disinterest in social relationships. Rather, it is the separation of 
the self of the offspring from the self of the primary caregivers. A 
distinct self is marked by the capacity to represent oneself accu
rately in the context of emotionally powerful relationships, such 
as human beings have with their parents, spouses, and children.

text:
A 
distinct self is marked by the capacity to represent oneself accu
rately in the context of emotionally powerful relationships, such 
as human beings have with their parents, spouses, and children. Differentiation is a way of being that comes with a way of thinking, 
feeling, and acting. Humans tend to be more emotionally entangled with family 
members than distinct from them, but the degree of distinction is 
significant. Degree of differentiation determines the level of reac
tivity an individual has to a wide variety of experiences, including 
threats to adequate emotional contact (Kerr and Bowen 1988). How 
distinct, or solid, the self is will determine the individual’s overall 
level of reactivity to separation experiences. Since separation is so significant an aspect of human life—from 
the milestones of birth, weaning, and leaving the nest to everyday 
separations like going to sleep or getting on a school bus—how a 
person responds to these experiences of separation will influence 
his overall anxiety level. Chronic anxiety, which is generated in the 
relationship system over generations, and comes to reside in indi
viduals based on their position in the relationship system, influences 
the amount of reactivity or imagined threat an individual adds to 
the stressor of separation experiences. Chronic anxiety pressures the 
individual and powerfully influences his degree of physical, social, 
and emotional symptoms.

Self-harm does not necessarily indicate low level of differentition. A person with a high level of differentiation (and therefore low level 
of reactivity to separation events) may, under great pressure, display 
extreme symptoms. For example, a highly differentiated individual 
put into isolation in a prison camp might engage in self-harm. In contrast, those at the bottom of the differentiation scale may 
interpret slight perturbations in their social environment as threats 
to adequate emotional contact and repeatedly engage in self-harm. ROLE OF THE PROTECTIVE RESPONSE
To further explore the social context in which self-harm occurs 
and to gain insight into the social context of responsiveness to social 
separation, I conducted twenty interviews with parents of people 
who engage in self-harm. My sample included any parent willing 
to be interviewed. Only two fathers were present for the interviews. The greater involvement of mothers calls to mind the finding that 
mothers typically have stronger responses than fathers to isolation 
calls in nonhuman species (Pettijohn 1977).

During that first year away from her mother, 
the daughter took a nonlethal overdose. FAMILY PROJECTION PROCESS
The family projection process, another concept in Bowen theory, 
accounts nicely for a relationship between self-harm and an envi
ronment of energetic protective responses. Bowen theory views all 
families as experiencing some degree of chronic anxiety and states 
that one way the chronic anxiety is regulated is via focus on a child. Similarly, Panksepp (1998) suggests that parents are hardwired by 
evolution to reduce their own distress by providing care for offspring. In the most common version, the primary caregiver, most often the 
mother, focuses anxiety on one of her offspring in the form of worry. This child, sensitive to the mother’s detection of threat, naturally 
reacts with increased anxiety. The mother notices the increase in 
the child’s anxiety and mistakenly views it as originating within 
the child, which again stimulates her sense of threat and deepens 
her worried focus. She is now more worried about her offspring, 
and she manages, or “binds,” her anxiety by sharpened focus on 
the child (Bowen 1978). This cycle, which cannot exist without the 
cooperation of other key family members such as the father, repeats 
with escalating intensity, resulting in a transfer of anxiety from the 
family to the child. The child comes to rely on caregivers to manage 
a pervasive sense of threat, while the parent manages with a chronic 
protective focus.

arena and gain momentum there. A clinician can prevent this by 
avoiding diagnostic language that locates the total family problem 
in a single family member. “Schizophrenogenic mother” is as far 
from Bowen theory as “borderline personality disorder.”   One 
cannot see the family projection process, or any aspect of systems 
thinking, when one marginalizes a party as “a borderline” or blames 
a supposedly controlling family member for what goes on in the 
system. Allowing a child to be the sole participant in treatment 
usually strengthens the notion that the problem is separate from 
the interactive family process. This occurs when the anxious par
ent presents her child to the clinician, and the clinician views the 
child’s anxiety as originating within the child. Bowen noted that 
the writing of a prescription or an insurance form that diagnoses 
the child, or any such gesture, could strengthen the projection of 
the total family problem onto the symptomatic child. A common way to isolate the problem is to label it “biological.” 
The articulate mother mentioned above, while able to describe the 
relationship to her daughter with great clarity, viewed her daughter’s 
problems as “mostly due to biology.”  Although all symptoms have 
a biological dimension, her statement conveys the idea that biology 
and relationship processes are mutually exclusive.

Any key member of a family system can decrease the weight 
of the family projection process. A father whose daughter had 
been cutting her arms for six months, for instance, came to realize 
that his efforts to get the daughter to try another, more intensive

therapy were not working. The daughter would always attend a 
few therapy meetings to appease her parents but then begin miss
ing most appointments. The father eventually saw his own agenda 
as part of a longstanding preoccupation with his daughter who, at 
seventeen, was largely beyond his direct control. He informed his 
daughter as much, saying he had underestimated the importance 
of letting people discover their own way of living. He apologized 
for trying to push her into therapy. During the next days the father 
feared the worst but forced himself to go outside and look at the 
stars rather than check on his daughter. The following week he and 
his daughter had a conversation about friends. He felt they were 
in better touch than they had been for a very long time. This case makes it sound easier than it is. Since the projection 
process is a system’s way of handling imagined threat, the members 
of the family will perceive any change in the process as dangerous, 
and oppose it. A member who can stay in good contact with those 
who experience the threat while remaining unmoved by provoca
tive behavior will emerge as a family leader.

A member who can stay in good contact with those 
who experience the threat while remaining unmoved by provoca
tive behavior will emerge as a family leader. “PROTECT ME; YOU CAN’T PROTECT ME”
The protective instinct is natural to caregivers. The family pro
jection process takes nature to an extreme. But the process does not 
imply a shift from blaming the self-harmer to blaming the protector. The self-harmer plays a full role in the process. To the degree she 
relies on others for protection, an individual will perceive more 
threats and will manage them more often by displays that say, 
“Protect me.”  Self-harm is one such display—an unusually intense 
one in that it further conveys the message, “You can’t protect me.” 
Conspicuous attempts to hide superficial wounds, for example, 
stimulate caregivers to discover them by signaling not just “Protect 
me” but at the same time, “You can’t protect me.” Mental health 
emergency teams regularly encounter individuals who engage in 
self-harm but time and again call for help immediately after the act, 
only to reject help when it arrives. One woman spent a week hint
ing that she was about to take another insulin overdose. When she 
finally did, she was immediately given aid but tried to flee when 
it arrived. Afterwards she said she considered overdosing under 
a bridge but instead chose a spot near the police station to ensure 
access to care. Such parties run from care with the knowledge that 
they will be chased and restrained.

chronic “Protect me; you can’t protect me” can become more defi
ant: “You can never catch me, but you can never stop chasing me.”
Seeking and defying help in the same gesture will frustrate 
caregivers who feel pulled and pushed at the same time. When they 
blame this frustration on the symptomatic party, caregivers become 
caught in reactivity, underestimating the option of managing the 
situation by managing self. When caregivers respond to “You can 
never catch me; you can never stop chasing me” with “Oh, yes I 
can,” they are in trouble. Controlling emotional reactivity can be as 
simple as responding, “How true.” If individuals engaged in self-
harm have two options, to be avoided or chased, they will choose 
battle. But if they have the third option of neutral emotional contact, 
they will often ease up. NEUTRALITY
Even when an action response is required, a caregiver can mod
erate emotional reactivity. For example, if a person tells a helper 
she intends to kill herself in the coming hour, some caregivers will 
be obliged to take protective action.

text:
For example, if a person tells a helper 
she intends to kill herself in the coming hour, some caregivers will 
be obliged to take protective action. But if this situation gets under 
their emotional skin, caregivers will convey “You shouldn’t be act
ing this way.” Such caregivers predictably telegraph the message, “I 
am personally invested in stopping you.” Less emotionally reactive 
helpers will be sure of what they need to do but feel less provoked 
by the “chase me” signal. They can say, in effect, “I respect you, I 
am obliged to take protective action, but I know that the ultimate 
responsibility for protection lies with you.” These helpers take the 
same action, but because they are less emotionally reactive, they 
also feel less pressure to find immediate resolution. Freer amidst self-harm, neutral parties can see the function in 
the dysfunction and express curiosity in how self-harm could help 
an individual solve problems. Rather than forcing the issue of 
protective action, they might ask of the self-harmer, “What led you 
to this decision?” or even “What is it like for you when people try 
to stop you?”  Such responses essentially say, “I can’t catch you; I 
suppose I have to act, but in the meantime I am interested in you.” 
The emotional tone of such statements is more important than the 
words. As Bowen theorist Dr. Daniel V. Papero (2008) has often 
pointed out, if a person is emotionally neutral, almost anything he 
says will be helpful.

As Bowen theorist Dr. Daniel V. Papero (2008) has often 
pointed out, if a person is emotionally neutral, almost anything he 
says will be helpful. Because it is uncommon, neutrality in response to self-harm 
is surprising and has the potential to awaken clearer thinking. Emotionally neutral people are funnier, too. Dr. Marsha Linehan, 


Vol. 9, No. 1        		
   Self-Harm and Bowen Theory	
  	
           41
the developer of dialectical behavioral therapy, reported the story 
of getting a patient involved with self-harm to laugh by saying, “If 
you kill yourself, I won’t work with you anymore.” (1993)
The challenge of living with heightened sensitivity is difficult 
to understand for those whose emotional life is less intense. Ex
treme actions are usually a best attempt to stabilize an emotional 
roller coaster that is hard to get off. The most common onlooker’s 
reaction to self-harm is that it has to stop. But those who engage in 
self-harm hardly see it that way. The key to neutral contact is a lack 
of pressured investment in changing the person who self-harms. THE “I” POSITION
Clinicians can convey neutrality in various ways, but it is es
sentially a state of being. Helpers who are emotionally neutral and 
less inclined to control what the other is doing are more successful 
at taking “I” positions—statements of what one will or will not 
do that are completely free of any message about what the other 
should do.

text:
People preoccupied with self-harm are more reactive 
to messages telling them what to do than those that clarify what a 
caregiver will or will not do. For example, one individual required 
expert stitching for damage to a nerve from a deep, self-inflicted 
cut. The stitches were covered with a cast to promote healing. Soon after discharge the individual began telling health care pro
fessionals that she intended to remove the cast. Most responded, 
“You must not do that.” She removed the cast. The cast was put on 
again. Again she initiated the dialogue about taking it off. But this 
time a hospital staff member took an “I” position. She decided she 
would not replace the cast again. The battle of the cast ended that 
day. The self-harming party stopped talking about the wound but 
continued her meticulous care for it, which had been her practice 
from the start. The self-harm was not about health; it was about 
relationships. People closely involved with self-harm would do 
well to think through their beliefs carefully regarding their degree 
of responsibility for protecting others and clearly define this to 
everyone involved. An “I” position that has proved particularly 
effective is, “I have come to realize that I can’t keep you safe.”  
A word of caution: The notion of an “I” position is not captured 
by the phrase “‘I’ statement,” which overemphasizes the words and 
underemphasizes the thinking behind them.

Again, it is the tone of 
speech, above all, that reflects the speaker’s thinking. The sentence, 
“I don’t believe hospitals keep you safe,” may reflect a well defined 
position or coercion, and listeners can tell the difference. 42	
	
  	
        Family Systems	
	
                     2012
We exaggerate the distance between those who engage in self-
harm and those who don’t. Alarming reactions to social separations, 
as well as alarmed counter-reactions, are everywhere. Humans 
are especially sensitive to their standing in their most significant 
relationships. When they experience a threat, they react. In the 
family, reactions are also signals. Going silent is a good example. Suppose two members of a 
family, a husband and wife, are continually allied when it comes to 
decisions. During a family visit with her father, the wife strongly 
disagrees with her husband. The husband reacts to the shift in 
the previously steady alliance by going silent. The silence sends a 
loud message to the wife. It protests the disruption in the alliance 
and stimulates alarm in her, pushing her back toward agreement. Family members can read these gestures with remarkable 
literacy. There are an infinite variety, including helpless gestures 
such as whining, pouting, and throwing up one’s hands, slumped 
posture, and talk of things being hopeless. Reactions to social sepa
ration include gestures that suggest aggression, such as tantrums, 
ultimatums, and intimidating looks.

SUICIDE AND SYSTEMS
Anthony J. Wilgus, MSW
The suicide of a sixty-eight-year-old woman affords a unique 
opportunity to move toward a greater understanding of this event 
that occurs in the life cycle of the human. While conventional 
psychiatric interpretations of depression and suicide focus primarily 
upon individual pathology, Bowen theory broadens the lens of 
analysis so that multiple relationships in several generations 
illuminate these phenomena. Of special importance in this 
exploration is the fact that the individual who committed suicide 
left an extensive volume of personal journals over a ten-year span, 
highlighting some of her thoughts and reflections prior to her death. Despite the writer having no prior knowledge of theory, the author 
contends that these documents vividly illustrate some of the core 
concepts of Bowen theory and substantiate the view that suicide 
is an event transcending the bio-psycho-social processes residing 
within any individual. INTRODUCTION
O
n an overcast September morning, police discovered the body 
of a sixty-eight-year-old Caucasian woman slumped over her 
laptop with an empty bottle of sleeping pills nearby.

her immediate circumstances and broadens the lens of analysis so 
that multiple relationships and generations can illuminate such 
events in the life of a family. Important to this particular exploration is the fact that Irene

highlighting her thoughts, observations, and feelings as she managed 
herself in an array of relationships. These documents, to which the 
author had access with the permission of surviving family members, 
offer detailed insight into both her internal processes and the larger 
relationship network of which she was a part. Employing concepts from Bowen theory, including differen
tiation of self, nuclear family emotional process, emotional cutoff, 
triangles, the multigenerational transmission process, and chronic 
anxiety, the major portion of the article situates this individual’s 
functioning within the context of her relationship system via her 
journals. Finally, the author concludes with the contention that 
suicide is an event that transcends the biological, psychological, 
and social processes residing within any individual. Examining the 
thoughts of this individual and her relationship network, paired 
with concepts drawn from Bowen theory, affords another way to 
conceptualize the suicide of a family member. Prior to embarking

Bowen described 
individuals at this end of the continuum: 
There are the people who are less flexible, less adaptable, and 
more emotionally dependent on those about them. They are 
easily stressed into dysfunction, and it is difficult for them 
to recover from dysfunction. (Bowen 1978, 362)
Throughout Irene’s eleven years of journaling, a major theme 
was her dependence on others. As she noted: “I’ve always had a 
strong need to be cared about, feel needed.”1 While the together
ness forces represented by this drive for connections are present in 
all humans, there is an intensity and desperation in her quest. In 
the mid 1990s, she described the “fear of being alone and finding 
it is lonely; not being able to survive it” along with her awareness, 
“I can’t seem to handle rejection.”  The intensity of this process

Title: Subjectivity, Homo Sapiens, and Science
Author: Bowen

101
SUBJECTIVITY, HOMO SAPIENS, AND SCIENCE
Murray Bowen, MD
E
arly in my psychiatric career, I wondered why psychiatry 
was not a real science, instead of a pseudo-science governed 
by a “scientific method.” I had no presumption about ever mak
ing a contribution in such a complex field. I was merely seeking a 
clarification for myself. Now, after almost forty years I am pleased 
with my life. To my own satisfaction, I think I know one way to
ward a major new theory about adjustment . The outcome may be 
a century away. The current situation is more chaotic than before. This might have been better predicted. I believe human behavior 
will eventually become a science. The major barrier appears to be 
subjectivity. It is part of human experience. It cannot be measured 
or verified. When subjectivity creeps into theoretical postulations, 
the result is more chaotic and less scientific. I will attempt to pres
ent a few ideas about the field. In the twentieth century, psychiatric thinking has been based 
primarily on psychoanalytic theory. It considers the human as unique 
and different from other forms of life. The contributions from psy
choanalysis have been tremendous, but it has never moved toward 
becoming an accepted science. I believe that has been blocked by 
basic formulations from literature, philosophy, mythology, and the 
arts.

text:
Life is generally divided into plant life and animal 
life, both tied to the Earth and both intimately interlinked. All life 
reproduces in clearly defined cycles, changing a little with each 
cycle. The animal world is mobile and it includes forms that extend 
from bacteria and other one-cell forms to the complexity of Homo 
sapiens at the other extreme. The animal world has some kind of 
a nervous system that operates either by some undefined chemi
cal mechanism or through a conglomerate of nervous tissue and 
chemical reaction. In its phylogenetic development, the nervous 
system proceeds through a series of orderly steps from the lower 
animals to the marvelous brain of Homo sapiens, about which we 
know too little. In addition to structure, the brain includes numerous functions 
that go back to instincts and are not clearly associated with any 
structure. Fairly late in phylogeny, the human developed the ability 
to stand upright and to think, reflect, and reason. This is not meant 
to be specific for anatomy and physiology. It is mentioned only 
for comparative reasons. Slowly the human developed a spoken 
language, cultures, philosophies, religions, mathematics, literature, 
the arts, and a host of other functions more subjective than factual. Science had to have a beginning. Along the way, man learned to 
figure out the nature of the universe, the properties of the Earth on 
which  he lived, and other subjects that had to do with pure science.

text:
My gallery of critics at NIMH helped me stay alert. Basic postulations had been based on natural systems in lower 
forms of life rather than general systems theory. Systems theory was 
used to convert certain items of subjectivity into the functional facts 
of systems. I have written about that. There are numerous examples, 
such as, “That man talks is a verifiable fact, but what he says is not 
a fact.”  Observers were not permitted to use interpretations or 
“loaded” words such as “depressed” in observations. Observations 
were based on fact, as far as discipline could go. Predictable actions 
that repeated over and over, in all the families, eventually found 
their way into concepts. Everything was based on facts as far as 
possible. Critics were fast to point out subjectivity in observer situ
ations. Critics suggested movies as more objective. Even the best 
plans of researchers can go awry. A dozen observers can watch a 
movie and emerge with a spectrum of different observations based 
more on the information in the brain of the observer than the actual 
situation. A trained and disciplined observer can be more accurate 
than the average less disciplined observer. To my critics I admitted 
the fallacies and merely said, “We are aware of the problem and are 
doing our best to deal with it.” The whole research stands on that 
effort. I believe we did a good job.

INTRODUCTION TO CONFERENCE
Kathleen B. Kerr, MSN, MA
This was the fifth interdisciplinary conference on the impact 
of relationships on individual variation. The conferences reflect 
Murray Bowen’s view that if a theory of the family were to begin 
to take its place in the overall effort to move toward a science of 
human behavior it must remain in viable contact with the natural 
sciences. A move toward science requires a view of the human as a 
product of evolutionary process and some form of systems think
ing. It has been almost fifty years since the development of Bowen 
family systems theory.

text:
It has been almost fifty years since the development of Bowen 
family systems theory. Evolution is now widely accepted as central 
to understanding human behavior. However, that the family func
tions as a largely interdependent unit regulating the development, 
physiology, and behavior of its members is still a radical idea. Seeing the family as more than a collection of individuals requires 
a conceptual shift. It is analogous to new knowledge of how bac
terial colonies function as a whole and of how the central nervous 
system, endocrine, and immune systems communicate and highly 
mutually influence each other. The individual components cannot 
be understood apart from the system. Another core tenet of Bowen theory is that the family rela
tionship system is central to the development of variation among 
individuals in their basic lifelong adaptiveness or differentiation of 
self. The theory describes this variation along a continuum based 
on what are seen as two related processes: (1) the degree to which 
an individual over the course of development attains emotional 
autonomy in relation to the family, and (2) the degree to which the 
emotional and cognitive systems are differentiated and integrated. The emotional system is seen as automatic, and the differentiation 
of the cognitive system allows individuals to respond to the envi
ronment with greater choice or flexibility.

text:
In recent years, the natural sciences have addressed the ques
tion of individual variation within species more systematically. It 
has taken some time to establish average ways that species behave. That knowledge needs to be in place before individual variation 
comes into view. As individual variation is increasingly studied, 
the impact of relationships on functioning becomes a focus. All 
members of a system influence each other. Relationships shape 
other relationships, especially through triangles. Interest in such 
individual variation in functioning and the developing science in 
this area of study led the conference organizers to develop the first 
of these conferences in 1996. The conferences have brought Bowen theorists and researchers 
together with natural scientists for mutually beneficial exchange. Participants in this conference come from the fields of psychology, 
anthropology, biology, endocrinology, neuroscience, epidemiology, 
family theory and research, and physiology. A number of them 
specialize in the study of the human’s nearest neighbors on the 
phylogenetic tree, the primates. Others study one-celled organisms, 
rodents, dogs, and even humans. Natural science is exploding with quality research on individual 
variation in functioning, the physiological underpinnings of such 
variation, and the variables in the social environment that contribute 
to it. Bowen theory has a way of understanding and interpreting 
such research.

Margaret Donley, MSW
The impact of the mother-infant relationship on individual 
variation made the first group of papers an obvious choice to provide 
the framework for the Variation Conference. Not surprisingly, these 
papers delivered exceptional insights into relationship systems and 
contributed important knowledge to the study of maternal effects, 
maternal style, and rearing effects. Although the perspectives were 
different, the presentations had in common the study of nonhuman 
primates which provides a gateway to understanding the common 
emotional processes that operate in natural systems. A shared feature of the presentations was the broader lens 
through which dyadic relationships were examined. The tradi
tional idea that maternal style, as a fixed trait, was central to infant 
development gave way to new perspectives on systems principles.

BEHAVIOR, AND OFFSPRING DEVELOPMENT  
Lynn A. Fairbanks, PhD
Murray Bowen recognized the value of studying natural social 
systems as an aid to understanding human family dynamics. Hu
mans and nonhuman primates share a strong and enduring bond 
between mothers and offspring, and ecological studies of repro
duction and maternal care in primate societies have shown that a 
mother’s investment of time and energy in her offspring is sensitive 
to her condition and access to resources. For primates in the wild 
and humans in past centuries, getting enough good quality food 
was the primary challenge for pregnant and lactating females, but 
now food is more readily available and over-nutrition has become

text:
Research on animal societies indicates 
that mothers who are underweight and have a restricted food sup
ply are more likely to limit investment in reproduction and infant 
care. Yet little is known about the consequences of diet and weight 
loss on maternal behavior in the overweight to normal range. For three decades, the Vervet Research Colony has contained 
multigenerational social groups of vervet monkeys that have been 
used for studies of maternal behavior, family relationships, and ge
netic and maternal influences on biobehavioral development. Over 
the years, the monkeys responded to a freely available laboratory 
chow diet by gradually gaining weight. In order to prevent over
weight and obesity and promote animal health, the diet at the Vervet 
Research Colony was changed in 2004 to provide a more natural 
level of fiber in the diet. The new diet was also higher in protein and 
lower in carbohydrate and energy density than the standard diet. Data on weight, mother-infant interactions, and yearling behavior 
for infants born from 2000 through 2006 were assessed for effects 
of the diet change (Fairbanks et al. 2010). The results showed that, even though ample amounts of food 
were available, females lost weight on the new diet. The average 
body weight of breeding females was 10% lower after the transition 
to the high fiber diet.

loss made the captive mothers less indulgent and more similar to

text:
In her groundbreaking study of the first year 
in the life of yellow baboons, Altman (1980) characterized maternal 
styl e dichotomously as laissez-faire or restrictive. Since then many 
studies investigating maternal behavior in primates and humans 
have combined specific behaviors into broader maternal styles. In 
cercopithecine monkeys, most variation in maternal behavior falls 
along the two independent axes of rejection (R) and protection (P) 
(Japanese macaques: Shino et al. 1995, Bardi and Huffman 2002, 
vervet monkeys: Fairbanks and McGuire 1993, rhesus macaques: 
Maestripieri 1998). The combination of these dimensions results in 
four different maternal styles: rejecting (high R and low P), controlling 
(high R and high P), laissez-faire (low R and low P), and protective 
(low R and high P). One study which examined maternal style in 
chimpanzees by De Lathouwers and Van Elsacker (2004) suggested 
that chimpanzee maternal style could be characterized along three 
dimensions: protectiveness, distance, and refusal. These studies are generally descriptive and atheoretical, based 
on factor analysis and principal components analysis. If there is a 
background theoretical viewpoint, it is frequently either covertly or 
overtly attachment theory (Weaver and de Waal 2003). The studies 
create typologies of variation in maternal behavior that are used to 
explain outcome in the functioning of offspring.

Examining behavior in such diverse species 
as marine sponges, harvester ants, and paper wasps did not detour 
the presenters from considering the similar principles that organize 
and influence individual and group behavior across all species, in
cluding the human. A common thread was the examination of the 
various ways systems adapt to changing conditions and the variation 
that occurs between groups within the same species. The impact of 
the relationship system on individual and group functioning was a 
central theme in these three presentations, providing insights into 
naturally occurring systems in nature. VARIATION AS THE FOUNDATION OF PERMANENCE IN 
SYMBIOTIC ASSOCIATIONS
Mary Beth Saffo, PhD
[The friend] told me. . . that no one can ever love someone 
constantly, equally, at all times. It has to rise and fall and wax 
and wane to maintain its permanence. That is its permanence. (Percy 2009, 28)
Symbiosis—the “living together” or intimate association, be
tween two or more species—pervades all of life. But mechanisms 
of self/nonself recognition and defenses against nonself are also a 
basic feature of living things. Among animals, even sponges show 
exquisite abilities for recognition of nonself, with the molecular 
tools for recognition and rejection of foreign genotypes bearing at 
least some resemblance to molecular mechanisms of graft rejection 
in humans.

But there are many important 
examples of nonhereditary mutually beneficial symbioses as well, 
including mycorrhizae (fungi associated with the roots of almost 
land plants (Brundrett 2002); lichens; symbioses between leguminous 
plants and rhizobia (a group of nitrogen-fixing bacteria); various 
species of fish and squid associated with bioluminescent bacteria; 
algal symbionts of reef-building corals; gut microbes in herbivo
rous animals such as ruminants and termites; and fungus-growing 
ants and termites (Aanen et al. 2009); and these symbioses are also 
maintained from generation to generation. In these nonhereditary 
but still tightly interacting symbioses, symbiotic partnerships are 
re-established each generation using a precise molecular “courtship” 
between hosts and symbionts, often cunningly integrated into the 
developmental patterns of one or both partners. Fidelity of partnership 
With symbiont transmission locked together with that of its 
hosts, it is not surprising that hereditary symbioses show strong 
host–symbiont fidelity. But, remarkably, strong partner fidelity is also 
seen in many nonhereditary symbioses, despite the fact that their 
mode of transmission provides at least the theoretical opportunity 
for changes in partnerships even within the life of a single plant or 
animal. Nevertheless, many of these nonhereditary relationships 
are quite constant, their partnership maintained in part by specific 
host-symbiont recognition mechanisms.

In 2000, Richard Lewontin, American evolutionary biologist 
and geneticist, wrote The Triple Helix, based in part on a series of 
lectures he initially gave in Milan, Italy. The book articulated the 
basic point that while DNA is informative, it is only a small part of 
a big picture that cannot be understood in isolation. In a series of brief chapters Dr. Lewontin discussed the complex 
interplay of gene, organism, and environment, emphasizing the 
role organisms play in constructing their own environment. He 
emphasized the reciprocal interplay of forces governing human 
characteristics, particularly those that are behavioral. In the final 
chapter, entitled “Directions in the Study of Biology,” readers were 
challenged to move beyond a reductionist approach to research to 
a more complex and larger one “that is more accurate and more 
useful.”(Lewontin 2000, 113)
Over the past twenty-five years, Deborah Gordon has inves
tigated collective behavior in red harvester ants (Pogonomyrmex 
barbatus) through field research conducted on a twenty-five acre site 
in the southwestern United States.

Her research has enlarged the

found in harvester ants Dr. Gordon identified in numerous scien

tific publications including two books Ants at Work (1999) and Ant 
Encounters: Interaction Networks and Colony Behavior (2010). Without central control, harvester ants build nests, forage for 
seeds, and conduct complex collective behavior through simple 
patterns of behavior that respond to moment-to-moment shifts in 
the environment. Colonies are highly efficient, although the process 
between ants is messy. The unit as a whole regulates the efficiency. Simple contact between two ants, mediated by chemical ex
change, conveys one of three messages: continue doing what you’re 
doing, become active, or change tasks. Ants are continuously regu
lating reactivity in the unit through patterns of contact and distance. When contact is too great, ants move away to avoid contact. When 
contact is not great enough, ants seek contact. Inactive ants may help 
to regulate reactivity within the unit as a whole so that reactivity, 
necessary for functioning, does not become overactive. Through development, harvester ant colonies become less re
active and more homeostatic.

Through development, harvester ant colonies become less re
active and more homeostatic. Since individual ants only live one 
year, the homeostasis is not based on differences in ants but in the 
organization of the unit as a whole. Recent studies focus on variation between colonies in collective 
behavior. Some colonies forage more days per year and are more 
consistent in foraging from year to year. While more active colonies 
are inclined to reduce foraging when perturbed, great variation ex
ists in this overall pattern. Some very low-activity colonies continue 
foraging when perturbed. There is also variation in this tendency. Colonies vary in response to harsh conditions. Some colonies con
tinue foraging at a high level while others refuse to forage. Dr. Gordon emphasizes the many new questions raised as an 
outcome of her work: (1) Does it help a colony to be sensitive to 
food availability, slowing down its foraging at the first sign that it 
takes a long time to find food? (2) Are colonies more successful if 
they make finer adjustment in the range of foraging, relative to the 
rate at which food is coming in? (3) On the other hand, it might be 
better for a colony to be more robust and keep going out to search no 
matter what. Natural selection could act on the function of interac
tion networks if within a population of colonies, some colonies use 
interactions in a slightly different way from others.

THE ULTRA-MODERN SYNTHESIS
Michael E. Kerr, MD
Using systems thinking to link facts about human emotional 
functioning, particularly facts derived from family research during 
the past six decades, with facts about Homo sapiens as a product of 
evolution, Bowen family systems theory (Bowen 1978) provides a 
valuable framework for appreciating how the forces that govern 
human behavior are similar to those that govern the behavior of 
other species. The important unique features of human beings not
withstanding, understanding the processes the human species share 
with all life is essential for understanding human nature. Since a 
framework for integrating human behavior with the behavior of all 
life is not part of the modern synthesis in biology, adding Bowen 
theory to the modern synthesis could advance the pursuit of a sci
ence of human behavior. THE MODERN EVOLUTIONARY SYNTHESIS
The publication of On the Origin of Species (Darwin 1859) con
vinced many people that evolution had occurred, but it convinced 
fewer that evolution by natural selection was the primary mecha
nism. The theory assumed inheritance of traits, but no one knew 
how such inheritance took place. A theory of inheritance based on 
a “blending” of traits was prominent at the time and was a serious 
challenge to trace variations in one generation being passed undiluted 
to the next, a fact on which evolution by natural selection rested.

text:
The Emotional System
Bowen theory conceptualizes three interconnected systems in 
the human body: the emotional system, feeling system, and intellectual 
system. The emotional system is that part human beings have in 
common with other forms of life. The human emotional system is 
not identical to even closely related species such as chimpanzees, 
but important commonalities exist. Bowen theory replaces Freud’s 
concept of the unconscious with the emotional system as the force 
that motivates human behavior. The intellectual system encompasses those aspects of the most 
recently evolved parts of the brain that make possible some of the 
brain functions that appear to be unique to human beings, such as 
abstract thinking, reasoning based on facts, and reflection. Addi
tionally, the intellectual system allows for some voluntary control 
over automatic emotional reactions. Importantly, at least to some 
degree, the intellectual system enables human beings to distinguish 
between thoughts and feelings and between objective and subjec
tive thinking. The feeling system functions as a bridge between the emotional 
and intellectual systems by bringing some aspects of the emotional 


Vol. 9, No. 2        	  The Impact of Relationships on Individual Variation                 135
system into awareness. If the intensity of a feeling state does not 
overwhelm the intellectual system, the feeling system appears to 
facilitate conscious decision-making in a variety of ways.

theory contributes another important way to study the emotional 
system because it conceptualizes families functioning as emotional 
units. The emotional processes within individuals drive the specific 
patterns of interaction in families that result in the family functioning 
as a unit. Furthermore, relationship patterns in families regulate the 
emotional functioning of individual family members. Therefore, it 
is possible to describe emotional functioning objectively by study
ing the how, what, when, and where of family relationship patterns. Theory of Human Development
Bowen theory describes the very involved early mother-infant 
emotional attachment as a normal symbiotic state that functions to 
promote the survival of the infant. The process of emotional separa
tion between mother and offspring in human beings is similar to 
what occurs in all mammalian species, but significant differences 
between species exist in how mature the offspring are at birth (hu
mans are quite immature) and how long the relationship endures 
beyond weaning (unusually long in human beings).
