This reliance on 
self-reports raises concerns related to the intention-behav -
ior gap, which highlights discrepancies between individuals’ 
stated intentions and their subsequent actions [41]. Self-reg -
ulation capabilities, a key moderating factor in this gap, have 
also been identified as a critical individual difference influ -
encing procrastination. Consequently, the present findings 
suggest that the intervention increased participants’ inten -
tions to complete the task but do not conclusively indicate 
actual task completion. Future research should address this 
limitation by examining the intention-action gap in procras -
tination. Specifically, employing longitudinal or two-part 
study designs where participants are followed up or recalled 
to report actual task completion, would provide more 
robust evidence of the intervention’s effectiveness. Second, the current study utilized a combined intervention 
targeting both outcome utility and task aversion simultane -
ously. It is uncertain which specific component of the inter -
vention—subgoal generation, the introduction of a small 
reward, or the recall of task benefits—was the most influen -
tial in driving the observed improvements in outcome util -
ity, mood, and reported likelihood of task completion. Future 
research should systematically evaluate each intervention 
component independently to identify which strategy exerts 
the greatest impact on reducing procrastination.

Future 
research should systematically evaluate each intervention 
component independently to identify which strategy exerts 
the greatest impact on reducing procrastination. Finally, although many results of the present study were 
statistically significant, the observed effect sizes were 
relatively small. This raises concerns about the practical 
significance of the findings and risks overinterpretation. The modest effect sizes suggest that while the interven -
tion may be effective, its impact compared to the control 
group is limited. Replication of the current study, along 
with extensions incorporating more robust and explicit 
interventions designed to further enhance outcome utility 
and reduce task aversion, is recommended to strengthen 
the evidence base and maximize practical relevance. Implications and conclusion
Developing cost-effective, low-threshold interventions 
to address procrastination is an urgent need, given the 
substantial negative impact of procrastination on indi -
viduals’ well-being and functioning. Overcoming bar -
riers such as limited treatment access, long wait times, 
and the demands of intensive therapy is crucial for wide -
spread intervention adoption. Although some interven -
tions have been designed to target procrastination, there 
is a scarcity of research on task-specific interventions 
validated through rigorous randomized controlled trials 
(see [38, 59]).

text:
The current study makes a meaningful contribution 
by demonstrating that a brief, low-effort intervention 
can effectively enhance outcome utility and increase the likelihood of task completion. By leveraging the Tempo -
ral Decision Model, this work provides valuable insights 
into how balancing task aversion and outcome utility can 
influence intentions to act upon procrastinated tasks. Practical implications to combating procrastination in 
educational, workplace, and clinical settings could utilize 
internet- and mobile-based interventions (see [10, 12, 23, 
37, 38]). Digital platforms and mobile applications could 
integrate brief, utility-enhancing strategies, such as gami -
fication elements or personalized incentives, to encourage 
task initiation and completion. By focusing on increasing 
outcome utility rather than solely attempting to reduce 
task aversion, such interventions may offer an accessi -
ble and effective means to reduce procrastination and 
improve productivity across diverse populations. As such, 
these findings pave the way for developing scalable, acces -
sible interventions to manage procrastination and offer 
a strong foundation for future research aimed at refining 
and optimizing strategies to support goal-directed action.

KerrThis  chapter examines the inﬂuence o f emotional factors o n the  develop-ment and course of cancer from the perspective of family systems theory.Family systems theory was  developed i n t h e 1950's a n d early 1960's byMurray Bowen, ﬁrst through the study o f families with a schizophrenicm e m b e r a n d later through s t u d y o f families w i t h symptoms spanning thefull range of emotional problems (Bowen, 1966;  Kerr, 1980b).Systems theory can be  contrasted with individually based theories suchas  psychoanalysis i n the  following way:  whereas individual theories con-sider schizophrenia a disease o f the  individual and s e e k its "cause" within
the  individual, systems theory conceptualizes schizophrenia a s a symptomof a disorder of the family emotional system. While systems theory has alsoconceptualized physical diseases as  symptoms o f disturbances i n thebalance of the family emotional system, the majority o f systems-basedresearch has focused on the emotional dysfunctions.

A systems model for conceptualizing thephysiological mechanisms involved i n illness is  proposed. Another model  ispresented that places cancer o n a continuum w i t h o t h e r disease states, em-phasizing the role o f the  exaggerated use  o f normal physiologic mecha-nisms i n the development of all of these conditions. these modeis is  t o a i d thinking about disease, not  as  something foreign thati s inﬂicted o n us  from the  environment, but  as  symptomatic of a distur-bance i n the balance o f our o w n bodily mechanisms.During any discussion about the inﬂuence of emotional factors incancer , it  is  prudent t o remind ourselves that c a n c e r is  not  conﬁned just lom a n , but  occurs in other animal species and i n plants. lese invaders o r even with the presence o f genetic defects without the

bercle bacillus causes tuberculosis o r that smoking causes cancer is  not
tirely accurate. I n recent years, a n attempt has  b e e n made t o deal  with
lis  issue  b y proposing a theory o f multiple causes (Cassel, 1 9 6 5 ) . This
leory states that several conditions or factors must b e present for a disease

text: The  systemmodel shifts attention from how others function to how weare  functioning. The  central focus is  not  the condition o f theother person (a  speciﬁc pathology o r character disorder) butrather the  degree t o which we  take responsibility f o r o u r ownfunctioning in the face of reactive behavior. Furthermore, thediagnostic model attends t o weakness rather than t o strength.Systems theory emphasizes one's o w n response t o challenge.Yet  as  long as  we  direct attention t o the  reactor's symptoms orweaknesses, we keep the focus on others not on ourselves. Wed o not  explore o r implement o u r strength.The condition of the reactor (paranoid, hysterical,narcissistic, passive, aggressive, or whatever) cannot by itselfmaintain the conﬂict. Reactivity i s not  a n isolated quantity. Itcreates a ratio that includes o u r o w n response. T o sustainitself, reactivity requires counter-reactivity. I f , however, wedeﬁne ourselves, focus on how we behave, and takeresponsibility f o r o u r o w n thoughts, behaviors, and feelings,we  set "appropriate" boundaries between others andourselves. We  d o not become emotionally enmeshed withthem. Instead we draw upon our own imagination and power.I f someone, for example, acts i n a passive-aggressivemanner, i t is  signiﬁcant only if it affects how we function.Consider Joan, who is  angry with Pastor B o b yet  afraid t o lethim know .

One  c a n t h e n recog-nize  that  what  appeared t o be  a symbiosis  whichwas  supposedly life-sustaining t o all members ofthe  family o r cultural group, was  i n fact moreaccurately a reciprocal parasitism i n w h i c h eachvoraciously depleted the  selfhoods o f those withwhom  he  was  "symbiotically" f u s e d . text:
WHAT KIND OF SY STEM I S THE FAMILY? Polly D. Caskie, MMH
The family movement's conceptual development has been influ -
enced by three important systems theories:  cybernetics, general 
systems theory, and natural systems theory. Careful examination 
of the basic assumptions, conceptual origins, and primary goals of 
these theories reveal important difference s—differences which have 
consequences for the future development of theory and research in 
the field of family. Darwin's theory of evolution by means of natural selection, a 
natural systems theory, contains the basic premise that, despite 
our uniqueness, human beings are a part of nature and subject to 
the same evolutionary forces as the rest of the living world. That 
premise is the bedrock on which Bowen family systems theory is 
built and is the vantage point from which Bowen developed a unique 
view of the family as a natural system. This view of the family as 
a natural system differs from other concepts of systems frequently 
applied to the family . INTRODUCT ION
Norbert Weiner's cybernetic theory (1948, 1950), Ludwig von 
Bertalanffy's general systems theory (1968), and Darwin's natural 
systems theory (1859, 1871) have influenced the family movement's 
conceptual development. In the search for ways to describe the 
important new discoveries from family research of the 1940s and 
1950s, consulting these existing systems theories was a logical step.

In the search for ways to describe the 
important new discoveries from family research of the 1940s and 
1950s, consulting these existing systems theories was a logical step. The family appeared to function as a whole unit rather than as  a 
collection of individuals. Some kind of systems concept was needed 
to characterize this phenomenon. However, basic to the develop -
ment of a systems theory of the family is determining what kind of 
system the family is. How one answers this question will influence 
how one thinks about the origins of human problems and the goals 
of psychotherapy. Ms. Caskie is a doctoral candidate in Counseling Psychology, Department of Human 
Services and Studies, College of Education, Florida State University, Tallahassee,

CYBERNETIC THE ORY
Norbert Weiner, a mathematician and engineer, first published 
his cybernetic theory in 1948. Two broad goals motivated his work. The first was to address the historical relationship between the 
fields of biology and physics, which were concerned respectively 
with knowledge about the living and nonliving aspects of nature. Questions about differences between the living and nonliving world 
had interested the Greek philosophers and continued to occupy 
nineteenth-century minds. In that century, these earlier differences 
became formalized into opposing philosophical positions.

text:
In that century, these earlier differences 
became formalized into opposing philosophical positions. At one 
pole were the mechanists who held that living organisms were ma -
chines and that their functioning could be explained by the laws of 
mechanics, chemistry, and physics. At the other pole were the vital -
ists who believed that the forces that governed living things could 
not adequately be described by invoking the laws which governed 
nonliving things (Mayr 1982). Guiding Weiner's work was an effort to find a way to connect 
these two poles of knowledge of the living and nonliving worlds. He believed accounting for the interactions between components of 
living or nonliving systems could be more effectively accomplished 
by extending concepts from the emerging field of communications 
engineering. He relied on concepts such as information and feedback 
rather than on earlier concepts from the field of power engineering 
such as thermodynamic laws. Weiner's second goal was to synthesize knowledge from various 
scientific disciplines which he considered too compartmentalized to 
permit intellectual cross-fertilization. He believed conceptual inte -
gration in the sciences could be achieved by developing a common 
language to describe both living and nonliving systems.

He believed conceptual inte -
gration in the sciences could be achieved by developing a common 
language to describe both living and nonliving systems. Central to 
developing a common language was developing a common concep -
tual base for understanding the principles that organized systems 
and the mechanisms that regulated relationships between their com -
ponent parts. For Weiner, these principles were (1) homeostasis, the 
maintenance of a predetermined steady state, and (2) self-regulation 
through communication of information between systems components 
and their environments. Communications theory supplied the prin -
ciple of feedback as the mechanism for self-regulation. Weiner thought his cybernetic theory might shed light on 
the nature of human behavior: "It is my thesis that the operation 
of the living individual and the operation of some of the newer 
communication machines are precisely parallel." (1948, 15)  Both 
 VOL. 1, NO. 1                      WHAT KIND OF SYSTEM IS THE FAMILY ? 9
living and man-made systems collect information from the external 
world through sensory receptors. This sensory information is then 
transformed into performance-motivating information by the central 
regulatory apparatus of the system. This process forms the basis for 
behavioral change, which Weiner believed was ultimately controlled 
by communication.

This process forms the basis for 
behavioral change, which Weiner believed was ultimately controlled 
by communication. Weiner applied his theory not only to the interaction of physi -
ological systems within individuals but also to the interactions be -
tween individuals in human society. He was familiar with Darwin's 
evolutionary theory but focused on the differences that distinguish 
humans from other life, particularly the human's capacity to learn. This attribute was the foundation for man's capacity for speech, his 
"greatest and most distinctive achievement."  (1950, 91)   It was this 
foundation and this capacity which made the human's social life 
different from that of the social insects. Weiner described the social 
lives of insect species such as ants and wasps as merely analogous 
to human society. They did not possess the uniquely human attri -
bute that cemented human society, the ability to communicate with 
speech (1950). Weiner's cybernetic theory assumes that human behavior and 
social organization were distinctly different from the behavior and 
social organization of other species. His theory's conceptual origins 
were drawn from the fields of physics, communications engineering, 
mathematics, and physiology. His first goal in building a theory was 
to smooth out the differences between the mechanistic and vitalistic 
positions in science through the use of common concepts derived 
from the field of communications engineering.

His second goal was 
to synthesize knowledge in the sciences and stimulate intellectual 
cross-fertilization. GENERAL SYSTEMS  THE ORY
Ludwig von Bertalanffy (1968) was one among many scientists 
in the 1920s and 1930s who saw the need for a shift in perspective 
in the sciences. The mechanistic, linear, reductionistic approach, 
which focused on isolating separate, discrete factors as causes of 
natural phenomena, had been successful in the physical sciences. However, he thought this perspective was not broad enough to 
permit the study of the essence of living systems—their wholeness. The broader perspective Bertalanffy proposed involved creating 
new concepts that could capture the dynamic, interactive proper -
ties of living systems. Terms such as "feedback," "circular systems," 
 10                           FAMILY  SYSTEM S               SPRING /SUMMER  1994
and "circular processes" were introduced to express the operating 
principles of self-regulating, self-orienting systems. Bertalanffy proposed to develop a systems theory that would 
be more general, leading to conceptual integration in the sciences 
through broadening the search for unifying principles rather than 
reducing science to the principles of the physical sciences. His ap -
proach was to deduce the structural similarity of laws among the 
different scientific fields.

His ap -
proach was to deduce the structural similarity of laws among the 
different scientific fields. He described his alternative to scientific 
reductionism:
We come then to a conception which in contrast to reduc -
tionism, we may call perspectivism. We cannot reduce the 
biological, behavioral, and social levels to the lowest level, 
that of the constructs and laws of physics. We can, however, 
find constructs and possibly laws within the individual levels. . . . The unifying principle is that we find organization at all 
levels. (1968, 49)
One of Bertalanffy's major contributions to thinking about 
living systems was his concept of open systems. Organisms, in 
contrast to nonliving systems like the system of reactions between 
chemical elements in a chemical compound, are not characterized by 
maintaining equilibrium. This distinction is seen in the differences 
between maintaining equilibrium in a chemical compound and in a 
metabolizing organism. The organism is not a closed, static system 
but rather an open system in which there is a continual interchange 
of material between the organism and the outside environment. Bertalanffy thought that concepts from general systems theory 
could be extended to the sciences that study human behavior and 
human social organization.

Bertalanffy thought that concepts from general systems theory 
could be extended to the sciences that study human behavior and 
human social organization. These concepts could bring some order 
into the "hodgepodge of contradictory theories in psychology." (1968, 
188)  He proposed that a new way of understanding the operation 
of complex living systems could lead to a mode of conceptualizing 
human behavior which viewed man as an "active personality system." 
(1968, 192)   Such a view would require psychology to adopt a holistic 
orientation, replacing the reductionistic perspective (which viewed 
human behavior as mobilized by drives, sensations, and reactions) 
with a perspective of the individual as a psychophysiological whole. Individuals would be seen as creators of their cognitive worlds, rather 
than as passive recipients of external stimuli. Like Weiner's, Bertalanffy's theory applied to human behavior 
and focused on aspects of human uniqueness. A basic assumption

was that human behavior was a consequence of our unique capacity 
for symbolic thought and language. He drew a distinction between 
the natural and social sciences based on his focus on human unique -
ness among living systems. He believed this uniqueness was based 
upon man's capacity for creating symbols and, thus, culture. He

He believed this uniqueness was based 
upon man's capacity for creating symbols and, thus, culture. He 
wrote:        ". . . the various symbolic universes, material and non-ma -
terial, which distinguish human cultures from animal societies are a 
part, and easily the most important part, of man's behavior system."  
(Bertalanffy 1968, 216-217)  Man's mental disturbances were thought 
to reflect a disturbance in man’s symbolic functions. The goals of Bertalanffy's general systems theory were similar to 
those of Weiner's cybernetic theory. Like Weiner, he was motivated by 
the desire to broaden the mechanistic and reductionistic perspective 
in the sciences and to synthesize scientific knowledge. The concep -
tual origins of general systems theory were the organizing principles 
found at each level of complex living systems. Bertalanffy believed 
that, ultimately, similarities between concepts at all levels of complex 
living systems could be expressed in logico-mathematical laws. FAMIL Y SY STEMS  MOD ELS BASE D ON

Such models postulate 
that the family is, above all, a communications system that operates 
on principles analogous to those governing communications among 
the various parts of man-made systems like computers and weapons. Codes or rules are assumed to regulate human relationships, and these 
rules are based on philosophy and religion. Relationship patterns 
are the observable manifestations of these rules. Thus the structure 
of the family, and the rules which govern family relationships, are 
grounded in uniquely human reason and mirror the unique structure 
of the human mind (Aponte and Van Deusen 1981). The principle 
of homeostasis, defined as the maintenance of an optimal, predeter -
mined steady state, is assumed to be the organizing principle for the 
family system as it is for mechanical systems. Homeostasis is the 
"goal" of the system, and governs relationships between individual 
components of this system. As a corollary, feedback of information 
 12                           FAMILY  SYSTEM S               SPRING /SUMMER  1994
between family members is considered an important mechanism for 
regulating the system’s homeostasis. Ideally, a main function of the 
cyclic interaction patterns observed between family members is to 
maintain the homeostasis of the system (Hoffman 1976). Therapy 
focuses on the communications, interactions, or transactional pat -
terns between components of the family system that produce and 
maintain a symptom.

Therapy 
focuses on the communications, interactions, or transactional pat -
terns between components of the family system that produce and 
maintain a symptom. A symptom in an individual family member 
functions as a homeostatic-maintaining mechanism within the fam -
ily system. Other family systems models have incorporated concepts from 
Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory as the basis for de -
scribing family organization and family regulating mechanisms. Such 
models envision the family as an "open system," in a continual state of 
becoming more complex as stimuli flow back and forth between the 
family system and the environment. Another concept incorporated 
from general systems theory into family theory is the concept of the 
family as a hierarchically organized system, with generations form -
ing the levels of the hierarchy. From a family perspective, standard 
hierarchical organization includes the levels grandparents, parents, 
and children. When the boundaries between the hierarchical levels 
of the family system break down, symptoms emerge (Minuchin 1974). Other models have incorporated a more global idea from general 
system theory, as a general way of describing the family as a living 
system without spelling out logical links that connect Bertalanffy's 
ideas with the family system.

At the same time, the term "system" has 
been used more as a descriptive metaphor for the family, and family 
relationships are not viewed as having a factual basis, but rather as 
convenient terms for descriptive purposes ( Duhl 1986). Cybernetics and general systems theory have been useful as 
models, on a microscopic level, to describe the operation of physiologi -
cal systems within the body or, on a macroscopic level, to broaden 
thinking by introducing a scheme which pictures the organization of 
the complex natural hierarchies from cell to solar system. However, 
careful reading of these theories and their basic assumptions about 
the nature of human behavior raises questions about the accuracy 
of their extension to the family system. Does the family relationship 
system operate according to principles of physics and engineering 
based on analogy with man-made systems? Does the family relation -
ship system operate according to mathematical laws deduced from 
common systems concepts in the social, biological, physical, and 
psychological sciences? Perhaps there are principles from another 
source which can directly rather than analogically describe the family 
as a system and explain how this system operates. VOL. 1, NO. 1                      WHAT KIND OF SYSTEM IS THE FAMILY ? 13

VOL. 1, NO. 1                      WHAT KIND OF SYSTEM IS THE FAMILY ? 13
NATUR AL SYSTEMS  THE ORY
Natural systems theory is not found in the work of one indi -
vidual. The term describes an historical tradition of studying the 
living world characterized by certain ways of thinking, and certain 
methods and assumptions. One central assumption is that the unique 
properties of life, while consistent with the principles of physics and 
chemistry, cannot be sufficiently described through physical and 
mechanistic laws. A second central assumption is that the human is 
part of all life, and all human qualities, including human uniqueness 
in cultural complexity and linguistic virtuosity, can be explained and 
accounted for by the same kinds of theories that apply to the rest of 
the living world. Therefore, separate theories and concepts are not 
needed to describe human behavior and the behavior of the rest of 
the living world. A characteristic method of scientific investigation 
within this tradition is one that relies more on personal observation, 
including the collection of facts, and on experiment, rather than 
on logic alone. The goal of the scientist becomes the discovery of 
natural laws that can explain the regularities in natural phenomena 
(Mayr 1982). Within the field of biology, Charles Darwin (1859, 1871) was 
an important natural systems thinker.

text:
Within the field of biology, Charles Darwin (1859, 1871) was 
an important natural systems thinker. He relied on observable and 
established facts from research in comparative anatomy and physiol -
ogy as well as on his own extensive field observations to strengthen 
his theoretical arguments about the processes of evolution. Darwin's 
theory of evolution held that all life was descended from a common 
ancestor and that present diversity among plants and animals ob -
served in the natural world was a product of continuing variation in 
each generation of life in combination with the differential reproduc -
tion and survival of individuals in each generation. Darwin's theory of evolution was a natural systems theory that 
saw nature as a system, organized according to reciprocal relation -
ships, mutually interdependent and mutually influencing. His theory 
described and proposed a mechanism which connected components 
of living systems.

His theory 
described and proposed a mechanism which connected components 
of living systems. He proposed that natural selection produces the 
beautifully synchronized co-adaptations we see between predators 
and their prey, between insects and flowers, between female pref -
erence and the appearance of these preferred characteristics in the 
males that become their mates, between the preferences of livestock 
breeders and the appearance of structural, functional, and behav -
ioral characteristics in later generations of stock they breed, between 
protective coloration and physical habitat, and between anatomical 
structures and the functions for which they were adapted. 14                           FAMILY  SYSTEM S               SPRING /SUMMER  1994
For Darwin, the following principles or "natural laws" accounted 
for the relationships between components of living systems: 
Growth with Reproduction; Inheritance, which is almost 
implied by reproduction; Variability from the indirect and 
direct action of the conditions of life, and from use and dis -
use; a Ratio of Increase so high as to lead to a Struggle for 
Life, and as a consequence to Natural Selection, entailing 
Divergence of Character and the Extinction of less-improved 
forms.

(1859, 459-460)
In The Descent of Man  (1871), published twelve years after The 
Origin of Species  (1859) ,  Darwin directly addressed the conclusion 
implicit in his earlier work:  that our own species is the product 
of evolutionary processes. Darwin reviewed the numerous facts 
that supported his conclusion:  similarities between our anatomy, 
physiology, instincts, and behavior and those of other life forms; 
exchange of diseases between humans and other animals; similar 
normal processes of gestation, maturation, and length of diseases 
which follow lunar periods; similarities between our reproductive 
processes and those of other mammals, including courtship and 
maternal care of the young; similarities in embryonic development; 
and the fact that our species retains "rudimentary parts" of physical 
structures found in earlier forms. Darwin wrote that the evolutionary origins of our human rela -
tionships can be seen both in our self-preserving instincts and in the 
social instincts we share with other social animals. He considered 
"sympathy" to be the fundamental element in these social instincts, 
observed in man's highly developed "instinctive love and sympathy 
for his fellows." (1871, 483)  This sympathy instinct results in man's 
sensitivity to the wishes, approval, and blame of his fellows and in 
his behavior in relationships being guided by this sensitivity.

CONC LUSION
How does one account for the family movement's ready ac -
ceptance of concepts from cybernetic and general systems theory to 
describe the family relationship system, and its missing the connec -
tions between biology, evolution, and the human family? What makes 
it so difficult for people to understand Bowen's concept of the family 
as a relationship system motivated by emotional forces, the same 
emotional forces that govern relationships in all forms of life? Darwin anticipated and addressed this problem of people's 
difficulty in accepting his theory of evolution. He wrote that this 
difficulty involved the mind's natural limitations in simultaneously 
comprehending all the steps involved in a gradual process of change 
and the outcome of that process. It is also difficult for the mind to 
comprehend the vast amounts of time required for this process to 
operate ( Darwin 1871). Our natural tendency to think of human 
behavior as the product of forces operating during the brief period 
from an individual's birth to his death seems to reflect the difficulty 
Darwin described. Another factor may be that we are naturally resistant to the idea 
that we are just one product of a long historical process, a process 
that has yielded diversity in life forms, and a process that makes us 
not so special.

Stephanie J. Ferrera, MSW
Many theorists have postulated an innate drive to explain aggres -
sion. Some have considered it a destructive and dangerous drive. A natural systems view is more neutral. It seeks to understand 
aggression both as a natural phenomenon,  an adaptation which 
evolved in many species due to its contribution to survival and 
reproductive success, and as a systems phenomenon,  a behavior 
which evolves and is shaped and regulated in the context of relation -
ship systems. Wilson views aggressive behavior as a spectrum of 
responses rather than a single drive, and delineates seven forms seen 
in animals and humans. De Waal observes that fighting in primates 
is usually followed by reconciling, and believes that the interplay 
of the two cements social bonds. Bowen‘s theory of the emotional 
system and differentiation of self makes it possible to understand 
the full spectrum of aggressive behavior, from the well-regulated 
level to the violent level on a single continuum without invoking 
a unique or pathological drive to account for violence. The effort 
toward a scientific and neutral theory of aggression informs the 
effort to develop ethical principles for regulating this behavior. Aggression
of the many dimensions of human behavior,  probably ag -
gression is the most difficult to be neutral about, especially when 
it goes to extreme, violent levels. People often invoke the concept 
of evil to explain it.

In 
1937, two years before his death, Freud wrote in Analysis Terminable 
and Interminable :  "Only by the concurrent or mutually opposing 
action of the two primal instincts—Eros and the death-instinct—, 
never by one or the other alone, can we explain the rich multiplicity 
of the phenomena of life." (Sulloway 1979, 412) 
Ethologist Konrad Lorenz published his influential On Aggres -
sion  in 1966. Drawing on his expertise in animal behavior, Lorenz 
put forward the thesis that man’s aggressive behavior is the expres -
sion of a phylogenetically programmed instinct that constantly 
seeks discharge. His view has been called "hydraulic" because it 
postulates an aggressive energy that builds up and must be released 
at a certain point. The effect of damming up the instinct is to lower 
the threshold of stimulation needed to trigger its release. Lorenz 
views the aggressive drive both as essential for preservation of the 
species and dangerous. In a chapter entitled "The Spontaneity of 
Aggression," he writes: 
Knowledge of the fact that the aggression drive is a true, pri -
marily species-preserving instinct enables us to recognize its 
full danger:  it is the spontaneity of the instinct that makes it 
so dangerous. If it were merely a reaction to certain external 
factors, . . . the state of mankind would not be as perilous as 
it really is, for, in that case, the reaction-eliciting factors could 
be eliminated with some hope of success.

far greater than that of the male. From a sociobiological point of 
view, which assumes that maximum perpetuation of one's genes 
in the next generation is the fundamental driving force of behavior, 
the female strategy for reproductive success should be to mate with 
the strongest, most reliable male available and to keep him around 
to help raise the offspring, while the male strategy for reproductive 
success should be to outcompete other males for access to females, 
to court and mate with numerous females, and at the same time to 
prevent these females from straying and mating with other males. These male-female differences in reproductive roles partially account 
for the fact that males are generally more aggressive than females. The high degree of male-male competition is a major selective pres -
sure favoring male aggressiveness, while the female specialization 
in parenting and corresponding male specialization in defense of 
territory is an additional selective pressure. Female aggressiveness 
is primarily activated by threats to her offspring.

costs and benefits accruing to a behavior. Applying this principle 
to aggression, we can say that, in any given environment and social 
system, there are factors which promote or favor aggression, factors 
which oppose or limit it, and an adaptive range that represents a 
balance among the various factors. Aggression is activated by the presence of limited food and 
resources worth fighting for, by the appearance of a stranger who 
represents a potential invasion of territory or disruption of the social 
order, by seasonal events such as the breeding cycle, and usually but 
not always by crowding. Crowding, which increases the frequency of 
encounters among animals, is often accompanied by more frequent 
aggressive interactions. J. B. Calhoun (1962) reported that captive 
rats in close proximity suffered breakdowns in their usual social order 
including rape and infanticide. On the other hand, several different 
studies of fish revealed that at high densities aggression breaks down 
and peaceful schools are formed. Barash (1977) distinguishes between 
density-tolerant species whose social and reproductive systems toler -
ate a great deal of crowding, and density-intolerant species in which 
reproduction drops off and aggression rises with crowding. The costs and risks associated with aggression are the limiting 
factors.

other living systems. This way of thinking led to two major con -
cepts:  the emotional system and differentiation of self. The family 
can be conceptualized as a system in that it, like other collectives in 
nature, is more than an assemblage of individuals. its members are 
functionally interrelated and interdependent. Their responsiveness 
to one another and influence on one another's behavior is profound. The individual members shape the system, and the system as a whole 
shapes the functioning of its members. Families operate at a certain level of emotional intensity on 
a continuum ranging from relatively calm (low intensity) to highly 
anxious (high intensity). The level of intensity in a family fluctuates 
over time related to the number and severity of stresses the family is 
dealing with and the way people manage that stress. People vary in 
the way they respond to life's stresses and pressures. Some can tolerate 
a good deal of stress without becoming very anxious or reactive. For 
other people, a relatively small amount of stress can trigger intense 
reactivity , and the ability to think and cope can be quickly compromised 
as people are caught up in an escalating cycle of reactivity to problems 
and to one another.

emotionally determined and anxiety-driven. A person’s level of

family begins to revolve around its most anxious members and 
lacks strong leadership from higher functioning members, it is on a 
regressive course. A family or, for that matter, any human system that is going

and the part each member plays in it. In a given violent event, some 
individuals have central roles, and thus a major responsibility, while 
others have more peripheral roles. As violent behavior runs out of 
control, it encompasses more and more people, and the likelihood 
increases that the targets of the behavior will be random outsiders 
who have had little or no part in igniting the process. The effort to understand aggression and violence on a neutral,

PERSPECTIVES ON GRIEF:  
PSYCHOANALYTIC, EVOLUTIONARY,  
AND FAMILY SYSTEMS 
Anne S. McKnight, MSW, EdD
Modern views on grief have been profoundly affected by 
psychoanalytic thinking. Freud wrote in “Mourning and 
Melancholia” that “the work of mourning” consisted of 
an unremitting focus on feelings of loss of the loved one. This view that, unless adequate mourning was carried out, 
the individual was prone to suffer difficulties in life, was 
elaborated on by other psychoanalysts and contributed to a 
body of ideas that became the basis for the five stages of grief 
m proposed by Kubler-Ross. Animal researchers have observed 
grief reactions in animals, and evolutionary biologists have 
identified a natural resilience in the response to death in 
the human population. Murray Bowen introduced a theory 
(Bowen theory) that provides a wider lens on grief than 
focusing on the individual—to examine the impact of death 
on the family system. This paper examines these different 
perspectives toward grief with a focus on how Bowen’s 
ideas on the expression of grief as reflective of the emotional 
functioning of the family can be of use to professionals and 
individuals who are facing bereavement.

Sigmund Freud: The Work of Mourning
In our Western culture, views about grief and how to grieve 
were profoundly affected in the 20th century by the writings 
of Sigmund Freud. Freud created the foundation for the pre -
dominant paradigm in the Western world for understanding 
grief by proposing that an individual could only overcome 
feelings of sadness over the death of a loved one by carrying 
out “grief work.”  
When his father Jacob died in 1896, Freud began a self-
analysis of his grief. In 1917, he wrote “Mourning and Mel -
ancholia,” in which he compared grief and depression. Freud 
presented the view that grief was comparable to depression 
because both involved suffering with a longing for something 
that is lost. In a letter to Ludwig Binswanger, who had lost a 
son, Freud wrote:
We find a place for what we lose. Although we know 
that after such a loss the acute stage of mourning will 
subside, we also know that we shall remain inconsolable 
and will never find a substitute. No matter what may 
fill the gap, even if it be filled completely, it nevertheless

remains something else. And actually this is how it 
should be. It is the only way of perpetuating that love 
which we do not want to relinquish.

He concluded that suffering was a natural part of the grieving 
process, necessitating “the work of mourning” to get relief. This 
effort required reclaiming the psychological energy, the constant 
longing for someone no longer there, that was invested in the 
deceased. The inhibition and loss of interest characteristic of 
grief are fully accounted for by the work of mourning in which 
the ego is absorbed. The work entails the ego detaching itself 
from the deceased so that it is free to attach to someone else 
(Gay 1989, 587). This process included engaging in a review of 
“each single one of the memories and hopes which bound the 
libido (life energy) to the object (the deceased).” This review, 
done “bit by bit” and “extraordinarily painful,” “was the only 
way to break the bond with the deceased, reclaim the libido, 
and move forward.” (Freud 1917, 150-72)
Freud believed that individuals respond to the loss of a 
loved one over the course of weeks and months by moving 
through a succession of phases. The phases included a phase 
of numbing, interspersed with outbursts of extreme distress, 
a phase of yearning for the lost figure, a phase of disorgani -
zation and despair, and a phase of greater or lesser degree of 
reorganization (Gay 1989, 587).

Psychoanalysts following Freud elaborated on his ideas 
on grief and the work of mourning. Helene Deutsch, a psycho -
analyst, published the “Absence of Grief” in 1937. Observing 
four patients in therapy, she concluded that certain symptoms 
such as uncontrolled, periodic weeping that were not con -
nected to any recent death were signs of “absent grief.” In the 
course of psychoanalytic treatment, she traced these symp -
toms to a loss the patients had experienced in childhood but 
had never mourned. She thought that the unconscious mind 
had an intelligence that, if denied, would express its needs 
in other ways. “Unmanifested grief will be found expressed 
to the full in some other way,” she wrote. (Deutsch 1937, 16) 
If the unconscious was not given the opportunity to grieve, 
then the subconscious feelings will make themselves known 
through various symptoms. Eric Lindemann, an American psychiatrist, expanded the 
idea of the absence of grief. He studied the survivors of the 
Coconut Grove nightclub fire in 1942 in which 500 people lost 
their lives. He concluded that no matter how healthy a subject 
might appear, a hidden unresolved grief lurked in their sub -
conscious. Current psychological problems were based  on that 
earlier unresolved grief reaction (Lindemann 1944, 1141-48).

Freud’s conception of grief and its treatment has had a 
major impact on psychiatry, mental health, and the field of 
grief therapy over the last century. His ideas on “the work 
of mourning” and the similarity of grief to depression have 
evolved and been reinterpreted by other theorists to include 
the ideas of disordered mourning, complicated grief, and the 
stages of grief work described by Kubler-Ross. The view of 
grief as a pathology, with the need for diagnosis, treatment, 
and medication, has been codified by psychiatry in the DSM V . In the DSM III,  the Diagnostic Manual of the American Psy -
chiatric Association  published in 1980, grief first appeared as 
“Uncomplicated Bereavement” and was defined as a “normal 
reaction to the death of a loved one” that occurs within the 
first two or three months. It was listed as a V code or non-
psychiatric problem. In contrast, in the newly published DSM V ,  bereavement 
is included in the diagnosis for major depressive disorder.

Grief as Part of the Natural World
The perspective of grief as a pathology is being challenged 
through observations in animal behavior and human research. The roots of thinking about grief from an evolutionary frame -
work surfaced as early as the work of Charles Darwin. Darwin, one of the first to initiate the scientific study of 
human behavior, observed that the expression of emotion was 
visible in the human. He believed that the universality of emo -
tional expression in animals and humans provided a thread 
of continuity in the evolution of species.

Bekoff speculates on the evolutionary value of grief among 
animal species:
 40               F amily SyStemS                        2015
Grief itself is something of a mystery, for there doesn’t 
seem to be any obvious adaptive value to it in an 
evolutionary sense. It does not seem to increase an 
individual’s reproductive success. Some theorize that 
perhaps mourning strengthens social bonds among the 
survivors who band together to pay their last respects. This may enhance group cohesion at a time when it’s 
likely to be weakened. Whatever its value is, grief is the 
price of commitment, that wellspring of both happiness 
and sorrow. (Bekoff 2007, 63)
Jaak Panksepp: The Neurochemistry of Grief
Jaak Panksepp, a scientist who has studied the neurochemistry 
of affectional bonds in humans and animals, elaborates on the 
evolutionary importance of the grief response. He views the 
neurobiology of grief as related to the disruption of feelings of 
safety and comfort in a social group.

We simply feel normal and comfortable when we are 
in the midst of friendly company, and that same feeling 
becomes warmer when we are among those we love 
deeply. ...We often take these feelings, like air itself, 
for granted. But we should not, for when this feeling 
of normalcy is suddenly disrupted by the undesired 
loss of a lover or the unexpected death of a loved one, 
we find ourselves plunged into one of the deepest and 
most troubling emotional pains of which we, as social 
creatures, are capable. In everyday language, this feeling 
is called sorrow or grief, and it can verge on panic in its 
most intense and precipitous forms. (Panksepp 1998, 261)
In an evolutionary sense, this psychic pain informs the 
individual of the importance of the loss of the loved one—
usually those with whom one has invested great genetic 
effort, such as children, or those who helped one thrive, such 
as parents, friends, or relatives. Panksepp believes that this 
type of psychic pain emerged from a brain emotional system 
that evolved early in mammals to inform individuals about 
the status of their social environment. The PANIC circuit is a neurochemical concept developed

most dependent on the one who died experiencing the most

human practices across cultures. Human reactions of grief and 
mourning lead to participation in a social acknowledgement 
of death through rituals, celebrations, or funerals. A death 
creates a void that draws humans together to reconnect with 
important others of their social group, thus restoring some 
feelings of safety and connection. George Bonanno: A Science of Bereavement
George Bonanno’s research is consistent with evolution -

of individuals who had lost a loved one and discovered that a 
natural resilience was a major component of grief and trauma 
reactions in people who face  the loss of loved ones.

The idea 
that individuals are resilient in coping with death challenges 
the conceptual framework of the Kubler-Ross model that grief 
must be processed through stages in order to prevent future 
difficulties for the individual. Bonanno (2009) found that the 
emphasis on having people talk or cry about a loss of a loved 
one can actually intensify the feelings of grief. He proposed 
that the focus of therapy should be on supporting the natural 
resilience in the individual. Bonanno’s interest in resilience in bereavement is linked 
to a broader area of research on resilience as a general human 
trait. In studying resilience in children who grow up with 
maltreatment and abuse, researchers have discovered that it 
is not unusual for children to cope well with adversity. Only a 
small percentage of children exposed to trauma emerge with a 
reaction that fits diagnostic criteria for trauma. This resilience 
of children in overcoming childhood difficulties is replicated 
in the resilience of adults (Bonanno 2009, 96). Bonanno found 
through his research that many traumatic events are simply 
forgotten over time. His research team studied a survey of 
the mental health of the population of New York City after 
 42               F amily SyStemS                        2015
the 9/11 attacks. They found that six months after the attack, 
a large majority of residents had no trauma symptoms, nor 
psychological problems from the event.

a large majority of residents had no trauma symptoms, nor 
psychological problems from the event. The exceptions were 
those who had witnessed the attack firsthand and those who 
had lost a loved one. For them, grief was more profound. Yet 
only a third met the criteria for PTSD, while two thirds did not 
(Bonanno 2009). In a survey of fifty-five widows one month 
after the death of a spouse, Toni Biscotti (in Konigsberg 2011, 
160) found a similar outcome in that those with the lowest 
amount of stress had dispositional resilience defined by three 
characteristics: they were connected to other people, they felt 
their grief was manageable, and they embraced and learned 
from new experience. . According to Bonanno, grief is a stress reaction in the normal 
population. It is experienced in waves in which an individual 
has periods of loss-oriented thinking, alternating with periods 
that are restoration oriented. Reflective of Panksepp’s theories 
of the neurochemistry of grief, he believes sadness is wired into 
the human brain and is “functional” in helping the bereaved 
take stock of their loss and reflect on its impact on their lives. Expressions of sadness engage sympathy and support for the 
bereaved from those around them, reinforcing social bonds. For the most part, people have a natural resilience that allows 
them to go forward in life while mourning the death of a loved 
one (Bonanno 2009, 96).

For the most part, people have a natural resilience that allows 
them to go forward in life while mourning the death of a loved 
one (Bonanno 2009, 96). For some who are dependent on a loved one, however, grief 
becomes more debilitating. Bonanno found that 10-15% of the 
population he studied had difficulty overcoming grief. Those 
overwhelmed by grief were characterized as excessively depe n-
dent, submissive, or clingy to the deceased. These individuals 
had an “exaggerated need for care, nurturance, and protection 
even when one is capable of functioning independently to meet 
normal everyday challenges.” (Bonanno 2009, 102) Their grief 
reactions were debilitating as they withdrew from life and 
remained endlessly preoccupied with the deceased person. FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY
Bowen Theory: The Family as an Emotional Unit
While Murray Bowen’s ideas about the function of grief 
fit into the evolutionary thinking of the animal behaviorists,

ing the impact of a death. Bowen proposed that the influence 
of a death is not simply on an individual who is grieving but 
on the entire family system, including succeeding generations 
over time. A person’s position in a family affects how their 
death influences the relationship system.

A person’s position in a family affects how their 
death influences the relationship system. Bowen theory’s view of death is based on the premise that 
the family is an emotional unit composed of interdependent 
family members adapting to their environment. Each member 
of the family interacts with other family members in recipro -
cal patterns involving emotions, behavior, and physiology. In these reciprocal interactions, the individual is balancing 
the competing emotional forces of striving for individuality 
and autonomy, while at the same time being sensitive to the 
expectations and approval of others. The more a person’s life 
is regulated by sensitivity to expectations, need for approval, 
and dependence on others, the more vulnerable that individual 
is to acting on emotions, including grief, rather than achieving 
a thoughtful management of his or her life based on principles. Two Variables in Grief: The Level of Anxiety and the Level of   
Differentiation in the Family
One factor that influences the equilibrium between togeth -
erness and individuality is the level of anxiety in the individual 
and family. Chronic anxiety reflects a basic core of emotional, 
physiological, and relationship reactivity in the family that is 
transmitted from one generation to another. This level of anxi -
ety in the family can be heightened by stresses, such as illness, 
unemployment, migration, and death.

ety in the family can be heightened by stresses, such as illness, 
unemployment, migration, and death. Symptoms develop in 
an individual when a family’s ability to adapt in the face of 
stressors is exhausted. The individual then absorbs the fam -
ily anxiety and, in bearing the symptom, allows others to be 
less anxious. Bowen also recognized from his research that humans 
vary in their ability to manage life thoughtfully in a calm con -
nection to important others. He labeled this variation in the 
capacity to preserve autonomy while maintaining connection 
to important others  “the scale of differentiation.” He wrote: 
A differentiated self is one who can maintain emotional 
objectivity while in the midst of an emotional system 
 44               F amily SyStemS                        2015
in turmoil, yet at the same time actively relate to key 
people in the system. (Bowen 1978, 485)
Bowen believed that how an individual and a family handle 
death varies according to their level of differentiation. At a 
higher level of differentiation, families are connected with a 
calm interdependence, allowing flexibility for individual life 
goals, even in the face of a death. Others can look symptom-
free until they experience a level of stress that they are unable 
to manage.

free until they experience a level of stress that they are unable 
to manage. Familes at a lower level of differentiation are 
more dependent on and reactive to one another and are more 
vulnerable to becoming overwhelmed by a death in the family, 
particularly of an important individual. For example, a grandmother in a family dies  and the mother 
is deeply affected. The son reacts to the mother’s grief and 
begins to have problems in school, at which point the father 
becomes angry at the son. Rather than diagnosing the grief of 
the mother as a pathology, Bowen theory describes how reac -
tivity and emotions such as grief travel from one member to 
another and across generations. According to Bowen, families can be “open” or “closed” 
systems in engaging the death of a family member. An “open 
system” is one in which a person can communicate his or her 
thoughts and feelings to another who can reciprocate. A “closed 
system,” is one in which sensitive subjects are instinctively 
avoided as a way to protect oneself from the anxiety of the 
other. Death is one of the most anxiety provoking subjects in 
human life, and discussing it is often taboo. People are fear -
ful of facing their own death, and they are afraid of upsetting 
their family members. In a similar way, a physician’s anxiety about a family’s 
reaction to death can affect the system.

reaction to death can affect the system. Medical professionals 
can contribute to the closed system when they speak obliquely 
of the dying process or offer treatment that will not actually 
prolong the life of the patient. When family members or pro -
fessionals can manage their own anxiety, discomfort, and reac -
tion to death, the individual close to death may be better able 
to talk and may be eager to discuss what they are thinking 
and feeling. A calm presence and willingness to engage and 
listen to the person dying can permit the living to hear their 
thoughts and observations. Funerals or community rituals around death have been 
documented since the emergence of mankind. The communal

...the best function of a funeral is served when it brings

contact with the harsh fact of death and with each other

In contrast to Freud’s emphasis on the individual review -

resolve the attachment to the dead, Bowen believed that fac -
ing the facts of the death , through family and community par -
ticipation in the dying process and the funeral , helped family 
members to move on. He encouraged families to visit dying 
relatives, to have children involved in the dying process and 
funerals, and to nurture “personal contact” between the liv -
ing and the dying. The goal is to bring the entire family system into the 
closest possible contact with death in the presence of 
the friendship system and to lend a helping hand to 
the anxious people who would rather run than face a 
funeral. (Bowen 1978, 332)  
This effort to be in contact with the dying also gives the living 
a view of death and the dying process that helps them accept 
and make responsible decisions about their own deaths. Bowen coined the term “emotional shock wave” (Bowen 
1978, 325) to draw attention to the emotional aftershocks that 
can occur in the extended family months or years after the 
death of an individual important to a family. This shock wave 
is based on the interdependence of the family members that is 
disturbed and realigned after a death. Families vary in how 
they react to death. A well-integrated family may be highly 
reactive at the time of death, but adapt rather quickly.

Families vary in how 
they react to death. A well-integrated family may be highly 
reactive at the time of death, but adapt rather quickly. A less 
integrated family may have significant symptoms emerge over 
a long period of time. Though not related to grief as such, this 
reactivity to a death can result in symptoms erupting in chil -
dren and grandchildren. The symptoms of a shock wave can be any human problem, 
including physical illness, behavioral difficulties, emotional 
symptoms, and social dysfunction (Bowen 1978, 326). The 
 46               F amily SyStemS                        2015
death did not “cause” these problems but created a ripple of 
anxiety that tipped the scale of emotionality and reactivity in 
the family to trigger the symptoms. The presence of a shock 
wave can highlight the underlying emotional dependency in 
a family, particularly when an emotionally important mem -
ber dies. Families may see these problems as unrelated, but 
a broader systems view of the functioning of the family after 
a death can highlight a pattern of problems following a sig -
nificant death. SUMMARY
A variety of conceptual framework for mourning and 
bereavement have developed over the course of human his -
tory. Freud’s ideas on the work of mourning laid a foundation 
for others, including Bowlby and Kubler-Ross, to formulate 
the stages of grief and the necessity for grief work as the pre -
dominant view in the mental health field in the modern era.

BRIEF REPORT
MARRIAGE PREPARATION PROGRAMS  
AND BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY
Kathleen F. Riordan, MSW
This article provides background information on marriage 
preparation programs and describes a unique interview 
format with engaged couples guided by Bowen family 
systems theory alongside traditional marriage preparation 
inventories. The unique format includes a review of 
individual and family functional facts and family emotional 
process. It also presents an opportunity for the pair to 
look beyond the courtship to early marriage. The author 
finds this combined methodology significantly broadens 
and enhances the more typical approach used in marriage  
preparation programs. BACKGROUND
For many years now churches, synagogues, and other faith 
based organizations have sponsored marriage preparation 
programs. One of the earliest examples of church sponsored 
programs would be the Catholic Church’s Pre Cana program. The program name is a reference from the biblical story in John 
2: 1-12 of the wedding at Cana. More about this program can 
be found at foryourmarriage.org. 1975 saw the enactment of the Family Law Act (FLA) 
and no-fault divorce. Both made it easier to obtain a divorce, 
resulting in a subsequent uptick in the frequency of divorce. Other variables that appeared to promote renewed interest in 
marriage preparation programs included a decline in church Brief Reports present important ideas in development and 
promising research in eary stages.

WITHIN-FAMILY VARIABILITY:  
THE FAMILY PROJECTION PROCESS  
IN AN ADOPTED FAMILY
Laura Brooks, MSW
The Adoptive Family Study (AFS) is a longitudinal, 
qualitative, prospective study of eight adoptive families. This 
paper uses a long-term case study design of one participant 
family composed of a mother, father, and their four children, 
two by adoption and two by birth. The family was recruited 
from a private adoption organization. Observations of the 
family were made over the first thirteen years of the study, 
with data collected in annual interviews with the couple in 
their home. Annual updates of changes in the three generation 
family included discussion of each child’s adjustment. Transcripts of the interviews were coded from the perspective 
of the family projection process, a key concept in Bowen family 
systems theory that describes the process in which parents 
project their anxiety onto a child. This process contributes to 
a child’s vulnerability to anxiety and dysfunction. Keywords: within-family variability, adoptive families, 
family projection process, adoption, Bowen theory, 
multigenerational emotional process
INTRODUCTION
Although exhaustive research has been done on why chil -
dren in the same family turn out differently, little is known 
about within-family variability from a systems perspective. Descriptions of the relational processes in families with both 
adopted and birth children are also lacking in the research.

text:
In contrast to the prevailing individual viewpoint of exist -
ing research, Bowen theory broadens the lens to a view of the 
family as a system of relationships that has regulatory effects 
on the functioning of the offspring (Bowen 1978). The effect 
varies depending on the intensity of the family projection 
process—the degree to which the parents project their anxi -
eties onto the children. In this process, the mother or father 
may be more tuned into one of their children. The child’s 
gender and birth order, the level of anxiety in the marriage, 
the extended family relationships at the time of the child’s 
birth, or a view of the child as special in some way, all may 
contribute to a mother’s heightened sensitivity to one of her 
children. This child focus may inhibit the child’s development 
towards higher levels of emotional autonomy and responsible 
functioning (Bowen 1978 and Kerr 2008). From this systems 
viewpoint, the Adoptive Family Study (AFS) explores how the 
family projection process—an indicator of emotional involve -
ment driven more by parental anxiety than the reality needs 
of the child—contributes to differences in the functioning of 
children, whether by adoption or birth, in the same family. LITERATURE REVIEW

In 1987, a seminal and comprehensive review of studies 
that used quantitative behavioral genetic methods, non-genetic 
influences such as differential parenting, extra-familial expe -
riences, and possibly luck, were synthesized, resulting in a 
conclusion that two children in the same family can be as 
different from one another as are pairs of children selected 
randomly from the population (Plomin and Daniels 1987 and 
Plomin et al. 2001). In other words, family influences are not 
determined by the family environment, but by each specific 
child’s experience of the environment (Plomin and Daniels 
1987). Studies of twins, adopted children, and birth children 
were included in the review. Plomin challenged researchers to 
identify the relevant family experiences specific to each child 
in the family that contributed to differential ou tcomes (2001). Conley (2004) examined three national sets of social and 
economic data and conducted in-depth interviews with 175 
individuals from 68 families longitudinally. He found that 
many factors contributed to social and economic inequality 
between siblings, including that: (1) parents learn as they 
go along, (2) a family is in constant motion economically, 
geographically, and in its makeup, (3) gender, birth order,

next section contrasts these hypotheses with Bowen family

The Family Projection Process
Bowen theory views the family as a regulatory system that 
distributes chronic anxiety among its members. The process is 
automati c and operates mostly out of awareness. This perspec -
tive was based on observations Bowen (1978) made in the 
 Vol.12, N o. 2                    W ithiN-Family Variability                111
1950s at the National Institute of Mental Health. He hospital -
ized several families with a psychotic adult child for up to 
three years, observing the differences in how parents variably 
projected their immaturities onto their children. In this way, 
children in the same family had different experiences. The more the adults in the family projected their anxi -
ety onto a child, the more anxiety that child absorbed. This 
affected their capacity to self-regulate or, as Bowen described it, 
to “differentiate a self.” (1978, 366) Bowen called this phenom -
enon the family projection process  that resulted in some children 
becoming more vulnerable to social, physiological, and psycho -
logical symptoms than other children in the same family.

Family projection exists in all families to some degree and 
represents one way that anxiety is managed. Parental anxiety 
takes many forms, but most commonly it can be observed in a 
preoccupation with a child, or being overly solicitous towards 
a child, doing things for the child that they can do themselves, 
and over-reacting to a child rather than responding realistically 
or objectively. In all forms, the anxiety begins with the mother 
and/ or father and the child reciprocates as a full participant. To the extent that an individual absorbs the anxiety of 
others—that is, to the extent the individual is regulated by the 
expectations and reactions of others—that person will have 
less capacity to think and act autonomously for self. On the 
other hand, autonomous, self-directed functioning correlates 
with lower levels of anxiety in the system and with higher 
levels of differentiation (Bowen 1978). Anxiety, Reciprocity,Triangles, and Emotional Cutoff
Anxiety is a response to a real or imagined threat. It is not 
unusual for family projection to intensify with increased anxi -
ety in the nuclear or extended family system. For example, if a 
mother and one of her daughters are predisposed to a mutual 
overinvolvement, an additional stress in the mother’s life, for 
instance her own mother’s death, would likely exacerbate the 
pattern. Reciprocity reflects an emotional interdependence 
that each reinforces, often out of awareness.

that each reinforces, often out of awareness. In the mother-
child relationship the daughter absorbs her mother’s anxiety 
and behaves in characteristic ways, such as tantrums or with -
drawal, that draw her mother’s focus away from herself onto

her daughter. Her daughter’s impairment is an outcome of 
this reciprocity. This systems process defies fixed traits or char -
acteristics, as each individual shapes and is shaped by the 
influence of the family relationship process. When anxiety is 
low, family projection is less visible. Bowen theory posits that a family dyad, such as a mother 
and child pair, is a fragment of a triangle that includes the 
father as well. The triangle is the smallest stable emotional 
unit in the family and interlocks with others in the nuclear and 
extended family. Each of the three relationships in the triangle 
is shaped by the other two in ways that become repetitive and 
predictable. The maturity in the marital relationship correlates 
with the degree of child focus. For instance, if there is tension 
or distance in the marriage, one or both of the parents may 
look to a child for a sense of well-being or steadiness. This is 
largely an instinctive, not a cognitive process. To the degree that spouses are in meaningful contact with 
their extended families, anxiety in their nuclear families is 
diffused.

The hypothesis for this study is that the parental triangle 
unevenly distributes anxiety to the children through the family 
projection process, thereby generating differential outcomes 
for children. The child who is the focus of the family projection process 
is likely to have more dysfunction that correlates with a lower 
level of differentiation than a child who receives less parental 
anxiety. Evidence of lower levels of differentiation include 
higher levels of emotional reactivity to the moods, feelings, 
and behaviors of important others in ways that shape how 
one feels, thinks, and behaves. Higher levels of differentiation 
manifest in more self-directed and responsible functioning 
while maintaining  contact with important others. 114               F amily SyStemS                        2017

contribute to the study. Information was recorded about 
changes in the functioning of each family member in three 
generations.

Three patterns of interactions in the parent child relation -
ships emerged from the data and are consistent with Bowen 
theory’s concept of the family projection process. These 
patterns include: (1) a mutual sensitivity between a parent 
and child, including worry, preoccupation, avoidance, or 
monitoring each other, (2) over-adequate/under-adequate 
interaction, with the parent acting more adequate and the 
child less adequate/helpless, and (3) difficulty being objective 
about the child, for example, being overly positive or overly 
negative. While there are similarities among all three patterns, 
each has distinctive attributes. Illustrative Data

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The effort to understand the severe impairment of individ -
uals led Murray Bowen to study the mother-child relationship 
in his research project at NIMH. The study, which lasted from 
1954 to 1959, initially involved mothers and adult daughters or 
sons living on the research ward. (Bowen 2013) Early on in the 
study, the intense, intertwined relationships between mothers 
and their adult children diagnosed with schizophrenia could 
be observed. This intensity was seen as a reciprocal process in 
which each could be seen as “living and acting and being for 
each other.” (Bowen 1978, 10) When it became clear that the 
process involved more than the mother-child dyad, fathers 
and siblings were invited to participate. Once the focus of study shifted from the individual to 
the family, a new order of observations not previously seen 
was possible. Most significant was the reciprocal influence 
the members had on the behavior of one another. An interac -
tional focus in the study led to a shift from a view of behavior 
as intrapsychically driven to one of response patterns at play 
among family members. Bowen’s observation that the family functioned as a 
unit led to the discovery of stable and predictable patterns 
of behavior which operated outside the awareness of family 
members.

EMOTIONAL PROCESS IN SOCIETY:  
A REVIEW AND EXPANSION OF THE CONCEPT
Katharine Gratwick Baker, PhD
Murray Bowen began thinking about human functioning 
in large nonfamily systems in the 1940s. Over the next 
thirty years, he returned many times to this subject in 
papers and presentations and, in 1974, he introduced the 
eighth concept—Emotional Process in Society (EPS)—in 
his family systems theory. Although Dr. Bowen did not 
fully flesh out the concept during his lifetime, others have 
continued to explore and expand it, relating it to the other 
concepts in the theory and to a broader understanding of 
large human social units. This article reviews Bowen’s 
original writing on EPS and offers specific examples of its 
interface with differentiation, triangles, projection, cutoff, 
and multigenerational family process. Key words: Bowen theory, progression and regression 
in societal process, differentiation, triangles, projection 
process, cutoff, multigenerational transmission process  
INTRODUCTION
With the eighth concept in his theory, Murray Bowen 
began to develop a theory of human society as an emotional 
system. This concept, emotional process  in society , led Bowen to 
observe and explore patterns in human social groups larger 
than the family as well as patterns in the human’s relationship 
to the larger natural environment over time.

describe societal variation, he also searched for a theoretical 
connection between family emotional process and societal 
emotional process. In the 1960s, he observed patterns of 
response in parents of teenage delinquents and noted that 
these parents tended to “give in to their [children’s] demands 
to allay the anxiety of the moment, hoping this will solve the 
problem. This sets the stage for new and greater demands and 
threats.” (275)
At the societal level, Bowen observed that public officials 
had also become increasingly “permissive” in the way they 
responded to pressures from clamorous social groups. He 
noted that,
Operationally, the vocal segment of society is in the 
position of the anxious teenager who is driven by 
anxiety and who is demanding rights, and the public 
official is in the position of the unsure parent who 
gives in to allay the anxiety of the moment. …Societal 
pressure is directed first at those who are most unsure 
of self, and most vulnerable to pressure. Then it extends 
to others. (1978, 275-276)
This pattern can become a prevailing response to social 
problems. The parallel in parental and societal responses to the 
demands for “rights” as opposed to “responsibilities” was 
striking to Bowen and led him to a beginning articulation of 
the concept of societal emotional process.

Differentiation
The concept of differentiation in Bowen theory describes 
how anxiety and integration of self vary along a continuum 
of functioning for individuals and families. At the level of 
organizations and larger social groups, anxiety manifests itself 
in the intense group response to real and imagined threats to 
the group’s existence. Integration of self at the societal level 
can be described as the internal integration of the group. A 
viable scale of differentiation on the societal level must address 
both societal anxiety and integration. It must be grounded in 
observable, natural phenomena and describe a continuum of 
societal harmony or disharmony with nature, both of which 
determine levels of societal anxiety. Leaders emerging in social 
groups reflect the anxiety and the level of internal integration 
of the group. To illustrate variation in the concept, two examples have 
been chosen from the extreme ends of a hypothetical societal 
scale of differentiation. The Great Famine in northern Europe 
from 1315 to 1317 is an example of societal regression, and 
the “Celtic Tiger” phenomenon in the Republic of Ireland 
from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s is an example of societal 
progression. The Great Famine commenced in the spring of 1315, with 
heavy rains that continued constantly until the summer of

that played out in their relationships with one another, their 
personal struggles for power, and the multiple revolutionary 
groups that appended to them at a time of high societal anxi -
ety and low societal differentiation in Russia. Numerous additional examples of triangles at the societal 
level exist in the history of international relations. During the 
Cold War, the dyadic polarization of the two Super Powers, 
the United States and the Soviet Union, frequently devolved 
into triangles and interlocking triangles, as each formed alli -
ances with other countries in order to strengthen its position 
in relation to the other Super Power. The United States formed 
the NATO alliance, and the Soviet Union then formed the 
Warsaw Pact shortly after the end of World War II. Smaller 
alliances, such as the US alliance with Israel and the USSR’s 
alliance with a number of Arab states in the Middle East, led 
to the formation of additional interlocking triangles that could 
be observed in shifting alliances and decision making in the 
United Nations. As countries locked themselves into these 
triangular alliances, it became increasingly difficult for them 
either to develop policies that were in their own best interest 
or to move toward a peaceful settlement that would be in the 
best interest of the whole region.

War—with its multiple interlocking international triangu -
lar alliances—came to an end. There was a brief period in 
international relations when the world was less polarized 
and there appeared to be more flexibility in problem solv -
ing. However, because of the anxiety generated by nuclear 
proliferation, population growth, a beginning awareness of 
climate change, and a lack of effective leadership, new trian -
gles rapidly formed that continue to the present day. Vol.13, N o. 1                emotioN al ProceSS  iN Society              27
Intense triangles can also be observed in smaller social 
systems, such as communities, work organizations, schools, 
and churches that function at low levels of differentiation. A common triangle in the workplace can develop between 
two employees and their boss. Both employees struggle to get 
closer to the boss, who may prefer one to the other, leaving a 
favored employee on the inside and the other on the outside, 
who is often blamed when problems arise. Similar triangles can develop in an anxious religious 
institution (Richardson 1996), when two members of a congre -
gation compete with each other for the attention of the senior 
minister or rabbi. Less intense triangles (and benign three -
some relationships) occur at higher levels of differentiation 
but generate fewer social symptoms.

The projection process  is a kind of triangle that is so 
common that Bowen made it a separate concept in his theory. The template for the projection process can be observed in the 
nuclear family when the parental relationship is anxious and 
unbalanced through conflict, overfunctioning, underfunction -
ing, or distance. Instead of working directly with each other 
to resolve the issues in their own relationship, parents often 
project their anxiety onto a child, who can pick up the projec -
tion and develop symptoms. At the societal level, this pattern reflects the hierarchies 
that exist between generations in families. A common example 
from the workplace would be unresolved issues between two 
business partners. A lower ranking employee may be held 
accountable for problems in the business that often have very 
little to do with that person’s actual functioning. The societal issue of homelessness in the United States is 
an example of a hierarchical projection process.

safety net for disadvantaged people, a fragmented mental 
health system, and inadequate care for disabled veterans 
returning home from war, those members of the population 
who end up homeless are often blamed for their plight. They 
frequently pick up projection from ineffective societal leader -

members of society, many of whom may make generous 
contributions toward the alleviation of societal distress. They 
have become part of a highly privileged economic minority

Bowen saw emotional cutoff  as a multigenerational mech -
