attachment across generations. The concept includes a descrip -
tion of variation in the intensity of emotional cutoff that reflects 
the family’s level of differentiation. In previous work (2003), this author proposes that, like 
triangles, emotional cutoff can provide a logical conceptual 
bridge between emotional process in the family and emotional 
process in society. Since “the salient characteristic of emotional 
cutoff is a range of emotional distancing behaviors between 
two contiguous generations in response to chronic anxiety 
and low levels of differentiation” (2003, 385) this distancing 
behavior can also be observed between generations at societal 
level. With increases in anxiety, 
...cutoff can extend outward [from the family] into other 
arenas of social polarization—between political groups, 
kinship groups, social classes, and religious groups, for 
example—and can be rigidified in institutions through 
laws and regulations that are difficult to change.”

and a Constitution that incorporated the institution of slavery 
into its earliest voting rights, the country’s historic struggle 
with racism can be seen as a multigenerational transmission 
process. Racial issues have emerged more or less intensely and 
continuously in response to societal anxiety throughout its 
two-and-a-half century history. Projection from anxious white 
leadership onto the African American population reached 
its highest level of intensity during the Civil War, but the 
subsequent Jim Crow period, and the recent period of police 
targeting, mass incarceration, and continuing inequality in 
education and social supports for African American citizens 
are examples of societal regression. The earlier Civil Rights 
Movement, the election of an African American president, and 
the emergence of a modern civil rights movement as seen in 
“Black Lives Matter” and “Stand Up For Racial Justice,” are 
reflections of societal progression. These fluctuations in the 
multigenerational transmission of anxiety in response to race 
will undoubtedly continue into the future in the United States.

FUTURE EXPLORATION OF THE CONCEPT OF  
EMOTIONAL PROCESS IN SOCIETY
This article reviews Bowen’s many years of original work 
in initiating and refining the concept of emotional process in 
society, including his search for “a logical bridge” between 
emotional patterns in the family and emotional patterns in 
larger human systems. Bowen was clear in his writings that he 
had not completed a study of this concept in the same depth 
with which he had addressed the other seven concepts.

DEVELOPING A SYSTEMS MODEL  
FOR FAMILY ASSESSMENT
Daniel V. Papero, PhD, MSSW
In personal conversations, Murray Bowen often floated 
the idea of a system of family diagnosis or assessment. He 
believed that it would be possible to create a family diagnostic 
system that could be used alongside or even in place of 
the DSM. In the book Family Evaluation , Michael Kerr 
proposed a general schema for such an assessment. Although 
several attempts have been made to informally follow the Kerr 
proposal, none has been extensively tested and validated. In 2011-2012, the NIMH began development of the Research 
Domain Criteria (RDoC), “…a research framework designed 
for studying the full range of human behavior from normal to 
abnormal based on biology, behavior, and context.” (NIMH 
RDoC Publications accessed September 28, 2017) The RDoC 
moves away from the categorical classification model of the 
DSM to a dimensional or continuum model. It currently 
comprises five domains, or areas of functional continua, 
and proposes two additional ones. The current domains are: 
(1) negative valence systems, (2) positive valence systems, 
(3) cognitive systems, (4) systems for social processes and, 
(5) arousal/modulatory systems. Two proposed additional 
domains include neurodevelopment and environment. The RDoC use of dimensions led the author to consider a 
new approach to family assessment that differs from the 
Kerr model.

Researchers have considered the 
response of the family to one or a series of stressful events. They 
refer to the family as a system (Hill 1949, Figley and Kiser 2013) 
and use terms like dynamic  stability  (Hill) and dynamic system  
(Figley and Kiser) to attempt to convey the fluid nature of family 
responses to challenge. McCubbin and Patterson (1983) expand 
Hill’s model of family response, pointing out that an initial 
stressor generally leads to other potentially stressful demands 
upon the family’s capabilities. This “pile up” (McCubbin and 
Patterson 1983, 13) introduces the dimension of time to the 
challenge of the family. Challenges and responses unfold over 
time. The dynamic and reciprocal nature of the interaction 
among family members results in shifts in the behavior of 
individuals, their perceptual frameworks, and the general 
emotional tone of the family system. The effect of these shifts 
can lead to greater strain on the family and its adaptive 
processes or to a reduction of that strain. Figley and Kiser (2013), drawing upon the work of Hill 
(1949) and McCubbin and Patterson (1983), suggest that a trau -
matic injury to one family member may affect the entire family.

dysfunction.” (2013, 6) They propose that the effectiveness of 
a family’s response to a high stress or traumatic event primar -

the current set of stressors, (2) the family’s perception of 
these stressors, and (3) the healing resources of the family

The benchmark of successful adaptation appears to be the 
family’s ability to continue to meet the needs of its members. Hill asserts that in well-adjusted families “…the basic needs 
of all members for affection, security, and growth are again 
being met in a satisfying fashion.” (1949, 97) McCubbin and 
Patterson indicate that good adaptation involves
…(a) the maintenance or strengthening of family 
integrity (a term used to refer to the degree of 
connection and affection in the family unit), (b) the 
continued promotion of both member development 
and family unit development, and (c) the maintenance 
of family independence and its sense of control over 
environmental influences. (1983, 20)
Indicators of poor adaptation include prolonged tension in 
the family and emotional impairment of one or more family 
members (Hill 1949), deterioration of family integrity, a 
decline in the health and development of one or more family 
members, a decline in the well-being of the family unit, and 
curtailment of family independence and autonomy (McCubbin 
and Patterson 1983). One can infer, therefore, that the term systemic dysfunc -
tion refers to a deterioration in the processes of coping with 
adversity that promote the maintenance of the family’s ability 
to meet the needs of its members.

In his annual report of his research project at the National 
Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) for 1959, Murray Bowen 
also directed attention to the reaction patterns of the family. Based upon the study of families with a member diagnosed 
as schizophrenic, Bowen noted that the families “…present a 
group picture of helplessness and inadequacy.” (Bowen 2013, 
39) He reported that the functioning of the family improved 
when one parent could become engaged in solving a life 
problem faced by the family. Bowen and his research team 
gradually came to view the family as a unit or system in 
which the symptoms of schizophrenia reflected the distraught 
family’s focus on a single individual (Bowen 2013, 25).

He 
proposed that the family become the unit of treatment rather 
than the individual, and that the therapy be directed at the 
family helplessness. Bowen’s research led him to view the family “…as a fluid, 
ever-changing, functional system…” (Bowen 1978, 159) The 
term fluid captures the many-sided reciprocal interactions of 
the family system as people respond to one another continu -
ously. It also includes the range of shifts in the emotional tone 
of the family in its interpretation of the challenge faced and 
the shifting emotional ground upon which the behavior of the 
family rests. The term functional  suggests that the family has a 
task to perform  or a purpose to accomplish . He added that the 
human family system is a natural system subject to the laws 
of other natural systems. (Bowen 1978, 151). If one views the 
family as a functional natural system, then a number of tasks 
can be inferred. The family unit must respond to the condi -

to meet the biological needs of its family members. It must 
extract resources from the environment — such as food, shel -
ter, and other critical resources— to sustain life. In this sense, 
then, the family has an economic function. In addition, it must 
provide a context for reproduction and the development of 
succeeding generations. It has, therefore, a regenerative or 
growth function.

time, and how well have they functioned. Specific family

FAMILY UNIT FUNCTIONING
To date it has been difficult to develop a family assess -
ment framework with Bowen theory as its foundation. Most 
proposed efforts, while broadly informative, have proved 
cumbersome and difficult to use clinically. A different 
approach, one that utilizes Bowen’s identification of the family 
as a dynamic functional system, may ultimately provide a 
more user-friendly framework for assessing the functioning 
of the family unit.

By extrapolating from Bowen’s descriptions of individual 
characteristics of differentiation of self, of systems thinking, 
of the role of leadership in the family, and of the effects of 
anxiety, stress, and tension on the dynamically shifting family 
system, it becomes possible to sketch out a dimensional or 
continuum-based framework for assessing family unit or 
system functioning. The creation of a dimensional model may 
allow the expansion of the NIMH’s RDoC model to include the 
functioning of the family as an element in the context of the 
emotional well-being of a person. It may also permit accurate 
conceptualizations of the complex interplay between indi -
vidual and family unit developmentally across the individual 
lifetime, between generations within the family system, and 
between the individual, the family system, and the broader 
social network in which all participate. The following five dimensions or continua represent a 
beginning effort to construct a dimensional model of family 
system functioning. The five dimensions, (1) resourcefulness, 
(2) family connectedness and integration, (3) tension manage -
ment, (4) systems thinking, and (5) presence of goal structures, 
will be described below. Resourcefulness

Bowen draws attention to the role of anxiety in family 
functioning, observing that the behavior of individuals and 
relationships shift in step with changing degrees of anxiety 
and stress or tension. He also adds the notion of chronic anxi -
ety to be considered as a variable influencing family behavior. The words “anxiety” and “tension” appear together often in 
Bowen’s writing. “As anxiety and tension increase, the adap -
tive patterns lose flexibility and symptoms erupt.” (Bowen 
1978, 263) In fact, in yet another passage, he equates anxiety 
with “emotional tension.” (Bowen 1978, 307) A prominent 
marker of tension in the individual and in relationships 
Bowen describes as emotional reactiveness . An important goal 
of family psychotherapy is to improve the ability of family 
members individually to control their own emotional reac -
tiveness (Bowen 1978, 541). The management of emotional 
reactiveness involves (1) the ability to recognize anxiety and 
tension in oneself and in others, (2) the ability to manage and 
decrease personal anxiety, (3) the ability to engage one’s think -
ing to enhance one’s own self-regulation and, (4) the ability to 
relate to others without attacking them, defending oneself, or 
becoming silent and withdrawing from the interaction.

Goal Structure
Well-differentiated people develop goals for themselves 
in life (Bowen 1978). One can infer from Bowen’s writings 
that the goals of well-differentiated people tend to be based in 
realistic assessments of their own capabilities, the challenges 
they face, and of their own resourcefulness. The development 
of a long-term goal for self automatically leads to the need for 
a plan that includes shorter-term goals seen as milestones on 
the way to the ultimate objective. Using systems thinking, it is possible to conceptualize two 
categories of goals: achievement goals and process goals. One 
can describe achievement goals fairly easily.

Using systems thinking, it is possible to conceptualize two 
categories of goals: achievement goals and process goals. One 
can describe achievement goals fairly easily. A person can aim 
to attain a particular career, to live in a particular part of town, 
to attain a certain social position, and so forth. Process goals 
reflect the individual’s ability to understand the functioning 
of relationship networks. Process goals may include tension 
management, reducing cutoff, and the activity Bowen called 
de-triangling (Kerr 1988, 145-146). The idea of goals for a family unit has not been explored 
within the context of Bowen theory. It is possible to concep -
tualize a set of family goals broadly. These goals reflect the 
evolutionarily based functions of the family unit—to repro -
duce and raise offspring to the point of sexual maturity and to 
locate and extract from the environment resources to support 
life and the reproductive function. From these most funda -
mental functions of the family unit, one can identify more 
complex goals related to the basic needs of family members. In 
a general sense the need-based goals involve (1) basic support 
for the development of children, (2) provisioning of resources 
to sustain life, (3) a defensive function when the family unit is 
faced with threat, and (4) a maintenance function of the mech -
anisms that underlie the previous three goals.

tion to change and threat. These goals should be reflected in 
people’s personal goals, in the goals of family leaders, and in 
the general psychology of the family unit. The framework of 
achievement and process goals can be extended to the family

The contrasting ideas of goals and no goals provides for 
yet another dimension that can be called Goal Structure. Two sub-continua become apparent immediately. One 
contrasts the presence of well-formulated achievement goals 
with the absence of such goals. A similar continuum contrasts 
the presence of well-developed process goals with the absence 
of such goals. CONCLUSION
The schema outlined above is intended to allow a clinician 
or a family member to formulate an impression of a family’s 
functioning as it faces challenge. It also provides a framework 
for tracking progress in the family. Each of the five dimen -
sions interacts with every other, and some of the sub-continua 
might be reflective of more than one dimension. The schema 
also may provide families with starting points for addressing 
a problem. If tension management, for example, is determined 
to be inadequate, a family member might begin to address 
his or her own management of tension and his or her interac -
tions with others who are tense.

FROM THE EDITOR
Robert J. Noone, PhD
The realm of subjectivity has been a major challenge in the 
effort to move toward a science of human behavior, especially 
with regard to dealing with the subject of emotions. During 
much of the twentieth century, the study of emotions was 
largely excluded from the world of psychological research, 
principally due to the view that it was not possible to directly 
observe them. Feelings could be acceptably dealt with in 
psychotherapy, but they were not seen as a proper subject 
for science. Charles Darwin and William James, of course, 
were among those who had previously included the study of 
emotions, but their influence was largely neglected in psychol -
ogy until the latter part of the last century. The view that emotions could not be properly studied in 
research has radically changed in the last several decades as 
neuroscientists took on the challenge of studying this basic 
human phenomeon. It is not surprising that at this point 
in time, there are significant differences among researchers 
about what is defined as an emotion, how it can be studied, 
and whether its study should be confined to humans or also 
include a wide range of nonhuman animals. Given the diversity of views, it is vital that definitions 
of the terms cognition, feelings,  and  emotions  be clearly stated 
in research and theory.

feelings and emotion, with emotion having deep evolution -
ary roots. Ralph Adolphs and David Anderson make a similar 
distinction and write: 
We will argue that feelings are quite distinct 
from emotions and need to be kept distinct for a 
science of emotion to make progress. (Adolphs and 
Anderson 2018,  24)
The fact that such differences exist in how feelings and 
emotion are defined and conceptualized by the above neuro -
scientists does not detract from the value of their work in 
understanding human behavior. Each of their contributions 
is considerable. In the development of his theory of the family system, 
Murray Bowen chose to define the family as an emotional 
system. He defined the term emotion broadly, using it to 
anchor the theory in evolution. He wrote: 
Emotional functioning includes the automatic forces 
that govern protoplasmic life. It includes the force that 
biology defines as instinct, reproduction, the automatic 
activity controlled by the automatic nervous system, 
subjective emotional and feeling states, and the forces 
that govern relationship systems. (1978, 304-305)  
Bowen defined the emotional system as present in 
all forms of life, from single-celled organisms to complex 
social systems.

In response to this RFI, the authors crafted and sent the 
following response to the NIMH. While the RDoC’s six domains represent a major step 
forward out of the categorical model of the DSM, they do 
little to convey the importance of context in the emergence 
of symptoms in an individual. For virtually everyone, that 
context consists of the network of interpersonal relationships 
into which a person is born, and in which he or she lives and 
dies. The family forms the center of that network. From an evolutionary perspective, the foundation of 
the family is biological. It has taken shape, within the line of 
mammalian evolution, to further the somatic and reproductive 
interests of its members. The family unit, or system, serves a 
number of functions. It is a reproductive unit, an economic 
unit, a system of logistics, a system for information distribu -
tion and processing, and a system for decision-making. The leap in understanding the emotional well-being of 
individuals occurs when the functioning of the individual is 
seen within the context of the family system. The individ -
ual both initiates and responds to the interactional processes 
of the family unit. As both an initiator and responder, the 
individual influences others and is influenced by them.

of the family unit. As both an initiator and responder, the 
individual influences others and is influenced by them. The 
influence occurs at all levels of organismic activity—physi -
ology, psychology, individual behavior, and the behavior of 
the family unit as a whole. From that perspective, the symp -
toms currently referenced as a mental pathology or illness 
can be reconsidered as the indicators of an adaptation the 
individual has developed to cope with the conditions that 
surround him or her. The adaptations made by an individual can reflect both long-
term adaptations—in that sense neurodevelopmental—that

migration and adversity that are currently characteristic of 
large human populations. It appears difficult for people to look at themselves as 
a part of a larger whole, a system that guides their physi -
ological, mental, and behavioral functioning. We can certainly 
perceive the interactional nature of the microbial world, where 
the individual cell can only be fully understood in terms of 
the context in which it lives.

We can certainly 
perceive the interactional nature of the microbial world, where 
the individual cell can only be fully understood in terms of 
the context in which it lives. We can also appreciate the inter -
actional reality of internal systems, for example the constant 
mutual exchange and influence between endocrine, immune, 
and stress systems within the body. And, we appreciate the 
interplay of forces in the physical reality of the solar system, 
where each solar body influences every other in a myriad 
of ways. But humans seem to balk at the idea that they are 
anything but completely free agents, even though a close 
observer can catalog the indicators of deep interdependence. That this deep interdependence is a principal influence on 
development and current behavior is becoming more difficult 
to ignore. Significant gains have been made in the neurosci -
ences regarding the degree to which experience and the social 
environment influence the development and functioning of 
the brain. The emergence of social neuroscience is testimony 
to this development. The co-regulation of physiology and 
behavior and phenomena such as emotional contagion are 
demonstrating the physiological substrates involved in the 
interdependent functioning of the family system. It is strik -
ing, however, that consideration of the family as more than 
one aspect of the social environment is neglected in the social 
neuroscience literature.

In the 1950s, Murry Bowen studied families under the 
auspices of the NIMH (Bowen 2013). From his work he devel -
oped a theoretical formulation of the family as an emotional 
unit or system. First called family systems theory, Bowen later 
called this work Bowen theory to distinguish it from other 
systems ideas emerging at the time. As a natural systems 
theory rooted in evolution, each concept was selected and 
defined to be consistent with biology and the natural sciences. As a result, the theory lends itself to the incorporation of 
knowledge from relevant advances in the biological sciences. For example, social neuroscience, epigenetics, and the physi -
ology of stress readily link to concepts in the theory offering 
rich opportunities for research in the context of family inter -
action. The nuance and specificity provided by Bowen theory 
enables its application in a wide variety of contexts using both 
qualitative and quantitative methodologies. Predominant paradigms in a given field sometimes give 
way to different paradigms. The addition of neurodevelop -
ment and the environment to RDoC as potential domains of 
research offers promise that the study of human behavior can 
move beyond a paradigm based on the individual to a systems 
model that studies the family as an emotional unit govern -

ing individual behavior and development.

BOOK REVIEW
Book reviews are a significant way to address and discuss ideas 
relevant to Bowen family systems theory. The journal will select 
reviews of books, chosen at a reviewer’s discretion, which 
critically engage the ideas presented in the text and address 
their significance to the ideas contained in natural systems 
thinking. Texts chosen for review should represent relevant 
scientific ideas that extend theoretical understanding of the 
natural world. Appropriate areas of inquiry include, but are 
not limited to, biology, sociology, sociobiology, anthropology, 
psychology, psychiatry, and medicine.THE DANGEROUS CASE OF DONALD TRUMP:  
27 PSYCHIATRISTS AND MENTAL HEALTH EXPERTS  
ASSESS A PRESIDENT
Bandy Lee, MD, MDiv. Reviewed by: Lorna Hecht-Zablow, MA
Shortly after the 2016 election of Donald Trump to the 
presidency, psychiatrists Judith Herman, MD and Bandy X. Lee, MD, MDiv., acted on their concerns about “the appar -
ent mental instability of the president-elect,” by sending 
letters to colleagues elucidating those concerns. Their goal 
was to muster a collective professional voice of warning 
about the emergent danger presented by the new president. Their efforts first led to a multidisciplinary conference, “Does 
Professional Responsibility Include a Duty to Warn?” that 
later evolved into the 2017 publication of The Dangerous Case 
of Donald Trump,  a compilation by twenty-seven contributors. Lee, Bandy. 2017.

One time, some of Donald’s friends were confused as

A person who thinks from a Bowen theory perspective, 
may “hear” in this story, even though she is not mentioned, 
the participation of mother in a mother/father/son triangle. It 
is likely that the younger Trump learned how to try to manage 
his father through his relationship with his mother, rather than 
figuring it out on his own. In fact, the functioning of the individual is often 
incomprehensible out of the context of the individual’s 
relationship to the group. (Kerr 1988, 30)
If a book about the Trump presidency had been (or will be) 
written using Bowen theory as a guide, the emphasis would be 
very different. Theory’s focus on facts of functioning over time 
would provide a dispassionate picture of economic, racial, 
migratory, environmental, and other societal processes out of

they are supposed to serve when they cross a line from diagno -

“Why ‘Crazy Like a Fox’ versus ‘Crazy Like a Crazy’ Really

mental health diagnosis has never been easily bridged. By 
consistently applying theoretical concepts and emphasizing 
facts of functioning, a natural systems perspective minimizes 
the all-too-human tendencies to judge and label. Murray 
Bowen recognized all this over seventy years ago.

Spring Conference of the Bowen Center for the Study of

increasing evidence of the reality of global warming and its 
many consequences for all life on Earth. The mission of the 
conference and of this issue of Family Systems  has been to look 
at the facts about climate change as well as interrelated crises 
that humanity is facing in this century, and ask: “What must 
we do to create a climate for change in our way of thinking, 
our behavior, and our way of life, in order to live in better 
harmony with nature and with one another?” These were 
core questions that Murray Bowen addressed in the 1970s in 
his thinking and writing on the human response to the envi -
ronmental crisis. Dr. Bowen was one of the early observers to see the 
dilemma that was emerging with “increasing societal anxi -
ety during one of the most secure periods in man’s history” 
([1974] Bowen 1978, 271). In his writings on emotional process 
in society, Dr.

UNDERSTANDING AND MANAGING THE IMPACT OF 
CLIMATE CHANGES ON ANXIETY: BOWEN THEORY 
AND AN EVOLUTIONARY PERSPECTIVE
Victoria Harrison, MA
This paper is an expanded version of a presentation for 
“Creating a Climate for Change,” at the Bowen Center 2020 
Spring Conference and part of a book underway titled The 
Dance of Life in Nature and the Family. It examines the 
functions of anxiety, defined in Bowen theory as “emotional 
reactiveness to a real or imagined threat,” in adaptation to 
climate over the human phylogenetic lineage as a backdrop 
for understanding the impact of climate changes in human 
evolution. Relationship patterns synchronize survival and 
reproduction with the environment and regulate the biology 
and behavior of individuals. Climate changes disrupt those 
relationships and stir threat reactions within the social group 
and family. The capacity of individuals to function and think 
somewhat independently in the face of anxiety is an additional 
resource in adaptation for the human. Responsibility for the 
impact of climate change is based in part on understanding 
anxiety as the capacity to recognize and adapt to real threats. This paper will include ways to take advantage of anxiety 
for thoughtful adaptation and conclude with directions for 
further study. Keywords: anxiety, adaptation, Bowen theory, climate 
change, evolution, family system

UNDERSTANDING ANXIETY IN TERMS OF BOWEN 
THEORY AND EVOLUTION: INTRODUCTION
 Murray Bowen defined anxiety as “emotional reactive -
ness to a real or imagined threat” (Bowen 1979). This paper 
examines the difference it makes to consider anxiety a natural 
capacity, part of human evolution, rather than a psychiatric 
diagnosis or pathology. A client of mine was in chemotherapy following successful 
liver surgery. He talked about the reactions to powerful drugs 
and to the cancer, reactions his doctors diagnosed as “anxiety.” 
He liked the idea that anxiety was, instead, a predictable part 
of successful recovery, one that fueled many steps he took to 
survive. He said, “It is really helpful to think about anxiety 
as a functional part of being a human being rather than a  
pathology.” He asked: “How did anxiety get such a bad name?”
 Certainly, psychiatry popularized anxiety as a pathol -
ogy.

The American Psychiatric Association included anxiety 
as the chief characteristic of neurotic disorders in the first 
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders  in 1952, 
institutionalizing a Freudian interpretation of repressed 
impulses underlying various symptoms. Each revision of the 
DSM maintained anxiety as an overarching category for symp -
toms. The association of anxiety with discomfort did not begin 
with Freud, however. The Latin anxietas  captured man’s reac -
tions to awareness of danger, death, and uncertainty (Croco 
2015). Even Charles Darwin in The Expression of the Emotions 
in Man and Animals considered “…the expression of grief and 
anxiety as eminently human” (1872, 149) not a fundamental 
capability of all life. A number of physicians, psychologists, and therapists 
write about anxious reactions to facts about global warming 
as a kind of pathology. Some have suggested a new diagnos -
tic category for the DSM: “eco-anxiety” and liken it to PTSD 
or trauma. Others, like Dahr Jamail, associate the feelings 
with grieving (Jamail 2019). Recommendations for manag -
ing emotional reactions to climate changes range from Native 
American healing rituals to sharing of feelings in group ther -
apy or meditation or five minutes in nature or to psychiatric 
medication. Climate activists and those who deny climate 
change are seen as antagonists rather than as versions of 
anxious reactions to a common threat.

patterns characteristic of reactions to threat that appear to be 
conserved and passed along over generations. The formation and variation of “emotional systems” 
appear to be a continuous pattern for adapting to climate 
changes and other conditions that threaten survival and 
reproduction. Murray Bowen defined “emotional systems” 
as characterized by variation in the capacity to function as a 
somewhat separate individual within intense emotional rela -
tionships. In 1973 he wrote:
In broad terms, the emotional system is conceived 
to be the function of life forces inherited from his 
phylogenetic past, that he shares with the lower forms, 
and that governs the subhuman part of man… (423) One 
is a built-in life growth force toward individuality and 
the differentiation of a separate ”self,” and the other, an 
equally intense emotional closeness.” (Bowen 1978, 424) 
 This paper describes what is known about climate condi -
tions, threat reactions, and variation in the capacity to survive 
as a separate individual and to survive as part of a group for 
species ancestral to the human. Although specific details about 
speciation and adaptive changes are not well understood, this 
comparative view of emotional systems is consistent with the 
work of several evolutionary scientists.

Although specific details about 
speciation and adaptive changes are not well understood, this 
comparative view of emotional systems is consistent with the 
work of several evolutionary scientists. Lynn Margulis, a pioneer in evolutionary biology, 
proposed trial and error symbiosis between independent cells 
as the adaptation of single cells, prokaryotes, to the challenges 
of changing climate on early Earth. Formerly independent 
cells, each with a survival capacity such as mobility or oxygen 
metabolism, were able to form a relationship with each other 
within a common membrane. These multicellular units were 
better able to survive, adapt, and reproduce together than they 
were as separate cells. These permanent associations created 
a new organism, eukaryotes, in which separate capacities 
contributed toward survival of the whole. Individual compo -
nents no longer survived as separate entities and reproduced 
the relationship system or association in future generations 
(Margulis 1981 and 1998). In an early paper on “Symbiosis, the Family, and Natural 
Systems,” Robert J. Noone described the evolutionary trajec -
tory of the parent/offspring bond as a “merger of individuals

into a functioning interdependence and, at the same time, the 
specialization of functioning within this unit” (Noone 1988,

EMOTIONAL SYSTEMS, CLIMATE, AND ANXIETY 
ALONG THE HUMAN PHYLOGENETIC LINEAGE
4.5 Billion Years Ago: Prokaryotes
Reactions to climate started with life on Earth. For the 
first three billion years, Earth was home to prokaryotic cells, 
currently represented by bacteria. Early prokaryotes carried 
DNA loose within a membrane and were solitary individual 
cells. Asexual reproduction by splitting or budding created 
almost identical replicas in rapid fashion. Each cell sensed the chemical environment through recep -
tors in its cell wall that detected food or toxins. Interaction 
with the environment was direct, through photosynthesis and 
the ability to obtain energy from inorganic chemicals. Temper -
ature extremes, biochemical toxins, oxygen, and limitations of 
nutrients were common threats for early cell life, and reactions 
to environmental threats were directly biochemical. Single 
cells, over time, evolved singular capacities for survival. One 
cell, for example, would be capable of mobility. Another cell 
could metabolize oxygen or other organic compounds. Contact 
and avoidance were accidental given the expanse of space 
for life to fill. The ability to avoid predators and threats arose 
within those first few billion years of life.

large animals. 200 Million Years Ago: Mammals

and fast enough to survive reptile predators and competitors,

the 45,000 species of mammals alive today. Adaptation for 
mammals included the evolution of diverse patterns of 
relationships between mates and with young within larger 
social groups. Species-specific patterns of avoidance and of

Murray Bowen observed that humans react to both real 
and imagined threats (Bowen 1979). Most often imagined 
threats involve relationships and competition for resources 
within the group or family. Becoming aware of real threats, 
such as global warming and its consequences, and recogniz -
ing reactions, such as conflict, exploitation, or avoidance, can 
increase the human capacity for more thoughtful, responsible 
adaptation. What makes this so difficult? Climate changes often operate “outside awareness.” 
They are incremental, subtle, and indirect. Global warming 
occurs over a long period of time. The erratic and extreme 
weather that brings storms, floods, and drought appears to 
be simply local and temporary. Changes in climate modify 
growing seasons for food or cash crops in erratic, unpredict -
able, and cumulative fashion. People expanding into Kansas, 
West Texas, and Oklahoma did not expect that plowing buffalo 
grass well adapted to preserve prairie land would interact 
with unexpected drought and high winds to produce a disas -
ter such as the Dust Bowl. Changes in climate affect sea levels 
far from melting glaciers. People are often not aware of the 
impact of climate changes until these changes become a crisis.

Much of perception itself operates outside awareness. The 
human brain comes with a stereotypical cause-and-effect focus 
that fails to see the interaction of forces and factors at play over 
time. The most typical reaction is to focus on what is visible 
as a cause or to imagine a cause. It is difficult to recognize an 
interplay of factors that produce a threat, and it is common to 
fail to recognize or address one’s part in those factors. The impact of anxious reactions is also often outside 
awareness. Brains that develop within a particularly anxious 
or chaotic family may not develop the capacity to recognize 
their impact on others and take responsibility for themselves 
(Henry, 1983). Brains that develop without contact with past 
generations or extended kin lack information and experience 
that moderate anxious self-interest. Greed, with exploitation 
of resources and of other people, often involves isolation from 
those who are affected. The absence of person-to-person rela -
tionships propels economic and social hierarchy as well as 
suspicion and competition. This is a multigenerational family 
factor that Murray Bowen called emotional cutoff (Bowen 
1978) and that could also be described as avoidance. Joseph LeDoux devotes a chapter in his book Anxious  to 
avoidance as a strategy for staying out of harm’s way. Success -
ful avoiding is “self-perpetuating” and automatic.

picture of what is to come. People who learn more about ways 
that past generations reacted to environmental and societal 
threats can better observe their own reactions and make more 
thoughtful decisions. Learn Facts about Local and Global Environments
It is important to find reliable sources of facts about climate 
change and its impact. Search for climate scientists with infor -
mative websites, books, and media. Please also see references 
at the end of this article for local and national organizations 
that provide information and organizing actions to consider. Define What You Believe 
Studying climate changes and their impact can strengthen 
the capacity to tolerate discomfort and engage curiosity. A 
focus on facts activates intellectual activity and the ability to 
distinguish real threats from imagined ones. This can lead to 
thoughtful action. Research projects hone awareness of what is 
not yet known and of subjective reactions, like climate denial, 
that fill the gaps. Defining what one believes about climate 
changes provides practice in distinguishing what one can 
modify and what one cannot influence.

MURRAY BOWEN’S CONTRIBUTION TO THE STUDY OF 
COMPLEX HUMAN SYSTEMS
Daniel V. Papero, PhD, MSSW
Complex systems consist of multiple connected parts acting 
together as a whole, a unit, or a system. This results in 
collective behavior of the unit that cannot be inferred directly 
from the behavior of the specific parts. For complex living 
systems, behavior emerges from the interaction among 
the various elements reflecting, among other things, the 
retained effects of past collective behavior, the environment 
in which the parts interact and to which they must adapt, the 
particular characteristics of the individual components, and 
the shifting degrees of metabolically produced energy within 
and among the parts as they interact. Bowen theory describes 
one kind of complex living system, the human family.1
Following his service in World War II in 1946, Murray 
Bowen entered the Menninger School of Psychiatry to begin 
his training in psychiatry. He later described the Menninger 
program as a rich environment where he was exposed to ideas 
and the leading thinkers of the day in the many symposia and 
lectures available to students (Kerr and Bowen 1988). He 
served on the library committee (personal communication) 
and used the excellent library to read widely across many 
disciplines.

At the NIMH, Bowen and his staff observed the interactions 
of family members—with one another and later with 
the hospital staff—of a severely impaired young adult, 
recording their observations in detail. Drawing upon his 
work at the NIMH and his continuing work with families 
less severely impaired, Bowen constructed a theory that 
considered the family a unit or natural system. Within the 
family, individuals react emotionally to one another. Those 
reactions reflect a deep connection and sensitivity among 
family members that regulate individual physiology and 
psychology as well as interactional sequences of behavior 
among family members broadly. He proposed that eight 
factors (theoretical concepts) plus a variable of amount of 
energy (anxiety)2 create the context from which dynamic 
family behavior emerges. Knowledge of the family system permitted Bowen to extend 
theoretical formulations to larger complex human systems 
like organizations and communities. He observed that many 
of the same processes evident in family system behavior 
exist in other human systems as well. These include, among 
others, the role of fearful emotional arousal (anxiety and

INTRODUCTION
The American biologist Richard Alexander wrote:
We do not hesitate to call the effort of the physicists 
“science,” but we are more apt to ridicule and dismiss 
the efforts of the behavioral scientists who study 
humans. In all the universe, the only topic we literally do 
not wish to be too well understood is human behavior 
(including, necessarily, our own) even, it would seem, 
if that kind of understanding represents the only clear 
way to diminish the threat of self-extinction. (1987)
Bowen echoed Alexander’s warning both in his conversa -
tions (personal communications) and in his 1973 paper, “The 
Systems Viewpoint of Human Behavior,” emphasizing the 
need for a science of human behavior. Also, in an essay entitled 
“The Odyssey Toward Science” he wrote,
If knowledge about the human ever becomes an 
accepted science, it can share new knowledge with the 
accepted sciences and proceed into the future with the 
other sciences. I support the view that the human is as 
scientific as the other forms of life on the planet, that it 
will finally be possible to construct a total human theory 
from scientific facts alone… (Kerr and Bowen 1988, 360)
In the current era, the need to better understand and 
develop a science of complex human systems has taken on a

heightened urgency.

disturbances in governmental systems, population migration, 
and deeply polarized groups competing with one another, 
individuals and families face serious challenges. How indi -

the degree of well-being of family members in the present and 
shapes the conditions influencing well-being in the future. Moreover, the relative competency of each family system to 
meet challenges affects the larger social groups in which the 
family system participates. In the years since the 1960s, when Murray Bowen formally 
proposed his theory, the study of complex human systems 
has developed exponentially. The term systems appears 
frequently in the scientific and popular literature, although 
specific definitions of the term are often lacking. New find -

Bowen’s theoretical work. The study of epigenetics, for exam -
ple, provides one of the mechanisms to support the idea of 
cross-generational transfer of aspects of behavior (Champagne 
and Curley 2015).

societal regression. He later changed the name of the concept 
to emotional process in society, a more objective term that 
included both the ideas of regression and progression. As in 
the case of the human family, Bowen proposed specific steps 
that could contribute to an improvement in societal function -

and his or her management of self. In 1988, Bowen condensed his understanding of his 
contribution to psychiatric research into fourteen ideas (Kerr 
and Bowen 1988, 346). Many of these relate directly to the 
study of the family and to applications of theory; for exam -
ple, the family diagram or the nuclear family emotional

OF COMPLEX HUMAN SYSTEMS
Bowen theory calls attention to and describes family 
emotional process (FEP), a dynamic system of interaction 
among family members. Bowen describes the theoretical model:
For the purposes of this theoretical therapeutic system, I 
think of the family as a combination of “emotional “and 
“relationship” systems. The term emotional refers to the

force that motivates the system and “relationship” to 
the ways it is expressed. ([1966] 1978, 158)
FEP places the individual in the context of the family 
relationship network, illuminating the behavioral linkages 
between family members, the shifting pattern of their interac -
tions linked to intensities of emotional energy, and the effects 
of individual variation on those interactions and on the func -
tioning of the entire system. Bowen theory contributes to the study of complex human 
systems in several ways.

Bowen theory contributes to the study of complex human 
systems in several ways. The first involves the process of 
systems thinking, placing the individual in a context of rela -
tionships, the family system, that regulates his or her behavior. Additionally, the theory contributes to the understanding of 
complex human systems in three general dimensions. First, it 
describes clearly the structure that lies beneath the swirling 
surface of human relationships. Second, it highlights the role 
of anxiety in motivating and shaping human behavior. Third, 
it addresses the importance of individual functioning in the 
behavior of complex human systems. Nine Salient Points
In 2019 the author received invitations to give keynote 
lectures at two conferences, the first addressing the challenges 
of climate change and the second more generally discussing 
Dr. Bowen’s thinking and its relevance to human dilemmas. Months of thinking and study followed these invitations, 
culminating in the author’s selection of nine ideas drawn from 
Bowen theory and considered directly relevant to the study of 
complex human systems. These ideas permit the development 
of potential applications to address problems encountered in 
managing complex human systems.

These ideas permit the development 
of potential applications to address problems encountered in 
managing complex human systems. The nine ideas include 
(1) systems thinking, (2) the foundational role of the family 
system in larger societal processes, (3) two guidance systems, 
(4) individual variation, (5) emotion as energy powering 
the system, (6) the effects of anxiety (fearfulness, stress), (7) 
dynamic flow and structure (infrastructure) of human relation -
ships, (8) the focus on functioning, and (9) the power of one. Systems Thinking
In a 2018 paper, Papero, Frost, Havstad, and Noone 
provided the following definition of systems thinking:
 Murray Bowen ’s Contri Bution  to the study of CoMplex huMan systeMs 49
Systems thinking represents an emerging paradigm in 
the life sciences. Rather than focus on the functioning of 
individual parts that make up a larger whole, systems 
thinking looks at the way in which the parts interact 
with one another to create the larger whole, and how 
the larger whole, in turn, regulates the parts which 
make it up. The back-and-forth interaction between 
the parts and the whole is observable and predictable 
in living systems. Systems thinking focuses on the facts 
of how the parts of a network interact and under what 
conditions the patterns of interaction change. (2018, 1)
Bowen developed the concept of the family as a system 
from direct observation of how individuals in the family func -
tion in relation to one another.

to the system and defensive actions when necessary. The 
system of relationships in the family requires certain func -
tioning positions in order to maintain its ability to adjust as 
effectively and efficiently to the stresses and challenges that 
face all living things. Context
Systems thinking involves a number of elements. When 
considering human behavior, people generally think about 
the individual. Behavior is often explained on the basis of 
the internal processes within the person. Systems thinking, 
however, places the person in a context of relationships. Indi -
vidual behavior emerges from the relational activity of the 
family system. From this perspective a number of questions 
become relevant when attempting to understand the behavior.

between reason and emotion. Around 370 BCE, Plato described 
the two as spirited horses pulling against one another. Goethe’s 
Faust (1808) describes the existence of two competing spirits. Darwin ([1872] 2009) also proposes a distinction between the

another for reason in the human brain. He describes an

of the brain that produce emotion as survival circuits produc -

opportunities exist” (2015, 139). Bowen says something similar 
in describing the emotional system.

To accompany the emotional system, Bowen describes an 
intellectual system—a source of reasoning and logic which 
is to some degree distinct from the emotional system. The 
intellectual system has the capability to (1) observe both the 
individual and the environment, (2) collect factual informa -
tion, and (3) analyze and establish a plan of action. Perhaps 
most importantly, the intellectual system is capable of project -
ing backward and forward in time, permitting the individual 
to review history and to anticipate future consequences of a 
decision taken in the present. Using the terms of the neuro -
scientist Jaoquin Fuster (2013), the intellectual system allows 
the individual to pre-adapt to anticipated situations. The abil -
ity to pre-adapt allows the intellectual system to influence 
and, to a degree, regulate the reactiveness of the emotional 
system, allowing the channeling of emotionally energized 
action toward cognitively determined goals. The capabil -
ity of the intellectual system to formulate novel responses 
to complex challenges adds flexibility when the emotional 
system response is inadequate. The interplay between the emotional and intellectual 
systems forms the core of Bowen’s concept of differentiation 
of self (DoS). The concept describes variation between indi -
viduals in how the two systems interact to shape the behavior 
of the person. Bowen proposed a continuum of variation based 
on whether the two systems are fused or differentiated.

A person’s degree of differentiation of self describes their 
ability to maintain separation of feeling and thinking and their 
ability to use the integrated pair to guide behavior and regu -
late emotional energy. At a certain degree of intense anxiety, 
the individual loses the ability to maintain that separation 
and begins to behave automatically or instinctively without 
thoughtful regulation and guidance. The point where the 
person loses awareness of separation between emotional and 
intellectual systems establishes a threshold for that individ -
ual—a tipping point from which behavior shifts from more 
thoughtful to more automatic. The lower a person’s level 
of differentiation of self is, the more sensitive the thresh -
old is to slight increases in anxiety. The higher the level of 
differentiation, the higher the threshold, increasing the abil -
ity of the person to maintain integrated functioning, even as 
anxiety increases. Based on these formulations, Bowen conceptualized a 
continuum of variation he called the scale of differentiation 
of self (DoS). At one end, he placed people with little ability 
to know the difference between emotional and intellectual 
functioning. He described people at this end of the continuum 
as highly dependent on relationships to others for direction 
and for stability.

THE IMPORTANCE OF THE INDIVIDUAL TO THE 
FUNCTIONING OF THE SYSTEM
Bowen theory’s concept of the scale of differentiation of 
self draws attention to individual variability along a specific 
continuum, the individual’s ability to know the difference 
internally between thinking and feeling (emotional and 
intellectual functioning), and how a person maintains the 
separation of these two functions when pursuing life objec -
tives. When compared to more differentiated individuals, the 
less well-differentiated person appears less able to regulate 
their emotional reactivity in interactions, appears more depen -
dent on the viewpoints of others than on those developed for 
oneself, and appears less able to follow their own direction 
when it runs counter to the norms and expectations of other 
family members. Bowen’s message is that when individuals can (1) 
manage their own emotional reactiveness, (2) engage in care -
ful thinking about their responses to challenges, (3) maintain 
consistency between carefully developed principles and 
actions, (4) remain in viable emotional contact with important

remain on course despite contextual ambiguity and the oppo -
sition of others, their functioning can influence the behavior 
of other members of the relationship network.

of societal regression, Bowen emphasized the importance of 
individual functioning in addressing societal dilemmas. The thesis here is that he might modify his future 
course if he can gain some control over his reaction to 
anxiety and his “instinctual” emotional reactiveness, 
and begin taking constructive action based on his 
fund of knowledge and on logical thinking. (Bowen 
[1974] 1978, 281)
TOWARD A SCIENCE OF HUMAN BEHAVIOR
In the last significant piece of writing of his lifetime, 
Bowen described his life work as an odyssey towards science 
(Kerr and Bowen 1988). There he laid out his effort to move 
psychiatry toward a science of the human based on facts, 
reducing subjectivity to the greatest degree possible. He said 
frequently (personal communication) that he thought such 
a science was possible and that systems thinking was a key 
element in the process. Systems thinking provides no magical answers, but it does 
provide a different way of conceptualizing human problems. It offers a more realistic evaluation of the difficulty in chang -
ing the basic patterns in any human dilemma, and it suggests 
ways to avoid some of the pitfalls of conventional thinking, 
and to institute progress toward long term goals.

AND LOGICAL THINKING

stem from the complex intersection of a host of factors and 
forces. Human population continues to increase with uneven 
geographical and age distribution. Segments of that popula -
tion are migrating in an effort to escape conditions fostering 
hunger, disease, and violence. Changing climate creates new 
weather patterns—affecting crops, water resources, and food 
supplies—and threatening the overall quality of life of large 
groups of people.

HUMAN NATURE AND SUSTAINABILITY: INDIVIDUAL 
BEHAVIOR IS NOT INDIVIDUAL
John Gowdy, PhD
“It is not the consciousness of men that determines their 
existence, but their social existence that determines 
their consciousness.” Karl Marx (1859)
“It is difficult to get a man to understand something 
when his salary depends on his not understanding it.” 
Upton Sinclair (1934)
At the root of public policy debates about sustainability are 
starkly contrasting views of “human nature.” If one believes 
that people are by nature selfish and greedy, one is likely to 
support public policies motivated by narrow self-interest. If one takes a more benign view that if left alone people will 
live in harmony, one is more likely to favor policies based on 
mutual aid, sharing, and cooperation. Findings from such 
diverse fields as anthropology, behavioral economics, and 
neuroscience suggest that behavior depends on the physical 
environment, neurology, cultural context, and individual 
and social history. Focusing on individual behavior alone 
misses the drivers of unsustainability—namely, a global 
economy whose viability depends on growth and exploitation, 
and the increasing concentration of wealth in the hands of 
an elite that controls the public policy agenda. Dr. Gowdy is Professor of Economics Emeritus, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, 
Troy, New York. He can be reached at gowdyj2@rpi.edu  or johngowdy@earthlink.net.

INTRODUCTION: HUMAN NATURE AND OUR 
EXISTENTIAL CRISES
We live in a time of contrasts and contradictions. Our scien -
tific accomplishments and understanding of the world around 
us have never been greater. We have a good understanding of 
how the universe formed and how Earth’s biosphere evolved. We know the evolutionary history of Homo sapiens and the 
structure of the human genome. We are close to solving the 
riddle of life itself. On the other hand, our rapacious economy 
and burgeoning population are undermining the planet’s life 
support systems to the point where our very existence as a 
species is threatened. We have carefully analyzed the threats of 
climate change, biodiversity loss, and inequality and we have 
carefully designed feasible policies to deal with these threats. Yet, so far, we have been incapable of seriously addressing 
any of them. Why is there such a gulf between understand -
ing and action?

this. It is not surprising that this view is held by supporters 
of unchecked exploitation and economic growth. But many 
environmentalists take the same position. Population ecologist 
William Rees (2010) blames all our problems on human nature:
Humans may pride themselves as being the best

need to look beyond conventional explanations—

will, resistance by vested interests, and so on—to 
what may well be the root cause of the conundrum: 
human nature itself. ( https:/www.sciencedaily.com/

If the evil-human-nature view is true, we are left with 
nothing but despair and handwringing over our inevitable 
demise. Collapse is the unavoidable fate of a flawed species. But if it is human nature to ravish the natural world how did 
Homo sapiens, living in a variety of cultures and local envi -
ronments, live sustainably on planet Earth for 300,000 years? Human societies lived within the bounds of local ecosystems 
for ninety-seven percent of human existence. Studies using 
genome sequencing indicate that the San (Khoisan) people 
inhabited Southern Africa continuously for over 150,000 years. The San were the largest human population group for most 
of human existence (Suzman 2019, Kim 2014). The Acheulian 
hand-axe tradition of Homo erectus  flourished for 1.5 million 
years. The Neanderthal Mousterian culture, with regional 
variations, lasted 300,000 years. Even after agriculture, many 
small-scale human societies lived in harmony with nature with 
stable populations and sustainable resource use. Humans are 
capable of almost any type of behavior depending on underly -
ing institutional structures and the behavioral patterns arising 
from the requirements of particular economic systems. Blam -
ing human nature for the current assault on the natural world 
is a defeatist position. If human cultures have always been 
unsustainable and characterized by overshoot and collapse 
nothing can be done.

It is obvious that 
world views are shaped by cultures we grow up in. But does 
it go deeper than that? Do specific kinds of cultures gener -
ate specific kinds of behavior? Are there universal patterns 
of human behavior? Is there a deep neurological basis for 
cultural values? In terms of formulating policy, a crucial ques -
tion is whether the values of society arise from individual 
choices or does the higher-level economic organization of soci -
ety (our social existence) determine individual values. In the 
first view, changing public policy comes when individuals 
are convinced one-by-one to support a certain issue (climate 
change, income equality, biodiversity protection) until a criti -
cal mass is reached. By the other view, values will be changed 
when the economic organization of society is changed. The Expansion of Evolutionary Theory
The expansion of evolutionary theory over the last few 
decades has changed our view of human nature. The nature 
or nurture debate has been replaced by the view that behav -
ior is a complex combination of interactions between genes, 
environment, and evolvability—the ability of encoded genetic 
information to call forth behaviors favorable to specific envi -
ronments. Twentieth century biology was dominated by a 
gene-centric view of evolution and natural selection. This 
view was developed by evolutionary biologists in the 1930s 
and 1940s and popularized by Richard Dawkins in The Selfish 
Gene (Dawkins 1976).

This 
view was developed by evolutionary biologists in the 1930s 
and 1940s and popularized by Richard Dawkins in The Selfish 
Gene (Dawkins 1976). Most evolutionary biologists took the 
position that the only inherited variations are genetic. There 
were several reasons why the gene-centric view came to be 
dominant. First, the selfish gene idea fits nicely within the 
prevailing paradigm of competition and selfish individualism. It is the biological equivalent of “economic man,” the rugged, 
rational individual independent of human society. Secondly, it 
was a reaction to some bad twentieth century science promot -
ing the inheritance of acquired characteristics—most notably 
the work of the Stalinist biologist T. D. Lysenko in the former 
Soviet Union. Thirdly, the mathematical formulation of the 
selfish gene model, and its derivative kin selection (inclusive

to contradictory empirical evidence (E. O. Wilson 2014, 69). The upshot was that environmental and social influences were 
usually downplayed in discussions about the mechanisms 
of inheritance. In recent decades the selfish gene position 
has been challenged by biologists (Jablonka and Lamb 2014, 
Pigliucci and Pigliucci and Muller 2010, D. S. Wilson 2015). Darwin saw the essence of evolution as variation, inheritance, 
and selection.

human nature debate include epigenetics, group selection, 
and ultrasociality. Epigenetic  evolution  refers to the nonDNA cellular trans -
mission of traits. The idea is that development can influence 
the transmission of genetic information. Inheritance is still 
based on genes, but how genes are expressed in phenotypes—
the physical characteristics of an organism—is determined not 
only by changes in the DNA sequence but also by nonDNA 
influences. Environmental factors such as temperature can 
switch genes on and off and affect how cells read genes. An 
example of this nonDNA influence is the effect of ambient 
temperature on the sex ratio of crocodile hatchlings. Tempera -
tures below 31.7°C produce more females and temperatures 
higher than that produce more males. Another example is the 
effect of zebra finch mother bird songs on the size and behavior 
of the hatchlings (Mariette and Buchanan 2016). Mothers sing 
a specific kind of song to embryos (in the egg) when ambient 
temperatures exceed 26°C and this song alters future nestlings’ 
begging behavior and growth, and their reproductive success 
and temperature preferences as adults.

As agriculture took hold, those societies having group 
traits most favorable to surplus production outcompeted other 
groups. Some groups gained a competitive advantage through 
the evolution of institutions—from religion and divine right 
to rigid caste systems—that supported surplus production. The requirements of the higher-level superorganism began 
to override the behavior, organization, human relationships, 
and ethical values that made us human as Pleistocene hunter-
gatherers. Today’s complex human societies are integrated 
systems consisting of technologies, power relationships, insti -
tutions, and belief systems that act to ensure the coherence 
and survival of the system as a whole, not necessarily for the 
benefit of individuals. These social variants are the products 
of natural selection, but “natural” does not mean “good” or 
“sustainable.” Natural selection favors those variants that are 
successful at a particular time in a particular place. Evolution 
cannot see ahead. Successful variants in one context can be 
dysfunctional in another. Cultural group selection depends on 
social learning and behavioral inheritance. This sort of evolu -
tion is most familiar to social scientists. Jablonka and Lamb 
(2014, 158) write:
We see culture as a system of socially transmitted patterns 
of behavior, preferences, and products of animal activities 
that characterize a group of social animals.

New techniques of analysis have allowed researchers to 
make inferences about the behavior of our Pleistocene ances -
tors. Sympathy and compassion for others are traits that were 
present in the Pleistocene. Spikins et al. (2018) discovered that 
Neanderthals cared for severely injured individuals, includ -
ing a male aged thirty-five to fifty at the time of his death, 
whose degenerative disease would have made it impossible 
for him to care for himself long before his death. A Neander -
thal individual found at the Shanidar I cave in Iraq showed 
extensive debilitating injuries including the loss of an arm, 
serious wounds to his right leg, and loss of hearing (Trinkaus 
and Villotte 2017). This individual would have required exten -
sive care by the community. Spikins observes: “Our findings 
suggest Neanderthals didn’t think in terms of whether others 
might repay their efforts, they just responded to their feel -
ings about seeing their loved ones suffering” ( Science Daily , 
2018). Evidence from the Sima de los Huesos site in Spain, 
dated at 400,000 years ago, indicates that a child with cranio -
synostosis1 and an elderly man who would have had trouble 
walking, received care for several years (Bonmatí et al. 2010, 
Gracia et al. 2009).

because of the “free rider” problem. Selfish individuals can 
out-compete altruists by taking advantage of their generosity. As an answer to this objection, Henrich et al. (2006) propose 
that altruism arose in humans hand-in-hand with punishment.

As an answer to this objection, Henrich et al. (2006) propose 
that altruism arose in humans hand-in-hand with punishment. Altruistic punishment—punishing others for violating social 
norms even at cost to oneself—is how humans deal with free 
riders and make cooperation work. Apparently, punishing

those who do not cooperate stimulates the same pleasure 
centers in the brain that are activated by, for example, eating 
something sweet (Vogel 2004). Some evidence indicates that 
punishing behavior is present in chimpanzees. In one experi -
ment, semi-wild chimpanzees were fed at a regular time only 
after all the chimpanzees in the compound came to the feed -
ing station. Late-comers who held up the feeding for all the 
chimps were punished by the group with hitting and biting. Altruism is a social attribute, not a strictly individual charac -
teristic, and it can be maintained by enforceable social rules. A sense of fairness is another policy-relevant behavioral 
attribute. Brosnan and de Waal (2003) found that brown 
capuchin monkeys exhibit a strong aversion to inequity. In 
one experiment, monkeys rejected rewards for performing 
a simple task if they witnessed another monkey receiving a 
more desirable reward for performing the same task. Pairs 
of monkeys were trained to exchange a small rock with a 
human in return for receiving a piece of cucumber.

For example, there exists observable structural 
differences between the brains of musicians and nonmusi -
cians (Gaser and Schlaug 2003). Brain plasticity allows for a 
remarkable degree of differentiation in the ability of individu -
als to adapt to different cultures and social institutions. There 
is evidence that humans have “social brains” that develop 
after birth to encode one’s culture (Frith and Frith 2010). A remarkable feature of the human brain is the presence 
of Von Economo neurons  (VENs) that apparently evolved to 
enable people to make rapid decisions in social contexts. These 
neurons are located in cortical areas positioned at the interface 
between emotional and cognitive processing. Allman et al. (2005) speculate that VENs are designed for quick signaling 
of appropriate responses in the context of social ambiguity. The ability to quickly respond in social situations would be 
particularly important in species with complex social networks 
and social uncertainties. Von Economo neurons are also found 
in smaller numbers in great apes, elephants, whales, and 
dolphins, all highly intelligent species with complex social 
systems. Pleistocene hunter-gatherers had fission-fusion 
communities where group size was seasonal. Small bands of 
a few dozen people were the group type for most of the year, 
but larger groups formed seasonally when resource availabil -
ity permitted. In this kind of social organization, groups are 
continually changing in composition.

When Michael died at the age of twenty-seven in 2000, an 
autopsy was performed to examine the structure of his brain. Remarkably, his endowment of Von Economo neurons was 
many times greater than found in any other gorilla studied, 
and, in fact, it was in the lower range for humans (Allman 
et al. 2011, 62). If such marked physical brain changes and 
changes in social behavior can occur in a nonhuman primate 
from a change in its social environment, imagine the profound 
change in human cognition and human sociality triggered by 
the agricultural transition ten thousand years ago. The social 
structure of our species changed dramatically from living in 
small, always familiar groups to populous, complex societies, 
massive built environments, complicated technologies, and 
daily interactions with total strangers. The latest neurological evidence suggests that human 
behavior is highly dependent on social conditioning and the 
critical neurological pathways enhancing intimacy and trust. These must be established in infancy for healthy emotional 
development. These are characteristics that make us human 
and they evolved deep in our evolutionary past.

HUMAN NATURE AND ULTRASOCIALITY
For most of human existence, people lived in small, 
egalitarian, and sustainable communities (See the articles 
in Gowdy 1998). With agriculture, our species joined the 
 Human  nature and SuStainability  | 81
social insects, ants, and termites, that also evolved socio-
economic systems organized for surplus production. The 
latest manifestation of this is the global capitalist economy. The radical change in the economic base of human societies, 
from small-scale, immediate-return foraging to large-scale 
production for surplus, fundamentally changed our relation -
ship with the natural world and with our fellow humans. The 
“cosmologies”—cultural belief systems—that came with the 
agricultural revolution, including exploitation of the natural 
world, caste and class-based social hierarchies, and power -

public policy. Humans were not the first species to make the journey 
from hunting and gathering to agriculture. We are not the first 
species to dominate the planet.

Humans were not the first species to make the journey 
from hunting and gathering to agriculture. We are not the first 
species to dominate the planet. We are not the first species to 
evolve large hierarchical societies of millions of individuals 
with a complex division of labor and a dependence on surplus 
production. Like their human counterparts, ant and termite 
farmers became dependent on cultivated crops and developed 
carefully articulated task-partitioned societies cooperating in 
large agricultural enterprises. The results of the agricultural 
transition in humans and social insects are strikingly simi -
lar—an explosion in population size, a complex division of 
labor, and the subjugation of individuals within the group for 
the good of the superorganism itself. Agricultural life enabled 
ants and termites to rise to ecological dominance, accounting 
for fifty percent of the Earth’s insect biomass, just as humans 
dominate terrestrial vertebrate biomass. These life forms—
ants, humans, and termites—overwhelmingly dominate the 
planet in terms of sheer numbers and environmental impact. These three kinds of organisms are the only ones that evolved 
complex agriculture and ultrasociality. This is more than an 
interesting analogy. Understanding the commonality between 
human and social insect ultrasociality can open the door to 
understanding our environmental and social crises. Why is it so hard to change the economic system toward 
sustainability and equality?

Why is it so hard to change the economic system toward 
sustainability and equality? With the emergence of large-scale 
state societies some five thousand years ago, human social 
evolution took a radical turn toward a kind of social organiza -
tion resembling an ant or termite colony. Humans are not ants, 
but the similarities are disturbing. One of the most troubling is 
 82 | F amily SyStemS 16:1 2021                     
the loss of individuality as the “needs” of the ultrasocial super -
organism come to dominate social evolution. One of the most 
powerful institutions to come out of the agricultural revolu -
tion and surplus production is “the market,” an institution 
that has taken on a life of its own. After agriculture took hold, 
belief systems promoted the idea of human uniqueness and 
the domination of nature. Today, economic ideologies promot -
ing deregulation, opposing social spending, and expanding 
the scope of the market are examples of downward causation 
in human social systems. Today’s free market ideologies, and 
the political expression of those ideologies, are the human 
social equivalent of the genetic mechanisms of behavioral 
control that evolved in social insect societies. Like ant and termite societies, humans evolved an ultraso -
cial system dedicated to the production of agricultural surplus. All three systems were the products of Darwinian natural 
selection: variation, selection, retention of favorable traits.

of ultrasociality is that current human behavior is not neces -

future. The loss of nonhuman nature is so severe that it has 
been termed “biological annihilation” (Ceballos et al. 2017). It is a tragedy but it has not significantly affected GDP , so 
it is ignored by policy makers. Climate change will become 
increasingly constraining in the coming decades in the form of 
extreme temperatures, frequency and severity of storms, and 
weather instability. How long will it take for climate change 
to end economic growth? We cannot say with certainty. But it 
will happen and will probably be the first important biophysi -
cal limit to growth. A complicating factor is that economically 
available stocks of fossil fuel energy and mineral resources will 
continue to grow in the near future with technologies enabling 
their continued extraction. The growth of the global economy depends on an expand -
ing supply of energy. Projections of the “end of fossil fuel” 
have been off the mark for several reasons. One is the under -
estimation of the ability of the market to find and exploit the 
resources it needs to keep expanding. Another is the confu -
sion over the fact that energy prices are indicators of relative 
scarcity, not absolute scarcity (Norgaard 1989). Massive energy 
inputs keep the economy growing.

limit to growth (Gowdy 2021b). Most ecological economists 
believe that global capitalism should be reformed so as to 
become a steady state system. According to Daly (2014) the 
steady state is achieved by (1) controlling the resource inflows 
through the economy using depletion quotas, and (2) control -
ling the outflow of wastes into the environment through 
pollution taxes. Following standard economic logic, Daly 
argues that the optimal scale of economic activity occurs when 
the marginal costs of growth equals the marginal benefits. This 
is not only a misapplication of the notion of the “margin” (a 
single small change in a system in equilibrium) it also assumes 
that costs and benefits of all the components of human well-
being, ecosystem functions, and geochemical processes can be 
measured and made commensurable in a common measure 
of value. A supplementary argument is that the economy can 
“develop” without growing, as in “sustainable development,” 
a concept Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called “snake oil” (see 
the discussion in Bonaiuti 2011, 41-45). Achieving a “steady state” global market economy is 
an ahistorical fantasy. The concept is fundamentally flawed 
because of a lack of an evolutionary perspective (see Daly’s 
anti-Darwinian views on evolution in Daly 2015). To achieve 
the steady state, all we have to do is freeze capitalism by 
controlling sources and sinks, then leave it alone.

beginning with large-scale agricultural empires some five

ultrasocial societies. The question is not when the scale of the

Discussions of effects of environmental impacts such 
as climate change are frequently cast in terms of the conse -
quences of going past a certain boundary such as a particular 
carbon dioxide (CO2) level or global temperature increase. The 
implication is, as in Daly’s MC=MB rule, that if we “just stop 
here we’ll be OK.” This assumes that the total effects before 
and after the tipping point can be calculated and appropriate 
policies instituted. But if we could magically reduce atmo -
spheric CO2 to its preindustrial level of 280 parts per million 
(ppm), and if the current socioeconomic system was still in 
place, we would be back to current CO2 levels in just a few 
decades. Climate change, biodiversity loss, and other major 
environmental disruptions cause a continuum of damages. There is no hard and fast level of atmospheric CO2 or global 
temperature that will be sustainable. The inertia built into the 
climate system means that the effects of climate change will 
not stop at a particular tipping point even if drastic measures 
are taken now.

In the 1970s, Eldredge and Gould (1972) established 
the importance of “punctuated equilibrium” in evolution -
ary history. The idea is that once a species is established in a 
particular stable ecosystem, it will exhibit stasis for most of 
its existence. Significant evolutionary change is the result of 
relatively rare and rapid (in geological context) events. One 
of the main forces causing such punctuations in evolution -
ary history is climate change. Major climate changes lead to 
bursts of rapid extinctions and a high turnover of new species. This is sometimes called the “turnover pulse” hypothesis as 
formulated by the paleontologist Elizabeth Vrba (1993). Peri -
ods of relatively rapid climate change were a major force in 
the biological evolution of Homo sapiens  (de Menocal 2011). Key environmental changes, such as the drying out of Africa 
and the creation of savannahs, and the pulses of ice ages in 
the Pleistocene, are recognized as drivers of human evolution.

Key environmental changes, such as the drying out of Africa 
and the creation of savannahs, and the pulses of ice ages in 
the Pleistocene, are recognized as drivers of human evolution. Richard Potts (1998) argues that key human traits—walking 
upright, large brains, tool use—evolved to adapt to environ -
mental variability and uncertainty. “Variability selection” is an 
evolved trait sometimes referred to as “the evolution of evolv -
ability.” Rapidly changing environments, driven by climate 
change, can favor the selection of attributes that enhance the 
genetic ability of an organism to generate inheritable pheno -
typic variation (Grove 2011). Climate change is accepted as a major driver of past soci -
etal collapse. The archeological and historical record of early 
agricultural state societies shows a common pattern of rapid 
expansion, followed by collapse and loss of complexity (Tainter 
1988). Examples include Angkor Wat, the Tang Dynasty, the 
Mycenaean Empire, the Classic Maya, and the Harappan 
civilization. These civilizations disintegrated due to the exploi -
tation of natural resources—the loss of soil fertility, erosion
