Misidentified Problems
Student problems can be misidentified in situations where 
staff members disagree not only about how to solve the prob -
lem but whether a problem even exists. Viewing problems 
using “cause and effect” thinking is common in schools, as 
part of educator training is to teach students to follow rules 
 142 | F amily SyStemS 2022 16.2                     
and operate within parameters placed on them. It is not typi -
cal to interpret student misbehavior as a product of both 
situational context and reciprocal interaction with others. Undesirable behavior in students is often referred to the 
school social worker or psychologist for resolution, often with 
the expectation that some form of change will follow which 
will alleviate the potential for the behavior to reoccur in the 
future. Attempts by systems-oriented practitioners to involve 
adults in conversations about context and person-environ -
ment interaction when seeking to solve student problems can 
be challenging, as these notions are generally not familiar to 
“cause and effect” problem-solvers. Mental health staff working with student problems from a 
systems perspective can, at times, be perceived by educators as 
remiss in addressing problems because, in their view, mental 
health staff are not doing anything to change the student.

FUTURE DIRECTIONS
History shows that for decades researchers have attempted 
to better understand anxiety using cross-sectional studies 
(Rapee 2012). These investigations, while ambitious, have 
produced little more than a series of isolated variables that 
may or may not contribute to anxiety’s development without 
increasing understanding of the etiological mechanisms that 
contribute to it (Lester et al. 2010). The closest most researchers 
have come to understanding children’s anxiety as a recipro -
cal process is the finding that an association exists between 
anxiety and parental insecure attachment patterns as parents 
model and transmit their own apprehension to their children 
in the next generation (Bogels and Brechman-Toussaint 2006, 
Muris 2007, Wei and Kendall 2014). To this end, the National Institute of Mental Health 
(NIMH) has adopted a broadened platform from which to 
more accurately understand mental health. This effort includes 
development of the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) frame -
work, which is designed to encourage and promote research 
studies that utilize a variety of approaches to more fully 
understand complex human behavior.

developed by Murray Bowen has been the engagement with 
the natural sciences by Bowen theory scholars and clinicians. Bowen believed that if the theory were to grow and contribute

contributed much to those seeking to become knowledgeable 
about natural systems as a basis for understanding human 
behavior through the lens of Bowen theory. In this essay, 
Michael Kerr reflects on his remembrance of Dr. Wilson 
and his contribution to a science of human behavior. — Robert J. Noone, PhD, Editor

A moment I relish was when Dr. Bowen and I went to the 
National Zoo where Dr. Wilson was being recognized for his 
major role in the development of the Ant House. This was in 
1988 or ‘89. What I had not expected is that the Zoo Director, 
Michael Robinson, after lauding Wilson’s contributions to the 
project, took him to task by asking him something like, “Ed, 
is there no place for free will in your thinking about human 
behavior?” After Robinson’s question, Murray Bowen who 
was sitting with me in the second row of the auditorium, 
blurted out, “Of course there is, it’s differentiation of self!” Dr. Robinson did not call on Dr. Bowen to elaborate. This vignette 
is more a Bowen story than a Wilson story, but I won’t forget it. Wikipedia has a very thorough description of Dr. Wilson’s 
career. I will not try to recap that here, but recommend it to 
readers of Family Systems. A notable Wilson quote in Wikipedia 
that relates to Robinson’s query states that 
…all animal behavior, including that of humans, is the 
product of heredity, environmental stimuli, and past 
experiences, and that free will is an illusion (italics mine). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._O._Wilson)
 I think it is important to end my remembrance of Edward 
O. Wilson by mentioning the rapidly growing field of systems 
biology. This field recognizes the need for natural systems 
thinking to describe and understand complex phenomena.

What makes Finding the Mother Tree so absorbing is 
Simard’s unfolding description of her life story as she devel -
ops her research. Growing up in the Canadian Northwest, she 
spent her childhood roaming the forests. After college, she was 
attracted to work for the forest industry as a way to continue 
her engagement with the woods she loved. For years, foresters functioned with a tree-farming para -
digm in which forests were cleared of vegetation to prevent 
competition to newly planted seedlings. The focus was on 
the survival of individual trees rather than on the reciprocal 
interactions between trees. Simard describes a particularly 
poignant episode in which her job was to spray glyphosate 
on the forest growth surrounding tree seedlings, already 
knowing this practice was harmful to regrowth. Simard was 
a neophyte in the forestry world and a female in a male-domi -
nated industry. She found herself marginalized and ignored as 
she made observations about the health of the seedlings that 
were being planted to reforest harvested areas of the forest. While her research led to an understanding that trees grow 
more vigorously in a habitat of mixed species, these ideas met 
laughter and resistance. The forest industry was not interested 
in changing its policies despite research to the contrary.

her breast cancer diagnosis and treatment, and finding a new 
partner who shares her joy in a forest life. Her honesty and 
insight about her personal struggles imbue her story with a 
humanness that is not always accessible in science writing. Undeterred by the difficulties she faced, Simard’s 
research on the underground networks of forests character -

these fungi and roots facilitate communication in an ecosys -
tem, she found  an exchange of carbon, water, nutrients, and 
defense signals between trees and plants. By using rare carbon 
isotopes as tracers to measure the flow and sharing of carbon 
between individual trees and different species, she discovered 
that  birch  and  Douglas fir  share carbon. Firs, which were in an 
interactive community with birches, grew larger as the birches 
lent them carbon resources.

lent them carbon resources. In a reciprocal process over the 
course of a season, birch trees receive extra carbon from Doug -
las firs when the birch trees lose their leaves. The benefit of this 
cooperative economy is that deciduous and coniferous trees 
vary in their energy needs during different periods of the year, 
leading to the overall health and resilience of the forest. In another fascinating study, Simard and her graduate 
student, Amanda, studied the Mother Tree and its surround -
ing saplings. Through carbon tracing, they discovered that 
the Mother Tree supplied more nourishment to her own seed -

through their underground networks, they are also able to

more do we not know about the forest—in which offspring 
nurturance, interchange of resources, and communication is 
exchanged by plant species with no identified brains? Simard’s research extends work done by her scien -
tific predecessors, such as Peter Wohlleben’s observations 
described in The Hidden Life of Trees. Her discoveries of a system 
of communication and resource sharing in a forest community 
transform our way of understanding the forest ecosystem. Her 
efforts have started a revolution in forest research and care.

Her 
efforts have started a revolution in forest research and care. What leads people to question given assumptions 
about living organisms and to have the capacity to under -
stand complex systems in which they live? Parallels between 
Simard and Murray Bowen are that both are pioneers who 
developed natural systems perspectives from their research 
on a particular species—tree communities and human fami -
lies. Both sought to understand the interactive nature of 
living species, questioning the reduction of the complexity 
of a natural system to the focus on the individual. Both were 
marginalized, and their ideas derided by their disciplines and 
professionals in their fields. They persevered, despite pres -
sures to change to the predominant views of the time. In the 
tradition of Galileo, Einstein, and many others who could see 
beyond accepted knowledge, Simard and Bowen have each 
laid the groundwork for understanding the systemic nature 
of the living world. For anyone interested in a systems view of the natural 
world, this book is well worth reading. The book is not only 
an interesting read for the discoveries the author made, but it 
also provides a fascinating window into how science is created 
through researching hypotheses generated from the curiosity 
of a creative and far-sighted scientist. ❖

Jacob B. tPriest  
Reviewed by: William A. Pickering, PhD
In The Science of Family Systems Theory, author Jacob 
Priest presents clearly stated arguments on several topics of 
crucial interest to students, practitioners, and researchers in 
family systems therapy. First, he argues that family systems 
theory (understood as a broad field of study) needs to take 
into account the considerable academic research on families 
that has accumulated in recent decades in order to test its 
hypotheses in light of this research and, if necessary, to revise 
its theoretical presuppositions accordingly. Without such an 
effort, according to the author, family systems theory runs the 
risk of becoming outdated.

central point. In any case, an acceptance of the sociological

A moment I relish was when Dr. Bowen and I went to the 
National Zoo where Dr. Wilson was being recognized for his 
major role in the development of the Ant House. This was in 
1988 or ‘89. What I had not expected is that the Zoo Director, 
Michael Robinson, after lauding Wilson’s contributions to the 
project, took him to task by asking him something like, “Ed, 
is there no place for free will in your thinking about human 
behavior?” After Robinson’s question, Murray Bowen who 
was sitting with me in the second row of the auditorium, 
blurted out, “Of course there is, it’s differentiation of self!” Dr. Robinson did not call on Dr. Bowen to elaborate. This vignette 
is more a Bowen story than a Wilson story, but I won’t forget it. Wikipedia has a very thorough description of Dr. Wilson’s 
career. I will not try to recap that here, but recommend it to 
readers of Family Systems. A notable Wilson quote in Wikipedia 
that relates to Robinson’s query states that 
…all animal behavior, including that of humans, is the 
product of heredity, environmental stimuli, and past 
experiences, and that free will is an illusion (italics mine). (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._O._Wilson)
 I think it is important to end my remembrance of Edward 
O. Wilson by mentioning the rapidly growing field of systems 
biology. This field recognizes the need for natural systems 
thinking to describe and understand complex phenomena.

 THE SCIENCE OF FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY
Jacob B. Priest  
Reviewed by: William A. Pickering, PhD
In The Science of Family Systems Theory, author Jacob 
Priest presents clearly stated arguments on several topics of 
crucial interest to students, practitioners, and researchers in 
family systems therapy. First, he argues that family systems 
theory (understood as a broad field of study) needs to take 
into account the considerable academic research on families 
that has accumulated in recent decades in order to test its 
hypotheses in light of this research and, if necessary, to revise 
its theoretical presuppositions accordingly. Without such an 
effort, according to the author, family systems theory runs the 
risk of becoming outdated. Secondly, by going beyond the 
familiar notions of systems thinking found in general systems 
theory and cybernetics and by making use of contemporary 
notions of system autonomy and adaptation, Priest argues that 
recent academic research supports the idea that families are 
in fact autonomous and adaptive systems.

If there is a defect to be found among the author’s exposi -
tions, in this reviewer’s opinion, it is seen in chapter 4, where 
Priest discusses sociocultural systems as the environments 
to which family systems are adapted. The entire chapter is 
devoted to discussing “power, privilege, and oppression” 
and the effects on families of the social inequities that result 
from them. Limiting the discussion in this manner leaves out 
all other characteristics of social systems when considered 
from the viewpoint of systems theory. In like fashion, and 
not entirely without reason, one could discuss family systems 
as vehicles for offloading stress onto more vulnerable family 
members as seen in spousal and other forms of within-family 
abuse. But, in limiting the discussion to these topics, one 
would certainly be missing much of the picture, if not the 
central point. In any case, an acceptance of the sociological 
analyses cited by the author is not essential to see the validity 
of his broader claim that the structural dynamics of the socio -
cultural systems in which families are embedded “shape the 
autonomy processes of the family system” (49). The Science of Family Systems Theory  is a valuable contribu -
tion to the literature. It forthrightly argues that family systems 
theory needs to go beyond the ideas of its founders and to 
absorb and utilize the results of current scientific research.

and Becvar 2013, and Carr 2016. Because Priest concentrates 
on defining autonomy and adaptation in a systems context 
and does not spend time going into the details of general 
systems theory as such, the book does not lose its focus on 
issues of concern to therapists. The supporting academic 
research cited by the author is not only interesting in itself, 
but his use of it provides examples of the kind of reasoning 
from empirical evidence that, he believes, family therapy must 
take into account if it ist to solidify its theoretical foundations 
and connect theory to improvements in clinical practice. In 
this book, students and therapists will find an accessible but 
penetrating discussion of the importance of theory and its rela -
tionship to practice, and researchers will encounter a sound 
and original approach pointing the way to future inquiries. ❖

how little a psychiatrist can realistically guarantee to the patient. He 
can guarantee time and perhaps an effort to understand the problem. He cannot realistically promise that he can understand, that his effort

an explicit request, to make explicit clear statements to meet only

3Family constellation theory revisited 
Part 2*
Walter Toman, PhD
After a brief historical introduction the theory of family con-stella -
tion is presented in a simple paradigm, followed by a review of the 
empirical data from our comprehensive research including double 
and triple checks where possible. Research of others in pertinent 
aspects of the theory is also reviewed. Basic and more complex sib -
ling positions, their combinations in partnerships and friendships, 
and their roles in parent-child relations are analyzed. The effects of 
losses of family members upon the development of individuals and 
families and family life are also analyzed. Their significance in the 
conduct of individual and family therapy is outlined. FRIENDSHIPS
As for friendships, incidentally, we found—besides many de -
scriptive features of people's individual friendships systems—that 
complementarity of sibling roles had an effect, among others, on the 
duration of friendships. Our subjects were asked to sit down com -
fortably, to try to relax and think of all the friends they have or once 
had, and jot down their first names or nicknames. Subjects listed an 
average of twenty-five friends (within a range of 6 to 102 friends) of 
both sexes and varying ages.

10.3 years when the friends had age-rank and sex conflicts of their 
sibling roles (p<0.02). In contrast to some of our own earlier findings 
with smaller samples of friendships (Toman 1972) complementarity 
was an even stronger factor in opposite-sex friendships than it was 
in same-sex friendships. Friendship studies of other researchers have dealt with just 
one or very few of their subjects' current friendships. Some of these 
studies confirmed the complementarity effect (Baxter 1965, Handy 
1968, Mendelsohn 1973, Mendelsohn et al 1974), and others did 
not (Schuh and Williams 1977, Birtchnell and Mayhew 1977). Our 
friendship studies, with their much broader database, support the 
complementarity concept of social relationships. Needless to say, I hope, that complementarity or non-comple -
mentarity of sibling roles or of other early relationships is an uncon -
scious guide to establishing new social relationships. We can't help 
using early experiences with a sibling or a parent or a childhood 
friend when making new social contacts. Doing so more knowingly 
may improve our chances of forming satisfactory and enduring 
relationships, but even knowingly people might err and sometimes 
fool themselves. Sometimes we do not know all there is to know, at 
least not right away.

The "duplication theorem" of social relationships (Toman 1961) 
which predicts that new social relationships are more likely to be suc -
cessful and enduring when they resemble old and familiar ones has 
intrigued sociologists (Secord and Backman 1964, 1974), psychologists, 
and psychotherapists. Several psychologists have done their own test -
ing of our general findings and of the theorem with their own samples, 
usually small ones, and confirmed our research.1  Mendelsohn, for 
instance, questioned sixty-four pairs of college students (selected from 
five hundred for greater statistical homogeneity and comparability) 
about their dating habits. He found a significant relationship between 
complementarity of their sibling roles (by sex and rank, sex only, rank 
only, neither) and satisfaction of dating as well as the number of actual 
dates. Other studies have failed to show clear effects.24	 	 			 	Family 	SyStemS 	 	 											S pring /Summer 	1995

because of its scale and delegated execution is that of Birtchnell and 
Mayhew (1977). They hired a market research organization to study 
a British national representative sample of some 2,000 subjects who 
received questionnaires about their marriages.

a British national representative sample of some 2,000 subjects who 
received questionnaires about their marriages. They were divided 
into those reporting "successful marriages" (982 subjects) and those 
reporting "unsuccessful marriages" (1,012 subjects). The authors claim 
they found no significant difference in sibling role complementarity 
between those two groups of subjects and their respective partners. Among other things they do report, however, is that a subgroup, 
namely men who were particularly fond of an older sister of theirs, 
were more likely to marry women who had a younger brother or 
else were only children. This and a few other particular effects can be spotted by so 
called configuration frequency analysis which we have conducted 
frequently with our data. Birtchnell and Mayhew did not try to ex -
plain such effects. We would have. In fact, I can think of a number 
of other subgroups to study. For example, those among the "unsuc -
cessful marriages" which actually ended in separation or divorce 
versus those which did not. Rating success or failure of marriage 
alone may not be a sufficient criterion to divide the sample in two 
groups.

Rating success or failure of marriage 
alone may not be a sufficient criterion to divide the sample in two 
groups. Children or no children, ages of children, ages of subjects 
at the time of marriage, time until the first child arrives, duration of 
marriage, and a few more easy-to-obtain characteristics of family 
structure would be meaningful moderators in defining subgroups 
or refining the criteria of success. Beyond that, I cannot recognize which selection principles 
prevailed when the hired market research organization approached 
the subjects for data gathering. Whether the subjects were gathered 
all over Britain, had different economic circumstances, housing or 
schools, or belonged to different ethnic or religious groups—all these 
may have exerted unforeseen influences. If the research focuses on 
relationships within a data complex, a circumscribed area of subject 
selection is usually more expedient. The condition "other things be -
ing equal" is more likely to be satisfied. It could also be that the British respond differently to such ques -
tions compared to americans and Germans. From small samples 
of families that I studied personally in London in connection with a 
research project on "individual friendship systems" (Toman et al 1986) 
I was surprised by the British subjects' eloquence and independence 
in love and partner relations as well as by their insistent thinking 
about social status.

had been known before. Freud and his early followers sensed those effects, but over -
estimated the events of loss and underestimated the permanent 
changes in reality which the event generates. Moreover, Freud called 
it trauma rather than loss and eventually reneged even on that. Imagined trauma is all he ultimately dared think of in his accounts 
of possible psychopathological consequences. Perhaps he and his 
school of psychotherapy had become too contained in the subjective 
worlds of their psychoanalytic patients, failing to use available cues 
about their patients' realities as treatment grew ever longer. Yet all 
kinds of reality cues were brought in by the patients and neglected 
by Freud and many other therapists. Inquiries with other family 
members and friends, not as an undeniable right of the patient or 
part of the treatment, but as permissible when occasions for such 
inquiries were good and taken tactfully, had often been discouraged 
by the therapists.

Where those inquiries had been tolerated or even 
encouraged, some therapists rushed to defend their patients and 
intimidate unsympathetic relatives which, in the long run, did not 
really help their patients either. Such views began to change only after Anna Freud and Dorothy 
Burlingham (1942) and, more convincingly and comprehensively, 
John Bowlby (1951, 1953) had studied separation effects of children 
in real life rather than in the mere introspections of adult patients. (See also Winnicot 1965; Sulloway 1979). Losses, especially of family members in early life, including their 
absence from the start, are at least as powerful a factor in generat -
ing psychopathology as are severe ongoing conflicts between living 
family members. Conflicts resulting from incompatible roles in the 
family systems count among them. Loss is rarer, though, than conflict. There are no families without conflicts, but there are many families 
where children have suffered no early losses of family members and 
even where their parents have not either. However, the percentage 
of those lucky families, once holding the absolute majority among 
families by far, has been on the decline. The psychological effects of the loss of a parent are usually 
graver than the loss of a sibling. Loss suffered within the first six 
years of life is graver than during late childhood and early adoles -
cence (seven to fifteen years).

qualitative losses are harder to evaluate. They require psychological 
understanding. All the other types of losses do so too, of course, but 
the time component should not be forgotten. The effects of losses show up in personal unhappiness, devel -

on the severity of the losses suffered.

Evaluation of anything like success of treatment cannot seriously 
be attempted without some appraisal of the client's objective condi -
tions at the start of the treatment. Tests of psychological ability or 
emotional stability of individuals or family members at the begin -
ning and end of treatment are not valid enough by themselves. The 
client's objective life situations and life histories need to be included 
too, by configuration frequency analysis or index aggregates. If 
neither shows significant differences in the expected directions, we 
cannot really be sure about treatment effects. If at least one of them 
does, we can be sure. Family therapists are in the fortunate position of having ac -
cess to the elemental details of life situations and life histories of 
individuals and families and ongoing opportunities inconspicuously 
to confirm them or put them into question. among the founders 
and fathers of family therapy are Murray Bowen (1959, 1960, 1965, 
1971, 1978), with his interest in getting an articulate picture of the 
family background in order to understand the family's present and 
possible future. Having developed his systems theory, he has not 
only been a very successful family therapist, but also a conscientious 
recorder of elemental details of family structures. The almost infinite 
variety of family life as well as the general principles spelled out that 
guide it can be used like silent levers in the conduct of therapy.

There are various types of family therapy. Some deviate more 
than others from classical psychotherapeutic principles. Those prin -
ciples of classical psychotherapy are something like this:  Listening 
attentively and benevolently, letting clients set the topics, but tak -
ing the liberty of coming back to them for more inquiry, expanding 
topics, asking for concrete examples, exploring feelings, meanings, 
also objective circumstances of events past, present, and future; also 
confirming, commenting, and interpreting the clients communica -
tions; all that without telling the patients about oneself or one's own 
life, family or work, —without asking for favors, giving lessons or 
orders or helping clients materially and practically in their daily 
lives; doing all that with regard to the family as a whole as well as 
to individual family members, thinking about affects and motives 
and longings and bonds and conflicts within and between family 
members revealed during sessions, letting the family discourse de -
velop as spontaneously as possible. All who deviate from classical psychotherapeutic principles 
 think they have good reasons, and they may be right as far as what 
they are doing in effect, if not always by design. Therapists are 
characters too, family therapists even more so, and apparently that 
is recognized and incorporated in the conduct of therapy.

recommend not to press for them or their completion during thera -

ordinary circumstances the therapist should take up, or expand on, 
only those family data that have been mentioned spontaneously 
during sessions. Neither individual nor group nor family therapy 
needs to be of just one kind, as long as the basic psychotherapeutic 
intent is intact:  to help others to help themselves. ❉

text:
MORALITY, NEUTRALITY, AND 
DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF
Stephanie J. Ferrera, MSW
Morality, neutrality, and differentiation of self are distinct but 
interrelated human processes. Neutrality arises from our effort 
to understand what is in nature; this is the hallmark of science 
and objective thought. Morality arises from our effort to deter -
mine and practice what ought to be  in human affairs; it involves 
subjectivity and a bias as to right and wrong. Neutrality cannot 
replace morality, but it can enlighten and guide moral thought and 
practice. Both neutrality and morality are inherent in the process 
of differentiating a self, the individual's development of increasing 
ability to think on a complex level, to define personal values, and 
to act responsibly. Darwin saw the moral sense as uniquely human, but rooted in the 
social instincts that humans have in common with other animals. Darwin suggested that altruism is the basic moral principle. Bowen's 
concept of the emotional system adds something to evolutionary 
theory. The emotional system provides a context for understanding 
the broad spectrum of moral thought and conduct, and the scale of 
differentiation sheds light on the ways that individuals and groups 
vary in their practice of altruism and other moral principles. This 
writer argues that the concept of differentiation of self is not only 
an accurate description of what is, but  also a trustworthy basis 
for determining what ought to be .

text:
The development of the capacity for neutral, objective thought, and 
the development of a moral self are two important aspects of the 
process which Bowen called differentiation of self, the movement of 
the individual toward increasing knowledge and ability to think on 
a complex level, toward definition of personal values and principles, 
and toward responsible action. MOrALITy
Human beings are moral beings who, to varying degrees, think 
about right and wrong and guide their behavior accordingly. Most 
people will state, "I know right from wrong," but when asked what 
they consider to be right and wrong, people have a wide range of 
views. Morality includes principles of right conduct, the thought 
upon which those principles are based, and the conduct guided by 
those principles. The thought upon which moral positions are based 
ranges from highly subjective and emotionally reactive to more 
objective and nonreactive. When moral issues are addressed on an 
emotional level, complex problems tend to be reduced to right/wrong 
categories, simplistic and rigid positions tend to be taken, and op -
posing views become polarized as either/or. At a calmer level of 
thought, people are able to see the complexity of issues involved in 
moral decisions, to consider different positions, and to weigh the 
positive and negative values of each position. The wide spectrum of human moral functioning is best under -
stood in the context of evolution and natural systems.

text:
The wide spectrum of human moral functioning is best under -
stood in the context of evolution and natural systems. Charles Darwin 
provides a good starting place. He was deeply interested in morality 
and devoted many pages of The Descent of Man to this subject because, 
as far as he knew, no one had approached it exclusively from the side 
of natural history,  and because he wished to see "how far the study 
of the lower animals can throw light on one of the highest psychical 
faculties of man" (Darwin 1981, 71). While Darwin saw "the moral 
sense," or conscience, as distinctly human and the most important of 
the differences between man and the lower animals, he also saw it as 
rooted in the social instincts which man has in common with other 
 animals. Darwin observed that animals seek and take comfort in 
one another's company, act with sympathy, kindness, and protection 
toward one another, join in mutual aid to defend against enemies, 
and at times risk and sacrifice their own lives for their comrades. He saw these "social instincts," evident in both man and animals, 
as the foundation of the moral sense, but believed that man alone 
can be considered a moral being because man alone has developed 
the intellectual powers to be able to reflect upon, and to approve or 
disapprove of, his own actions.

text:
Prompted by the moral sense "which 
tells us what we ought to do" and conscience "which reproves us 
if we disobey it" (Darwin [1871] 1981, 93), man will, through long 
habit, acquire the self-command needed to keep his social instincts 
predominant over his instinct for self-gratification. Darwin's statements strongly suggest that he equated moral vir -
tue with altruism, self-sacrifice for the benefit of others. At one point 
in the discussion of the evolution of  moral qualities, he states:  
To do good unto others—to do unto others as ye would they 
should do unto you,—is the foundation-stone of morality. ( 
[1871] 1981, 165) 
He saw "disinterested love for all living creatures" as the most noble 
attribute of man (Darwin [1871] 1981, 105). Darwin con-ceptualized 
moral functioning along a continuum from lower to higher with the 
highest morality based in the social instincts, expressed by sympa -
thy and concern for the welfare of others. For most humans, this 
concern is limited to members of one's own tribe or group, but as 
individuals develop a higher level of morality, this concern extends 
beyond persons known to include all members of one's nation, and 
beyond that to include humans of all nations and races, and even 
beyond humanity to include all sentient creatures.

text:
Other features 
of high level morality cited by Darwin are reason and the ability to 
see long-term consequences of behavior, the power of self-command, 
and the ability to control even the thought of bad actions (Darwin 
[1871] 1981, 100-103). Building on the foundation laid by Darwin, Murray Bowen 
developed a natural systems theory of human behavior. Like Dar -
win, he saw the human as part of all life and saw human behavior 
as largely guided by instincts inherited from ancestral species. The 
automatic, instinctual behaviors in human families and groups 
include the sympathy and benevolence which Darwin called the 
"social instincts," but also include behaviors which Darwin might 
have considered anti-social:  conflict, distance, aggression, domi -
nance, side-taking and alliances. Families can operate cooperatively 50      faMily  SySteMS              S priNg /SuMMer  1995
 in ways that benefit all members, but they can also operate in ways 
that generate tension and division and that result in the gain of some 
members at the expense of others. Bowen's effort to understand 
these seemingly disparate phenomena within a single framework 
led him to a conceptualization not present in the thinking of Darwin 
or others who had grappled with this problem:  the  theory of the 
emotional system and differentiation of self.

text:
The seedbed for this theory was the research project on schizo -
phrenia that Bowen designed and directed at the National Institute 
of Mental Health from 1954 to 1959. Here entire family units, father, 
mother, and an adult child with a diagnosis of schizophrenia, were 
hospitalized together, and family inter-action was observed on a 
close, day-to-day basis. Bowen was impressed by the intensity of 
emotional attachment between family members, by the automatic and 
instantaneous responsiveness between members. Physically, each 
was a separate individual, but functionally, the members appeared 
bound together in a larger whole. Bowen called this larger whole "the 
emotional system," and his early papers contain detailed descriptions 
of the patterns of interaction. All family members participated in the 
family "togetherness" or undifferentiation, but the greatest intensity, 
he observed, was often in the dyad of mother and one child.

text:
All family members participated in the 
family "togetherness" or undifferentiation, but the greatest intensity, 
he observed, was often in the dyad of mother and one child. Bowen 
describes the mother and child as "being for each other:"
Once the child enters into this "being (helpless) for the mother" 
and the mother enters into the opposite "being (strong) for 
the child," they are both in a functional bind of "being for 
each other."  When the child's self is devoted to "being for the 
mother," he loses the capacity of "being for himself." (Bowen 
[1960] 1978, 63) 
This togetherness phenomenon, "being for each other," which 
Bowen originally observed in the mother-child relationship, is pres -
ent at varying degrees of intensity in all human relationships. Each 
member of a relationship system appears to maintain a level of 
comfort and security for self by attempting to keep others comfort -
able, and also by seeking responses from others that will keep self 
comfortable. Much of this adaptation to others is done instinctively, 
with little or no awareness of the behavior. While such a process 
operates primarily on an emotional level, it is often explained on 
an intellectual level as based on love and protectiveness. People 
believe they are being what others "need" them to be, and getting 
others to be as they "should" be. While the conscious rationale may 
be altruistic, the consequence of reactively giving up self and "being 
for each other" is often the opposite.

be altruistic, the consequence of reactively giving up self and "being 
for each other" is often the opposite. In "being for each other," there Vol. 2, N o. 1          M orality , Neutrality , aNd differeN tiatioN  of Self                        51
 is a fusion and blurring of boundaries between people, diminishing 
the capacity of each person to function as a separate, self-directed 
individual, thinking and acting for self. The sacrifice of "self" or in -
dividuality carries a cost in terms of the growth and development 
of each member and, consequently, a cost to the overall strength of 
the family or group. Bowen's concept of differentiation of self refers to the degree 
to which a person matures emotionally and becomes a self-directed 
individual. The concept came from Bowen's observation that, within 
the family emotional system or "togetherness," each member did 
indeed strive to develop a separate and autonomous "self."  Bowen 
saw the force for individuality, like the force for togetherness, as a 
natural phenomenon. Each living organism is a "self" like others of 
its kind but still unique and different; each has a boundary which 
separates it from the surrounding world, and each has an internal 
guidance system which allows it to steer its own course to some ex -
tent.

text:
Bowen defined the "intellectual system," rooted in the human's 
more recently evolved higher brain functions, as a human capacity 
which has the potential to operate somewhat independently of the 
emotional system. The intellectual system, operating in counterbal -
ance to the emotional system, is the key to the human's ability to 
"differentiate a self."  This capacity to observe and reflect, to think 
factually and objectively, frees one from the automatic responsive -
ness of the emotional system, allowing one to see a range of options 
and choices in responding to the issues and dilemmas which life 
presents. An optimal balance between intellectual and emotional 
functioning is reflected in an individual's ability to be for self without 
being selfish and to be for others without being selfless (Kerr and 
Bowen 1988). The concept of differentiation of self and the scale of differentia -
tion are products of Bowen's looking at what is in nature,  at the facts 
of human behavior, and trying to describe these facts as objectively 
and scientifically as possible. In seeking to define the most basic 
process underlying human behavior, Bowen chose a concept well 
established in biology, the concept of differentiation. Differentia -
tion is a life process that humans have in common with all living 
organisms (Bonner 1994).

Differentia -
tion is a life process that humans have in common with all living 
organisms (Bonner 1994). Placing human behavior in a biological 
context and using biological language was consistent with Bowen's 
fundamental premise that the human is part of all life and that hu -
man families and groups are natural systems. Differentiation of self is a fact of nature; it is not a moral im -
perative. The scale of differentiation is an attempt to describe what 52      faMily  SySteMS              S priNg /SuMMer  1995
 is, not an attempt to prescribe what ought to be. to read it as a scale 
of moral virtue, and to conclude that better differ-entiated people 
are more virtuous than poorly differentiated people, would be to 
misconstrue the concept of differentiation. People at all points on 
the scale of differentiation are moral insofar as they function morally; 
that is, insofar as they consider their lives in relation to the lives of 
others, define their own views of what is right, and attempt to live up 
to what they have defined. It is, however, accurate to apply the scale 
of differentiation toward understanding the variation among people 
in moral functioning. The two key features of differentiation—the 
ability to distinguish between thinking and emotion within self, and 
the ability to function as an autonomous individual while actively 
relating to others—influence moral functioning as they influence all 
dimensions of human behavior.

text:
In general, poorly differentiated 
individuals would be more togetherness-based in their approach 
to moral issues, prone to automatically adopt or reject the views 
of others, reactive to differences in views, and  likely to become in -
volved in monitoring and regulating the behavior of others rather 
than focusing on self. Better differentiated people would be more 
individuality-based, more able to balance emotional reactions with 
reflective thought, to maintain their own independent views while 
also considering the merits of other views, to relate calmly to those 
with different views, and to focus on their own responsibilities rather 
than on the behavior of others. Altruism provides a helpful illustration of the difference that the 
level of differentiation makes in an individual's moral functioning. Altruism guided primarily by instinct is one thing; altruism guided 
by a balance between thinking and emotion and a boundary between 
self and other is something else. A highly differentiated individual 
might certainly choose to act altruistically in many situations by 
contributing personal resources to benefit others. However, differen -
tiation would require something more than a sympathetic, altruistic 
impetus as the basis for giving. Whatever anxiety was raised by being 
in contact with the need or distress of the other would be managed 
within self, rather than automatically acted upon.

between self and recipient. When help was given it would be with 
respect for the autonomy of the other, in a way that promoted, rather

people have drawn valuable moral insight from their knowledge of 
differentiation. Many who have studied the theory of the emotional 
system and differentiation of self have observed that the qualities 
of personal and social functioning associated with high levels of 
differentiation are fully consistent with the qualities espoused by a 
variety of spiritual and moral traditions. The features of high-level 
morality defined by Darwin—concern for others that is inclusive 
of all humanity and all living creatures, ability to understand the 
consequences of one's actions, and the capacity for self-observation 
and self-regulation—are consistent with the features of differentia -
tion of self defined by Bowen. NEuTrALITy
Many scientists and philosophers have seen nature as neutral. This view recognizes that nature does not operate according to hu -
man values and beliefs about what ought to be. While the human is 
a product of nature, nature is not a product of the human. Nature's 
only bias is the perpetuation of life. Nature has no investment in 
which individuals, or even which species, survive or in the means 
that living organisms devise in order to survive. Nature also teaches 
that there is no one "right" way for living organisms to deal with 
such basic imper-atives of life as survival, growth and development, 
reproduction, and death.

one can appreciate the complex balance of forces operating in hu -

the neutrality of systems thinking. Systems thinking, when applied 
to human situations, transcends fault and blame, freeing the indi -
vidual to see more sides of a problem and more options for solving 
it. In moments of neutral thinking, one can glimpse, deep beneath 
the elaborate surface details of human situations, the beautiful bal -
ance that characterizes all natural systems. Systems thinking and neutrality lay the foundation for, and 
operate in the service of, responsible moral functioning. Moral 
decision-making (deciding what is "right" for oneself in a given situ -
ation) and moral action (doing as one "ought") are called for many 
times in the course of life. Systems thinking and neutrality do not 
give the answers to moral questions, but they do allow one to see 
the bigger picture, to see self as part of the picture, to see options 
and responsibilities, and to see how one might act so as to make a 
difference in the picture and in the outcome. DIFFErENTIATION OF SELF

when it begins to serve some function in the relationship system. It 
may become a focal point for the collective reactivity of the family, 
a rallying point for family unity, an overshadowing concern which 
draws attention away from other areas, or an avenue for enhanced 
functioning of some members. As problems become embedded in 
the system in these ways, they become more intractable. Seeing one's part in the projection process and in the develop -
ment of problems requires deep reflection. It is one thing to accept 
the idea that one has played a part, and another thing to understand 
specifically  how o ne has personally contributed to problems. This 
level of self-awareness comes in small increments through studying 
one's family and other systems, understanding how these systems 
evolved over time to become what they are, and seeing how one's 
own functioning has been shaped in these systems. Bowen's theory 
of the emotional system provides a detailed map to guide this study. As a person comes to know the context, triggers, relationship patterns, 
and automatic behaviors that make up his emotional functioning, 
he also begins to see his part in shaping the systems to which he 
belongs. With this knowledge comes almost unlimited opportunity 
for personal growth in the direction of increased self-regulation and 
responsibility.

In the intricacy of human interdependence, an individual has 
many impulses to dominate, coerce, lean upon, co-opt, steer, blame, 
pity, and otherwise impinge upon others. There are an equal num -
ber of opportunities to function more responsibly. Differentiation 
of self goes beyond the altruistic impetus in what it requires from 
the individual. The work of differentiation calls one to conceptual -
ize at a complex level, to become aware of self at a deep level, and 
to contribute to the common good at the optimal level possible for 
self. This work takes continual reflection and consistent effort. The 
person who is committed to managing self in this way provides 
leadership and strength to his family and society, thus increasing 
the potential for others to function more thoughtfully and respon-
sibly. As individuals come forward with this kind of leadership, 
they make a unique contribution to the maturity and stability of their Vol. 2, N o. 1          M orality , Neutrality , aNd differeN tiatioN  of Self                        59

process designed by nature that has the potential to lead us "beyond 
nature," beyond automatic functioning, toward understanding and 
solving some of the binds and dilemmas that are part of our natural 
heritage.

The Faculty Case Conference is held twice monthly at the Georgetown 
Family Center. Faculty members take turns presenting a case from their 
clinical practices. The conference is not intended as supervision, nor as a 
meeting to arrive at consensus about how to manage specific cases. It is 
intended as a learning experience for the faculty and to keep them aware 
of one another's general approach to clinical problems. Presenter:  Roberta B. Holt, DSW
This clinical case report is based on a presentation at a Faculty Case 
Conference in November 1994. Identifying data including the family sur -
name have been altered to insure confidentiality. This case was presented 
to summarize emotional processes within a family and stimulate thinking 
about the ongoing course of the con-sultation. The presentation was selected as an example of the applicability of 
Bowen theory to a poor family with multiple problems. Bowen theory is 
grounded in biology and applies to all humanity. In spite of its inclusive -
ness it has been overlooked and underutilized as relevant in thinking about 
the most intense human problems that come to the attention of public social 
service agencies. PRESENTING PROBLEM
This case was a referral in my work in a co unty welfare child 
protective unit. The family had been on welfare and the mother was 
participating in a project designed to train clients for self-sufficiency 
as part of the larger goal of reducing welfare rolls.

In society there currently is pressure to get people off welfare. This is not a new idea. Programs have been in existence for decades 
and have met with varying degrees of success. Examples are programs 
provided by the Welfare Amendment of 1962, The Economic Oppor -
tunity Act of 1965 that provided training and work experience for 
public assistance recipients and other qualifying low income people, 
and the Work Incentive Program (WIN) of 1967. Each generation 
becomes aware of those who are not self-sufficient and tries to do 
something effective to deal with the problem. New programs are 
designed to overcome the deficits of previous programs. Logic has 
suggested that if recipients cannot attend training or work because 74      Family  systems              s priNg /summer  1995
 a lack of resources prohibits participation, then these resources need 
to be provided if the program is to succeed. While reality issues are 
important variables, I believe subtle emotional processes that occur 
in families are the critical bedrock upon which most of the reality 
issues exist.

A premise derived from Bowen theory is that variation in the basic 
adaptiveness or lifetime fitness of individuals is based in a nonran -
dom multigenerational transmission process which includes, but 
involves more than, genetic transmission. Among humans, and 
probably other species, it involves an orderly relationship process 
which during prenatal and postnatal development shapes the overall 
responsiveness and functioning of individuals to their environment 
throughout the life course. The nongenetic transmission of behavior is generally regarded 
as learned. Recent research related to maternal influence on the 
prenatal neuroendocrine development of offspring suggests that 
another phenotype transmission process is involved. It is posited 
that a third form of heritable variation, in addition to those of ge -
netic and cultural transmission may exist and that it is consistent 
with and an element in the  multigenerational transmission process 
defined in Bowen theory. A principal question in the effort to understand human 
behavior  has been how to account for the basic differences among 
individuals. The question generally leads to the nature/nurture is ‑
sue which, in recent years, has moved from a less polarized debate 
toward an effort to understand the interplay between genetic and 
environmental influences on the development of individual differ ‑
ences.

what mayr terms “essentialism.”  It is the tendency to conceptualize 
individual differences as deviations from what is perceived to be an 
underlying essence or norm of a particular category or group. From 
an evolutionary perspective, individual differences simply represent 
variations. The notion of an essence or norm is more a product of 
the human brain than a phenomenon in nature. Darwin was able to observe that each form of life is unique. In the process of reproduction, offspring vary slightly from both the 
previous generation and from each other. he observed that life forms 
produce more offspring than can be sustained in the environment. Some variations increase an offspring’s chances of surviving and 
successfully reproducing; most do not. The complexity and diversity 
of all life, according to Darwin’s theory of natural selection, is seen 
as resulting from the accumulated variations selected for over the 
course of evolution. The existence of heritable variation could be observed by Dar ‑

types; it does not rigidly determine each cell’s destiny. Which type a 
particular cell will become is determined on the basis of interactions

larva has the genotypic potential to develop into a member of one

however, is transmitted. As Bonner (1988) states, “ultimately both

is further removed from the direct gene instructions and more influ ‑

Adaptiveness, as it is used 
in this paper, refers to within species variation of lifetime fitness or 
flexibility in responding to environmental challenges. Bowen theory 
posits that the variation in adaptiveness found among individuals 
and families is to a significant degree determined by the multigen ‑
erational family relationship system. offspring can be observed to vary in the degree to which they 
resolve their emotional dependence on the parental family and be ‑
come self‑directed. The expressed variations along this continuum of 
differentiation of self are subtle and complex. The basic adaptiveness 
of an individual can be assessed, according to this theory, when the 
nuclear family relationship patterns, life stressors, and other variables 
entailed in the concept of differentiation of self are considered. The 
degree to which an offspring develops basic, as opposed to reactive, 
emotional autonomy in relation to the parental family is equivalent 
to an individual’s basic level of adaptiveness. Individuals at higher 
levels of differentiation of self are predictably more adaptive in that 
they are less likely to develop prolonged physical, psychiatric, or 
social symptoms in response to stressors than are those toward the 
less differentiated end of the continuum. Their life courses, and those 
of the other members in their family, are more orderly and based 
more on self than on reaction to others.

and postnatal development. It is hypothesized that chronic anxiety

are exposed to higher levels of testosterone than those which gestate 
between two female fetuses. The exposure to this hormone, which 
crosses the fetal membrane between contiguous siblings, influences 
the course of development and adult reproductive behavior. Clark et al. (1993) have shown that the intrauterine position 
of gerbils also influences the sex ratio of the littermates’ offspring. Since this in turn influences the sex ratio of the littermates in the next 
generation, it represents an example of a phenotypic transmission 
process. An acquired characteristic, the sex ratio of litters, is transmit ‑

not directly related to Homo sapiens  due to morphological differences 
in the rodent uterus, but it does suggest the potential for the pheno ‑
typic transmission of physiological and behavioral characteristics 
mediated by hormones or neuropeptides in the mother‑offspring 
blood exchange. The principal functions of the family (mating, reproduction, 
affiliation, child-rearing) have been found to involve biological me ‑

the regulation of these behaviors (Gubernick 1990, hofer 1984, Insel 
1992). Such informational substances are components of a vast array 
of mutually influencing factors, at many levels, which are involved in 
the regulation of behavior.

by behavioral means, most particularly by the process of teaching 
and learning” (Bonner 1980), is clearly a factor in the variation in 
adaptiveness of individuals inheriting such information. There is evidence to suggest that there may be additional phe ‑

relationship, among mammals at least, is an important factor in 
regulating the adaptiveness of offspring to their environment. The 
evolution of prolonged parent‑offspring involvement along with 
more complex and integrated neural, hormonal, and immunological 
systems, have resulted in processes influencing physiological and 
behavioral functioning which are not genotypic and which entail 
more than what is generally thought of as learning. These processes 
are active in both the prenatal and postnatal periods. A number of experimental animal studies have demonstrated 
that the stressing of one generation results in observable behavioral 
and physiological changes in the adult lives of that generation’s off ‑
spring. It has been further demonstrated that the influence of such 
stressors can be transmitted not only postnatally, but prenatally, and 
not only from one generation to the next, but over several genera ‑
tions.

that variation in the basic adaptiveness or lifetime fitness of individu ‑
als is based in a nonrandom multigenerational transmission process 
which includes but involves more than genetic transmission. Among 
humans, and probably other species, it involves an orderly relation ‑

shapes the individual’s overall responsiveness to and functioning 
in his or her environment.

Basic adaptiveness is seen as roughly corresponding to the 
basic level of anxiety each individual inherits from the preceding 
generation. The transmission of anxiety is mediated by the family 
relationship system and involves physiological and psychological 
processes. Individual offspring in the family vary in the anxiety 
transmitted to them and as a result their families of procreation will, 
in turn, vary in their level of chronic anxiety. This process can be 
observed to occur over the generations with some order. The nongenetic transmission of behavior is generally regarded 
as based in learning. Recent research related to maternal influence on 
the prenatal neuroendocrine development of offspring suggests that 
another phenotypic transmission process may be involved. It also 
suggests an additional mechanism involved in the multigenerational 
transmission process. The biological literature primarily cites “maternal effects” 
in discussing the phenotypic transmission of traits. The multigen ‑
erational transmission process described by Bowen posits a more 
complex process. The influence of the mother -infant relationship 
in the regulation of the behavior and physiology of the developing 
offspring is itself seen as reciprocally influenced by the emotional 
system of the family. The regulation of individual development and 
behavior due to the interactions of members of a highly integrated 
group is not unique to humans or even to mammals.

The effec Ts of sTalin’s Purge on 
Three genera Tions of russian families
Katharine G. Baker, DSW and Julia B. Gippenreiter, PhD
This article reports the results of a joint Russian-American research 
project that studied the multigenerational impact of the 1930s Stalin 
Purge. It has been estimated that between twenty and forty mil -
lion people died in the purge. Through in-depth interviews in the 
winter of 1993-94 with fifty grandchildren of purge victims, the 
study explored the impact of this historical event on family life. It 
also examined the functional variation of family members in the 
third generation in relation to the way families had dealt with the 
loss of grandparents. The results of the study indicated support 
for the hypothesis that cutoff from grandparents was significantly 
inversely associated with aspects of functioning in the grandchild 
generation. Additionally, a personal research effort into family 
history and the ability to actively protest political coercion were 
positively related to social functioning. IntroductIon
In the 1930s, Stalin launched a purge of the communist Party 
leade rship and red Army senior commanders that spread, through 
personal denunciation, to all levels of Soviet society in the years 
leading up to the Second World War (conquest 1990; daniels 1985), 
with the most intense phase occurring from 1937 to 1939.

Anxiety, behavior, and emotional patterns are transmitted from one 
generation to the next through the substance of relationships between 
grandparents, parents, and grandchildren.1
this study looks at the three-generational relationship cluster 
of grandparent-parent-grandchild but focuses on the grandchild 
generation as interview subjects. According to Bowen family systems 
theory, one would expect the functioning of the grandchild generation 
in present-day russia to be consistent, to some extent, with family 
response to prior historically catastrophic family events such as the 
purge. In other words, families that had been able to maintain a 
reasonably stable level of functioning following the purge might be 
expected to produce grandchildren who would continue to manage 
themselves reasonably effectively in present-day russia. Families 
that were unstable in the aftermath of the purge might be expected 
to produce grandchildren with higher levels of anxiety and family 
disarray, possibly including cessation of reproduction. Cutoff  is an aspect of the multigenerational transmission process 
that reflects the nature of connection-disconnection in a family. It can 
be part of “vertical” relationships between generations, as well as 
“horizontal” relationships within the same generation.

Memorial  (Adler 1993) is a russian nongovernmental organi -
zation that began informally in 1987 for the purpose of erecting a 
monument to the victims of the purge. It quickly became a repository 
for information about victims of the purge. originally it was entirely 
a grassroots organization. Its founding conference took place in Mos -
cow in January 1989, and after the end of the Soviet union in 1991, 
it was officially registered with the Russian government and began 
to receive some government support. Its central office is in Moscow 
and it has branch offices throughout the former Soviet Union. A high 
percentage of its members are the daughters and grandchildren of 
victims of the purge.

Because this was a relatively small pilot study with a strati -
fied random sample, the findings cannot be fully generalized to the 
wider population of russia. nevertheless, they indicate directions 
for future research which could be significant. The concept of cutoff 
as an aspect of multigenerational process can be useful in describing 
and defining family and societal response to mass trauma, not only in 
larger samples of the russian population, but also in other societies 
that have experienced extensive losses of significant family members 
in past generations. Solid and replicated findings could also have 
value in predicting the basic functioning of future generations in such 
currently traumatized societies as rwanda and Bosnia. In addition, 
knowledge about the impact of cutoff on the functioning of succeed -
ing generations may lead to the development of clinical interventions 
with at-risk populations such as those in refugee camps. the phenomenon of cutoff at the societal level is also deserving

GENDER  AND  BOWEN THEORY
Roberta B. Holt, DSW
Little has been written about the contribution of Bowen theory 
to a discussion of gender and gender issues. With its base in 
the natural sciences, Bowen theory addresses gender from the 
perspective of emotional process in relationships. This paper 
selects several of the prevailing themes in the literature about 
gender and addresses them from the perspective of Bowen 
theory. It then discusses how the theory can be useful in the 
resolution of gender issues. INTRODUCTION
In the years since the development of Bowen theory,  little has 
been written about its contribution to a discussion of gender and 
gender issues. The reasons for the absence, for the most part, are 
embedded in the grounding of the theory in biology (Papero 1990) 
and its central focus on how emotional systems operate. Defining 
basic mechanisms  and patterns in emotional behavior has been a 
central inquiry of Bowen theory. The discipline of science, to which 
Bowen theory aspires, has directed the work to discovering the 
nature of emotionality and how it functions. The findings suggest 
commonalities in the processes that govern emotionality that apply 
to all of life. Gender considerations as a topic of societal discourse emerged 
from real concerns that have tended to be economic and political.

Gender considerations as a topic of societal discourse emerged 
from real concerns that have tended to be economic and political. Much 
of the literature deals with institutional inequities that are societally or 
culturally determined. Individual societies or cultures vary in privileges 
extended to members on the basis of sex, social status, religion and 
other considerations.1  When the literature on gender has addressed 
biology, it has tended to focus on the structural and functional differ -
ences between the sexes rather than on their similarities. 521 Anonymous member of the editorial review board helped to define more clearly 
the scope and limitations of this paper by offering these remarks. Dr. Holt is on the faculty of the Georgetown Family Center. © Georgetown Family Center, 1996

This paper addresses gender from the perspective of emotional 
process in relationships. Since Bowen theory is a context for con -
sidering gender, it may be useful to  define the scope of biology to 
which the theory aspires and the scope of culture from which gender 
studies have emerged. A principle for defining a boundary between 
biology and culture is:  If all cultures perform a particular activity, 
then that activity probably is embedded in biology. How the biology 
is expressed varies among different nations, tribes, groups, families, 
or individuals.

text:
How the biology 
is expressed varies among different nations, tribes, groups, families, 
or individuals. These variations with all of their  innovations are an 
expression of culture (DeVore). Culture, psychology, sociology, economics, politics and a host 
of other societal considerations are part of the human condition. As 
such, the literature about these subjects makes an important contribu -
tion. There is a place for them in Bowen theory, but these subjects 
have not been a central consideration of the theory. The central 
focus of Bowen theory is on biology which provides observations 
that are universal and apply equally to all humans. The concepts in 
the theory are applicable to gender and culture and may extend to 
relationships in all forms of life across various species. SOME CONSIDERATIONS ABOUT GENDER
As long as there have been males and females, there have been 
differences between the sexes. The most obvious differences are vis -
ible. They are  a given for each individual and are deeply embedded 
in biology. These differences have been part of the evolutionary pro -
cess as long as there have been humans on earth. They emerged with 
the transition to bi-sexual reproduction and are thought to provide 
diversity that increases the margin of survival of the species. Although the presence of difference contributes to survival, the 
presence of any difference provides a fertile field for the development 
of misunderstanding and conflict.

text:
Although the presence of difference contributes to survival, the 
presence of any difference provides a fertile field for the development 
of misunderstanding and conflict. Difference creates an opportunity 
for an individual to react to something “foreign” to the “self.”  The 
perception that another is not part of the self sets up the potential 
for arousal, discomfort, excitement, or tension. These, along with 
other emotional states, alter how an individual thinks and increase 
the potential for subjectivity to emerge in interaction. Humans vary greatly in their capacity to be comfortable with 
difference. Most people have a range of tolerance for dealing with it 
intellectually and abstractly. Some can talk comfortably about appre -
ciating difference as long as it is perceived to belong to the external 
world and does not touch the core of the self. Actual interaction with 
another creates a potential for emotionality to be stirred in the reality 
 54	 	 			 						F amily	SyStemS 	 	 												S pring /Summer 	1996
of one-on-one interaction. Under such circumstances, the thinking 
system turns off and the ability to be in the presence of difference 
erodes. It dissolves in proportion to the amount of emotionality 
generated and the amount of solid self available to the individual. Many individuals appear to tolerate difference and actively 
seek variety. A portion of these people operates out of a polarity 
that “needs” the  environment to define self.

text:
Many individuals appear to tolerate difference and actively 
seek variety. A portion of these people operates out of a polarity 
that “needs” the  environment to define self. They make decisions 
based on doing the opposite from the other rather than from care -
fully considered beliefs from within themselves. To have a concur -
rent opinion with another would be more “togetherness” than such 
an individual can manage. The self is defined in relationship to the 
other. In interaction such individuals automatically pick up on the 
opposite side of thoughts expressed by another. The presence or 
absence of  another influences the direction of thinking. The result -
ing interaction is described in the literature as relationship oriented 
and not autonomous (Bowen 1978). The greater the perceived difference, the more individuals can 
polarize as opposite from the other. The process provides little op -
portunity for neutrality. Negative contact can be maintained until it 
escalates to a level of discomfort that requires cutoff. Generally this 
is a formula for creating and maintaining divisive and ineffective 
interaction. The end point is a climate in which it is not possible to 
respect the ideas of others sufficiently to form cooperative bonds

Goal Orientation
Much of the prevailing psychological commentary  about the 
sexes supports a view that men are goal oriented and women are 
relationship oriented. While this view makes a valid point and pro -
vides useful information about prevailing traits of individuals, the 
ideas neither elucidate nor apply to an understanding of the scale of 
differentiation in Bowen theory. Importing a premise about gender 
differences leads to the erroneous conclusion that there is a gender 
bias in the theory. This interpretation introduces an individually 
oriented bias that is unrelated to Bowen systems theory. More specifically, Bowen theory neither states nor implies that 
goal orientation is a characteristic of males and that relationship 
orientation is a characteristic of females. The scale of differentiation 
applies equally to both sexes. The balance between individuality 
and togetherness varies on a continuum for both sexes. Women who 
function at higher levels of differentiation are highly goal directed 
(Bowen 1978). Goal direction is generated internally, whether in 
the arena of own family, of community in civic activities, or in the 
workplace. The more a female is emotionally reactive, the lower her 
level of functioning, the less she has an ability either to define goals, 
or to pursue them effectively in any arena. Vol. 3, N o. 1            G eNder  aNd BoweN  Theory                                  59
The same principle applies equally to males.

Relationship orientation is another area for considering about 
gender. All humans would prefer satisfying relationships. The need 
for relationships and the demands for togetherness is not gender 
specific. How much relationship is needed to keep an individual 
calm  and functioning optimally varies along the scale of differen -
tiation. At higher levels of functioning, individuals of either sex 
have less relationship orientation (Bowen 1978). At lower levels of 
functioning there is intense relationship orientation with emotional 
dependence on others and a focus on them.

Feelings
All humans whether male or female have the capacity for 
thinking and feeling. In well differentiated individuals these capaci -
ties operate as a “friendly team,” in which the ability to arrive at a 
thoughtful position contains within it an awareness of the feelings 
of self and others, along with the motivation and an ability to deal 
with emotional reactivity. In much of the literature on gender, feelings tend to be described 
as a property of females. Males are considered to be “cerebral” at 
best, or “unfeeling” at worst. Bowen theory postulates, and clini -
cal practice provides observations to support, that both males and 
females are equally intense creatures when it comes to emotionality 
and the feeling system. How emotionality is expressed is a matter of personal style 
that may be related to gender but is not confined to it. For example, 
in emotional interaction there is the individual who expresses emo -
tionality readily. This individual is often the one who can be a pro -
jector, or be considered to be the expressive “feeling one.”  Such an 
individual often operates in close interaction with an associate who 
becomes anxious in the presence of emotionality, puts a lid on the 
expression of feeling, and distances from it. This individual appears 
as “wooden” or “unfeeling” but is just as anxious and feeling as the 
more openly emotional one.

Although a modification of anxiety can contribute to 
reducing polarities, it is not sufficient to eliminate them. Reducing 
anxiety creates an environment in which it is possible to hear the 
other person’s position more accurately. Once this occurs, more 
workable ways of living with differences emerge. While consideration of gender issues has made a significant 
contribution, many are based on assumptions about characteristics 
that pertain uniquely to a particular sex. Those who do not contain 
those characteristics are recognized emotionally as “different.”  A 
focus on differences can generate, if not fuel, anxiety. An unintended 
consequence of defining the differences is further separation of in -
dividuals into discrete categories. The greater the anxiety, the more 
differences become important. When differences become a primary 
consideration, a focus on the commonalities of the human condition 
is lost. The possibility of resolution of interpersonal issues becomes 
increasingly remote. Bowen theory provides an “escape hatch” for society in its 
struggle to deal with differences and human conflict. It contains 
major concepts that accept differences in human interaction as 
a given without further polarization. It defines useful ideas for 
reducing anxiety as the driving engine of increased polarity. To 
those concerned about relationships between the sexes, it provides 
an important avenue for exploration.

The following brief report conveys a line of emergent thinking that 
may ultimately contribute to a deeper understanding of the rela -
tionship between individual functioning and emotional processes 
in the broader unit—family, neighborhood, community. If that 
relationship can be more precisely delineated theoretically and sup -
ported by observation, new insights may follow about the nature of 
individual functioning, about the concept of differentiation of self, 
and about the functioning of emotional units. The relationship between stress, anxiety, individual variation 
in terms of degree of differentiation of self and the functioning of 
individuals and groups forms a central tenet of the Bowen theory. As anxiety intensifies, both for the individual and for the broader 
emotional unit (family, work group, etc.), theory posits that function -
ing becomes compromised initially for those with the lowest levels 
of differentiation of self. If the severity of anxiety increases, the func -
tioning of others can become compromised as well. The restriction 
of individual functioning is expressed in the relationship system, 
producing the markers of anxiety in the relationship process itself 
(the destabilizing of two-person systems, the emergence of triangling, 
high degrees of relationship reactivity, and so forth).

The neuroscientist, biologist and primatologist Robert Sapolsky 
(1992, 1990) has observed a similar process in a colony of feral baboons 
in Kenya, spelling out both the physiological processes that mark 
the shifting degrees of stress for individuals and the markers of that 
shift in the group. During periods of group stability (marked by a 
clearly established hierarchy with well-defined rank for each animal), 
higher ranking animals display less stress (measured physiologically 
and observed behaviorally) than do lower ranking animals. During 
such interludes higher ranking animals display low basal levels of 
cortisol, rapid elevation of that level in response to threat, and rapid 
return to basal levels upon cessation of the threat. Lower ranking 
animals display elevated basal cortisol levels, slow elevation of that

Collectively, these studies show that there is not a single 
physiological profile of dominance among social primates, 
particularly as it pertains to adrenocortical function. Instead, 
it depends on the type of society in which it occurs, and a 
critical variable seems to be whether it is a stable or unstable 
one. It is my feeling that the psychological advantages and 
disadvantages of dominance, varying according to the so -
cial setting, are the critical variables in this stable/unstable 
dichotomy. (1992, 276-77)
As the group shifts from social stability towards instability, 
the increasing instability finds expression in behavioral changes 
of individual animals and in shifts within the animals’ network 
of relationships. Aggressive behaviors increase, and Sapolsky has 
measured an increased frequency of dominance interactions (the 
dominant reinforcing his position with a subordinate or a subordinate 
challenging the position of the dominant or both). The increasing 
instability reveals itself in the rapid formation and dissolution of 
coalitions among the animals. During periods of social instability 
in the group, the advantages of rank disappear, at least in terms of 
relative freedom from stress, and dominant animals display elevated 
basal cortisol levels and the behaviors indicative of high levels of 
stress. In fact, the basal cortisol levels of dominant animals during 
such periods of instability may be higher than those of subordinate 
animals.

of reversal of dominance present an elevated profile of basal cortisol,

rank (1992, 277). In that instance, the dominant animal is in effect 
losing ground to the lower ranking animal, and the stress response 
relates to that loss of position. In essence, the animal may be argued 
to experience a loss of control in interactions, lack of predictability 
(the animal is confronted with behaviors of others that differ from 
those that he or she expects), and a general sense of a worsening of 
his or her individual positon in the group. The stress response is 
linked to the apparent change in those psychological variables. Sapolsky has also demonstrated that individual animals differ 
in their capabilities related to the assessment of the security of their 
own position (1992, 278-79). A particular class of animals consistently 
display the lowest levels of basal cortisol. These animals displayed a 
constellation of stylistic traits, reflecting those differing abilities. In 
general these animals excelled at distinguishing between threatening 
and neutral or non-threatening interactions and events.
