Sapolsky’s descriptions of primate behavior under differing 
intensities of stress parallel Bowen’s descriptions of the human 
family’s response to differing degrees of anxiety. Both point to the 
role of social interaction in triggering and managing physiological 
stress and anxiety, and both describe the process by which a shift in 
social stability (defined in the individual’s terms as social control and 
predictability and the personal sense of holding one’s own or gain -
ing ground socially) can produce individual changes in anxiety and 
behavior that in turn can lead to a spreading of social instability in 
the group as a whole. Their descriptions of the behaviors expressing 
social instability (and therefore individual stress among a significant 
proportion of the group) are remarkably similar. ❉

CONSULTANT DISCUSSION
The consultation with Mr. B and his aunt represent a rare clini -
cal opportunity to learn from a family where both a perpetrator of 
violence and another significant adult family member not associated 
with the violence were interested, motivated, and available. In this 
consultant’s experience, the standard clinical configuration in families 
with violence  has been either the adult perpetrator, the adult victim, 
or both. Involvement of other family members in the consultation is 
unusual. Consulting with Mr. B and his aunt has reinforced previous 
assumptions that the potential for a more complete and thorough 
understanding of the multigenerational context of family violence 
requires contact with family members who occupy positions of 
significance within the triangles of the family. It is expected that 
future interviews with this family and others can yield a greater 
understanding of the emotional processes that provide the context 
for violence in relationships. FACULTY DISCUSSION

FROM THE EDITOR
Thi, irr,r. of Family Systems features several articles about the
emotional functioning of nonhuman species. The articles are de-
rived from presentations at the Georgetown Family Cente/s con-
ference on "Individual Variation and the Relationship System"
which was held in April1996. In the last issue of this journal, which
also published articles from that conference, I commented on the
difficulty of comparing human behavior to the behavior of other
species. I mentioned E. O. Wilson's view (1975) that such compari-
sons are difficult because human intelligence has evolved to such an
extreme degree that it greatly distorts basic primate social qualities. Wilson's view implies that basic primate social qualities exist
in human beings but are often difficult to discern. However, even
when obvious similarities exist between aspects of human behavior
and the behavior of other species, another problem arises in assess-
ing the basis of the similarities. This problem concerns the distinc-
tion between analogy andhomalogy. Wilson defines analogy as "a resemblance in function, and
often in appearance also, between two structures, physiological
processes/ or behaviors that is due to evolution rather than common
ancestry." ('1975, 578) The resemblance results from convergent
evolution.

text:
What aspects, if any, of the human emotional system are
homologous with the emotional system of a very distantly related
species such as harvester ants? The Distinguished Guest Lecturer
for the 1997 Annual Georgetown Family Symposium, Dr. Deborah
Gordon of Stanford University, has been studying harvester ants f or
more than a decade. Her presentation beautifully described a
harvester ant colony as a natural system. If an increase in food
resources occnrs near a colonp the number of colony members
foraging for food increases, and the increase in the number of
foragers is followed predictably by a decrease in the nqmber of ants
engaged in other tasks such as nest maintenance. This reciprocal
functioning is quite similar to what Murray Bowen described in
human families; namely, that a change in functioning of one family
member is followed predictably by compensatory changes else-
where in the system. Most biologists would probably say the similaritybetween the
pattern of reciprocal functioning in a harvester ant colony and a
human family is based on analogy, not homology. The existence of
reciprocal functioning in these very distantly related species prob-
ably reflects convergent evolution. In other words, reciprocal func-
tioning has been adaptive in the environments where the social units
of harvester ants and human beings have evolved each species has
developed the pattern independently.

Prima Te Social relaTioNShiPS
Frans de Waal, PhD  and Molly Embree
A review of current literature on coalitions and alliances among 
primates indicates that primates may understand social relation -
ships within their groups at a higher level of sophistication than 
most other mammals. Apparently of critical importance to pri -
mates’ social complexity is triadic awareness, a term from biology 
which refers to the ability to understand relationships of others 
independently of one’s own involvement. This ability to recognize 
relationships among multiple items (whether individuals or ob -
jects) in the environment may lie at the heart of primates’ success 
using tools to achieve a physical goal (that is,  obtaining termites 
from inside a mound) or using coalitions and alliances to achieve 
social goals (that is, secure the alpha position with the support of 
another). Though humans have developed this “triangulating” 
capacity to an extreme, expanding research on primate species 
shows this ability to be characteristic of the primate order rather 
than a human invention. IntroductIon
Among biologists and anthropologists, there is considerable 
speculation about the evolutionary origin of the large brain relative to 
body size typical of humans and, in fact, all primates. one popular 
hypothesis, particularly among primatologists, emphasizes social 
intelligence (Jolly 1966, Humphrey 1976).

the most common form of triadic interaction among primates 
is a coalition or alliance of two individuals jointly opposing a third. In general, coalition may be described as two individuals cooperating 
in what may be a temporary, opportunistic, and aggressive encounter 
against a third, while alliance implies a more stable, long-term rela -
tionship between two individuals, often based on affiliative behavior 
such as grooming, resulting in regular support during agonistic 
encounters with others (de Waal and Harcourt 1992). Coalitions between males in the context of fights may greatly 
influence the outcome of fights, the dominance ranks of those in -
volved, and ultimately, the reproductive success of the winning 
males. Smuts and Watanabe (1990) describe the importance of 
greeting rituals between two adult male baboons in maintaining 
their coalition prior to a fight with a third. In chimpanzees also, in 
captivity and in the wild, males can dominate other males who may 
be even larger and stronger, if they are supported by other males or

Among adults, the interactions involved in forming coalitions 
can be subtle and complex. de Waal describes many such examples 
in Chimpanzee Politics  (1982), based on his observations of an island 
colony of twenty-five chimpanzees in the Arnhem Zoo, in the Neth -
erlands. In one example, the young alpha male, nikkie, was able to 
dominate the other males in the group only with the support of the 
old leader, Yeroen, whom he had replaced. nikkie was able to pre -
serve his coalition with Yeroen (and therefore, his own alpha status) 
only by allowing Yeroen mating privileges that he did not have to 
allow lower ranking males. When he interfered with Yeroen’s mat -
ing privileges, Yeroen had only to withdraw his support during the 
next aggressive interaction between nikkie and other males in the 
group to make the importance of his role in the coalition evident. In 
addition to these observations of the chimpanzees’ triadic interactions 
on the island, incidents in their night cages made clear that, while a 
third male might dominate either nikkie or Yeroen individually, he 
could not dominate the two of them. Bonobos, a close relative of chimpanzees and humans, provide 
another example of the importance of coalitions in primate social 
systems.

Bonobos, a close relative of chimpanzees and humans, provide 
another example of the importance of coalitions in primate social 
systems. (Nishida and Hiraiwa-Hasegawa 1987) Despite the bonobo’s 
close relation to humans and chimpanzees, it has a completely dif -
ferent social system. Although caution is advised in interpreting 
direct comparisons of humans and bonobos or chimpanzees, it is 
interesting to note the apparent evolutionary flexibility in the social 
systems within our lineage (McGrew et al. 1996). one critical difference between bonobo and chimpanzee so -
cieties is the strong alliances among female bonobos which allow 
them to dominate males in spite of the dimorphism in size. Among 
captive as well as free-ranging bonobos, an alpha female typically 
dominates other group members, and females form coalitions to secure 
priority of access to resources and to dominate males (Kano 1992, 
de Waal 1997). In chimpanzees, males are individually dominant to 
all females and form aggressive coalitions to dominate other adult 
males, but in bonobo society a male’s rank is permanently linked 
to the status of his mother (Furuichi 1992). Female bonobos form 
strong alliances by engaging in sexual interactions such as genito-
genital (G-G) rubbing, during which they rub their genital swellings 
together.

vention, where one individual separates two others. typically, this 
strategy is used by alpha male chimpanzees to cut off the affiliative 
actions of other adult males in the group whose formation of a coali -
tion could potentially undermine the alpha’s power. For example, 
when nikkie, the alpha male of the Arnhem colony, saw his main ally 
grooming with another adult male, he began an intimidation display 
which included loud hooting, slapping the ground, and charging 
around the two males. this kind of display is effective in separating 
the two other males and possibly in preventing the formation of a 
coalition between them. the fact that nikkie intervened in all the 
grooming sessions of his ally and his rival he witnessed during his 
three-year tenure as alpha male suggests that a coalition between his 
ally and another male might threaten his role as leader in the group. Similar divide-and-rule strategies among adult male chimpanzees 
have been documented by nishida and Hosaka (1996) in the wild. Another incident requiring triadic awareness involved mother 
chimpanzees in the Arnhem colony whose juveniles’ play suddenly

on a hot day two mothers, Jimmie and tepel, are sitting in the

wild and captive chimpanzees. reconciliation, consolation, and mediation are relatively new

animals must compete selfishly to survive and reproduce to their 
greatest advantage. What we are beginning to understand more

FAMILY EMOTIONAL PROCESS, REACTIVITY, 
AND PATTERNS OF OVULATION    
                                               
Victoria Harrison, MA
This pilot study investigated aspects of family emotional process, 
levels and patterns of reactivity, and patterns of ovulation for ten 
women over three months. Basal body temperature and physiologi -
cal and hormonal measures indicated differences between women 
who did and did not ovulate. Sustained levels of reactivity were 
present for women with anovulatory cycles. Anovulatory women 
and their mothers reported absence of contact with a higher number 
of family members than did those women who ovulated. For those 
who ovulated, patterns of delayed ovulation were consistent with 
increases and decreases in reactivity in the course of family life. These observations about contact and emotional cutoff between 
family members, about reactivity and about patterns of ovulation 
suggest ways in which relationships within the family influence 
variation in human reproduction. Although the small number 
of subjects prohibits statistical correlation, the differences noted 
in this pilot study provide a basis for extending this study to a 
broader population. IntroductIon
In all of nature, the capacity to reproduce exceeds actual 
reproduction. the human population is no exception. In several 
generations of any family, some reproduce and some do not. Some 
family members have many children and others have one or a few.

text:
Bowen Theory and evolu Tionary Theory
Michael E. Kerr, MD
Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection explains how highly 
integrated social systems evolve. Bowen’s family systems theory 
describes how relationship systems function. This article reviews 
the contributions of Darwin and others to the theory of natural 
selection, describes basic concepts in Bowen theory, applies Bowen 
theory to naked mole-rat colonies, and discusses ideas in Bowen 
theory that might expand evolutionary theory’s understanding of 
living systems. These ideas include multigenerational emotional 
programming, emotional r egression, and an individuality-together -
ness balance in relationship systems. The article does not attempt 
to integrate the two theories or to explain one theory in the context 
of the other, but to delineate their different perspectives on the same 
life processes. The principal goals of this article are to compare the perspec­
tives on living systems of Bowen family systems theory and the the­
ory of evolution by natural selection and to explore Bowen theory’s 
potential contributions to the understanding of all living systems. The article does not attempt to apply the theory of natural selection 
to the human family. Family systems theory was developed by psychiatrist, Mur ­
ray Bowen (1978). The theory conceptualizes the human family as 
an emotional unit.

text:
Family systems theory was developed by psychiatrist, Mur ­
ray Bowen (1978). The theory conceptualizes the human family as 
an emotional unit. The term “emotional” means that there are basic 
forces and patterns operating in families that have evolved over 
several billion years. Man’s large brain has spawned language, a 
complex psychology, and an elaborate culture but, as important as 
these developments have been, the most fundamental forces and 
patterns governing family functioning appear to have evolved long 
before the human neocortex evolved. The term “unit” means that a 
family is a well­organized system of interlocking relationships. This

text:
Bowen theory and Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by 
natural selection (1859) are distinct in that the former describes how a 
system functions  and the latter describes how a system evolves. Bowen 
theory describes the functioning of the human family emotional 
system. Natural selection describes the interplay of forces that lead 
to the evolution of, for example, the social system of a hive bee or 
the anatomy of a giraffe. The myriad observations on which natu­
ral selection rests include detailed studies of the organization and 
functioning of the social systems of many species, but the theory 
itself is not about how these systems function. Natural selection ex­
plains how individual traits, both anatomical and behavioral, and 
types of social organization function in the service of survival and 
reproduction. Evolutionary biologists distinguish between proximate cau -
sation  and ultimate causation. Proximate causation describes how 
certain stimuli in an organism’s environment and processes operat ­
ing within the organism trigger ways of reacting and functioning 
that the organism has evolved. For example, a seasonal decrease in 
daylight hours triggers migratory behavior in birds. Ultimate causa ­
tion, in contrast, attempts to explain why an organism has evolved 
its particular morphology and ways of functioning. For example, 
migration results in birds living in an area where food resources are 
more plentiful in the winter.

For example, 
migration results in birds living in an area where food resources are 
more plentiful in the winter. Family systems theory, by describing 
how a relationship system functions, how relationship patterns 
regulate individual r esponses, appears to fall under the category of 
proximate causation. However, although Bowen did not necessarily 
develop family systems theory to explain how an emotional system 
evolves, the theory may have some relevance to that question, some 
relevance to ultimate causation. The thesis that family theory may be relevant to ultimate as 
well as proximate causation is rooted in the recognition that living 
systems have important similarities in organization and functioning. Bowen refers to these similarities when he states: “Man’s family is a 
system  which I believe follows the laws of all natural systems.” (1978, 
 151)  John Bonner notes the similarities of living systems when he 
states: “There is a fundamental sameness in how cells group togeth­
er to form a multicellular organism, how individual animals come 
together to form a social group, and how members of a human 
family form an integrated unit.” (1994, 20)  Because family theory 
describes how human relationship systems function, and because 
similarities exist in relationship systems across species, the theory 
has the potential to amplify an explanation of how a system evolves 
by natural selection.

The “lens” of family theory can facilitate ef forts 
to discern common processes in living systems, pr ocesses that may 
shape as well as reflect evolution, and it can also facilitate the study 
of relationship systems as forces in natural selection. DARWINIAN EVOLUTION
Darwin developed the theory of evolution by natural selection 
to explain the great diversity of species in nature. The theory can also 
explain the evolution of well ­integrated social or relationship sy stems. Understanding the theory begins with recognizing the earth has a 
multitude of environmental niches that can sustain life. Niches vary 
enormously and new niches keep being added. Living or ganisms 
continually change as their structures and instincts undergo slight 
variations. Some variations are heritable, thus can accumulate in 
descendants over generations and spread slowly through a popula­
tion. After many generations, an accumulation of slight variations 
may modify the structures and instincts of the individuals in a popu­
lation suffi­ciently to endow its members with enough distinguishing 
traits to demar cate the population as a new species. The heritable variations that spread through a population are 
those that render an or ganism and its descendants more adaptive, 
more able to survive and reproduce.

The heritable variations that spread through a population are 
those that render an or ganism and its descendants more adaptive, 
more able to survive and reproduce. Nature “selects” the organ ­
isms that have the adaptive traits in the sense that these individu ­
als will gradually monopolize a niche’s life­sustaining resources, 
consequently making it diffi­cult for their less adapted competitors 
to survive. If a new trait enables an organism to access a new life­
sustaining resource in a niche, this reduces competition and allows 
both the variant and original populations to co­exist. This leads to 
an increase in the diversity of life forms in a niche. Survival in an environmental niche depends on an organism’s 
abilities to cope with the physical environment and to manage in ­

text:
Thus, natural 
selection shapes the character of relationships. Natural selection not only shapes relationships, but relationships 
are a selective force in their own right. Darwin states: “In social ani­
mals it (natural selection) will adapt the structure of each individual 
for the benefi­t of the community; if each in consequence profi­ts by the 
selected change.” ([1859] 1979, 135)  The statement seems to imply 
that if a change in the functioning of an individual in a social group 
benefi­ts the reproductive success of both that individual and others 
in the group, the relationships other group members have with that 
individual act as a selective force to pr eserve the change. Robert Triv ­
ers describes this process in the socially minded herring gulls when 
he states: “These social characteristics evolve because other gulls are 
part of each individual gull’s environment and, like all other parts 
of the environment, may have selective effects.” (1985, 16)
Provided that the environmental niche and other factors favor 
such an outcome, the selection pressure of relationships in a social 
group can increasingly integrate the functioning of individuals into 
the group. As the fun ctioning of individuals becomes more int egrated, 
the group evolves from a loose aggregation of fairly independent 
individuals towards a cohesive unit in which the survival and repro­
ductive success of individuals depend heavily on the unit.

In this 
way, natural selection can lead to the evolution of highly integrated 
social systems. In some species with highly integrated social systems, the social 
unit contains sterile individuals with adaptations of structure and 
instincts that make them very different from other members of the 
unit. Worker castes in social insect colonies are one example. The 
existence of such individuals confronted Darwin with the theoretical 
problem of explaining their evolution. He states: “The great diffi­ ­
culty lies in the working ants differing widely from both the males 
and the fertile females in structure, as in the shape of the thorax and 
in being destitute of wings and sometimes of eyes, and in instinct.” 
([1859] 1979, 257)  How can sterile individuals transmit their highly 
specialized traits to the next generation without having offspring 
of their own? Vol. 4,	N o. 2	 																	B oweN 	theory 	aNd	eVolutioNary 	theory 																											 123

selection can operate at the level of the family as well as at the level 
of the individual. He uses the term “community” in his discussion 
of selection at the family level, but is apparently referring to a group 
of related individuals (Wilson 1975, Alexander et al. 1991).

text:
He uses the term “community” in his discussion 
of selection at the family level, but is apparently referring to a group 
of related individuals (Wilson 1975, Alexander et al. 1991). The 
hypothesis is the following: If a community generates slightly mod­
ifi­ed, sterile individuals whose actions promote the welfare of the 
community, the community’s fertile members flourish and transmit 
to their fertile offspring the tendency to produce the sterile, slightly 
modifi­ed members. As the process repeats over generations, the 
fertile and sterile members gradually evolve very dif ferent struc tures 
and instincts. Selection is not for the modifi­ed, sterile individuals, 
but for the community’s capacity to generate them. Worker caste insects exemplify an exaggerated form of what 
many evolutionary biologists now classify as altruism,  which is func­
tioning that potentially increases the number of surviving of fspring of 
others as it potentially decreases the number of one’s own surviving 
offspring. Examples of altruism include risking one’s life to pr otect 
others, sharing food with others, and caring for others’ of fspring. Such acts become more prevalent and appear in more exaggerated 
form as social systems evolve greater complexity (Wilson 1975). Altruism is one of the hallmarks of a well­integrated or “eusocial” 
society according to Charles Michener (1969).

text:
Altruism is one of the hallmarks of a well­integrated or “eusocial” 
society according to Charles Michener (1969). Eusocial species live 
in colonies of overlapping generations, one or a few individuals 
produce all the of fspring, and all other individuals are functionally 
sterile, helping to rear the young and protect the colony. Altruism, 
along  with cohesion and cooperation are key properties of social 
existence according to Edward O. Wilson (1975). The hypothesis of family selection answers the question of 
how sterile altruists can evolve by natural selection, but it does not 
answer other important questions about the evolution of complex 
social systems. For example, the hypothesis does not explain why 
exaggerated forms of altr uism and other features of eusociality have 
evolved in certain taxonomic groups and not in others (Alexander 
1991). Fu rthermore, Darwin’s theory i ncludes the pri nciple of 
inheritance, but does not include an understanding of the basis of 
inheritance. Mendel’s insight into the basis of inherited variation 
was not appr eciated until the beginning of this century, some years 
after Darwin’s death. As the science of genetics emerged and de ­
veloped, evolutionary biologists began integrating it with natural 
selection. Their efforts have generated new formulations that expand 
on Darwin’s ideas about the evolution of social systems.

NATURAL SELECTION SINCE DARWIN
This section describes the ideas of a number of influential 
biologists, but leaves out many others who have made important 
contributions to understanding how social behavior evolves. The 
principal purpose of this section is not to present a complete survey 
of the fi­eld, but only to illustrate, especially to those not familiar with 
the biological literature, some of the attempts that have been made 
to integrate genetics with the theory of natural selection.1 
 
Inclusive Fitness
A formulation of natural selection based on inclusive fitness  to 
explain the evolution of social behavior was developed by William 
Hamilton (1964). This type of formulation is also referred to as kin 
selection. The basic idea is that the greater the degree of genetic re­
latedness among individuals in a community, the stronger their ten­
dency to evolve social behaviors such as altruism. In other words, a 
close genetic rel ationship is the primary incentive for social evol ution.

individuals in the following way: if the average inclusive fi­tness 
of the individuals in a kin network displaying altruism is higher 
than the genetic fi­tness of individuals in otherwise comparable 
networks not displaying altruism, the networks displaying altru ­
ism will flourish (Wilson 1975). Since the communities of a species 
displaying altruism flourish (greater reproductive success) relative 
to the communities of the same species not displaying altruism, the 
genes encoding for the altruism will gradually become a feature of 
the species as a whole. According to Hamilton, the concept of inclusive fi­tness ex ­
plains why so many species that have evolved eusociality belong to 
the or der Hymenoptera (ants, wasps, and bees). Females in nearly 
all hymenopteran species have a closer genetic relationship with 
their full sisters than is true in almost all other sexually reproducing 
species. This does not result from inbreeding, but from an unusual 
system of genetic inheritance. Therefore, a sterile worker ant tending 
her colony’s larval brood is aiding the survival of sisters who have 
an unusually large number of genes identical to her own.

cies in all other taxonomic groups combined. In other words, the 
existence of subsociality in a species is a stronger predisposition for 
the evolution of eusociality than the degree of genetic relatedness 
in the subsocial units themselves. This model can be extended to 
other taxonomic groups. For example, well­integrated societies with 
altruistic behaviors have evolved in birds and mammals. All birds 
and mammals exhibit parental care, but the subsocial units in these 
species do not have the unusual degree of genetic relatedness seen 
in hymenopteran species. Mutualistic Social Behavior

or dies, then take over as the new queen. Another way is for her to 
lay her own eggs surreptitiously in the nest. Thus, the insects can 
gain individual fi­tness because they are capable of altering their 
functioning in reaction to changes in the system and of modulating 
their functioning in reaction to what the system will allow. Semisocial colonies can evolve into primitively eusocial ones (in 
a similar way to the evolution of eusociality from subsociality) when 
the type of nest and conditions of a habitat favor a queen’s mature 
daughters remaining at the nest rather than leaving to start nests of 
their own. The daughters function as partially or completely sterile 
workers, performing tasks previously performed by the unrelated 
auxiliaries. Unneeded, the auxiliaries eventually die or the queen 
drives them off. At this stage, queen and workers (mature daughters) 
function very differently but are similar in appearance. Furthermore, 
the workers are capable of starting nests on their own. If a sterile 
worker leaves to found her own nest, she will become fertile.

The 
concept is similar to mutualistic social behavior. Reciprocal altruism 
occurs in the following way: an individual behaves altr uistically 
towards an unrelated individual; the action induces the unr elated 
individual to behave altruistically in return (immediately or later); 
the recipr ocated altr uism produces a net gain in individual fi­tness 
for the individual who fi­rst acted altruistically (the help he r eceives 
increases his fi­tness more than the help he gave decreased it); thus, 
natural s election pr eserves the genes encoding for a ltruism in the fi­rst 
individual. The evolution of reciprocal altruism r equires r epeated 
interactions between the cooperating individuals. The tendency of members of baboon troops to form coalitions 
may have evolved by reciprocal altr uism (Trivers 1985). Coalition 
members aid one another recipr ocally in disputes with other troop 
members. Reciprocal altruism can explain the evolution of a number 
of human behaviors; for example, gratitude, sympathy, and guilt 
may be favored by natural selection because these feelings motivate 
individuals to reciprocate altruistic acts (Wilson 1975). Evolution of Similarities in Complex Biological Systems

organization and functioning of all complex biological systems were 
developed by John Bonner (1988). The ideas address aspects of how 
systems function as well as general principles about how systems

and in social species presumably depends on the selection of genes 
encoding for tendencies towards specialized structures or functions. However, the processes that create differentiation during the devel­

time of an or ganism, colony, or society, are not under direct genetic

A termite colony is an example of relationship processes 
regulating gene expression and individual development. Reciprocal 
functioning is important in role differentiation in a termite colony. Every nymph in a colony carries genes encoding for the potential 
to be a queen, worker, or soldier, but only some nymphs become 
soldiers—most of the others become workers. The mature soldiers 
in a colony have genes directing the pr oduction of a pher omone that 
“turns off” soldier genes in a nymph when the pheromone contacts 
it. However, when the soldier ranks deplete for whatever reason, 
the soldiers as a group produce less pher omone, and this allows the 
developing nymph’s soldier genes to “turn on.”  The nymphs develop 
into soldiers, the soldier ranks fi­ll to their most adaptive proportion, 
and the consequent rise in pher omone level inhibits other nymphs 
from becoming soldiers. Another universal property of complex biological systems is a 
“tug of war” between forces for integration  that bring the components 
of a system together and forces for isolation  that work in the opposite 
direction (Bonner 1994). Examples of isolation include trees spacing

Examples of integration 
include baboons forming into troops, lions into prides, and fi­sh into 
schools. Both the forces of integration and isolation are evident in 
a social unit; for example, the members of an insect colony form an 
integrated unit around their queen, but they also kill or expel indi­
viduals from other colonies (even members of the same species). These forces that appear to be working in opposite directions 
are really the same; they are the forces of natural selection (Bonner 
1988). For example, selection for tendencies toward integration 
may occur because they increase the effi­ciency of a system; selection 
for tendencies toward isolation may occur because they distribute 
the members of a species or social unit more evenly in the area of a 
needed resource. Having reviewed some basic ideas about how social systems 
evolve by natural selection, the discussion will now shift to Bowen 
theory’s description of how family systems function. One distinction 
between the theory of natural selection and Bowen theory is that 
while both theories address the phenomena of complex biological 
systems, Bowen theory’s vantage point is the system as a whole and 
natural selection theory looks at the system through the “eyes” of 
its individual members.

relationship system and on how the patterns regulate individual

enhance its genetic fi­tness by maintaining a pattern of interaction 
in a relationship system. BOWEN FAMILY SYSTEMS THEORY
There are many defi­nitions of what constitutes a family. Bowen 
(1985) defi­ned a family as the total number of individuals attached to 
an emotional nucleus . By this defi­nition, an individual is part of a 
family if the forces and patterns operating in the family unit af fect 
his emotional functioning and his emotional functioning affects 
the forces and patterns in the unit. The defi­nition encompasses 
single­parent families, two­parent families, and families with three 
or four generations living together; it can include unrelated people 
and people living at great distances from one another. These forces 
and patterns operate in nonfamily groups as well, but usually with

The term “system” is applied to family relationships because 
they have that quality. The behaviors between family members are 
automatic and predictable. For example, a change in the functioning 
of one family member is followed by compensatory changes in the 
functioning of other members. Systems thinking conceptualizes the 
total chain of events that play out within and between individuals, 
addressing the interrelationship of the events rather than assigning 
“cause” to any one event. Systems operate at all levels, from genes 
to societies. Bowen theory is a specifi­c theory about the facts of hu ­
man emotional functioning, but some of its concepts probably have 
application to other species. The theory distinguishes between an emotional system,  a feeling 
system,  and an intellectual system  in human beings. The emotional 
system “includes the force that biology defi­nes as instinct, reproduc­
tion, the automatic activity controlled by the autonomic nervous 
system, subjective emotional and feeling states, and the forces that 
govern relationship systems.” (Bowen 1978, 305)  The human emo­
tional system is not necessarily identical to the emotional systems 
of other species, but it has evolved gradually during the long line 
of species ancestral to Homo sapiens. This makes it likely that some 
common denominators exist between the human emotional system 
and the emotional systems of other species.

Differentiation and chronic anxiety are interconnected 
in that well­differentiated people tend to react less anxiously than 
poorly differentiated people to relationship disturbances. For exam­

he is to real or imagined shifts in distance from or involvement with 
important others. People sometimes express these reactions as feel ­

Relationships can generate chronic anxiety, and anxiety can 
affect the character of r elationships. For example, one individual 
may be anxious, but become even more anxious in reaction to others’ 
anxious reactions to him. Chronic anxiety can escalate in a relation­
ship system as a result of this interactive process. Therefore, family 
relationship systems have a level of chronic anxiety that reflects 
how everyone in the system is functioning. The level fluctuates 
over time in all families as stresses within and surrounding a family 
change. However, chronic anxiety tends to be highest in families 
composed of poorly dif ferentiated people because their members 
are unusually reactive to one another’s anxiety. In well­differenti ­

anxiously to him. As anxiety increases in a relationship system, people’s auto ­

text:
As anxiety increases in a relationship system, people’s auto ­
matic response is to attempt to reduce anxiety in themselves. (A 
more thoughtful response might be to tolerate the anxiety.)  An 
automatic response when people feel isolated or unsupported is to 
make more emotional contact with others; an automatic response 
when people feel crowded or adversely affected by others is to get 
more distance. Because everyone in an anxious system is attempting 
to get comfortable, the system is unstable. However, all relationship 
systems have patterns of emotional functioning  that help stabilize the 
system by “binding” anxiety in certain parts of it. Family theory describes four patterns of emotional functioning: 
emo­ti o­nal distance, em o­tio­nal co­nflict, recipr o­cal functi o­ning, and triangles. The patterns reduce individual anxiety by binding or integrating it 
into the structure of relationships. Emotional distance (by physical 
withdrawal or internal mechanisms) reduces anxiety generated by 
too much contact. Emotional conflict (verbal or nonverbal) reduces 
anxiety generated by too much contact or too much distance. The 
dual function results from conflict being a way to have contact and 
maintain distance at the same time. Reciprocal functioning r educes 
anxiety because each person is fairly comfortable in his particular 
“overfunctioning” or “unde rfunctioning” position in the relatio nship.

A decline in system functioning is termed 
an emotional regression. Usually one of two scenarios unfolds after clinical symptoms 
develop in a relationship system. In one scenario, a family gets 
highly focused on the symptoms and symptomatic member, and 
the symptomatic member becomes (to varying degrees) chronically 
dysfunctional and dependent on the family. This type of “caretaker ­
patient” interaction can bind family anxiety and thus allow a system 
to regain stability. The stability occurs, however, at the expense of 
the group becoming preoccupied with its internal problems and hav ­
ing a chronically ill member. In another scenario, the symptoms so 
threaten a family that they generate even more anxiety and intensify 
the regression. As the r egression deepens, symptoms may appear in 
multiple people. In contrast to these scenarios, symptoms sometimes 
serve as a stimulus for a system to pull out of a r egression. A multigenerational transmission process determines the 
levels of differentiation of self of the members of a family unit and 
the consequent vulnerability of the unit to regressions in emotional 
functioning. The information determining level of differentiation 
is transmitted through genes, intrauterine effects (Noone 1995), be ­
havior, and the communication of attitudes, values, and beliefs.

THE NAKED MOLE­RAT (HETEROCEPHALUS GLABER)
Having discussed some basic ideas in Bowen theory, the theory 
will now be applied to a nonhuman species, the naked mole­rat of 
east Africa. This species lives in colonies exhibiting a degree of social 
integration so extreme that the colonies very obviously function as 
emotional units. The extreme degree of sociality in naked mole­rats 
meets the criteria of a eusocial species. Considerable research data 
exists on these animals from extensive studies done both in the wild 
and in laboratory settings.3
The purpose of describing this species in such detail is to illus­
trate that the fundamental forces and patterns operating in human 
families operate in a distantly related mammalian species.

The forces 
and patterns could have evolved independently in the phylogenetic 
lines leading to human beings and naked mole­rats, but it is more 
likely that both species exhibit them because they evolved before 
the phylogenetic lines split. If this is true, it supports the idea that 
fundamental and highly influential aspects of human emotional 
functioning evolved long before the human neocortex evolved, long 
before the emergence of a complex psycho logy, elaborate culture, and 
language. The far more complex brain of Homo sapiens  adds myriad 
details to human behavior that make human beings different from 
naked mole­rats in important ways, but the similarities between the 
two species are as important for understanding human behavior as 
the differences. Ecology
Naked mole ­rats are subterranean ­dwelling rodents that inhabit 
the semiarid and desert regions of the horn of Africa. Their fossil 
record there extends back three million years (Van Couvering 1980). They are hairless creatures small enough to fi­t into the palm of a 
human hand. Colonies range in size from 25­295 members, with an 
average being seventy to eighty members (Brett 1991a). Naked mole­rats have two large protruding incisors they use 
for digging, feeding, and fi­ghting. They excavate extensive burrow 
systems by forming digging teams composed of a long line of ani ­
mals. The lead animal in a line digs to extend a tunnel, then pushes 
the excavated dirt under itself to the animal behind it.

breeding female nurses the pups for about four weeks, and then 
weans them by physically pr eventing them from nursing (Lacey 
and Sherman 1991). After weaning, the pups begin to eat the feces 
of other colony members and to nibble on solid food transported to 
the nest by workers. Only one female breeds, but successful reproduction depends 
on a group effort—the colony as a whole could be considered the 
unit of reproduction. The entire colony changes in some interesting 
ways as a bree ding female’s pre gnancy progresses. Only the breeding 
female nurses the pups, but the teats of all colony members (males 
and females alike) enlarge during the breeding female’s pregnancy 
(Jarvis 1991). As the breeding female nears parturition, colony 
members sharply increase the amount of time they spend huddled 
together with her in the nest area. After a litter is born, colony 
members (especially the younger ones) exhibit a heightened alarm 
response. It seems the whole colony participates (physiologically

nonbreeding males, nor do they show sexual interest in her or other 
females (Jarvis and Bennett 1991). Relationships
Strong pair ­bonding exists between a breeding female and 
each of the breeding males, and an especially strong bond typically 
exists with one male. These relationships persist outside as well as 
during the mating period (Jarvis and Bennett 1991). The breeding 
female and her primary consort are usually in proximity. If she 
leaves the nest to roam the burrows, he soon follows her. The bond 
between a breeding female and a breeding male also manifests in 
frequent “ano­genital nuzzling.”  In this activity, two animals rest 
side by side in the naso­anal position, rousing periodically to smell 
or rub the partner’s genital area (Jarvis 1991).

range from harmonious to highly conflictual. The most common 
vocalization in a colony is a “soft chirp.”  Soft chirping accompanies 
harmonious interactions, and may serve as a contact or cohesion call 
among colony members (Pepper et al. 1991). Aggressive interactions 
are accompanied by loud chirps. In general, an animal reacts ag ­
gressively if a colony mate interferes with his getting something he 
wants or tries to take something he has. For example, if an animal 
is behind another in a tunnel and wants to pass, the lead animal 
may block him, triggering both animals to emit loud chirps. After 
a brief vocal exchange, the lead animal may squat down and let the

The breeding female is the most dominant animal in a colony, 
dominating males and females alike. Others usually defer quickly 
to her but, if not, she may act very aggressively. She might gape 
her jaws, threaten with her incisors, emit hissing sounds, shove the 
inadequately submissive animal down a tunnel, and even bite it 
(Reeve and Sherman 1991). To avoid such treatment by a breeding 
female, a confronted animal may double up, roll on its back, and 
stay motionless for several minutes (Lacey et al. 1991). Aggressive interactions are commonplace in the daily routine 
of a colony, but the animals spend a majority of their time huddling 
together peacefully in the nest area. Pressing against and lying on 
top of one another reduces the energy demand of a colony (Brett 
1991b). This is because the physical contact helps the animals control 
evaporative water loss and body temperature (Jarvis and Bennett 
1991). In other words, naked mole­rats have evolved to use external 
processes such as relationships to help regulate certain internal func­
tions. Presumably, such adaptations have evolved because they are 
more effi­cient for this species in this environmental niche than other 
types of water and temperature control (Alexander 1991). Relationships and Physiology
Relationships affect the physiology of naked mole­rats in other 
important ways. One way is that the number of animals living in a 
colony constrains the physical growth of the colony’s members.

One way is that the number of animals living in a 
colony constrains the physical growth of the colony’s members. This 
socially induced constraint on growth is evident in a young colony 
founded from a pair of naked mole­rats. Pups from the pair’s fi­rst 
two litters tend to grow rapidly and become large adults, but pups 
from their subsequent litters grow more slowly (on average) and are 
less likely to become large adults (Jarvis et al. 1991). A mark of the 
unusual flexibility of naked mole­rats, however, is that all the ani ­
mals in a colony retain the ability to resume growing if the colony’s 
confi­guration changes. For example, if some large adults in a colony 
are lost through predation or fi­ghting, the smaller adults can r esume 
growing and quickly replace the lost animals. This socially induced 
constraint on growth may be adaptive by preventing a colony from 
carrying an excess of large animals (Jarvis et al. 1991). Having more 
 large animals than necessary to defend a colony would strain the 
colony’s precious energy resources. Relationships also regulate the physiological dif ferences be ­
tween breeding and nonbreeding naked mole­rats. The breeding 
female’s behavioral dominance of the nonbreeding females results 
in their having poorly developed uteri and ovaries and low levels 
of the hormones involved in reproduction (Faulkes et al. 1991).

Group Agonistic Interactions
Another aspect of life in a naked mole­rat colony is coordinated 
group attacks on predators, on for eign naked mole­rats, and even 
on colony mates. If a poisonous snake enters a colony in search of 
prey, the individuals that discover the snake hiss and bite at it, sound 
alarm grunts, and often push dirt into the tunnel to block its further 
entry (Lacey et al. 1991). The alarm calls rapidly summon large 
nonbreeding colony members to the site. The defenders may stalk 
the snake to trap it in a tunnel, then attack and kill it with vicious 
bites from their incisors (Alexander 1991). Naked mole­rats are highly xenophobic (Brett 1991a). One 
way colony mates seem to recognize foreign naked mole­rats is by 
smell. The members of a colony acquire a distinctive colony odor by 
rubbing themselves frequently with the excr etory products in their 
toilet ar eas (Lacey et al. 1991). If for eigners are detected in the burrow 
system, some of the animals discovering the intruders threaten them 
and others run back to the nest area, emitting trilled vocalizations as 
they go. The alarm calls quickly recruit defenders to the site of the 
developing conflict (Pepper et al. 1991). The defenders often form a 
two­tiered wall of threatening animals to repel the intruders (Lacey

Considerable variation exists in how well naked mole­rat colo­
nies function. One measure of this variation is litter survival rate, 
which refers to the percentage of pups in a litter surviving to wean­
ing. Studies of captive colonies reveal signifi­cant variation in litter 
survival rates both between colonies and in the same colony over 
time (Jarvis 1991). The range of variation extends from none of the 
pups in a litter surviving to nearly all of the pups surviving. Appar­
ently low litter survival rates can also occur in wild colonies. The fate of a litter can usually be predicted within twenty­four 
hours after parturition (Lacey et al. 1991). In colonies where most 
of the pups in a litter will wean successfully, the pups are kept in 
the nest area, the breeding female nurses them regularly, and other 
adults spend considerable time with them. Large nonr eproductive 
adults baby­sit pups born in the tunnels until they can be carried 
to the nest (Jarvis 1991). These baby­sitters lie on their sides with 
a pup sheltered within the curve of their bodies, gently nudging 
and grooming it. In sharp contrast, in colonies where a low litter 
survival rate can be predicted, tunnel­born pups may never make it 
to the nest.

cannibalize newborn pups. One factor affecting the survival rate of a litter is the functioning 
of the breeding female (Jarvis 1991). Some breeding females spend 
most of their time in the nest area lying quietly with their nursing 
pups. These breeding females are not highly aggressive in their dom­
ination of the nonbreeding females, but somehow order prevails in 
their colonies. In contrast, other breeding females appear conti nually 
threatened by the possibility of losing reproductive control. They 
spend so much time in the tunnels hissing at and shoving other fe ­
males that they neglect their pups. Not surprisingly, colonies with 
a quieter breeding female appear to rear young more successfully 
than colonies with a breeding female that acts continually threatened 
and stays on the move.

Not surprisingly, colonies with 
a quieter breeding female appear to rear young more successfully 
than colonies with a breeding female that acts continually threatened 
and stays on the move. Many captive colonies rear pups successfully for a time, but 
then their litter survival rates drop precipitously. One factor appear ­
ing to contribute to this decline is the absence of predation in captive 
colonies (Jarvis 1991). Without pr edation, a colony may grow large 
very rapidly and contain a dispr oportionately high number of young 
animals. The surplus of subadults (an ener getic class of individuals 
that often help care for pups) can result in over ­stimulation and ex­
cessive movement of pups, thus increasing their risk for trauma and 
other problems. Artifi­cial predation (the periodic r emoval of a few 
animals from a colony) can sometimes prevent a decline in a colony’s 
litter survival rate. This suggests that naked mole­rat colonies are 
adapted such that an average level of pr edation helps maintain an 
optimal balance of individuals of different ages and sizes in a colony. Many instances of rearing failures are unexplained. Application of Bowen Theory

Application of Bowen Theory
The facts that have been presented about naked mole­rats are 
consistent with a core concept in Bowen theory that the basic social 
group functions as an emotional unit. It is highly predictable in na­
ked mole­rat colonies that a change in the emotional functioning of 
one member is followed by compensatory changes in the emotional 
functioning of other members. As in human families, systems think­
ing is necessary to address the complex array of processes that con­
nect the functioning of the colony as a whole with the psychological, 
physiological and behavioral functioning of each member. Naked mole­rat colonies operate as if they are governed by 
 146 	 	 			 								 	Family 	SyStemS 	 	 									 	 					1998
the counterbalancing life forces of individuality and togetherness. Every action by an organism probably reflects the influence of both 
forces, but it appears the balance of the two forces can vary among 
species. Naked mole­rats, for example, appear to function with less 
individuality and more togetherness than human beings. These 
rodents exhibit some autonomy but, like the cells of a multicellular 
organism, directive signals received from other members of the unit 
(these si gnals are hypothesized to be part of the to geth erness process) 
largely control their activities.

text:
The togetherness force in naked mole­rat colonies manifests 
itself in many ways; for example, in a marked dependence of each 
individual on the group and a consequent group cohesiveness. To­
getherness processes are also evident in the synchronous functioning 
of colony members such as increased huddling, teat enlargement of 
all members, and heightened alarm r esponse when a reproductive 
female nears parturition. Furthermore, togetherness processes allow 
individuals to use the relationship system to regulate body tempera ­
ture and evaporative water loss. The togetherness force could play 
a role in the many cooperative behaviors of naked mole­rats such as 
digging teams, sharing food, and helping in the care of the young. This force seems central to group defense of the colony in that indi ­
viduals from the same colony band together to repel foreigners. The individuality of naked mole­rats is harder to discern than 
the togetherness processes, but, like the cells of a multicellular or gan­
ism, these rodents have some capacity to function autonomously and 
separately. One example of their individuality is the rapid r eproduc­
tive development of a nonbreeding female if she is r emoved from her 
colony. Relationship forces largely suppress her reproduction, but 
she r etains a r eproductive potential. In other words, she functions 
with less individuality within the “emotional fi­eld” of her colony 
than she does outside that fi­eld.

A nonbreeding female that moves 
into the functioning position of breeder transforms anatomically, 
physiologically, and behaviorally. One remarkable transformation 
is the shift from having no apparent inclination to pair ­bond as a 
nonbreeder to having the propensity, as a breeder, to form intense 
and often long­lasting emotional attachments with males. Another 
example of the effect of functioning position is an adult naked mole­
rat’s resuming growth following the death of one of the colony’s 
large defenders. An example of the impact of functioning position 
on development is the phenomenon of an average­sized adult act ­
ing as if he is a large animal because years earlier he had been the 
largest pup in his litter. All four patterns of emotional functioning described by fam ­
ily systems theory appear to exist in naked mole­rats. The pattern 
of emotional distance is most easily observed in solitary species of 
mole­rats where the young distance from one another and from their 
mother soon after weaning. Naked mole­rats live in such physical 
proximity that it may take a period of colony strife to make their use 
of emotional distance obvious. For example, in the colony that had 
two breed ing females, the reigning breed er and her mate co nsistently 
avoided areas in the burrow system where fi­ghting was most intense 
(Jarvis 1991).

Another area where chronic anxiety seems to have an impact on 
naked mole­rats is the suppression of GnRH in nonbreeding females. This may occur in the following way. The interaction between a non­
breeding female and the breeding female generates chronic anxiety 
because each animal per ceives the other as a threat, and they are in 
frequent contact. The anxiety gets bound in a dominant­subordinate 
interaction. The anxiety is bound in the sense that the nonbreeder’s 
subordinate posture calms the breeder and the consequent reduced 
aggressiveness of the breeder calms the nonbreeder. However, the 
dominant position (or perhaps the absence of subordinate behavior) 
is associated with GnRH production and reproductive maturity and 
the subordinate position is associated with GnRH suppression and 
reproductive immaturity. The concept of differentiation of self describes individual 
variation in levels of emotional functioning. Naked mole­rats lack 
the well­developed intellectual system that has an important role in 
differentiation in human beings, but these rodents still exhibit some 
individual variation in emotional functioning. One example is the 
difference between breeding females in how they preside over their 
colonies.

TIONARY BIOLOGY
Having reviewed some of the central ideas in both evolution ­
ary theory and Bowen theory, and having applied Bowen theory 
to naked mole­rats, the next question to address is whether Bowen 
theory describes important aspects about the functioning of emotional 
systems that current evolutionary theory either does not address 
or does not address adequately. The thesis to be developed here is 
that Bowen theory, particularly with its emphasis on relationship 
processes, addresses phenomena that are not presently emphasized 
by evolutionary theory but that can contribute to evolutionary 
theory. Furthermore, the complexity of the phenomena may of fer 
a challenge to evolutionary theorists to explain their evolution by 
natural selection.4
Three phenomena or emotional processes described by Bowen 
theory will be discussed. The fi­rst process is emotional programming. Emotional programming is an important process to consider for 
understanding the transmission of information across generations 
and it may also provide a link between role differentiation and level 
of differentiation. The second process, emotional regression , will be 
described in considerable detail because, of the three processes, it 
has the most obvious potential for extension to nonhuman species.

Emotional Programming in Human Families
Emotional programming occurs through the ongoing interac ­
tions parents and other family members have with a child during 
his developmental years. Some programming may occur during in­
trauterine development. Emotional programming appears to affect 
a child’s biochemical, physiological, psychological, and relationship 
functioning. Differences in the intensity of family triangles r esult 
in siblings being programmed dif ferently. In other words, parents 
typically focus more on one child than on the other(s). Chronic anx­
iety drives the more intense focus, not the reality needs of the child. Parents commonly say they are more involved with or worry more 
about one child because  that child has more problems or needs but 
miss how they unwittingly program the child to need more of their 
energy and attention. Their unrealistic needs for and expectations 
of the child pr ogram him to have unrealistic needs for and expecta­
tions of them. The pr ocess is anchored in the emotional system but 
includes complex feeling and psychological components. The more focused ­on child develops more of a “relationship ori­
entation” than his sibling(s). This means his functioning and ability 
to maintain a feeling of well­being (and accompanying physiological 
equilibrium) are more dependent on the approval, acceptance, and 
reinforcement of others than is the case with his sibling(s).

Multigenerational programming of levels of emotional attach­
ment may not occur in naked mole­rats in the way it does in human 
beings, but emotional programming as described in human beings 
may provide a link between a phenomenon that is evident in naked 
mole­rats, role differentiation, and level of differentiation. The hy­
pothesized link can be addressed by comparing the development 
of clinical dysfunctions in human families with the development of 
functional sterility in naked mole­rat colonies. The comparison is 
informative because the clinical dysfunctions are linked to level of dif­
ferentiation and functional sterility is a type of role differentiation. Role differentiation presumably evolves in the social units of 
a species because it is adaptive—its presence in the unit raises the 
average genetic fi­tness of the group’s members. The evolution of 
role dif ferentiation involves selection both of the traits that charac­
terize a particular role and of the relationship processes that regulate 
expression of the traits such that only a percentage of individuals in 
a social unit manifest them.

The different levels of social integration exhibited by the many 
species of mole­rats (taxonomic family Bathyergidae) illustrate that 
the evolution of role differentiation parallels the evolution of other 
social behaviors. The levels of social integration in mole­rats range 
along a continuum between the extreme of mole­rat species whose 
members live solitary existences, forcefully maintaining distance 
from one another, and the extreme of the naked mole­rat species 
 154 	 	 			 								 	Family 	SyStemS 	 	 									 	 					1998
whose members energetically affi­liate with one another. The more 
socially integrated a mole­rat species is, the more developed are its 
courtship, mating, pup care, and attachment behaviors, and its role 
differentiation (Jarvis and Bennett 1991). Hence the capacity to gen­
erate functionally sterile, nonbreeding females in naked mole­rat 
colonies has evolved along with other morphological and behavioral 
traits that render naked mole­rats more adaptive to their environ­
mental niche. The clinical dysfunctions that occur in a multigenerational 
family exhibit a wide range of severity and chr onicity, with some 
nuclear families that comprise a multigenerational family having a 
low incidence of serious clinical problems and others being awash 
with problems. The most serious dysfunctions tend to occur in the 
least differ entiated (least adaptive) nuclear families.

capacity is exceeded. Thus, from a Bowen theory perspective, clinical 
dysfunctions are a by-product of the adjustments individuals make to the 
anxious emotional milieu of their families. The idea that clinical dysfunctions are linked to adjustments 
human beings make to the emotional milieu of the family unit is 
similar to the idea of behavioral scaling  that Wilson (1975) describes in 
nonhuman species. Many species change their social interactions in 
response to increased population density. The changes are presum­
ably mediated by anxiety. At low density, individuals of the same 
species e xhibit little or no a ggressive b ehavior towards one a nother; at 
moderate density, they are more reactive to one another and display 
intermittent territorial d efense; at high de nsity, they exhibit sharp ter­
ritorial defense, but allow some joint occupancy of land under strict 
dominance hierarchies; and at extreme density, the system breaks 
down and “social pathology” emerges.

an emotional system. The loss is in functional level of differentiation, 
not in basic level of differentiation. Basic level refers to the adap­
tiveness of an individual or a family unit that is the outcome of the 
multigenerational transmission pr ocess. Once established during 
development, an individual’s basic level rarely changes. Functional 
level refers to the level of emotional functioning of an individual or 
family unit. Functional level can fluctuate widely depending on the 
level of chronic anxiety in a family system. It appears that relationship systems from cells to human soci­
eties are vulnerable to emotional regressions. The description that 
follows is of r egression in a two ­person system, a marital rel ationship. This is a less complex system than an entire family or society, but it 
appears to illustrate some of the basic processes involved in r egres­
sions of other relationship systems. The focus on a marital relation­
ship in isolation from the larger family and social context simplifi­es 
the discussion, but the narrow focus does not imply that a marriage 
is unaf fected by the relationship systems in which it is embedded.

text:
Regression in a Marital Relationship
Relationships exist in a state of balance  between the life forces 
of individuality and togetherness. When two people form a pair 
bond relationship, each automatically invests an equal amount of 
emotional energy in the other. The ener gy each person invests in 
the relationship is suffi­cient to promote a state of calm and sense 
of well­being in the other person; consequently, the relationship 
enhances the functioning of both people. Emotional ener gy that is 
not r equired to keep a r elationship in balance is available to people 
for the autonomous pursuit of other life goals. The balance of a relationship is a dynamic  process in that each 
person continuously and carefully monitors the other person and 
makes the adjustments necessary in his or her own communications 
and behaviors that keep the relationship in balance. For example, a 
wife invests more emotional energy in her husband in r esponse to 
perceiving discomfort in him; or, a wife r esponding to her own dis­
comfort behaves in a way that triggers an increase in her husband’s 
emotional investment in her. Despite being a dynamic equilibrium, 
the adjustments people make are so automatic and precise that, like 
basic level of differentiation, the basic  balance of a relationship usu­
ally does not change over time.

Emotional regression on a societal level can man ifest in a variety 
of symptoms and problems. One symptom of societal regression is 
greater instability in personal relationships; for example, a higher 
divorce rate and more single­parent families. Another symptom of 
a regression is individuals and institutions operating in more selfi­sh 
ways, emphasizing their “rights” over their responsibilities and not 
respecting the integrity of others. Paralleling the rise in selfi­shness 
by some is a rise in selflessness by others. The selflessness manifests 
in people acting unsure of themselves and yielding to selfi­shly mo ­
tivated pressure from others. One other common symptom is more 
splintering of society into “we­they” factions. Subgroups adopt 
more dogmatic positions and get polarized with other groups that 
have the “wrong” viewpoint.

similar in appearance and many aspects of nonsocial behavior, but 
they have very different social organizations. Prairie voles are highly 
affi­liative throughout their life span. Their affi­liative nature mani­
fests itself in the following ways. Pups become markedly distressed 
if separated from their par ents and socially isolated. Vir gin females

high levels of parental care. Prairie voles live in multigenerational 
family groups. In contrast, montane voles display little affi­liative 
behavior except during the postpartum period. Adults live in iso­
lated burrows and avoid other montane voles except to mate, which 
they do often and indiscriminately. Mothers nurse and care for their 
pups, but lose interest in the pups after weaning and abandon them. Males never see their of fspring. Pups show little distress in r eaction

viduality and togetherness do not necessarily indicate that they have 
evolved to dif ferent levels of emotional functioning. The reason for 
this conclusion is the observation in human beings that emotional 
reactivity increases to both individuality and togetherness threats as 
basic level of dif ferentiation decreases. In the two vole species, how­
ever, increased r eactivity to threats to one force appears balanced by 
decreased r eactivity to threats to the other force. Each species reacts 
to different stimuli, but each species seems equally reactive. Extending the individuality ­togetherness concept across species 
is similar to Gadagkar’s (1995) speculation that each entity compos­
ing any interactive group, from groups of self­replicating molecules 
to groups of warring nations, has both an “individual identity” and 
a “group identity,” the relative strengths of which affect the mix of

Whether social systems are described in terms of individuality 
and togetherness, individual identity and group identity, or integra­
tion and isolation, the evolution of differences between sp ecies in their 
social systems can perhaps be entirely explained by the selection of 
genes promoting either more social or more solitary existences. This 
view implies that the eusociality of naked mole­rats and honeybees 
arose de novo  in each of their phylogenetic lines from the selection 
of genes favoring sociality and other aspects of social integration. Biologists refer to similar evolutionary outcomes in distantly related 
species as convergent evolution. However, because emotional pro­
gramming plays such an essential role in producing the variations 
in individuality­togetherness balance within  the human species, it 
might also have a role in the evolution of dif ferences in social orga­
nization between  species. Some support for the idea that emotional programming plays 
a role in the differences in social organization between species may 
come from research by John B. Calhoun (1967). He created an exper­
imental condition that required rats to coor dinate their activities to 
obtain water. In the process of the rats having more social contact, 
they not only became more cooperative, but they exhibited much 
more social tolerance than before the experiment.

increased social tolerance might involve a relationship­induced ex­

In directing energy to 
address the external threat, the group members might relate fairly 
calmly to one another. Could calm and sustained contact gradually 
program the individuals both for more social tolerance (with associ ­
ated decreased reactivity to individuality threats) and more affi­lia ­
tive tendencies (with associated increased reactivity to togetherness 
threats)? The assumption in this scenario is that the capacities for 
social tolerance and affi­liation are inherent in the phylogenetic line 
of the species r esponding to the environmental change. That a species can shift from one type of social or ganization to 
another and that the shift can involve relationship system regulation 
of gene expression (for example, increased social contact “turning 
on” genes that control the expression of certain receptors in parts 
of the brain) are hypotheses consistent with current knowledge in 
biology. However, for the emotional programming of one generation 
to contribute directly to evolution and speciation, the programming 
has to be transmitted with fi­delity to future generations, a hypothesis 
that treads the borders of current knowledge in biology. The tran smission of programmed levels of emotional attachment 
in human beings is highly predictable, but most of this transmission 
appears to occur after a child’s birth. Prairie voles display affi­liative 
tendencies and social tolerance at birth.

birth. The transmission could occur in utero  (the programming of the 
parents somehow regulates the expression of genes in a developing 
fetus) or by some other yet undiscovered system. This attempt to extend the individuality ­togetherness concept to 
help explain the evolution of different social organizations in species 
poses questions, but draws no fi­rm conclusions. The principal reason 
for speculating about the possibility that emotional programming has 
a role in evolutionary change is that this system of multigenerational 
transmission described by Bowen theory is new to biology. Perhaps 
the concept of multigenerational emotional process can eventually 
be integrated with genetics in ways that are presently unimagined. CONCLUSION
The observations of naked mole­rats, social insects, cellular 
systems, mammals, and other life forms lead to the conclusion that 
Bowen theory describes emotional processes that are widespread in 
nature.

3COMPLEXITY, VARIABILITY, AND CHANGE IN 
SYMBIOTIC ASSOCIATIONS
Mary Beth Saffo, PhD 
Symbiosis—the intimate association between two or more spe -
cies—is a surprising biological phenomenon, because the presence, 
in all organisms, of defense mechanisms against “nonself” would 
seem to preclude the persistence of intimate, protracted interspe -
cies associations. Nevertheless, symbiosis is a very common way 
of life. This paper reviews several examples of this evolutionarily 
and ecologically important interaction, illustrates some of the com -
plexities of symbiosis dynamics, and introduces some questions and 
methodological issues of symbiosis research. Five generalizations 
about symbiotic dynamics are addressed: (1) The evolutionary conse -
quences of symbiosis often defy simple definition. (2) The dynamics 
of symbiotic interactions change over time. (3) Symbiotic life has 
a cost. The cost/benefit balance of symbiotic associations can be af -
fected by environmental changes. (4) The most important aspects 
of interspecies interactions may not be the most obvious ones. (5) 
Symbiotic interactions reflect both the conflicts and the connections 
between species individuality and species partnerships. Marriage is a far more complex 
collaboration than that of romance .

collaboration than that of romance . —Kathryn Harrison
A fundamental feature of being alive is the ability to distin-  
 guish between “self” and “nonself”—DNA, proteins, cells, or 
bodies of other genotypes or other species—and to isolate or de -
stroy such foreign material that makes its way into one’s body. The 
immune systems of vertebrates are particularly elaborate variants 
of such systems, but they are far from the only defense systems in 
nature: microorganisms, plants and invertebrate animals also pos -
sess chemical, antibiotic defenses against predators, competitors 
and pathogenic organisms. Even animals as different from humans 
as sponges have mechanisms which can distinguish with exquisite

But another widespread feature among organisms is symbiosis 
(Saffo 1992b), the “living together,” or intimate association, of two 
or more species, including antagonistic (parasitic, pathogenic), com -
mensal (beneficial to one partner, of apparently “neutral” effect to 
the other) and mutualistic (mutually beneficial) symbiotic associa -
tions. This species-togetherness is defined spatially by intimacy of 
structural contacts (attachments between cells of two species, or the 
habitation of one species inside the cells, organs or body cavities of 
another species) and temporally by consistency and length of inter -
action (interactions which always occur with a particular species 
or group of species, or persist for lengthy or crucial portions of the 
species partners’ life cycles). Given the universal presence of anti-”nonself” mechanisms 
among organisms, it is surprising that symbiotic associations exist 
at all. Yet symbiosis is everywhere. Why does symbiosis coexist with 
defense mechanisms against nonself? How does the prevalence of 
symbiosis affect the physiology and ecology of organisms, and how 
might it shape their evolutionary history? What can the complexi -
ties and varieties of symbiosis tell us about the nature and impact 
of interspecies interactions in general, or of interactions between 
individuals within a species?

The wide taxonomic and geographic distribution of symbiosis 
(Saffo 1991b, 1992a, 2001; Paracer and Ahmadjian 2000) provides 
evidence for the evolutionary importance and ecological impact 
of these associations, through the sheer number of species that are 
involved in such associations, and the impact these symbioses have 
on many ecosystems. All species are involved in symbiotic associations in some way; 
it can be further argued that most species on Earth may be obligately 
symbiotic in their way of life. Drawing from examples of antagonistic 
symbioses, many large taxonomic groups of invertebrate animals, 
 including tapeworms and flukes (two classes of flatworms), leeches (a 
class of annelid worms), several orders and suborders of nematodes 
(roundworms), an order of barnacles, numerous families and orders 
of insects, and at least four entire phyla (the largest taxonomic divi -
sion below that of kingdom) consist only of parasitic species (roberts 
and Janovy 2000).

Finally, all plant and animal species are hosts to a 
variety of parasitic or pathogenic symbionts, many of which show 
narrow host specificity; for these reasons, biologists have concluded 
that the species numbers of parasites and pathogens must exceed the 
species numbers of free-living species. To that number can be added 
the numerous species of commensal and mutualistic symbionts, some 
of which are noted below. mutualistic symbioses play key roles in many different ecosys -
tems and, like many parasitisms, are also often correlated with the 
radiation of a number of microbial, plant and animal taxa (margulis 
and Fester 1991). For instance, several microbial symbionts of plants 
provide crucial contributions to plant nutrition, with consequences 
to plant growth of global ecological and agricultural importance. Among these symbioses are mycorrhizae—fungi which inhabit 
the roots of most land plants—and nitrogen-fixing bacteria which 
inhabit the roots of legumes, alders and several other plant species. in addition to the very wide distribution of mycorrhizae among land 
plants, both molecular and fossil evidence indicate that mycorrhizal 
fungi have been associated with plants for about 400 million years, 
at or close to the same time as the first appearance of land plants 
in the fossil record (Smith and read 1997), suggesting in turn that 
mycorrhizal symbiosis might have been correlated with the earliest 
evolution of land plants (Pirozynski and malloch 1975).

Lichens, 
which are symbiotic associations between fungi and algae, are also 
important contributors to terrestrial ecosystems: although found at 
all latitudes, they are especially conspicuous colonizers of alpine 
and high latitude habitats. in the Arctic, lichens provide the main 
forage for reindeer, and they are the source of ninety percent of the 
photosynthetic productivity in the Antarctic (Saffo 1991b). Among animal hosts, the presence of symbiotic algae can allow 
hosts to live a plantlike life, relying on the photosynthetic activities 
of their algal symbionts as a major or main source of their organic 
food (Smith and Douglas 1987, Douglas 1994). Numerous aquatic 
invertebrates, including giant clams, soft corals, ”green” hydras, 
and several species of sea anemones, jellyfish, flatworms, and sea
