Because of the physical and ecological 
base provided by the algal-coral symbiosis, the plants and animals in 
coral reef communities form one of the most diverse and productive 
ecosystems in the world. microbial symbionts also assist animals who eat plants, espe -
cially those who specialize on the lowest-nutrient plant tissues, such 
as leaves, phloem and wood. microbes in animals as diverse as aphids, 
grain weevils, termites, surgeonfish, ruminants, horses, rabbits, koalas 
and kangaroos carry out cellulose digestion and produce carbon-rich 
fermentative products and nitrogenous compounds (including amino 
acids and vitamins), which allow their hosts to thrive on nutrient-lim -
ited plant diets (Saffo 2001). We omnivores also harbor an extensive 
microbial flora in our guts; though we do not depend on our gut 
microbes to the same extent as ruminants do, the usefulness of our 
“commensal” microbes is suggested not only by personal experiences 
of digestive discomforts following use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, 
but also by recent research (Hooper et al. 2001). All of the above examples document the nutritional benefits 
of many of the most ecologically important and best-known sym -
biotic mutualisms.

Symbiotic associations are intricate, complex, and variable 
associations, by many measures: in kinds of metabolic interactions, 
in degrees of structural and physiological intimacy and degrees of 
dependency between symbiotic species partners, in consequences of 
the symbiosis for the evolutionary success of each species partner, 
and in ecological context and impact of the symbiosis. Symbioses are, 
 quite literally, entanglements between species at many organizational

Lynn margulis (1993) has characterized symbiosis as a “para -
sexual phenomenon,” and, indeed, symbiosis resembles in many 
ways a “marriage” between two species. Like marriages, symbioses 
are a diverse category of relationships, varying from symbiosis to 
symbiosis in their internal dynamics, in the consequences of the 
association for the partners in the association, and in the factors 
which keep the association together. Both are long-term intimate 
relationships, with significant impact on the lives of the partners; 
both can shape, and be shaped by, the environment around them 
(interpersonal, social, and economic environments for human 
marriages, biological and physical environments for symbiosis); 
and both are shaped by their histories (family and interpersonal 
histories for marriages; developmental and evolutionary histories 
for symbioses). As international diplomats and family therapists 
could attest, human relations can rival the complexity of symbiotic 
associations, and the maintenance of long-term, productive associa -
tions can seem, in practice or in theory, a challenge both in marriage 
and in symbiosis (with symbiosis adding the extra evolutionary 
challenge of protracted physical contact between different spe -
cies). Finally, both present a challenge for study: understanding the 
dynamics of the many levels and intricacies of either interpartner 
or interspecies dynamics is a difficult, and sometimes seemingly 
intractable, enterprise.

Symbiotic species partnerships can also change over time. Trees 
are most commonly associated with ectomycorrhizal fungi (truffles 
and mushroom “fairy rings” around trees are the reproductive struc -
tures of ectomycorrhizal fungi). The roots of some trees associate 
with only a single species of fungus and maintain that association 
throughout their lives. other tree species, however, including beeches 
and pines, not only associate with more than one (sometimes even 
tens or hundreds) of fungal partners over their lifetime, but the com -
munity of fungal symbionts changes over time, generally increasing 
in species diversity as trees (and the forest communities of which 
they are a part) mature. interactions also change over larger-scale evolutionary time. Reflecting the widely held perspective that mutualism is a more 
“advanced” symbiotic association than parasitic or pathogenic 
interactions, biologists have often proposed that mutualism is the 
invariable end result of properly coevolved symbiotic partnerships. But, in fact, symbioses do not invariably evolve from “primitively” 
pathogenic associations to “advanced” mutualisms. Studies of chang -
es in pathogenic organisms and other symbioses over time suggest 
that interactions can evolve in virtually any direction: from virulent 
to less virulent, less virulent to more virulent, from antagonistic to 
mutualistic symbiosis, and from mutualistic or “benign” interactions 
to antagonistic ones (Saffo, 1991a).

SUICIDE: A FAMILY EMOTIONAL REGRESSION
Hal DeShong, PhD
When an individual suicides, an anxiety storm sweeps through the 
family system and overwhelms objectivity. In calmer moments, those 
involved perceive that many individuals and variables have played a part; 
but when the pressure is on, the seductive tendency is to explain what has 
occurred through reductionistic speculations and conclusions. Members 
of the family system are drawn toward blaming a person, a relationship, a 
substance, an event, or a simplistic combination of these. The interactive 
broader picture is lost in the effort to subdue enormous anxiety. Suicide, viewed from a Bowen systems perspective, is a manifestation 
of a family emotional system in disorder. This paper examines the facts in 
one family’s regressive emotional system. It is hoped that this examination 
will stimulate interest in the question:  If a family had a way of understand -
ing emotional process—how the functioning of each member influences 
the system, particularly how certain positions collect uneven portions of 
chronic anxiety, and how the functioning of each member either promotes 
or undermines this process—could a regression be slowed enough to reduce 
the lethality of the situation? Suicide defined
Suicide, as it is presented here, does not include such events as  
ritual suicide, acts or customs motivated by cultural and/or 
historical processes, or acts of suicidal terrorists.

particular ecosystem is conceptualized through understanding the 
competition between forms for occupation of niches, defined as “the 
function or position of an organism within an ecological community” 
(The American Heritage Dictionary 2000). A niche, therefore, is either 
a place for which an organism is best suited or fitted, or the pattern 
of relationships between organisms and their environment. A posi -
tion is defined by the pattern of relationships between a particular 
organism and its environment. from an ecological perspective, a human family can be thought 
of as an ecosystem, a biological community of interacting organisms 
and their physical world. As noted by Robert Wright,
 
. . . the environment of human evolution has been human (or 
prehuman) beings. . . . The evolution of human beings has 
consisted largely of adaptation to one another. (1994, 27)

a complicated process involving, among other interactive behaviors, 
cooperation, avoidance, exploitation, mutual affection, and acquiring 
an ability to know “which people warrant which sort of treatment, 
and when they warrant it.” (27)  A functioning position, generated

Robert H. Dysinger, MD was a co-investigator with Dr.Murray  
Bowen on a research project at the National Institute of Mental Health 
studying hospitalized families with a schizophrenic family member 
from the project’s inception in November 1954 through its termination 
in July 1959. His career path was within the Public Health Service. After the project ended he remained on staff at the National Institute 
of Mental Health until 1962. There were two other co-investigators 
on the project: Warren M. Brodey, MD and Betty Basamania, MSW. In the first year of the research, it was observed that a change 
in the emotional functioning of the schizophrenic offspring could 
be followed by physical problems in a parent. Initially a medical 
internist took care of the physical complaints of the family. But as 
the evidence grew that emotional problems and somatic problems 
could have something to do with the family relationships, several 
changes were made in operating procedures. These changes made 
it possible to more readily make use of the wealth of details from 
observing the families. The procedural changes were also made to 
assist families to understand and begin to solve their own problems 
better. In Dr. Bowen’s research, there was always an integration of 
hypothesis and therapy.

This is a part of a continuing clinical research project which 
began by undertaking to study intensively in a specifically designed 
treatment situation, three symbiotic mother-daughter relationships in 
which the daughter was schizophrenic. The treatment plan was based 
on the concept that the character problem underlying the psychotic 
symptoms is a dysfunction of a persisting intense mother-daughter 
symbiosis. The main features of the plan were a supportive indi -
vidual psychotherapy relationship of a specific kind for the mother, 
another for the daughter, and a living situation in which the mother 
was encouraged to take an active part in the hospital work with the 
daughter, including living on the ward herself if she wished. From

A central consideration was that for 
the observer action phenomena are definable as objective facts. A first step to explore this direction of study was the prepara -
tion of a chart on which the major action events of each day were 
recorded chronologically in columns headed mother-daughter rela -
tion, daughter-mother relation, staff-daughter and staff-mother rela -
tions. All available records were used to construct the chart. These 
included psychiatric notes, social work records, nursing notes and 
reports, and sound recordings of staff discussions. The review of the 
chart was valuable in achieving a perspective in which previously 
isolated clinical conceptions began to fall into place. Two steps were then taken to bring greater precision to the 
study. The first was to limit the scope of further detailed study to 
the mother-daughter relationship alone. Several considerations led 
to this. One was simply that the observations were more reliable in 
this area. It was considered also that a clarification of patterns of the 
family relationship would help define obscure transference-counter -
transference aspects of the staff-family relationships. Furthermore, 
it seemed the major forces governing the course of events were 
contained in the mother-daughter relationship and that staff rela -
tions to either were of secondary magnitude.

contained in the mother-daughter relationship and that staff rela -
tions to either were of secondary magnitude. So long as the focus of 
the study was on major patterns it was considered that study of the 
mother-daughter relationship as an isolated entity could be profitably 
done. The second step was an attempt to refine the conceptualization 
of action phenomena. Toward this end the concept of the “move” 
was developed. The term “move” is meant in a sense like that of common usage 
as when one says, “That was a good move,” or “It is his move now.” 
This usage is obviously related to the language of games, which has 
provided a valuable source of analogies for thinking in this way. Two kinds of moves were defined in detail for use in this study. These were approach moves and engaging moves. An approach

full answer would illuminate the biological mysteries of the mother 
infant relationship and its vicissitudes into later life. SUMMAR y AND CONCLUSIONS
A method was developed as a part of a clinical study of an 
intense symbiotic mother-daughter relationship which was helpful 
in working from a large volume of clinical observations toward a 
definition of some of the striking features and general characteristics 
of the relationship. The approach is described and its application in 
the study of one relationship is presented. Although the relationship 
discussed is the only one extensively studied in this way to date, the 
thinking that went into the method has been valuable in sharpening 
the clinical perception of gross and subtle moves and response in 
clinical work with other relationships. In general, the experience has been that the detailed study of 
the action phenomena served to focus and order significant events 
of those relationships, which although obvious in the clinical obser -
vations are very difficult to appreciate in any perspective. By first 
clearly distinguishing the moves from what is concurrently presented 
in other ways, it has been possible to develop a perspective of the 
move and response patterns over substantial periods of time.

Kathleen B. Kerr, MSN, MA
What a beautiful illustration of systems thinking research this 
paper is. With an unusual opportunity to continuously watch the 
behavior of an intense mother-daughter pair, the author was able 
to abstract patterns of behavior. Using the daily clinical records of 
the parties, he defined objective behaviors, such as the move, the 
approach, or the engagement. He ignored subjective data and fo -
cused on what people did, not what they said, thereby following the 
adage “actions speak louder than words.” As you read this paper 
you can almost see the researcher backing up from the subjectivity 
and detail to see broad recurring patterns of movement between 
the two. There is an excitement to his journey as he uncovered the 
skeleton of emotional process underneath the verbiage and detail. The recurrent cycle: mother approaches, daughter ignores and de -
mands, mother withdraws, daughter approaches, holds each captive. Neither evidences ability to bargain, negotiate, or set limits with the 
other. No resolution occurs.

text:
ADDRESSING CUTOFF IN RESIDENTIAL CARE OF 
DISTURBED ADOLESCENTS
Roberta M. Gilbert, MD
In our society, it is customary to remove children with severe emo -
tional or social problems from the home of parents who are abusive 
or neglectful. Medication, psychotherapy for parents and child, and 
residential treatment are the usual forms of intervention. Contact 
between parent(s) and child is restricted. Rarely is the functioning 
of the family emotional system addressed. Rarely are the problems 
in the child seen as a function of the relationships in the family. The 
author consulted to a residential facility for disturbed adolescent 
girls and reports here on dramatic improvements in the girls after 
she implemented ideas from Bowen theory that encourage contact 
with family to reduce emotional cutoff and improve functioning. BACKGROUND
Our society views some families as toxic. In them, children fail  
to thrive or become overtly ill in a variety of ways. When the 
children get far  enough from the norm in physical, emotional, or 
social symptoms, or when parental abuse or neglect comes to light, 
society’s way of trying to lend a hand is to remove them from the 
home. Various forms of intervention may be offered, including 
psychotherapy for both parent(s) and children, medication for the 
children, tutoring and, sometimes, continued residential treatment. Rarely, if ever, is the functioning of the family relationship system 
(the emotional unit) addressed.

(the emotional unit) addressed. Rarely are problems in the child 
seen as difficulties in the relationships in the family itself. Rather, 
when one person in a family is not doing well, that person is seen 
as having–or being–a problem. Professional attention is not focused 
on the relationships within the family emotional unit but on the 
individual with the problem. This individual is seen as a victim of 
various acts of omission or commission by parents who are seen as 
the cause of the problem. Murray Bowen began formulating the basis for a radically new 
way of conceptualizing the human in the 1940s. In what came to be

affects the other. Emotionally, individuals are not independent of 
each other. From that one postulate, several other major concepts 
derived (such as triangles, the importance of the multigenerational 
emotional heritage, the family projection process, societal process,

Therapists, in a neutral or “research” 
position try to learn from the family. They also try, partly by man -
aging themselves well and partly by applying the lens of theory 
to the situation,  to help the family function better. In the begin -
ning, efforts are aimed at lowering the anxiety level of the family. Anxiety’s effects in a family group are especially elaborated in 
Bowen theory. The movement of anxiety often crystallizes itself 
into one of several patterns that repeat over time. These are conflict, 
distance, cutoff, overfunctioning-underfunctioning reciprocity, and 
triangling. Cutoff, which can be seen as an extreme form of distance 
in a relationship, was important enough in Bowen’s thinking to be 
given the status of one of the eight formal concepts. Indeed, the 
powerful effect of emotional cutoff in human lives is observed on 
a regular basis by psychotherapists working from a perspective of 
Bowen family systems theory. Routinely, people are seen whose 
severe symptoms are lessened after bridging emotional cutoffs in 
their families. For this reason, Bowen theorists have decried the tendency in 
our society for societal agencies, while well intended, to take children 
out of their homes without addressing the effects of the separation 
and cutoff that may ensue. These agencies and helping profession -
als within them may actually add to the problems of the individuals 
they are trying to assist.

the staff intentionally tried to assist families and adolescent daughters

teenage homes were administered by a residential treatment center, 
at the edge of the city,  for disturbed children of all ages. Two of the  
group homes were in suburbs of the city. The center was a private 
nonprofit institution and funded by private donations, third party 
(insurance) payors and fees for service.

problems of helping disturbed girls to grow up in an institutional 
setting away from their families. A beginning understanding of Bowen family systems theory 
as applied to the group home seemed to indicate that consultant 
and staff were promoting cutoff between residents and their parents 
simply by following the norm in societal treatment guidelines. These 
guidelines indicate that when symptoms are severe and unmanage -
able by the parents, or when abuse is present, the children must be 
separated from the family. In this separation process, any institution 
is often at risk for developing a negative attitude toward the parents. With this polarization in place, however mild, it is understandable 
that no particular effort would be made to keep children in contact 
with families while in the care of the institution. As staff and consultant understood more Bowen theory and as 
they tried to take it seriously and apply it in the group home setting, 
several things became apparent:
(1)  In most cases, consultant and staff became convinced that 
the residents had become involved in a blame and cutoff pattern with 
their families. This attitude was endorsed, however insidiously, by 
staff. The attempt to learn a different, “systems” way of thinking 
highlighted our own blaming tendencies. We had been seeing  the 
parents as the problem.

serious acting out. Some of the parents were overtly rejecting and 
did not want to provide a home for the girls. Moreover, had they 
been discharged to home, serious cutoff would have, in many cases,

With this much clarity on the subject, consultant and director 
began to devise a plan to promote increased connectedness between 
residents and their families. Our hypothesis, drawn from Bowen 
family systems theory, was that if the teenage girls were in better 
contact with their families, they would do better. We were not sure 
how they would do better, but we thought that if we watched we 
might see some differences. We would explain the idea to the girls 
and, over time, to their parents. We would encourage residents to 
stay in better contact with their families through unlimited phone 
calls to them, letter-writing, and visits with family whenever they 
and the family could arrange them. If money was lacking for travel, 
we would provide it where trips would be needed. METHOD    
In the beginning we realized that some extra funds would be 
needed  to implement our plan. We brought our ideas to the adminis -
tration of the wider institution, proud of its “pro-family” posture. We 
explained, to the best of our ability, the theoretical base from which 
we were operating. Our plan was received well and supported.

explained, to the best of our ability, the theoretical base from which 
we were operating. Our plan was received well and supported. We 
were granted the needed funds for phone calls, bus trips, and even 
staff time to accompany people on trips to their family homes when 
parents were unable to visit. The staff explained to the residents that we believed that when 
people had more contact with family they did better in life. To that 
end, we asked them to write or call home at least once a week. Tele -
phone access would be provided whenever residents wanted to call 
parents. Bus tickets and chaperones for trips would be provided for 
girls to visit parents in other cities. Similar explanations were given 
to parents. Contacts between staff and parents did not change. VOL. 6, NO. 2       A DDRE SSING CUTO FF IN RESIDENTIAL CARE OF DISTURBED  ADOLE SCENTS           141

which it is actually better to cut off?”  In one family both mother 
and father had physically and sexually abused each of thirteen chil -

through the courts, found her way to the group home. Sometime 
later, her sister followed. The parents were both in jail in another

arranged by bus, with a staff member, on a periodic basis for the 
girls to see their parents. The girls, for their part, began cooperating by writing, phoning, 
and visiting home more often. If staff members noticed someone to 
be a bit behind in contacting family, they encouraged the resident 
to do a little more. OUTCOME
Within a few months after instituting the new policy of en -
couraging girls to increase their connections with their parents, 
the director described some interesting changes. There were 
noticeable differences for the better in the behavioral, physical, 
academic, and emotional symptoms of the residents. Delusions 
and hallucinations decreased. Depressive symptoms improved. Sleep improved. Grades in school went up for almost every girl. The phenomenon of the decline of mental and emotional symptoms 
was quantified by the author who was prescribing medications. In almost every case, doses of medications went down from what 
they had been at the beginning of the study and for some were 
discontinued. Occasionally a girl would become more disturbed after a visit 
or an intense phone call. But these disturbances were short-lived, 
less intense, and more easily managed than those we had been deal -
ing with before the project began.

ourselves how more contact with parents had led to such a positive 
outcome in the lives of the girls and of the home itself. The author, 
steeped in analytic theory, asked why, wanting to interpret. Why 
would making more frequent contacts with family—most of them 
intense, “disturbed” families—make such  a difference? We tried to 
use old theory to explain what new theory had directed.

Why 
would making more frequent contacts with family—most of them 
intense, “disturbed” families—make such  a difference? We tried to 
use old theory to explain what new theory had directed. One of the 
favorite explanations for the phenomenon we had observed went 
as follows:  The girls, without adequate contact with their parents, 
fantasized them to be either angels whom they missed intensely or 
devils with whom they were ashamed to be associated and whom 
they blamed for all their troubles. In either case, the fantasy produced 
a great deal of anxiety leading to acting-out behavior and emotional, 
social, or academic problems. When they actually made contact 
with their real, human parents, the need for fantasy was gone. They 
could deal, we thought, with the reality of their parents—even those 
in jail—better than the fantasies, exaggerated versions of who their 
parents really were. In retrospect, however, that explanation was 
probably only one sign of the author’s recent association at that time 
to psychoanalytic theory and its propensity for asking “why” and 
then constructing intrapersonal, individually based “explanations” 
or interpretations for the answers. With more experience in “thinking systems,” there was an al -
ternative way of seeing what took place in the home that was more 
consistent with Bowen family systems theory. That was to simply 
observe that  cutoff increases anxiety. Increased anxiety is associated with 
symptoms of various sorts.

diagram. They noticed several relatives that were potential contacts 
for this girl. They encouraged her and supported her in her efforts 
to contact as many of them as possible. One member of her family was a great aunt who lived across 
the state. This aunt was especially receptive to the overtures of the 
resident (and sometimes the staff on her behalf). The aunt came to 
visit. It turned out that she had always wanted to have children but 
had never married and so had none. The child and the great aunt 
made friends. There were visits back and forth by the child to the

positive about the relationship. The girl's symptoms of schizophrenia disappeared and her

LESSONS FROM THE OTHER TWO GROU P HOMES
There were two other group homes in the same system to which 
the author consulted. Lessons learned there may not have been as 
dramatic but they were as real. In the second home, where girls with conduct disorders tended 
to be placed, the parents were often available for staff meetings. In these situations, with the symptom-bearer cut out of the family 
emotional system, if only temporarily, what could we see? Here, it 
could be seen most often that when, by virtue of the parents’ fatigue 
(deriving from their own over-focus, inconsistencies with the child, 
and their marital relationship problems) and society’s removing the 
 144                                   FAMILY  SYSTEM S                                                  2003
child from the situation, the parental focus on that particular child 
was lessened. In that circumstance the conflict of the parents could 
easily be seen. It was most often played out in the rearing of their 
child. If one parent would impose a consequence for behavior, the 
other would undercut it. If one parent said “no” the other would 
play the rescuer and say “yes.”  If and when the parents began to 
work on and resolve their problems with each other, the child’s 
conduct improved. Diminution of symptoms and discharge usually 
soon followed. The remaining group home offered still other lessons.

soon followed. The remaining group home offered still other lessons. There, 
when a child was cut off or out of the family system by being ad -

focus move to another child in the family. The next child to draw 
the parental focus was usually the next one in age to the admitted 
one. It was not unusual for one child in a family to be discharged 
home, only to admit the next one in the family, who apparently had 
drawn the focus during the admission of the first one. In each of the group homes there seemed to be at least one 
resident who was overly focused on the problems of the others. She 
would take their problems on herself, try to solve them, and worry 
excessively about them. The staff’s understanding of this pattern 
and pointing it out to the person repeatedly was to no avail. It 
could often be seen that the girl had a similar position in her family, 
often an outcome of underfunctioning parents who had placed her 
in charge. Sometimes, of course, the child herself seemed to be the 
object of an intense focus, seeming to have taken on from her parents 
this way of relating. CONC LUSIONS AND I MPLI CATIONS FOR

tives, ideas derived from Bowen family systems theory. Some of the 
lessons learned are as follows:
(1)  Society’s first impulse, when a family symptom becomes 
intense, is to remove the symptomatic person from the family. This 
is so much a part of human reactivity as to be almost at the level 
of reflex. It is an intervention to which we as a society have given 
little thought. (2)  In many instances, if there had been trained and experi -

would need to be removed from their homes less frequently. Where 
separation was still necessary, Bowen theory-guided therapy with 
parents could be expected to make it possible for the child to return 
home earlier than is now the case. (3)  When children are removed from their homes, parents are 
usually seen by society as “bad parents”— abusive or neglectful of 
the child in some way. Blame of the parents is routine. (4)  As society’s agents, caretakers rarely stay emotionally neu -
tral. If the parents are seen as abusive or neglectful, traditional logic 
dictates less contact between parents and child rather than coach -
ing in family relationships. Therefore, when children are removed 
from their homes by societal agencies, cutoff between parents and 
children is usual.

little more than common sense. However, Bowen theory is actually 
counterintuitive on several points. The concept of cutoff is one. Common sense in our culture says that in cases involving abuse, 
neglect, suicide, or risky behavior endangering life, better break the 
family up and find surrogate parents—the children will be better off 
in the long run. Bowen theory points out, against common sense, 
that if people are yanked out of significant family relationships, their 
anxiety will escalate and their problems will actually intensify. (6)  The group home experience indicates that removal of chil -
dren from their homes and subsequent promotion of cutoff between 
the generations is not the best approach. When possible, the better 
way is to “think systems” and let Bowen theory be the guide. Even 
though families may be separated, it is possible to avoid emotional 
cutoff between parents and children in residential treatment. In this 
project, emotional cutoff was reversed by promoting letter-writing, 
phone calls, and family visits. Use of internet e-mail could conceiv -
ably be used in the same way. (7)  Economically, many institutions might balk at the budget -

FAMILY PSYCHOTHERAPY IN OFFICE PRACTICE 
Murray Bowen, MD
introduced by
Ruth Riley Sagar, MA 
Catherine Murphy Rakow, MSW
INTRODUCTION
From his earliest years of practice, Dr. Bowen had an interest in 
families. While at the Menninger Foundation (1946-1954), he departed 
from common practice and had contact with families, sending them 
monthly updates on their ill family member, having a social worker 
meet with the families, and involving families in treatment planning. He also used different therapy approaches to assess their effectiveness 
and to develop comparison groups for research purposes. The “in-residence” family research project at NIMH (1954-
1959) provided the laboratory for the observation that the fam -
ily is an emotional unit. This idea guided the research and the 
method of therapy that developed from it. Eleven families lived 
in the hospital for extended periods of up to three years, and eight 
families were seen on an outpatient basis. Once it was possible 
to see the patterns of emotional interdependence in the research 
families, it was possible to extend these observations to all families. Dr. Bowen's  presentation of his work with families from his clinical 
practice was made in 1961, almost two years after the NIMH project 
had ended. In this presentation he describes how difficult it is for 
a family member to change and the influence on the system when 
even a small change occurs.

This manuscript was found among a small collection of admin -
istrative, clinical, and meeting files that had traveled with Dr. Bowen 
from his first office on the Georgetown campus. The rediscovery of 
this manuscript in the Bowen Library offers an opportunity to see 
the evolution of Dr. Bowen's thinking and to  sense the excitement 
of the discoveries he was making about families. ABSTRACT
This paper will describe some experiences with family psychotherapy 
for a wide range of problems treated in the office practice of psycho -
therapy. The starting point was a formal family research project in 
which fathers, mothers, and normal siblings lived on a research ward 
with psychotic patients in a continuing “in residence” observation 
and treatment situation. A few months later, I began using it with 
an increasing number of families in my part-time private practice. The research provided the ideas, and the practice provided clini -
cal experience with different kinds of problems. In five years, this 
method of family psychotherapy was used with ninety-four families, 
for problems ranging from those with an overtly psychotic family 
member to those with fairly simple neurotic problems.

How 
does one conceptualize an intrafamily psyche? In 1955-56 we used 
a term for it that was later dropped because it was not completely 
satisfactory. Recently I have come back to it as a term that conveys, on a 
descriptive level, a fairly accurate notion of the concept. It is the 
term undifferentiated family ego mass. According to the concept, cer -
tain children differentiate themselves almost completely from the 
“family ego mass,” developing well-defined autonomous “selfs.”  
This is synonymous with our familiar concept of a “mature person” 
or a person with a strong ego. Especially important is their ability 
to function as contained emotional units. This person would marry 
a spouse with an equal level of ego development. They could be 
emotionally close without either one losing self or without the 
obliteration of ego boundaries between themselves. Children who 
later become psychotic are examples of those who achieve least dif -
ferentiation of self. They function as extensions of the family ego 
mass. They might separate themselves from the family and function 
as dependent attachments to others who will guide and direct them. They might have so little “self” that they collapse in psychosis when 
they attempt to function autonomously. Children who later become 
parents of psychotic children are among those who achieve poor 
levels of differentiation of self.

Children who later become 
parents of psychotic children are among those who achieve poor 
levels of differentiation of self. They do not “grow away” from the 
“family ego mass.”  Instead, after reaching physical maturation, they 
“tear” themselves away, maintaining a kind of pseudo-separateness 
from the family by means of angry rebellion or distant indifferent 
positiveness. They function satisfactorily in business and intellectual 
pursuits,  but when such a person marries a spouse with equally 
poor ego differentiation, they immediately find themselves “fused” 
in a new “undifferentiated family ego mass” with its characteristic 
over-dependence, over-distance, and emotional turmoil. Children 
who later become parents of neurotic children are among those with 
higher levels of ego differentiation. There are a variety of ways that 
this husband-wife “family ego mass” attempts to resolve its problems. They may remain appended to one of the old family ego masses; they 
may establish a network of new, less intensive interdependencies; or

For our original research project, we chose families with 
one maximally impaired schizophrenic offspring that had lived in 
geographical separation from the parents' own families. There are 
definite patterns to the way the husband and wife deal with the prob -
lem within the new ego mass. When they are emotionally close they 
“fuse into each other,” experiencing conflict and “loss of identity.”  
They keep sufficient emotional distance for each to maintain a fairly 
workable level of “self.”  For this we have used the term emotional 
divorce . Resolution of the parental conflict goes in one of two opposite 
directions. The conflict may remain largely between the parents with 
comparatively little involvement of the children, or the conflict may 
transmit itself to one or more children with relatively less problem 
between the parents. However, in practical terms, there is almost 
always some degree of involvement in both parents and children. In 
these ninety-four office practice families, the principal problem was 
in the child in forty-nine percent, and between the parents in fifty-
one percent. There were those in the middle of the scale in which 
it is hard to determine the location of the principal problem. When 
children are involved, it is characteristic for one child to be maximally 
involved, leaving the others relatively less involved.

theoretical basis from which the psychotherapy evolved. I believe 
psychotherapy is profoundly influenced by the way the therapist 
views man and his struggles, and particularly by the therapist's 
theoretical concept of the nature of the problem he is treating. For 
instance, a therapist who views the problem as a product of early 
maternal deprivation will think , be, and act differently than a therapist 
who sees the problem in another way. Whether this concept proves 
valid or profitable as a way of viewing family problems, it has been 
used as a thinking model for this method of family psychotherapy, 
and for that reason, it is included here. The intrafamily psyche, 
or the “undifferentiated family ego mass,” is an undifferentiated 
amalgamation of emotional selfs that occurs when these people with 
poorly defined ego boundaries are in a living interdependence with 
each other.

Now to a brief summary of family psychotherapy with a psy -
chotic offspring. Functionally, the child is “welded” into the ego gap 
between the parents and he functions there, as an ego “nothing,” to 
permit the parents to be an ego “something,” until the passing years 
and his own growth make this into an untenable resolution. As I see 
it, the phenomenon is no one's fault,  and there is no malevolence 
or chicanery involved. Given this particular situation between the 
parents and a child, consciously or unconsciously conceived to fill 
this gap, the triadic union is consummated just as automatically as 
the force that causes the sunflower to always keep its face to the sun. It occurs in spite of conscious forces to oppose it, just as the alcoholic 
gets another drink in spite of conscious resolutions to the contrary. When psychosis erupts, the functioning of the triad is disrupted. There are powerful forces to restore triadic equilibrium, as well as 
growth forces to differentiation and separation. An example was a 
family with a withdrawn, psychotic daughter. After a year of family 
psychotherapy, the daughter became a vigorous, aggressive par -
ticipant in family life. This seemed to be a hopeful change, but the 
change caused anxiety in the parents. They had her institutionalized 
and tranquilized.

Shelly Fine, MASc
Neither a man nor a crowd nor a nation can be trusted to act humanely or 
to think sanely under the influence of a great fear. – Bertrand Russell     
There is much debate about the origins and perpetuation of the Israeli-
Palestinian conflict. With all the deep-seated emotional issues that 
are triggered it is almost impossible to come up with an objective 
understanding of the issues involved. People and countries seem 
to take sides and focus on what is wrong with the other rather than 
try to understand this phenomenon as an emotional process that 
much of the world contributes to and sustains. This paper will use 
Bowen theory to suggest that the Israelis and the Palestinians, in 
their chronic anxiety, have become locked in an overfunctioning/
underfunctioning reciprocity which has been reinforced by the 
triangling of, primarily, Britain, Russia/Soviet Union, other Arab 
entities, and the United States. As a result, none of the parties 
have been able to think rationally about what is best for the long 
term. They stay stuck in an emotional process from which they have 
not been able to extricate themselves. During times of increased 
societal stress, this process produces symptoms in the form of the 
terrorism we see today.

a previous paper (Fine 2006) I examined this conflict up until World

will focus more extensively on the time period from World War I to

Arab entities, Britain, France, the United States, and Russia/the 
Soviet Union, all of whom intervened in this dyadic conflict out of 
their own anxious interests, contributed to this emotional process, 
intensifying and perpetuating the problem. Bowen theory suggests that, like a marital couple under stress, 
two groups experiencing high chronic anxiety (threat, whether real 
or imagined) and low levels of differentiation of self (the ability to 
separate thinking based on principle and fact from thinking based 
on fear) are likely to come into conflict when they confront a threat to 
their survival. This threat can come in the guise of scarce resources, 
such as limited land or water, or from fear of attack or competition. The parties manage their differences with distance but, as the threats 
multiply, their relationship becomes polarized and various postures 
are taken to deal with the ever-increasing differences. This can take 
the form of conflict, projection onto a third party, or an overfunction -
ing/underfunctioning reciprocity. Once these processes are activated, 
the groups are not able to consider the threats realistically and take 
action based on the facts and for the common good. Dr. Murray Bowen provided a comprehensive theory about fam -
ily functioning that can be extended to explain this kind of societal 
process.

Dr. Murray Bowen provided a comprehensive theory about fam -
ily functioning that can be extended to explain this kind of societal 
process. In fact, Bowen said that “the study of the family provided 
a completely new theoretical dimension for conceptualizing the 
total human phenomenon” (Bowen 1978, 269) and he believed that 
the “greatest gain from the family movement would come, not from 
family therapy, but as the basis of new theories about man and his 
efforts to adapt.” (Bowen 1978, 269) 
In the case of the Zionists and the Palestinians, the overriding 
pattern was and continues to be an overfunctioning/underfunction -
ing reciprocity. Throughout the various time periods in the Middle 
East, such as the expansion of the European presence in the Ottoman 
Empire, the British Mandate after World War I, the Cold War, and 
presently United States predominance, the Jews, in their insecurity, 
became overresponsible, acting like they knew what to do and how 
to do it; reciprocally, the Palestinian Arabs, in their insecurity, took

It occurred to Bowen that societies tend toward progression or 
regression just as families do, and he demonstrated the latter in his 
study of delinquency in society (1978, 275-276). With his personal 
knowledge of public officials, an examination of newspaper articles 
on the national scene, and file-keeping on the principal people who 
made landmark decisions, Bowen noticed that just as the number of 
families who were becoming overly permissive with their delinquent 
children was increasing, there was also a higher incidence of this 
same behavior in society (1978, 275). He demonstrated a definite 
similarity between the functional differentiation of “permissive” 
parents as they dealt with their delinquent children and the func -
tional differentiation of society, as it, too, dealt, comparably, with 
these same behavior problems. Bowen believed this regression is propelled by periods of 
prolonged stress in families and in society where people’s need for 
“togetherness” outweighs their need for “individuality.”  What are 
the togetherness/individuality forces?

“The togetherness forces are 
derived from the universal need for ‘love,’ approval, emotional close -

other to keep the peace or to gain approval. The individuality force, 
on the other hand, is “derived from the drive to be a productive, 
autonomous individual as defined by self rather than the dictates 
of the group” (Bowen 1978, 277), allowing for rational and creative 
thinking for the long term. Under sustained anxiety, the togetherness 
forces outweigh the individuality forces to produce an “increase in 
decisions designed to allay the anxiety of the moment, an increase 
in cause-and-effect thinking, a focus on ‘rights’ to the exclusion of 
‘responsibility,’ and a decrease in the overall level of responsibility.” 
(Bowen 1978, 279)  The effect on society is that “individuality is 
submerged, decision-making ability is lost, viable members desert 
the group, and there is overwhelming emotional reactivity, violence, 
and chaos.” (Bowen 1978, 278)  This “prolonged increase in societal 
anxiety can result in a gradual lowering of the functional level of

the human’s increasing consciousness of acting in conflict with na -

product of the population explosion, the disappearance of new 
habitable land to colonize, the approaching depletion of raw 
materials necessary to sustain life, and growing awareness 
that “spaceship earth” cannot indefinitely support human life 
in the style to which man and his technology have become 
accustomed. (Bowen 1978, 272)
 
The origins of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in the late 1800s and 
early 1900s seem to be related to similar fears for survival, but more so 
about the fear that one’s family, religion, or group might not endure 
the changes that were occurring in society. With the fragmentation 
and decline of the Ottoman Empire that had controlled the area of 
Palestine for the previous 400 years, the Europeans, the Jews, and 
the Arabs all viewed themselves as in contention for their share of 
the same region. Under this kind of sustained anxiety, groups made 
decisions based on their own short term goals to the exclusion of the 
goals of others. This kind of automatic reactivity and inability to work 
together has continued until today. In the present day, fear for the 
survival of the group is intensified by the same problems described 
by Bowen.

survival of the group is intensified by the same problems described 
by Bowen. For instance, there are some very real issues fueling the 
conflict such as “huge population growth, intensive agriculture, 
insensitive urban planning, road-building on a vast scale, and the 
development of an industrial economy” which have all wreaked 
havoc on the ecology of Palestine (Wasserstein 2003, 73). It is difficult to grasp the origins of the difficulties between the Jews 
and the Christians, but it seems apparent that their relationship has been 
characterized by a type of “marital conflict” whereby the Christians, in 
times of societal stress, saw the Jews, in their difference, as a threat and 
thereby victimized them. The Jews, reciprocally, saw the Christians 
as a threat, felt victimized and apparently insulated themselves. This

dilemma they are in and negotiate productively (Zittrain-Eisenberg 
and Caplan 1998, 20). Bowen theory, likewise, would imply that two parties in a dis -
pute will have added trouble working out their differences when 
others are taking sides. This kind of triangling prevents the kind 
of objectivity that is needed for two groups to calm their reactivity 
enough to think more reasonably about their actions. Bowen stated 
that conflict between two people will resolve automatically if both 
remain in emotional contact with a third person who can relate 
actively to both without taking sides with either and remaining  
emotionally detached (Bowen, 1978, 174-5). Bowen also believed 
that this person would have to be “sure of self on all life principles 
that involve himself and his family,” have “the courage to take action 
on his convictions,” and devote “primary attention to becoming the 
most responsible possible person” (Bowen 1978, 449) so that if the 
participants become anxious and reactive, he can continue to stay 
committed to his principles and connected to both parties.

 and The neurobiology of aTTachMenT  
and sTress reacTiviTy
Robert J. Noone, PhD
Progress toward a science of human behavior requires the development 
of theory and concepts which can be subjected to testing. This testing 
of rich concepts and theories entails observation, comparative analysis, 
and research from a range of fields of investigation. The concept of 
the multigenerational transmission process in Bowen theory is a 
testable concept, and findings from the fields of the neurobiology of 
attachment and stress reactivity are presented in this context. These 
areas of research focus on the limbic-HP A system and provide some 
initial support for: (1) how family interactions can have such profound 
effects on development; (2) how such effects might vary among siblings; 
and (3) how they can be transmitted nongenomically over multiple 
generations. In particular, the research in these areas indicates that 
behavioral interactions in the maternal-offspring relationship can 
significantly influence the neuroendocrine and behavioral development 
and adaptiveness of individuals. Central to science is the development of formal concepts which 
attempt to account for observable phenomena in nature. As the 
evolutionary biologist Ernst Mayr states:  
The contribution made by new concepts or by the more or less 
radical transformation of old concepts is equally and often 
more important than facts and their discovery.

comprise his systems theory of the human family. The development 
of this concept was based on research and related to the question of 
how to account for individual differences in the basic adaptiveness1

change significantly in just one generation. Slight variations which 
appear to be based on family interactions do, however, occur which

in characteristics as basic as height, weight, and intelligence. Bowen observed that variations in basic adaptiveness, which ap -

directly. The Family history Data Base Project, being developed at the

hPA reactivity. The release of oT has been found to have a dampen -
ing effect on anxiety and stress reactivity (Carter 2003). Oxytocin and 
its receptors have been found to be influenced by social experience, 
especially early in development. This influence continues in adult -
hood as positive social interactions have been found to release oT 
(Uvnas-Moberg 1998). The physiology of primates and other mammals is highly re -
sponsive to the relationship environment. They also seek to regulate 
this responsiveness through the use of relationships. This is most 
evident early in development when the proximity or presence of 
the caretaker is central to an offspring’s responsiveness to perceived 
threat or novelty (Gunnar 2005). For humans and other primates, the 
use of relationships to regulate their physiological responsiveness 
continues throughout the life course in varying degrees. In the human family, members can be seen as engaged in an 
ongoing process of regulating states of tension and calm by means of 
relationships. Parents serve not only to regulate such states in their 
children but reciprocally regulate their own physiology through 
caretaking.

Parents serve not only to regulate such states in their 
children but reciprocally regulate their own physiology through 
caretaking. The concepts of the triangle and nuclear family emotional 
process in Bowen theory describe how this process functions, and the 
multigenerational transmission process describes how this process 
plays out over the generations. It hypothesizes that there will be varia -
tion among siblings in the degree to which the principal caretaker 
or caretakers rely on them for their own physiological regulation. The degree to which a child serves this function will determine the 
degree to which he or she emotionally separates from the family and 
the degree to which he or she will rely on or avoid relationships for 
self-regulation. This process is seen as determining basic adaptive -
ness throughout the life course. It is posited that, among siblings, 
variation in this process is transmitted into the next generation and, 
over the course of generations, will lead to a wide range in the basic 
adaptiveness of descendants. CoNCluSIoN

neurobiology of attachment and stress reactivity suggest they will 
play a central part in testing the concept of the multigenerational 
transmission process. Current research in this area provides support

101EMOTIONAL NEUTRALITY AND THE QUEST FOR PEACE: 
NORTHERN IRELAND AS A CASE STUDY
Stephanie J. Ferrera, MSW
   
Emotional neutrality or de-triangling as defined in Bowen theory is 
a basic principle of family psychotherapy. The question addressed 
here is what application this principle may have to larger systems. Large-scale conflict is driven primarily by emotional process, a 
process that operates in communities and whole societies much as it 
does in families. Escalating conflict puts pressure on a community 
or a society to intervene. Intervention often involves the use of 
force, with the possibility of calming a disturbed system but also 
with the risk of further escalating conflict. Northern Ireland was a deeply divided society from the time of its 
creation in 1921 until recently. In a decades-long peace process, 
the people of Northern Ireland have found ways to resolve their 
differences through negotiation rather than violence. In Paths to 
a Settlement in Northern Ireland, Farren and Mulvihill studied  
this remarkable change from the perspective of Bowen theory . They 
propose that shifts in key relationships, particuarly Britain’s move to 
a neutral position, were the essential changes that freed the Northern 
Ireland communities to find their own way to peace. DEFINING NEUTRALITY
Emotional neutrality was defined by Murray Bowen as the 
ability to be in contact with disharmony without taking a 
side.

text:
DEFINING NEUTRALITY
Emotional neutrality was defined by Murray Bowen as the 
ability to be in contact with disharmony without taking a 
side. Bowen’s concept of emotional neutrality, as defined in theory 
and practiced in psychotherapy and in life, is significantly different 
from the conventional understanding of neutrality. Webster offers 
several definitions of neutrality: not taking part in either side of a 
dispute or war; without strongly marked characteristics; indefinite; 
indifferent; middling. Emotional neutrality is none of these things. Rather it is a way of functioning in an emotional field of tension. Such 
functioning requires that one stay outside the tension while actively 
relating to those who are involved in it, and that one understand the 
problem with a systems perspective that goes beyond blame. Ms. Ferrera is in private practice in Oak Park, Illinois and on the faculty of the Center 
for Family Consultation in Chicago. © Georgetown Family Center, 2011
 102             F amily SyStemS                        2011
Bowen noted that the stances of “That’s not my problem” or 
“I’m not getting into it” were indicators of emotional reactivity, not 
emotional neutrality. The connotation of passiveness or indifference 
is especially antithetical to Bowen’s concept of emotional neutrality.

text:
The connotation of passiveness or indifference 
is especially antithetical to Bowen’s concept of emotional neutrality. Michael Kerr notes: “Neutrality does not mean fence-straddling or a 
wishy-washy posture toward life problems.” (Kerr and Bowen 1988, 
111)  One can have clear positions on the issues in a family or society 
and still be emotionally neutral. EMOTIONAL NEUTRALITY
A basic principle in this theoretical-therapeutic system is 
that the emotional problem between two people will resolve 
automatically if they can remain in contact with a third person 
who can remain free of the emotional field between them, 
while actively relating to each. (Bowen 1978, 251)
In this carefully crafted statement, Dr. Bowen defines emotional 
neutrality or de-triangling as the key to therapeutic change. “Actively 
relating to each” means keeping the right degree of emotional distance 
and emotional contact, knowing what to say, and balancing serious -
ness with humor. What the third person brings is not an answer to 
the problem between the two, but a way of relating that improves 
their chances to calm down, think, and find their own answers. The neutral one, being non-reactive or at least less reactive than the 
involved persons, is freer and more flexible, more able to see both 
sides, and more able to engage others on a thinking level.

The neutral one, being non-reactive or at least less reactive than the 
involved persons, is freer and more flexible, more able to see both 
sides, and more able to engage others on a thinking level. Lowering 
reactivity and enhancing thinking is what makes the resolution of 
the problem possible, or even, as Bowen asserted, “automatic.”
CONFLICT AS EMOTIONAL PROCESS
From a systems perspective, conflict is defined as reactivity to 
differences. Differences per se  do not create conflict. Under calm 
conditions, people live with differences and much of the time handle 
disagreements with good will and good humor. Kerr notes:
  
People do not have trouble getting along because of issues. These issues tend to bring out the emotional immaturity of 
people, and it is that immaturity, not the issues, that creates 
the conflict. (Kerr and Bowen 1988, 188)
 Vol. 8, N o. 2            emotioNal  Neutrality  aNd the QueSt For Peace          103
On a continuum, conflict ranges from mild to moderate to intense, 
based less on the issues in play than on the levels of maturity of the 
people involved. Relatively minor issues can generate intense conflict 
while more serious issues may be managed with only mild conflict. At the mild level of conflict, people are somewhat reactive but 
still calm enough to hear one another, exchange information, and 
access thinking. As ideas and information are exchanged, creative 
thinking allows for problem solving. Jokes and endearments are 
possible.

As ideas and information are exchanged, creative 
thinking allows for problem solving. Jokes and endearments are 
possible. The engagement reduces tension, and the ability to see 
solutions brings a sense of success, underscoring trust and confi -
dence in the relationship. Mild-level conflict is an anxiety-binding 
mechanism that actually works to reduce anxiety. At the moderate level, reactivity is higher and thinking is more 
difficult. More energy goes into attacking and defending; there is 
more right-wrong polarization, overseriousness and overperson -
alization. Without a strong effort to manage reactivity, people can 
easily move into escalation or will end their contact with reactive 
distancing and triangling. At the intense level, reactivity is near or at the point of people 
losing control over their behavior. Emotion dominates thinking so 
that the intellectual system is more geared to winning than to finding 
an accord with the opponent. Polarization is intense and people see 
little room to move. There is a sense of stalemate, discouragement, 
and loss of confidence in the relationship, as well as increasing danger 
that the conflict will spread. LARGE-SCALE CONFLICT
Every conflict in history is unique and deserves to be understood 
in its own historical and cultural context, with its own set of facts:  
people, places, issues, events.

LARGE-SCALE CONFLICT
Every conflict in history is unique and deserves to be understood 
in its own historical and cultural context, with its own set of facts:  
people, places, issues, events. On the other hand, stripped of the 
myriad detail that makes each conflict unique, it is possible to observe 
an underlying emotional process that is common to all. National and international relations are magnitudes more com -
plex than family relationships, yet from the perspective of emotional 
process they are families writ large. All of the anxiety driven patterns 
that Bowen observed in families are involved in large-scale conflict. Reciprocal grievances, blame, attack, defense, and retaliation drive 
people to increased polarization. Through triangling, more people 
are drawn into the conflict. The result is side-taking and projection 
of the problem to the other side, which creates the divided “us-them” 
 104             F amily SyStemS                        2011
system. As conflict expands and deepens, civil contact between 
opposing sides becomes increasingly difficult. Emotional cutoff  
intensifies unity among “us” and isolation from “them” which, in 
turn, fuels the projection process and fear of the other. Large-scale conflict is multilateral. Issues and competing interests 
multiply and more factions emerge. Large-scale conflict is also multi -
generational.

Large-scale conflict is multilateral. Issues and competing interests 
multiply and more factions emerge. Large-scale conflict is also multi -
generational. As current issues activate memories of old grievances, 
people who have lived together as neighbors may turn against one 
another. Children born into a divisive emotional field are educated 
on a deep, visceral level to a way of life that perpetuates the divisions. Children may be recruited to defend a partisan loyalty with little or 
no understanding of the origins and nature of the problem. INTERVENTION

important thing to understand from the perspective of emotional

parties and moves toward the outside “peacemaker.”  When people

manage their own conflicts, they become subject to external control. The “peacemaking” third party—be it a parent, teacher, mediator, 
judge, court, police or military—is then in the position of trying to 
manage the behavior of others.

THE USE OF FORCE
As it pertains to relationships, force may be defined broadly as 
any action that places pressure on others to change. Ways that force 
has been used to bring about social change include moral pressure, 
such as marches and demonstrations; legal sanctions, such as fines 
and imprisonment; political mechanisms, such as boycotts, embargos, 
or strikes; physical restraint, physical aggression and, ultimately, 
armed aggression. Bringing force to bear on a conflict has the potential to either 
calm or inflame the emotional level. Those involved in conflict that 
is running out of control, or those in the vicinity, may welcome the 
arrival of an authority who is equipped to restore order.

arrival of an authority who is equipped to restore order. Conflict 
may be brought under control, at least for the moment. On the other hand, the use of force introduces serious obstacles 
to settling conflict. One is that force often begets more force, resulting 
in escalation. As conflict becomes increasingly harmful, the number 
of issues and grievances between combatants increases, providing 
fuel for further conflict. A second pitfall is overkill. The use of force, 
unless strictly disciplined, easily becomes excessive. In his writing 
on aggression, Edward O. Wilson (1978) observes that humans are 
strongly predisposed to slide into deep, irrational hostility when faced 
with external threats, and moreover that we are inclined to escalate 
hostility to a level that will overwhelm the source of the threat by

themselves are vulnerable to emotional reactivity: fear, excessive use 
of force, side-taking, or retreat. A third obstacle is that force hardens 
the polarization between the parties. Even when force does succeed 
in changing the behavior of others, it is most likely to stiffen their 
inner resentment and resistance behind a façade of submission until 
an opportunity to retaliate presents itself.

HISTORICAL ROOTS OF THE CONFLICT
Strife between the Irish and English has been almost incessant 
since the twelfth century. Attempts by England to control Ireland 
were largely unsuccessful as each wave of settlers was absorbed, 
becoming, as the Irish say, “more Irish than the Irish themselves.” In

of settlers. Large numbers came from England and Scotland. Backed 
by British authority, they confiscated land that had been owned and 
occupied by native Irish for generations. In the context of its colonial 
expansion, England’s encouragement of the settlements was widely 
seen as an effort to gain control and governance over Ireland. By 
then Protestant, the English Crown saw the native and still Catholic 
Irish society as a threat to its security. The dispossession of natives was profound. In 1641, 61% of land

single most important factor in the evolution of relationships in the 
English-Irish system. Along with losing their land, native Irish lost 
social status in the new political arrangement, becoming cheap labor 
with no important role in governance and subject to degrading penal 
laws that deprived them of civil and religious rights.

The Irish Position
Following partition, relationships between the North and 
South became more distant as the two parts of Ireland grew apart. “The South, preoccupied with building its own Catholic-National -
ist state…found little energy and less inclination…to address the

that the Irish state would pursue unification of Ireland and jurisdic -
tion over the whole island. Unionists have pointed to these Articles

existence of Northern Ireland.” (Farren and Mulvihill 2000, 189)

Like Hume, Farren and Mulvihill view the Anglo-Irish Agreement

in the hands of the majority of its people, Britain moved for the first 
time to a more neutral position. From a systems perspective, the 
meeting of the two “parent” governments, Britain and Ireland, to 
work together moved the problem of Northern Ireland into the larger 
context in which it had been created and in which it would need to be 
solved. John Hume and the SDLP had long believed that the British 
and Irish governments working together would be necessary:  
The reason we were continually failing to reach agreement 
was that we were not discussing the real problem. …the 
real problem wasn’t just relations within Northern Ireland; 
it was a British-Irish problem. It was the failure of Britain 
and Ireland to resolve their differences in the 1920s and they 
pushed the failure into a corner called Northern Ireland. The 
time had come for both governments to work together to 
solve the problem. (Hume 1997, 61-2)

Farren and Mulvihill describe with clarity how systems change

  Neutrality locates the cause of conflict in the emotional 
processes of a system, not in the dispositions of a particular 
person, group, or event. Natural systems theory argues that 
the relationships that comprise the system can be altered if 
one of the parties…adopts a neutral or differentiated position 
within the emotional triangle. That is, the neutral actor remains 
connected to the other parties, but is not entrapped by them. While the idea of an emotionally driven triangle reveals how 
and why conflicts expand, the alteration of the triangle in certain 
ways will also reveal how conflicts can be transformed. ...The 
major strategic contention of Bowen theory is that the emotional 
neutrality of one in the system will produce higher neutrality 
or differentiation in the other members of the triangle, though 
not necessarily simultaneously. De-triangling becomes the 
single most important peacemaking mechanism in the natural 
systems framework. (Farren and Mulvihill 2000, 132-3)

Britain’s shift to a neutral position was a necessary but far from 
sufficient step in the resolution of Northern Ireland’s conflict. The 
Anglo-Irish Agreement was met with a broad spectrum of emotional 
reactivity, from the positive response of the SDLP , to the disbelief and 
mistrust of Sinn Fein and the IRA, to the outrage and opposition of 
the Unionists. It would take years of dedicated work by thousands 
of committed people, with countless pitfalls along the way, to realize 
the promise that the 1985 Agreement held. To understand the resistance to change, it is helpful to consult 
Bowen’s writing on the predictable process that follows when one 
member of a family takes a step toward differentiation:
The family system is disturbed when any family member 
moves toward a slightly higher level of differentiation, and 
it will move as automatically to restore the family system to 
its former equilibrium. …This pattern is so predictable that 
the absence of an emotional reaction is good evidence that the 
differentiating effort was not successful. (Bowen 1978, 495)
Predictably then, Britain’s assuming a neutral, de-triangled 
position would be rigorously tested and opposed by those who saw 
it as a threat or a ruse. Vol. 8, N o.

While this perspective sees Britain’s shift to a neutral position as 
essential and pivotal to progress toward peace, it also recognizes other 
major concurrent developments that moved the peace process. First 
was the influence of changing economic realities. Economic disparity 
between North and South increased as the Irish Republic joined the 
European Union and enjoyed dramatic economic prosperity—“the 
Gaelic Boom”—in the 1990s. This rising standard of living in the South 
placed pressure on Northern Irish leaders to settle their differences so 
that their people could partake in the new economy. Second was the 
changing social climate of the Irish people, who increasingly rejected 
force as the agent of change and lent their support to more moderate 
organizations such as SDLP and the Alliance Party. These organiza -
tions represented moderate, negotiable approaches and shared the 
Irish people’s increasing ability to envision a power-sharing solution. A third factor was the active involvement of “outsiders”—President 
Clinton, Senator Mitchell, and European Union leaders—who pro -
vided neutral third party function, expertise in mediation, and an

Northern Ireland was back on the front pages on March 26, 
2007. Two of the most prominent and controversial figures in the 
past forty years of struggle, Gerry Adams and Ian Paisley, met face-
to-face for the first time, sitting down together in the Stormont Par -
liament building in Belfast to announce their agreement to form a 
power-sharing government. The agreement means that Britain will 
hand back responsibility for running Northern Ireland’s affairs to an 
administration of Protestants and Catholics. Paisley, as the leader of 
the DUP , now the largest party in the province, will be first minister, 
and Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein’s chief negotiator, will be deputy 
first minister, a post with equal power. Other parties will have seats 
in the government in proportion to their electoral showing. (Quinn 
and Cowell 2007)
Commentators note that the hope for the success of this agree -
ment is that it was reached by the parties themselves in contrast with 
past agreements that were imposed upon them. The New York Times  
editorial page of March 27, 2007 acknowledged the “vision, steadi -
ness, and timely pressures” contributed by Prime Ministers Blair 
and Ahern in the peacemaking process, but went on to say, “In the

presented to summarize and consider the emotional process within 
a three-generation family. This presentation was selected as an example of the context that

individual with multiple functional difficulties (substance abuse, 
chronic physical problems, and chronic pain) within the family 
emotional system in which they are embedded. PRESENTING PROBLEM
This case was referred to my private practice from a pain 
management clinic at a local hospital. I have seen a number 
of such referrals, whose chronic pain the referral source considers

intense emotional involvement and attachment. The shape of that 
doesn’t always look positive on the surface, but it’s very involved. And, as Dr. McKnight said, she’s living out with her son some version 
of what went on between her and her mother, which in attachment 
theory terms would be called an insecure or ambivalent attachment. The intense involvement indicates too much attachment, not too little. So I was wondering, is floundering too strong a word? Dr. McKnight:  Adrift? Ms. Kerr:  Adrift. Good word. And what does she do when you say, 
“Well, I don’t think this is all because you’re adopted, and I do think 
your mother is very invested in you.” And when you present an 
alternative view. Can she engage it at all? Mr. Murphy:  That, along with a couple of other comments. I re -
member saying, “That’s an interesting hypothesis. I have a different 
hypothesis.” And there was a moment of a marked awakening and 
she replied, “I never thought of that before.” Kind of taking it into 
consideration. Mobilizing her, putting it into practice, or somehow 
trying to make something more of that is not necessarily something 
that she gets. She’ll get swamped by the next desperate call from 
her son. Or her husband.

Georgetown University School of Medicine 
VOL.1 NO. 1 4380 MACARTHUR BLVD., WASHINGTON, D.C. 20007 JAN/FEB 1979 
ABOUT THE FAMILY CENTER 
AND ITS FACULTY 
Murray Bowen, M.D. This is the twentieth year of "family" at George­
town. The events of this period represent an impor­
tant nodal point in our history. The motivation of the 
faculty to start this Family Center Report is a part 
of this sequence of events. Some five years ago I 
began an informal newsletter called "News and An­
nouncements.'' I was too busy with other things to 
continue it regularly so the "Report" is now a total 
faculty effort. With Scott Meyer to see that the work 
is done, and Ruth Riley Sagar to supervise the detail, 
and with a dozen others to contribute, it will go out 
on schedule six times a year. In anticipation of this event, I put out a final issue 
of "News and Announcements" in November­
December 1978. I wanted to present an overview of 
the phenomenal growth of the Family Center since 
the end of 1975, and especially to correct some 
erroneous assumptions about our financing that 
work to our disadvantage. In this first Family Center 
Report I will amplify and clarify some points from 
the November-December letter. Several forces converged to create the rapid growth 
of the past three years. One important force has to do 
with theory. Systems theory provides a unique new 
dimension for conceptualizing every facet of human 
behavior.

One important force has to do 
with theory. Systems theory provides a unique new 
dimension for conceptualizing every facet of human 
behavior. I "knew" this in the 1950's when I began 
working toward a total systems orientation, long 
before systems ideas were acceptable in the 
profession. As the years have passed, systems con­
cepts have gradually come into favor and an in­
creasing number of professional people are seeking 
knowledge about systems theory and therapy. Our 
twenty-year experience in developing and refining 
systems theory has put Georgetown in a position of 
prominence in this new field. A second factor in the 
rapid growth has been the contribution of the 
faculty. It requires years to train people who are ex­
perts in systems theory and therapy. Through the 
years I have had a large volunteer faculty of well­
trained people who were employed or in private prac­
tice in the local area who gave generously of their 
time for teaching and research at Georgetown. Until the end of 1975 the Family Program was housed in 
two small offices in the basement of St. Mary's Hall. The faculty worked wherever there was a vacant 
office or classroom. At the end of each year we had 
enough reserve funds from postgraduate tuition and 
the Annual Symposium to distribute a token payment 
of some $3.00 per hour to the most active members 
of the volunteer faculty. A critical factor in the rapid growth was the space 
provided by the move to the new Family Center.

A critical factor in the rapid growth was the space 
provided by the move to the new Family Center. The 
move to the 4,000 square foot off-campus rental 
space in December 1975 was possible because we had 
enough funds to pay our own expenses. We still had 
the undistributed funds from 1974-75 and a gift to 
the University in my name that would insure our sur­
vival in case of financial reversals. We were "on our 
own" with huge fixed, expenses and a dedicated fac­
ulty determined to make the Family Center a success. The space permitted the faculty to begin im­
plementing systems programs held in abeyance for 
years. Each new program raised questions and new 
areas to be studied. The evolution of symposia 
provides one index of the development of new in­
terest. In three years the number of symposia in­
creased from one to eleven. In addition to the large 
general symposium, ten small specialized symposia 
represent the interest of the faculty member who 
sponsors it. In the last "News and Announcements" 
I listed all the symposia for 1978-79, and some of the 
most important programs being developed by the 
faculty. In addition to these, my monthly one-day 
clinical conferences were moved from Richmond to 
Washington which adds another eleven full-day 
meetings to the Family Center schedule. The gifted 
and inspired faculty is engaged in so many clinical­
teaching-research activities it is impossible to detail 
them in a brief communication.

The gifted 
and inspired faculty is engaged in so many clinical­
teaching-research activities it is impossible to detail 
them in a brief communication. The increased 
faculty activity on a national level has paralleled the 
increase in other areas. In three years we have 
outgrown our space. Every section of the Family 
Center is "bulging at the seams." Equipment that 
will not go into the offices is in the halls, and the 
waiting rooms have been converted to improvised 
classrooms. On busy days the Center swarms with 
students, trainees, families for research, and families 
for clinical service. The main impediment to the continued growth of 
the program is the lack of finances. The total support 
from the University is about $25,000 a year of which 
$15,000 is my half-time salary. Three years ago we 
hoped the University would be able to provide us 
with faculty salaries in return for teaching time in the 
Medical Center. This has not been possible. We 
hoped we could provide some faculty income from 
research grants. The faculty worked diligently at this 
for a year and a half but were not successful in 
securing a single substantial grant. Faculty energy 
went back to postgraduate teaching and symposia on 
which the monetary return is low considering the 
time and energy involved. The Family Center has 
been successful financially in that our net income is 
always greater than our expenses.
