The Family Center has 
been successful financially in that our net income is 
always greater than our expenses. But we still have 
not found a way to reimburse the faculty members 
who must make a living from part-time private prac­
tice of family therapy and who donate as much of 
50% of their time to the Family Center and the Uni­
versity for little or no pay. Erroneous assumptions about the Family Center 
finances have hurt us. It has been easy for people to 
assume we are supported by Georgetown University 
and that the salaries of the faculty and staff, and the 
rent, are all paid by Georgetown. Such assumptions 
result in requests for tuition free instruction in our 
postgraduate courses, free admission to symposia, 
"scholarships," and student rates. These are the in­
come producing activities that enable us to pay our 
bills. Among those who make the requests are 
University employees. It is important for me and the 
faculty to be an integral part of the University. We 
have given much of our time teaching in the Medical 
Center and the University and we have been lenient in 
providing Georgetown people free admission to ac­
tivities for which we would charge others. The more 
lenient we are in this area the more the faculty must 
work to make up the deficit. There have also been problems on the other side of 
the ledger.

The more 
lenient we are in this area the more the faculty must 
work to make up the deficit. There have also been problems on the other side of 
the ledger. There are Georgetown administrative of­
fices that assume we are supported by research grants, 
that we have a lot of money, and that they are en­
titled to their percentage of it. These notions may 
have started when we once had a gift donated in my 
name. If we were funded by gifts, or grants, or by 
university salaries, we would be glad to contribute 
our fair share. To make these kinds of demands on 
the Family Center at this time is equivalent to 
"killing the goose that lays the golden eggs." The 
"goose" has quite a potential for future con­
tributions if Georgetown can lend a hand until she 
gets on her feet. These erroneous assumptions are the 
result of poor communication. A goal of these com­
ments is to correct the distortions about Family 
Center funding. We at the Family Center are pleased with our ac­
complishments of the past few years. The faculty is 
alive and healthy and working on the problem. We 
cannot continue our present level of productivity without some outside source of funds. Currently we 
are working on research proposals with renewed 
energy and are seeking gifts and contributions in any 
amount. There is no panic or immediate urgency 
about the problem but, unless we can find some solu­
tion, the faculty will have to revert increasingly to 
private practice.

currently includes fifteen teaching tapes available to

CLINIC 
The Family Center has been operating a sliding-fee 
clinic since January 1975. Requests from the com­
munity as well as the need for a clinical service for 
training of fellows in family psychiatry stimulated 
this development in July 1975. Faculty volunteered 
time to establish the clinic before the first fellows ar­
rived. Therapy rooms were scarce in those early days 
in the basement of the Georgetown Nursing School 
and Ruth Riley Sagar not only had to pull rooms out 
of a hat, but administrate the operation as well. With 
the opening of the Family Center and the addition of 
administrative staff, the clinic was able to begin ex­
pansion in 1976. Currently 125 to 150 families are seen for a total of 
250 therapy hours a month. A third of the referrals 
are for biofeedback training while the remainder are 
for "standard" family therapy. Twenty to thirty new 
families are added to the case load each month. The 
clinic provides therapy for the full range of human 
problems, from psychotic families to those dealing 
with serious physical illness such as cancer or social 
problems such as delinquency or alcoholism. A major misconception about family therapy is 
that it is designed only for "families" with "family 
problems." Couples and entire families are seen at 
the Center, but therapy is done predominantly with 
individual family members in individual sessions.

"Family therapy" is defined by the theoretical orien­
tation of the therapist which guides the conduct of 
the therapy rather than the number of family mem­
bers that might attend the sessions. The average family is seen about twice a month 
and many are encouraged to enroll in the Community Course in Family Systems Theory. Most people who 
participate in this course while in therapy make 
remarkably faster progress than those just in family 
therapy. This observation suggests a number of new 
directions to improve the effectiveness of therapy for 
the future. REVIEW OF IDEAS 
This column is designed to report interesting and 
significant ideas of relevance to clinicians, theoreti­
cians, and researchers in family theory. The criteria for selection of material for the review 
will include some of the following. The ideas must be 
compatible with systems thinking and be consistent 
with an understanding of natural living systems and 
their operations. To this end, highest priority will be 
given to articles from biology, medicine, and com­
parative animal behavior. Particular priority will be 
given to articles that address a search for basic prin­
ciples of nature, and long-term outcome; as well as 
items of interdisciplinary interest and those grounded 
in research. Selection will also focus on new dis­
covery and, from time to time, on old ideas re-dis­
covered and considered worthy of reconsideration.

the results of their own selective reading. When pos­

the reviews. The scope of this column, however, dic­

This column was conceived as an outgrowth of in­
terest at the Family Center in its alumni. One recent 
project to evolve from this emphasis was the Alumni 
Luncheon held at the Annual Symposium last Octo­
ber. The Family Center is attempting to be in better 
touch with those who have been an integral part of 
the organization in the past. As in many other 
schools and training centers, the students and teach­
ers often drift apart after the shared learning experi­
ence. Although some of this is inevitable, we would 
like to influence better contact when possible. The success of this column depends on the input of 
the alumni and is designed as a "what ever happened 
to" column in which an alumnus or an alumni group 
will be highlighted so that our readers can be brought 
up to date on their lives and activities. Rather than 
requesting information from people arbitrarily, we 
would pref er to hear from those of you willing to give 
the Center an update on your lives. So herein lies the 
plea!

Center initiated its most ambitious series of sym­

tion to the family field, his twenty years at George­
town, and the publication of his book, Family Ther­
apy in Clinical Practice. Ninety experts whose profes­
sional paths crossed Dr. Bowen's were invited to 
attend. More than sixty were able to come and, of 
that number, thirty guests participated in a series of 
panels outlining the emergence of family con~..!pts 
and the flowering of family therapy as well as contri­
butions made by psychiatry and the social, biological 
and-natural sciences. One highlight of the day was an 
audiotape from Dr. Karl Menninger who was unable 
to attend because of poor health. Dr. Menninger 
spoke of his "long relationship with Murray" and 
said that he was pleased that Dr. Bowen was getting a 
"well-deserved, warm, fuzzy day." 
The meeting was followed two weeks later by the 
Second Conference on Children organized by 
Patricia Meyer.

be the forum for papers that represent an extension

Harvard University. He is best known from his 
column "This View of Life" in Natural History 
Magazine. Dr. Gould did a special lecture at 
Georgetown University Medical School on the 
evening before the symposium entitled "Ontogeny 
and Phylogeny." At the Symposium on Friday, Dr. Gould presented a general critique of human 
sociobiology. A special feature of the Symposium was a program 
presented at the banquet.

On November 13, the Family Center sponsored the 
Second Conference on the Emotional and Biological 
Aspects of Cancer. This annual meeting was 
organized by Dr. Michael Kerr who brought together 
six well-known clinicians and researchers who have 
approached this subject from different and unique 
vantage points. Dr. Martin Lewis, Chairman of the 
Department of Pathology at Georgetown, discussed 
developments in the field of tumor immunology and 
the relationship of the immune system to the 
emotional state. John J. Mulvihill, Director of the 
Clinical Genetics Sections of the National Cancer In­
stitute, reported on his extensive research with high 
incidence cancer families and his interest in the 
relationship of the emotional state and the genetic 
predisposition to cancer. Dr. Robert Picard whose 
long research career has been primarily in psycho­
somatic medicine concentrated more on life exper­
iences that make individuals prone to cancer than on 
events that may provoke it. Dr. Wolf who has also 
had a distinguished career in psychosomatic research 
presented findings from his exhaustive study of 
Roseto, Pennsylvania which suggests that the cohe­
siveness of family units in a community effects the 
incidence of illness in that community. Dr. Murray 
Bowen focused on multigenerational emotional 
factors specific to the development of mental versus 
physical illness. Dr. Kerr presented information on 
family emotional process and the onset and course of 
cancer.

A few people have been extremely active in pursu­
ing their research ideas on a regular basis for a num­
ber of years. A larger number of people have parti­
cipated from time to time, working on one of their 
own ideas, or as part of a team effort. Areas in 
various stages of research and development include 
cancer, aging, biofeedback for stress management, 
education, bereavement, divorce, nursing, and chil­
dren. At present, no project is currently being 
funded. Very few people have actually applied for 
funds, and statistically, about one in five nationally 
is funded. It takes so much effort to apply for fund­
ing that some, the very committed people, would 
rather spend their time doing the work than applying 
for funding. There is always the issue of how much 
effort to place on "translating" Bowen Theory so 
that others such as NIH and other review boards can 
hear it. At present, one goal is to develop service 
projects which would allow the opportunity to pro­
vide a service and to expand theoretical knowledge 
simultaneously.

member at the Family Center largely in charge of 
sponsored programs and development of contract 
funds. Knowledge of funding and numerous other 
issues are already making a significant contribution 
to development of research at the Family Center. Without research, the theory per se eventually 
becomes either useless or a "movement" with 
"believers" rather than thinkers. More important, 
not doing research is an indicator that not only the 
theory, but those who use it, are no longer 
developing. There are a number of ways in which people can 
participate in research at the Family Center. Policy 
has developed such that two positions have been

goal is to become active on a regular basis; that is, 
that the Family Center, rather than another institu­
tion, is their primary orientation and intended place 
of activity. The other criterion, is that they may be 
considered for a faculty position at a future time.

Two events of the past year have stimulated a new 
level of interest at the Family Center in the evolution 
of the family field nationally. The Human Family 
Symposium provided an opportunity for Family 
Center associates to become acquainted with such in­
dividuals as Virginia Satir, Salvador Minuchin, 
Donald Bloch, and other authorities in the family 
field as well as persons from related disciplines such 
as sociology and biology. As a result, a new aware­
ness of the evolution of the family field and those in­
dividuals in the field using diverse theories, ap­
proaches and techniques has developed. The creation of the American Family Therapy 
Association in November 1977 also enhanced this in­
terest. Dr. Bowen, a member of the Board of Direc­
tors, was elected the first President and, con­
sequently, the Family Center faculty has become 
keenly aware of the difficult task of defining prin­
ciples and standards for the new organization.

These two factors stimulated the inclusion of this 
"Guest Column" in the Family Center Report. In 
each edition, a guest author will contribute his views 
about the development and extension of family 
theory and the practice of family psychotherapy. This column promises to provide a broader scope to 
the Family Center Report by not only continuing to 
report on the development and extension of Bowen 
Theory but also to acknowledge the ideas of other 
recognized authorities in the family field. TRAINING 
Several training programs existed prior to the

WELCOME TO THE HUMAN FAMILY 
Timothy S. Healy, S.J. In selecting guest authors for this special column, there 
seemed to be no more appropriate author for the first col­
umn than the President of Georgetown University, 
Timothy S. Healy, S.J. Father Healy, the forty-sixth 
President of Georgetown and a member of the Society of 
Jesus, was born in New York City in 1923. He was 
graduated from Woodstock College in Maryland and was 
ordained at the University of Louvain in Belgium. He 
holds a doctorate in English Literature from Oxford 
University. An author of numerous articles on higher 
education, Father Healy has also written two books on 
John Donne. Below are Father Healy's comments and 
welcome on the occasion of the Human Family Sym­
posium on September 9, 1978. Welcome to this modest extension of Georgetown. The 
University is blessed with several halls, but none quite large 
enough to hold you in the brilliantly lit comfort in which 
you are seated here. Those titles, memberships, and boards [enumerated in 
Dr. Kerr's introduction] are sort of academic barnacles 
you pick up by staying in the water long enough. I guess what is most moving about this occasion is that, 
like everybody in the room, I am the product of several 
dozen teachers, probably forty or fifty, of whom a dozen were good and three were great.

I spent the summer at Ox­
ford writing a chapter for a professor, the greatest among 
them, or as we say in New York, "my rabbi," Dame Helen 
Gardner, who handed me my doctorate on a platter by 
holding my hand as I went through it. To see this many former students, associates, and ad­
mirers come together to honor a Georgetown faculty 
member reminds me first of all that the university is still 
about what the university ought to be about, which is good 
teaching and good scholarship. Dr. Bowen, for making 
this possible, on behalf of Georgetown, its medical school, 
its forty-six past presidents, and I hope another forty-six to 
come -if we survive the late eighties - I would like to say 
thank you. It is also reassuring to see that the family still exists and 
that somebody fusses about it. Let me tell you two reflec­
tions on that, one serious and one not so serious. Every 
now and then it does seem to me that probably one of the 
bad things that has happened to medicine since the 18th 
century is its marriage to the university. In a sense, the 
university is the one place in Western society which 
apotheosizes trivia; the larger the pile of it you get, the 
closer you are to divinization. I am not really sure that be­
ing able to deal with Plato, to choose something out of my 
world, or with the upper anterior surface of the left toe 
is that much of a benefit either for the university or 
for medicine.

and as dignified as the family as a subject for study is 
reassuring. The second story that I would like to tell is to encourage 
you lest you lose heart. Fifteen years ago, the received 
wisdom loudly trumpeted on every minor sinai by every 
minor prophet who could find a sinai to trumpet off, most 
of whom were from the departments of political science, 
was that the four-year liberal arts college was finished. It 
was perfectly clear that the drift of the future was going to 
be that the community colleges would eat the bottom of it 
and the university would eat the top of it· and that you 
would go from community colleges into Cornell Universi­
ty, one of the principal proponents of this thesis, where 
Mr. Perkins would welcome you with open arms into the 
serious research world of the university. The four-year college with its dilettantism, its breadth of 
scope, its care for the past and, in a very curious sense, its 
love for youngsters would disappear into history with the 
dodo and the Parthenon. If yo'u have followed the news­
papers you know that the dodo and the Parthenon are 
 coming back strong and that no place has discovered the 
fact that the liberal arts college matters more than Mother 
Harvard who, in trumpeting the core curriculum about 
which you have read so much, has also just simply knock­
ed on the head the whole theory which was so popular fif­
teen years ago.

In each issue of the Family 
Center Report I will elaborate on some of these activities. The Community Course may be one of our most important 
and interesting experiments. On the simplest level it is designed to teach the fundamentals of family systems 
theory to people not in the mental health professions. Over 
the years there have been several abortive efforts to 
develop such a course. The present course was started after 
the move to the new Family Center when we had sufficient 
classroom space in the building and available faculty to 
teach it. As a course rather than a lecture series, reading is 
required and written homework is expected. The class 
meets for two hours twice a month beginning in September 
and ending in June. There are currently two sections, one 
which meets from 12:30 to 2:30 p.m. on alternate Tuesdays 
and the other from 10:00 to 12:00 noon on alternate Satur­
days. Mental health professionals are excluded to prevent 
the classes from being over-run by those who seek training 
in family therapy. Tuition for the Community Course is 
$250.00 per year. The course focuses on learning about families through 
the part self plays in his own family. When class members 
can begin to observe the part that self plays in the family, 
and can resist the automatic urge to change others, they 
can begin to assume responsibility for self, and begin to ex­
perience the favorable results that can occur throughout 
the entire family.

Obviously it is not possible to do more 
than scratch the surface in a single course but the trainees 
are exposed to the principle of objective observation as a 
step toward emotional control. The teaching of such a course is a subtle process that 
goes far beyond lecturing about a body of knowledge. The 
ability to communicate emotional process in the midst of 
emotionality is the key. Most mental health professionals 
are better qualified as preachers than teachers for a course 
such as this. It is a bit incongruous when the teacher 
preaches at the class members to stop preaching at their 
children. Mrs. Patricia Meyer is in charge of the Community 
Course. She has a special interest in this kind of teaching, 
in staying in contact with a majority of class members, and 
in modifying the content and manner of presentation in a 
way that can be heard by most of the trainees. This course 
provides a way to learn about self in the context of one's 
own family, and the ways that change can predictably 
result. For the Family Center faculty, this course is a 
unique laboratory for developing and refining a special 
kind of teaching skill. At the Family Center we do not have 
"students." If we use a term to refer to people in courses, 
it is "trainee." 
The Community Course is also used to supplement the 
therapy of people already in family therapy. Some kind of 
didactic teaching is essential in clinical work with families.

didactic teaching is essential in clinical work with families. This is marginally successful for the therapist involved in a 
transference. Over the years I have tried numerous devices 
and methods to communicate about emotional systems 
without being emotionally involved with the family. The 
effort is directed at helping family members to get outside 
the emotionality to have a calmer look at the total 
situation. In the 1950's there was the family diagram which has 
now become a cornerstone of most family therapy. Then 
came tutorial teaching during the family sessions which is 
really not successful unless the family and the therapist can

ing is effective within limits but it is time-consuming and 
there is the ever-present problem of the family responding 
to the emotionality rather than the content. Multiple family therapy offers some advantage over 
therapy with one family. A fair level of teaching is possible 
when a family member can attend family lectures, confer­
ences and symposia. A still better level of teaching is pos­
sible during family therapy with mental health profes­
sionals when a family member is enrolled in the George­
town Postgraduate Program. There are special dis­
advantages even with this. In summary, some kind of 
teaching is essential in clinical work with families.

are many variables to this which have to do with the fam­

degree to which the teacher is emotionally contained within 
self, and the method of teaching. After the present Community Course began, I referred 
people from my private practice. No method tried thus far 
has offered as many advantages and as few disadvantages 
for people already in family therapy. Some chronic fam­
ilies that never got beyond symptom relief have been able 
to start slow basic change. Families doing well have made 
faster progress. Most chronically fixed families for whom 
basic change is realistically remote have been able to gain a 
little from the course. Certain families have started in the 
course as a preparation for family therapy. Some do fairly 
well without therapy. The average family seems to require 
much less therapy later on. Thus far we have no more than educated guesses to ex­
plain the effectiveness of the Community Course. That it is 
a subject-oriented course may partly explain its effective­
ness. Most of the class members are seriously involved in 
the subject matter and in dealing with the instructor about 
subject matter, rather than in having a workshop orienta­
tion. Another factor is Mrs.

Another factor is Mrs. Meyer's personal interest in 
refining and developing this kind of teaching, and the inte­
rest that has developed among the other instructors. Still 
another part is the fact that the course is held in the Family 
Center classroom in close proximity to all other Family 
Center activity. The Community Course is mentioned 
often in Training Committee meetings where the primary 
focus is on the development and refinement of Postgradu­
ate Programs for family therapists. In many ways the 
Community Course has become a kind of pilot project for 
developing new teaching methods and techniques for all 
teaching at the Family Center. From my perspective, this course represents a step for­
ward in developing more effective preventive and com­
munity psychiatry. Although there are successes and 
failures with any approach, this course presents the most 
advantages and the fewest disadvantages I have seen with 
any approach thus far. Among people from the communi­
ty who have never had experience with any kind of psycho­
therapy, the greatest success is with those who are seriously 
motivated, who do their reading and homework, and who 
work seriously to apply the principles they have learned. Several of these repeat the course year after year, probably 
learning more from repeating than from their first ex­
posure. They appear to have mastered principles that will prevent future emotional problems in their families.

mid-ground are the less motivated who are lax about 
reading and homework, who are also lax in applying what 
they have learned, who expect that mere attendance will 
change something, who tend to blame the course or the in­
structor if they fail to grasp a point, and who discontinue 
at some convenient point along the way. Among the 
failures are those who attend out of compliance with so­
meone's request, who never engage the subject matter, and 
who fail to see their part in the relationship system of their 
own families. They are so relationship-oriented they spend 
more time criticizing the instructor and other class 
members than listening. Thus far we have not announced the Community Course 
except in restricted circles because we do not yet have the

divorce represents a lack of resolution in the mourning 
process of prior family relationships. Through his presen­
tation of a couple contemplating divorce, Dr.

mental health system and the legal system on the marital 
dyad. Joseph Steinberg, trained as a family therapist and now 
a practicing family lawyer, discussed the therapist-lawyer 
relationship. His experience demonstrated that coopera­
tion between professionals can allow spouses to be their 
own best negotiators and thereby avoid the negative 
aspects of the adversarial process. Lawrence Gaughan, 
Professor of Law at Washington and Lee University, 
presented a paper on various practical and theoretical 
models for the lawyer-client relationship. Professor 
Gaughan will be a legal fellow in residence at the George­
town Family Center while on a sabbatical during 
1979-1980. He will study family systems theory and its ap­
plication to family law.

fluence on the lawyer-client relationship. The panel discussions permitted participants and speak­

within a divorcing family and a divorcing society. The Second Conference on Nursing, organized by Kath­

by the patient in the hospital setting as it relates to per­
sonality characteristics and family situation as well as to

Many dis­
cussions among Family Center faculty and staff are cur­
rently focusing on ways to better assess the quality of ser­
vice and how it can be improYed. It seems reasonable to 
assume that the more that is known about what is being 
done, the more likely it will improve. But a systematic 
method for gathering this knowledge has been lacking. Evaluation of outcome is particularly important now in 
this era of "anti-psychotherapy" feeling within ever 
enlarging segments of psychiatry. There are loud voices 
proclaiming psychotherapy to be "non-medical" and not 
legitimately within the province of psychiatry. These voices 
would have you believe that psychiatrists should concern 
themselves with psychopharmacology and the treatment of 
the "organically" based mental disorders, while leaving 
the interpersonal, the family, the neurotic problems to the 
''counselors.'' 
The contributions of research into brain chemistry and 
the development of psychoactive drugs cannot be under­
estimated. Some great research has been done and volumes 
of exciting new information await us. But, like anything 
else, long-term problems develop when one area is over­
emphasized at the expense of another. The prevailing view prior to Freud was that mental illness was the result of 
brain pathology. Freud's view that such disorders could be 
based on functional rather than structural disturbances in 
the brain was not initially well-accepted.

Freud's view that such disorders could be 
based on functional rather than structural disturbances in 
the brain was not initially well-accepted. Gradually, 
psychoanalytic theory and a method of psychotherapy 
firmly based on that theory gained acceptance. Now, it is 
popular to be "anti-psychoanalytic," as if Freud had been 
terribly wrong. This attitude extends to even being anti­
psychotherapeutic. It seems like a case of "throwing out 
the baby with the bathwater." 
The orientation of the Family Center is not opposed to 
psychopharmacology or to brain chemistry research. The 
Center does, however, specialize in a method of 
psychotherapy that has been effective in the full range of 
mental, physical, and social disorders. Psychotherapy can 
be based on sound medical principles, principles that 
evolve from a systems theory of human functioning which 
can ultimately be integrated into the mainstream of medi­
cine. Systems theory can make a major contribution to­
ward the development of a much needed theory of medi­
cine. But if this is to be more than a belief, it is imperative 
that the Family Center do more to demonstrate that what is 
thought to be effective in any given clinical situation, is, in 
fact, being realized in the actual therapy. The Family 
Center faulty and staff will be working very hard to develop 
methods to assess effectiveness during the upcoming year.

systematic, patient study and investigation in some field of 
knowledge, undertaken to discover or establish facts or 
principles." That process can be, and usually is, done 
largely in the cerebral cortex, and need not be funded nor 
directed by others. It does, however, have to result from 
the personal challenge and drive within the individual for 
excellence. Research is a major cornerstone of the Family Center. It 
not only supports the ongoing activities in psychotherapy 
and training, but also provides the foundation on which 
future activity and growth will be built. Even more impor­
tantly, research is the primary vehicle for engaging one's 
own thinking. To reify Bowen Theory is not research. Without continued engagement of the mind into the 
sciences and the unknown, one risks becoming sterile, dull, 
and merely a mimic of someone else's ideas and tech­
niques. Research is not exclusively the business of those 
who are funded by a contract or a grant. Research is the 
business of every person at the Family Center.

 provides a specified product at the end of a specified

The hard work is in the therapist's maintaining and 
improving his personal functioning or differentiation. Many trainees absorb the concepts of family systems 
theory at an intellectual level, without applying them in 
their own lives. The existence of this gap between being in­
tellectually aware of systems concepts and "operationaliz­
ing" them becomes obvious in all but the easiest therapy situations. As anxiety increases in the family, a therapist 
who does not have the concepts well-integrated in his own 
life becomes mechanistic in his approach and loses the 
family. The therapist, for example, may be viewed as too 
distant or uninvolved. Paradoxically, a therapist who is 
really operating outside the emotional field of a clinical 
family is not perceived as distant. In fact, the farther out­
side of the emotional field he is, the more comfortable it is 
for the family to relate to him. A significant part of the faculty's responsibility in train­
ing is to know when the trainee is not operationalizing the 
concepts. To supervise effectively is to help trainees bridge 
this "gap." To do this, faculty members must continuous­
ly be aware of the degree to which this gap exists within 
themselves and strive to close it. When a trainee is at least 
aware of the gap between intellectual awareness and the 
emotional change still to occur within self, he at least has a 
direction toward which to work.

ON EMOTIONAL PROCESS IN SOCIETY 
Murray Bowen, M.D. This is a report about the least understood concept in my 
Family Systems Theory. Few things in life have provided 
more personal satisfaction than the discovery of a logical 
conceptual bridge between emotional process in the family 
and emotional process in society. I had worked on this as a 
background project for over fifteen years. We had detailed 
knowledge about the family. Many of the same patterns 
also operated in society. The answer seemed so obvious 
that anyone could know it, but it was so elusive it could 
evade discovery for decades. Awareness came suddenly 
while writing a paper late in 1972 and early in 1973. It was 
a minor version of finding a "missing link." Time has not 
permitted writing a paper in sufficient detail for the con­
cept to be understandable to any but the most serious 
students. This will be a report ABOUT the concept. All my life I have been interested in explanations for 
societal and international events. At any one time in 
history writers have pronounced society to be in the most 
decadent state since the beginning of time and have 
predicted doomsday as just around the corner. In the same 
periods others have predicted the glories of future civiliza­
tions.

periods others have predicted the glories of future civiliza­
tions. There has never been an explanation for war that 
goes far beyond the usual cause and effect thinking. On a 
more serious level there have been the analyses of 
historians, philosophers, and political and social scientists. Most of these have used logical deductive reasoning that 
explained events in retrospect. There are a few fascinating 
predictions of the future that appear to have been based 
more on intuition than known fact. When I came into psychiatry I was delighted with a dif­
ferent order of reasoning that might provide better 
answers. Then I discovered that psychoanalysts tended to 
make sweeping generalizations from specific knowledge 
about the individual. For instance, there were generaliza­
tions that societies went through the same stages of 
psychosexual development as the individual. Perhaps the 
best explanations were the Jungian concepts such as a 
group unconscious. The average psychiatric explanation 
made the error of applying the psychology of the in­
dividual to society as a whole. The family research of the 1950's added a completely 
new dimension to theoretical thinking. For the first time it 
was possible to view the family, rather than the individual, 
as a single emotional-psychological unit.

For the first time it 
was possible to view the family, rather than the individual, 
as a single emotional-psychological unit. Most family researchers and family therapists continued, to some 
degree, to see the family as a collection of individuals, and 
to see emotional "stuck togetherness" as a pathological 
state. There is an accuracy to this individual view but it 
misses the emotional bonding, of varying intensity, that 
welds all families into a unit. This beginning new view of 
the family as a unit quickly led some therapists toward 
superficial comparisons between the family and social 
groups. There were numerous early efforts to extend family 
thinking to work and social groups. Emotional process in a 
family is similar to emotional process among people who 
work together. Early family therapists were quick to 
assume that work and social groups WERE families. This 
practice is still so prevalent that many accept it as fact. However much the relationships at work are similar to 
relationships in the family, there are important differences 
that are missed when people talk and function as if they are 
the same. I was super-sensitive to false analogies. In my 
NIMH research I went along for a time with the notion the 
ward staff WAS a family. By 1956, we were following a 
strict interpretation of "family" in the research which 
helped to focus on the differences between relationships in 
families and in work and social systems. Then came the triangle concept.

Then came the triangle concept. The triangle is the 
molecule of any emotional system. It operates between any 
three people who come together for a task. I had hoped the 
triangle would eventually become the bridge to understand 
the specific connection between emotional process in the 
family and larger groups of people. This never evolved. Knowledge about triangles provided an important dimen­
sion but it was not the key to the puzzle. I was sure that 
somewhere in this increasing body of knowledge about 
families there was a logical conceptual bridge that would 
lead to a more precise understanding of emotional process 
in society. During the 1960's I avoided quick analogies and 
premature speculations, and devoted myself to keeping 
files and bibliographies from the literature, pertinent 
clinical data, and writings from newspapers and magazines 
that seemed to highlight the process. In the meantime the 
"family" profession continued to use loose analogies and 
make inaccurate comparisons between family process and 
societal process. For me, the societal issue became a huge 
puzzle that was always in the background awaiting some 
new bit of evidence. The next chapter evolved in 1972 when Anton Schmalz 
asked me to prepare a paper for a meeting of the Environ-
 mental Protection Agency. He was bringing together a 
broad spectrum of scientists to meet with important 
government figures.

government figures. The scientists were researchers in 
population explosion, pollution, energy problems, the 
dwindling food supply, waste disposal, and alternative 
solutions to environmental problems. He asked me to ad­

of human reactions as man damaged and then attempted

province of societal agencies. The schools, police, proba­
tion officers, social agencies, juvenile judges, and other 
higher societal authorities become involved in the process. It is possible to establish a fairly accurate functional level

momentary symptom relief which leads ultimately to a 
deeper step into the regression. The same pattern applies to

measures to relieve the anxiety of the moment. In 1973-74, 
I wrote about this process as "societal regression" which 
since then I have tried to present as one phase of a process

~iofeedback is a process of providing ·a person with 
relatively immediate and continuous information of some 
bioelectric response of which the individual is often 
unaware. Information, usually in the form of audio or 
visual signals, is "fed back" to the individual to indicate 
the presence or degree of bioelectric responses within the 
body. Biofeedback training is the process of learning to 
control the automatic responses, first with the help of the 
biofeedback instrumentation and eventually without the 
assistance of any external equipment.

The purpose of learning to control bioelectric responses 
such as muscle tension, skin temperature, skin conduc­
tance and sometimes brain waves is to permit the indi­
vidual to change the degree of arousal within the body. Under stress, the organism tends to respond with what 
Cannon called the "fight or flight response" which is ac­
companied by certain physiological changes. Under sus­
tained stress, or the perception of stress, the organism loses 
its ability to return to homeostatic baseline. Eventually, in 
this high arousal state, one or more systems of the 
organism give way or dysfunction, resulting in any one of 
numerous stress-related problems such as hypertension, 
tension headache, migraine and others. By learning to 
reduce the degree of arousal, the individual can reduce the 
likelihood or severity of the stress-related symptoms. Biofeedback training facilitates this self-regulation by pro­
viding cues to the individual which are then used to: 
(1) decrease the intensity of the over-reaction to the 
stressor; (2) decrease the frequency of the over-response; 
(3) facilitate a more rapid return to baseline; and (4) in 
general, decrease the state of arousal. In biofeedback training, the equipment "senses" and 
picks up minute changes, such as in muscle tension, 
amplifies this bioelectric signal, and converts it to light or 
sound. The individual learns to control the bioelectric 
response by learning to control the light or sound.

The individual learns to control the bioelectric 
response by learning to control the light or sound. There 
are many ways of providing feedback based on different 
rationales. In general, the most common purpose of pro­
viding biofeedback in this laboratory is to facilitate op­
timum arousal, including optimum balance between the 
parasympathetic and sympathetic branches of the auto­
nomic nervous system. The only purpose of the equipment 
is to provide physiological cues to facilitate the shift in 
arousal. The equipment includes an electromyograph 
(EMG) measuring muscle tension; electroencephalograph 
(EEG) -specifically Alpha/Theta trainer; electrodermal 
response (EDR) which measures the same response as the 
Galvanic Skin Response (GSR) but uses conductance in­
stead of resistance; and digital skin temperature. All the sensors are non-invasive. They are usually ap­
plied to the skin which has been specifically cleansed for 
this purpose and, depending on the equipment and func­
tion, a cream is used to facilitate conductance of the 
bioelectric activity from the body to the equipment. It is important to understand that the equipment is only 
monitoring the activity of the body, not introducing any 
electrical activity into it. Further, it is important to 
remember that the equipment is only providing signals or 
cues to the individual. It is the individual who is learning to 
reduce the degree of arousal.

anymore than anyone can precisely describe how to walk, 
write, or throw a ball. The organism is remarkable, and 
most motivated individuals begin to learn some self­
regulation in six or eight one-hour sessions in the 
laboratory with related practice without instrumentation at 
home. Like most learning processes, the more practice the 
better the result. The learning curve for becoming an 
"autonomic athlete" is highly dependent on the in­
strumentation in the initial stage but, in time, the in­
strumentation becomes a very small part of self-regulation. REVIEW OF IDEAS

or not the project is funded, the ideas will continue to 
develop for additional future research and service. REPORT ON THURSDAY EVENING 
PROFESSIONAL MEETING ON 
JUNE 21, 1979 
The Third Thursday professional meeting on June 21, 1979 
was a highlight of the year. The presenter was George Stid­
worthy, Ph.D., a biochemist and cell biologist of Boston. His slides and movies of human fibroblasts, from the 
beginning of life to death, were a feature of the evening. He set up a laboratory situation in which fibroblasts 
multiplied at maximum speed and then was able to follow 
----the-life course of a single fibroblast and all the progeny of 
that fibroblast to the death of the colony. His study of one 
human cell provides basic knowledge of the human 
phenomenon. Dr. Stidworthy is Marian Merrifield's 
cousin.

Department of Psychiatry 
Georgetown University School of Medicine 
VOL.1 NO.4 4380 MACARTHUR BLVD., WASHINGTON, D.C. 20007 SEPTEMBER/OCTOBER 1979 
TWENTY YEARS AT GEORGETOWN 
PART I 
Murray Bowen, M.D. The Family Program began its twenty-first year at 
Georgetown on September 11, 1979. The story of those 
twenty years could be told in a dozen different ways. For 
this anniversary message I have chosen to review the history 
of the family in psychiatry as it evolved in the 1940's and 
19SO's, and as Georgetown came to play its role in the 
evolution. My move from NIMH to Georgetown in 1959 was 
governed by two major factors. One was theoretical and the 
other practical and prophetic. The theoretical part is re­
lated to the way the family idea took root and began to 
grow. Any evolutionary process begins with tiny separate 
roots largely unnoticed for long periods. When the time 
and situation is right, one of the roots begins to grow. In 
this sense the process continues on its course, as much in 
spite of as because of the people who happen to be there to 
develop the ideas. And so it was with the evolution of the 
family research of the 1940's and 1950's which was impor­
tant in the development of family therapy in the 1950's. The family idea evolved directly from psychoanalytic 
theory, and specifically in well-known psychiatric centers 
that practiced the most disciplined version of psycho­
analytic therapy for severe mental problems in adults.

The 
professional disciplines of sociology, anthropology, child 
psychiatry, psychology, social work, and marriage 
counseling were far removed from the mainstream in this 
evolution. In the 1940's psychoanalysis offered a new era of hope for 
understanding and treating mental illness. It helped to 
make psychiatry into a popular medical specialty. The 
theory defined mental illness as a pathology in the person of 
the patient. The therapy was designed to resolve the 
pathology through careful analysis of the patient-therapist 
transference. The therapist could contaminate the transfer­
ence, and jeopardize the outcome of therapy through con­
tact with the patient's relatives. The best centers were 
diligent in guarding the privacy of the therapeutic relation­
ship and perfecting thereapeutic technique. It was difficult 
to maintain therapeutic discipline with schizophrenia and 
other severe emotional problems. Psychologists were employed for more precise diagnosis of the pathology in 
the patient, and social workers were hired to see the 
relatives and help protect the patient-therapist relation­
ship. That was the strict professional orientation of the 
time. Schizophrenia is the most complex of the emotional 
illnesses. It is sufficiently complex that psychiatry cannot 
account for it with the same frame of reference used to 
understand milder problems. Conceptually it is difficult to 
delineate the family from the pathology in the patient.

Conceptually it is difficult to 
delineate the family from the pathology in the patient. Most 
of the therapists who did psychotherapy with schizophrenia 
in the 1940's worked toward excluding the family from the 
patient-therapist relationship. That resulted in an im­
portant body of knowledge, known as the psychoanalytic 
psychotherapy of schizophrenia. A smaller group of thera­
pists began to study the family involvement in schizo­
phrenia. That course led into a conceptual thicket. There 
were powerful prohibitions against a REAL therapist 
having contact with the patient's relatives. There were 
practical reasons for this discipline. Few therapists could 
have contact with the family without become so emotionally 
involved they lost their value to the patient. I believe the nature of the theory and the therapeutic 
discipline about the therapeutic relationship led to the early 
family researchers operating secretly and underground for 
almost a decade. Certainly my early work with families was 
in the evenings and on weekends, away from the critical eyes 
of supervisors and colleagues. In the early 19SO's I began 
looking for a research center in which it would be possible 
"to do new things in the name of research." When I moved 
to NIMH in 1954 I already had a well developed hypothesis 
about the origin and nature of schizophrenia.

Years later I 
was to learn that other therapist investigators in widely 
separated centers had also been experimenting with schizo­
phrenia and the family at the very same time. This FACT 
lends support to the evolutionary nature of the family move­
ment. I use the term "family movement" to designate the 
early years of "family research" and also the "family 
therapy" era which was to come later. Family research with schizophrenia played the most 
critical role in the evolution of family theory and therapy. There were three major research projects in the 19SO's. Lidz 
began his interest in schizophrenia in the 1940's at Johns 
Hopkins and continued with a formal research team at Yale 
in the early 19SO's. He was a psychoanalyst who never really 
 became a family therapist, but the contributions of the Lidz 
group were enormous. Another was Jackson who had been 
trained at Chestnut Lodge and who started his research 
group in Palo Alto in the early 1950's. The other was 
Bowen, trained in Topeka and on the Menninger Clinic 
staff until he began his "live-in" research at NIMH in 1954. There were other early investigators who did not go on to 
formal research nor publish very much. The researchers 
began reporting an order of data never previously recorded 
in the literature. This resulted from the focus on relation­
ships between family members.

The researchers 
began reporting an order of data never previously recorded 
in the literature. This resulted from the focus on relation­
ships between family members. The researchers each used 
slightly different terms to describe their observations but 
they were all describing the same relationship patterns. The 
psychiatric world reacted positively, as if these relationship 
patterns were specific to the etiology of schizophrenia. My experience will help illustrate the events of the 
1955-57 period. I had entire families living on the research 
ward which provided a clear view of the process we all were 
seeing. It began in 1954 with live-in mothers and patients. That provi~ed a new view of the mother-patient emotional 
fusion and evidence that this was merely a fragment of a 
larger family system. Within months plans were made to 
admit families with fathers. A preliminary method of family 
psychotherapy had been developed when the first entire 
family was admitted in December 1955. Observation of the families provided a strikingly 
different panoramic view of the human phenomenon. The 
emotional "stuck-togetherness" between family members, 
and the ways they rejected and distanced from each other to 
cope with the emotional bondedness, defied many common 
explanations of human behavior. An exciting new 
theoretical world had suddenly come into view.

An exciting new 
theoretical world had suddenly come into view. I have no 
better frame of reference than to compare it to the possible 
reaction of Darwin when he finally saw the evidence for 
evolution. After it was possible to see this in families with 
schizophrenia, it was automatic to see less intense versions 
of the same patterns in people with less severe emotional 
problems, and even in "normal" people. I was elated. The 
implications of this went in every direction. Here was 
evidence that schizophrenia was not qualitatively different 
from the other men1-a1-mnesses, and that schizophrenia, 
neurotic level problems and the concept of "normal" all 
somehow belonged on the same continuum. Here was 
evidence that a "so-called" pathology in one family member 
was a functional manifestation of anxiety elsewhere in the 
family. The ramifications of shifting from thinking of THE 
INDIVIDUAL AS THE UNIT OF ILLNESS to THE 
FAMILY AS THE UNIT OF ILLNESS are so complex that 
most health professionals still comprehend this as a distant, 
abstract collection of words. After seeing the family as an 
emotional unit, it was logical and automatic to devise a 
method of psychotherapy directed at the unit rather than at 
individuals in the unit. The clinicai use of family therapy 
provided more clues about emotional forces within the unit.

provided more clues about emotional forces within the unit. I believed these new observations contained the building 
blocks for a completely different theory of emotional illness, 
if it was possible to sort and assemble them. I wondered why it had taken so long to SEE this different 
view of the family. I had worked with schizophrenia for years without seeing it. Three main factors seemed related 
to this ability to SEE: (1) the previous years of THINKING 
TOWARD the family, (2) families living together on the 
ward, and (3) the intensity of relationship patterns in 
families with schizophrenia. The absence of any one factor 
could have obscured the view. Jackson was the only other 
family researcher who talked about the potential for a new 
theory of emotional illness, but his thinking went toward a 
communication theory and mine toward a more biologically 
oriented theory. One can wonder what would have evolved 
had he lived into the 1970's. There were reactions when it was discovered that relation­
ship patterns, originally considered specific for schizo­
phrenia, were also present in all other people. In the late 
1950's and early 1960's this resulted in several research 
projects to study "normal" families. To my knowledge all 
that research confirmed that the relationship patterns were 
also present in normal families.

psychiatry associated the relationship patterns, and also 
family therapy, with schizophrenia until early to mid 
1960's. Then the new knowledge was absorbed into the 
literature, as if it has always been there, without specific 
connection to anything. Very slowly bits and pieces of it 
have been appended to conventional individiual theory. I consider March 8, 1957 the national birth date of family 
THERAPY. For some years John Spiegel, Chairman of the 
Family Committee of GAP, had been unsuccessful in his 
search for psychiatrist researchers for his Committee. He 
began to hear about the family researchers in 1956. In 
March 1957 he arranged an all-day panel for family 
research papers at the annual meeting of the American 
Orthopsychiatric Association, the first such family section 
at a national meeting. Mendell, Spiegel, Lidz, and Bowen 
read papers for their research teams. The notion of family 
psychotherapy was discussed briefly. The THERAPY idea 
mushroomed. It was as if the discussion had made family 
therapy legitimate. Increasing numbers of therapists started 
their own version of family therapy. In may 1957 at the 
annual meeting of the American Psychiatric Association, 
there was a section on "Schizophrenia and the Family" with 
papers by Bowen and Dysinger of NIMH, Lidz of Yale, and

the concept of psychotherapy for the family while in Europe 
in 1951. He developed his own intuitive method of family 
group therapy which he continued on a rather private level 
for most of a decade. Satir was a social worker in a state 
hospital setting who had worked with families for years. She 
became an eager member of the family therapy movement 
in the 1958 period. The numbers of pioneers who become 
identified with family therapy in the late 19SO's and early 
1960's increased each year. In the 1957-58 period the family therapy movement 
spiraled into its own orbit that by-passed theory and 
research and went toward developing family therapy as a 
technique. I have referred to this as a "healthy unstructured 
state of chaos," expecting this wild period would soon 
correct itself when therapists could begin to see the 
FAMILY AS AN EMOTIONAL UNIT rather than as a 
collection of individuals. This did not occur. Now, after 
twenty years, the field is still in its "THERAPY" orbit and a 
prolonged "unstructured state of chaos." Hundreds of new 
therapists from various professional disciplines and 
different types of training are joining the field each year.

In 
terms of numbers, a majority of therapists are using a few 
therapeutic methods and dozens of different techniques, 
many based on rather simplistic notions about the nature of 
emotional illness. However, the number of theoreticians, 
serious scholars, researchers, and solid clinicians is slowly 
increasing and providing more structure to the field. The prophetic part of the move to Georgetown began in 
1957. There was a spectrum of different reactions to the 
evidence that relationship patterns in families with schizo­
phrenia, originally considered specific for schizophrenia, 
were present in all other people. At one end of the spectrum 
was that of a senior consultant at NIMH who said, "Since 
these findings are not specific for schizophrenia, you should 
discontinue the family research and devote your time to 
schizophrenia." At the other end of the spectrum was 
George Raines, M.D., Chairman of the Department of 
Psychiatry at Georgetown. In 1957 he asked how the NIMH 
research was going. I said, "About as perfect as it could 
be." He responded, "When you reach the end of your string 
with the government, do not leave Washington without 
coming to see me." As the NIMH string ended in 1959, 
there were numerous job offers, most of which I investi­
gated. No other chairman had as much comprehension of schizophrenia and the family research as George Raines.

No other chairman had as much comprehension of schizophrenia and the family research as George Raines. He 
said, "When you started the research I knew you would not 
find the expected answer to schizophrenia but I also knew 
you would discover all kinds of other things important for 
psychiatry, and I wanted that for Georgetown." He already 
had potential funding to move my entire research staff from 
NIMH to Georgetown. He was realistic about his symptom­
free state and his life expectancy after an operation for lung 
cancer a year before. I terminated at NIMH in July 1959 
and was to start at Georgetown after the first meeting of the 
Executive Committee in September. During the summer 
Dr. Raines' cancer reoccurred and he died in September. I 
went to his funeral and burial in Arlington Cemetery on 
Friday morning, September 11, 1959, a few hours before my 
appointment to the Georgetown faculty that afternoon. After his death the potential funding for the family research 
did not materialize. The story of the Family Program under the chairmanship 
of Dr. Steinbach, and its relationship to the family scene 
nationally, will be continued in future issues of the "Family 
Center Report. " 
SOME THOUGHTS ON THE FAMILY 
Norman Paul, M.D. I was pleased to be asked to review "off-the-cuff' some of 
my current views on the family. The nature of paradoxes 
and how they influence our lives, perceptions, and thinking 
mechanisms has been intriguing to me.

text:
The nature of paradoxes 
and how they influence our lives, perceptions, and thinking 
mechanisms has been intriguing to me. One of these para­
doxes is the whole belief about consciousness or awareness 
of the self and how every person prides himself on being 
conscious when such awareness occurs. It seems that we all 
live with an illusion of consciousness, regardless of 
farfetched, grandiose notions to the contrary. We do have 
an awareness of what we call a self and, at various times, an 
awareness of feelings and thoughts about various matters. However, we have no idea what we look like to the other, no 
idea what is being projected to the other (in non-verbal 
language), while at the same time we harbor notions that we 
are capable of editing the behavior we generate externally. This at times approximates a delusional state as evidenced 
by periodic defensiveness when confronted with inputs from 
others which we have vigorously screened out. This state of affairs so clearly indicates the validity of 
using close-circuit T. V. This technological advance par 
excellence confronts one with the evidence of what is 
unknowable about the self to oneself in an almost majestic 
way. It confirms all too clearly that, like it or not, we are by 
far more unconscious than conscious. Inevitably, this situation leads to other semi-delusional 
views about ourselves and our experience, such as the belief 
that one can learn from one's experience.

Inevitably, this situation leads to other semi-delusional 
views about ourselves and our experience, such as the belief 
that one can learn from one's experience. Here, too, it feels 
good to think and believe that one is learning from one's 
experience. How can one learn from one's experience if the 
crucial data, i.e. self-data about the self, not the edited 
fragments that one remembers, is not available. In The Psychology of Man's Possible Evolution, P.D. Ouspensky discusses the question, "What Is Lying?" 
 As it is understood in ordinary language, lying means 
distorting or in some cases hiding the truth, or what people 
believe to be the truth. This lying plays a very important 
part in life, but there are much worse forms of lying, when 
people do not know that they lie. I said in the last lecture 
that we cannot know the truth in our present state, and can 
only know the truth in the state of objective consciousness. How can we lie? There seems to be a contradiction here, but 
in reality there is none. We cannot know the truth, but we 
can pretend that we know. And this is lying. Lying fills all 
our life. People pretend that they know all sorts of things: 
about God, about the future life, about the universe, about 
the origin of man, about evolution, about everything; but in 
reality they do not know anything, even about themselves. And every time they speak about something they do not 
know as though they knew it, they lie.

In the summer of 1%6 I was seeing a family that con­
sisted of a couple and three children, two girls and a boy. The particular problem was the second girl, Sally, who at 
the time was sixteen years old. The mother had a 
tremendous amount of antipathy and hatred for Sally, and 
Sally, in response to her mother's distancing, began to seek 
the company of questionable peers who were involved with 
drugs and were potential runaways. The more Sally would 
solicit the company of such children, the more abrasive and 
violent her mother would become. The mother and father had had a strained relationship 
for years, the typical scene of the husband being successful 
in his business and the mother waiting out her time for the 
three children to grow up so she could be free. Yet, at the 
same time, in spite of her expressed wishes for the children 
to mature, her actions threw barriers in their paths. This 
situation was confusing for her children and for her 
husband. The principal problem was her lingering 
antipathy toward Sally. One day in June of 1%6, the mother reported that Sally 
came home after wrenching her elbow playing tennis. Because she was unable to internally rotate her right arm, 
Sally asked her mother to snap her bra for her. The mother 
became irate and abusive.

Paul MacLean, M.D., Director of the National Institute 
of Mental Health's Laboratory of Brain Evolution and 
Behavior, will be the visiting guest expert at the Sixteenth 
Georgetown University Symposium on Family Psycho­
therapy to be held November 16 and 17 at Stouffer's 
National Convention Center in Crystal City, Virginia. Dr. MacLean will speak on the "triune" brain, a concept he has 
developed from thirty years of research on the functioning 
of the human brain. "Triune" is one of many neologisms coined by Dr. MacLean. It refers to evidence that the brain is really three 
brains in one: the ancient reptilian core, (which MacLean 
calls the R-complex) the old mammalian brain (or visceral 
brain, or limbic system); and the neocortex, (the main 
reason humans differ from animals). Dr. MacLean has 
demonstrated the anatomi,cal separateness and chemical 
distinctness of the three brains and maintains that they 
control distinct groups of behavior. His work raises interest­
ing questions about the differences between instincts, 
emotions, and thinking, and where the locus of control for 
human behavior lies. The selection of Dr. MacLean as the visiting guest expert 
is a reflection of the Family Center's interest and commit­
ment to learning about man's physiological functioning and 
its relationship to emotional behavior. Dr.

For a long time I have been thinking of how best to make 
changes in the research program at the Family Center. Certain issues are involved: (1) the development of ideas, 
and (2) the willingness to work for long-term goals. Clinic 
fees and course tuition produce income for the Family 
Center that assures that the rent will be paid and that staff 
salaries will be met. Faculty members are already over­
worked and over-committed, by and large, and if an x 
amount of money is needed for their personal budgets, they 
are likely to choose to see families to assure their personal 
income. I have known all along that the Center has not alloted 
either the time or the budget for research. Doing projections 
for one and five years away in terms of goals and ways to get 
there has been a very worthwhile experience for me. On 
Scott Mcyu's ·recommendation and with Ruth Sagar's 
assistance it became necessary to make budget projections 
so that as a Center we could better plan the amount of space 
required before the lease expires next year. To make these projections I began to look at the past. It 
was a real eye-opener to discover that only 1 % of the Family 
Center's income supported research. This is particularly 
interesting since research is said to be one of the priorities of 
the Center and of all those involved in it.

The Symposium was special for many reasons. Many attendees "heard" and "saw" connections be­
tween family systems theory and the life sciences that 
had formerly eluded them. This "hearing" and "seeing" 
appeared to transcend the customary analogizing be­
tween human and subhuman life forms that has char­
acterized many past symposia. The presentations taken 
as a whole seemed to make it irrelevant to formulate 
notions about human behavior that do not begin with 
man's similarity to all life. What was also clear was 
that if man's tie to nature is a reality rather than a 
philosophical position, then comprehending the dif­
ference between the realms of science and philosophy 
is more than an academic exercise. Careful distinctions 
are essential for advancing knowledge about behavior. There were other factors that made this symposium 
unique. It was held at the newly opened Leavey Cen­
ter on the Georgetown campus, marking the return of 
the Symposium to Georgetown for the first time since 
1970. The new hotel and meeting facility was ideal. It 
had the conveniences of off-campus convention facili­
ties and the added bonus of the Georgetown Univer­
sity ambiance.

made during the ninety-minute panel discussion was 
Dr. Bonner's view that most biologists specifically 
avoid extending their conceptualizations to human 
behavior. This avoidance may result from human be­

all living systems, not just human systems. Bowen had

Andrea Maloney-Schara 
At the Thursday Professional Meeting in July 1988, 
Andrea Schara presented a broad overview of the theo­
retical ideas that guided her clinical research project 
on AIDS and the Family. This research effort with 
eight families where one person in the family has AIDS 
. or tested positive for HIV influenced a rethinking of 
ideas about differentiation and anxiety. Many variables are involved in the development of 
symptoms. The hypothesis guiding the research was if 
one person in a family could modify his emotional 
reactivity to others while maintaining contact with 
them, his immune system and the family would reflect 
a greater ability to function. The research was designed 
to move away from a focus on pathology and towards 
a focus on the individual's ability to manage self in 
the emotional system. The basic foundation of this 
effort was: I) on separating a self from patterns of 
behavior which the individual had defined as dysfunc­
tional and 2) on lowering anxiety which was defined 
as the responsiveness that makes it difficult to know 
self. A broad way of thinking about differentiation at 
various levels in nature seemed to provide intellectual 
space for both therapist and client. The effort to think 
about self as part of a system is more obvious when it 
can be factually noted in other parts of the natural 
world.

The effort to think 
about self as part of a system is more obvious when it 
can be factually noted in other parts of the natural 
world. Processes which involve the push to be an indi­
vidual and the pull to go along with others occur in 
various forms of life. For example, an ant colony is 
 activated by a stimulus from the environment. The 
needs of the colony for workers or soldiers influence, 
or perhaps even determine, what kind of genes are ex­
pressed. A biochemical process is activated. This sig­
naling process allows the colony to regroup and adapt 
to the changing conditions. It is easier to see these 
processes in other systems in nature than it is in the 
human family. These kinds of emotional organizations 
are predominant in nature. These processes place con­
straints on the members of any emotional unit. In the 
human family, this can be seen when one member be­
gins to separate a self. Reactivity to others and to different ideas increa­
ses during times of anxiety. In this research biofeed­

vided for a period of learning to calm self after encoun­
tering differences. The thinking part of self can be 
used to manage the physiological reaction to differen­
ces. In general, symptoms tend to be less intense when 
anxiety is lower. Yet the effort to be a self in relation­
ship to important others usually increases anxiety. Biofeedback is one way to mediate the short term re­
action.

On December 8, 1988, Victoria Harrison examined 
the concept of "stress" in light of the history of the­
ory development in the natural sciences. She described 
the extent to which a concept such as "stress" has de­
fined the direction of scientific research of human 
functioning. Ms. Harrison contended that this direction 
has limitations and may be misleading in the search 
for a science of human behavior. Ms. Harrison's questions about the concept of 
stress grew from her evaluation of the scientific litera­
ture on a variety of physical symptoms, especially re­
productive functioning. In reviewing this literature, 
she began to see limitations in research methodologies 
and findings. Stress is a concept underlying much of current re­
search. Ms. Harrison discussed this topic in three gen­
eral areas: 1) the history and definitions of science, 
2) the literature on stress and its shortcomings, and 
3) the study of emotional systems as another avenue 
for understanding these phenomena. In describing the history of Western science, Ms. Harrison painted broad brush the early efforts of the 
human to describe nature based on observation rather 
than on imagination. These early organized observa­
tions included mathematics, the calendar, agriculture 
and astronomy and, in later centuries, anatomy, bio­
logy and the taxonomy of living things. In the l 800's 
the effort moved beyond description to defining the 
way in which nature is organized.

In the l 800's 
the effort moved beyond description to defining the 
way in which nature is organized. Darwin's theory of 
natural selection expanded the laws of inheritance de­
fined by Mendel. However, the impact of Darwin's 
theory on philosophy and the arts seemed to oversha­
dow its application in the natural sciences at the time. In the 1900's scientists focused initially on the gene 
as the unit of observation. The l 930's saw knowledge 
from evolution and genetics combined to form what 
has been called "the grand synthesis." More recently, 
 thinkers such as Dr. Bonner and Dr. Kerr have claimed 
there are many unanswered questions and great leaps 
are still required to account for how evolution occurs. In the 1900's the field of psychology reflected an 
organized effort to study the human. William James, 
Freud, and Pavlov based their theories on principles 
other than evolution. Freud drew from classical litera­
ture to describe the two-person relationship. Other 
prominent ideas were stimulus/response and operant 
conditioning. In the 1920's the field of physiology moved be­
yond human anatomy with Walter Cannon's concept 
of "fight or flight" which defined a systemic response 
of the human organism to a challenge. The concept of 
stress originated with Hans Selye, who attempted to 
unify medicine with the natural sciences.

Murray Bowen, M.D. Reviewed by Daniel V. Papero 
On Thursday, January 23, 1989, the audience 
attending the Family Center's Third Thursday Profes­
sional Meeting was privileged to hear Dr. Murray 
Bowen speak on the topic Science and Therapy. The 
title turned out to be slightly misleading as Dr. Bowen 
concentrated on the development of theory and his 
lifelong odyssey toward science. Dr. Bowen recounted precisely the steps toward 
the development of a natural systems theory of the 
human. Medicine is a mixture of science (the develop­
ment of knowledge) and practice (the application of 
science). Dr. Bowen had always been interested pri­
marily in the scientific side of medicine. After early 
interest in surgery and experience as a general practi­
tioner in rural Tennessee, he emerged from medical 
service in the Second World War with the belief that 
the work of Sigmund Freud had made psychiatry into 
a science. He matriculated at the Menninger Founda­
tion, where he immersed himself in the new theory of 
Freud and the details of contemporary psychiatric 
practice.

He matriculated at the Menninger Founda­
tion, where he immersed himself in the new theory of 
Freud and the details of contemporary psychiatric 
practice. He realized that although Freud had defined a 
body of scientific fact, his theory was not scientific. With the belief that a science of the human was pos­
sible, Dr. Bowen reported spending several years im­
mersed in the literature of other disciplines for clues 
to and a basis for a science of the human. From this 
effort emerged his view that Darwin and the theory 
of evolution had the greatest value to his effort. There 
was no way, however, to connect the facts of Freud 
with evolution without some sort of systems theory. Although others at that time were developing a 
systems theory that has come to be known as general 
systems theory, Dr. Bowen reported only minimal ex­
posure to these ideas. Instead he created the way of 
thinking which he called natural systems theory. With 
natural systems theory as his guide, he combined the 
facts of Freud, Darwin and the reproductive human 
family to produce a new theory of the human family. The facts articulated by Freud applied to the two per­
son system, the analyst and the patient. The new the­
ory could move beyond the two person system to one 
comprised of multiple people. In 1954, Dr. Bowen 
moved to the NIH, where the new theory was put to 
work with entire families.

attributed them to conventional theory. The fact of 
the existence of a new theory was ignored. Later ver­
sions of this process treated all systems theories as 
equivalent, and the uniqueness of natural systems the­
ory was lost. A variety of erosive forces operated to 
maintain conventional viewpoints and wear away at 
foundations of a new way of thinking. Such erosive 
pressures have not abated with time and are present among the Family Center faculty as well as in the 
broader professional community. Science, according to Dr. Bowen, is proven fact. No one today seriously argues that the Earth is flat. Earth's spheroid shape has become science. One of the 
great dilemmas in developing a science of the human 
is the tendency to substitute the products of the hu­
man brain (subjectivity, thought, imagination, feeling) 
for proven fact. The output of the human brain can 
be called mind. The brain is science, but its products 
are not. When science is mixed with mind, theory is 
lost. The future of knowledge of the human is bound­
less. There are many facts currently known, and many 
that remain to be discovered and proved.

TOWARD THEORY 
Murray Bowen, M.D. There have been an increasing number of unsolici­
ted communications about the way lives have been 
changed by Bowen Systems Theory. Many have taken 
the form of 'My life has been different since/ learned 
your theory." There were frequent questions, "What 
was so helpful?" Responses were as personal as the 
original statement. The wonderment was often discus­
sed in regular theory meetings. Roberta Gilbert, M.D. attended most of the meetings. She did a paper that 
combined her own personal reasons about the way her 
professional life changed after learning the theory. It 
was detailed enough for the Family Center Report, 
but took the form of a personal testimonial rather 
than an objective report. As such, it was not publish­
able. If it were possible to rewrite the paper, eliminate 
most of the personal pronouns, and put the content 
into the third person, the theoretical content might 
qualify for publication. A lesser writer might not have 
been intrigued by such a rewrite. A new report was sub­
mitted within days. It is printed here for the readers. A good theory is usually an impersonal thing, fash­
ioned from universal knowledge and careful observa­
tion. It is usually free of personal pronouns, unless 
used to convey meaning, or unless there is specific 
reason to delineate self from others in the field.

This statement, taken as a challenge,

at the interface of life and theory, trying for more ob­
jectivity and clarity. It would, of course, be impossible 
to speak for all the people who have written, but one 
can speak for oneself. As a result of being in touch 
with a different way of thinking, certain changes have 
taken place. WHAT HAPPENED 
Professional changes. Solid residency training pro­
grams equipped psychiatrists to use two main tools: 
psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy and drugs. Clinical experience and the demands of the training 
were such that facility with both was obtained by the 
time one graduated. These tools were doubtless of 
value. Countless people were "helped.'' As one's career 
unfolded, however, there were some areas where the 
training, and perhaps traditional psychiatric theory, 
fell short. Traditional methods seemed inadequate 
when it came to parents who were having difficulty 
with their children. Traditional theory said little about 
how to deal with people who were having relationship 
problems. Addicted people were completely off limits. Unfortunately, a very high percentage of people who 
ask for help fall into these categories.

Addicted people were completely off limits. Unfortunately, a very high percentage of people who 
ask for help fall into these categories. Theoretically, it was possible to assist people to 
attain a higher level of functioning than they had had 
before their "illness" but there were very few guide­
lines to use other than uncovering and understanding 
"psychopathology." It was believed that if people un­
derstood their pathology they would automatically 
go on to a higher level of functioning. However, ex­
perience showed all too often that: 1) they did not 
always improve as a result of uncovering and under-
 standing and 2) if they did, it was only to their for­
mer level, not to higher and higher levels of emotional 
maturity or functioning. Ultimately, if a person could 
get to where they had been prior to the onset of symp­
toms, the clinician learned to be content. In addition, people often found theoretically 
sound interpretations ludicrous, irrelevant, or not 
helpful enough, even when these interpretations were 
carefully timed and gently delivered. Working with a 
theory which did not speak to wide areas of human 
existence and which was not appreciated by much of 
the patient population took an inevitable toll on the 
clinician. When Bowen Family Systems Theory became 
available, clinical work became an exciting mental 
workout - a scientific project to discover if and how 
the principles matched the field.
