When Bowen Family Systems Theory became 
available, clinical work became an exciting mental 
workout - a scientific project to discover if and how 
the principles matched the field. Here was a way to 
think about relationship problems between adults or 
between parents and children. There was no need to 
exclude addicted people from the broad, inclusive 
theory. People did not find theory ludicrous or irrele­
vant. They found it useful. They often put it into use 
immediately, and they got positive results in their 
lives. Best of all, they talked of higher levels of func­
tioning than they had ever experienced. Once, after 
something about the concept of the scale of differen­
tiation had been explained to a person, he came back 
the next session saying, "In all the seven years I have 
been seeing you, that is the most helpful thing you 
have ever told me. Why haven't you ever told me that 
before?" The more theory one mastered, the better 
the clinical results. Family relationship changes. It is difficult to explain 
the effect of bridging cutoffs in a family, but the ef­
fect is profound. Loss of symptoms, improvement in 
all areas of functioning (emotional, intellectual, and 
physical) and a sense of steady groundedness were 
some of the tangible results. There is more interaction 
and that interaction is of a higher quality among all 
the members of the family. Functioning of less func­
tional members has steadily gone upward.

Dr. Peter Titelman presented a paper on the uni­
versal taboo, incest, for the Professional Lecture Series 
on February 16, 1989. Incest has been an area of special study for Dr. Titelman for several years. He has gained clinical ex­

this time. He believes that the current trend toward 
outspokenness about incest may at times result in re­

seen in positions of blaming the offender and isolating 
him from his family, which only results in intensifying 
family triangles and reactivity. For that reason, Dr. Titelman worked to find a way to explore the problem 
from a family systems point of view, looking for a 
way to keep a neutral position himself. He found more 
neutrality in what he called a "multiperspectival 
approach." This approach meant that he could see 
through the eyes of everyone in the family; not only 
the child, but also the mother, the other siblings and 
the offender. Dr.

universal taboo, but is universally broken in all socie­
ties. Although the taboo is not defined in precisely

society is mother-son, father-daughter or brother-sister

age between genetic evolution and cultural history."

NATURAL SELECTION THEORY 
AND THE EMOTIONAL SYSTEM 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. Family systems theory describes precise, predictable 
patterns of human emotional functioning and behavior. These patterns are assumed to be embedded in an emo­
tional system that is a product of man's evolutionary her­
itage. An important question raised by Bowen's de­
scription of these patterns is whether their existence is 
consistent with present evolutionary theory. Is the evo­
lutionary outcome of the human family being an emo­
tional unit, a unit governed by the counterbalancing life 
forces of individuality and togetherness, consistent with 
what is known about how natural selection shapes evolu­
tionary change? Research by biologist Leo Buss suggests that natural 
selection theory can explain how the family evolved into 
an emotional unit that exhibits a fundamental conflict 
between the individual and the group. It would appear 
from Buss' ideas that for natural selection to explain such 
an outcome, selection would have had to have acted on 
the family or social group as well as on the individual. There are some emotional processes in the human family, 
however, that may not fit easily into current evolutionary 
theory.

There are some emotional processes in the human family, 
however, that may not fit easily into current evolutionary 
theory. A family process that may indicate the need for 
amplification or modification of evolutionary theory is 
the regression in functioning and symptom development 
associated with heightened chronic anxiety. However, 
before discussing those aspects of human emotional pro­
cess that may or may not fit with evolutionary theory, 
Buss' argument for how natural selection can explain the 
patterns of embryonic development (ontogeny) will be 
described. The striking parallels between the developing 
embryo as an emotional unit and the multigenerational 
family as an emotional unit stimulated this presentation. Development is one of the great puzzles of biology. How can the progression from a fertilized egg to a fully 
formed fetus be explained? Normal development de­
pends on cells dividing the right number of times, 
growing to the right sizes, migrating to the right places, 
and differentiating into specialists that are essential for 
the integrity of the whole. What forces make develop­
ment an orderly and predictable process? How did the 
order and predictability come to be? How did the varia­
tions in development that produce the vast diversity of SUMMER 1989 
life forms evolve? In Buss' book, Evolution of Individ­
uality, the patterns of ontogeny are explained through the 
application of natural selection theory.

In Buss' book, Evolution of Individ­
uality, the patterns of ontogeny are explained through the 
application of natural selection theory. It is a pioneering 
attempt to apply natural selection theory more broadly 
than it has generally been applied since the modem syn­
thesis (the wedding of population genetics and natural 
selection theory that occurred early in this century). Buss considers this broader application of natural selec­
tion to be more consistent with Darwin's original theory. Darwin observed that all the offspring of a given or­
ganism are not exactly the same, and that these differ­
ences among offspring can be passed to their descen­
dants. The existence of heritable variation among off­
spring means that organisms can evolve to be increas­
ingly suited to their natural habitats. Since the diversity 
of natural habitats and ecological pressures is great, the 
diversity oflife forms is great. This is the theory of nat­
ural selection. The original theory lacked any mechanism 
by which variation might be inherited. In addition, the 
original theory envisioned natural selection acting on 
groups as well as on individuals. In Buss' view a tacit 
assumption of the modem synthesis is that the individual 
is the sole unit of biological organization upon which 
natural selection acts. Buss holds that natural selection 
can act on many "levels" of biological organization si­
multaneously.

Buss holds that natural selection 
can act on many "levels" of biological organization si­
multaneously. If natural selection is assumed to act on 
more than one level, and if the conflict between the inter­
ests of the component cells of an organism and the inter­
ests of the organism as a whole is appreciated, then the 
evolution of many basic patterns of ontogeny can be ex­
plained. It is generally thought that life originated when certain 
molecules developed the ability to replicate themselves. Transitions to more complex life forms followed. One 
theory about the progression to greater complexity is that 
autonomously replicating molecules were associated into 
self-replicating complexes, self-replicating complexes 
were incorporated into cells, autonomously replicating 
organelles such as mitochondria were also incorporated 
into cells, cells associated to become multicellular indi­
viduals, and individuals associated to become multimem­
ber groups. Buss theorizes about one of these transitions 
or steps towards the development of complex life forms. This transition, which occurred sometime in the 
Precambrian period, was from free-living, totipotent 
(undifferentiated) cells to multicellular individuals with 
division of labor (cell differentiation). When cells that had been living independently began 
living in groups, the "group" represented a primitive 
multicellular organism. At first none of the cells in the 
group perfonned any specialized functions.

At first none of the cells in the 
group perfonned any specialized functions. Over time, 
however, random genetic mutations resulted in some 
member cells being different from other member cells. If 
a change in a member cell produced a specialized func­
tion (differentiation) that resulted in the total organism 
being at an advantage relative to other organisms in its 
ecological niche, natural selection acting at the level of 
the individual organism would have favored preservation 
of the new function. It would have favored it because 
the organism with the advantage would be more likely to 
survive and reproduce than its less specialized competi­
tors. Since the new function increases the reproductive 
success of the total organism, it also increases the 
chances of the member cell specialist's genes being rep­
resented in the next generation. The basis of the new 
function would have to be heritable, but the details of the 
heritability are too complex for this presentation. There is a problem, however. When a member cell 
specializes, it disadvantages its own reproductive poten­
tial. By directing its cellular "machinery" to perf onn a 
specialized function, it has less "machinery" available to 
clone itself. So while the specialist is behaving altruisti­
cally (in reference to the organism as a whole) and com­
promising its own reproduction, its undifferentiated cel­
lular neighbors are behaving individualistically.

The in­
dividualists preserve their cellular "machinery" for repro­
duction and, as a consequence, reproduce faster than the 
specialist. Herein lies the dilemma. Natural selection 
acting at the level of the individual organism that has the 
advantage by virtue of its member cell's specializations 
favors preservation of that organism. However, natural 
selection acting at the level of the cell lineages (member 
cells and their descendants) favors lineages that are pro­
ducing the most descendants, the undifferentiated lin­
eages. So how did evolution manage to preserve repro­
ductively disadvantaged specialists? Why does the or­
ganism not become overrun by undifferentiated cells? Had this overrun occurred, life as we know it would not 
have evolved. For a harmoniously functioning, differentiated, multi­
cellular unit (such as Homo sapiens) to evolve, mecha­
nisms had to evolve to control the propensity of cells to 
reproduce without contributing any specialized functions 
to the group. Natural selection at the level of the individ­
ual organism had to effectively oppose selection at the 
level of cell lineages. Over millions of years the propen­
sity for continued self-replication of cell lineages was in 
fact (according to this theory) subjugated to the interests 
of the whole.

fact (according to this theory) subjugated to the interests 
of the whole. Buss considers the principal innovation of 
metazoans (animals having a body composed of cells 
differentiated into tissues and organs) to be the evolution 
of processes ("epigenetic controls") that restrain the in­
herent propensity of cells to self-replicate. The competi­
tion between the "rights" of the cell and the "needs" of 
the group has, through natural selection, achieved a bal­
ance that preserves the integrity of the group. This in­
tegrity is evident in the orderly patterns of cell division, 
cell growth, cell migration, and cell differentiation that 
characterize the development of metazoans. Buss refers to the controls on cellular self-replication 
as "epigenetic" because the specialized destiny of any 
component cell of an organism is not detcnnined by that cell's base sequences of DNA. A cell's outcome is de­
termined, rather, by the interactions between the cell and 
its environment. The dependence of a cell's outcome on 
its environment is illustrated by an experiment with an 
amphibian embryo. For a period in the embryo's devel­
opment, if cells that would normally develop into an eye 
are transplanted to other areas of the embryo, the cells 
will develop into structures appropriate for the area to 
which they have been transplanted.

If the cells are sim­
ply cut out of the embryo and allowed to develop in a salt 
solution, they form no recognizable structures whatso­
ever. So the cells of an embryo early in development 
have no capacity on their own to develop into any one 
structure. Their ultimate fate depends on external influ­
ences. These external influences, which are assumed to 
be encoded in the genomes of other cells, comprise the 
epigenetic controls. Several types of epigenetic controls have evolved. One control is "maternal predestination." When the 
mother produces an egg, some of her cytoplasm contain­
ing messenger-RNA and gene activators is deposited in 
that egg. This means that after the egg is fertilized, the 
embryo's own genes do not direct its early development. The mother directs it. No opportunity exists for a cell in 
the young embryo to "do its own thing." Any increase in 
selfish individualism is simply not possible. Another 
important epigenetic control is "induction." Cells, 
through electrical or chemical stimuli, can induce neigh­
boring cells to specialize. In response to inductive influ­
ences, however, cellular "competence" has also evolved. Competence describes whatever capacity cells have to 
resist attempts by other cells to dictate to them. Complex 
interactions during the course of development (consisting 
of cells pressuring and resisting one another) eventually 
lead to a developmental outcome of groups of cells dif­
ferentiated into organs and tissues.

any cell lineage to know the "master plan" of the organ­

behaviors that natural selection has perfected over evolu­

behaviors is the way cells interact with other cells. Since 
the activity of one cell cannot be explained out of the 
context of its relationship to other cells, the concept of a 
relationship system is essential. Furthermore, since the 
characteristics of a cellular relationship system at any 
given moment depend on the characteristics of earlier

an organism indicates a primary change having occurred 
in normal cells that transforms them into cancer cells. Buss reflects this view in stating that cancer cells 
"succeed because mutations giving rise to them ultimately 
endow them with a greater replication rate than their 
neighbors." A transformed cell has the ability to evade 
normal host controls on its reproduction and to mobilize 
resources in its environment to support its growth. The 
question for evolutionary theorists is the following: If 
cell differentiation during development depends on epi­
genetic controls, why should such controls not continue 
to be of paramount influence in adult organisms? Could 
not the primary disturbance in cancer be a disturbance in 
the epigenetic controls on cell differentiation? A cell in 
an adult organism may continue to replicate rather than 
differentiate because it does not receive the signals from 
other cells on which its differentiation depends. Cancer 
may reflect a disturbance or regression in cellular rela­
tionships that is fostered by heightened chronic anxiety. Viewing cancer as primarily reflecting a disturbed bal­
ance of cellular relationships appears to extend Buss' 
ideas about the evolution of developmental processes.

Among the distinguished speakers at Georgetown 
University's Bicentennial Colloquium, Utraque Unum, 
on April 4-5, 1989, was E.O. Wilson of Harvard 
University. His talk, entitled Biological and Human 
Determinants of the Survival of the Species, covered four 
general areas: 1) the biological basis of human nature, 2) 
the close genetic affinity of the human with other organ­
isms, 3) the diversity of life on earth and how human be­
havior affects it and, 4) the need to join science and the 
humanities more closely in consideration of the human's 
place in the world and in relation to all other life. Two general views currently appear at odds with one 
another. The first might be called scientific humanism. It essentially incorporates the general view of modem 
biology that life is self-assembling, i.e., that an au­
tonomous process of random mutation and extreme natu­
ral selection across innumerable ecological events and 
across millions of years can produce the reduced set of 
genes now known to be human. A key element in the 
definition is the word autonomous. Life, from its be­
ginnings to the present, requires no more explanation 
than mutation, recombination, and rigorous natural se­
lection to account for what has evolved. Life has pro­
duced itself without any direction.

spectrum where little ambiguity exists as to the basic

human sensory system determines how color vocabulary 
has developed in many different languages. In a second 
example, Wilson cited research which appears to 
demonstrate that human arousal is greatest when pre­
sented a figure having the complexity of a ten to twenty 
tum maze.

Scientists have described 1.4 million species to date, but 
it is estimated that the total number is between 10 and 30 
million. The majority of these known and unknown 
species exist in the tropical rain forests. The diversity of 
life occurs through a process called adaptive radiation 
and has occurred repeatedly in the history of life. The fate of the Earth, according to Wilson, is mir­
rored in the destruction of the unique ecology of St. Helen's island. Over the past century and a half, that 
ecology has been virtually destroyed by human action. This destruction is now occurring on a worldwide basis. The destruction of the tropical rain forests is the latest 
and perhaps most serious manifestation of this process. Wilson speaks of the four horsemen of the ecological 
apocalypse: 1) ozone depletion, 2) the greenhouse ef­
fect, 3) toxic pollution and, 4) the depletion of species 
due to the destruction of environments. The destruction 
of the rain forests is the most serious and current of these 
developments due to the tremendous profusion of life 
that exists there. The rain forests now have been reduced 
to 50% of their original extent and are currently being 
destroyed at the rate of half a football field per second. Wilson calls the effect of this destruction on species di­
versity catastrophic. He estimates that ten thousand 
species per year are lost due to cutting the rain forests 
alone.

stood it, and we only think we have control. We don't 
even know why we respond a certain way to other or­

Noone discussed the process of symbiosis in the 
history of evolution, from the unnucleated cell through 
the nucleated cell and multi-cellular organisms to the par­
ent/child relationship in the animal world. Central to understanding the evolution of natural sys­
tems is the concept of natural selection. Although 
Darwin's theory continues to undergo modifications, the 
basic notion that life reproduces itself with some varia­
tion remains unaltered. The variants that "fit" better in 
the environment are selected for; that is, they are more 
likely to mature and reproduce than those which "fit" less 
well, accounting for both stability and gradual change in 
life forms. What has been modified in Darwin's theory of natural 
selection is defining what constitutes "the unit of selec­
tion." He did not define the mechanism by which varia­
tion is inherited. The framers of the modem synthesis, 
who integrated Mendelian genetics with Darwin's the­
ory, defined the individual organism as the unit of selec­
tion. They posit that the genetic material determines what 
is inherited and what varies. The individual organism, as 
the expression of the genome, interacts with the envi­
ronment and is selected for or against on the basis of this 
interaction.

phylogenetic tree. Usually multicellular organisms have 
resulted from the banding together of offspring of the 
same parent cell, but in some cases cells of different par­

such an example. Cells themselves, if they are to func­

so the clustering together of cells into larger organisms 
has been nature's solution to this problem. Among multicellular life forms the degree to which 
cells adhere to one another, communicate, and develop 
specialized functions varies widely. On a continuum of 
cellular integration and differentiation, at one end can be 
found loosely integrated cells which are identical in 
structure and function and which have the capacity to live 
apart for periods of time.

He pursued his 
studies first at the Arnhem Zoo in the Netherlands and 
more recently at facilities in the United States. Dr. de Waal drew upon this work in discussing four 
aspects of primate behavior: 1) the political life of chim­
panzees in the colony of the Arnhem Zoo; 2) the degree to 
which chimpanzees depend upon one another and develop 
reciprocal relationships, including food sharing; 3) domi­
nance style among primates; 4) the function of sexual be­
havior among bonobos in regulating group tension and 
behavior. The chimpanzee colony at Arnhem is the largest in 
captivity. Twenty-five animals are maintained on a large 
island, approximately 2.5 acres, surrounded by a moat. Dr. de Waal studied the behaviorof this group extensively 
for several years. The shifting social structure of the 
group provided ample opportunity to observe the interplay 
of dominance, aggression, and reconciliation among the 
animals. Dominance behaviors can be both formalized and 
aggressive. Formalized dominance behaviors are WINTER 1990 
expressed in rituals in which no aggression occurs. Among chimpanzee males, submissive greeting rituals 
characterize dominance. Such rituals are always 
unidirectional; that is, the less dominant always greets the 
more dominant and never the reverse. Aggressive 
dominance behaviors are self-evident, consisting both of 
bluff and, rarely, actual violence. Dominance structures can be stable for long periods of 
time in a chimpanzee troop.

Aggressive 
dominance behaviors are self-evident, consisting both of 
bluff and, rarely, actual violence. Dominance structures can be stable for long periods of 
time in a chimpanzee troop. The group at Arnhem had 
been stable for approximately three years before Dr. de 
Waal's study began. Shortly after he arrived, however, 
the dominance order among the males was challenged, 
and a fascinating process began to unfold. When the 
hierarchy among male chimpanzees begins to change, a 
predictable sequence of developments occurs. The first 
indication of the process is the refusal of a subordinate 
male to greet the higher ranking individual. A second 
stage follows in which the challenger engages in threats 
and bluffs directed at the dominant or alpha individual. These displays culminate in actual violence .4% of the 
time. Most injuries are not fatal, but under certain condi­
tions chimpanzees can and do engage in systematic 
killing. At Arnhem, dominance is determined by coalitions in 
which two or more individuals join together to defeat an­
other. A male can employ two strategies in his pursuit of 
higher rank. He can find a male ally of sufficient strength 
that the two together can force the submission of the alpha 
male, and he can court the support of females in maintain­
ing and enhancing his position. Much like a human 
politician, the chimpanzee courts the backing of the fe­
males by interacting with their offspring and socializing 
with the mothers themselves.

politician, the chimpanzee courts the backing of the fe­
males by interacting with their offspring and socializing 
with the mothers themselves. Researchers believe the 
support of the females is less important in the wild, where 
the females are able to move away from the males when 
necessary. Coalitions are essentially triadic in nature, a situation 
of two against one. Often a minimum winning coalition is 
established; that is, a coalition of two weaker individuals 
who together are strong enough to defeat a stronger indi­
vidual. One of the winning coalition becomes the domi­
nant or alpha individual but is totally dependent upon the 
coalition partner for the maintenance of his dominance. The supporting partner gains certain advantages in terms 
of sexual opportunity and status. The alpha male has only 
intimidation to keep his partner in line, because direct ag­
gression might lead to the latter's switching allegiance, 
ending the farmer's ability to maintain his position. Predictable patterns of behavior can be observed re­
peatedly in the triadic coalition. The outsider can attempt 
to woo one of the alliance, seeking a shift in alignment. He can also attempt to gain the assistance of others in 
neutralizing the alpha's partner in order to meet the domi­
nant one on more even terms. The dominant individual 
can respond by interfering in his partner's social 
interaction with others (a separating intervention in Dr. de 
Waal's terms).

servable, frequently following moments of conflict or 
aggression which are the outcome of the behaviors de­

to another, followed by grooming and kissing. In this 
manner fences are mended and tensions abated, although 
sometimes only temporarily. Females engage in what De 
Waal calls mediation behavior. This occurs when two 
males are in conflict. The female will approach one and 
begin to groom him. Then she leads the first male to the 
second, whom she begins to groom. She then moves 
away from the pair, who continue grooming one another. The consistency with which one animal supports an­
other varies from totally consistent to somewhat less. Males are generally less consistent than females, and the 
older males of the group are the least consistent. This 
suggests what one might expect: that older males rely 
more on alliances to maintain their position in the group as 
their own physical strength declines. Dr. de Waal's 
research indicates that male chimpanzees are twenty times 
more likely to engage in conflict with one another than are 
females.

females. On the other hand, males reconcile much more

necessary among male chimps in the wild in order to 
maintain a territory, and one can never know who one's 
next partner will be. Therefore, relationships must be 
maintained and repaired to meet basic requirements. Females in the wild are more dispersed and less reliant on 
cooperation. Some anthropologists have argued that food sharing is 
the cornerstone of reciprocal relationships among hu­
mans. Among chimpanzees, hierarchies seem to disap­
pear during food sharing. The interactions are character­
ized by the various reassurance behaviors described 
above. However, immediately prior to the food sharing, 
when the food is shown, the animals engage in a flurry of 
status communication behaviors and kissing and embrac­
ing just before the distinctions are reduced during the ac­
tual sharing of the food. Aggressive interactions among 
the animals during food sharing cannot be predicted on 
the basis of hierarchy. Some animals refuse to share their 
food and can be characterized as "stingy." These animals 
are recipients of the most aggression. They are not at­
tacked, however, when they refuse to share their food.

fonn a matrilineal system in which kinship is important. Daughters inherit the social rank of their mothers. While

the dominance hierarchy is predictable in direction, (a 
fairly rigid system) and aggression is severe. Among

less predictable and its intensity is milder. Stumptails en­
gage in aggressive behavior twice as frequently as rhesus, 
but the intensity of the aggressive interaction is much less. Consequently stumptail macaques arc injured far less 
often than their rhesus counterparts, even though stump­
tails interact aggressively much more frequently. Dr. De 
Waal concludes that dominance style is determined by 
how much the dominant individual needs the subordinate: 
the more the dominant needs the subordinate, the less 
despotic his behaviors will be.

How can the differences in the ways people respond

the development of physiology in the human generally 
begins with birth. Ms. Friesen presented information on 
important aspects of the environment before birth. Ms. Friesen presented many interesting findings culled 
from reading The Roots of Human Behavior by Myron Hofer.* First she noted that he makes no distinction be­

opmental biology, but sees the development of behavior

constant interaction of gene, behavior, and environment 
from the very beginning. Organisms at any stage of de­
velopment can move toward more development only in in­
teraction with the environment. There are innumerable 
environmental factors acting on different levels of devel­

Reviewed by 
Michael E. Kerr 
The presentation for the Monthly Professional Meeting 
in February was given by Steven M. Stanley, Ph.D., 
Professor of Paleobiology, Department of Earth and 
Planetary Sciences, The Johns Hopkins University. His 
title was, Brain Size, Bipedalism, and Climatic Forcing in 
the Evolution of the Human Genus, Homo. Among the questions asked by evolutionists, one of 
the oldest pertains to whether man walked upright before 
his big brain evolved or whether his big brain preceded 
his bipedalism. Darwin dealt with this question by 
reasoning that the big brain evolved to facilitate tool use, 
so until the hands were free to use tools (which would 
have accompanied bipedalism), natural selection would 
not have favored the evolution of a larger brain. The 
discovery of Lucy, the 3.5-million-ycar-old specimen of 
Australopithecus afarensis, confirmed Darwin's view. She walked upright, but did not have a big brain. Dr. Stanley presented his hypothesis about the forces that 
favored evolution of a larger brain once our ancestors 
were walking upright.

She walked upright, but did not have a big brain. Dr. Stanley presented his hypothesis about the forces that 
favored evolution of a larger brain once our ancestors 
were walking upright. An important component of Dr. Stanley's argument is 
the phenomenon of neoteny. When certain structures of a 
developing organism are delayed in reaching their final 
mature state, the result is an adult organism (or an 
organism at some intermediate stage of development) that 
has features normally present only in the more immature 
stages of that organism. The retention of immature 
characteristics in a more mature stage is called neoteny, 
and when it occurs, these characteristics are subject to 
natural selection. In other words, if a delay in the 
maturation of certain structures favors survival, the 
factors that promote this delay will spread through a 
population. An important aspect of neoteny is that a 
maturation delay in one structure or system is 
accompanied by delays in certain other structures or 
systems. Stanley argues that neotenic development of the brain 
was critical to the evolution of a larger brain. During fetal 
development, both in Homo sapiens and subhuman 
primates, brain size constitutes about 10% of body 
weight. In chimpanzees (and presumably in the distant 
ancestors of human beings), brain growth slows quickly 
after birth, becoming 1 % of body weight.

text:
In chimpanzees (and presumably in the distant 
ancestors of human beings), brain growth slows quickly 
after birth, becoming 1 % of body weight. In human 
beings, however, rapid brain growth continues after birth 
(neoteny), the brain remaining at 10% of body weight 
until the end of the first year of life. Its development then 
slows and the brain becomes a much smaller percentage 
of body weight, but neoteny allows the brain to grow 
much larger than would have otherwise been the case. Important to Stanley's argument is the fact that with 
neotenic development of the brain, the maturing of certain 
other body structures (for example, the musculature) also 
has to be delayed. These maturation delays result in a 
more helpless infant. The distant ancestors of human beings could not have 
lived in trees and managed a helpless infant. For a mother 
to move through the trees, her infant would have to have 
been strong enough to hold on to her (as infant 
chimpanzees do). So to be able to pay the price of a 
helpless infant to allow development of a larger brain, our 
ancestors, reasons Dr. Stanley, would have had to come 
out of the trees and spend most of their time on the 
ground. A mother could manage a helpless infant much 
more easily if she were walking rather than swinging 
from branch to branch. Although Australopithecus did walk upright and, no 
doubt, spent considerable time on the ground, Stanley 
believes that it was primarily arboreal.

Although Australopithecus did walk upright and, no 
doubt, spent considerable time on the ground, Stanley 
believes that it was primarily arboreal. He bases this view 
on the following evidence. The toes, hands, arms, and 
shoulders of Australopithecus appear to be far better 
adapted to an arboreal life than to a terrestrial one. Its teeth 
were good for eating fruit rather than meat, and the fruit 
was primarily in the trees, not on the savannahs. Perhaps 
Australopithecus could have lived on meat if it could have 
cooked it, but it did not have fire. Another disincentive to 
terrestrial life was that Australopithecus was slow afoot 
compared to chimpanzees and baboons and had no 
weapons to speak of. It would have been easy prey for 
lions and other predators on the savannah. For Australopithecus to have survived on the ground, 
it would have had to operate in cooperative groups. Group cooperation usually depends on less competition among the males and is often associated with some degree 
of pair bonding. When pair bonding does not characterize 
a species, there tends to be marked sexual dimorphism, 
with males being much larger than females. The males 
grow large to compete with each other, thereby earning 
copulation rights. A considerable male-female size 
difference existed in Australopithecus, suggesting that 
they were not pair-bonded and probably had not evolved a 
sophisticated level of group cooperation.

A considerable male-female size 
difference existed in Australopithecus, suggesting that 
they were not pair-bonded and probably had not evolved a 
sophisticated level of group cooperation. The point is that 
Australopithecus could have survived without evolving 
these characteristics if it was primarily arboreal. The particular adaptive features of Australopithecus 
made it highly successful in its habitat. This is suggested 
by the fact that the species was around for 1.5 million 
years without changing very much. If it was not doing 
well, selection pressures would have favored change. However, eventually it did begin to change and, in the 
process, gave rise to the terrestrially adapted genus, 
Homo. An interesting question is, "If Australopithecus 
had adapted successfully for so long, why did it change?" 
Stanley posits that it was the environmental impact of the 
Modem Ice Age (2.5 to 2.4 million years ago) that created 
new selection pressures on Australopithecus and triggered 
the processes that fostered the eventual evolution of the 
big brained species, Homo sapiens. An ice age is associated with cooling and drying of the 
planet: deserts spread, woodlands decrease, and 
savannahs increase. As a consequence, during the 
Modem Ice Age, forest dwelling species extincted in large 
numbers and terrestrial species, those adapted for cool 
and dry conditions, flourished. In order to survive, 
Australopithecus spent increasing amounts of time on the 
ground.

In order to survive, 
Australopithecus spent increasing amounts of time on the 
ground. With its new terrestrial existence came new 
selection pressures and, as a consequence, new 
adaptations. Whereas neotenic brain development would 
have been selected against in an arboreal species, it could 
be selected for in a terrestrial one. Mothers could better 
guarantee the survival of helpless infants. So 
Australopithecus could evolve into our first big-brained 
ancestor, Homo habilis. Homo habilis used early stone tools and had an 800 cc 
brain size. This compares to the 400 cc brain of 
Australopithecus, who did not use tools, and the 1300 cc 
brain of modem man, who uses highly complex tools. The earliest skull and femur of Homo habilis, which are 
about 2 million years old, suggest that the species was 
close to the physical size of modem man. Stanley says 
that the evolution of a larger brain being based on natural 
selection acting on neotenic brain development is 
supported by the finding of delayed development 
(compared to apes) of the teeth of Homo habilis. In other 
words, neotenic development of teeth suggests that 
neoteny was occurring in other structures as well. Neoteny would be occurring in the brain, teeth, and other 
structures that rendered the infant more helpless. Homo erectus, which had a 900 cc adult brain, 
evolved from Homo habilis, and had completely replaced 
Homo habilis by 1.5 to 1.4 million years ago.

evolved from Homo habilis, and had completely replaced 
Homo habilis by 1.5 to 1.4 million years ago. Homo 
erectus had a narrow pelvis and small pelvic opening. By 
estimating the birth size of the head from measurements of 
the pelvic opening, and by knowing the adult brain size, 
Stanley concluded that brain development was far from 
complete in Homo erectus newborns. This is further 
evidence of the importance of neoteny in the evolution of 
a larger brain. 5 
 In the evolution from Australopithecus to Homo 
habilis, sexual dimorphism was greatly reduced, a change 
that persisted through Homo erectus and Homo sapiens. It is known that changes in behavior can precede changes 
in the anatomic structure of an organism. The behavioral 
change creates a selection pressure for structural change. Stanley posits that the terrestrial dwelling Homo habilis 
would have required a sophisticated level of group 
cooperation to permit survival. The cooperation facilitates 
the hunting of meat (less fruit is available) and it facilitates 
defense against lions and other predators on the savannah. So selection would favor males who could cooperate 
rather than compete, which permits a reduction in the size 
of males, and it would also favor the cooperation and 
improved care of the young that is promoted by pair

It was a pleasure to listen to Dr. Stanley's clearly 
presented, carefully reasoned arguments for an 
environmental crisis having set in motion a chain of 
evolutionary events that lead eventually to the adaptive 
features that characterize Homo sapiens, the most 
remarkable of those features being a 1300 cc brain. DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF AS PROCESS 
Roberta B. Holt, D.S.W. A cornerstone of Bowen theory is differentiation of 
self. This concept refers to the amount of self available to 
an individual. It includes an individual's level of function­
ing, and the degree of fusion between that individual's 
thinking and feeling system. In its broadest sense it is a 
concept that, at the level of action, refers to over-all level 
of maturity; the degree of responsibility for self, family 
and community; the ability to be productive; the develop­
ment of a cooperative and social self that lives in harmony 
with its fellow humans while remaining a solid self; the 
capacity to stand up and be counted in matters of princi­
ple; and the ability to retain one's thinking ability in 
stressful circumstances. In its more evolved state it refers 
to a life based on principle that orients and guides every­
thing one does. Differentiation is part of nature. It, therefore, was not 
invented, but discovered. In this respect, unraveling the 
mystery of how differentiation in the family system 
evolves is one of the great frontiers of science.

It, therefore, was not 
invented, but discovered. In this respect, unraveling the 
mystery of how differentiation in the family system 
evolves is one of the great frontiers of science. Differentiation transcends not only the intrapsychic but in­
terpersonal process and looks at the larger system in 
which the individual has binding emotional ties. Since the 
process is part of nature, the "evidence" of how the pro­
cess of differentiation unfolds and develops is available to 
anyone who takes the time to work on observing, identi­
fying the observations, and articulating accurately what is 
fact. As currently understood, the process of differentiation 
relates to the clarity of thinking available to an individual, 
one's ability to think broadly enough to understand some­
thing about the system in which one lives, and an emo­
tional system under sufficient control that it can discrimi­
nate the facts of a given situation from the emotionality 
always present in human organisms from birth to death. Evidence suggests that differentiation of self is both 
constitutional, or basic, and functional. This discovery, if 
accurate, negates the need for polarized debate about na­
ture versus nurture. The individual is born with a basic 
6 level of differentiation. Much of this basic level is fixed, 
yet there is the functional level of differentiation which is 
fluid and changing.

The individual is born with a basic 
6 level of differentiation. Much of this basic level is fixed, 
yet there is the functional level of differentiation which is 
fluid and changing. In the arena of the functional level of 
differentiation the self can, over time, develop a small in­
crease in the basic level of self. The beginning stages in developing an increase in the 
level of differentiation appears to be related to reactivity 
and calm. Those who can decrease the reactivity and op­
erate from a level of reduced anxiety describe the process 
as one that permits new and important information to be 
introduced. The new information has an impact when it is 
recognized as discrepant with what is previously known 
about emotional issues. The organism is presented with choices --either to dis­
card the new observed "fact" and continue with the old 
emotionality or to recognize the information as discrepant 
with the old perspective. If the laller process takes place 
the individual "sees" in a way that defuses anxiety in the 
system. How efforts to reduce emotional reactivity in self sets 
the possibility of further development in motion is not 
fully understood. Those who can lower the level of emo­
tional reactivity often indicate it enables the individual to 
"see" more of the process within the system of which he 
is part. Seeing differently, in tum, enables the discovery 
of new information.

Seeing differently, in tum, enables the discovery 
of new information. To the degree the new information is 
factual, and emerges from calm thinking and observation, 
the individual becomes more grounded in reality, and can 
become aware of a new more workable set of options 
available to self. One individual seen in clinical practice described the 
process of discovery as similar to having a car that had 
become stuck in one gear. This gear permitted the car to 
only press forward as a way through a morass. The defus­
ing of anxiety enabled the driver to stop pressing forward, 
and discover a reverse gear and even a parking gear that 
had been present in the "car" all along, but had not been 
accessible to the individual. The reduction of reactivity promotes increased access 
to the thinking part of the brain, which perceives and 
translates the perception into thoughts that govern behav­
ior. In the presence of reduced anxiety, the feelings of the 
limbic system do not guide the process, rather the think­
ing part of the brain is utilized to define what self can and 
can not do. As a consequence, increased demarcation in 
the degree of fusion between the intellectual system and 
the emotional system emerges in the development of a 
more thinking, responsive self. The thinking and the 
emotional system operating autonomously, but in cooper­
ation with each other, is a hallmark of the process of dif­
ferentiation and a critical component in its successful evo­
lution.

In natural systems it is striking that the evolution of 
differentiation is dependent not only upon a reduction of 
personal anxiety, and the emergence of thinking translated 
into action, but the presence of social interaction with 
significant others with whom the individual has binding 
emotional ties and interdependency. The self emerges, 
develops and matures in the context of the social colony 
of which it is emotionally a part. The process does not oc­
cur in a vacuum, and only rarely can it evolve success­
fully outside the family unit. Since differentiation evolves out of interaction in the 
larger system in which the individual is embedded, the 
concept of a person-to-person relationship is important. Broadly stated, the person-to-person relationship refers to 
 the solid self of one individual relating to the calm solid 
core of another in a way that the emotionality in each does 
not guide the interaction. In the presence of the other, 
each is operating from a position of objectivity in which 
one individual can know and can hear the thinking of an­
other individual. On matters of subjectivity it is possible 
to express the feeling part of sell' without the other cross­
ing the boundaries of self. Each can be a self in the pres­
ence of the other. The development of a person-to-person relationship 
appears to be deceptively simple.

Each can be a self in the pres­
ence of the other. The development of a person-to-person relationship 
appears to be deceptively simple. The challenge of differ­
entiation , however, is not synonymous with the reactivity 
in immature people who use the relationship system to 
send their feelings to others in the system. The development of the person-to-person relationship 
is achieved in the presence of all other relationships to 
which the principals are connected. It is here that reality­
based issues of significant consequence to all in the sys­
tem emerge. These provide the possibility of deciding 
whether to be present and engage self in them or not. To 
the degree that one does or does not define self in relation­
ship to these issues, further evolution of differentiation in 
self can occur. It is here that the family system operates 
and it is at this level that decisions about the family takes 
place. Interaction, while important, is not sufficient for the 
development of differentiation. To many this means par­
ticipation in the social events of the family. This may or 
may not be related to continued differentiation. The yield 
on attendance at family group events such as major holi­
days, wedding, funerals is correlated with whether the 
individual retains a focus on self.

can relieve the anxiety of the moment but at a significant 
price to self and to the system in the long term. The pro­
cess of differentiation continues in the direction of the de­
velopment of autonomy, but in connection with the emo­
tionally significant others in the family colony. Successful efforts toward differentiation cannot be 
conferred to self by others, nor is domination of others 
part of the process of developing a more solid self. Differentiation is self-contained and focuses on the self, 
not on the other. As such, the concept of power is dis­
crepant with Bowen theory. In nature there are neither 
winners nor losers. Power, as used in popular parlance, 
implies something that one individual relinquishes to an­
other. The use of power over another is part of the pro­
cess in an unsure, immature self that is not consistent with 
differentiation. As such it emerges from the pseudo self, 
and is connected to the borrowing and trading of selves.

As such it emerges from the pseudo self, 
and is connected to the borrowing and trading of selves. This kind of domination compromises the self of one in­
dividual in the service of an inflated pseudo self of an­
other who feels more dominant. The one who gains a 
feeling of having more self does so at the expense of the 
one who either is seen as giving up self or who, in fact, 
chooses to do so. Power increases polarity and tension in 
the system, resulting in the system becoming increasingly 
rigid and unyielding. As the process evolves, it requires 
greater amounts of energy to sustain until one side gives 
up self to resolve the polarity. While the one who "wins" 
may have a temporary sense of increase in self, the 
amount of self that goes into maintaining the domination, 
or into "propping up" the yielding one, creates a long­
term situation of less, rather than more self in the system. Consistent activity in the direction of differentiation 
produces modifications for the individual and has an im­
pact on the system. In time it becomes easier to see pro­
cess. The development of differentiation gradually 
evolves into a cumulative experience that represents a 
change in feelings, in thoughts, and in the ability to act. This cumulative experience becomes distilled into a 
knowledge of principle that increasingly guides the differ­
entiation of self.

CHANGES AT THE FAMILY CENTER 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. Several major changes are taking place at 
the Family Center. During the past six months 
there has been a significant change in Dr. Bowen's 
involvement in the daily activities of the Center. He has been gradually turning the responsibility 
for the Center over to others for several years, so 
the recent changes are not sudden ones. A change 
in the Center's relationship to Georgetown 
University will occur on July 1, 1990. Also a move 
to new office space will occur later this summer. Dr. Bowen was in the hospital in December, 
January and May. Based on his ongoing 
assessment of his physical resources and based on 
what is involved in getting into and out of the 
Family Center premises, he has decided that for 
the foreseeable future he will make himself 
available to Family Center faculty, staff, and

In 1971, the California legislature. quoting 
the Church of England's document for support. was 
the first to pass no-fault divorce laws which 
pemtltted marriages to terminate, not for offenses 
previously considered unpardonable, such as 
adultery or physical or mental cruelty, but because 
of tempermental incompatibility or disappoint­
ment that married life was not as the couple hoped 
it would be. These legislative changes have spread 
rapidly throughout the states so that now no-fault 
divorce is a law in all 50 states. The net effect of 
these societal changes has been to facilitate the 
entrance and exit from marriages. It is arguable 
that the predicted divorce rate. variously estimated 
from 50% to 70% for a thirty-year marriage (3). is 
more a function of these societal influences than 
an acute change in the evolved characteristic of the 
human family called the marital bond. DIFFERENTIATION AND DIVORCE

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. The 1990 Annual Family Symposium, was 
held November 10-11 at the Leavey Center on the 
Georgetown University campus. The Symposium 
was preceded by the Clinical Conference on 
November 9th, which was also held at the Leavey 
Center. This Symposium was unique in that it was 
the first to be held since Murray Bowen's death. Although Dr. Bowen was not present physically, he 
was there in people's memories, in people's private 
and public comments about him, and in the 
theoretical thinking reflected in the professional 
presentations. He was also very much there by virtue of 
being on several videotapes. The magnitude of his 
influence on so many lives simply stood out. Unmistakable as well was the commitment of 
many to amplify, to extend, and to communicate 
the ideas Bowen labored so long and hard to 
develop. There were tears, but the transition was 
remarkably smooth and perhaps complete. Currents of sadness were strangely mixed with 
heartfelt gratitude and vibrant enthusiasm. The 
gratitude, of course. was for what Bowen had given. He once said that he had tried to live by the 
principle, 'You only have what you give away." The 
enthusiasm at the Symposium seemed primarily 
generated by the prospects for an exciting future for 
those willing to work on the theory's further 
development. Dr.

Dr. Michael Kerr did the Clinical 
Conference. The day began with a videotape that 
Dr. Bowen and Dr. Kerr had made in April 1981. It 
followed the diagnosis of Dr. Bowen's aortic 
aneurysms, and just prior to two operations, the 
first of which would forever change his voice. The 
tape perhaps provides a unique look at Bowen the 
man, at the principles upon which he had tried to 
base his personal and professional life. Among 
many other subjects, he talks about his own death 
and the possibilities for a future without him. As 
always. the dedication to theory shines forth. WINTER 1991 
The two families interviewed by Dr. Kerr 
for the clinical sessions were families that Dr. Bowen had interviewed many times for past 
Clinical Conferences. The family members talked 
about the effort to live theory in their personal 
and professional lives and also described what 
Bowen said and did that was especially helpful to 
their moving towards a different way of thinking 
about human behavior. What they described 
extended beyond Bowen the man in that his words 
and actions reflected theoretical principles that 
could be learned and practiced by others. Their 
remarks were consistent with the view that an 
understanding of theory coupled with an ability to 
talk, feel, and act in ways consistent with that 
theory are more important influences on the 
success of therapy than the personality of the 
therapist. The theme of this year's Symposium was 
the nature and importance of theory.

the nature and importance of theory. The 
Distinguished Guest Lecturer, Dr. Lloyd Motz, 
Professor Emeritus of Astronomy at Columbia 
University, was chosen with this theme in mind. Professor Motz has a remarkable perspective on 
the importance of theory for advancing knowledge. He did not draw analogies between nonliving and 
living systems, but concentrated on how theories 
in the physical sciences are developed and how 
those theories guide the gathering of further 
knowledge. Professor Motz addressed how much more 
complex living systems are when compared to 
nonliving systems. Murray Bowen believed that 
we are not condemned to a subjective morass in 
understanding human behavior. There is a way 
out of the morass, by "distinguishing what man is 
from what man thinks and says he is." Bowen 
attempted to develop a theory about the nature of 
man, that is anchored in provable facts and that is 
predictive. However, probably few living in the 
first half of the seventeenth century imagined 
anyone could develop a theory that made 
absolutely amazing predictions about the physical 
world until Newton developed it. Similarly, few 
living in the first half of the twentieth century 
imagined that a theory could be developed that 
describes an amazing level of predictability in 
human emotional functioning until Bowen 
 developed it. It was fascinating to reflect upon 
what Bowen had attempted to accomplish as one 
listened to Dr.

The past ten years have been among the

have not been coming to the Annual Symposium

appreciate how the thinking has progressed. One of the family members interviewed for 
the Clinical Conference commented during her 
videotaped session about how Bowen's shift in the 
early l 980's to a greater focus on theory and 
science has been invaluable to her effort to move 
towards systems thinking. I think this has 
probably been true for all of us. Bowen's ten-year 
effort to clarify concepts such as functional facts, 
functional dysfunction. emotional objectivity, the 
distinction between science and philosophy, the 
distinction between the brain and the products of 
the brain, the notion of a "science of subjectivity," 
and the distinction between lww to think versus 
what to think has been extraordinarily useful to 
many of us. A better understanding of those ideas 
was reflected in many of the papers presented this 
year. Bowen could have died in 1981. I am glad he 
did not. Not only did we have Bowen the man for 
ten years--with his sense of humor. his dedication.

Michael Robinson, Ph.D. reviewed by Douglas Murphy 
On January 18, 1991, Dr. Michael 
Robinson, Head of the Smithsonian Zoo, was the 
presenter at the Thursday Professional Meeting 
sponsored by the Georgetown Family Center. Dr. Robinson's topic was on predator/prey 
relationships and how they have evolved in 
nature. The reciprocal interactions between 
predators and their prey have always generated 
interest among biologists and researchers in 
animal behavior. Dr. Robinson, whose field of 
study is entomology, has specialized in this area of 
predator /prey interactions among insects. Dr. Robinson characterized predator/prey 
relationships as a two-sided arms race, which 
throughout evolutionary history has escalated on 
both sides. A predator advances and produces 
novel ways of catching prey while the prey 
advances and produces new ways of defending 
itself. This interaction across evolutionary time 
leads to greater degrees of perfection on both sides 
of the relationship.

Certain species of 
bats utilize this same ability to catch fish 
swimming close to the surface of a body of water. Because the bat's mouth is not designed for 
scooping up fish from the water, it has evolved a 
spiked back toe that acts as a fisherman's gaff to 
spear the fish. It then places its prey in a sack-like 
fold in its wing and carries the fish back to a place 
where it can be eaten. Another species of bat, the frog eating bat, 
does not utilize echolocation to find its prey, but 
instead responds to the mating call of male frogs in 
its environment. One type of frog has developed 
the most complex mating call that exists in frogs. The mating call consists of two separate 
vocalizations. When one male vocalizes alone 
there is first a whine-like sound, which is followed 
by a "chuck" sound. When two male frogs are in the 
same area they both produce a whine-like sound, 
then two "chuck" sounds. When there are three or 
more male frogs vocalizing in a chorus they add 
three "chuck" sounds. Experiments have shown 
that females of this species of frog respond more 
readily to the more complex vocalization of the 
three "chucks." The question raised by these 
behaviors is why the solitary male frogs don't 
vocalize the more complex songs and therefore 
attract more females. Researchers have found that 
the less complex vocalization makes it more 
difficult for the frog-eating bat to locate the 
solitary frog.

 Spiders' Webs: Ladder webs of a spider in 
New Guinea are similar to spiral webs found in 
common spiders except for the addition of a 
ladder-like extension at the bottom of the web. Such ladder webs are specialized to trap moths. Moths have evolved a defense against the sticky 
surfaces of spider webs. Their wings are covered 
with loose scales which readily fall off, leaving 
them more able to escape. However. when a moth 
comes into contact with a ladder web it will flutter 
up and down the ladder. just as it will when it 
comes upon any kind of impediment. The shape of 
the ladder web along with the fluttering up and 
down causes the wing scales of the moth to 
completely peel off. leaving it finally attached to 
the sticky web. Another spider holds a single thread of web

On April 18, 1991 John B. Calhoun, Ph.D. presented the Third Thursday Lecture. Dr. Calhoun is a distinguished ecologist whose work 
has long been studied by many connected with the 
Family Center. His research, using animal models 
of mice and rats, studied the effects of crowding on 
behavior and teased out mechanisms whereby 
these effects occur. Dr. Calhoun began his presentation by 
noting his lifetime focus on individual variation 
or, what makes one animal different from 
another. He also spoke of differences between 
species being more of degree than of kind. Rats 
and mice do many of the things chimps do. The 
question is how far back does the resemblance go. The simple neivous system of flatworms is the 
building block for more complex neivous systems. With evolution, more of the building blocks are 
simply linked together. So if we understood 
flatworms better we might understand more of 
what humans are about. This view fits with Dr. Calhoun's definition of an animal as a set of 
probability functions working from a nervous 
system. The evening's particular focus was on 
universal autism, how animals get there and what 
they look like along the way. In situations of 
optimum density, 12% of the genetically 
homozygous mice or rat populations studied 
develop extreme behavioral disturbances of a 
hypoactive nature.

behavior deviates from a species specific ideal for 
survival. The extreme segment of this group are 
called autistic and are unable to express 
reproductive, social, or conceptual behaviors 
essential for species survival. They are arrested at 
an early stage with only contact and nursing 
behavior learned. The most extreme segment are SPRING 1991

of the population demonstrates various social 
pathologies deviating from the species norm. A 
greater percentage of the group falls into the 
autistic category. If the population is allowed to 
increase in a finite space, crowding reaches very 
high levels. The population then becomes 
universally autistic, incapable of reproducing, and 
dies out. This is the phenomenon Dr. Calhoun 
described as universal autism. Not all the animals studied manifest social 
pathology and reach the stage of autism at the 
same rate.

Roberta M. Gilbert, MD 
For therapists forced to struggle with 
objectivity amid family polarizations on a daily 
basis, the March 21 Professional Lecture provided 
a fascinating look at the problem of objectivity as 
it arises in another profession--journalism. Jack 
Germond, a well-known political reporter, 
columnist and television commentator, intrigued 
the audience with his thinking, brought alive by a 
ready stock of illustrative stories. Objectivity in newspaper reporting, Mr. Germond emphasized, is first and foremost related 
to accuracy. Facts are the foundation and primary 
requirement of the journalist's work. For 
example, Peter Arnett. reporting on the Persian 
Gulf War from behind enemy lines, stayed factual 
by continually reporting on the restrictions under 
which he was operating. In wartime, accuracy can be hard to come 
by. In the recent war the Allied forces deliberately 
misled the press for military purposes--in this way 
the enemy was misled also. Another aspect of objectivity is fairness.

journalists, especially in conflictual and

necessarily giving both sides equal space, but by 
giving a balanced, fair picture. Unfortunately, when there is controversy, 
neither party understands that the other side must 
be presented. Therefore, neither side is totally 
happy with the outcome. News analysis presents other problems to 
the journalist seeking objectivity. Mr. Germond 
thinks that even when the subject is emotionally 
charged. it is possible to be objective and detached 
in making Judgments, tf the writer is a seasoned veteran. The best analysts cannot allow 
themselves to care who wins a given political 
campaign, for example. It is not a violation of objectivity in 
journalism, however, to remind readers of past 
patterns which might influence the outcome of a 
political campaign. It would be a betrayal of the 
reader's trust to treat all political candidates as 
though they all had equally serious prospects for 
election. In this instance, while it is not difficult 
to be accurate and balanced, it may be difficult to 
be fair and judicious. Certain pressures operate on journalists to 
mitigate against objectivity.

If any of Mr. Germond's ideas sound 
similar to those of Dr. Murray Bowen, if they ring 
true to the experience of people working in the field 
of human behavior and the human family, 
perhaps it is because objectivity--a respect for the 
facts--is objectivity wherever one finds it. And 
perhaps it is best served when attention to 
accuracy, fairness, and detachment, as well as 
emotional force fields, is meticulous, regardless of 
the content. DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF AND LEARNING 
Daniel V. Papero 
In his theory of human functioning, Murray 
Bowen outlined a theoretical construct which he 
called d![ferentiation of self, which described how 
people differed from one another in terms of 
functioning. At the heart of the concept is the 
balance between reflection and instinct in any 
person. Behavior can be automatic and reflexive, a 
direct response to an internal or external stimulus 
or set of conditions. Life decisions can be based on 
what feels right and what seems easiest at the 
moment of decision. How one behaves can also be 
carefully thought out, guided by principles worked 
out and tested over time. Both have value for the 
individual in the varied conditions of life. Bowen observed that the ability of people to 
utilize these guidance systems varied greatly. Some people seemed only capable of automatic 
responses to any stimulus or condition, while 
others displayed varying degrees of ability to 
employ either.

Some people seemed only capable of automatic 
responses to any stimulus or condition, while 
others displayed varying degrees of ability to 
employ either. Some could be somewhat objective 
and thoughtful if circumstances were favorable but 
resorted easily to automatic, feeling-based 
behavior. Others could make choices between 
guidance systems more independently of the 
conditions they faced. Those with no ability to distinguish between 
thinking and the automatic or emotional guidance 
system received a rating of zero on the scale of 
differentiation. Their guidance systems were in 
fact undifferentiated, and their behavior was 
governed solely by automatic processes. From 
zero, individuals could be assigned a scale number 
based on their ability to separate thought from 
emotion under differing conditions and guide 
their behavior accordingly. A person rated 100 on 
the scale of differentiation would have the ability 
to employ either guidance system no matter what 
the circumstances and to change between them as 
he or she saw fit. In fact, Bowen never identified 
anyone whom he rated at 100, but theoretical 
completeness required that the potential for such a 
person be included and described. Bowen described the functioning 
characteristics of people in different quarters of 
the scale of differentiation. Those whose level of 
differentiation falls into the first quarter of the 
scale (0-25) live essentially in a world of feeling 
and automatic behavior.

Those whose level of 
differentiation falls into the first quarter of the 
scale (0-25) live essentially in a world of feeling 
and automatic behavior. Their actions are 
determined largely by what feels right, and they 
are extremely sensitive and reactive to the feelings 
and behavior of others. People within this 
quadrant have great difficulty functioning without 
another human being to attach to and from whom 
they draw functioning strength. At the very lowest 
levels of the scale, even the feeling world can be 
overwhelming, leading people to retreat into a sort 
of paralysis or numbness. People in the next quadrant (25-50) live with 
increasingly more choice between the automatic 
response and a more reflective, thoughtful 
alternative. While much of life is lived 
automatically, people in this range show 
increasing flexibility to operate with both 
guidance systems. Behavior can be self­
determined and based on well thought out 
principles, although in the lower ranges outside 
authority may be drawn upon to bolster one's own 
viewpoint. Ideas about personal responsibility are 
drawn less from the relationship matrix and other 
important people than from the person's own 
thought and assessment. The borrowing and 
lending of functioning strength among people can 
occur, but the person is also better able to function 
when such is lacking.

While maintaining clear views

of complexity. They establish goals for themselves 
based on thought and principle and have 
considerable energy free to pursue them. From a theoretical perspective a second 
variable, anxiety, alongside differentiation of self 
affects functioning . Defined as the fear of real or 
imagined threat, anxiety can be further divided 
into the categories acute and chronic. Acute 
anxiety refers to the response of the individual and 
the group to real threat or challenge. A pianist's 
pre-performance butterflies, a pedestrian's 
automatic leap from the path of an oncoming 
vehicle, the worry of concerned relatives while a 
person undergoes surgery all illustrate some 
common manifestations of acute anxiety. The 
term acute implies that the reaction is specific to a 
particular threat and time-limited. Chronic 
anxiety is less easily illustrated than described. As 
the term suggests, chronic anxiety is a persistent 
state in the individual and the group. While there 
is no clear threat, people report a fear of what 
might occur. Among its manifestations are a 
continual wariness, suspicion, physical tension, 
fear of what might happen, fatigue, irritability and 
so forth. Chronic anxiety wears away at people, 
and its debilitating effects tend to reduce people's 
ability to handle episodes of acute anxiety. From a theoretical perspective, chronic 
anxiety and level of differentiation go hand-in­
hand.

From a theoretical perspective, chronic 
anxiety and level of differentiation go hand-in­
hand. The lower the basic level of differentiation 
of self, the more chronic anxiety becomes a factor 
affecting the resiliency and the functioning of the 
individual and the group. The more modest the 
basic level of differentiation and the more 
pervasive chronic anxiety, the more easily acute 
anxiety can be paralyzing and lead to further drops 
in functioning and increased chronic anxiety. Level of differentiation plus the effects of chronic 
and acute anxiety are principal variables affecting 
functioning. Functioning, for the purposes of this 
discussion, can be roughly equated with behavior. It incorporates all that goes into what the person 
does to bring the best of his or her capabilities to 
bear upon the challenge of adapting successfully to 
the changing environment. In this context, 
learning refers to the process through which the 
individual retains the effects of experience which 
then influence present and future situations. Leaming can occur with or without the person's 
awareness or intent. It can also be actively 
pursued. If learning can be considered a part of 
functioning, it varies with all functioning 
according to the level of differentiation of self and 
anxiety of the learner. Assuming a steady level of anxiety, varying 
levels of differentiation of self can, theoretically, 
have implications for the motivation to learn.

relationship to significant others becomes to the

From such a climate leaders can 
emerge whose only qualifications are charisma 
and demagoguery. Learning for individuals with 
higher levels of differentiation is directed 
increasingly toward goals selected by self and for 
self in accordance with well-defined ideas of value 
and responsibility. Knowledge of the role of differentiation of 
self and anxiety in learning also presents certain 
implications for anyone with the responsibility to 
assist another's learning. For simplicity's sake, 
that individual will be called a teacher, although 
that person is potentially as much a learner as the 
designated student. Self-knowledge may be the 
most important qualification for the teacher. Specifically, the ability of the teacher to recognize 
automatic processes in self, particularly those 
associated with anxiety, and to manage self 
responsibly are essential to maintaining sufficient 
relationship to the student to assist motivation 
and maintain contact. A general knowledge of the 
characteristics of differentiation of self at 
differing levels can assist the teacher to 
understand how important a relationship will be 
to the learning process and what the student is up 
against in his or her effort to maintain self in the 
world. The teacher's knowledge of his or her own 
level of differentiation of self may assist in 
recognizing better the manifestations of a 
togetherness process in self which impedes or 
biases the learning process in the student.

the Georgetown University campus. This year's Distin­
guished Guest Lecturer was Dr. Howard T. Odum, an 
environmental scientist from the University of Florida. In 
addition to Dr. Odum's featured lecture, Dr. Michael Kerr 
did an hour long presentation on Sunday morning, filling 
Dr. Bowen'straditional slot in the program. Over the two 
days, fifteen 15-minute papers were presented. They were 
grouped in threes and followed by panel discussions. The meeting began with papers by Roberta B. Holt, Laura Brooks and Walter J. Smith. Dr. Holt described 
the social work profession from a historical perspective, 
emphasizing how the field had changed during this century. Given that Bowen theory is in many ways consistent with 
the original direction of social work, Dr. Holt puzzled over 
how social work gets such a distorted image of Bowen's 
ideas. In her presentation, Ms. Brooks discussed human 
aging in the context of aging in other species, and com­
mented on how human aging gets defined as a "problem" 
rather than as a fact of nature. Looking at relationship 
systems rather than just at individuals allows one to study 
the function older individuals have in a group, both in 
human and subhuman species.

in an inpatient setting. Attempting to treat patients as part of 
a family emotional system often puts Hasselle at odds with 
conventional medical practice. He commented that he is 
trying to implement change from within the system rather 
than from outside. Mrs. Flynn, a psychiatric liaison nurse in 
a general hospital, described the impact of a hospital on the 
family, as well as the impact of family process on the 
patient's progress.

Roberta M. Gilbert M.D. The Family Center's Professional Meeting in De­
cember featured a presentation on Sigmund Freud's con­
tribution to the study of human behavior from the perspec­
tive of Bowen family systems theory. Freud's greatest accomplishment was fathering 
psychoanalysis, both a theory and a method for understand­
ing the effect of past experiences on the present. It is the 
foundation upon which most present day therapies are built. Childrearing, a burgeoning school of psychoanalytic criti­
cism, and even everyday language have all been influenced 
by his thinking. Freud's place in history was recently empha­
sized by the Wall Street Journal. (12/2/91) He was one in a 
series of three ''Thinkers Who Shaped the Century."Yet, 
despite its palpable impact on present day society, Freudian 
theory remains a theory, not a fact. The evening's presentation focused on transfer­
ence, the one formal psychoanalytic concept Bowen did not 
reject.

text:
The evening's presentation focused on transfer­
ence, the one formal psychoanalytic concept Bowen did not 
reject. Freud defined the phenomenon, in 1924, as follows: 
"In every analytic treatment there arises, without the 
physician's agency, an intense emotional relationship be­
tween the patient and the analyst which is notto be accounted 
for by the actual situation. It can be positive or ... negative 
. . .It becomes the principal tool of the resistance. . .A 
universal phenomenon of the human mind." Freud believed 
that transference occurred in the unconscious mind, a con­
cept he developed to explain mental phenomenon that were 
outside awareness. Transference could be dealt with by 
analysis, which could bring unconscious content to aware­
ness, at which point it was thought to be resolved. Countertransference, the transference of the analyst 
in regard to the patient, was also ever present. Countertransference could be dealt with in the same way, 
and this was the prescription for any aspiring analyst. Is anything like transference apparent in other spe­
cies? Dr. Paul MacLean views the reptilian brain as a 
"homing" or repetitive brain, seeing it as responsible for 
repetitive behavior. Lorenz described imprinting in other 
species, in which behavior which occurred early enough 
could persist for a lifetime. Dr. Walter Toman, in his descriptions of sibling 
position and how it affects character and relationships, may 
be describing a special case of transference.

Dr. Walter Toman, in his descriptions of sibling 
position and how it affects character and relationships, may 
be describing a special case of transference. How does Bowen family systems theory change the 
idea of transference? Differentiation of self, an idea absent 
in Freudian thinking, is especially pertinent. Higher on the 
scale, people would be presumed to be more self aware, and 
3 
 so transference would be weaker, more manageable, and 
more recognized for what it is than at lower levels of 
differentiation. The family projection process may happen at times 
through the mechanism of transference. Also, the form 
transference takes, since it is a relationship phenomenon, 
may take the form of any of the four relationship patterns 
described by Bowen. Freud's idea of transference assumes the existence 
of-an unconscious mind which is part and parcel of the 
psychoanalytic definition of it. In Bowen theory, there is 
no unconscious. For that reason, the phenomenon as under­
stood from the new theoretical point of view may need a new 
name. "Repetitions," is one which describes the continua­
tion of old patterns in ·the MacLean sense, and may best 
describe what is being seen. The concept of the ego and the concept of basic self 
were contrasted. Psychoanalysis defines the ego as "a 
coherent system of functions for mediating between the 
instincts and the outside world. Its development from infancy 
to adulthood was traced in the presentation.

Its development from infancy 
to adulthood was traced in the presentation. The concept of the basic self was described in terms 
of both automatic and thought-out guidance systems. The 
basic self is surrounded by a functional self which is nego­
tiable in relationships though basic self is not itself nego­
tiable. Boundaries in the functional self are permeable 
depending upon the level of differentiation of self of the 
individual. How is it that two such careful observers such as 
Freud and Bowen can come up with such different descrip-_ 
tions of the core of the self? First, this difference can be 
understood in terms of the emotional unit. If the emotional· 
unit is the individual, the ego serves well conceptually to 
describe an intrapsychic phenomenon. If, however, the 
emotional unit is the family or an emotionally connected 
group, then the basic self, which is defined in relationship 
terms, becomes necessary and extremely useful in describing 
the connectedness between the self and the emotional unit. Secondly, the impact of the concept of differentiation is 
readily apparent in the differences between the two concepts. Other areas to consider from a Bowen family sys­
tems view include the ego mechanisms of defense, the 
relationship between subjectivity and objectivity in the 
human, the neo-Freudians, Freudian views on women, and 
object relations. Studying the two theories is a way for the presenter 
to see how they relate to each other now and over time.
