Studying the two theories is a way for the presenter 
to see how they relate to each other now and over time. On 
that subject, Lloyd Motz, in Conceots of Science stated: 
" ... the introduction of a 'new theory' does not completely 
invalidate the previous theory, but rather incorporates it into 
a more general and larger theoretical structure. The old 
theory remains valid in a restricted domain but is replaced 
4 by the extended theory to explain observations and experi­
mental data that lie outside the restricted domain. The old 
theory thus becomes a special case of the extended theory." 
Just as Einstein's new ideas about gravity did not do 
away with Newton's theory, so Bowen theory, while more 
useful and more explanatory, does not do away with the old 
theory about human behavior entirely. THE FUTURE FUND

has said before in other contexts, changing the wording 
somewhat and shifting the emphasis a little. It would be 
refreshing to hear some other ideas on this subject from 
Family Center faculty, who presumably address the subject 
of training in their endeavors and might have fresher view­
points to present. Papero began his presentation with a rather lengthy 
story about Robert E. Lee in his role as president of Wash­
ington College after the War of Northern Aggression. Lee 
apparently was a rather innovative educator, if the stories 
can be trusted, who placed a great deal of emphasis on the 
student's responsibility for learning. At Washington Col­
lege, Lee introduced a number of elective courses for stu­
dents, including the first university course on journalism 
offered in the United States.

VOL. 13, N0.2 
RESPONSIBILITY FOR SELF 
Daniel V. Papero, PhD, LCSW 
An increasingly common procedure in mental health 
practice today assigns several therapists to a family. A 
person may have an individual therapist, a married pair 
may have a couples therapist, a child may have a child 
therapist. Additional specialty therapists such as a biofeed­
back therapist, a hypnotherapist, or a psychiatrist may also 
be involved. A somewhat different version of the same 
phenomenon links several therapists to one person. In the 
arena of clinical supervision, a clinician may also have 
several clinical supervisors. An employer may require' a 
supervisor within an agency, the clinician may select an 
additional supervisor in a particular area of interest, and 
may also see a therapist about some personal dilemma. The likelihood is high that each of these therapists or 
supervisors has a different way of thinking about the nature 
of human behavior, of human problems and of how best to 
approach them. Even with a common orientation, transfer­
ences may exist between family members and the various 
therapists ( or between supervisor and supervisee ), compli­
cating each person's ability to be responsible for and to 
represent self.

symptoms are a product of the family emotional unit, and 
to divide them into separate problems to be addressed by 
different practitioners confuses the situation and adds ad­

extremely complex. The main thrust of the effort to learn and apply the 
Bowen theory occurs outside the clinical hour in the impor­
tant relationships of the family, the work system, and the 
community. The learning occurs in each family member's 
efforts to become familiar with the emotional system of 
family, work, and community and to manage self differ­
ently within it. The effort to improve functional differen­
tiation of self is continual. A person's or family's efforts 
may occur in spurts and may or may not involve a clinician. Basic to the effort to learn and apply the Bowen 
theory is the person's understanding of responsibility for SPRING AND SUMMER, 1992 
self. On a simple level, responsibility for one's life in­
volves thinking through situations, making decisions and 
accepting the consequences of those decisions. The pro­
cess is more complex than it appears at first glance. How 
much thought and how much feeling should influence the 
decision-making process? And how do thought and feeling 
influence the acceptance of the consequences of decisions? Where do facts fit into the process? And what about 
relationships to other people?

How can a museum engage people in a discussion 
about the future? Where next, Columbus? invites people to 
explore their own thinking, to weigh the puipose of further 
space exploration, to review the challenges involved tech­
nically, and to consider the process of the exploratory 
enterprise. Four themes generally define how people think 
about exploration. The first defines exploration as a part of human 
nature, a manifestation of biological programming. To be 
on the move is to be human. This theme is linked to the 
concept of conquest, an inevitable next step, to gain some 
sort of benefit such as spreading out, or gaining wealth or 
power. While the focus is on the benefit to the explorer, the 
effect of exploration on the New World is often ignored. Columbus's example clearly links exploitation with explo­
ration. The second incorporates the notions of the frontier 
and of manifest destiny. Space as the high frontier, the 
American destiny, the national character, mandates a pio­
neering effort. The metaphor invokes notions of courage, 
ingenuity, self-reliance and taming the wildnerness, but the 
discussion often ignores what went wrong in the pioneering 
effort of the last century. Space as the frontier is often cited 
in U.S. space policy documents and in government rheto­
ric. Exploration as a badge of character, a mark of 
leadership and superiority lies at the heart of the third 
theme. Exploration is linked to competitiveness and eco­
nomic strength.

matter of choice. The endeavor is a social and cultural

stellar exploration, these same challenges are even more 
complicated. In the meantime, exploration continues from the 
Earth. Humans scan the heavens with complex telescopes 
and instruments looking for other signs of life and for 
greater factual knowledge of the universe. Like the ancient

new domain. Whether or not exploration is within our

One of the 
central facts of life is that it ends in death. Perhaps only 
humans are aware of death as a future event. Nevertheless, 
the distinction between the living and the dead is essential 
to most species, and the death of an individual can have a 
powerful impact on the survival of the social unit. In a two-day conference at Georgetown University 
on April 25-26, the issue of death was a springboard for 
exploring many dimensions of family systems theory. During the first day, papers discussed death in social 
systems of different species, and as a reflection of the 
emotional process in the human family. An integrating 
theme of the day was approaching death as a fact which 
both expresses and intensifies the emotional forces in a 
system. Theoretical concepts such as the emotional sys­
tem, cutoff, the level of anxiety in the system, differentia­
tion, and triangles were used to explore the nature of death 
in a system. In the second day of the conference, the presenters 
applied theory to their professional and family experience 
with death. These included papers about the process and 
impact of dying in family systems, as well as in hospitals, 
nursing homes, institutions, and the religious community. A focus of several papers was the ethical and emotional 
issues that arise for families in the overlap of these various 
systems around death.

Dr. Michael Kerr gave the keynote address. Quoting 
several times from Lewis Thomas, Dr. Kerr described 
death as a part oflife, something occurring around us all the 
time in nature. People who have feared death most of their 
lives typically discover that when it is imminent, they can 
face it calmly. People around the dying person actually 
have more anxiety than the dying person himself, and their 
anxiety can emotionally isolate the dying person. The 
emotional isolation, which is a consequence of a relation­
ship process, is responsible for much of the withdrawal and 
depression a dying person experiences, although such 
reactions are often blamed on the fact that the person is 
dying. Similarly, the relationship system generally has 
more impact on a survivor's adjustment to a death than do 
the survivor's reactions to the death itself. Dr. Kerr also 
commented on how Murray Bowen helped so many people 
recognize the importance of the funeral for enhancing the 
functioning of the survivors. Dr. Loretta Nowakowski presented her observations 
on the process of dying. She placed the ability to choose to 
die along a continuum based on the level of differentiation 
and the relationship forces in the family. Dr. Papero 
discussed searching for an objective view of death, rather 
than becoming mired in reactivity to it.

with the human and transferring dominance to familiar 
humans, they play a part in their own domestication. When allowed to roam completely free, they may 
revert to the wild form such as the aurch, a predecessor of 
the cow, or wild boar, a predecessor of the pig. However,

revert to their wild state. They were, to some extent, kept

projects. SPECIAL POSTGRADUATE PROGRAM 
Priscilla J. Friesen, LCSW 
The Special Postgraduate Program began in the 
mid-seventies to address the question of how to provide 
formal training to mental health professionals who lived 
10 too far from Washington to participate in the Tuesday 
evening Postgraduate Program. Requests for training had 
been coming from people who had heard Dr. Bowen speak 
at meetings around the country as well as those who had 
done reading about family theory and therapy. Most people come to the Family Center to learn to 
do therapy. "Training" implies that there is something one 
can learn to do either in one's own family or with clinical 
families. This is a dilemma that is present with all "train­
ing" or "teaching." Training at the Family Center is an 
effort to assist people to see the world differently, to see 
their automatic assumptions and perceptions and to thereby 
affect their functioning.

People learn "to do" therapy or to 
manage themselves more effectively within a clinical rela­
tionship as they think differently about themselves and the 
nature of human relationships. What one does follows 
from how one thinks. This is often elusive to describe. Presentation of theory is only a portion of train­
ing. The training program must represent what is theoreti­
cally consistent and based upon differentiation. That is, the 
training program must simply represent being "outside" of 
the emotional system be it in the supervisory relationship or 
in the presentation of a content area, in administrative 
actions, even in considering how theory guides whether 
coffee is served. This past year twenty-four people were in the 
training program. Eleven were new to the program. Many 
had been introduced to Bowen theory through another 
training program established by someone trained previ­
ously at the Family Center. Others became interested after 
hearing various faculty members speak around the country. Participants came from California, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, 
Tennessee, North Carolina, New Mexico, New Jersey, 
Pennsylvania, Missouri, Massachusetts, Vermont, lliinois, 
Virginia, and British Columbia. The program is held four times a year: September, 
December, March, and June. Each session is held Monday 
through Wednesday. On Tuesday evenings, trainees from 
the Special Postgraduate Program join those in the local 
program for an evening of trainee presentations.

Each session is held Monday 
through Wednesday. On Tuesday evenings, trainees from 
the Special Postgraduate Program join those in the local 
program for an evening of trainee presentations. The four times a year model was developed in­
stead of the more typical intensive training of one, two or 
four weeks because it simply takes time to think, to relate 
theory to family and clinical situations, and to integrate 
theory into one's work and life. The training program 
provides a format of disciplined study of theory through 
presentations and discussion as well as supervision be­
tween times by phone or letter. A common question is, "How long is the training 
program?" The training program is available for as long as 
it is a useful format for learning. Most who are serious 
continue for at least three years; some continue for longer; 
others move to other Family Center programs to learn and 
 contribute. Initially most people involved in the training 
program are interested in theory to assist them in their 
personal and professional lives; with time many move to 
another level of interest in theory and ideas for their own 
sake. Each day includes two morning lecture and discus­
sion periods. During the first morning session, different 
faculty and staff present their current theoretical interests.

Each day includes two morning lecture and discus­
sion periods. During the first morning session, different 
faculty and staff present their current theoretical interests. Presentations this year included history of the Family 
Center, its programs and how theory guides the develop­
ment of an organization; what are the difficulties in learn­
ing theory; marriage from a family systems perspective; 
reproduction in evolution and in the human family; under­
lying assumptions of general systems and family systems 
theory; societal regression and child protective services; 
AIDS; the physiology of marriage; and physiology and 
Bowen theory. The second morning session is conducted each day 
by Dr. Kerr, Director of the Family Center. This provides 
continuity in addressing the basics of theory, misconcep­
tions, and questions from the group. Over the lunch hour, videotapes are shown from the 
large collection of teaching and clinical tapes available at 
the Family Center. Each trainee is assigned a supervisor when they enter 
the training program. This supervisor typically follows a 
participant through their entire training period at the Family 
Center. Each group is composed of four to six participants 
at varying levels of experience with theory. The supervi­
sion group meets each afternoon for three hours.

Each group is composed of four to six participants 
at varying levels of experience with theory. The supervi­
sion group meets each afternoon for three hours. This time 
is available for more in depth discussion of theory as well 
as the opportunity for individuals to present efforts in their 
own families, in clinical relationships and in the organi­
zations where they work. Supervision is also conducted 
between the sessions by phone or letter. On Tuesday evenings each participant has the oppor­
tunity to present. This is often the most anxiety producing 
and challenging opportunity of the year, but most say it is 
also the most useful. Each person is challenged to organize 
his thoughts about an area of theory and to present it 
publicly. The range of topics is striking. Perhaps most 
important for this evening is the opportunity to put one's 
self "out there" with one's colleagues, an opportunity to 
define a self. Each year is a bit different. People, faculty, staff and 
trainees continue to push their own understanding of theory 
--pushing to get beyond their own subjectivity. The 
Georgetown training program represents one format to 
challenge one's selfat multiple levels: within self, in one's 
family, in one's clinical work, in one's professional envi­
ronment, and in the world of ideas and science. It is a 
learning and "training" environment for all, including 
faculty and staff.

HOMELESSNESS, HELPFULNESS 
AND PULLING BEANS 
D. Vail, PhD 
The neighborhood is haunted. In broad daylight appa­
ritions drift along the street, stand idly on the street corner 
or outside the liquor store-deli, or move between lines of 
stopped cars. They are easily recognizable, these shades of 
modem city life. Like Scrooge's ghosts, they rattle chains 
of anxieties. Even in warm weather they sport several 
layers of clothing, sometimes augmented by a blanket. In 
some parts of the city they carry their belongings with them 
in battered shopping carts or faded chidren's wagons. Around here they carry usually only the tools of the 
panhandling trade-their voices, their appearance and 
their boldness. At the comer of Wisconsin and Nebraska, at Tenley 
Circle, across the street from the American University 
dormitories and Sears, a half a block from MacDonald's, a 
ghost has set up camp. He's done it now for several years. From his shopping cart piled high with stuff, he produces 
a Coleman stove, a folding camp stool, a dozen eggs, and 
assorted other items for breakfast. Mornings find him 
cooking his breakfast, surrounded by rush-hour traffic and 
pedestrians streaming to the Metro. This year he's added 
a pop-up domed tent as well, although I haven't noticed it 
recently.

Armed always 
with a large cup and sometimes with a sign invoking God's 
blessing, they move along the lines of stalled traffic, 
sensing where coins can be had and where not. Last 
summer, a blond woman worked this stretch. Sometimes 
alone and sometimes with a man, she moved among the 
cars efficiently. Locals commented on her. She could have 
stepped from her Volvo wagon a few minutes earlier, in 
between her luncheon in a Georgetown bistro and picking 
up her kids at Georgetown Day School just up the street. In 
the late afternoon, she and her companion, who always 
seemed to turn up whether he had worked the traffic or not, 
walked to the local liquor store-deli, where they purchased 
whatever. They usually appeared to be in deep conversa­
tion. I never saw either one of them initiate contact with 
another person, although she would respond to a hello. I 
haven't seen either one of them in a while. The frequency of divorce in the United States and 
western Europe has risen sharply in the past few years. Now around half of all first marriages end in divorce, and 
an even higher percentage of second marriages. The 
number of attorneys has increased dramatically as well. If 
the graphs and reports of the press can be believed, people 
resort to litigation to resolve differences more frequently 
than ever before.

the graphs and reports of the press can be believed, people 
resort to litigation to resolve differences more frequently 
than ever before. The threat of litigation has changed the

businesspeople and their customers to be more guarded in

Crown Heights or south central LA are now intensely 
focused on the differences among people, and violence 
appears to be only a spark away. An entire generation of 
young males now resolves dic.putes, and even indulges its 
~ with deadly force. Failed relationships fill the 
prison system to the bursting point. Robert Reich, in his book Work of Nations, comments 
on the "secession of the successful." He suggests that the 
 more fortunate elements in society have been separating 
themselves increasingly from the less fortunate. William 
Schneider in a recent Atlantic Monthly makes a related 
point when he describes the shift of political action from the 
cities to the suburbs. Upset, displeasure and disagreement 
seem increasingly to be handled by a cutoff from the other 
perceived as noxious, dangerous, or crazy. The wealthy 
retreat to secure compounds, often complete with police 
security, while others, like the Branch Davidians ofWaco, 
Texas, build fortresses to shut out the rest of the world. In nice weather, workers in the building often eat their

lunch at a picnic table on the plaza outside the front door. Kids from the MacArthur School frequently sit there work­
ing on their projects in the sunshine. When I saw the 
specter, she was alone at the table. It was a very cold, sunny 
January afternoon. Her eyes peered out from a mountain of 
clothing. An old green acrylic blanket, heavily pilled, 
topped the entire ensemble. Taken aback, I said hello. She 
responded with almost a gaiety, but we got no further than 
an exchange of greetings. I see her now and then, never 
again at the picnic table. Maybe someone has made her 
move. Yesterday she was sitting on the steps of the house 
across the way. I recognized the green blanket. When I see 
her, she never seems to be doing anything-never panhan­
dling, just mostly sitting wherever she can find the sun. In her 1984 article in Scientific American, Ellen L. Bassuk wrote: "To talk with homeless people is to be struck 
by how alone most of them are. The isolation is most severe 
for the mentally ill. Family and friends grow exhausted or 
lack the ability to help; overburdened social workers may 
be less responsive; the homeless themselves may be un­
willing or unable to communicate their needs and to make 
use of the support available.

Some 7 4 percent of the shelter 
residents we interviewed said they had no family relation­
ships, and 73 percent said they had no friends, even within 
the shelter community."1 Stephanie Golden, in her 1992 
book The Women Outside: Meanings and Myths of 
Homelessness, writes: "The most important factor was the 
loss of family and other relationships. In the years before 
an accelerating loss oflow-cost housing in New York City 
made cheap hotel rooms virtually impossible to find, this 
was perhaps the most frequent reason for homelessness that 
the Dwelling Place staff heard. The issue was not necessar­
ily that the women were unable to maintain relationships 
but rather that they were unable to carry on when these were 
lost. The great majority had lived within society, to some 
extent at least, and became homeless only when their 
network of support was destroyed. Because most were 
products of a generation that socialized women to be 
dependent and not to work, the determining factor that 
broke up their lives and plunged them into homelessness 
was usually not economic but relational. ,,z 
Some of the spirits sleep back in the brush along the 
canal and on the tangled slopes of the hill below the 
University. Their crude shelters can be found there, par-

whatever else comes to hand. I've never actually seen 
anyone in these shelters, but someone has used them, and 
recently too.

one poor, female-run family manages to maintain a home

ticularly susceptible to homelessness. Research suggests

less is the inability to remain in viable relationships to 
important others, then that problem is surely not limited to 
those at the lowest functioning level of society. It appears 
that people are having trouble with relationships at all 
levels of functioning in society. Seen from a broad perspec­
tive, the indicators of relationship disruption across the 
entire society appear undeniable.

In another context, Papero paraphrased Calhoun's find­
ings in the following manner. "Individuals withhighsocial 
velocity showed appropriate territorial behaviors. As so­
cial velocity declined, however, animals showed behaviors 
that appeared to deviate increasingly from those consid­
ered optimally "mouselike." On the lower end of the curve, 
animals tended to avoid contact with others and to be 
ignored by the more dominant individuals altogether. As 
environmental stress increased ( due to population density), 
fewer and fewer individuals were able to maintain a high 
social velocity and ever greater numbers of animals exhib­
ited behaviors common to the lowest end of the curve. Although the curve and the differences between individu­
als tended to be intensified under environmental stress, 
Calhoun concluded that even under optimal environmental 
conditions, the social velocity curve, with attendant alter­
ations in behavior, will develop. "5 
If there be accuracy to this view of disturbance in the 
ability of people to relate to one another throughout 
society, then each person plays a direct part in the emer­
gence of homeless people.

Our own inability to get along 
with others, our side-taking, our fault-finding, our divorc­
ing, suing, robbing, killing and incarcerating, our intrusive 
helping, our egregious territoriality, our feelings (even 
delusions) of entitlement, our greed and "I know best" 
attitudes that provoke others to defend themselves against 
us create the environment in which the least able collapse. But have we a choice? Must we not defend ourselves 
against the others who are doing their own version of what 
we do to a greater or lesser degree? Was Malthus not 
correct? Are we not, as creatures of nature, red in claw and 
fang? Are we caught in an ecological trap, to borrow 
another of Calhoun's ideas, in which our most basic pro­
gramming (whether genetic or learned) exacerbates and 
even creates the very problems with which we must contend? If one accepts, for sake of discussion, the proposition 
that relationship disturbance is an expression of the dis­
ruption of the entire society and effects all sorts of rela­
tionships, then some of the current approaches to social 
problems, and in particular homelessness, may require 
reconsideration. Is it possible for homelessness to be 
addressed without addressing the functioning of the entire 
society in terms of the management of relationships?

society in terms of the management of relationships? Does 
the intense polarization that seems to characterize the 
human approach to any sensitive issue actually maintain 
and exacerbate the very dilemmas that stimulate the partisan 
response initially? Would it really be of greater long term 
benefit to the homeless for people to learn how to manage 
themselves responsibly with their rivals, their parents, their spouses than to spend a week or a weekend serving food to 
homeless people in a soup kitchen? Does the key to 
functioning begin at home, in one's own backyard, and 
with the people most important to self? Murray Bowen 
occasionally commented that one can't make a bean grow 
by pulling on it. If the simple proposition-that people's 
ability to manage relationships responsibly in society is 
deteriorating- is in any way accurate, then many of the 
ways humans currently address social dilemmas certainly 
resemble pulling on the bean. Bowen hypothesized that increased reactivity, the basis 
for increased difficulty relating to others, is an expression 
of the agitation, disturbance, or anxiety in the person and 
the family. He extended this idea to society as well.

He extended this idea to society as well. Theory 
would go on to suggest that the better functioning people in 
the family maintain their ability to manage relationships 
under greater pressure than do the poorer functioning 
members, but as the disturbance in the unit (family, orga­
nization, society) increases, more and more people have 
greater difficulty maintaining good functioning relation­
ships. In families, when the anxiety, agitation or distur­
bance can decrease, relationships become easier to manage 
and the entire unit functions more productively. In the family, when functioning of the unit slips, as 
relationships become more difficult, increasing amounts of 
energy and resources tend to be directed to the person(s) 
perceived to be the problem. Those efforts tend to produce 
short-term relief but often lead to a more intense version of 
the original problem, prompting a greater response from 
the family. It tends to be a vicious, escalating cycle. The 
less able become more vulnerable, and the more able more 
frustrated and fatigued. Polarizations develop between 
those who favor one remedy and those who favor another. More energy and resources are used up in the polarized 
stalemate, the family may stabilize at a reduced level of 
functioning and even come to accept the compromised 
state as the norm. The efforts to blame, cajole, bribe, or 
even force the most sensitive, least able to function are 
notably unsuccessful in anything but the very short run.

family therapy field came from varied theoretical back­
grounds and had different goals for their theoretical con­

Ludwig von Bertalanffy. He was trained as a biologist and 
worked in the quantitative study of metabolic processes. Disenchanted with applying a reductionist/mechanistic 
approach to the study ofliving organisms and theirprocesses

was without a means of scientific verification, von 
Bertalanffy sought to develop an overarching theory that 
would account for both living and non-living systems and 
eventually lead to the unification of all of the sciences. The originator of cybernetics was Norbert Weiner. It 
was with his background in physics, philosophy, math­
ematics and engineering that Weiner, with others, devel­
oped the necessary thinking which lead to the creation of

consensus. Bowen natural systems theory's method of inquiry is

communication and control in mechanical systems. The 
human family is conceptualized as a trivial machine; that it 
is a self-regulating system which utilizes covert communi-cation and control processes which are unique to man.

nature of humanity's predicament not because under­
standing its nature will enable us to escape it, but because 
if we do not understand it we shall continue to act and 
react in ways that make it worse." 
Thus begins the preface of Overshoot by William 
Catton, teacher and writerofhuman ecology and environ­
mental sociology. This book puts in ecological terms the 
two million years of human cultural evolution (Catton, 
1982, p.5). In particular it focuses on the repetitive 
processes of humans "taking over additional portions of 
the earth's total life supporting capacity, at the expense of 
other creatures." Each time this has occurred, by taming 
fire or developing tools, horticulture, metallurgy, agricul­
ture, technology, or medicine, human population has 
increased dramatically. However, the latest way human 
population has expanded can lead to the end of the 
process.

Earth. Carrying capacity for any species is the number that 
can be supported without permanent harm to the ecosys­
tem. For example, the ecosystem can restore itself from 
temporary overgrazing, but destruction of the rootlets 
under the soil line leads to a permanent process of deserti­
fication. This conclusion is based on levels of two resources: 
energy and ground water. Energy usage has depleted finite 
sources of fossil fuel. We are not living on the solar energy 
 coming in each year but are using irreplacable energy of the 
past. Likewise we are draining ground water from existing 
aquifiers holding supplies from thousands of years ago. The water table in central Arizona has dropped approxi­
mately 150 feet in the last 30 years. Closer to home, the 
Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission estimates that 
the metropolitan area will begin to run out of water in 2004. A drop in the water table below the roots of large trees is a 
first step toward desertification. When these trees die the 
understory and grasses are unable to maintain themselves 
in the glare of the sun and die.

Island, North Africa, Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and 
the Mayan Empire are examples. Some sections of desert 
in the U.S. are results of such processes. Evidence for 
global desertification is that currently there are 24 billion 
ton less topsoil on the planet each year. Wallace presented a number of other environmental 
effects on population pressure. Methane, carbon dioxide, 
and nitrous oxide gases contribute to global wanning. Many byproducts of increased population, especially de­
forestation, fuel the extinction of species. Forests are being 
cut because of settlement, collection of wood, and sale of 
lumber. Desertification occurs primarily by overgrazing 
and cutting of wood for fuel. Increased population leads to 
all these effects especially by deforestation and desertifica­
tion. These in tum decrease the food supply needed for 
increased population, thereby promoting famine and in­
creased susceptibility to disease both of which lead to 
increased mortality.

Teleki described the isues in Africa as complicated and 
difficult to fix. The African people themselves are strip­
ping their countries of their assets. Both farmers pressured 
by subsistent needs and purposeful greedy leaders engage 
in consuming natural resources. A corporate element 
drives a process where a few, often from outside the 
continent, benefit from the sales of animals, trees, minerals 
and cash crops. A country's natural resources are removed 
with little direct benefit to the country. For example, a large 
mahogany tree nets the country $200-$300 but the wood 
sells in Europe for about $300,000. Political colonialism 
has been replaced by economic colonialism. Foreigners 
trying to "help" are not always helpful. For example, 
religious missionaries are often avid hunters, and religious 
policy toward population control can counteract a country's 
public policy efforts. AID programs designed to be benefi­
cial see little of their funds actually reach the target country 
due to administrative costs and graft in the country. In terms of the ecological state of the continent Teleki 
reported that in earlier times there were few people and 
much wildlife. Now there are many people and mrukedly 
decreasing wildlife. There has been large scale burning of 
forests. The eastern and western portions of the belt of 
equatorial forest are burned off. Slash and bum agriculture 
generates ash that temporarily improves the thin tropical 
soil.

lntheFall 1992issueoftheFamilyCenterReport,Louise 
Rauseo described the Georgetown Family Center's efforts to 
develop a computerized database of multigenerational family 
histories to conduct family research. In response to this 
article, a number of people volunteered to participate in the 
project Some people offered to assist in developing the 
family history questionnaires, while others volunteered to 
provide their own family histories. Since then, significant 
progress has been made in moving toward the initial data 
collection phase. This report describes progress in defining 
the Family History Database Project, clarifying responsibili­
ties between project participants and the Family Center, 
developing methods to preseIVe confidentiality and collect 
and store data, and defining research expectations. Project Definition: The purposes of the project are to 
create and maintain a database of rigorously and systemati­
cally collected observations about family functioning and to 
make the database available to qualified researchers inhuman 
behavior. The database will contain multigenerational 
histories about family functioning, collected both retro­
spectively and contemporaneously. The project will be long term.

COMPLEX BIOLOGICAL SYSTEMS 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. A year ago I wrote an article for the Family Center Report 
entitled, "Bowen Theory and Evolutionary Theory." The 
article was an attempt to define some distinctions between the 
two theories. Bowen theory describes the human family as an 
emotional unit, and it uses systems thinking to deal with the 
complex, interdependent processes that occur in the unit. Besides describing some specific patterns of emotional func­
tioning present in all families, the theory holds that two basic 
life forces, differentiation and togetherness, account for 
variations in the intensity of the patterns. The theory does not 
address how the human family evolved to function as an 
emotional unit; it only assumes that it did. In contrast, 
Darwin's theory attempts to explain how evolution occurs, 
principally by the process of natural selection. It attempts to 
explain how human beings and other species have come to 
look and act the way they do. Whether the forces and patterns 
described by Bowen theory evolved solely by natural selec­
tion is, at this point, an unanswered question. During the past year, based on continued reading in 
biology, on discussions with biologists Stephen Emlen and 
John Bonner, and on exchanges with colleagues in my own 
field, I have thought more about the relationship between 
Bowentheoryandevolutionarytheory.

Symposium was radical. Family and family systems ideas 
were not a part of psychiatry although they were being 
taught in a department of psychiatry. The concept of 
looking at the family as a unit, or thinking of this unit as 
the focus of treatment, was a radical departure from the 
conventional view of psychiatry. Theoretical ideas com­
municated to the young residents at Georgetown had 
proved powerful, effective and useful. Many were mov­
ing to areas where family psychotherapy was "either 
unknown or poorly understood."1 Joseph Sebastian, a 
resident from the class of 1964 expressed interest in 
meeting again after completion of training, and proposed 
an annual family "homecoming" at which alumni could 
read papers to each other about their clinical experiences 
with families. In tum, "they could hear about new devel­
opments in the Georgetown program and in the family 
movement nationally."2 
6 The Symposium was designed to provide a forum for 
alumni to present their work to professional colleagues 
and provide time for professional exchange after each 
paper. In addition to the "alumni," a distinguished guest 
speaker was invited to attend the meeting and present his 
or her own work. The addition of a guest lecturer brought 
ideas from a broader professional circle and helped keep 
the Family Symposium from becoming "ingrown." Many 
of the original distinguished guests were personal and

REFLECTIONS ON THE THIRTIETH 
ANNUAL SYMPOSIUM 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. The Thirtieth Annual Family Symposium was notable 
both for a recognition of its origins and for a vision of the 
future. The focus on origins occurred at the Symposium 
banquet; the vision of the future threaded through two days 
of professional presentations. The First Annual Symposium was held in May 1965. The psychiatric residents who finished at Georgetown in 
June 1964 and Paulina Garcia McCullough, a social worker 
in the department then, planned and implemented the first 
conference. Three of the fonner residents, Francis "Bud" 
Andres, Tom Fogarty, and Joe Sebastian, spoke after 
dinner at the banquet. Paulina McCullough gave her 
recollections following their remarks. Others who had 
participated in early symposia then spoke. These included 
Lida Beth Cavanaugh, Lilian Rosenbaum, and Mary 
Goepfert. Finally, Roberta Holt, whose careful review of 
Murray Bowen's writings about the early symposia was 
central to planning the banquet program, described how 
much she had gained from the experience. Bud Andres, 
reminiscent of meetings past, moderated the evening. It would be difficult to summarize all the comments 
made during the banquet program. This is an era in society 
when history is often neglected or rewritten, usually heavily 
encumbered with the bias of the writer.

This is an era in society 
when history is often neglected or rewritten, usually heavily 
encumbered with the bias of the writer. The goal of this 
effort to review history was to be as factual as possible. The 
people who spoke were the people who did the planning, 
perfonned the administrative and logistical tasks, and 
presented many of the papers in those early years. In 
listening to their recollections, it was clear that each of the 
people had had the courage to follow Murray Bowen out of 
the mainstream, pursuing radically new ideas about human 
behavior and a method of therapy with unusual promise. It 
was fascinating, moving, invigorating, enlightening, and 
entertaining to listen to them describe how the Symposium 
began, particularly considering that their remarks were 
being made as part of the thirtieth conference. WINTER 1994 
The Symposium itself had a somewhat different design 
this year. The thinking behind the changes was that the 
natural sciences seem to be discovering new facts about 
living systems at an increasingly rapid rate. A goal was to 
increase the infusion of these facts into the Symposium. The new facts from many disciplines should both push the 
development of Bowen theory and further energize people 
knowledgeable about the theory who are attempting to 
make contact with the accepted sciences. Amplifications 
and extensions of Bowen theory can only enhance the 
effectiveness ofits applications in therapy and other arenas.

speakers. Many of the papers addressed two important 
dimensions that Bowen theory adds to the study of mind­
body connections: (1) the theory addresses individual 
variations in response to stress with its concept of the scale 
of differentiation; and (2) the theory describes the relation­
ship system component of stress by defining the forces and 
patterns that govern anxiety in families and other groups. Whereas Ors. Lumpkin and Pert described aspects of how 
the body functions as a system, many of the other presenters 
described how broaderrelationshipprocesses regulate each 
individual's physiology. The research on individual func­
tioning and relationship system functioning were certainly 
not integrated during the Symposium, but it was clear that 
the presenters were looking at different aspects of the same 
elephant A number of the papers emphasized the evolu­
tionary basis of human relationship systems. This is not a 
new theme, but the fruits of years of reading and thinking 
were evident. Two papers addressed the implications of 
natural systems thinking for the field of psychology. One 
paper amplified the distinction between Bowen theory and 
conventional theory concerning family reaction to death. The content of the Annual Symposium has changed 
significantly over twenty-nine years. Theory has guided the 
change.

decade. In the 1990s, science has increasingly dominated 
presentations at the Annual Symposium. Presenters are 
assemblingmorefactualknowledgefrom the sciences, viewing 
that knowledge through the lens of natural systems thinking, 
posing even better questions, and tentatively suggesting a few 
possible answers. Things are in flux. Little is proven, 
analogies still dominate presentations, but there is movement 
towards something more solid. A few presenters are getting 
very close to extending theory. By Bowen choosing more 
than forty years ago to anchor his theory in man's similarity 
to all life, he set in motion a process that would inevitably 
move the Annual Symposium towards more and more sub­
jects relevant to developing a science of human behavior. Presentations about clinical research will continue, as they too 
contribute to science. As the science progresses, the effec­
tiveness and innovativeness of the theory's applications will 
progress in parallel. Progress in applications can, of course, 
also add to theory. The only thing that can sidetrack. the 
forward movement of this process is human subjectivity. Thus far, the meeting is on track. DIRECTOR

Family Systems is the only journal based on Bowen family systems theory. Bowen theory is widely accepted asa well­
developed theory about the human family, one that views human behavior in the context of all life. Journal articles may 
either reflect Bowen theory or be relevant to it. Articles about elephant families, the brain, insect societies, flatworm 
behavior, and ancient civilizations may be as relevant as articles about Bowen theory itself, clinical research, and family 
therapy. Rather than a fixed body of knowledge, new facts are gradually amplifying and extending the theory. Therapy 
based on Bowen theory is also evolving. Research and applications using Bowen theory in disciplines such as biology, organizational development, anthropology; 
the law and medicine are generating new and exciting developments. The many disciplines represented on the Advisory 
Board reflect the theory's relevance to other fields. A new journal is needed to keep pace with the rapidly occurring changes.

Michael E. Kerr, MD 
The inaugural issue of Family Systems was published in 
June 1994. This is an interdisciplinary journal based on 
Bowen family systems theory which is published by the 
Georgetown Family Center. It will appear semiannually in 
the beginning and quarterly in the next two to three years. Murray Bowen's basic research direction was towards 
the accepted sciences. He believed that viable contact with the 
sciences would keep family systems theory open, enabling it 
eventually to be a science. Bowen wrote in detail about all the 
major components of his theory and therapy. Over the years, 
however, he repeatedly emphasized that the theory was 
incomplete,notfixed in stone; it could be modified, amplified, 
and extended by new facts. Death ended Bowen's work on the 
theory, but this journal is dedicated to the future of the theory 
and its many applications. It seems apt that Bowen suggested 
the journal's title, Family Systems. Bowen theory defies conventional categorization. It is 
more than a psychological theory. It is not an outgrowth of 
general systems theory. It is more than the basis of a fonn of 
family therapy.

Bowen theory defies conventional categorization. It is 
more than a psychological theory. It is not an outgrowth of 
general systems theory. It is more than the basis of a fonn of 
family therapy. It has potential applications in fields as 
diverse as medicine, biology, anthropology, law, sociology, 
and organizational management A natural systems theory 
can transcend the various compartments of knowledge con­
cerned with human functioning. A steady influx of factual 
knowledge and ideas from these various compartments or 
academic disciplines is critical for shaping the future of 
Bowen theory. This journal is not trying to create a new 
discipline, but to provide a forum for exchange between 
existing disciplines. N atura1 systems thinking, which can deal 
with the complex interactions that occur within and between 
multiple levels of living systems, is a framework that allows 
for exchange between disciplines. Natural systems thinking 
allows the six men of lndostan to communicate more effec­
tively, regardless of which part of the elephant they are 
touching. F amity Systems has an Advisory Board that reflects the 
journal's multidisciplinary orientation. This Board is com­
posed of distinguished scholars, writers, and researchers from SPRING 1994 
the natural and social sciences who, although not necessarily 
experts on Bowen theory, are sufficiently familiar with it to 
appreciate its relevance beyond the field of family therapy.

intended to represent the thinking of the Georgetown Family

evolutionary base of Bowen theory. One reason for this 
emphasis is that Bowen theory is commonly misperceived to 
be a psychological or sociological theory-its base in biology 
is totally missed. Another reason for the emphasis is to 
distinguish Bowen theory from Freudian theory. Many 
people erroneously view Bowen theory as an outgrowth of 
Freudian theory. Freud made important discoveries about 
human behavior, some of which can be incorporated into a 
natural systems theory, but his psychoanalytic theory treats 
man as a special case in nature. Freud conceived of a collision 
 between the instinctual urges of the individual. which he 
thought push continually for expression, and the civilizing or 
taming forces imposed on the individual by family and 
society. Toe collision creates a tension that psychoanalytic 
theory uses, in part, to explain the development of clinical 
symptoms and other aspects of human motivation.

to its environment, including others with whom the organ­
ism is in relationship. A natural, living system is one that 
is shaped by the selective forces of nature which affect 
whether and how the system survives from generation to 
generation. Each member of a natural, living system 
responds to these selective forces in basic, fundamental 
ways; that is, in emotional ways. Emotions may be trans­
mitted between and among individuals who are members 
of the system and it is through this emotional process that 
each member of a natural living system may affect the 
functioning of other members of the system. Emotions organize an individual's biology. One class 
of emotions is captured by the tenn anxiety. Anxiety is the 
response of an organism to a threat. The threat may be 
imminent, in which case the response is one of acute 
anxiety. The threat may be remote and may never even 
occur, in which case the response is one of chronic anxiety, 
extending over an indetenninate period of time. Anxiety, 
including chronic anxiety, constrains the range of respon­
sive options available and in this manner limits functioning 
across the full range of responses. Sometimes an emotion, especially anxiety, is so intense 
and sustained that it becomes impossible to contain it 
within the organism or within a two-person relationship. A 
third person is then brought into the relationship through 
the operation of emotional process.

LCSW gave a stimulating presentation about marriage as it 
relates to Bowen theory at the Thursday Professional 
Meeting. The presentation was grounded in a basic assumption 
that attachment is a requirement and characteristic of all life 
forms. In humans the need for attachment is variable, and 
is consistent with the variations on the scale of differentia­
tion. The variation along the scale of differentiation 
represents a range of behavior, from those able to function 
out of reality needs to those operating consistently from 
emotional need. Where an individual fits along the con­
tinuum of need is a function of togetherness forces and how 
they are managed. In many respects these are influenced by 
family process. 5 
 According to Ms. Robeau, the need for togetherness 
and its management can give rise to intensity and conflict. Over a period of time, conflict in a marriage can create a 
climate of chronic anxiety in which the ability to think is 
compromised for one or for both partners. When this 
occurs, the likelihood of cutoff increases.

Public speaking and writing are activities that can trigger 
anxiety. Fear of public speaking is a prevalent fear and can 
reach phobic proportions. Being stared at by a large number 
of people for an extended period of time, being subjected to 
possible criticism, or not representing oneself well are all 
aspects of this anxiety. The fear of writing, sometimes known 
as writer's block, can interfere with the productivity of even 
the greatest authors. Being subjected to criticism and not 
representing oneself well, as well as the added sense of 
pennanency of the written word can add to the intensity of a 
writer's problem. Writers and speakers may begin to doubt 
their knowledge of the subject, or find themselves procrasti­
nating. A writer may begin to worry about and let their work 
be influenced by the feared opinions of family members, 
readers or particularly "important" people.

TWENTY YEARS AT GEORGETOWN­
PART II 
Murray Bowen, M.D. There are three major areas of professional in­
volvement in this twenty years at Georgetown. One deals 
with my own evolution and the development of the theory 
and therapy. The second deals with my relationship with 
Georgetown, the development of the teaching and research 
programs, the evolution of the various symposia and 
meetings, the formalization of the structured postgraduate 
training programs in 1969, and finally the move to our off 
campus Family Center in December 1975. The third area 
deals with my participation in the family movement na­
tionally and the part Georgetown has played on the na­
tional scene. It is impossible to clearly separate one area 
from the others. No one area could have developed with­
out contributions from the other two. This report will 
focus primarily on the development of the theory and the 
therapy. My NIMH research from 1954-1959 had opened up 
dozens of new areas for research and clinical work. When I 
started at Georgetown in the fall of 1959, the initial goal 
was to start one regular teaching conference, to secure the 
financing for my NIMH staff previously promised to 
George Raines, to spend a year or so writing up the NIMH 
research, and then to move into new research with some 
teaching. I proceeded cautiously into teaching.

I proceeded cautiously into teaching. From the 
Menninger experience I had learned that teaching can so 
occupy energy that research is more fantasy than action. My move to NIMH created a full time research situation. At NIMH I learned that research and administration did 
not mix. It is possible to divide time between two separate 
activities but a good administrator is thinking about press­
ing administrative problems on his research time and the 
research suffers. A good researcher is thinking about 
research on his administration time and his administration 
suffers. I could have functioned well as an administrator at 
NIMH but I had made a significant life sacrifice for the 
research position and I resigned all administrative posi­
tions except those to keep my project alive. I believe this 
enchanced the research but probably hastened my termina­
tion at NIMH. All these factors influenced my decisions 
when I started at Georgetown. During 1959-60 much time was spent with John Rohrer, 
Ph.D., Chief of Psychology in the Department of 
Psychiatry. He had been involved in my early talks with 
George Raines and he knew the foundations that had pro­
mised Dr. Raines the funds to move my NIMH operation 
to Georgetown. We did not get the money but Dr. Rohrer 
made important indirect contributions in the early 
Georgetown years. His fund of knowledge was extensive 
and he was a genius in putting complex concepts into sim­
ple terms.

made important indirect contributions in the early

and he was a genius in putting complex concepts into sim­

than all the name psychologists with whom I had been 
previously associated. In 1960 I was again "alone," a one 
man operation in a new place. An agreement with Dr. Steinbach provided half time at Georgetown, most of it for 
writing and research planning. My busy half time private 
practice was my clinical research laboratory. I was the first 
family therapist in the area. Numerous referrals provided 
ready access to all kinds of families except low income and 
underprivileged people, who were seen in the clinic at 
Georgetown. The 1959 to 1965 years were exciting. The earlier de­
tailed theoretical concepts and therapeutic methods were 
rapidly extended to the entire spectrum of less severe emo­
tional illnesses. In 1959 I had a contract for a book about 
the NIMH research. The rush of new ideas made it 
frustrating to write about schizophrenia. In 1961 my 
editorial consultant believed I was close enough to a new 
theory to spend the next several years on that. I was 
pleased about the opinion, and glad to be free of writing 
about "ancient" material. In the 1960-61 period Bill Meissner spent summers help­
ing with detailed multigenerational histories on three 
families back as far as 300 years.

In the 1960-61 period Bill Meissner spent summers help­
ing with detailed multigenerational histories on three 
families back as far as 300 years. That fabulous experience 
provided data for the concept about the multigenerational 
transmission process and the refinement of the family 
diagram. It started the trend toward multigenerational 
histories in all families, and resulted in the detailed study 
of my own family. Very early in that work, I reasoned that 
one could spend years on a single family history, that all 
families are pretty much alike if one goes back into history, 
and my family would always be available for study. The development of theory led to changes in therapeutic 
methods which in turn produced data for extending the 
theory. My earliest method of family therapy with neurotic 
level families was developed in the 1956-59 period, along 
 side the schizophrenia research. Each spouse listened to, 
and "analyzed" the dreams, fantasies, verbalizations, and 
actions of the other spouse. Although a workable and suc­
cessful format, the psychoanalytic focus missed important 
new systems concepts and was gradually replaced. The no­
tion of "differentiation of self" was always in the 
background and I was constantly working to contain my 
own emotional reactivity in the midst of emotional chaos, 
so that one family member would take steps to define self.

This led to my notion of "staying outside the emotional 
arena" which is still generally misinterpreted as distancing 
from it. In the 1956 to 1959 period I had used the term "family 
therapy" when two or more family members were present, 
and "individual therapy" when only one person was pre­
sent. I still had no way to avoid a transference with only 
one person. By 1960 I had gained enough emotional con­
trol over my own functioning to be in the midst of emo­
tional turmoil without becoming part of it. When I began 
using the term "family therapy with one person" it was 
considered an inaccuracy in me. This issue could be 
debated forever without resolution, without the other side 
having a systems framework to evaluate it. In twenty years 
there has been some acceptance of the idea among systems 
people. The concept "The Triangle" required a long time to 
define. The first preliminary notions about the triangle 
were evident by 1956, but it was not until about 1963 it was 
sufficiently defined to be used as a precise theoretical and 
therapeutic concept. It is not possible to really see the 
precision of triangles until one is reasonably outside the 
emotional system, and not part of it. This is true of the 
other concepts to a lesser degree. The definition of 
triangles opened new conceptual horizons. Most impor­
tantly it led to precise knowledge about the triangle be­
tween two spouses and the therapist and to exact techni­
ques for modifying it.

Most impor­
tantly it led to precise knowledge about the triangle be­
tween two spouses and the therapist and to exact techni­
ques for modifying it. This was rather well perfected by 
1964. The practice of changing the entire family through 
changing one central triangle is still a cornerstone of this 
theory and method of therapy. The triangle concept also 
led to ways to conceptualize emotional systems in social 
and work situations, and to consult in office and work 
situations to validate the theory. The first six concepts of the theory were fairly well 
developed by 1964. In October 1964 I did the first of four­
teen years of regular trips to the Medical College of 
Virginia. In 1965 I agreed to do a paper for the journal, 
Comprehensive Psychiatry, without knowing I would have 
to integrate the six concepts into a "theory" before the 
paper could be considered finished. In May 1965 we had 
our first Georgetown Family Symposium. Later that 
month I made my section of the movie, "The Hillcrest 
Family." Writing the 1965-66 paper was one of the most 
frustrating and difficult experiences in my life. Hundreds 
of hours went into it. By fall I was so bogged down the 
paper was set aside for several months. In the spring of 
1966, at the urging of the editor, I began again. The task 
was still difficult.

By fall I was so bogged down the 
paper was set aside for several months. In the spring of 
1966, at the urging of the editor, I began again. The task 
was still difficult. Certain concepts would not mesh into 
what I could call a "theory." Completion of the paper 
finally took several days from a family vacation with ex-
2 tended families in August. A load was lifted when that 
paper finally went into the mail. At that point I felt free to 
proceed with a long postponed book. On the family trip in August 1966 there were the begin­
nings of the anxiety episode in my family of origin, later 
reported in the "Anonymous" paper. The year spent 
writing that paper had opened the door to a brand new 
area of investigation and research that was to take another 
six years. I had been working toward the "differentiation" 
of my self in my family of origin for years with minimal 
success. New knowledge about interlocking triangles led to 
new insights in my own family. All available free time 
from October 1966 to January 1967 was spent drawing 
family diagrams and triangles, making telephone calls and 
writing letters, all designed to bring important family 
triangles into focus for a long planned trip home in 
February 1967. The success of that visit was one of the 
most exhiliarating experiences in my life. I was able to stay 
outside the family emotional system an entire week in con­
trast to a few minutes or a few hours on previous trips.

I was able to stay 
outside the family emotional system an entire week in con­
trast to a few minutes or a few hours on previous trips. To 
me it meant the triangle held the secret for understanding 
emotional systems, and most especially IT MEANT THE 
THEORY WAS RIGHT. Events followed one another in rapid succession after 
the breakthrough in February 1967. In March 1967 I was 
scheduled for an important paper at a national family 
meeting. I had already spent a dozen years trying to com­
municate my concepts to the profession without really be­
ing heard. The "family of family therapists" is another 
"undifferentiated family ego mass." 
Instead of presenting yet another paper, which would 
not be heard by many, I decided to present the experience 
with my own family. It would be an action presentation 
about the theory. Most importantly it would help me begin 
to differentiate a self from the family of family therapists. Few therapists have more than superficial knowledge of 
triangles or of differentiation but the paper helped to begin 
a national focus on the extended family. I have now spent 
another dozen years working to differentiate a self from 
the family of family therapists who respond exactly as 
members of my own family. DIRECTOR

presentation, I began using examples of triangles and dif­
ferentiation from my own family in my teaching con­
ference at Georgetown. Residents began using this 
knowledge on visits to their families of origin and report­
ing the successes and failures to the conference. Within a 
year I discovered these residents were doing better dealing 
with spouses and children than similar residents in weekly 
formal family therapy for their own problems. This chance 
discovery that a little time spent working in their parental 
families was more successful than a direct focus on spouses 
and children was startling. This led to extensive research 
and experimentation in refining this method of ''coach­
ing" with all kinds of family groups as well as with one 
person. Within about two years this had become the core 
curriculum in our large postgraduate family training pro­
gram and is now the trademark of the Georgetown Family

Within about two years this had become the core 
curriculum in our large postgraduate family training pro­
gram and is now the trademark of the Georgetown Family 
Programs. Since the early 1960' s there had been some focus on the 
extended family in all family therapy, but never by ex­
cluding the primary focus on the nuclear family and never 
with specific methods for differentiation and detriangling. For ten years this has remained the method of choice with 
those motivated to assume responsibility for this task. For 
more anxious people we use a mixture of focus on the 
nuclear family before moving to the extended family. The 
results are far less successful when the two approaches are 
mixed. Another important method of family therapy over­
lapped with this focus on the extended family. Beginning 
in about 1964 I had the blueprint for a method of multiple 
family therapy which combined the principles of differen­
tiation in the husband-wife-therapist triangle with prin­
ciples of conventional multiple family therapy used at 
NIMH in the 1950's. The Georgetown Clinic never had 
enough new families to start such a group. Shortly after 
Lida Beth Robinson Cavanuagh joined the social work 
staff in 1965, she found enough families and in January 
1966 I started a research study to develop this method of 
multiple family therapy. By 1967, I and members of the 
research staff were using this method widely in places 
where they worked.

research staff were using this method widely in places 
where they worked. The research continued until 1970 and 
resulted in numerous papers. A chance discovery with this 
method led to infrequent appointments in all methods of 
therapy. In June 1967 I started a monthly multiple family 
therapy project on videotape at the Medical College of 
Virginia with families also seen weekly by psychiatric 
residents. Two of these families terminated with moderate 
symptom relief after a few months. I knew this was 
somehow related to the involvement of two therapists. In 
June 1968 I filled the vacancies with new families who 
could be seen only in the monthly video sessions. The new 
families did as well or better than similar families seen in 
routine weekly appointments. That was the beginning of 
scheduling less frequent appointments across the board in 
all methods of family therapy. This method of multiple 
family therapy still exists as one of our standard 
therapeutic methods. The next evolution in my own theoretical-therapeutic

It was asked to address the 
predictable reaction of the human to environmental stress. For many years I had been interested in the difference be­
tween emotional process in the family and emotional pro­
cess in society. I expected to do a paper on random 
thoughts about emotional reactions to crisis situations. In 
the months of writing the paper, it was possible to define 
specific connections between the family and society, which 
then made it possible to do fairly accurate predictions 
about the future of society. In 1973 this concept was 
presented as "Societal Regression" which accurately 
describes the current situation but misses the fact that 
societal regression and progression cycle in knowable 
ways, exactly as in families. The last major change in the theory was in 1974 when 
the name of the theory was changed from Family Systems 
Theory to The Bowen Theory, and two new concepts were 
added to the original six concepts, I had started the term 
Family Systems Theory in the 1960's, but it was being used 
so loosely by so many different people to mean so many 
different things the term had become meaningless. I dislike 
the use of personal names to describe theories and had 
searched unsuccessfully several years for a brief descriptive 
term. Finally, I agreed to use my name to designate the 
theory.

searched unsuccessfully several years for a brief descriptive 
term. Finally, I agreed to use my name to designate the 
theory. The seventh concept, "Emotional Cut-off," 
specifically defines emotional process between the genera­
tions, a process which was poorly defined by the other con­
cepts. The eighth concept, "Emotional Process in 
Society," includes both regression and progression. The 
past five years my effort has gone from schizophrenia at 
one end of the spectrum to societal issues at the other, and 
to the use of systems ideas to conceptualize physical, emo­
tional, chemical, and genetic factors as part of a function­
ing unit, rather than as separate entities. When I first began to grasp systems ideas in the 1950's I 
was sure that systems theory would eventually replace con­
ventional theories about living things. As time has passed, 
I have come to believe it may take another two generations 
for there to be a great enough systems base to begin to 
validate the various ideas. Every idea in the theory had 
been researched to my satisfaction before it had been in­
corporated in the theory. The generations of the future will 
decide whether or not it is on the mark, or how much it has 
missed the mark. Georgetown University has been a 
favorable place in which to work.

FAMILY CENTER REPORT 
James L. Framo, Ph.D. When I was asked to write this guest column I decided 
that of all the issues worth discussing about the family field 
the most important one concerns the politicization of the 
family therapy movement. I think the time has come for 
thinking about how the various theoretical models in fami­
ly systems theory can approach some integration. (I can 
just picture Murray Bowen's immediate reaction: "I hear 
you, Jim, but that push toward 'togetherness' can have 
many disguises."). In essence, I believe there should not 
only be exploration of the commonalities among the 
theories, but also how each can possibly supplement or 
enrich the others. I will first try to explain briefly how I 
think we arrived at this point of pseudo-differentiation. If one were to examine in simplistic fashion the develop­
ment of a field of endeavor, the following stages might be 
postulated: 
I. The state of observation and discovery of 
phenomena. 2. The formulation of theories about the observations.

The state of observation and discovery of 
phenomena. 2. The formulation of theories about the observations. (Theories consist of functional statements about the 
relationships which produce phenomena.) 
3. The organization of the observations into categories, 
based on the theories. (One could succinctly define 
science as systematized knowledge.) 
4. The splitting of the field into various theories or 
schools. The process of separation of a field into diverse schools 
is fascinating to observe. Insofar as psychotherapy is con­
cerned, I have wondered if, therapists find a way of work­
ing that is comfortable for them, and then build a theory 
on those methods compatible with their personality. In any 
event, the history of various movements reveals a repetitive 
pattern of initial unity and then division into various fac­
tions, sometimes resulting in denunciations between the 
''true believers'' and the ''revisionists.'' The bitterness 
among Freud, Jung, Adler, and others within the psycho­
analytic movement is well known. Unlike psychoanalysis, 
which stemmed from a single towering figure, family 
therapy developed independently in various places, thus 
naturally giving rise to different viewpoints. Every family 
therapy student knows there are a number of family 
therapy "schools," classified variously as communication, 
systems, strategic, structural, psychodynamic, experien­
tial, behavioral, gestalt, intergenerational, and problem 
solving.

eminence, but they also care for each other. As far as I 
know, there are no major family therapy figures who do 
not talk to each other. It is always difficult to separate ideological differences

The dangers of partisanship are less readily ap­
parent. The schools can become dogma and subject to self­
deception; that is, they tend to become closed frameworks 
in the sense that information or data that challenges basic 
assumptions is not allowed entry into the system. One sear­
ches only for confirmation or refinement of basic con-
 cepts. I think this is one of the reasons psychoanalysis has 
declined. Are the schools of family therapy the new 
religions? In substance, there are two basic conceptual approaches 
in the field. There are the schools which focus on interac­
tional patterns and restructuring of relational sequences; 
the past and mental representations are considered irrele­
vant. At least this is the stance taken in publications. It is 
obvious to anyone, however, who observed treatment ses­
sions conducted by these family therapists that they are 
making constant but implicit use of their psychodynamic 
knowledge. Then there are those schools, in the minority 
now, which build on what is known about human ex­
perience and behavior, which take history into account, 
and believe that what goes on inside peoples' heads is just as 
important as what goes on between people. From my point 
of view, it is the relationship between the intrapsychic and 
the transactional which is central.

From my point 
of view, it is the relationship between the intrapsychic and 
the transactional which is central. One advantage, by the 
way, of different belief systems in science is that contro­
versy can be settled by research; thus far almost no system­
atic studies have been done comparing the different treat­
ment methods. In my judgment all the schools have value, 
and training programs should expose students to all the 
family therapy models. It is my thesis that the family therapy field needs more 
communication among its schools, should search for 
similarities and concordance among the theories, and when 
true differences are found they should be tested. I'm not 
very sanguine that the originators can do it since they are 
much too invested in their own theory. I have even 
speculated that devotion to one's theory can supplant 
devotion to one's intimates. I also don't think that the in­
novator's followers can do it because of their loyalty or 
special relationship to their leader. Perhaps it rests with the 
third generation of family therapists. IDEAS FROM ADVANCED TRAINEES

public and private outpatient mental health settings. Following the com­
pletion of an M.S. W., she has practiced as a family therapist in addition 
to having administrative and supervisory responsibilities. The following is a beginning effort in the development 
of my thinking about the applications of Bowen Theory to 
organizational systems. I will briefly highlight some of 
these comparisons and applications. Bowen Theory describes the human phenomenon in 
terms of the forces and counterforces that operate within 
family relationships. Similar forces also operate within 
organizations. The relationship process among the in­
dividuals within an organization throughout the genera­
tions of its management and employees and the relationship 
of that organization to society is similar to relationships 
among members of a family throughout the generations of 
the family and the relationship of that family to society. Thus, the process inherent in human relationship systems 
provides the basis for comparing organizations and 
families. The way a person functions in his or her life is influ­
enced by the way that person relates (or does not relate) to 
family of origin.

The way a person functions in his or her life is influ­
enced by the way that person relates (or does not relate) to 
family of origin. An individual's ability to manage self in 
relation to family provides the foundation for managing 
self in other relationships. For example, when an in­
dividual's attachment to family of origin is extremely in­
tense, there is a greater potential for the individual to relate 
to the organization and/or the individuals within in an ex­
tremely intense way. The degree of intensity may be con­
ceptualized on a continuum with extreme closeness or 
overinvolvement with emotional process on one end, and 
extreme distance or cutoff from emotional process on the 
other. An individual with highly intense family relation­
ships is likely to have highly intense work relationships 
which, like in families, may be characterized by either 
distance or by overinvolvement. That is, the level of inten­
sity in both family and work is extreme, but may be mani­
fested either way. Thus, the level of intensity within an 
organizational system is affected by the relationships of 
the individuals within that organization to their families of 
origin. Another factor that may affect the level of intensity 
within an organization is the nature of the organization 
itself, its history, its leadership its source of funding, as 
well as the product or service it provides.

manifestation may reflect that person's tolerance and 
management of anxiety within his or her own family. Symptoms of increased anxiety within an organization 
may be exhibited by tardiness, absence, apathy, conflict, 
accidents, sudden unprovocated threats of unionization 
and a general decrease in efficiency and productivity.

As in a family, individual members of an organization 
fill certain functional roles which serve to maintain the 
equilibrium of the system. For example, in a family where 
a woman dies leaving three children, the oldest daughter 
may automatically assume the mothering responsibilities 
regarding job tasks and emotional relationships. A similar 
process may take place in an organization. When an 
employee leaves an organization, he or she not only 
vacates the position and its job responsibilities but 
established emotional alliances as well. The attraction of a 
new employee to the job and the employer to the employee 
may be related to the perceived ability to fulfill not only 
the job tasks but the emotional alliances as well. If 
members of a family or of an organization are aware of 
their automatic responsiveness to assuming functional 
roles, they may be able to modify the process. The more automatic the process, that is, without 
thoughtful decision-making, that propels an individual's 
functioning in his or her family, the more automatic will be 
the responsiveness to fulfilling functional roles in an 
organization, especially at times of high anxiety. The way a 
particular person relates to parents, grandparents, aunts, 
uncles, and siblings may affect the way that person relates 
to bosses, administrators, supervisors, and coworkers.

the position and the cpnflictual relationship serve a func­

getting involved in the automatic alliances that come with

and keeping the relationship with the medical director as 
calm as possible. Learning as much as possible about the 
organization and its operation, developing relationships 
with as many significant people as possible without getting 
locked in particular relationship patterns, and keeping the

ty of modifying the process.

To assess the overall functioning of an individual within 
a family and the family itself demographic characteristics, 
symptoms of physical, emotional, and social dysfunction, 
and responses to nodal events must be observed. Because 
normal fluctuations of anxiety can distort the assessment 
at any one particular time, functioning must be observed 
over time and throughout generations. Higher functioning 
is characterized by the ability to distinguish between feel­
ings and thoughts, to operate from either a feeling or a 
thinking position, and to make thoughtful objective life 
decisions. A higher functioning family faced with high 
anxiety and resultant dysfunction will predictably have the 
capacity to regain functioning more quickly. To assess the overall functioning of an organization, the 
data must also be viewed over time, through different 
generations of administrators and through different phases 
of development to allow for normal fluctuations of anxiety 
and to identify characteristic response patterns to these 
shifts. Facts about the process of decision-making, 
whether by exploration of options and thoughtful con­
sideration of outcome or "because it's always been done 
that way," definition of objectives and goals with plans 
for implementation consistent with goals, tolerance for 
differences of opinion, and shifts in leadership and policy 
throughout the organization's life cycle are indicators of 
the level of organizational functioning.
