more thoughtful, objective functioning is usually in­
dicative of a higher functioning organization. Higher func­
tioning organizations have the potential for greater pro­
ductivity, less staff conflict, fewer employee symptoms, 
more open communication among and within levels of 
hierarchy, more tolerance for differences and, in general, 
more responsible functioning of individuals within the 
organization and of organizations to their employees and 
to society. As in families, organizations may appear to be 
high functioning because they are symptom-free only when 
anxiety is low. The slightest increase in anxiety may result 
in symptom formation. Defining a self in an organization is based on the same 
principles as defining a self in a family. The basic goal is to 
increase the responsible functioning of self. Progress in 
defining a self in one system no doubt has benefits for the 
other, although greater gains seem to evolve from progress 
in defining a self in family of origin. Some of the ways to 
implement this goal within an organization parallel some 
of the ways to define self in a family.

BIOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF CANCER 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. A widely accepted view about the etiology of cancer is 
that a normal cell is transformed into a cancer cell as the 
result of damage to genes in the cell's nucleus. This 
damage or change in a gene, referred to as a mutation, can 
be caused by a variety of agents, chemicals, viruses, or ex­
cessive exposure to radiation, among others. Such a 
genetic mutation, which is an irreversible change, is con­
sidered to be the basis for a normal cell acquiring the 
characteristics that make it a cancer cell, namely, the 
capacity for unrestrained growth in the body, referred to 
as autonomy, and the capacity for direct invasion and 
migration into tissues the cell does not normally occupy. Professor Armin Braun of Rockefeller University in 
New York has proposed an alternative to the genetic muta­
tion model for cancer. Based primarily on his research 
with plant tumors, Dr. Braun has developed an epigenetic 
model for cancer, a model he presented at the Family 
Center's sponsored Symposium on the Emotional and 
Biological Aspects of Cancer on October 15, 1979.

Braun has developed an epigenetic 
model for cancer, a model he presented at the Family 
Center's sponsored Symposium on the Emotional and 
Biological Aspects of Cancer on October 15, 1979. Braun 
believes that the genetic information necessary to establish 
a cancer cell is already present in a normal cell. The normal 
cell usually does not become cancerous because this infor­
mation or cancer potential is represented by an as yet poor­
ly understood regulatory process. This cancer potential, 
which was presumably acquired by the cell at some earlier 
stage in evolution, only emerges when disturbances in cell 
regulation permit the derepression of this potential. Braun believes that this repression-depression process 
involved in the transformation of a normal cell to a cancer 
cell may be similar to the normal process of cell differen­
tiation. Most cells of the body, through the process called 
differentiation, become specialists. As specialists, they per­
form a narrow range of tasks, yet retain the potential to do 
a wide range of other tasks. Red blood cells, for example, 
make hemoglobin but not albumin, while liver cells do the 
opposite. Both cells, however, seem to have the genetic 
potential to make both substances. Braun considers the cancer cell a type of specialist too, a specialist in making 
the substances that enable it to keep reproducing itself.

Braun considers the cancer cell a type of specialist too, a specialist in making 
the substances that enable it to keep reproducing itself. If Braun's concept that disturbances in cell regulation 
are critical in the development of cancer is correct, then to 
what extent is this process reversible? Dr. Braun presented 
fascinating evidence from plant and animal studies that 
reversal of the cancer transformation process can occur 
both spontaneously and as the result of certain experimen­
tal techniques. He suggested that further research into this 
reversal process might have more potential value for 
cancer treatment than the current effort to find better 
methods to kill cancer cells, either through chemotherapy 
or radiation techniques. The issue of regulating cell functioning and its relation­
ship to cancer poses some interesting questions for systems 
theory. Systems theory focuses on the relationships be­
tween the parts of a system, defining the influence of the 
nature of those relationships on the functioning of the 
parts. The nature of relationships is viewed as critical 
regulatory influence on the functioning of the individual 
parts. Genes can be thought of as part of such a system. Rather than being independent entities that are dictating 
the functioning and behavior of a cell, Braun's work sug­
gests that genes are subject to regulatory influences, both 
from within and from without the cell nucleus.

nature is one grand interdependence of all its various parts 
mutually influencing and regulating one another. Com­
plete autonomy does not exist. Attempts to ~xplain cancer 
by looking inside the cell nucleus for a defect is like trying 
to explain the movements of the earth by studying its core. Presumably, the fundamental disturbance in cancer is in 
relationships, and this relationship disturbance is likely oc­
curring at multiple levels ranging from the family relation­
ship system down to the relationships between cells and 
even to relationships within individual cells. Following Dr. Braun's presentation about the biological 
aspects of cancer, Dr. Murray Bowen and Dr. Michael 
Kerr made presentations about the emotional aspects of 
cancer. Dr. Bowen's interest in cancer and its relationship 
to emotional forces spans most of his psychiatric career. Other interests and responsibilities have kept him from 
concentrating his research energies on this area, but it was 
he who steered Dr. Kerr towards cancer some years ago. Dr. Bowen believes that there are important lessons to be 
learned about theory and therapy from the study of family 
process in cancer, lessons that may not be so obvious from 
the study of the emotional dysfunctions.

Dr. Kerr's last area of discussion was his personal ex­
perience with psoriasis and its relationship to chronic an­
xiety. Psoriatic skin lesions reflect excessive cellular 
reproductions with the piling of these cells on the skin's 
surface and the formation of scaling lesions. In Dr. Kerr's 
personal experience the level of activity of the lesions are a 
perfect reflection of the degree of chronic anxiety. When 
anxiety is low, the lesions disappear completely. Dr. Kerr 
then presented a series of slides showing that all skin condi­
tions ranging from psoriasis to benign tumors to precan­
cerous lesions to squamous cell skin cancers could be 
viewed on a continuum with the same basic physiological 
mechanisms involved in each process. It seems reasonable 
to assume that not only did anxiety play a role in psoriatic 
activity but in the benign and malignant tumors as well. This Symposium is part of a general long-term effort at

In mammals, the counterpart of the reptilian forebrain 
is represented by a massive group of ganglia which Dr. MacLean refers to as the "R-complex." Research con­
ducted at his field laboratory in Poolesville, Maryland sug­
gests that the role of the R-complex in everyday behavior 
includes selecting and defending a homesite, foraging and 
hunting, mating and breeding, forming social hierarchies, 
homing and migrating, engaging in repetitious and super­
stitious behavior, showing obeisance to precedent, and 
imitating and promoting deceptive behavior. His experi­
ments demonstrate for the first time in a mammal that the 
R-complex plays a basic role in species-typical ritualistic 
behavior. These are behavioral indications that the rep­
tilian brain, which has only a rudimentary cortex, is poorly 
equipped for learning to cope with new situations. In the 
extinct transitional forms between reptiles and mammals, 
the cortex is presumed to have undergone great elaboration 
and differentiation, so that animals would have a better 
means of viewing the environment and learning to survive. In all existing mammals, the old cortex has undergone a 
large convolution called variously the great limbic lobe or 
the limbic system.

In all existing mammals, the old cortex has undergone a 
large convolution called variously the great limbic lobe or 
the limbic system. Clinical and experimental studies over 
the past forty years have provided evidence that the limbic 
system (limbic cortex and brain stem) derives information 
in terms of emotional feelings that guide behavior required 
for self-preservation and preservation of the species. MacLean notes that clinical observations provide the 
best evidence of the role of the limbic system in emotional 
behavior. Epileptic discharges in or near the limbic cortex 
result in a broad spectrum of vivid emotional feelings. MacLean believes that it is one of the wonders of the brain 
that limbic discharges tend to spread in and be confined to 
the limbic system not directly involving the neocortex (neo­
mammalian brain), and suggests that this underlying fac­
tor may contribute to the inexplicable conflicts between 
what we feel and what we know. It is also significant that 
limbic discharges may result in symptoms characteristic of 
10 the toxic and endogenous psychoses, such as feelings of de­
personalization, distortions of perception, paranoid delu­
sions and hallucinations. MacLean divides the limbic system into three subdivi­
sions. The two older ones are closely related to the ol­
factory apparatus. His studies have shown that these two 
subdivisions are involved in oral and genital functions 
respectively.

bypasses the olfactory apparatus. MacLean suggests that 
this subdivision, most highly developed in humans, may 
reflect a shift from the olfactory to the visual in socio­

ian and paleomammalian brains pass through the hypo­
thalamus and subthalamic regions. According to MacLean 
these pathways provide the avenues to basic personality. MacLean believes that these pathways hold the key to the 
expression of "prosematic" behavior, another word 
coined by MacLean which denotes any kind of nonverbal 
signal, whether vocal, bodily, or chemical. Compared with the limbic cortex, the new cortex (neo­
mammalian brain) is like an "expanding numerator," 
according to MacLean. It mushrooms late in evolution and 
culminates in human beings, affording a vast neural 
"screen" that makes symbolic language and the associated 
functions of reading, writing, and arithmetic possible. "Mother of invention" and father of abstract thought, the 
neomammalian brain promotes the creation and preserva­
tion of ideas. MacLean believes that the concept of the triune brain 
has significant implications for psychiatry and the social 
sciences.

Some clinical conference days provide feedback on 
things I had sort of forgotten. There was such a day in the 
spring of 1980 when some in the audience placed too much 
importance on the "kinesics" of body posture, man­
nerisms, facial expression, and other expressions of body 
language. I have been interested in this order of data for a 
long time. It is easily over-interpreted or misinterpreted. That is the subject of this clinical note. Experience with these issues goes back to the early years 
of my NIMH research. Most of our theories about human 
ralationships include the concepts of love, hate, devotion, 
anger, rage, and numerous other subjective states. It is 
next to impossible to prove scientifically the presence or 
absence of these feeling states, or measure them, without 
depending on what the human SAYS about subjectivity. The difference between what the human SAYS and what 
he DOES is notoriously discrepant.

The difference between what the human SAYS and what 
he DOES is notoriously discrepant. Decades ago, psychology devised the "scientific 
method." It was designed to find common denominators 
in this shifting sea of subjectivity, and ultimately to make 
the study of human relationships into a science acceptable 
to the accepted sciences. This has not occurred. I do not 
believe this ever can occur. Early in the NIMH research I was looking for ways to 
define the VERIFIABLE FACTS of human relationships, 
and to bypass concepts based on subjectivity. The effort 
resulted in my beginning effort to view the human 
phenomenon the way Darwin had viewed the subhuman 
world. My critics of that period said it could not be done. They were right within their frame of reference. I was 
distantly right within my frame of reference. It is impossi­
ble for the human observer to get beyond his own bias and 
subjectivity in viewing the emotional phenomenon of 
which he is a part. I was asking only for an opportunity to go as far as I 
could in containing my subjectivity, in becoming the most 
objective observer that was humanly possible, and in 
avoiding the intermix of my uncontained subjectivity with that of the family. My effort contradicted one of the main 
premises of individual psychotherapy in which the 
therapist works for an effective emotional connectedness 
with the patient, which is known as transference, and 
which is viewed as the principal modality of change in 
psychotherapy.

Part of my early effort was to focus on ACTION which 
could be measured and validated, and to defocus subjec­
tivity which could not be verified. In 1956 a research 
associate, Robert H. Dysinger, M.D., did a paper, "The 
Action Dialogue in an Intense Relationship." It was a very 
simple premise in which words were tuned out and the rela­
tionship between a mother and daughter was evaluated in 
terms of gross action between them. The action told a 
more consistent story about the relationship than anything 
that was said. The paper was presented at the annual 
meeting of the American Psychiatric Association in May 
1957. Neither the discussant nor the audience could really 
"hear" the concept, the professional response was 
negative, and the paper was never published. It did repre­
sent an early effort to get beyond subjectivity and into 
verifiable FACTS about relationships. 2 In the late 1950's, Scheflen and Birdwhistell began their 
research on body language at Eastern Pennsylvania 
Psychiatric Institute. Theirs was a sophisticated study in 
which they tuned out the sound and analyzed family rela­
tionships from microscopic action on sound movies. I was 
so fascinated by their effort that I stayed in personal con­
tact with them and learned all I could as they developed the 
professional discipline of "kinesics." The ACTION bet­
ween people tells its own story.

From the standpoint of 
conventional theory, the action is out of conscious 
awareness and could be called the language of the un­
conscious. From a systems viewpoint I now think of it as 
automatic emotional reactivity. I worked hard to incor­
porate the knowledge of kinesics directly into family 
therapy. It was not as effective as I had hoped. By the early 
1960's I abandoned it except as background knowledge for 
the therapist. By the early 1960's kinesics was being taught in profes­
sional schools. At my various demonstrations of family 
therapy, there appeared an increasing number of young 
professional people who were zealous in their effort to 
read body language meaning into therapy sessions. At first 
I was pleased with the interest in this new body of 
knowledge. People tend to veiw any situation through 
what they have already learned and the new knowledge 
seemed to provide a different dimension than the usual 
psychodynamic explanations. As a group, the kinesics peo­
ple seemed more dogmatic. The attraction to kinesics may 
have been the promise of a new key to the language of the 
unconscious. However it came about, the kinesics people 
were persistent. It was not unusual for them to imply, 
''Through my knowledge, I know something about you 
that you don't know." Any attempt by me to explain a dif­
ferent way of viewing the clinical situation was often heard 
as my defensiveness and denial, and further evidence of the 
accuracy of their observations.

Other experiences add another dimension to this note. In 
the 1950's mental health professionals began visiting the 
established family centers to learn about family therapy. My family programs have always attracted visitors and the 
number has increased each year. Average mental health 
professionals have fixed ideas about the nature of mental 
illness and psychotherapy and little ability to comprehend 
a theory different from the one they learned in training. They have no frame of reference to HEAR that the way a 
therapist THINKS about a problem can be more important 
than what the therapist DOES in therapy. The visitors 
wanted to hear about family therapy and they viewed it as 
method, style, and technique appended to conventional 
theory. The average professional visitor would say, "I 
want to see you WORK with families so I can know exactly 
what you DO in family therapy.'' In the beginning I would 
attempt to explain some of the basic differences hoping it 
would enable them to get more from the visit. Very quickly 
I learned that the basic posture of a visitor was not likely to 
change and the explanations about differences could be 
counter-productive. I have kept explanations to a 
minimum except when the visitor's curiosity is aroused and 
they have a basis for hearing something different. Instead 
of offering explanations, I try to ask for the visitor's opin-ions about their perceptions.

want to know what the therapist "thought" he was DO­
ING in therapy,. If they did want the therapist's opinion, it 
was to contrast it with what the therapist actually DID, as 
revealed by their scientific studies. Most of the students 
had well designed research plans for the numerous 
variables in the therapeutic relationship, but none had con­
sidered variables that would detect differences in theory.

The video program began at a time when I was still 
teaching the "reversal" as therapeutic technique. The 
phenomenon that I have called reversal has been further 
developed by Haley and later by Selvini Palazzoli as the 
"therapeutic paradox." In the early 1970's I gave up the 
teaching of reversals as technique because poorly differen­
tiated therapists were inept in the use of the reversal, and 
better defined therapists automatically used it successfully. The "reversal" has a long history at Georgetown. It was 
developed in the early 1960's as part of the theoretical con­
cept, triangles. Until that time my activity in 
psychotherapy had been rather formal, serious, and 
restrained. Then came the precise knowledge about 
triangles. When a family member, or the therapist, could 
"see" the step-by-step development of the triangle emo­
tional complex, and that person could assume an opposite 
or different emotional posture than that dictated by the 
family emotional system, the emotional complex would 
immediately resolve or be "detriangled." This knowledge 
of triangles was used in two ways, First, it was taught to in­
dividual family members as a way for the individual to 
quickly resolve the immediate family problem. It was 
magical when it worked. This was developed into a precise 
therapeutic method that I used extensively in the early to 
mid 1960's.

It was 
magical when it worked. This was developed into a precise 
therapeutic method that I used extensively in the early to 
mid 1960's. I abandoned the method because the 
motivated family members seemed to be acting more on in­
formation from outside self than from inside self, the 
change tended to be transient, and the family never seemed 
to know what to do when symptoms returned. The method 
was amazingly successful for short term therapy. I believe 
that variations of this method have been incorporated into 
behavior modification therapy and parent effectiveness 
training. The knowledge of triangles was also used by the 
therapist in avoiding emotional incorporation in the family 
system, or in "detriangling" self when he became emo­
tionally involved. The term "reversal" came from the ef­
fort to find an opposite or different posture from that dic­
tated by the family system. The reversal was an effective 
way for the therapist to defuse the intensity of emotionali­
ty in the family, and stay in contact with the family while 
staying outside the emotionality. When a family is emo­
tionally involved in an issue, the climate becomes overly 
serious. The reversal involves an ability to see the other 
side of the issue, to interject a bit of humor, to change the 
pace, and to remain casual in the face of family 
seriousness. There are literally dozens of techniques in­
volved in this.

members that he had brought with him a God. The tribe, 
naturally, welcomed the new God, expecting that He 
would become a part of the harmony. However, faithful to 
the call of the culture he represented, the missionary began 
advocating that there can be only one God, and all other 
gods should be discarded. Regardless of the outcome of 
the story-probably a tragic one-how unreligious, how 
insane, how egocentric this missionary must have looked

A FAMILY THERAPY TREATMENT 
AND TRAINING PROGRAM 
By Patricia H. Meyer, ACSW 
In 1978, the Virginia Department of Corrections decided 
to explore how family therapy could assist juvenile of­
fenders and their families to improve the "quality and 
diversity of their personal and interpersonal lives." Three 
major family therapy models were selected for evaluation: 
communication (Satir), systems (Bowen), and structural 
(Haley). It is anticipated that "the results of the project 
would provide a systemic view whereby the viability of 
family therapy as the treatment model of choice in working 
with juvenile offenders and their families could be deter­
mined." 
The effectiveness of the three models will be compared 
longitudinally. A minimum of sixty families are being 
referred to each center by four Virginia court districts. A 
control group will receive traditional court-directed ser­
vices.

The following column represents one of several interests that have 
evolved during her training at the Family Center. Since receiving her M.S. W. from the University of Michigan in 1968, 
Anne has worked in a child welfare agency in California, a home for un­
wed mothers in Texas and, since moving to the Washington area in 1975, 
as a psychiatric social worker at the Alcohol Center in Arlington, 
Virginia. Bowen Theory has many implications for the understan­
ding and treatment of the development of and recovery 
from alcoholism in a family. Bowen states that, in general, a person marries a spouse 
with an equal level of differentiation. That is, over a 
lifetime, people have a certain degree of ability to act as 
autonomous, functional individuals, as well as a certain 
degree of dependence and reactivity to the emotional 
forces in their families. People marry spouses with the 
same relative level of autonomy/dependence. This concept is difficult for many people to accept. We 
all know families in which one spouse is more functional, 
creative, responsible, efficient, conscientious, or outgoing 
than the other. All of us have seen marriages where one 
spouse is psychotic, alcoholic, depressed, dysfunctional, or 
clearly operating below the capacities of his partner. In 
fact, many mental health professionals find themselves 
"working" with the functional spouse to get the "sick" 
partner into therapy or into a hospital, or onto medication.

In 
fact, many mental health professionals find themselves 
"working" with the functional spouse to get the "sick" 
partner into therapy or into a hospital, or onto medication. In traditional psychotherapy, the goal of therapy generally 
points toward treating this sick partner and then returning 
him to society or to the family "cured." 
The concept of equal levels of differentiation of spouses 
points to a completely different approach to the dynamics 
of dysfunction in a family. Bowen argues that each spouse 
enters marriage with a similar kind of "programming" for 
emotional closeness from his extended family. Two in­
dividuals come into a marriage with a mutual degree of 
need for emotional satisfaction from their mate, and in 
marriage they become an emotional amalgam. They have 
areas in which they operate autonomously, but each is sen­
sitive and reactive to the other's thoughts and actions. In 
one sense, each begins to function as a part of the other. They become an organism or a system. This concept of 
emotional fusion makes it inconceivable to think of one 
spouse's dysfunction as independent of the other spouse. Traditional psychotherapists argue that when psychosis 
or alcoholism develops in a spouse, the other spouse only 
reacts to it by leaving, becoming depressed, or angry. Bowen theory poses this duality in another light. Each 
spouse enters the marriage with a level of emotional need.

Bowen theory poses this duality in another light. Each 
spouse enters the marriage with a level of emotional need. In the process of pooling their emotional selves when the 
needs are intense or the stress is high, problems in the mar­
riage emerge. Bowen identifies three areas of dysfunction: 
an emotional, social, or physical problem in a spouse, con­
flict between the spouses, or a focus and development of a 
problem in a child. 5 
 6 Traditional psychotherapy veiws dysfunction as an in­
trapsychic problem. A system's viewpoint sees the problem 
as part of the interactional process in the family. Dysfunc­
tion develops in one person which in fact serves to keep 
that system in balance or to allow the rest of the system to 
function. In a marital relationship, it is theoretically predictable 
that as one spouse functions less effectively or responsibly 
the other begins to function in a way to compensate for 
that change. It is as if the organism of the marital system 
develops extra muscles in its back to compensate for the 
withering away of muscles in its arms. Another way of viewing dysfunction in a spouse is as a 
seesaw. In the marriage each partner deposits his level of 
functional self on one end of a seesaw so that the seesaw 
balances. As the marriage progresses, however, one side 
begins to borrow from the other so that one functions bet­
ter at the expense of the other.

As the marriage progresses, however, one side 
begins to borrow from the other so that one functions bet­
ter at the expense of the other. This borrowing is typical of 
most marriages and becomes the obstacle to seeing two 
spouses operating at equal levels of differentiation. In families with high anxiety or intense emotional needs 
for togetherness, the borrowing of self triggers a reciproci­
ty in which the more spouse A functions, the less spouse B 
functions, so the more spouse A functions, and so on. The 
seesaw begins to tip progressively until one spouse is 
dysfunctional or dead. Although many people have found 
this concept confusing or difficult to understand, I was 
stunned by the clarity and exactness with which it describes 
the development of alcoholism within families I have 
observed, and explains readjustments families have to 
make when the alcoholic stops drinking. Alcoholism develops in families of various levels of dif­
ferentiation. The progression of the problem, or the 
amount of dysfunction, varies with each individual over 
time. Some people may take forty years to develop symp­
toms that others have after two years of drinking. However, if the drinking continues, the progression of the 
symptoms and the intensity of the problem is predictable 
to an endpoint of death or institutionalization.

However, if the drinking continues, the progression of the 
symptoms and the intensity of the problem is predictable 
to an endpoint of death or institutionalization. When a person stops drinking, however, the ability to 
function is not determined as much by the gravity of the 
alcohol problem, as by the level of functioning of the per­
son when he began to use alcohol. That is, a talented 
businessman may make a million dollars, drink it up, stop 
drinking, and make another million. Another person may 
be unemployed and drifting and drinking. When both stop 
drinking, they become a little more functional than when 
they were drinking. That is, their level of involvement with 
alcohol is less important than the level of self already 
established before they started drinking. The process of interaction between the alcoholic and the 
spouse becomes so predictable and definable that it is 
useful to list the characteristics of alcoholic families. The basic dynamic in alcoholic families is a reciprocity 
of over/under functioning in which one spouse is efficient 
and self-reliant, treating A like a child. The more capable 
the spouse is at maintaining the functioning of the system, 
the more quickly A will fall into total dysfunction and 
death.

Many mental health professionals totally miss the duali­
ty of this process, and underestimate the durability of these 
alcoholic marriages. They tend to offer services such as 
programs on domestic violence shelters for abused women. They assume that if families could separate from the 
alcoholic, they would. Similarly there is a recognized 
frustration in emergency rooms and in police stations at 
the unwillingness of "battered wives" to press charges 
against their spouses. This behavior is explicable and predictable from a fami­
ly systems viewpoint. The alcoholic is not the "problem," 
but an expression of the functioning of the family system. Each spouse plays a role in this dysfunctioning/ overfunc­
tioning relationship, and to view one as the victim and the 
other as the "problem" is to contribute to the family pro­
cess rather than to modify it.

Clearly, the development of alcoholism cannot be reduc­
ed simply to the functioning of a marital relationship. Alcoholism, and marriage to an alcoholic, is a 
multigenerational process to the extent that a child of two 
alcoholic parents has an 800Jo chance of becoming an 
alcoholic. Some professionals believe that a chemical reac­
tion in the brain or a genetic susceptibility to alcoholism 
explain this multigenerational process. However, these 
physiological explanations do not explain the number of 
daughters of an alcoholic who marry an alcoholic. In a family systems context, the process of taking 
responsibility for another's functioning is the complimen­
tary and reciprocal dynamic of not taking responsibility 
for one's own behavior. This is a balanced relationship 
with a certain inherent stability. Superficially one spouse 
may look highly functional the other dysfunctional. But as 
Bowen points out, their need for emotional togetherness is 
the same. Although much has been written about the dynamics of 
the family process in the development of alcoholism, there 
is little in the literature about the family process whan the 
alcoholic stops drinking. Observing these "dry" families 
can give the therapist other important clues to the 
reciprocal process in the family.

that the alcoholic's functioning is essential to the 
equilibrium of the family, and a change in the behavior of 
the alcoholic throws the family out of balance emotionally. l j Thinking of the seewaw, the overfunctioning spouse is in 
balance with the underfunctioning spouse. They are com­
plimentary. When the alcoholic becomes more functional, 
he takes on responsibility for self. The family is thrown in­
to a transitional stage in which a shift takes place. The 
seesaw begins to move under the momentum of the better 
functioning alcoholic. If the spouse does not readjust from 
the overfunctional role in a corresponding manner, the 
family will be thrown into stress and anxiety. This process 
of transition for both spouses is more stressful than the 
original drinking. The predictable reaction of a spouse to an alcoholic who 
is not drinking is to become highly anxious. Spouses often 
describe this anxiety as "walking on eggshells." Some will 
openly state that they were more relaxed when the 
alcoholic was drinking since they knew what to expect. They describe their fear of having the alcoholic drink again 
as more intense than the fear they had knowing that the 
alcoholic was drinking.

stops drinking is another indication of how the stability of 
the family was maintained by the family's intense focus on 
the alcoholic's drinking. It is as if the family had a certain 
quota of anxiety which was manageable for them when the 
alcoholic became dysfunctional. However, when he stops 
drinking and becomes more responsible, it is as if the anxi­
ety he has absorbed is pushed back into the family. The family at this time is very vulnerable to problems. Bowen points out that in a family with high degree of anx­
iety, problems can develop in a spouse, in a child, or in the 
marital relationship. The family begins to realize that the 
alcoholic is not responsible for all the problems in the 
family. They may try to refocus the problem by saying that 
the alcoholic didn't change when he stopped drinking, or 
that he acts like he's drinking. A son may openly voice the 
desire for his father to drink, as the family begins to focus 
its attention on his own marijuana use. One family illustrates this process in terms of a dysfunc­
tion developing in a spouse.

One family illustrates this process in terms of a dysfunc­
tion developing in a spouse. The husband and wife were 
married five years with one five year old son. Each had 
been married before. The wife had been married to a man 
who beat her regularly, and her second husband had rarely 
been sober during their marriage. She worked, raised her 
children, and coped with these problems. When her hus­
band stopped drinking, she went into an alternately 
agitated and despondent state. She left her job stating she 
could no longer handle the pressure. She described herself 
as suicidal and on the verge of a nervous breakdown. She 
became paranoid and obsessed with problems she had 
when her husband was drinking. This kind of extreme 
reversal in the spouse well illustrates the process that takes 
place in many families. The seesaw tilts in the other direc­
tion. My clinical experience shows the most common area of 
problems for families with a non-drinking alcoholic is 
marital conflict and divorce. Surprisingly, the majority 
divorce after the alcoholic is sober. In my clinical ex-perience, these divorces are usually initiated by the 
alcoholic after a period of non-drinking. Although a fairly commonplace occurrence, separation 
and divorce after sobriety is at face value a paradoxical 
phenomenon. Sober alcoholics have many explanations 
for their divorcing. "My sobriety came first" is one. Another is that "both of us were sick when I was drinking.

Sober alcoholics have many explanations 
for their divorcing. "My sobriety came first" is one. Another is that "both of us were sick when I was drinking. I got well, and she didn't." Or "When I stopped drinking, 
I had the courage to get out." 
Yet whatever the explanation of the process, the 
homeostasis of each family became unbalanced by the 
change in the alcoholic. It is as if only one half of the 
seesaw moved. The alcoholic becomes more functional, 
and establishes more boundaries for self, and the spouse 
does not make a corresponding shift. In a sense, the over­
functioning spouse cannot "give back" the borrowed 
share of responsibility for functioning to the alcoholic 
without lapsing into dysfunction. The marriage becomes 
unbalanced and breaks apart. Therefore what seems 
paradoxical-a more functional individual threatening the 
stability of a marriage-is predictable when viewed from a 
family systems perspective. Some mental health professionals debate whether the 
goal of intervening in a family should be toward having the 
alcoholic stop drinking if the problem only shifts to other 
family members. This dilemma certainly highlights the im­
portance of treating the whole family so as to minimize 
these shifts and problems in other family members. However, my experience shows that little actually is ac­
complished in the family if the alcoholic does not stop 
drinking.

However, my experience shows that little actually is ac­
complished in the family if the alcoholic does not stop 
drinking. Other mental health professionals see their mis­
sion to sober up individuals without considering the treat­
ment or the overall functioning of the family. They often 
say that most alcoholics who become sober no longer have 
any emotional problems. This viewpoint ignores the im­
pact of the recovery process on the family, the resulting 
anxiety, and symptomology in other family members. In 
contrast to this viewpoint, a family systems therapist sees 
that to stop drinking is only the beginning of changes to 
more functional behavior for the entire family. Bowen's theoretical hypothesis that people marry 
spouses with equal levels of differentiation is strikingly 
confirmed in the study of the alcoholic family. A mental 
health professional with this theoretical orientation can in­
tervene in a family with an eye to helping the entire family 
understand and change these patterns. SUBSCRIPTION FORM

band. Dr. Derdeyn went on the compare the differences 
between the gradual dissolution of the marital bond and 
the sudden rupture between parent and child at the time of 
divorce.

The third speaker, Dr. Edward Beal of the Georgetown 
Family Center, spoke about the decision-making processes 
and emotional attachment in families. He presented three 
multigenerational family histories which showed how ex­
tended family decision-making processes highlight how a 
family may involve itself in custody determinations. Behavior that might look unusually eccentric from a one 
generational standpoint may be consistent with patterns 
persisting throughout many generations. Beal believes that 
custody decisions should be made with a view toward fin­
ding the least damaging alternative for the whole family 
within the entire network of its emotional relationships. He went on to describe what he considers an inappropriate degree of "child focus" whereby a parent under stress 
devotes more attention to the child than the child's cir­
cumstances seem to warrant. The child's perception of the 
parent's anxiety then leads to a reciprocal relationship bet­
ween parent and child in which the child becomes more 
relationship oriented and less task or goal oriented. This 
process may untimately impair the child's future develop­
ment. Dr. Beal then explained the differences between a 
mildly child focused family and a severely child focused 
family and the manner in which each deals with divorce 
and custody matters.

In a presentation entitled, "Divorce and the Evolving 
Social Structure," Dr. Murray Bowen, Director of the 
Georgetown Family Center, reiterated his belief that two 
parents living together is the most effective way of nurtur­
ing children. He believes that the best adjusted families will 
continue that way in spite of current societal pressures. Dr. Bowen also stressed that more people think they want 
custody than actually do. He urged avoiding custody if one 
is uncertain, and avoiding a court decision on custody if at 
all possible. Although he acknowledged the high and still 
rising divorce rate, he indicated that one way of stopping 
or slowing down this trend would be to abolish marriage. He cited evidence to show that it is not necessarily essential 
that marriage exist for the nurturing of children. As to the 
objection that the adversarial process is an integral part of 
the law and that there is no way a lawyer could desert the 
adversarial role and be ethical, he responded that many 
modern practices were once considered unethical. Dr. Richard Wolman, the principal investigator in a 
custody research project at Harvard University funded by 
the Department of Health, Education and Welfare, out­
lined his plan for a new court procedure in dealing with 
custody situations. The court in his particular 
Massachusetts jurisdiction spaces temporary and perma­
nent custody hearings approximately 12 to 18 months 
apart.

disorders are stress related. Such findings have led to an 
extension of the medical concepts of disease to include 
homeostatic imbalance and maladaptive stress responses. Healthy individuals exhibit the capacity to cope with 
stressors, usually regaining homeostatis within a relatively 
short period of time after "emergency response" episodes. This inherent quieting response allows their bodies to 
restore needed energy reserves, preparing them for subse­
quent, inevitable stress periods. On the other hand, per­
sons who are predisposed to or are actually suffering from 
"stress illness" generally recover homeostatic balance 
much more slowly, if at all. While many biological factors 
such as organic disease or hostile environmental conditions 
may contribute to such recovery deficits, most stress-prone 
individuals compound the problem by gradually learning 
to override their inherent homeostatic mechanisms. Accor­
ding to Dr. Stroebel, the resulting hyperreactive automatic 
behavior pattern eventually becomes so routinized that the 
individual comes to regard it as "normal."

scholar, Dr. Musto is both Senior Research Scientist at

intergenerational continuity. He also touched on the very­
ing degrees of successful aging among members of the 
Adams family which ranged from John Adams who lived 
into an active old age after beng President to his grandson, 
George, who committed suicide at the age of twenty-eight. Speakers from the Family Center focused on different 
aspects of family systems theory and aging. Dr. Murray

wide angle lens and addressed broad theoretical aspects of 
anxiety patterns in present and past generations. Mary

Walter Toman, Ph.D. It is our pleasure to have Professor Walter Toman as our guest 
columnist for this issue of the Family Center Report. Dr. Toman 
was recently our guest at a two-day symposium on the importance 
of sibling position in family therapy. Dr. Toman, author of Family 
Constellation, is well recognized for his studies on birth order. His 
work is distinctive in its focus on at least three generations of the 
family. He has provided a comprehensive systems understanding of 
the impact of birth order on a person's life course which is consist­
ent with the concept of sibling position later developed by Dr. Murray Bowen. In addition to Dr. Toman's presentation, this issue features 
selected papers presented by other speakers. Regularly featured 
columns will resume in the next issue of the Report. -R. Sagar

Recently, the trend has been more toward having one child, 
particularly in the larger cities. The average age difference 
between parents is three years with the husband being the 
older of the two. The parents are approximately 27 and 24 
when they marry and they remain childless for two years 
before beginning to have children who are born at intervals 
of three to four years. There is far more variation in Ameri­
can families. In ninety percent of families with children, the parents are 
present at least until their children reach adolescence. In ten 
percent, children have suffered the loss of a parent from 
death, divorce, separation or even absence since birth. In five 
percent of these families, children have lost a parent before 
they are six years old. Fatherless families are about five times 
more frequent than motherless families. In the United 
States, there are more incomplete and disrupted families 
than in We_stern Europe, particularly in the larger cities. Sizeable deviation from this average family structure is 
usually psychologically significant. Large age differences 
between the spouses often imbue the older of the two more 
clearly with the parent role. Exceptionally large age differ­
ences from the children can transform the parents into psy­
chological grandparents. Very small age differences from the 
children can transform the parents into psychological siblings. Both situations tend to weaken the role of parents as educa­
tors.

FRIENDSHIP SELECTION 
OF FIRST BORN FEMALES 
Mary Ann Ames, M.S.N. Since 1972, I have been influenced by Bowen Family 
Systems Theory. One of the concepts of this theoretical 
framework is the importance of sibling position in determin­
ing the psychological characteristics of an individual. Bowen 
has adopted and developed this idea from the lifelong 
research of Dr. Walter Toman. Dr. Toman has spent much of his professional career 
researching the psychological traits of individuals and how 
these traits influence the life course of an individual in terms 
of career choice, mate selection, and friendship selection, to 
name a few. His duplication theorem for instance states that 
" ... new (extra-familial, non-incestuous) interpersonal re­
lationships will duplicate the earliest (intra-familial, incestu­
ous) interpersonal relationships in degrees varying from 
complete duplication to none at all ... " 
Toman's research has been largely based on empirical 
data. In terms of studying friendships, he found that, in 
general, the oldest sibling tends to choose friends who had 
been younger siblings, especially in relationships that are 
successful. In 1976, I became more curious about investigating the 
variables in friendship selection, and conducted a single pilot 
study of one individual's friendship history which was later 
replicated with a larger sample.

ALCOHOLISM AND SIBLING POSITION 
Anne McKnight, A.C.S. W 
Alcoholism is characterized by a set of describable symp­
toms associated with excessive drinking. These symptoms 
may include physical problems such as cirrhosis of the liver, 
pancreatitis, memory loss, nerve damage, and blackouts, 
social problems such as legal, professional, or marital diffi­
culties, and emotional problems such as paranoia, irritabil­
ity, and violent outbursts. Yet, despite the fact that alcoholism is an identifiable 
process with common characteristics, alcoholics function at 
widely divergent levels. Society tends to characterize alco­
holics as "irresponsible" people who shirk the demands of 
their jobs and the responsibilities to their families. In observ-
4 ing alcoholics in their families. it is evident that many people 
who are becoming more open about their alcoholism, are 
very functional individuals. They are often the $100,000 a 
year lawyers. the stars of stage and screen, the super-moms, 
the well-known politicians. Despite the fact that the specific 
symptoms of alcoholic process are present in both, it has 
become increasingly apparent that some alcholics are tal­
ented, aspiring people, while others function at a very mini­
mal level. In the family context, birth order particularly may 
provide a basis for such divergent patterns in alcoholism. Sibling position is one of the most objective and quantifiable 
factors in family research.

Sibling position is one of the most objective and quantifiable 
factors in family research. The most complete review of the research on sibling posi­
tion and alcoholism is a 1973 article written by Howard 
Blane and Herbert Barry who studied birth order and schizo­
phrenia, delinquency, and obsessive-compulsive personal­
ities. They reviewed all available studies on alcoholism and 
birth order between 1937 and 1971 in the United States, 
Canada, England, Scandinavia, France, Austria and Australia. From the twenty-seven studies they reviewed, they con­
cluded that the birth position most significantly at risk for 
alcoholism is the youngest. This finding seemed stable in a 
variety of cultures and over a period of decades. They found 
that the larger the family the more probability that the 
youngest would develop alcoholism. Blane and Barry hypoth­
esized that the youngest siblings may develop alcoholism in 
such significant numbers from being unwanted, rejected, 
subject to maternal deprivation in a large family, or through 
a dependence conflict in which "alcohol may serve as a 
vehicle whereby the individual can experience personal 
power through fantasy or aggressive behavior." 
Although the largest percentage of alcoholics in one birth 
position are youngests, when analyzing the raw data, the fact 
emerges that the second most frequent birth position is the 
oldest, particularly from small families.

text:
A key factor in the development of a dysfunction such as 
alcoholism is the unattainable nature of the goals these 
oldests set for themselves. Dr. Bowen describes the super­
functional alcoholic in a 1975 article entitled Alcoholism 
and the Family: "He might be a dynamo in his profession or 
business and appear to be doing well with his immediate 
family. Such a person usually has an exaggerated sense of 
responsibility for others. He tries hard to live up to this 
responsibility, but since it is ultimately unattainable, the 
outcome is irresponsibility and broken promises. This per­
son's life is burdened by his high self-expectations and 
unrealistic sense of responsibility. The harder he works, the 
more he becomes emotionally isolated." 
The oldest brother, in setting out to succeed, immerses 
himself in his work whether politics, law, acting, construc­
tion or business. In investing himself in his work, he becomes 
distant from his family. An oldest tends to work at such a 
pace that only with alcohol can he slow down and relax. At 
the same time, drinking begins to take the place of the 
relationships that have been displaced by his efforts at work. The pattern for the oldest sister is somewhat different. Her 
efforts generally tend toward a caretaking role toward her 
husband and children. She attempts to be a great wife, a 
great mother, a civic organizer, or more recently a mother 
and a career woman.

anything for themselves. Dr. Bowen describes a youngest

son as one who is so fused into the family system, particu­
larly in his relationship with his mother, that he never devel­
ops a functional life. Although he may collapse into drinking 
later in his life, this person was never able to develop into an 
autonomous individual before the drinking began. He labels 
these youngests as "the emotional refugees from the family 
relationship system." In contrast to Blane and Barry's con­
tention, it is not deprivation or rejection, but rather the 
intensity of family focus on youngests that makes them 
vulnerable to dysfunction in alcoholism. Even for those who 
stop drinking, the overall level of functioning does not shift 
too dramatically. In summary, sibling position plays a role in shaping pat­
terns of behavior. A process of dysfunction can proceed with 
an entirely different pattern according to the family "mold­
ing" which takes place according to the birth order of the 
child. Since alcoholism can develop in strikingly different 
ways with oldest and youngest siblings, knowledge of sibling 
position can give the therapist clues for recognizing these 
patterns and helping families to change them. PROGRESS IN CLINICAL WORK

practice and reports on some observations about my own 
clinical practice and its development. Background. I am an oldest child with one younger 
brother. My father is the youngest of three brothers. My 
mother is the second of four, preceded by an older sister and 
followed by two brothers. In relationship to females, she is, 
therefore, a younger sister of sisters. I grew up in the home­
town of my paternal grandparents. My grandfather was the 
youngest of four brothers. His wife, my paternal grand­
mother, was the youngest daughter and next to youngest 
child in a family of five. Indeed, by programming and child-
5 
 hood experience, there is a rich background in dealing on a 
day-to-day basis with youngests. In contrast to my family background, I have had a history 
of almost universally choosing oldests and only children in 
social relationships. My female friends interestingly enough 
were mostly oldest sisters of sisters and onlys, and my male 
friends were oldest brothers of brothers and onlys. Not until I had begun to work on relationships with all the 
youngest siblings in my own family, and particularly with 
my mother, was it possible to relate better to theyoungests in 
my own clinical practice. One advantage an oldest has in growing up surrounded by 
youngests, is having the freedom of a naturally built-in 
outside position.

One advantage an oldest has in growing up surrounded by 
youngests, is having the freedom of a naturally built-in 
outside position. This outside position could quickly dis­
solve under stress, and I could become entangled in situa­
tions of high anxiety by what I perceived as helplessness in 
others. The reciprocal response to helplessness is to perform 
the task at hand for the other, with the danger of becoming 
bossy or pushy in the process. At the point I found I was no 
longer stepping in and doing, there was a new order of 
functioning which provided some flexibility. However, I 
could then find myself standing on the side lines playing the 
"Monday morning quarterback," assessing the efforts others 
were making. Clinical Practice. Early in my fourteen years of clinical 
practice, I became aware that I was more successful with 
oldests and only children. Nothing was done at the time to 
objectify this thought. Recently, I decided to subject some of 
my clinical records to review in order to take a more accurate 
reading on my clinical performance as it relates to sibling 
position. Clinical review. I collected all the clinical records that I 
could find that had information about sibling position. I 
then divided them into all records between 1970 and 1975, 
and all records between 1975 and 1980. These two piles were 
then divided into two categories each: one with all cases seen 
more then ten times; the other pile those cases I had seen less 
than ten times.

tics were far more pronounced than was my unofficial 
observation. Among those seen more than ten times before

the same minimum number of sessions were youngests. The 
figures for those who terminated before ten sessions were

few friends I had who were not oldests, I made a conscious 
effort to do something about it. The closest person I had to a 
younger sister is a cousin, five years my junior, whom I had 
spent a fair amount of time avoiding when I was 10 and she 
was 5, and when I was 15 and she was 10. At that time, our 
interests were very divergent. A conscious effort was made to 
contact her, learn something about her life, and know her 
better. Simultaneously I continued the same effort with my 
mother. This was a more difficult arena, yet some of the 
reactions and processes found in the less intense relationship 
with my younger cousin of my own generation were present 
6 , in more subtle and intense forms in the relationship with my 
mother.

Being different with my mother resulted in the 
initiation of some new patterns of behavior in self that 
quickly translated into a more "automatic," "easy" and 
"comfortable" relationship with my brother. This latter shift 
was a by-product that could not have been achieved by 
trying to do something differently in the relationship with 
my brother directly. In general, some of the basic observations made as part of 
this process are: I) To the degree that I was doing my bossy, 
lecturing oldest act, youngests in my life would predictably 
distance. This would occur whether or not the lectures were 
justified. As a corrollary, and more important to a focus on 
self, as soon as I would slide into lecturing and telling others 
what to do, I was impairing my own ability to hear the other. 2) As soon as I could control myself to the degree that I 
could hear the other, intellectually as well as emotionally, it 
was possible to also discover who the other really is, and 
what that person is attempting to do in life. Once it was 
possible to make some progress with this in my own family, 
and only then, was it possible to operate in the much richer 
environment of relationships and to have a wider perspective 
on the human condition, in general, including an awareness

THE IMPORTANCE OF BIRTH ORDER TO 
THE JOURNEYMAN FAMILY THERAPIST 
Daniel V. Papero, Ph.D., M.S.S.W. There comes a point in the learning process where the 
therapist-trainee is no longer a novice. Although the trainee 
is clearly not a master therapist, knowledge, skill and expe­
rience have progressed beyond the beginner stage. This 
intermediate stage can be viewed as the journeyman stage of 
development, in analogy to the structure of medieval guilds. For the journeyman, learning involves continuing to stretch 
the mind, to question, and to consolidate knowledge about 
the family. It is a phase, however, when it is easy to pretend 
to know what one really only guesses or half knows. It is also 
a time when it is easy to doubt one's knowledge, skill, and 
ability. Those who see the journeyman either as more 
knowledgeable or less skilled than is accurate can foster this 
pretense or uncertainty. To the extent that the j oumeyman is 
caught in pretended knowledge or doubt, development can 
slow or stop. Toman's work is directly applicable to the journeyman 
therapist in four areas. It provides: 1) a reliable framework 
or matrix for the development of a research orientation to 
the family; 2) a bridge between reactive patterns in the 
nuclear family and those in the family of origin; 3) specific 
guidelines useful in the actual practice of therapy; 4) a rigor­
ous model to aid in the development of knowledge and skills.

Developing a research orientation is important to family 
therapists at all levels. Beyond understanding how a particu­
lar family functions, a research orientation attempts to inte­
grate the work with many families to arrive at an under­
standing of families in general. In each case structure and 
objectivity are required. A working knowledge of birth order characteristics can be 
useful in establishing a research orientation. The actual 
behavior and relationships of family members can be com­
pared to Toman's basic profiles. Where differences are 
noted, a micro-research project becomes available to both 
therapist and family. The range of questions is endless. Of 
particular interest is Toman's discussion of the loss of family 
members. If the therapist-researcher has a working knowl­
edge of Toman's seven rules governing the severity of loss it 
is possible to investigate the type of loss and its impact on 
family functioning. This line of questioning can lead quickly 
back to the extended family and the operation of multi­
generational processes. In short, Toman's work provides a 
reliable guide for maintaining a research orientation. The journeyman therapist can benefit from the effort to 
understand the mechanisms by which reactive patterns of 
one generation are passed to subsequent ones. Information 
about sibling position can account for part of this phenom­
enon.

Information 
about sibling position can account for part of this phenom­
enon. According to Toman, marriage partners have com­
plementary, partially complementary or non-complementary 
sibling positions. The level or degree of complementarity depends upon the presence or absence of rank and/ or sex 
conflict. For example, two oldest children or two youngest 
children would have a rank conflict. While each could iden­
tify with the other, each would tend to seek the same role. The expectations and behavior of one would not comple­
ment the other. A brother of brothers or a sister of sisters 
would have a sex conflict; that is, neither would have had the 
experience of a sibling of the opposite sex. Marital partners 
with complementary sibling positions would have neither 
rank nor sex conflict. Partially complementary relationships 
involve partners with middle sibling positions. Each spouse 
would have at least one sibling relationship which would 
complement at least one sibling relationship of the other. Partners with non-complementary sibling positions would 
present either or both a rank and sex conflict. Toman sug­
gests marital partners with non-complementary sibling posi­
tions have greater difficulty in marriage than partners with 
complementary or partially complementary relationships. Degrees of complementarity can also be applied to parent­
child relationships.

text:
Degrees of complementarity can also be applied to parent­
child relationships. Parents and offspring with rank and/ or 
sex conflict could be expected to have greater difficulty 
adjusting to one another than those who do not. The interac­
tional expectations of the parent would not fit the behavior 
of the child. Whatever the degree of complementarity, how­
ever, each person comes to a marriage with a series of 
expectations and reactive types of behavior which are 
determined by one's own sibling position. If into this interactional matrix one adds anxiety, the fuel 
of family process, it is possible to begin to define the mechan­
isms by which reactive patterns cross generational boundar­
ies. Toman suggests that the earliest contexts influence the 
perception and shaping of contemporary contexts. A person 
approaches the marital relationship with a perceptual con­
text and types of reactive behavior shaped by the past, 
primarily the family of origin. In the best of circumstances 
the marital relationship represents the blending of such pat­
terns. If one postulates a relationship between anxiety and 
the emergence of ingrained reactive patterns, one would 
expect anxious marriages would be more highly influenced 
by the past then less anxious ones. The greater the anxiety in 
the marital pair, the greater the reliance on old patterns to 
manage anxiety and the greater the tendency for the anxious 
patterns of one generation to appear in another.

As anxiety rises in a new marriage, each partner reacts in a 
pattern brought from the family of origin. As such reactive 
patterns are repeated, one would expect them to be modified 
to fit the new family environment. The longer such a reactive 
marital pattern has been developing, the more it could be 
expected to assume a unique character of its own, although 
the original patterns of each partner would lie at its core. This would account for the nuclear family patterns which 
seem unique yet familiar if one has collected accurate infor­
mation on past generations of the family. Using Toman's 
profiles and information on family functioning, a map of the 
multigenerational process of a family can be constructed. Such a map can reveal chronic patterns of reactivity and 
suggest entry points and goals for therapy. Toman's work is also useful directly in therapy. If sibling 
position is indeed such a factor in the cross-generational 
7 
 8 transmission of reactive patterns, it argues powerfully for 
focus on extended family in therapy. This is, of course, a key 
point in Bowen Family Systems Theory. On a more practical 
level, a knowledge of sibling profiles can help the therapist 
locate family members who can be both objective about and 
significant to the family. In the more intense dysfunctions, 
the therapist may be presented with an intense, chronically 
emotional triangle.

In the more intense dysfunctions, 
the therapist may be presented with an intense, chronically 
emotional triangle. It can be extremely difficult for members 
of this triangle to gain any detachment from the intensity of 
the emotional process. Armed with a knowledge of sibling 
characteristics and the process map of the family, the thera­
pist can search for other significant family members who 
may be able to gain some objectivity. Through the manage­
ment of self in the emotional context of the family, these 
people may affect the intensity of the central triangle. Infor­
mation about sibling position can also help the therapist 
unravel tangled family patterns. Once the patterns are 
understood, data on sibling position can suggest ways to 
reduce anxiety and work with the family. Toman's work is important at the journeyman level in a 
final dimension. At the journeyman level there appears the 
temptation to slow down or stop the search for understand­
ing the family. This is both natural and problematic. It is 
natural when one considers the years of training and thought 
that precede attainment of journeyman status. It is difficult 
to challenge one's assumptions repeatedly and to work to 
train the mind to look objectively for facts. A small amount 
of knowledge is seductive, and it is easy to think one knows 
what one really only supposes. The temptation to stop learn­
ing is especially problematic in a field as new as family 
therapy.

The temptation to stop learn­
ing is especially problematic in a field as new as family 
therapy. The journeyman therapist operates continually on 
the basis of theory which he has borrowed from someone 
else. It takes considerable effort and hard work to move 
from the position of accepting another person's theory, to 
the position where one has worked with the theory, chal­
lenged its assumptions, and learned from its concepts. It is 
the difference between believing something is accurate and 
knowing it is. A disciplined effort to learn about the family is 
vital if the therapist is to move beyond the journeyman level. Toman's work provides an excellent model of depth and 
rigor for this effort. Family Constellation provides specific 
tools and suggestions for continued study of the family. Toman discusses quantitative aspects of family constella­
tions and specific formulas he has developed for measuring 
conflict and loss in families. There is even a procedure sug­
gested for attaining a combined index of the conflict and loss 
indices. While the measures are themselves interesting, the 
more important lesson for the journeyman lies in Toman's 
efforts to be objective and to look for facts. What makes 
Toman's formulas and quantifications particularly signifi­
cant to the journeyman is the multigenerational context in 
which they are set.

Toman's formulas and quantifications particularly signifi­
cant to the journeyman is the multigenerational context in 
which they are set. To be objective and to look for fact in the 
matrix of the multigenerational family is a primary devel­
opmental task at the journeyman level. Toman has, in fact, 
defined the task and developed an approach for accomplish­
ing it. TWINS AND TRIANGLES 
Barbara Bershon, M.A. I am the first born twin of a family with two sets of twins, 
and I am married to a man who was raised as a twin since he 
was adopted only two months after his sister. The mother­
father-child triangle in my family and in my husband's fam­
ily is different than in a family where the births occur singly. During courtship, a comfortably close twosome exists. As 
soon as a couple decides to have a child, the automatic 
emotional triangling process begins. The arrival of the baby 
provides much excitement and anxiety for the family. The 
mother may become very close and involved with the new 
baby, which leaves the father in the outside position. Now 
the father, who had enjoyed a closeness exclusively with his 
wife, pursues her which can either cause conflict in the 
marital relationship or can push the mother even closer to 
the child. As the excitement of the baby's arrival subsides, 
the triangle can stabilize allowing both parents to be 
involved with the child and conflict between the couple to 
decrease.

As the excitement of the baby's arrival subsides, 
the triangle can stabilize allowing both parents to be 
involved with the child and conflict between the couple to 
decrease. But when anxiety reoccurs, the emotional process 
will resurface in the same way. The birth of two children makes this process occur differ­
ently. Rather than one primary triangle, there are several 
interlocking ones. In the situation of twins, the emotional 
focus on both children becomes more diffuse, or focus on 
one child becomes especially intense. At birth my twin brother had physical complications that 
took my mother's attention. But since there were two of us he 
did not become dysfunctional since my mother's focus had 
to be shared with me. In addition, my mother's focus on one 
child (my twin brother) did not leave my father outside the 
triangle, because the other child (me) was available to him 
for focus. Six years later when the second set of twins was born, the 
focus again remained diffuse. There were always several 
family members in an outside position. Sometimes these 
were the comfortable ones, and sometimes they were the 
uncomfortable ones. Because the children arrived in twos, a 
diffusion of the emotional process occurred. In some families with twins, such as my husband's, the 
over-focus/ under-focus pattern predominates. Since my 
husband and his sister were adopted only two months apart, 
they were raised as twins and faced the world as a twosome.

in my family, my husband's family had one over-focused, 
not very functional child, and one lucky, under-focused 
child. Marital conflict between my husband's parents re­
mains minimal and, as long as my sister-in-law remains 
underfunctional and over-focused, the rest of the family 
continues to function well. The automatic emotional triangling process of diffusion 
and over/under focus which occurs in all families seems 
more obvious and possibly more intense in families with 
twins than it does in families with children born singly. THE OLDEST DAUGHTER

Clinical observations using Bowen's Family Systems 
Theory and Toman's extensive research on the significance 
of birth order provides the framework for these comments. Functioning Characteristics. An oldest daughter of a 
youngest mother is usually a "super mother." This is not a 
label or a diagnosis of pathology, but a composite of forces 
in the multigenerational family which contribute to these 
particular functioning characteristics. She functions as an 
over-responsible caretaker whose energies are primarily 
invested in nurturing and guiding children and significant 
others as if she is solely responsible for their well-being. With 
varying degrees of intensity, her physical and emotional self, 
her whole being, is tuned in to the health and welfare of those 
who are important to her. She is vulnerable to an anxious 
emotional field in which she attempts to solve dilemmas and 
restore emotional equilibrium during periods of disruption, 
often at the expense of her own goals. Her own mother has 
usually reinforced this caretaking role by expecting her to 
look after other siblings, protect them from harm, and func­
tion as a mother substitute in her absence or during illness. Her functioning is also reinforced by her father who has 
tended to support his wife in her expectations. The mother looks to her daughter to alleviate family 
anxiety. Even during early childhood, the mother's expecta­
tions are an integral part of the mother-child relationship.

The mother looks to her daughter to alleviate family 
anxiety. Even during early childhood, the mother's expecta­
tions are an integral part of the mother-child relationship. The most common pattern is one in which the mother and 
daughter are overly invested in each other and the father 
functions in a peripheral position. An oldest daughter of a 
youngest mother tends to make decisions that would pro­
mote comfort in the parental relationship by monitoring the 
behavior of her siblings and maintaining the emotional bal­
ance in the family. Implicitly or explicitly, the family conveys an impression 
that she must solve dilemmas, reduce friction between her 
parents and her siblings, and rescue her siblings and mother 
from stressful situations. If she functions well in this posi­
tion, she is rewarded and reinforced by attitudes in the 
family. When she is anxious, the feeling of responsibility for 
others influences her automatic responses to emotionally 
laden situations. Her caretaking functions surface, espe­
cially unsolicited helping or rescuing others from what she 
perceives as pain, anxiety, or harm. When she finds solutions 
to problems, she is pleased with her functioning but finds it 
difficult to understand why others in the family are not as 
pleased as she. Since her major energies are invested in the service of 
others, however, she is prone to neglect her own goals.

others, however, she is prone to neglect her own goals. The 
oldest daughter of a youngest mother has a high level of 
expectations of self and of others. If she comes from a 
blaming family, she tends to blame herself first for perceived 
failure in meeting expectations. She may blame others if her expectations remain unfulfilled. She is an absorber of family 
anxiety, a balancer of the emotional budget in the relation­
ship unit. Major Variables Which Influence Functioning, A mother 
who has lost a nurturing grandparent, parent or an older 
sibling early in life tends to be an anxious parent who has 
difficulty in allowing her own daughter to grow away from 
her. During her daughter's adolescence, conflict may devel­
op as she feels the stress of her daughter's attempt to separate 
emotionally. In extreme situations, mother and duaghter may become 
so reactive to each other that an emotional cut-off may 
result. The daughter uses distance in the relationship as a 
mechanism for dealing with the discomfort of a conflictual, 
intense attachment to her mother. She may seek other rela­
tionships of equal intensity with peers. When she marries, 
she continues to function as a "super mother" until problems 
arise in the marriage, at which time she may seek psycho­
therapy. Another variable which influences functioning is the level 
of family anxiety at the time the oldest daughter is born.

and from the multigenerational past, each member of the

for relationship sustenance and fulfillment of expectations.

CLASSICAL YOUNGEST FUNCTIONING 
CHARACTERISTICS: A HANDICAP IN 
BOWEN SYSTEMS THERAPY 
Patricia H. Meyer, A.C.S.W. For purposes of this presentation a classical youngest is 
defined as any individual whose functioning centers around 
the environment when defining an action for self; that is, 
problems are viewed as being in another, and solutions to 
problems are believed to be dependent upon the environ­
ment's producing the change. One of the cornerstones of Bowen Family Systems Theory 
is personal responsibility, assessing areas of underfunction­
ing and overfunctioning and working towards greater 
responsibility for self in all facets of one's life. The classical 
youngest enters adulthood without a working knowledge of 
personal responsibility. The classical youngest is unable to 
proceed through this proces of change in therapy until he 
first comes to terms with the helpless, dependent forces that 
have dictated his life. The Process of Differentiation. Differentiation may be 
described on the basis of the following hierarchy: feeling­
the automatic response; thought-the automatic response 
with facts that allow objectivity; belief-a calm, factually 
based foundation of personal principle and the ability to act 
on principle when anxiety is high. Feelings are automatic responses all people experience. For those who are dominated by feelings, life has few choi­
ces. The capacity to think and to perceive fact provides 
objectivity about alternatives.

text:
For those who are dominated by feelings, life has few choi­
ces. The capacity to think and to perceive fact provides 
objectivity about alternatives. It is also possible, however, 
that a person can KNOW something without having the 
emotional knowledge, conviction, or discipline to activate 
the thought. For example, an individual may think that 
jogging is a great idea which provides fitness, a vigorous 
mind and a vigorous body. Yet, that individual is unable to 
integrate regular jogging into his life. Belief is a principle that an individual follows through his 
lifetime. This is not to say that a belief is the answer to a 
dilemma. It is, rather, a guide for evaluating any particular 
decision. The more personal principles an individual has, the 
more self-directed he is. The less personal principle an indi­
vidual has, the more other-directed he is. This person sees 
problems as existing because of others. Focus is directed 
toward people and organizations in the environment: 
teachers, schools, the county or federal government. The classical youngest has had minimal experience with 
assuming responsibility. Decisions have been made and fail­
ures avoided through the efforts of protective parents and 
elder siblings. It is possible that such a person has never 
experienced the burden of feeling that any problem is really 
his own. In less severe cases, the youngest may admit to 
playing a part in a problem and may even have an awareness 
of the changes needed.

In less severe cases, the youngest may admit to 
playing a part in a problem and may even have an awareness 
of the changes needed. However, expectation for change will 
be directed toward other people and the environment. Any 
expectation that self can carve a different environment is 
lacking. Focus on Dependency. In therapy, it is impossible to 
introduce a classical youngest (a definition that can also be 
applied to any ultra-dependent person) to the concept of 
defining a self until he has first come to terms with the 
helpless, dependent forces that have dictated his life. This 
process occurs by asking questions that highlight the 
dependent nature of the youngest. In focusing on a specific 
incident, for instance, questions should underline that the 
youngest never had a notion about what self did or should do 
but was clear on what others did or should do. It seems to 
take a repulsion and disgust for the characteristics in self 
which do not contribute to any situation. Until the indi­
vidual begins to be disgusted with himself for these depend­
ent characteristics, the suggestion that he define a self is 
fruitless. If he comes to terms with his dependent character­
istics, he can then proceed through the course of therapy like 
any person who has a working knowledge of responsibility 
for self. Clinical Example. I began to see a man, the youngest of 
sisters and brothers, with his wife. The husband was pushed 
into sessions by the threat of divorce.
