Clinical Example. I began to see a man, the youngest of 
sisters and brothers, with his wife. The husband was pushed 
into sessions by the threat of divorce. His participation in 
sessions was similar to what would be expected of a young 
adolescent. He had nothing to say, no thoughts to contrib­
ute. This happy pair came in together for a short time until 
one day the husband was absent because he was ill. I 
informed the wife that I believed her husband's presence was 
a waste of time unless he decided he wanted to grow up. I 
informed the wife that I thought she could accomplish more 
in sessions for herself without her husband's being there. Later the husband began to come in alone as a result of a 
new threat of divorce from his wife. At this point, without his 
wife to draw focus in the sessions, he was able to focus on 
patterns of dependency and irresponsibility. Questions were 
asked to highlight these patterns: "I get the impression that 
your wife considers your participation as a parent to be 
minimal. How can you account for her having such a view?" 
It has been a year since, and many changes have occurred. The husband was often very uncomfortable and clearly res­
istant to allowing any focus for problems to be directed 
toward him. On the surface, he complained that the therapy 
was too slow, that it was very expensive, did not work, and 
he did not want to discuss or change his role in the family. Acting out occurred.

he did not want to discuss or change his role in the family. Acting out occurred. For months, the husband insisted his 
wife pay me. He would neither write the check nor hand it to 
me. At home he referred to me as MEYER in non-friendly 
tones. He would often make comments about his displeasure 
with being present at the sessions. However, a second process began during that year. Fight­
ing every step of the way verbally, the husband began to 
behave in his nuclear family and extended family in a 
manner that surprised me. For the first time, he actually 
directed issues at others and stayed around for the "flack." 
He began to handle issues in his family and to leave his wife 
out of doing so-a total reversal in the pattern. To date, he 
has achieved more than I would have predicted. I believe he would probably have remained in his depend­
ent position had that dependency not been so forcefully 
underlined in therapy. Unless a therapist has a working 
knowledge of this predictable pattern of classical youngests, 
therapy that pushes for differentiation is doomed to failure. The youngest will wait until the end of time ... when in the 
next session, the therapist will finally tell him what to do, or 
the environment will produce the answer. DEPARTURES FROM

Paulina G. McCullough, A.C.S.W 
James B. Smith, M.A. This is a study of fifty students enrolled in a course for the 
purpose of learning more about their families, particularly 
their own roles in them. The study is an analysis of their 
characteristics in terms of Walter Toman's sibling profiles. For those students who represented a departure from the 
profiles, an effort was made to ascertain those factors in the 
dynamics of family process which appeared to account for 
the departure. The data came from genograms and other 
required reports for the course. The rationale for this analysis was based on the idea 
advanced by Murray Bowen that intense family dynamics 
such as the multigenerational projection in the case of schi­
zophrenia substantially obscures profile characteristics. Our 
assumption was that if intense family dynamics can obscure 
profile, less intense versions might also affect sibling roles 
and responses. The students were grouped by first, middle and last born. A major objective was the identification of those variables 
which appeared related to overfunctioning and underfunc­
tioning with special reference to sibling position. The vari­
ables used were: sibling position, age, motivation, degree of 
responsibility, degree of"worry," "stuckness" and dysfunction. Half of the students were first born, even though this 
group was only 14% of all siblings in the families repre­
sented.

much greater for the last born (an interquartile range of 
seventeen years compared to only five years for the first 
born). This was the first indicator that first and last born had 
different reasons for applying for the course. A significant distribution emerged when studying respon­
sibility. Following predictions, firstborns rated high in both 
responsibility and overresponsibility. Middle borns clus­
tered in the middle range of responsibility, also following 
predictions. Last barns showed the same pattern for their 
age distribution in the overresponsible category as first 
borns, a clear departure from their profile. When we considered the degree of "worry," roughly the 
same distribution was present. A closer scrutiny of the 
departures from characteristic profiles revealed that oldests 
who underfunctioned were also high in dysfunction. In all 
but two cases, youngests who overfunctioned seemed to be 
"making up" for some family deficit such as premature death 
of one or both parents, dysfunction in one parent or in an 
older sibling (generally in a sibship of two), or serious con­
flict between parents or between a parent and an older 
sibling.

possible explanation is that first borns who applied to the 
course were feeling overresponsible and stuck, while last 
barns were overfunctioning, worrying, and compensating

A SYSTEMS MODEL FOR DISEASE* 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. For many centuries medical diagnosis was restricted to a 
description of the patient's signs and symptoms. The dis­
covery by Pasteur of the relationship of germs to disease dra­
matically changed medical diagnosis. It became possible to 
classify disease based on specific etiological agents, such as 
the tubercle bacillus as the cause of tuberculosis, for example. Most cancer research today continues in this mode of trying 
to identify specific viruses, genetic defects, or carcinogenic 
substances that might "cause" certain cancers. Such research 
is invaluable if specific agents or defects can be identified and 
treated so that a particular cancer may be rendered harmless. Identification of the pneumococcal bacterium and specific 
antibiotics to treat it, for example, has greatly lessened the 
danger of that type of pneumonia. As time has passed, it has become evident that invasion by 
a bacterium or virus does not necessarily lead to the develop­
ment of a clinical disease. In fact, in the majority of instances 
people can live in perfect harmony with these invaders or even 
with the presence of genetic defects without developing a 
clinical syndrome.

In fact, in the majority of instances 
people can live in perfect harmony with these invaders or even 
with the presence of genetic defects without developing a 
clinical syndrome. With this in mind, saying that the tubercle 
bacillus causes tuberculosis or that smoking causes cancer is 
not entirely accurate. In recent years, an attempt has been 
made to deal with this issue by proposing a theory of multiple 
causes (Cassel, Health and the Community: Readings in the 
Philosophy and Science of Public Health, Katz and Felton, 
eds. 1965). This theory states that several conditions or factors 
must be present for a disease to develop. The presence of 
bacteria itself is not enough. A systems model goes a step beyond the multiple cause 
model, conceptualizing the balance of the relationships be­
tween the various "causes" or factors as the critical deter­
minant in the development of clinical disease. A systems 
model for understanding the mechanisms of disease attempts

systems model does not preclude the possibility that a specific 
defect or agent may be found for a given disease, but the im­
portant question is what disturbs the harmonious balance of 
biological relationships that leads to clinical symptoms. Acne vulgaris 
The author was taught the systems model of disease by one 
of his own diseases, acne vulgaris. Acne is a perifolliculitis, an 
inflammation surrounding the sebaceous follicles in the skin. Muir has defined the following mechanism in the develop­
ment of an acne lesion (Muir's Textbook of Pathology, 
Anderson, ed., 1976). Corynebacterium acnes is a bacterium 
that finds an occluded sebaceous follicle suitable for growth. This bacterium produces a potent lipase, an enzyme, that 
chemically reacts with sebum, the neutral fat substance nor­
mally produced by sebaceous glands, splitting the sebum into 
substances called free fatty acids. Unlike sebum, when these 
free fatty acids leak into the tissues surrounding the sebaceous 
glands they are potentially quite irritating to the tissues.

Unlike sebum, when these 
free fatty acids leak into the tissues surrounding the sebaceous 
glands they are potentially quite irritating to the tissues. The 
presence of the free fatty acids is usually associated with a 
significant inflammatory response, causing the area sur­
rounding the sebaceous glands to become swollen and packed 
with white blood cells. It is this inflammatory reaction that 
produces the redness and swelling that gives the clinical pic­
ture of acne. It is the response of our own bodily armies, our 
own immunological system, that creates the picture of chaos 
and destruction we call disease. Since these are our own im­
munological armies, to what extent is their mobilization 
under our control? To what extent is the deployment of these 
armies in disease an unnecessary, even counterproductive 
overreaction to the situation? There are many other interesting questions posed by the 
disease acne. For example, why do some people never get it? People with high sebum output and people with high concen­
trations of the corynebacterium on their skin have never ex­
perienced an acne reaction. Why do people have exacerba­
tions and remissions of the disease? Dr. Michael Kerr presiding al discussion by panelists Mrs. Patricia 
Meyer, Mrs. Marilyn Krasner, Mrs. Paulina McCullough, Dr. Murray Bowen and Dr. George Vail/ant. Several years ago I began trying to identify some of the fac­

Paulina McCullough, Dr. Murray Bowen and Dr. George Vail/ant. Several years ago I began trying to identify some of the fac­
tors that influenced these cycles of activity in my own case. My exploration contributed significantly to the development 
of a systems model for disease. The first factor I identified was the consumption of foods 
with high sugar content. I speculated, perhaps inaccurately, 
that the extra sugar energized the bacteria in some way, trig­
gering more lipase production, free fatty acids and eventually 
an inflammatory response. Efforts to reduce sugar intake did 
lead to some improvement in the acne. The second factor I 
identified was mechanical irritation of the skin, by shirt col­
lars and shaving, for example. What was interesting, how­
ever, was the gradual realization that excessive sugar and 
mechanical irritation did not always trigger an acne response. At times these stimuli were tolerated or adapted to rather 
well. The third factor identified proved to be the most difficult 
of all to really see. For some time my wife had been telling me 
that she thought that when I was under more stress the acne 
was more evident. It is one thing to be told that stress can be 
associated with acne, but it is another thing to really see a 
clear association between stress and the activity of a disease 
process within oneself.

associated with acne, but it is another thing to really see a 
clear association between stress and the activity of a disease 
process within oneself. For me it took time and careful obser­
vation during repeated cycles of the disease to become con­
vinced of a clear association between fluctuations in my level 
of chronic anxiety and fluctuations in the activity of the 
disease. But I did become convinced. When anxiety was low, 
significant sugar consumption and mechanical irritations 
could be tolerated with only mild skin reactions. When anxi­
ety was high, severe exacerbations of acne could be avoided 
by carefully avoiding excess sugar and mechanical irritations. The combination of all three factors in high "dosage" pro­
duced the worst reactions. The interplay fascinated me. Later on, I resorted to the use of low dosages of tetra­
cycline on a regular basis to control the acne. College students 
flock to clinics around exam type for tetracycline to get 
through school pressures without having a full flowering of 
their acne. It usually works for them and did for me. Since no 
one is entirely certain about the exact mechanisms involved in 
acne, no one is sure why tetracycline can help control the 
disease. Originally, I had imagined it controlled the reprod~c­
tion of bacteria. Later I heard that tetracycline interfered with 
the production of free fatty acids, thereby reducing the 
iflflammatory reaction.

2 am one to take aspirin reluctantly, I never liked the idea of us­
ing tetracycline to control the acne. I did like the idea of no 
longer having to worry about eating foods with high sugar 
content. The reliance on tetracycline continued for about two years. During that period, I learned a good deal about my anxiety 
and my ability to control it. Acne had been an important 
teacher about anxiety. Eventually it became possible to get 
along without the tetracycline, even while consuming foods 
high in sugar content and continuing to experience various 
mechanical irritations of the skin. The fact that I could con­
trol the activity of the disease process through the control of 
my anxiety was mind boggling. To what extent is this possible with other diseases? This is 
not to say that the acne only disappears by reducing anxiety. Certainly other biological variables influence it. But when 
acne continues to be active, anxiety is unquestionably an im­
portant variable influencing the clinical course. Nor is this to 
say that people who have acne have it because of "psycho­
logical" problems. Anxiety is a universal phenomenon and 
acne is but one of a myriad of ways anxiety can be manifested. It would be tempting to say that anxiety in acne is reflected 
in an overzealous inflammatory reaction.

It would be tempting to say that anxiety in acne is reflected 
in an overzealous inflammatory reaction. But it seems more 
accurate to think in terms of a systems model and say that 
anxiety disturbs the balance between all the various biological 
factors involved. What probably occurs is that as the process 
gains momentum, the activity of each factor (the bacteria, the 
enzymes, the white blood cells) is increasingly modified by the 
activity of every other factor through a series of feedback 
loops. The disturbance is in the total balance of the system 
rather than any one part being the culprit. In other words, the 
activity of the inflammatory cells may reflect what is going on 
with the bacteria, sebum, lipase, and free fatty acids but also, 
the activity of the bacteria, sebum, lipase, and free fatty acids 
may be a function of the overzealous inflammatory response. The important point is not to pick out any one factor and 
blame the process on it. All of the players are capable of liv­
ing in harmony. The anxiety disrupts that harmony and turns 
peaceful coexistence into polarized confrontation. A quotation from Lewis Thomas offers a fitting conclusion 
for this idea: 
Our arsenals for fighting off bacteria are so powerful, 
and involve so many different defense mechanisms, that 
we are in more danger from ourselves than from the in­
vaders. (Lives of a Cell, 1974.)

Lorraine Lougee, L.C.S.W. The multigenerational transmission process describes how 
children emerge from the same family with different levels of 
differentiation and marry a spouse with the same level of dif­
ferentiation. Over time a family system produces branches 
with members who become more functional and competent 
(or differentiated), and branches where individuals become 
increasingly less competent. Does genetics play a role in this 
process? Linking transgenerational familial patterns with heredity is 
not a new idea. In 1869 Galton in Hereditwy Genius proposed 
that sons could become increasingly more precocious than 
their fathers. A physician named Mott reporting in The 
British Medical Journal in I 910 noted the earlier and more 
severe forms of mental disease in succeeding generations and 
explained this as a progressive degeneration of the germ 
plasm.

By his account, senile psychosis occurred in the first 
generation, involutional psychosis followed by dementia in 
early life in the second and third, and idiocy leading to infer­
tility in the fourth generation. He believed that the human 
race was continually being purged of disease in this manner. This phenomenon, known as anticipation or antedating, was 
widely observed and documented during the 1930's and 40's. Anticipation was subsequently dismissed as being a function 
of selective data collection rather than a bona fide biological 
phenomenon. Since these old studies did not use systems con­
cepts in analyzing the data, the conclusions may be inaccurate, 
however. The association between genetics and psychiatry dates from 
the earliest writings of Freud. Much of the research in the 
field of psychogenetics has concerned itself with transmission 
studies-how traits are transmitted from parent to offspring. The emphasis has been on discovering the gene or groups of 
genes that determine personality or mental illness. Pedigrees 
are then pieced together and the classical laws of segregation 
and recombination are utilized to understand how the gene is 
passed among the various family members. The over-emphasis on the existence of a genotype as a 
causative factor in human functioning is the "gene as destiny 
approach." The application of systems thinking to genetics 
has, however, more relevance to understanding the role of the 
gene in physical and mental dysfunction.

The gene is not a 
static entity whose presence alone always determines the ex­
istence or absence of a given illness. The gene is part of a 
complex system involving both neural and endocrine control 
mechanisms and their interaction with the environment. It is estimated that there are about two to three million 
genes contained in the DNA of every cell. Not all of these 
genes are being expressed at the same time. What leads genes 
to be turned on and off is a subject of intense interest. Systems regulating the expression of genes are thought to 
exist, yet an understanding of gene regulation is quite in­
complete in higher organisms. In 1959 Jacob and Manod 
discovered how this process operates in bacteria, and 
O'Malley of Baylor College of Medicine has described the 
same process operating higher on the phylogenetic scale with 
chicken cells. O'Malley has found that a complex formed by a steroid hormone and its receptor controls protein synthesis 
by acting directly on the genetic material of the cell. The 
steroid hormones include the sex hormones, androgen and 
estrogen, and hormones secreted by the adrenal glands, the 
corticosteroids. There is a substantial body of literature which 
suggests that emotional stress can alter the balance of these 
hormones. Steroid hormones, for example, induce gene expression in 
chicken cells as follows. After diffusing into the cell thev

Steroid hormones, for example, induce gene expression in 
chicken cells as follows. After diffusing into the cell thev 
become coupled with their receptor molecule in a target cell. Cells that do not respond to a given hormone lack receptors 
for that hormone. Receptors sequester the hormone in the 
target cells and concentrate them in the cell nucleus. Acceptor 
sites for hormone and receptor complexes have been observed 
only on the chromatin of target cells. Chromatin consists of 
DNA and two kinds of protein, histone and nonhistone. The 
ability to bind the complexes resides in a particular fraction of 
the nonhistone proteins, the AP3 fraction. The complex 
stimulates the transcription of particular genes so that RNA 
encoding the information in these genes is synthesized. Ac­
cording to O'Malley the cells' response appears to be related 
to concentrations of receptor proteins in the cells which are 
not fixed. It can be altered by aging, by changes in the 
physiological state of development, and even by the presence 
of other hormones. For example, in the chick oviduct, 
estrogen stimulates the production of progesterone receptors, 
and tissues treated with estrogen are therefore more respon­
sive to progesterone. The stability of the hormone and recep­
tor complex also influences the magnitude of a target cell's 
response to a steroid hormone. Some cells must be bathed 
continuously in a high concentration of hormone if the 
response is to be maintained.

Gene amplification is a process in which one or 
more genes are duplicated selectively within a chromosome, 
and organisms likely evolved from single forms to more com­

to metholtexate, a drug used in cancer treatment, because the 
gene which codes for the emzyme to which the drug binds 
becomes amplified, or duplicated many times over. This 
allows much more of the enzyme to be produced, thus block-

leads to a change in the genome in a manner not considered to 
be a classical mutation. Transposable genetic elements or transposons are segments 
of DNA which can move genes around among such segments 
and can cause the rearrangement of genetic information on 
chromosomes. Prior to the discovery of transposons it was 
assumed there were only two major ways of achieving bio­
logical diversity-mutation and homologous recombination. Since transposons involve neither, they are referred to as "il­
legitimate" recombinational processes. They are common in 
bacteria that exchange genes in nature, and there is evidence 
that some can move among very different bacteria species 
that have not previously been known to exchange genes. Their ability to bring together unrelated DNA segments has 
led them to be spoken of as nature's genetic engineers.

Their ability to bring together unrelated DNA segments has 
led them to be spoken of as nature's genetic engineers. Stanley Cohen, a molecular geneticist at Stanford University, 
has stated that because transposons can join DNA segments 
that have little, if any, ancestral relationship, evolution can 
take quantum leaps as well as small steps. Finally, can emotional process affect the germ or reproduc­
tive cell in some type of "genetic programming"? While this 
is considered highly unlikely and dismissed as Lamarckian 
when considering human heredity, it is quite fascinating to 
look at how what is tantamount to acquired characteristics 
can be incorporated into the genome in other life forms. A 
major argument raised against such an occurrence in the past 
has been the so-called "central dogma," which held that the 
fundamental flow of information in all biological systems 
was unidirectional from DNA to RNA to protein. In 1970 
this assumption was shattered by the discovery of "reverse 
transcriptase," an enzyme found in certain RNA-containing 
viruses which catalyzed the synthesis of DNA using viral 
RNA as a template. The DNA can then be incorporated into 
the cell's pool of DNA and is passed from cell to cell during 
DNA replication. Other mechanisms for inserting acquired information into 
the DNA have also been shown to exist and are known as 
genetic insertion mechanisms. Transformation and bacteri­
ophage-induced transduction are two examples.

tion was first demonstrated in the work of the bacteriologist 
Griffith in 1928 with pneumococcus. In this process DNA is 
released by cell death or natural processes and enters a new 
cell from the environment by penetrating the cell wall. The 
entering DNA is permanently incorporated into the chromo­
some of the new cell and therefore affects its heredity. In bac­
teriophage-mediated transduction, phages, which are viruses, 
enter a bacteria, sometimes carrying foreign genes into the 
bacterial chromosome they have entered. These examples show that there may be a genetic basis to 
the multigenerational transmission process operating through 
the regulation of gene expression. That actual "genetic pro­
gramming" involving an alteration in the germ cell can occur 
is still generally considered doubtful. However, knowledge in 
the field of genetics doubles every two years. That a theory of 
the magnitude of Darwin's is currently under challenge by the

This quarterly report of the 
activities of the Georgetown University Family Center pub­
lishes reports on the training, research, and clinical services 
provided at the Family Center. It also features regular col­
umns by Dr. Murray Bowen, by a noted guest expert in the 
family field, and by a Georgetown postgraduate trainee, as 
well as periodic reviews of articles from scientific journals on 
biology, medicine and comparative animal behavior con­
sidered relevant to family clinicians and researchers. In previous issues of the FAMl/,Y CENTER REPORT, noted 
authorities in the family field such as Dr. Normal Paul, Dr. James Framo, Dr. Carlos Sluzki and Dr. Walter Toman have 
discussed topics as varied as a man's illusion of self-awareness 
in relation to the validity of using closed-circuit television in 
therapy, the rivalries among family therapy schools and ways 
to encourage cross-fertilization of ideas and methods, collid­
ing epistemologies in the systems paradigm, and the impor­
tance of sibling position in family relationships. Each issue 
also features Dr. Bowen's series of articles reviewing his twenty 
years at Georgetown and the parallel development of the field 
of family therapy. Recently, the REPORT has expanded to in­
clude articles by advanced trainees reporting on ideas they 
have developed while in the Postgraduate Training Program, 
and to include abstracts of presentations by speakers at an­
nual symposia and conferences.

G. Mary Bourne, A.C.S.W. This paper began as a report about a two-year experiment 
in teaching family practice residents about family systems. But as I developed the paper it became apparent that I hadn't 
just taught something called family systems. I had taught 
Bowen theory to those residents in a relatively pure sense. Every time we, as therapists, are asked to enter another 
"system" -like family practice medicine, or public schools, 
or small business -we have an immediate decision to make in 
terms of what we will teach. We can water down what we 
know to be true about families, compromising with the 
system in a sense, by teat:hing techniques that are palatable 
and seem to fit with what they already believe.

We can water down what we 
know to be true about families, compromising with the 
system in a sense, by teat:hing techniques that are palatable 
and seem to fit with what they already believe. Or we can 
maintain as much integrity as possible-much as we would 
when dealing with our extended families- by focusing on 
process, moving slowly and calmly, not expecting we will 
change things but recognizing and reinforcing change if it 
happens. Dr. Kitty LaPerriere and Dr. Bowen discussing Dr. Albert Scheflen 's 
videotape "About Science and Medicine and One's Own Cancer."

and probably not always wise to attempt. But there are a 
number of professional areas, including family practice medi­
cine, where people are much more eager to find a theory base 
from which to view family than are family therapists them­
selves. This certainly proved true at a clinic in Minneapolis, where 
the director, the social worker and eighteen family practice 
residents with whom I worked over the past two years just 
seemed to soak up the information I gave them without any 
evident disruption in the everyday workings of the clinic. I 
went there once a month, thinking I was teaching them about 
family systems, and learning at least as much as I taught.

Eventually, the three of us met to discuss the possibility of 
my teaching a two-hour monthly course on "family systems" 
to six residents. Two hours a month seemed so little time, 
especially since the residents were being exposed to many 
other methods of treatment by the Medical School and the 
two hospitals with which the clinic was affiliated. These in­
cluded marriage counseling, human sexuality, communica­
tions theory, chemical dependency counseling and the ventila­
tion of feelings. I suggested that the three of us meet periodically to talk 
about theory, thinking there might be more value in teaching 
them than in teaching the residents. What they chose to do, 
instead, was to be a part of every class session, learning with 
the residents and reporting on what they were doing with their 
own extended families. Because of the small amount of time, I taught from two 
family diagrams each session, using information from Toman 
at the start, and a lot of anecdotal material for comparison. After the first few sessions, people began to draw their own 
diagrams, and anyone who was making new moves in ex­
tended family reported on them. My own teaching at this 
point became more theoretical and dealt more with ways to 
most effectively work with one's own family. I certainly could expect no commitment from the residents 
that they would do anything significant with their own 
families.

needs seems only to get longer: interviewing and communica­

fields and apply them in a coordinated preventive-curative

But, what does this mean? There is the adolescent who is 
on school grounds from eight to three, but attends only three 
classes a day. Is he truant? There is another child who misses 
two of every five school days due to illness. She always 
returns to school with an excuse note from her mother. She 
has permission to be away from school. ls she therefore not 
truant? What about the sixteen year old who is no longer 
bound by law to attend school? When he begins absenting 
himself from his classes, can he really be considered truant? Another child cowers ar home, petrified by the crowds at 
school. Is he phobic or is he truant? Each student described above is unable to accomplish a 
primary developmental task of adolescence. He is failing to 
gain the skills and credentials necessary for independent adult 
survival in our society. Thus, he may be truant as much from 
adolescence as from school. I have been the family therapist in a therapeutic day school 
for adolescents for the past two years. At first I was mystified 
by the range and contradictory nature of the symptoms these 
adolescents exhibited. Gradually I came to recognize that 
beneath the fascinating, fluctuating adolescent dramatics 
there were some similar, sad family scenarios.

been able to identify two clinically distinguishable families 
which I have named The Addictive Truanting Family and The 
Allergic Truanting Family to distinguish how active emotional 
dynamics, seemingly opposite in these two types of families, 
have prompted a common symptom, adolescent truancy. By 
means of an exploratory research project, I have discovered 
that, despite their differences, these families share some 
critically important multigenerational trends. The Addictive Truanting Family 
Under stress, members of an addictive truanting family 
fuse into an almost visible ego mass. There are four 
characteristics by which this family can be recognized. First, 
the parents are over-responsible for their symptomatic child. Their greatest fears are for the child, and their greatest 
burden, accepted with willingness and sometimes joy, is to 
give comfort to this child. In some addictive truanting 
families boundaries blur so that while the parents are busy 
taking on an inordinate amount of responsibility for the stu­
dent's health or school tasks, the child is busy taking care of 
parental tasks such as household management. The reason given for parental overconcern is the second 
common trait.

its members. Although the allergic adolescent's symptom, 
truancy, resembles the addictive adolescent's symptom on the 
surface, the underlying family dynamic and function of the 
symptom is quite different. 7

characteristics. First, each parent delegates parental respon­

high standards of the family must be communicated to the 
adolescent. The parents try to enlist the school, the police, the 
court, the church and the hospital to follow through with the 
structure and consequences they themselves are unable to 
provide for their child. Secondly, the adolescent is perceived as hopelessly evil.

Additionally, I compiled data from

suggest that all the families might share some critically impor­

The most striking characteristic of the families of our 
students is their geographical isolation. An impressive 
number of family histories revealed that the student's grand­
parents had migrated from Europe and Asia two generations 
before the student's birth. I hypothesized that dynamics of 
emotional cutoff from long distance migrations might have 
been activated in the emotional projection process of these 
families. Research data gives tentative support to this 
hypothesis in both the grandparent and the parent genera­
tions. Fifty-four percent of all grandparents in our sample 
have migrated from the state or country of their birth. This 
migrating phenomenon is seen more dramatically in the 
parental generation where parents are separated geograph­
ically from both the preceding generation and from their own 
generation. Sixty-six percent of the parents in our sample 
has no sibling residing within the same state. Seventy-two 
percent of all the siblings of the parents in our sample is 
either deceased or living out of state.

come. What moves people and their relations to exchange 
their nest of origin for one purported to be populated by 
cuckoos? Which nest, home or hospital, is best for a rest? I 
have also wondered about the people who come. Do they 
bring their craziness with them or do they leave it behind? These and other related questions have arisen throughout 
my career as a minister working in a psychiatric hospital.

Do they 
bring their craziness with them or do they leave it behind? These and other related questions have arisen throughout 
my career as a minister working in a psychiatric hospital. In 
the past five years or so I have adopted three assumptions as a 
basis for responding to these questions: (I) the presence of in­
tense emotional turmoil in the family, (2) the effort of family 
members to resolve their distress by "selecting" one member 
as the source of their difficulties, and (3) the attempt by the 
family to gain relief from the crisis by relinquishing a signi fi­
cant degree of responsibility for reduction or resolution of its 
anxiety to the hospital. In my place of work it is common for the staff to assume a 
major degree of responsibility for human problems. There is, 
in fact, little that can be done to avoid taking responsibility. When a person is admitted he must be diagnosed, treated, 
returned to the community, and then referred for follow-up 
care. Each staff member plays a part that potentially contrib­
utes to the family problem. To the extent that the hospital 
assumes responsibility for treatment of one member, the 
family and others in the person's social system are relieved of

The project I designed entails conducting a family inter­
view with people who arrive seeking voluntary admission for 
the first time and who are accompanied by at least one 
member of their family. This interview is conducted before 
the admitting physician decides about admission. To admit or 
not to admit, that is the question. Deciding this question is 
perhaps the most critical aspect of the project. The goal is to 
define this as a decision for which the family is responsible. In 
practice it is difficult to maintain this posture completely. The 
family interviewer usually confers, exchanges information, 
and discusses the advisability of admission with the physician, 
thus entering into the decision. If the person is admitted, follow-up interviews are held 
with the family by the family therapist who originally met 
with the family during admission. This person is responsible 
for coordinating his efforts with the treatment team regarding 
the patient's course in the hospital, the progress of the family, 
and referral for possible follow-up care. The project began on November I, I 979 with a staff of 
seven who were on call for initial family interviews. Currently 
there are eleven people working on the project, each con­
tributing a maximum of one half day per week.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. Many people recover from cancer. A few have experienced 
dramatic remissions of widesdpread disease. Regardless of 
clinical outcome, the quality of life of patient and family is 
quite variable. The Family Center is sponsoring a symposium 
on cancer on April 11, 1981. This conference is intended for 
helping professionals as well as cancer patients and their 
families. It brings together guest experts from several medical 
disciplines as well as cancer patients to explore some of the 
factors that may influence differences in outcome. Factors to 
be explored include the impact of belief systems of the pa­
tient, the family and the medical treatment setting, and society 
in general; the influence of different types of emotional re­
actions and adjustments; and the importance of relationship 
networks. Several patients will describe their own recovery 
and the factors they believe to be important in that process. The guest speakers will be Charles H.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. On April 11, 1981, The Georgetown Family Center sponsored 
its fourth symposium on cancer. The distinguished guest experts 
were Charles H. Goodrich, M.D., Clinical Associate Professor 
of Medicine at Cornell Medical College and Harold Wise, 
M.D., Associate Professor of Community Health at Albert 
Einstein College of Medicine and Director of The Family 
Center of Holistic Health at Montefiore Hospital in New York. Joining Doctors Wise and Goodrich on the program were Dr. Murray Bowen and Dr. Michael Kerr from Georgetown. The conference was well attended and generated an atmo­
sphere that is difficult to capture in writing. Wise and Goodrich 
brought two families from New York, both of which had members 
who have experienced complete regressions of widespread 
cancers. The families presented their views on what had been 
important to them in the recovery process. In the afternoon, 
videotapes were shown of Albert Scheflen and Gregory Bateson, 
each discussing the thinking stimulated by their own experiences 
with cancer. Murray Bowen discussed both tapes. Perhaps one of the strengths of the day was the avoidance of 
simplistic explanations about the interrelationship of emotional 
and biological variables in cancer.

In fact, such a view, the old theory of cancer, was the 
basis for the radical surgical treatments of cancer. Cancer was 
initially thought to be a local disease that remained localized for 
a period of time and then spread in a predictable way, mostly 
through the lymph channels. The lymph nodes were viewed as a 
barrier to the spread. The old theory assumed that a cancer acted 
as an independent, autonomous entity, unaffected by the body's 
defense system, and that it did not spread by way of the blood. In the mid l 950's, the bloodstream was revealed as an 
important route for spreading tumor cells from the primary site to 
distant organs. It was also learned that although lymph nodes 
may destroy tumor cells, they were not really a barrier to their 
spread. The idea that a tumor was an autonomous entity was also 
modified as their growth or dormancy was shown to be related to 
conditions in their environment, such as the body's defenses. So, 
rather than cancer being thought of as a local affliction that 
ultimately spread, a growing belief developed that it was a 
generalized, or systemic disease, probably from its inception. This change in thinking about cancer obviously has had great 
implications for therapy. We have moved from radical to more 
conservative surgical measures, such as, from the radical 
mastectomy to even just the removal of the lump itself. Also, 
more systemic therapies such as chemotherapy have been 
emphasized.

more systemic therapies such as chemotherapy have been 
emphasized. There are some other interesting facts about cancer. Cancer 
is often multi-focal. Besides primary site, there is frequently 
microscopic evidence of tumor cells at other sites in the same 
tissue. This does not mean these other sites are the result of 
spread from the primary site, but, rather, they are probably 
separate tumors arising at the same time. It is as if the whole 
tissue has become carrier-prone, rather than one cell running 
wild, multiplying and spreading. This, again, is a more systemic 
view of the problem. Interestingly, these microscopic cancers 
often do not progress to actual "disease." For example, 25% of 
breast cancer patients show evidence of cancer cells in the 
uninvolved breast, but far fewer develop a second tumor. Autopsy data of women over 70 who died of causes other than 
breast cancer showed that the percentage of those with micro­
scopic breast cancer was nineteen times greater than the actual 
incidence of overt breast cancer in that age group. The point is

cancer, some of the work in the field of cancer is also reflecting a 
slight shift towards a systems view of the emotional factors of 
cancer. Mostly, however, our work in the emotional area has 
been based on theories rooted in the study of the individual, such 
as a psychoanalytic conceptualization of the cancer patient. Yet the field has been and is loaded with innovative thinkers 
and courageous therapists. The word courageous may seem 
overstated, but there has been no great stampede to work in this 
area and those who have worked in it have been labeled, at times, 
"kooks indulging in unscientific mysticism." As far as I am 
concerned, there is a science to this field. It is just that there are 
so many not easily defined variables that the patterns are not 
clear. Man's thinking about the solar system was in a similarly 
confusing state before Copernicus, Kepler, and Newton brought 
us to a systems framework there. The literature about emotional factors in cancer is extensive

Lawrence LeShan, 
working from a psychoanalytic framework, has contributed 
extensively to the field. He emphasizes the significance of a loss 
of a relationship eight years to a few months prior to the 
diagnosis, a point emphasized by almost everyone who has 
worked in the field. He describes the person vulnerable to cancer 
as faced with insoluble life situations and an accompanying 
feeling of despair over the fact that they feel they have done 
nothing. He adds that these people are unable to express anger or 
resentment or to become aggressive in their own defense. He 
describes them as nice, cooperative people who want to get 
along, but who tend to alienate themselves. In my own work with cancer, I have found LeShan's 
observations quite consistent with my own. Dr. Caroline 
Thomas, the distinguished guest expert at our first symposium on 
cancer in 1977, has done extensive longitudinal studies of 
medical students at Johns Hopkins. The former medical students 
who later developed cancer reported different family attitudes in 
youth from those of their healthy classmates. They are described 
as "low gear people, little given to expressions of emotion, 
whose relationships with their parents had been cold and 
remote." William Green and Arthur Schmale have both empha­
sized that disease occurs in a setting of emotional distress 
characterized by separation from a significant person or the loss 
of a major goal.

Harold Wise and Charles Goodrich, this year's symposium 
experts, also look at relationship networks. Wise has made 
extensive studies of the healing process in tribal medicine, 
discovering that the oldest healing form involves bringing the 
whole clan together and "working things through" for 24 to 72 
hours. Wise and Goodrich presented the view that there is a 
healing force within the family. When people get emotionally 
isolated from their family network, they seem more vulnerable to 
getting sick. If they do get sick reactivating that network around 
the patient has tremendous healing potential. Wise and 
Goodrich are innovators. They are comfortable with what they 
don't know and have the motivation and courage to try new 
things. For a small percentage of cancer families in their 
practice, they have helped arrange family network meetings, 
sometimes at the bedside. In a still smaller percentage of 
instances, complete reversal of the cancer process has occurred. Wise believes that some day there will be a way to explain this 
observable phenomenon in scientific terms. What is important to 
me about their work, along with that of Dr. Stewart Wolf, is that 
it broadens the field of observation from just the individual 
patient to the relationship network. This broader view invites 
new conceptualizations. Murray Bowen presented the videotapes of Albert Scheflen 
and Gregory Bateson. These, again, are tapes that must be seen 
to be fully appreciated.

current blindness in understanding cancer is tied to being 
embedded in a cause-and-effect paradigm dating back at least to 
Aristotle. While man has moved toward systems in the physical 
sciences, he remains quite enmeshed in cause-and-effect 
thinking in the biological sciences. Much of Scheflen's thinking 
in the area was stimulated by dealing with the medical profession 
during his own illness. Bateson also described a different way of 
thinking about cancer, talking about disturbances in the ecology 
of the body that permit cancers to grow. He too had fascinating

of my family, I now know myself a bit more objectively. Through 
a review of the history of the nursing profession, I have 
attempted to objectify my view and define my relationship with 
the nursing profession more clearly. PERSONAL PERSPECTIVE 
In a conversation with my mother last year, she said, "Even 
as a child you cared a great deal about people and things." 
Health" care" is an interesting term and a commodity that the 
nursing profession appears highly invested in providing. In a four 
page pamphlet on the standards of nursing practice published by 
the American Nurses' Association, the word care is used 26 
times, 16 times preceded by the word nursing, 6 times preceded 
by the word health and five times by the words comprehensive 
and professional. Fourteen of the 26 total uses are in association 
with planning. So it would seem that care is something that 
nurses can do and ought to plan. Although I had a vague suspicion that I should already know 
its meaning, I decided to refer to Webster's for a clearer 
understanding of the word" care." In addition to grief and mental 
suffering, I found care to mean a "burdensome sense of 
responsibility" and "heavy anxiety." As a verb, it means to pay 
"painstaking or watchful attention," and "to heed." These 
meanings opened a new awareness of the origins of my 
difficulties both in my profession and in my family.

likely to belong on the regressive side. Returning to Webster, I found that a nurse is a woman who 
suckles and takes care of an infant and, more generally, one 
6 (usually a woman) who furnishes nutriment, fosters growth or 
well-being, and one who is trained to care for and wait upon the

short, a nurturer, a caretaker, and an assistant. Although there is 
nothing inherently wrong with nurturing, caretaking, and assist­
ing, there can be "too much of a good thing." Although still 
undecided about whether this concept of nursing is progressive 
or regressive, I keep wondering if any profession could function 
effectively with nurturing as a foundation. I am reminded of the 
infantilizing aspects of hospitalization and of how often I have 
observed nurses play a part in reinforcing and even in promoting 
dependency in the form of doing for, deciding for, and protecting 
patients. A nurse mentioning "my patients" often seems to 
indicate the kind of possessiveness that does not allow the 
necessary space or information for patients to make their own 
decisions.

A nurse mentioning "my patients" often seems to 
indicate the kind of possessiveness that does not allow the 
necessary space or information for patients to make their own 
decisions. A way to classify aspects of the nursing profession as 
progressive or regressive is to assess them as manifestations of 
differentiation and fusion as defined by family systems theory. An underlying premise is that both differentiation and fusion are 
innate forces operating simultaneously within human organisms. Progression is the product of the human tendency to strive 
towards individuality and autonomy of self while effectively 
relating to others. Regression is the product of the tendency to 
unite, to conform, and to seek approval, agreement and the 
immediate relief from the anxiety of the moment. Progression 
occurs when one is able to recognize anxiety and the push for 
immediate action, but is nonetheless able to make decisions that 
will have long-term beneficial effects for all concerned. Regres­
sion occurs when one responds to the anxiety of the moment and 
either acts or reacts in relatively automatic, unthinking ways that 
temporarily reduce pressure or "feel right" but do not solve 
problems, resolve issues, or result in long-term gain.

Progression 
is a result of being able to reason, while maintaining an 
awareness offeelings and emotional forces; regression is a result 
of automatically reacting to emotional forces while having little 
or no awareness of what reason might be like. The following are some characteristics of a profession that is 
progressive -moving toward differentiation -and some char­
acteristics of a profession that is regressive -remaining or 
becoming more undifferentiated. A profession is in a state of progression to the degree that: 
( 1) Self-definition is based on an established, thoughtful 
philosophy or system of beliefs. (2) Goals, principles and standards of practice are clearly 
delineated and consistent with self-definition and 
philosophy. (3) Those goals, principles, and standards are clearly com­
municated to its members and to other professions with 
which it interacts. ( 4) Self-definition is maintained while remaining in contact 
with other related professions. A profession is in a state of regression to the degree that: 
( 1) Self-definition is governed by outside influences. (2) Goals, principles, and standards have unrecognized 
discrepancies. (3) More emphasis is placed on rights than on responsibility. (4) Contact with other professions is limited to reinforce 
a sense of identity. (5) The organization and its members are overvalued or 
undervalued.

The origins of nursing in recorded history stem from military 
and religious orders whose guiding principle was charity. It is 
common in modern nursing texts to equate or parallel the 
development of nursing to the "history of women." As early as 
1946 a rather romantic historian wrote, "The nurse is the mirror 
in which is reflected the position of women throughout the ages." 
Factually, the majority of nurses are women, but to equate 
nursing with womanhood misses how emotional process has 
influenced the course of its development. The attempt to merge 
or to compare the two is reflective of emotional process. Nursing developed from a societal acceptance of responsibility 
for providing services to members of society who were tempor­
arily or permanently unable to function independently. Although 
the move to educate or train people to perform this function 
seems a reasonable, responsible course of action, the growth of 
nursing appears to have been determined by emotional (regres­
sive) forces rather than by intellectual (progressive) forces. Interestingly, the issues have changed little in the past 100 years. In the United States nursing was not commonly practiced by 
respectable women prior to the Civil War.

Interestingly, the issues have changed little in the past 100 years. In the United States nursing was not commonly practiced by 
respectable women prior to the Civil War. Until that time 
hospitals were, in fact, not respected places, since they catered 
only to the indigent, the homeless, the ill and infirmed. It was 
common also for "poorhouses" or almshouses to be located 
under the same roof as hospitals. Conditions were extremely 
unsanitary. Bleeding, purging and administering large doses of 
alcohol were standard medical procedures of the day, and nurses 
were recruited from the dregs of society. The majority of nurses 
at that time were uneducated and often "morally unfit" to 
assume the care of patients. For example, former inmates of the 
workhouse on Blackwell's Island in New York staffed Bellevue 
Hospital. In 1861, shortly after the outbreak of the Civil War, the 
publication of Florence Nightingale's Notes on Nursing ac­
quainted American women with the concept of professional 
nursing. One author credits this publication with stimulating 
nearly 10,000 women to volunteer to serve as nurses in spite of 
the social stigma still attached to "nursing strange men on the 
battlefield." There were about 9,000 volunteer nurses for the 
Union Army and about 1,000 for the Confederate. Dorothea Dix, known for her efforts to reform "insane 
asylums," was appointed by the Secretary of War to super­
intend women nurses.

A REVIEW 
Francis L. Giove, ACSW 
For a person who is trying to think toward a systems view of 
the human phenomenon, the title of the book Why Males Exist, 
by Fred Hapgood is a first clue that the book is a cause and effect 
presentation. I've got nothing against cause-and-effect thinking, 
but the view it presents is too narrow. From my perspective, 
cause-and-effect thinking is a historical part of an ongoing 
process in the big picture of all life. When I saw E.O. Wilson's positive comment on the front 
cover, I decided to scan the contents of the book. What I saw 
impressed me. Here was a presentation of life in all forms, with 
lots of good examples. One example that struck me was the 
opening of Chapter IV, "An Overview of Some of the Cons and 
Pros of Sex." The author talks about "wasteful males." Sex is 
placed in a wide-ranging context. Hapgood says: 
There are three alternatives to wasteful males: males, like 
beavers or nesting birds, that work; bisexuals; and creatures 
that reproduce asexually. The key feature of these three 
systems is that the organisms in them clearly channel their

The lionessess of a pride all come into and go out of a short

THE BOWEN FAMILY THEORY AND ITS USES 
A REVIEW 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. This book by Dr. Margaret Hall is the first book on Bowen 
Theory to be published other than Murray Bowen's own book of 
collected papers, Family Therapy In Clinical Practice. (Writing 
a book such as this is a major task) and it is difficult in a brief 
review to do justice to the effort it represents. Dr. Hall has spent 
years writing and rewriting this text, striving to represent the 
theory as accurately as she could. Ha!J is a well-known 
sociologist and much of the book appears aimed at trying to 
communicate Bowen Theory to that discipline. She raises 
numerous issues of interest to sociological researchers, and 
attempts to show how family systems theory may facilitate 
research in these areas. Several sections of the book are the product of lengthy 
discussions Dr. Hall had with Dr. Bowen about his theory, 
particularly its development. She now has in writing many things 
Bowen has talked about over the years, but has never written 
himself. It provides insight into the kind of mental discipline it 
takes to develop a new theory. Few people who were not part of 
the pioneering family research of the l 950's appreciate the 
magnitude of the task in making what Bowen has called the 
"quantum leap" to a new level of conceptualization, namely, 
toward systems thinking. The book is divided into three parts: (I) Theory, ( 2) 
Applications, and (3) Issues and Implications.

The book is divided into three parts: (I) Theory, ( 2) 
Applications, and (3) Issues and Implications. The part on 
Theory is the longest and contains detailed presentations of each 
ofBowen's eight concepts. Some ofHall's discussion of theory is 
an attempt to present it as Bowen has talked and written about it, 
while other aspects of her presentation of the concepts reflect her 
10 own interpretation of Bowen's ideas. Hall weaves ideas devel­
oped from sociological research into Bowen's concepts, draws 
what she believes are parallels in thinking, and often suggests 
where these juxtaposed ideas can enhance each other. This effort 
by Hall may make the book of particular interest to sociologists. The part on Applications begins with a chapter about Dr. Hall's efforts to differentiate a self in her family of origin. This 
discussion about her own family is brief and may mislead the 
reader, as it underemphasizes the complexity and gradual nature 
of the effort toward differentiation. The next chapter is entitled, 
Healing Processes, and examines the different qualities of 
family response to symptomatic behavior, particularly physical 
symptoms. A chapter called, Aging and Institutionalization, 
underlines the importance of meaningful emotional contact 
between older and younger generations as an ingredient in the 
healthy functioning of both generations. Brief clinical vignettes 
are provided to amplify these ideas.

chapter. Hall expresses the view that the field of sociology has 
biased conceptualizations about women and that Bowen Theory 
can provide a new perspective. I imagine many sociologists 
would disagree with Hall's views about such a bias. The last 
chapter in this part of the book, Formal Organizations, 
describes some applications of systems ideas to work systems. The third and final part of the book, Issues and Implications, 
contains chapters entitled, The Bowen Theory As Theory, 
Science, Evolution, Psychotherapy as a Secular Religion, and 
Toward a General Theory of Human Behavior. These chapter 
titles suggest the extent to which Hall attempts to look at 
Bowen's ideas in the perspective of a wide range of other fields. Brief examination of Dr. Hall's book gives the impression 
of a fairly short book that could be read in a brief period of 
time. Appearances are quite deceiving. Once into the book, the 
reader is confronted with one complex issue after another, each 
having extensive references. Hall, herself, does not promise 
answers to the many questions raised in her book, but does 
provide an interesting account of the threads in her own thinking 
as she attempts to integrate the ideas. The Bowen Family Theory and Its Uses, by C. Margaret Hall, New York,

 MY PHYSICAL FUNCTIONING 
Murray Bowen, M.D. This is prepared to answer some of the hundreds of questions 
that come every day. Many are the product of misassumptions 
rather than reality in me. Until March 1981 I led a charmed medical life. My father 
lived to 87 and my mother is still going at 95. I never missed a 
day from school because of illness and no more than two or three 
days from work in over forty years. I had lived in and around 
hospitals all my life and professional contact with doctors had 
been for routine physical examinations. My brief absences from 
work came when I had a cold or flu and I did not want to risk 
contact with others. My last hospitalization was for German 
measles in the Army in 1941 and that was to isolate me from 
others during the contagious phase. The experience in 1981 has been a new one for me. I went to 
the hospital in March 1981 for sudden chest pain assumed to be 
a heart problem. The coronary arteries were good. The diagnoses, 
often the product of medical guesses, shifted from day to day.

The coronary arteries were good. The diagnoses, 
often the product of medical guesses, shifted from day to day. Arterial radiography revealed an asymptomatic aortic aneurysm 
in the adomen and a probable aortic aneurysm in the chest that 
could have caused the chest pain. Surgical repair of the 
aneurysms was recommended. I had never taken drugs of any 
kind. In the hospital I was extremely sensitive to drugs. After 
eight days I went to my nearby home for over a month to be 
followed closely in the outpatient department. The goal was to 
avoid expensive hospitalization, to recover from the ordeal of 
medical tests and the drug experimentation to stabilize the blood 
pressure, and to make a decision about surgery. On May 5 I 
returned to the hospital for more arterial radiography and repair 
of the chest aneurysm on May 6. Recovery was fairly rapid and 
on May 17 I returned home for another period ofrecovery. The 
major complication was a traumatized recurrent laryngeal nerve 
and a partially paralyzed vocal cord. Recovery from that is still 
in progress. On May 25 I returned to the hospital for surgical 
repair of the abdominal aneurysm on May 26. Recovery was 
rapid and I returned home for good on June 2, 1981, to be 
followed by the cardiologist and a speech therapist for the 
whisperish voice. National professional meetings are most frequent in the fall 
and spring months.

National professional meetings are most frequent in the fall 
and spring months. In April and May 1981 it was necessary to 
either cancel my participation in meetings or to get Mike Kerr to substitute for me. On June 11, 1981, little more than a week out of 
the hospital, Mike Kerr helped me get to the Ackerman 
Memorial meeting in New York City. Since then I have been to 
selected national meetings. Microphones do a fair job compen­
sating for the weak voice. My doctors warned me that recovery 
from cardiovascular surgery is far slower than recovery from 
other major surgery. The process also involved a major weight 
reduction. I returned to work part-time by about mid-June 1981. It was a surprise to discover I could not bounce back, and that 
recovery is so slow. I was out of commission for most of three months. The back 
work that accumulated was horrendous. It included mountains 
of correspondence, material to be read, and all kinds of 
administrative and writing chores. I assumed that catching up 
would be like an ordinary absence ifl applied myself. I thought I 
would be current in a matter of weeks or a few months. Then 
came the surprise. I was not physically able to apply myself. Every small task required several times as much energy as it 
previously required. A short time at my desk would bring out the 
current symptom and the symptom demanded physical rest. I 
could no longer ignore symptoms as I had done in past years.

A short time at my desk would bring out the 
current symptom and the symptom demanded physical rest. I 
could no longer ignore symptoms as I had done in past years. To 
ignore a symptom only multiplied the recuperation time. My 
periods of productive work were limited and new work was being 
piled onto the back work. Gradually the admonitions of my 
doctors began to make sense. I could not recover as fast as I 
thought I could. I had MAJOR chest surgery and major 
abdominal surgery in little more than three weeks and the 
recovery process required a change in life style. It became clear 
that it may take a year to catch up with back work and the future 
will require more selectivity about the amount of work I do 
personally, and that much more work must be delegated to my 
Family Center faculty. My physical functioning for the future appears bright, ifl can 
calibrate the amount of work an oldest son automatically 
assumes for himself. Recovery from the medical crises of 1981 
has not been as fast as I would like but it has been slow and 
gradual. The weak voice has been a major problem but it does not 
interfere with meetings and I expect it to improve. My head 
works a mile a minute with all kinds of theoretical and 
therapeutic problems which I shall try to record and implement 
along with my new lifestyle. I am working to make the 
experience of 1981 into something positive for the long term 
future.

ACUTE AND CHRONIC 
PHYSICAL DYSFUNCTION 
Edward W. Beal, M.D. At some point in their lives eight of every ten people on earth 
will experience back pain. Lower back pain currently affects 
seventy-five million people in the United States alone and ac­
counts for approximately ten percent of all visits to physicians. There are seven million new patients with low back pain each 
year. Although it is difficult to substantiate, early man and his 
predecessors, while walking on all fours, had virtually no back 
pain. When man evolved from that four-legged individual to 
this more upstanding individual, he moved from a relatively per­
manently prone position to a more upright posture. Although 
walking in an upright position greatly enhanced man's mobility 
and range of functioning, this evolutionary advantage was 
solidified only at great expense in body adaptation: virtually 
100% of the American population by age 20 has evidence of 
lumbar disc disease. This paper will illustrate the advantages and disadvantages of 
this development and the necessary body adaptation. It will 
focus on the response patterns of bones, muscles and the in­
dividual person and their systematic interaction in the evolution 
of physical functioning and dysfunctioning known as low back 
pain.

text:
The spinal column is a chain of blocks (the vertebrae), stack­
ed one on the other and kept from collapsing by an exact system 
of muscles and ligaments that acts with synergistic and an­
tagonistic precision. The lumbar vertebrae in particular are 
large and massive because of their weight-bearing function. The 
task and function of the vertebrae, in conjunction with the 
pelvis, is to support the rest of the body. Individuals who cannot 
stand up for themselves in confrontation are frequently referred 
to as "spineless." This metaphysical concept obviously derives 
from the physical importance attached to the spine. The vertebrae have two types of bony projections, one to 
which muscles attach and the other to which other bones attach, 
forming joint processes. The spinal cord floats through the cen­
ter of the vertebrae, and the spinal nerves proceed through these 
tiny, bony notches, serving as the body's communications 
system, reporting pain from the periphery to the brain and sen­
ding messages from the brain instructing muscles to function in 
certain ways. Between each vertebra lies the inter-vertebral space occupied 
by the inter-vertebral disc. A conceptually easy way to think 
about the spine is to look at the spine as a stack of alternating 
hockey pucks and jelly donuts. The hockey pucks correspond to 
the vertebrae and the jelly donuts (slightly stale and tough) cor­
respond to the inter-vertebral discs.

text:
The hockey pucks correspond to 
the vertebrae and the jelly donuts (slightly stale and tough) cor­
respond to the inter-vertebral discs. The vertebrae are insulated 
from one another by the jelly-donut-like consistency of the 
discs. The soft discs also permit the flexibility of bending the 
spine in any direction. Man's spinal column functions best when it stands erect like a 
telephone pole. Yet what keeps it from falling apart or coming 
down? Just as a telephone pole has guide wire to weather the 
winds of a storm, similarly the spinal column has muscles and 
ligaments which function to attach it to all that surrounds it. As 
the telephone pole and guide wires bend with the wind of a 
storm, so do the spinal column and muscles bend with the stress 
of their environment. When man developed the ability to stand erect and thereby 
increased his potential for mobility, his ability to maintain 
balance became more problematic. Switching from four feet to 
two is like turning a soda-pop bottle upside down. A man 
standing erect has the same inadequate base of support as does 
the inverted soda-pop bottle. This difference is highlighted by 
the fact that it takes man between two and three years to be able 
to learn to walk satisfactorily while it takes most four-legged 
mammals only a few weeks. However, maintaining one's balance while maintaining one's 
mobility is not the only problem. Evolutionary adaptation to 
the advantage of walking is incomplete.

text:
However, maintaining one's balance while maintaining one's 
mobility is not the only problem. Evolutionary adaptation to 
the advantage of walking is incomplete. The table of the pelvic 
bones upon which the spinal column rests is carried neither level 
to the ground nor perpendicular to the spinal column, but 
rather is tilted forward at a forty-degree angle. Thus, to keep the 
appropriate spinal alignment and body weight evenly 
distributed, an individual should walk with his/her body tilted 
forward at a forty-degree angle. Yet, for a variety of reasons, 
parents encourage children to walk and sit upright. Adhering to 
parental commands to walk upright with shoulders back re­
quires a child to force the lumbar spine to bend backwards. This 
spinal adaptation, enabling one to walk upright, changes the 
body's weight distribution and badly deforms the entire spinal 
structure. An exaggerated forward lean keeps the spine in 
perfect alignment as it was at birth, whereas the acquired, erect

ducing a pronounced hollow in the back referred to medically as 
lumbar lordosis, or, more commonly, as swayback. While maintaining the acquired erect posture, the body's 
weight is redistributed to the back edges of the vertebrae, 
significantly decreasing the spinal column's stability.

text:
While maintaining the acquired erect posture, the body's 
weight is redistributed to the back edges of the vertebrae, 
significantly decreasing the spinal column's stability. A com­
mon analogy would be changing a stack of children's blocks 
from one that is evenly stacked to one in which the blocks were 
aligned less evenly along their edges. The second column of 
blocks is significantly less stable, Therefore this curve of the 
lumbar spinal column enabling man to walk upright requires a 
major shift of weight distribution to the back edge of the 
vertebrae and the discs. This added force and weight is trans­
mitted to the soft discs, causing them eventually to bulge and/ or 
rupture onto the spinal nerves passing alongside each disc. This 
compensatory mechanism of shifting the weight in order to 
walk upright is sufficiently prevalent that by twenty years of age 
100% of the American population has a deformed lower lum­
bar disc. This adaptive mechanism (shifting the weight on the structure 
of the spine) creates both acute and chronic problems. The 
chronic process, through the destruction of the disc, allows 
bone to grate on bone resulting in gradual dislocation of that 
joint which, in turn, puts constant pressure on the nerve. The 
chronic, constant pressure on the disc leads to periodic acute 
situations when the bony passage is so reduced that during any 
extreme backward bend of the spine the nerve is pinched, pro­
ducing severe back and leg pain.

The pinching of the nerve 
sends an immediate message to the brain in which the latter, 
without the intervention of consciousness, responds with a 
message to the muscles to pull tighter in order to enhance the 
stability of the lumbar vertebrae. Unfortunately pulling tighter 
is helpful in stabilizing the spinal column up to a point, after 
which it simply pinches the nerve more, possibly causing 
paralysis and requiring total bedrest. The specific muscles involved in this process include the 
muscles of the back, buttocks, and abdomen as well as the 
short, strong muscles along the spinal processes of the spinal 
column. The back and abdominal muscles are the guide wires of 
the spinal column and exert their effect through interaction on 
the pelvic table. The back muscles lift the back of the pelvis and 
thereby increase the hollow in the back. They are opposed by 
2 the abdominal muscles which lift the front of the pelvis and 
decrease the hollow in the back. All things being equal, the 
strength of the back muscles should be equal to the strength of 
the abdominal muscles in order to keep the spinal column 
straight. However, the back muscles win hands down. Yet the 
side effect of becoming the strongest is that the back muscles 
become the shortest and the tightest and therefore increase the 
pressure on the back edges of the vertebrae and on the discs that 
separate them. The function of muscles is the development of tension and 
shortening.

The function of muscles is the development of tension and 
shortening. Muscle contraction depends upon stimulation of 
the muscle by the nerve. Between contractions the muscles 
assume a relaxed state. The reactivity of the muscles to stimula­
tion is an important characteristic -one over which the muscle 
itself exercises no control. If a muscle is stimulated once, there is 
a brief lag period between the arrival of the stimulus and the in­
itiation of tension development. When the tension reaches acer­
tain value, the muscle contracts. This contraction is transient and 
the muscle subsequently lengthens and returns to its relaxed 
condition. However, if the muscle is subject to repeated fre­
quent stimuli, a condition over which the muscle has no control, 
the muscle will not relax between each stimulation but rather 
will remain in a contracted state referred to as tetany. The 
plateau of contraction is maintained until the muscle begins to 
fatigue, at which time it relaxes and goes into dysfunction. Cons­
tant stimulation results in a state of constant functioning or over­
functioning that eventually leads to temporary dysfunction. Although the muscle can exercise no control over this process, 
the mind/body complex of each individual can. The basic reac­
tivity to stimuli is a characteristic of all protoplasm.

The intellectual and emotional systems can be thought 
of as a complex unit of protoplasm. The task of the individual is 
to maintain some balanced, integrated functioning between the 
two. The stimulus for the development of functioning is signifi­
cant emotional contact with others, beginning with one's 
mother and own family. This stimulus/response pattern for 
mature intellectual/emotional systems can be measured just as 
the stimulus/response pattern of the adult muscle functioning. Adult individuals who return for significant emotional contact 
with their extended families report a period of time with 
enhanced functioning followed by a period of time in which 
there may be an acute or chronic imbalance between intellectual 
and emotional functioning. The loss of functioning comes for 
some people with just a one or two-hour exposure to extended 
family and for other individuals after a two or three-day ex­
posure to extended family. Just as the constant stimulus to the 
muscle results in fatigue and underfunctioning, a constant ex­
posure to the stimulus of the extended family almost always 
results in a loss of functioning unless interrupted by physical 
space or time. Constant exposure to stimulation of muscles may 
result in the loss of functioning unless interrupted by physical 
space or time. Constant exposure to stimulation of muscles may 
result in the loss of functioning of the physical self.

ON CORPORATE INTERACTION 
The corporate organizational chart often depicts the flow of 
power and responsibility as a static, two-dimensional process 
without focusing on the true cause of success---how people, 
three-dimensional beings, interact. On December 7, the Georgetown University Family Center 
sponsored a day-long symposium, "People at Work: 
Understanding Organizations," to explore Bowen Systems 
Theory within the context of the workplace. According to the 
Family Center, systems theory has direct application to increas­
ing the effectiveness of organizational life by teaching a calm 
and studied approach to the predictable elements of corporate 
life. Developed by Murray Bowen, M.D., Director of the Family 
Center, systems theory views the family as an integral unit and 
contends that what affects one family member will affect the 
entire family unit.

After receiving her M.S. W. from the Medical College of Virginia in Richmond 
in 1979, Ms. Keenan has been employed at the Arlington Community Mental 
Health Center. Ms. Keenan worked for seven years as a probation counselor at 
the Fairfax Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court before returning to graduate 
school. My purpose in presenting on this subject is two-fold: 1) an ef­
fort to gain some perspective on a theme that has played and 
continues to play an overly important role in my family, and 2) 
an effort to tie one family process theme to Bowen's concepts. The term holiday derives from "holy day" and is, according 
to Webster, a day of freedom from labor, a day set aside by law 
or custom for the suspension of business, usually in celebration 
of some event. The word holiday is also used to mean joyous 
and gay, as in "holiday spirit." So holiday, by definition, has 
connotations of purpose and expectation, and therein lie two 
clues to the emotional forces that surround a holiday event. The 
more purposeful the holiday the greater the expectation, and the 
greater the expectation, the greater the emotional forces. Holidays are defined or interpreted by the individual, by the 
family, by the legal, religious and educational institutions in 
society, and are influenced by economic, cultural, and en­
vironmental factors. For the purpose of this paper, I narrowed the focus to one 
holiday-Christmas.

For the purpose of this paper, I narrowed the focus to one 
holiday-Christmas. The themes, issues, and questions that ap­
ply to this one holiday are also present to some extent for all 
holidays, or for any other special event where families and 
social groups come together for celebration or ceremony. But Christmas is different from other ceremonial occasions 
or celebrations in that it not only occurs every year at the same 
time, but is a special day not only for individuals and for 
families, but for work systems, friendship systems, community, 
country and for the entire Christian world. It comes close to be­
ing the universal holiday celebration and as such, it has great 
impact in both subtle and not so subtle ways. In case there is 
anyone who would argue with the fact of the emotional impact 
of Christmas, Holmes and Rahe gave it 12 of 100 points as a 
stress factor on their Social Readjustment Scale. 6 SOCIETAL PERSPECTIVE 
If Bowen's concept of societal regression is correct, then what 
American society is doing with Christmas seems to be a good in­
dicator of that process. Over the last decade, an increasing 
number of magazine and newspaper articles such as the one in 
1977 entitled, "Holidays are Threatening," or the one in 1978 
entitled, "If Holidays are for Merry-Making, How Come I Feel 
So Blue?" have appeared in the popular press.
