Then 
there are the families or family members who run from one pole 
to the other-sometimes during the same holiday season. Most families fall somewhere between these two poles, and I 
know I am not unique in coming from a family where some 
members have hugged or at least leaned on one pole while 
others lean on the opposite. I myself am, of course, in the mid­
dle, the more flexible and functional position, and am not sur­
prised to observe that the more I pull up my functioning and 
tone down the general level of anxiety in me, and the more I 
take control of myself and my Christmas, the more my family 
also moves toward a more flexible, middle position between the 
two poles. PERSONAL EFFORTS 
For me to have arrived at a more functional, flexible, middle 
position on Christmas has taken seven years of hard work. The 
progress has not only been slow but often hard to spot. In trying to think through and work through some of the 
themes and issues that get in the way of my effort to function at 
maximum capacity during Christmas, I have done several 
things: 
1. I've tried record keeping, and make annual attempts to 
plan what I want to do and not do, predict what I will do, take 
action, record what happened and evaluate the results. Except 
for the first year of my marital separation, when I coincidentally 
wrote down nothing, I now have seven years of Christmas 
observations and evaluations which have been invaluable for 
seeing how slow the progress has been. 2.

OBSERVATIONS ABOUT 
HOLIDAYS AND FAMILY PROCESS 
1. A family with energy for or interest in only one holiday, 
such as Christmas, is different and brings a different degree of 
emotional intensity to bear on that one holiday than a family 
with energy for and interest in celebrating various holidays 
throughout the year. And both families are different from the 
family with an allergy to or avoidance of celebrating any 
holidays or special occasions. 2. A family with energy for orjnterest in celebrating holidays 
only for children and only when those children are young is a 
different family and brings a different degree of emotional in­
tensity to bear on those children than a family which has energy 
for and interest in participating in and focusing attention on 
holiday celebrations fairly evenly among the various age groups 
and throughout a lifetime. 3. The higher the degree of importance given to an event, the

adults watch with anxious anticipation. Children are discourag­
ed from spending their own money on gifts for each other or for 
the adults. When the children are older, the adults will offer to 
buy something for the children to give, and the child can pay 
them back if he insists, but he is told that it's silly of him not to 
save this money or spend it for something he needs for himself. The adults in such a family play a strange game of unwrapp­
ing presents to themselves in an embarrassed manner, either 
half-heartedly or over-enthusiastically, and this adult exchange 
occurs only after the children have been the center of attention 
until they are dropping from exhaustion. The parents may not 
exchange presents, having taken a pledge to save money. What 
frequently happens is that the wife agrees to give nothing, but 
then slips in a new arm chair or suede coat because she cannot 
stand to hurt her husband's feelings, and besides, in the child­
focused family, the husband is often confused as "one of the

Louise Rauseo, M.S.N. This paper presents an approach to thinking about symptoms 
as physiological process and as family process. At a physiolog­
ical level, certain symptoms appear when balance is lost in the 
autonomic nervous system. At the family level, symptoms ap­
pear as part of a parallel process in which relationship balance is 
lost. Clinical practice with individuals and families exhibiting 
asthma symptoms stimulated some of the thinking reported 
here. In these disorders, there is a loss of homeostasis in the 
autonomic nervous system (ANS) which is in a finely tuned 
balance during times of health. In the family relationship 
system this loss of balance is evident as a parallel process when 
observed taking place over a long period of time. In the physiological process, the hypothalamus is now 
recognized as a regulator of emotional and autonomic reactivi­
ty.

recognized as a regulator of emotional and autonomic reactivi­
ty. This structure has two small areas located close together 
which are largely responsible for the directions of most internal 
physiological responses. One direction of response is termed 
ACTIVATION (A). In general, this direction of response 
moves the organism toward activity and alertness. It includes 
the "fight or flight" mechanism under the control of the sym­
pathetic nervous system (SNS), along with additional factors 
related to brain activity and muscle tone. The opposite direction of response is called RESTO RA TI ON 
(R). RESTORATION involves a generalized response observed 
in the internal responses associated with relaxation, rest, and 
digestion. These are known as parasympathetic nervous system 
(PNS) responses and other associated somatic changes. During times of health, the body maintains a dynamic 
balance between these two directions of response according to 
the demands of the organism and the environment. There is 
also a process described by Gellhom as "tuning" in which the

TRAINING 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. I have been thinking for the past several weeks about what I 
would write in this particular column about training. Sometimes I think our training program at the Family Center is 
pretty good and sometimes I am not so sure. We do a lot of dif­
ferent kinds of teaching and training, but the bulk of our ener­
gies are devoted to the postgraduate training of mental health 
professionals. As I finally sit down to write, it is late on the Sun­
day evening after Thanksgiving. I have a fire going, a com­
fortable chair, and have spent much of the day reading The 
Dancing Wu Li Masters, by Gary Zukav. What an experience! Nothing is more intellectually humbling than theoretical 
physics. Zukav does a masterful job of presenting the ideas, but 
my pitiful mind has been so twisted and bent out of shape by 
particles that are waves and waves that are particles and the 
space-time continuum that I may never recover. What a delight­
ful day! In the last few months, for teaching purposes and because my 
mind has been stretched by the idea, I have been drawing an 
analogy between the development of Newton's theory of 
universal gravitation, a theory that proposed an organizing 
principle to account for the motions of the planets, and the 
development by the early family researchers of a systems way of 
thinking about the human family. Newton gave us cosmos 
(order and harmony) where we had chaos in reference to the 
universe.

text:
Newton gave us cosmos 
(order and harmony) where we had chaos in reference to the 
universe. The theory of emotional systems and counterbalanc­
ing life forces gave us cosmos where we had chaos in reference 
to the activity of the human family. Suddenly we could break 
free of ascribing all kinds of interlocking motives to individuals, 
unconscious or otherwise, and begin to think in terms of emo­
tional fields and patterns. What an absolutely glorious 
discovery. The publication of Newton's theory in 1666 came only 123 
years after Copernicus published his concept of a sun-centered 
universe. What a period in history. Things were again a bit quiet 
again on a conceptual level until 1900 when Max Planck 
discovered that the basic structure of nature is granular and that 
energy comes in packets or quantums. We now talked in terms 
of quantums, and in only a few more years we had Einstein's 
special theory and then the general theory of relativity and the 
theory of quantum mechanics. I envy the excitement people in 
the field experienced with each conceptual breakthrough. These 
were truly "quantum leaps" and all within just a couple of 
decades. Then I look at our own Family Center training programs and 
ask myself what it is we are trying to accomplish. Training can 
become so dull and routine, just like psychotherapy can become 
dull and routine if the therapist lets it. So is the problem in the 
trainee or in the person who trains?

Training can 
become so dull and routine, just like psychotherapy can become 
dull and routine if the therapist lets it. So is the problem in the 
trainee or in the person who trains? I think much of the problem 
is in the trainer. I suppose there were .teachers who, even in the 
1920's, could make physics dull. They could make it dull even 
when theory was evolving around them with such rapidity it 
could make their heads spin. So what was wrong with those 
physics teachers and what is wrong with us when our training 
becomes routine? I suppose the "average" trainee that enters a family training 
program is not particularly interested in theory. Most want to 
 be taught about theory, but few have had the experience of what 
it means to try to think on a theoretical level. Most enter the pro­
gram with the belief that the thinking that leads to theory can be 
done by others, the "pioneers" perhaps, and what they want to 
learn is the applications of the theory, namely, in therapy. So 
what happens to a training program that tries to orient itself 
around what the "average" trainee wants? It gets adept at turn­
ing out technicians. It gets a faculty that starts to experience train­
ing as a chore best relegated to junior faculty.

Are we as part of the family movement sitting on a theoreti­
cal revolution anything less exciting than the theoretical revolu­
tions in physics that centered on Newton and Einstein? I don't 
think we are. The potential gift of the systems paradigm to our 
understanding of living systems is great. I say potential because 
we have not even begun to realize or even imagine the size of this 
gift. But it is so easy for family systems to be seen as just another 
type of psychotherapy and to be categorized with that morass of 
other psychotherapies. To the extent that it is categorized that 
way, it will be of interest mainly to mental health professionals. Mental health professionals, by themselves, are not capable of 
developing family systems theory to its potential. Realization of 
that potential will clearly depend on viable contact with all the 
scientific disciplines. To the extent that our training program 
views family systems as a therapeutic method and not as a new 
theory, it will be working against the development and exten­
sion of the systems paradigm in the natural sciences.

When I originally thought about writing this column, I was 
simply going to discuss the curriculum I have designed this year 
for the second year of our regular postgraduate program. Then 
when I began writing it, I started thinking about all the thinking 
that was behind setting up the program in this particular way. And that is what led me into all this background about the 
development of theory in physics. First of all, when I inherited 
this second year program, I was not looking for more to do. My 
reaction was, this is another chore. Then I thought if I am going to do this, I am going to make it interesting, at least to me. I 
decided that if my thinking was stimulated, then chances are 
that the thinking of my trainees would be stimulated too. Cer­
tainly it seems to work this way in psychotherapy. When the 
family problem becomes a resource for my own learning, the 
family seems to begin almost automatically to learn more about 
itself. I also decided to keep the year focused on theory and not 
worry too much about whether I was teaching people to do 
therapy. The year is going very well. Oh, some of our less 
theoretical heads are dragging a bit, but I am still waiting to see 
what the year will bring. I had no idea about the wealth of ideas 
that abound in the heads of our trainees, once they get free of 
being taught and begin to learn. The program is organized on a 
seminar format, with me assigning most of the reading and 
guiding the discussion.

seminar format, with me assigning most of the reading and 
guiding the discussion. I made it clear at the beginning that I am 
not an expert in all these areas, but that my thinking has been 
stimulated by the reading. The books we are reading include 
Cosmos, by Carl Sagan; Sociobiology, by E. 0. Wilson; Paul 
MacLean's work on the triune brain; Jack Calhoun's mice 
studies; and Why Males Exist: An Evolutionary View of Sex­
uality, by Fred Hapgood. Later in the year Levels of 
Schizaphrenia, by Al Scheflen and some of the more theoretical 
papers from family research will be discussed. Systems thinking is slowly emerging in the natural sciences. There are embryologists in England working toward what they 
call a biological field theory. It would appear that the systems 
thinking that has emerged in the family movement is but a small 
part of what is developing on a larger scale. In most respects I 
think that the systems ideas that have emerged from family 
research are ahead of the other fields. For example, all the 
fabulous new information emerging from research in animal 
behavior appears conceptually imprisoned by old ideas that per­
tain to individual cells and individual organisms. I do think, 
however, that we may be on the verge of a theoretical explosion 
in the natural sciences akin to what happened in physics during 
the first quarter of this century.

TRAINING PROGRAMS AT THE FAMILY CENTER 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. We have been thinking and discussing the training we do 
at the Family Center a lot in recent months. Murray Bowen 
has stimulated this interest, and his ideas on the subject have 
stimulated me to clarify my own. Bowen's main message is that people in training are prob­
ably capable of a better level of systems thinking than the 
program stimulates them to achieve. Trainees have difficulty 
being aware of the various paradigms in psychiatry and the 
degree to which their thinking is influenced by them. People 
can be "taught" that there is a biological, psychological and 
sociological paradigm, but saying they exist and really seeing 
their influence on one's thinking are two different things. Mental health professionals have been thoroughly indoc­
trinated with the psychological paradigm and the individual 
frame of reference. The indoctrination began in their families, 
was reinforced by society, and given the stamp of approval in 
professional school. The commitment to an individual frame­
work is strong enough in everyone that it is easy to miss that 
systems is even a new paradigm. Missing that fact, most of us 
retain our individual psychological orientation and append a 
few of the new systems ideas onto it. So, how does a training 
program help people see paradigms?

Missing that fact, most of us 
retain our individual psychological orientation and append a 
few of the new systems ideas onto it. So, how does a training 
program help people see paradigms? What does a faculty do to 
continue to work on these issues for themselves? In the last few years, my ability to think systems has been 
aided by reading in the sciences. When designing the second 
year of our postgraduate program, I decided that what had 
been useful to me might also be useful to others. As described 
in the last issue of the Family Center Report, I structured a 
seminar that included books such as Sagan's Cosmos, Wilson's 
Sociobiology, Scheflen's Levels of Schizophrenia, and Mac­
Lean's work on the triune brain. I wanted to emphasize man as 
a part of nature and to increase people's awareness of systems 
in nature. I believed that trainees who could think on this 
broader theoretical level would be less likely to fall victim to 
simplistic explanations about the human process. I do not think that most people deep down believe that 
man is a part of nature. Most see nature as something man is 
intertwined with, but still separate from. This view is suppor­
ted by two observations. The first is that man tends to consider 
himself more important than other life forms. I do not think it 
is consistent to see oneself as part of nature and yet more important than everything else in it.

I do not think it 
is consistent to see oneself as part of nature and yet more important than everything else in it. The second observation is 
that man's search for "meaning" in literature, religion, and 
philosophy almost always involves defining himself as special 
and unique and distinct from other living things. A recent National Geographic article and the television 
series Life on Earth seem to support this view. The article 
about Mono Lake in California described the impact of divert­
ing many of the streams and rivers that feed Mono Lake into 
Los Angeles water reservoirs. The lake and life forms that 
depend on it have clearly been placed in jeopardy by this diver­
sion. The lake is regularly visited by huge flocks of migrating 
birds that thrive on the lake's abundant brine shrimp. One of 
these bird species is a type of gull. When the head of the Los 
Angeles Water Authority was interviewed about Mono Lake 
and asked about the growing threat to the gulls he replied, 
"People are more important than a bunch of gulls." 
I suppose an advantage to man in considering himself more 
important than gulls or other creatures is that it provides some 
justification for doing things that threaten their survival. Com­
petition between species is the rule in nature and that is just 
the way nature works.

petition between species is the rule in nature and that is just 
the way nature works. But I think that if man did not try to 
justify his competition with other species on the basis of his 
being more important, he could be more objective about the 
process and live in more harmony with the environment. As it 
is, a staggering number of species are becoming extinct because 
of man's encroachment. So many other aspects of the environ­
ment are deteriorating as well that our present course will 
eventually invite corrective measures by Mother Nature. David Attenborough's series, Life on Earth, is a marvel. He brings together more portraits of nature in thirteen hours 
than one would normally hope to see in an entire lifetime of 
research. The basic point of the series is rather simple. As life 
evolves it gets packaged in a seemingly infinite variety of ways, 
ranging from the simple to the complex. The various packages 
have found their way into just about every nook and cranny 
on the planet, thriving under the polar ice, growing out of 
dead logs or high above urban sprawls. Might we not seem 
quite strange and even a bit chaotic to such orderly creatures 
as the whales and social insects? Do you think it possible that 
the social organization of whales generates less individual dys­
function than is produced by the human herd? I think it is 
possible that the whales are doing better in this regard than we 
are.

are. If this turns out to be the case, could we still consider our­
selves the most "important" species on earth? In addition to seeing man as a part of nature it is impor­

ining nature. it is now fairly easy to see systems in operation. The value of systems thinking in reference to the solar system 
is obvious to everyone, although that was not the case prior to 
Copernicus and Newton. The ability to think systems in refer­
ence to the social behavior of animals is a more recent event. A treatise on insect behavior pubiished only fifty years ago 
was replete with references to individual motivations of the 
organisms. A soldier ant was seen as responding from "a sense 
of duty," for example. In essence, the colony was seen as a 
collection of individuals, each motivated in their own particu­
lar way, without conceptualizing any kind of organizing princi­
ple that influenced and regulated the functioning of the indivi­
dual organisms. In the 1940's, T.C. Schneirla made a significant 
conceptual leap in the µnderstanding of insect colonies as 
superorganisms. The following quote is from an article by 
Girard Piel about Schneirla's ideas: 
The organization of colony behavior does not pre-exist in 
any one type of individual worker, brood, or queen~ nor 
is it additive from these alone.

The social insects have elaborate caste systems and the various 
organisms that comprise a colony have considerable differen­
tiation in structure and function. Yet each organism in the 
colony usually has precisely the same genetic potential. Whether an egg turns into a queen, a worker, or a soldier is 
determined when it begins to develop and is based on the 
particular type of interaction it has with the colony. The bio­
logical system of the superorganism, so to speak, is determining 
the structure and functioning of each of its parts. Systems concepts such as these abound in animal research, 
yet the field is still lacking a true systems theory. It is a little easier to see systems in the social organization 
of smaller organisms. One can look at an ant colony and get 
some sense of how the organisms are responding to and being 
influenced by each other. As was the case with the solar sys­
tem, however, it took someone to point this out before a 
majority could say, "Well, that's obvious." It is not so easy to 
see how a colony of chimpanzees or a family of humans is 
being influenced and regulated by one another. We have been doing this seminar for nearly a year now. Has it helped people toward a better level of systems thinking 
in reference to the human family?

in reference to the human family? Has it helped people be 
more aware of paradigms and the influence of those paradigms 
on their thinking? I'm not sure. The seminar has been enjoy­
able and people certainly have an easier time seeing systems in

seeing systems in the physical world or in the social insects, 
but immediately lose that ability when concentrating on the 
human process. The one dividend reaped from this way of 
approaching knowledge, is that all of us are a little more aware 
of the incredibly narrow perspective mental health profession­
als have on the human process. One of my favorite comments 
on this point was made by Isaac Newton just before his death: 
I do not know what I may appear to the world; but to 
myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the seashore, and diverting myself and now and then finding a 
smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, while 
the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me. UNDERSTANDING ORGANIZATIONS:

On December 7, 1981, the Family Center sponsored its 
second symposium on Bowen family systems theory and its 
application to work organizations. The conference format was 
designed to bring together eight individuals, who in their roles 
as consultants, managers, and employees, have applied their 
knowledge of Bowen theory to the organizations in which they 
live and work. Entitled "A Dialogue: Understanding Organiza­
tions," the conference focused on using a systems perspective 
to conceptualize the functioning of work systems. Emphasis 
was placed on stimulating the audience to apply the theory to 
their own organizational experience rather than on presenting 
specific answers to organizational dilemmas. The presenters included: Dr. Murray Bowen, Mr. Scott 
Meyer, Mr. David Bork, Ms. Kathy Wiseman, Mr. Doug Stern, 
Mr. Tom Gilmore, and Mr. Ray McCain. They were chosen for 
their familiarity with Bowen family systems theory and their 
experiences in a variety of work settings. In spite of the varied backgrounds of the presenters, several 
important themes emerged. The first was the importance of 
identifying and managing triangles and interlocking triangles. Triangling is a process whereby issues between two people 
stretch to include a third when anxiety increases. A second is 
the importance of defining responsibility as a leader, employer, 
or consultant so that functioning is focused and less vulnerable 
to the emotional process.

responsible functioning of those working with him. Dr. Bowen maintains that the knowledge to get through 
emotional and administrative systems is available. Knowledge 
of triangles and interlocking triangles is key. Triangles operate 
in emotional systems predictably. As in a family, triangles 
project problems away from possible solutions and carry the 
process elsewhere in the system, a process which often results 
in symptoms. It is these symptoms that most management 
techniques attempt to remedy. Primary to the optimal functioning of an organization is the 
ability of leaders and employees to take positions on what they 
will and will not be responsible for. If the head of an organiza­
tion can identify his beliefs and define his responsibilities to each important part of the system, the emotional organization 
will function more thoughtfully and less reactively. From this 
lessened emotionality comes the importance of holding em­
ployees accountable for their work, without making excuses 
for inadequate performance. This principle can be summarized 
as taking an "I" position and not letting emotions interfere 
with what is right. Understanding and applying theory is a process for living 
effectively ,vithin emotional fields in organizations. The pro­
cess begins with the head of the organization being the most 
responsible person he can be.

Mr. Doug Stern's experience as a student of family systems 
theory and as an executive in a leading motion picture company 
provided a fascinating example of how to apply the theory to 
a large, complex industry. Mr. Stern viewed the motion picture 
industry as representing a degree of organizational dysfunction 
not unlike the schizophrenic family. In describing this compar­
ison, Mr. Stern delineated several principks adapted from 
Bowen Theory: 
l. Higher reactivity. This is reflected in decisions based on 
relationships rather than objectives. These decisions are 
often influenced by rumors and are often subject to 
sudden change. 2. Triangling. T riangling behavior is evident in unstable 
alliances between producers and executives and in the 
transfer of senior level anxiety to lower levels in the 
organizational chart. Closed cliques and high executive 
turnover also indicate these processes operating to a sig­
nificant degree. 3. Projection process. This process is indicated by feuds 
fought at lower levels that are the result of problems not 
resolved between senior executives. This process is also 
reflected in over-valuing new employees and undervalu­
ing them as their tenure increases. 4. Closed system. A closed system is characterized by inade­
quate relations with the external environment and rigid 
internal boundaries that maintain high emotional inten­
sity. Familiar players tend to move from one organiza­
tion to another with little room for outsiders.

ments than they would be in a presentation about family sys­

we had had at the Human Family Symposium in September 
1978 entitled "The Natural Forces That Resist Change" and 
suggested we show a videotape of that panel to the AAP. Dr. Bowen agreed and Andrea Maloney-Schara went to work get­
ting the tape edited into presentable form. She did a beautiful 
job. I began the workshop with a brief review of how the 
Human Family Symposium had come into being and described 
the thinking behind having a panel on the subject of resistance 
to change.

A member of the audience asked Bowen if 
 he thought the term "biopsychosocial" was a useful step toward 
integration. Bowen did not think the term would contribute 
very much, recalling the excitement in the l 940's over the 
term "psychosomatic." The term was an effort to wed the 
psyche and the soma, but Bowen did not think that the thirty­
five years since the introduction of the term had produced 
much in the way of theoretical integration of the two domains. Bowen also discussed some of his reasons for wanting to 
remain connected to psychiatry and medicine. He thought 
schizophrenia would remain the province of psychiatry into 
the foreseeable future and believed it critically important that 
family thinking not lose its involvement with schizophrenia. Many mental health professionals still compartmentalize emo­
tional illness. Diagnostic categories such as schizophrenia, 
manic-depressive, and organic brain syndrome are viewed as 
primarily biologically-based problems that belong in the psy­
chiatric domain. The neuroses and other less intense emotional 
problems are viewed as different entities, more as problems in 
living, that are best managed by the non-medical mental health 
disciplines. This way of thinking sees family as more relevant 
to these less intense problems. This split is more profound than 
simply a choice of the most appropriate therapeutic techniques. The split implies that family theory is not especially relevant

nation, and encouragement to those with potential problems 
to take action.) 
The Biofeedback Program staffed the learning center, and 
offered participants the opportunity to observe physiological 
indicators of stress such as sweat response and peripheral skin 
temperature. Participants could observe changes in these phy­
siological responses as they tried to relax or tried to think 
stressful thoughts. As well as introducing ways to learn about 
physiological responses to stress, the Georgetown Biofeedback 
staff explained the applications of biofeedback and relaxation 
for treating physical disorders such as hypertension, headaches 
and ulcers, for treating emotional responses such as generalized 
anxiety, depression and phobias and for treating behavioral 
indicators of anxiety such as drinking, overeating and smoking.

Introduction 
It is a basic assumption of the Bowen Theory that to the 
degree one emotionally cuts off from past family relationships, 
one shall over-invest in present relationships. Although this 
process has been amply documented in clinical work and family 
therapists' work with their own families, it has not yet been 
applied to the ways one handles mentors-guides, teachers and 
coaches who were once emotionally significant. I have come to 
believe that an analogous process does occur with past mentors, 
making one especially vulnerable to the extremes of disciple­
ship, in which an enormous amount of effort is invested in 
gaining the approval of a present mentor. This paper describes

with past mentors. The first section of the paper describes

mentors during the last eighteen months. Part I: Facts Influencing the Fusing Cutting-Off Process 
My father was the youngest in a very large family, and my 
mother was the only child of the five born to her parents to 
live beyond five years old. My parents married secretly in a 
mixed marriage that was only revealed to their families of ori­
gin when mother was pregnant for the first time with my twin 
brother and me.

My parents married secretly in a 
mixed marriage that was only revealed to their families of ori­
gin when mother was pregnant for the first time with my twin 
brother and me. As a second-born twin, I have tended to func­
tion as a younger brother of a brother, a position that makes 
one especially vulnerable to the extremes of discipleship. But 
as a twin, I am also an oldest since our births were followed by 
a younger brother and two younger sisters. Consequently, I 
also tend to move as a middle child and as an older brother of 
a brother and sisters. Sharing a mixed Jewish and Irish-Catholic 
heritage, I was acutely aware of being different from the 
Protestant kids with whom I socialized through most of grade 
school and high school. For thirteen years, I was a member of 
a religious community and for five and one-half years an 
ordained priest. My clinical master's degree is in pastoral psy­
chology, which makes my credentials as a mental health profes­
sional a bit unusual, and for some, questionable. Early in my work on changing self within my family, it 
became very clear that my basic way of handling emotionality 
was to distance through geographical cut-off whenever possible. The intensity of the cut-off would parallel an intense invest­
ment in the educational institution or group that I became 
part of. In an attempt to gain what I perceived as qualities 
lacking in self I fused with these institutions and those super­
vising my work there.

When I first began thinking of this project, I decided to 
get in touch with all those who influenced me as a clinician. This included three supervisors and a Jungian analyst with 
whom I worked for a few months. It soon became apparent 
that what I believe clinically is rooted in my fundamental 
beliefs about life, and I quickly decided to include those who 
influenced my beliefs about ultimate concerns: life and death, 
God and the Church. I then decided to include those who had 
been important to me while I was in the religious community, 
especially a former superior with whom there had been a total 
cut-off after I received permission to marry in the Church.

hood? Is the female of the species inherently better able to 
cope with all types of challenges?

Moreland, Lee Keenan, and Priscilla Friesen. This panel, en­
titled, "The Unmarried Female in Family and Society," addres­
sed both societal factors and family factors that lead to being 
an unmarried female. Each participant presented a case study 
with specific clinical details and principles about this phenom­
enon. The panel defined an unmarried female as one who has 
not maintained significant contact with a male for a prolonged 
period of time. Hence, individuals with multiple marriages of 
short duration would be in fact defined as unmarried females. One panelist offered the idea that it may be only in degree 
that all females are unmarried. The panel members also made 
comparisons about various members of the animal kingdom 
and the human family regarding the kind of mating and attach­
ments they develop. In general the panelists thought that un­
married females function in service of their own mothers and 
families in a way that makes attachment to a male significantly 
more difficult than for those females who remain married.

Department of Psychiatry 
Georgetown University School of Medicine 
Vol. 4, No. 2 
SUBJECTIVITY, HOMO SAPIENS 
AND SCIENCE 
Murray Bowen, M. D. Early in my psychiatric career, I wondered why psychiatry 
was not a real science, instead of a pseudo-science governed by 
a "scientific method." I had no presumption about ever making 
a contribution in such a complex field. I was merely seeking 
clarification for myself. Now, after almost forty years I am 
pleased with my life. To my own satisfaction, I think I know 
one way toward a major new theory about adjustment. The 
outcome may be a century away. The current situation is more 
chaotic than before. This might have been better predicted. I 
believe human behavior will eventually become a science. The 
major barrier appears to be subjectivity. It is part of human 
experience. It cannot be measured or verified. When subjecti­
vity creeps into theoretical postulations, the result is more 
chaotic and less scientific. I will attempt to present a few ideas 
about the field. In the twentieth century, psychiatric thinking has been 
based primarily on psychoanalytic theory. It considers the 
human as unique and different from other forms of life. The 
contributions from psychoanalysis have been tremendous, but 
it has never moved toward becoming an accepted science. I 
believe that has been blocked by basic formulations from liter­
ature, philosophy, mythology, and the arts. None of these 
disciplines came from scientific facts.

beings. Anything generated in the human brain is vulnerable to 
feeling contamination, unless some discipline can insure reason­
able objectivity. Freud was aware of the deficiencies in his 
theory but his followers were not. They tended to treat his 
writings as eternal truths. Most people are not aware of the 
great difference between truth and fact. Truth is subjective. Fact is scientific. Practitioners are rarely aware of the small 
points and discipline that goes into theory or science. Psychia­
tric practice and research produced volumes of subjectivity. It 
could not pass muster in serious research. Psychologists came 
into the field to help with research. They developed an ex­
tremely complex scientific method designed to handle the sub­
jectivity in a structured scientific way. They hoped it might 
raise the entire field to the status of a science. Debates about 
this have continued for decades. I do not believe human beha­
vior can become a science as long as we use the scientific 
method. In the 1940's teachers and experts could not answer speci­
fic questions about theory. I sought answers from the literature. I was on the library committee with easy access to past and FALL 1982

I sought answers from the literature. I was on the library committee with easy access to past and FALL 1982 
present writings. My quest led through science, psychiatry, 
psychoanalysis, psychology, sociology, anthropology, ethology, 
evolution, astronomy, philosophy, mythology, physics, mathe­
matics, biology, religion, and all the disciplines about human 
behavior. The basic goal was common denominators on which 
the disciplines were based. My reading eventually led to the notion of the human as 
a phylogenetic development from the lower forms of life. I 
believed it would bring us closer to science if we could see the 
human as related to all other living things. It is a scientific fact 
the earth is part of the larger universe; that the earth is made 
up of all kinds of inorganic elements that behave according to 
scientific principle; and the earth abounds in all kinds of life 
that came from the primordial ooze. Life is generally divided 
into plant life and animal life, both tied to the earth and both 
intimately interlinked. All life reproduces in clearly defined 
cycles, changing a little with each cycle. The animal world is 
mobile and it includes forms that extend from bacteria and 
other one cell forms, to the complexity of homo sapiens at the 
other extreme. The animal world has some kind of a nervous 
system that operates either by some undefined chemical 
mechanism or through a conglomerate of nervous tissue and 
chemical reaction.

The animal world has some kind of a nervous 
system that operates either by some undefined chemical 
mechanism or through a conglomerate of nervous tissue and 
chemical reaction. In its phylogenetic development, the nervous 
system proceeds through a series of orderly steps from the 
lower animals to the marvelous brain of homo sapiens, about 
which we know too little. In addition to STRUCTURE, the brain includes numerous 
FUNCTIONS that go back to instincts and are not clearly asso­
ciated with any structure. Fairly late in phylogeny, the human 
developed the ability to stand upright, and to think, reflect, 
and reason. This is not meant to be specific for anatomy and 
physiology. It is mentioned only for comparative reasons. Slowly the human developed a spoken language, cultures, phi­
losophies, religions, mathematics, literature, the arts, and a 
host of other functions more subjective than factual. Science 
had to have a beginning. Along the way, man learned to figure 
out the nature of the universe, the properties of the earth on 
which he lived, and other subjects that had to do with pure 
science. Science worked well as long as he focused on the uni­
verse and the inanimate world. It worked less well when he 
focused on animal forms. It was least effective when he focused 
on himself. Terms developed for the pure sciences are blurred 
when applied to other fields. The literature and dictionaries 
are not clear about things such as science and theory.

could fade when other thoughts or emotion intervened. The

different way of thinking. Over time, they could SEE too. The 
ability to see was based on their level of maturity and not their

therapy was a superficial manifestation and not a primary

quite different. Theory was very important to me. I had spent years work­

is a verifiable fact, but what he says is not a fact." Observers 
were not permitted to use interpretations or "loaded" words 
such as "depressed" in observations. Observations were based 
on fact, as far as discipline could go. Predictable action that 
repeated over and over, in all the families, eventually found 
their way into concepts. Everything was based on FACTS as 
far as was possible. Critics were fast to point out subjectivity 
in observer situations. Critics suggested movies as more objec­

observers can watch a movie and emerge with a spectrum of 
different observations based more on the information in the 
brain of the observer than the actual situation. A trained and 
disciplined observer can be more accurate than the average less 
disciplined observer. To my critics I admitted the fallacies and 
merely said, "We are aware of the problem and are doing our 
best to deal with it." The whole research stands on that effort. I believe we did a good job. After it was possible to see the potential for theory in the 
research, a major goal was to package the observations as accu­
rately as possible and preserve the clues for future research.

similar to medicine in the late nineteenth century when a few 
doctors with a hospital could start new medical schools, which 
produced poorly trained doctors in volume. In the I 915 period 
the Flexner Committee closed the poor schools and required 
others to meet standards. The family therapy movement had 
no controls beyond a few self imposed controls and those are 
questionable. The rush to family therapy continues, as a thing 
unto itself, responding more to the popularity and private 
practice income, than to the level of professionalism in the 
therapists. The family therapy rush is seen more as a phenomenon in 
society than the action of any one person or group of people. The family idea is one of the most significant contributions in 
this century. The need was there, social regression had increased, 
societal anxiety was higher, and new people rushed in to fill the 
gap. I think the whole thing could have been better predicted. The whole thing has the marks of a regression which will run 
its course and eventually settle down to a period of societal

accepted science that can grow and develop with all the scien­

AND EVOLUTIONARY THEORY 
Michael E. Kerr, M. D. Twenty-five years of family research has clearly established 
the importance of viewing the family as an entity in its own 
right. The family could not be adequately understood by some 
extension of the concepts from individual theory. Something 
new was required. Those who could made the break from indi­
vidual theory were able to see the family as a system, as an 
emotional unit, and not just as a collection of individuals. Family research had defined an order to human interaction 
that was previously unknown. One of the most important contributions of family research 
may be that it has provided a way of thinking about a living 
system, namely the family, that has application beyond the 
family itself.

One of the most important contributions of family research 
may be that it has provided a way of thinking about a living 
system, namely the family, that has application beyond the 
family itself. The order that characterizes a family system is 
but a small segment of the order that characterizes all of na­
ture. Things in nature fit together and our present theories 
about nature have barely begun to help us comprehend this fit. Darwin contributed immensely to our understanding, but we 
remain a long way from any comprehensive understanding of 
the way nature is ordered. From the windows of a spacecraft we can see The Whole 
Earth, but our "mastery" of natural law has proceeded no 
further than the group of some elementary laws of physics. Compared with the unchartered, infinitely more intricate 
laws of biology and behavior that govern the human spirit, 
this mastery is trivial, a mere conjurer's trick. The mastery 
of the physical law can no longer save us while we are 
grounded in a tangle of ignorance of the natural laws that 
govern our behavior. -Melvin Kanner 
Recently I have been learning more about whales, dolphins, 
and insects that look like twigs. I have been trying to under­
stand existing theory in evolutionary biology and to learn 
more of the facts that theory has difficulty accounting for.

text:
I have been trying to under­
stand existing theory in evolutionary biology and to learn 
more of the facts that theory has difficulty accounting for. Learning about how land and sea mammals have remained the 
same and also have developed differences over the long course 
of their evolution has given me more appreciation of some of 
the unanswered questions about the natural forces that guide 
evolution. Whales are among that group of mammals that live 
in the sea, although their evolutionary ancestors are thought to 
have lived on land. Sea mammals are in many ways quite simi­
lar to land mammals and the new adaptations they have made 
to life in the sea appear to be orderly modifications of the 
structures and functions of land mammals. What are the forces 
that keep so many things the same and simultaneously permit 
and foster change? Someone might answer, "Oh, that's genetics 
and environment." But it appears that genetics and environ­
ment is not a very complete answer. Current estimates are that it has been over fifty million 
years since the sea and land mammals parted evolutionary 
company. What are some of the changes that have and have 
not occurred over that span of time? The vertebral column of 
the whale has undergone some interesting modifications that 
render it more adaptive to life in the sea. The whale's spine is 
much more flexible than that of most land mammals, an obvi­
ous aid to efficient swimming.

The whale's spine is 
much more flexible than that of most land mammals, an obvi­
ous aid to efficient swimming. This flexibility derives from an 
increased number and enlargement of the soft discs between 
the vertebrae. What is particularly impressive is how this modi­
fication in the spine has remained well integrated into the total 
3 
 "plan" of the organism. Detroit automakers could not put 
smaller and less powerful fuel-efficient engines in their cars 
without also reducing the total weight of the car. By the same 
token the vertebral column of a whale could not be altered 
without attention to all the other structures with which it is 
closely integrated. Evolution must keep the "master-plan" of 
the organism in mind. Current theory does not help us much 
in understanding how this is regulated. The patterns of social organization in sea mammals and 
the communication systems that serve to maintain those pat­
terns is another intriguing area of study. Because sea mammals 
live in such a significantly different environment than land 
mammals, one might expect changes both in their social organ­
ization and in the ways they communicate. It appears, how­
ever, that social organization has remained much the same in 
terms of the range and distribution of possible types of organi­
zation, while the communication systems have undergone 
some interesting adaptations.

Like the land mammals, sea 
mammals may live in large, tightly knit groups which demon­
strate a highly sophisticated level of cooperation. Examples are 
the killer whales and the dolphins. Sea mammals may also live 
a more anti-social existence. The fin-back whales who are close­
ly associated only for mating and maternal care of the young 
are such an example. Like the land mammals, the organization 
of a given species of sea mammals may cycle or change depend­
ing on the state of the environment and/or the mating recep­
tiveness of the females. Dominance hierarchies have been 
demonstrated in both land and sea mammals. When it comes 
to communications systems, however, the sea mammals have 
made some fascinating adaptations, and whales provide one of 
the best illustrations. The overall adaptation in communication has involved 
well-integrated changes in several bodily systems and, again, 
each change fits smoothly into the total plan of the organism 
and into the functioning of the social group. Darwin puzzled 
over how the various evolutionary changes in an organism 
could be so well meshed with one another. The evolution of 
such a complex structure as the eye provides a good example. Did the various parts of the eye evolve independently and then 
just happen to fit together or are there some yet to be defined 
organizing principles that orchestrate the process and make the 
fit of things more understandable?

The evolution of the highly 
complex system of communication in whales poses no less dif­
ficult questions than those posed by the evolution of the eye. Whales have evolved to rely very little on a sense of smell 
or sight to "read" their environment and to know what their 
fellow whales are doing. They do rely on sound waves. Based 
on their ability to send, receive and interpret these sound 
waves, they can assess the state of their environment and com­
municate with other whales with extraordinary precision. To 
accomplish this, whales' ears have had to develop a kind of 
"independent suspension." When we humans are under-water, 
we have a difficult time discriminating the source of sounds. Regardless of which ear picks up the sound first, the sound 
waves quickly trigger vibration in the entire skull, not allowing 
the human to separate reception of its two ears. Whale ears 
have undergone a number of important changes including being 
surrounded by air-filled cavities which reestablish separate 
function and allow directional interpretation by the brain. Integrated with these changes in the ears are remarkable chan­
ges in the whale brain that improve its ability to receive and 
interpret sound. Structurally the whale's cerebral cortex is 
strikingly similar to that of man, although it is highly special-
4 ized for sound.

Structurally the whale's cerebral cortex is 
strikingly similar to that of man, although it is highly special-
4 ized for sound. It is as if language has been a critical stimulus 
for the development of the human cerebral cortex and sound 
has served a similar function in the evolution of the whale 
brain. And what of the insects that have evolved to look just like 
twigs? What are the forces that guided the evolution of this 
particular insect and made it far less vulnerable to predators? Nature is just full of these perfect copies and perfect fits that 
enhance adaptiveness. Awareness of them helps us to recognize 
that evolution is a beautifully orchestrated orderly process and 
yet, while we know evolution has occurred and is occurring, 
our knowledge about how it occurs is limited. It was Charles Darwin who established evolution as a fact, 
and proposed the process of natural selection as the primary 
force shaping evolutionary change. Darwin observed that in 
nature parents tended to produce more offspring than neces­
sary for replacement and that these offspring were not all 
exactly the same. He assumed that these differences in the off­
spring rendered some more adaptive to their environment than 
others and that these better adapted ones had an increased 
chance of surviving and reproducing, and passing their particu­
lar traits onto yet another generation.

In this way, nature would 
be "selecting" the better adapted ones and shaping the direc­
tion of evolutionary change. While Darwin considered natural selection the primary

cell nucleus, is responsible for directing the orderly series of 
cleavages that lead to the blastula stage. The genes on the chro­

thinking about embryogenesis does not adequately explain the 
phenomenon, and argues instead for what he calls a "field 
treatment" of organism development. Rather than thinking

determine where cleavage planes develop, and of shifts in ener­

ideas from mathematics he attempts to explain why the various 
planes of cleavage occur where they do as the egg develops. Goodwin's ideas are complex and I have little capacity to 
evaluate their validity. What intrigues me, though, is that he is 
trying to develop a new way of thinking about organisms.

Goodwin's ideas are complex and I have little capacity to 
evaluate their validity. What intrigues me, though, is that he is 
trying to develop a new way of thinking about organisms. He 
is trying to develop concepts that pertain to the organism as a 
whole rather than falling back on the genetic program as the 
cause for what happens. My interpretation of his ideas is that 
he is trying to view the organism as a unit and not just as a col­
lection of cells, each cell being guided by its genes. While it 
may seem obvious that it is important to be able to view a bio­
logical organism as a unit, there is no theory currently available 
that lends itself to that broader view. To quote Goodwin: 
"The organism as a real entity, existing in its own right, 
has virtually no place in contemporary biological theory. " 
The controlling or causal aspect of the genetic program 
permeates much of scientific thinking about living things. Try­
ing to think in structural terms requires letting go of the causal 
aspect of the genetic program and viewing the organism as a 
system. If the organism can be legitimately thought of as a sys­
tem of relationships, governed by organizing principles or laws, 
then the genetic apparatus can be thought of as occupying a 
functioning position in the system. The genes would both reg­
ulate and be regulated by the organism. Now I am aware that it has almost become fashionable 
today to apply the word "systems" to all kinds of things.

reminiscent of what the early family researchers were trying to

found most interesting. When most of us think about evolu­

it is equally important to keep in mind that for generations 
after generations, organisms remain mostly the same. Again, 
current theory assigns responsibility for this stability of organ­

that the organizing principles that pertain to the organism as a 
whole play an important role in stability as well as in change. To illustrate this point, Goodwin describes an extremely 
thought-provoking experiment done with Drosophila, the fruit 
fly. There is a gene "eyeless" in Drosophila whose presence 
results in failures of eye development. This "eyeless" gene is 
recessive, so a fruit fly would have to inherit two such genes, 
one from the male parent and one from the female parent, for 
the failure in eye development to occur. Failure of eye develop­
ment implies that that fly is homozygous recessive for the 
"eyeless" genes and therefore has no dominant genes for eye 
development. One would normally expect then, that if fruit 
flies who have experienced failures in eye development are 
mated, all of their offspring would also experience such fail­
ures. Well, in fact this holds true for only a few generations, 
after which time flies with normal eyes begin reappearing!

mal eyes, direct descendants of homozygous recessive parents 
without eyes, can be demonstrated through standard back­

Mendelian genetic theory, adherents to that theory do propose 
possible explanations for why they believe it really is not 
inconsistent with classical theory. Furthermore, Goodwin con­
cedes that the empirical findings of classical genetics are, for 
the most part, consistent with the concept of the genetic pro­

that just because many empirical results are consistent with a 
model does not mean they necessitate that particular model to 
explain them. A majority of empirical observations fit with 
Ptolemy's model of the solar system, but not all the facts fit it. It was these things that did not quite fit which presumably 
stimulated people like Copernicus and Newton to develop a 
much broader and more comprehensive conceptual model. Goodwin suggests that there are enough Drosophila- like exper­

genes as a central directing agency determining the stability of

residing in the cell nucleus. Now let's extend structural thinking into the realm of 
evolutionary change. As mentioned earlier, prevailing evolu­
tionary theory ascribes a central role to random genetic chan­
ges, mutations and recombinations, to provide the new forms 
on which the forces of natural selection can then act. For 
some years this way of thinking about evolutionary process 
has struck me and an increasing number of others as somewhat 
haphazard. Not only would the genetic mutation have to lead 
to a change in the organism's form and/or function that ren­
dered it more adaptive to its environment, but it would also 
have to be sufficiently constrained that the change would be 
compatible with the overall plan of the organism. If this were 
not the case, the "new" organism would die in utero or soon 
5

genetic changes certainly occur, their effect on the organism 
would be determined by broader principles or forces that gov­
ern the organism as a whole. Another way of saying this is that 
the "effect" of a given "cause" would be determined by the 
system in which it is occurring. The idea of "organizing principles" and "forces" sounds a 
bit vague, but that is because no one has yet defined what they 
are.

similar body forms. The explanation given was the conven­

that, on the basis of natural selection, their evolutionary paths 
have converged to produce quite similar forms. This conven­
tional explanation certainly could be adequate for explaining 
what has happened, but possibly it is an incomplete model. To expand the natural selection model, let's go back to 
what I was saying earlier about thinking of organisms as law­
governed systems that can be stimulated toward change through 
the effects of genetic mutations and/or environmental pres­
sures. If we think of organisms in this way, then it seems likely 
that organisms would evolve as systems as opposed to the var­
ious parts of an organism evolving relatively independently of 
one another. Such an idea was first proposed in 1917 by 
D'Arcy Thompson. Goodwin proposes that not only do organ­
isms evolve as systems, but that these systems evolve through 
orderly states of transformation. The "states of transforma­
tion," he theorizes, are governed by the relatively small number 
of generative rules or laws mentioned in his earlier quote.

of generative rules or laws mentioned in his earlier quote. This 
way of thinking would not eliminate natural selection as an 
important force in evolutionary change; it only proposes that 
there is an equally important non-random process occurring 
within organisms that influences the outcome. That such unre­
lated species as the shark and the whale could converge so 
much in their evolutionary pathways, would be related not 
only to experiencing similar selection pressures, but also to the 
organism being governed by internal principles of change or 
transformation that shape the course of its evolution. Another implication of the idea of organisms evolving as 
rule-governed systems takes us back to our earlier discussion 
of the whale. If the whale has evolved as a system, then the 
whale's ability to produce sounds, the capacity of its ears to 
accurately receive sounds, and the capability of its brain to 
interpret sounds, would not be thought of as having occurred 
6 independently. A systems view of the organism would imply 
that each inclination toward change in one part of the system 
would be fostered or dampened by the activity of the system 
as a whole. In addition, each inclination toward change in one 
part of the system would be a stimulus for adaptations in other 
parts of the system.

organism is a part also evolves as a system. Not only would the

is dependent on "genetic" change, and here I am using the 
word "genetic" in the conventional way. If the conventional 
genetic view is correct, how could different ways of respond­

by an animal in its lifetime, influence its genetic program and

to influence the functioning of its genes. We have known for 
some time that even "simple" organisms can learn from exper­

on its experiences. Eric Kandel at Columbia has done some fas­

concluded that learning is a universal feature of nervous sys­

involves changes in the amounts of neurotransmitters released 
at synapses. Furthermore, he suggests that because changes in 
the structure and function of synapses produced by learning 
can be enduring, and are thought to require new protein syn­

expresszon. Were you aware that trees can "learn?" The thickness of a 
tree's trunk is, in part, regulated by the tree's experiences bend­
ing in the wind. I assume the process is similar to the thickness 
of the skin on the bottom of the foot being regulated by the 
foot's repeated experiences with the terrain on which it walks. Feet and trees adapt in this way.

leaves at the top of many trees are remarkably different in

been found that the shape of leaves at the top of the tree is 
much more efficient for getting rid of excess heat than the 
shape of those at the bottom. The obvious adaptive value of 
this is that leaves near the top of trees in fairly dense forests 
are exposed to much more sunlight than those near the bottom 
and require, therefore, a system for cooling themselves to avoid 
damage. It can probably be assumed that the genetic makeup 
or genetic potential of all the leaves on the tree is the same and 
that the variation in leaf shapes would reflect differences in 
which genes are expressed. The obvious question, then, is what 
 regulates this gene expression. I think it is possible, although I 
do not know that it has been established, that the shape of the 
leaf is regulated by the experiences it is having interacting with 
environmental forces as it is developing. Thinking of it this 
way would be suggesting that developing leaves "learn" in the 
same way developing trees learn how thick their trunks need 
to be. The other possibility, of course, is that this information 
is all programmed into the tree's genes before it even starts 
growing and, irrespective of its experiences as it grows, the tree

very little knowledge about how the systems that surround the

as relatively unimportant probably is due to the difficulty of 
studying larger systems, and perhaps also due to the view that 
the genes are somehow in charge and direct the course of events. The thinking appears to be that if we learn enough about the 
genes and how they work, we will eventually have the solutions 
to most of our biological puzzles. Thus far, however, it has not 
worked out this way in cancer research. We have learned a very 
great deal about the mechanics of cancer cells, but, in spite of

forces that drive, regulate, and determine the emergence of 
cancer cells. The learning experiments and observations that I have

such exact balance. It is these processes of regulation that pre­

plasm, and within the environment external to the cell, that I 
presently conceive of as the system or the organizing principles

teaching and culture. But, obviously, an evolutionary theory 
would have to apply equally well to simple one-celled organ­

say it must be passed on through the genes.

mals would have experienced a chance genetic mutation that 
resulted in a degree of enlargement and hardening of the 
middle toe of at least some of their offspring, These offspring 
would have been a little faster because of the change, more

would have favored retention of this gene in the population.

toward a hoof. Perhaps further favorable mutations would be 
required to bring the process to its present state. An alternative to the above described conventional expla­
nation would be the role of functioning in the evolution of the 
zebra hoof. As the three-toed zebra's evolutionary ancestor 
began living in the open and spent much more of its time run­
ning, it made increasing functional demands on its feet, parti­
cularly the more central and forward portions. Now the feet of 
some of these early pioneer runners may have shown some 
adaptive responses within their lifetime, responses drawn from 
their existing range. An example might be some thickening of 
the skin in areas experiencing the greatest pressure. This would 
not mean that their offspring would necessarily be born with 
this thickening; more than likely they would be born with no 
noticeable changes. But the speculation is that they are born 
with some kind of record of at least some of the previous gen­
erations' experiences in this regard. If the zebra ancestors con­
tinued to live on the plains and their experiences in adapting 
were continually reenforced in a particular direction, then an 
eventual shift in the range of response may occur. In this in­
stance it may mean that after ten or twenty or fifty genera­
tions, offspring would begin appearing who demonstrated visi­
ble changes in their middle-toe toward hypertrophy.

In this in­

tions, offspring would begin appearing who demonstrated visi­
ble changes in their middle-toe toward hypertrophy. Can we 
call this "evolutionary hypertrophy" and consider it a slowed 
version of a physiological process that, within a narrower range, 
can occur within an animal's lifetime? Meanwhile, the two 
lateral toes are beginning to show signs of "evolutionary disuse 
atrophy." As the changes in the feet are evolving, this would 
create pressures for change in other parts of the system as well, 
for example, the particular configuration of the leg muscles. Natural selection would continue to play an important role in 
all this in that it seems likely that not all the offspring of a 
given generation would be equally capable of learning and 
adapting and not all offspring would occupy the same position 
in the social group. I am assuming that position in the social 
group would also influence learning opportunities. There are 
numerous other examples in nature that are consistent with 
the idea of an important role for functioning in the learning 
that may shape evolutionary change. The absence of eyes in 
animals who live out their lives in the dark; the streamlining of 
the fish that live in the sea; the vestigial pelvic girdle and hind 
limbs of the whale (a mammal who has not walked for over 
fifty million years) and, of course, the neck of the giraffe.

The 
collective diversity of evolutionary adaptations made by all life 
on earth can appear overwhelming; but there is also a basic 
simplicity to all of it. In one sense, nothing in evolution is real­
ly new; the processes underlying all the changes are very old 
indeed. It's like a symphony, with variations on basic themes 
played out over and over again. Some variations are variations 
of variations, achieving such complexity that it is easy to lose 
sight of commonality with the rest. The tusks of a walrus are 
"nothing more" than exaggerated canines from the upper jaw. Whale skin consists of the same three basic layers as human 
skin. The ear canal of some whales has a conical plug thought 
to function as a sound transmitter. What is it made of? Kera­
tin, the same substance we make everyday to cover our bodies. No, humans do not lay eggs, but in terms of cellular and phy­
siological processes the developing chick embryo and human 
fetus are more similar than different. Even when quite radical 
 innovations are made by a species, it does not mean that the 
capacity to do it the "old way" has been completely lost. Kol­
lar and Fisher have been able to produce four complete teeth, 
derived substantially from the embryonic tissue of a chicken!

WHAT IS THEORY? WHAT IS SCIENCE? The Third Thursday Professional Meeting has a long history 
of dedication to the refinement and expansion of knowledge 
and theory. In July, 1983, four members of the Family Center 
faculty presented short papers addressing the general question, 
"What is science and what is theory." Although each of the 
papers was relatively simple, and by itself incomplete, the 
evening as a whole illuminated the difficulties and struggles 
involved in an effort to study the human. The general response 
to the papers suggested that they were helpful to others inter­
ested in science and the study of human functioning. Conse­
quently they will be presented in the Family Center Report 
over the next two issues. THEORY AND SCIENCE 
Daniel V. Papero 
Science is the study of "starstuff." Whatever starstuff is, 
everything that exists is composed of it. On a very basic level 
all sciences study starstuff, the substances and processes of the 
universe. The scientific study of the human is but another var­
iant of the study of starstuff. A common denominator among life forms is the ability to 
perceive and respond to stimuli. S~ch ability to respond is a 
basic distinction between life and non-life. The human is fully 
capable of perceiving and responding -to the cycles of nature 
and the presence or absence of other living forms.

The human is fully 
capable of perceiving and responding -to the cycles of nature 
and the presence or absence of other living forms. In addition, 
the human appears to have the capacity to observe the response 
of self to the world and of other life forms to self. Observation 
is coupled with the ability to reflect about the act of observa­
tion as well as what has been observed. All disciplined ways of thinking are based on the capacity 
for observation and reflection. Science, like religion or philo­
sophy, is first and foremost a disciplined way of thinking. How 
science regulates thinking sets it apart from other disciplines of 
thought. Science as a way of thinking attempts to control the 
influence of imagination in describing and explaining the natu­
ral world. The product of science is knowledge, which is always 
considered imperfect. The degree of imperfection is seen as 
depending, in large measure, on how well imagination has been 
controlled and examined during the process of scientific think­
ing. The accuracy of observation is always open to question. Science essentially questions the process of observation. It FALL1983 
attempts, by means of various checks and balances, to guaran­
tee an accurate description of what has been observed. The 
process of scientific observation attempts to eliminate the in­
fluence of the observer's biases. Science is concerned primarily 
with accurate observation of what exists.

text:
The 
process of scientific observation attempts to eliminate the in­
fluence of the observer's biases. Science is concerned primarily 
with accurate observation of what exists. It is less concerned, 
at least in terms of observation, with whether a phenomenon is 
right or wrong, good or evil. Facts are the output of scientific 
observation. The observer must arrive at an operational defini­
tion of fact to be adhered to in reporting what has been ob­
served. Imaginative thought in science attempts to connect facts. Such an effort to define connections, at least in science, must 
address all known facts about a phenomenon. The more facts 
are considered selectively, the further the process moves away 
from science. The rigorous inclusion of all known facts in the 
thinking process is an important hallmark of science. The initial thinking which follows observation would best 
be called an idea or notion. The process of science, then, at­
tempts to challenge the accuracy of such an idea or notion 
with further observation and, if possible, new facts. Science 
always moves back to the observational position in the natural 
world. The process of taking an idea back to the world for 
observation is simple. The idea should explain any observed 
facts. The discrepancy between what the idea leads one to 
expect and what is actually the case is of great importance. Assuming that observation is as accurate as possible, such dis­
crepancy is the basis for further refinement of thought.

text:
Assuming that observation is as accurate as possible, such dis­
crepancy is the basis for further refinement of thought. With­
out that discrepancy, there is no way of taking that idea and 
moving beyond it. When one finds a discrepancy, it is possible 
to rework imaginative thought, to create a new notion. Once 
the idea has been further refined, the process again returns to 
observation. In this way the process of science cycles from the 
idea to the observed world and back to thinking, until thinking 
and observations are in accord. When no further unexplainable 
discrepancy remains between thinking and observation, the 
idea can be called a concept. Several concepts can be formula­
ted together to account for various aspects of a phenomenon. When such concepts are sufficient to explain what can be 
observed about a whole, it is reasonable to call that collection 
of concepts a theory. The use of the term theory only occurs 
after a long process of refinement. A well constructed theory 
highlights the imperfection of knowledge. It provides a frame­
work against which discrepancy can be noted. Theory, there­
fore, is never final. It is merely the best current statement of 
refined imaginative thought and fact. As such, it always re­
mains open to further refinement.

reading and learning. Such thinking makes learning a luxury. Those of you who were at the Symposium in the fall 
know of the focus there on "what is science." This focus, the

uate program this year, and other foci have led me to some

vels found in Northern Europe. In an empirical monograph, 
Rev. Buckland attributed the cave deposits and external gravels 
to a single flood. In fact, they were produced by several epi­
sodes of glaciation which he had misinterpreted.

text:
When my head is working well, family systems theory 
provides a broad base from which to take on the ongoing chal­
lenge of thinking through important life events and pheno­
mena. One of the fascinating characteristics about this theory 
is that while it allows one to view the world as broadly as one 
is capable, at the same time it also allows one to zoom into a 
more narrow field or phenomenon. Like some other professions, nurses are in a position of 
dealing with "the profession," each other, and people who are 
either interested or in need of certain services. Most of my 
efforts in utilizing the theory have been in connection to my 
personal life and to my clinical work. Some, but certainly less, 
energy has gone into applying theory to "the profession." This 
is certainly a relevant area, and I will be working to carve out 
the time it takes to think through the details. Clinically one of the more useful aspects of the theory is 
the way it provides a way of looking at a system and focusing 
on all aspects of the emotional processes in that system, not 
simply the presenting symptom. Another is knowing that the 
system can for the most part re-equilibrate itself if I don't 
hover, try to fix or "meet all the needs." In other words, if I 
can be a thoughtful, interested outsider to the situation, peo­
ple can figure out how to manage their symptom. To maintain 
this interested but not imposing position takes knowledge of 
self and respect for the other.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. On October 9, 1982 the Georgetown Family Center spon­
sored a one day Symposium on Family Evaluation and Diagnosis. Symposium speakers included Dr. Walter Toman, Professor of 
Psychology at the University of Erlangen-Nurnberg in Ger­
many; Dr. Murray Bowen, Clinical Professor of Psychiatry and 
Director of the Georgetown Family Center; and Dr. Michael 
Kerr, Clinical Assistant Professor of Psychiatry and Director of 
Training at the Georgetown Family Center. The meeting was 
an outgrowth of the interest in developing a family diagnostic 
system that has been stimulated by the publication of DSM III. Georgetown is one of a number of groups around the country 
working on a method of family diagnosis. This symposium was 
designed to present Georgetown's progress to date, and, in 
addition, to present the research of Walter Toman, who has 
been working on his own version of family diagnosis for many 
years.

Toman gained an international reputation following the 
1961 publication of his book, Family Constellation, which is 
now in its third edition. Bowen was immediately attracted to 
Toman's research on sibling position, seeing Toman's concep­
tualizations as filling an important gap in Bowen's then devel­
oping family systems theory. Toman had assembled discrepant 
and partial facts about family configuration into a precise 
body of systems knowledge, a body of knowledge Bowen 
viewed as having considerable applicability in family systems 
therapy. Georgetown-trained people quickly became well ver­
sed in Toman's profiles of the various sibling positions. Sibling position is only one aspect of what Toman assesses 
in evaluating a family. He systematically collects a wide range 
of data about several generations of the family and has a unique 
method of recording it. The system of recording is too com­
plex to be described here, but it is explained thoroughly in 
Family Constellation. While Toman 's theoretical basis for in­
terpreting the data and his method of recording it are quite 
different than Georgetown's, there is considerable similarity 
between the two approaches in terms of the type of data that 
is collected.

For example, Toman looks at at least three gener­
ations of the family and gathers the following information 
about family members: ages, dates of birth and marriages; de­
tails about deaths and other losses, such as long separations or 
divorces; educational and occupational histories; clinical prob­
lems; where people have lived and are currently living; and the 
amount of contact people retain with their families of origin. Toman's reason for collecting this extensive data about the 
family configuration, past and present, is that he is trying to 
define the facts in a person's life and the real social contexts in 
which they developed and now live. To quote Toman: 
The data helps us understand a person and his family on 
the basis of what he and people around him have been do­
ing in reality and in the context of options that reality has 
offered him, rather than on the basis of his introspections, 
expressions and evaluation of feelings alone. Knowing 
facts, social contexts and important events in a person's 
life permits more valid interpretations. It means not only 
knowing a person's responses and actions, but also know­
ing what it was and is that he has responded to and acted 
upon. *Reprinted with permission from the American Journal of 
Family Therapy, Vol 11, No. 1, Spring 1983. 4 Dr. Walter Toman, special guest at the Symposium on Family Evaluation 
and Diagnosis, discusses his system of collecting and ordering data on sev­
eral generations of a family.
