and Diagnosis, discusses his system of collecting and ordering data on sev­
eral generations of a family. Many people balk at accepting the amount of predictability 
that Toman's sibling profiles imply, but, to my knowledge, his 
research on the subject is more systematic and precise than 
anyone else's in the field. His sibling profiles appear to be as 
accurate for people who lived a hundred years ago as they are 
for people living today. The profiles transcend social and cul­
tural differences. If you present Toman with three or four gen­
erations of family data, it is impressive how he can accurately 
describe people in the present generation even without meeting 
or talking with them. Not that he is implying family configura­
tion is all there is to understanding a person, only that it is an 
important variable to be included in the overall assessment. The Georgetown Family Center group's work on a system 
of family diagnosis has yet to reach their goal of a book or 
manual on the subject. Many people have asked, "Why family 
diagnosis? Isn't diagnosis precisely what family therapists have 
spent years trying to get away from?" Questions such as these 
reflect misconceptions about the purpose of family diagnosis. Bowen and his Georgetown group have been doing a type of 
family diagnosis for many years in the form of the family dia­
gram.

Bowen and his Georgetown group have been doing a type of 
family diagnosis for many years in the form of the family dia­
gram. The family diagram has provided a systematic method 
for collecting data and recording them in such a way that facil­
itates interpretation. In spite of years of using family diagrams, 
the thinking that guides their use has never been spelled out in 
detail, and that's one of the goals of a book on diagnosis. A major concern about proposing a diagnostic system 
relates to how it would be applied. While the system would be 
developed from an understanding of theory, overzealous thera­
pists might miss its theoretical underpinnings and make simplis­
tic applications. Ideally, a diagnostic system would help broad­
en therapists' theoretical understanding of families by forcing 
them to consider many more variables in their assessment. Many clinical evaluations focus almost exclusively on the nu­
clear family and limit knowledge of the extended family to 
characterizations like "rigid" father or "alcoholic" mother. Not that the problem is solved by collecting more data; peo­
ple can collect it then not know how to interpret it. An exam­
ple is when people claim they are using "the Bowen model" 
because they have collected four generations of family data 
and made a family diagram.

help therapists think differently about families and contribute 
to their understanding of theory. ., 
 Most family therapists have now become reasonably fami­
liar with family diagrams. It would be interesting to let 10 
therapists interpret the same diagram, then compare the re­
sponses. I suspect the range of interpretations would be broad, 
that subjective responses would have considerable influence, 
and that a lot of the assumptions made about the family would 
be a product of individual theory. Individual theory, developed 
from the study of individuals, does not offer a basis for under­
standing the family as an evolving multigenerational emotional 
unit. Something new is required. The understanding of the 
family diagram is a manifestation of these underlying emotion­
al forces, forces that have a characteristic balance, intensity, 
and pattern of flow in each emotional field. There is the emo­
tional field of the nuclear family unit, the emotional field of 
the mother's immediate family of origin, of the father's imme­
diate family of origin, etc. The fields are said to be interlock­
ing because they have influenced and continue to influence 
each other emotionally.

The fields are said to be interlock­
ing because they have influenced and continue to influence 
each other emotionally. It is this theoretical understanding 
that brings the family diagram to life and provides important 
information about prognosis and planning the conduct of 
therapy. Although Georgetown still lacks a formal diagnostic sys­
tem, the direction of the current thinking was presented at the 
Symposium. Family diagnosis involves the assessment of four 
areas: 1) symptomatic person, 2) nuclear family emotional 
process, 3) nuclear family adaptiveness, and 4) family intact­
ness. Dr. Bowen, Dr. Toman and Dr. Kerr participate in a panel discussion on 
family evaluation and diagnosis. Symptom Diagnosis. An important parameter that family 
theory has added to symptom diagnosis is the assumption that 
emotional, physical and social symptoms are equivalent in the 
sense of being different manifestations of a common underly­
ing emotional process. Symptom diagnosis tells you where the 
system problem is being expressed, in which family member or 
family relationship, and whether it is expressed as physical, 
emotional, social or marital dysfunction. Nuclear Family Emotional Process. To what degree is the 
basic problem or immaturity of the nuclear family unit charac­
teristically bound in marital conflict, dysfunction in a spouse, 
or projection to a child? Does the emotionally driven process 
consistently get played out in the same way or does it shift 
around?

Does the emotionally driven process 
consistently get played out in the same way or does it shift 
around? In some families people take turns being symptomatic, 
while in others the process is rather rigidly focused on one per­
son. Flexibility in where symptoms are expressed suggests a 
better prognosis. At this level of diagnosis, the symptomatic 
person or relationship has been placed in the context of the 
underlying flow of the emotional forces in the nuclear family. Dr. Kerr presents Dr. Louis Rittlemeyer, Acting Chairman of the Depart­
ment of Psychiatry with pictures taken of Dr. Richard Steinbach who 
made introductory remarks at Family Symposia since 1963. The presenta­
tion was made prior to Dr. Toman 's introductory lecture at the Thursday 
Professional Meeting the evening before the Symposium. Nuclear Family Adaptiveness. Assessing the adaptiveness 
of a nuclear family is a complex task that requires looking at 
the entire history of the nuclear family as well as at more 
recent circumstances. What is the capacity of the nuclear fam­
ily as a unit to adapt to stress? The word adaptiveness has been 
chosen over differentiation because the latter has been subject 
to so much misinterpretation. A poorly adaptive family would 
be one where a routine stress, such as the birth of a baby, trig­
gers intense and protracted anxiety culminating in a clinical 
symptom.

A poorly adaptive family would 
be one where a routine stress, such as the birth of a baby, trig­
gers intense and protracted anxiety culminating in a clinical 
symptom. A fairly adaptive family is one that, while experien­
cing clinical symptoms, has only a moderate level of emotional 
reaction in face of tremendous stresses. Family Intactness. There are two main variables to be 
assessed under family intactness, the emotional stability of the 
extended family and the degree of emotional cutoff from ex­
tended family. The complexity of variables to be considered in 
making this evaluation makes it one of the most difficult of all 
aspects of family diagnosis. Impressions about the stability of 
each extended system come from looking at all the data: lon­
gevity of family members, amount and seriousness of clinical 
problems, divorces, productiveness of lives measured within 
the constraints of opportunity, to name but a few things that 
need to be considered. Stability and instability is a continuum 
and a complete three generation diagram would be an absolute 
minimum for gaining an accurate impression about it. Assess­
ing the level of emotional cut-off is also quite difficult and 
requires considerable understanding of theory. It is not some­
thing that can be adequately measured by counting up the 
number of trips home or the frequency of letter and phone 
contacts. The implications of family diagnosis for prognosis and 
therapeutic planning cannot be examined briefly.

The implications of family diagnosis for prognosis and 
therapeutic planning cannot be examined briefly. The implica­
tions can be summarized by saying that before beginning fam­
ily therapy it is essential to evaluate the nature of the problem 
being dealt with and to have some initial plan for approaching 
it. The ability to make prognoses is greatly enhanced by the 
recognition that the clinical course of a symptom is significant­
ly influenced by the family emotional field, nuclear and exten­
ded. Therapeutic planning is greatly enhanced by the recogni­
tion that it is frequently more profitable to direct therapy at 
parts of the family system seemingly quite removed from the 
symptom itself. 5 
 THURSDAY PROFESSIONAL SERIES 
1983-1984 Program 
Roberta B. Holt, L.C.S.W. History and Purpose 
The Thursday Professional Series began in the early 1960's 
as a forum for the presentation of family systems ideas. Initi­
ally, the meeting provided a central place for mental health 
professionals with work experience in diverse settings to hear 
emerging family systems concepts and results of work in pro­
gress. The meetings also provided informal exchange and op­
portunity to renew social contact. Today the program continues many of the same functions 
and has expanded into an evening that concentrates on theo­
retical issues, ideas peripheral to family systems theory, and 
innovations to existing family systems therapy.

characteristics:

the dysfunction. 4) a history of marital issues addressed and dealt with. 5) more openness in the system. Families with a secondary child-focus can more often be 
engaged in clinical work to see beyond the narrow focus on

problem through exploration of family patterns, old issues, 
and multigenerational themes. Attention to self and the part

relationship patterns can contribute to more thoughtful, more

The M Family 
A secondary child-focus process is discernible in the M 
family. Both Mr. and Mrs. M grew up in large Italian families 
in Texas. Their move East was experienced as difficult for 
both of them, and they have worked hard to establish a net­
work of friends through their church and community. There 
are visits several times yearly between the family in Texas and 
the family in Virginia. Contact is also maintained by mail and 
telephone. Mr. and Mrs. M describe their marriage as having begun 
too early. Both were 20. They make note of "ups and downs" 
in the relationship, with problems generally getting worked 
out when Mrs. M gets "so exasperated that screaming and slamming brings it to a head." They report that in the past two 
to three years, Mr. M's involvement in work has increased with 
a corresponding investment by Mrs. M in the needs of their 
two teenaged daughters. Mr. and Mrs. M recognize a gradually 
increasing sense of emotional disconnection from each other 
over the past two years. In the past year or so, their older daughter, Joyce, who is 
15, has begun to give the M's cause for concern. Her grades 
began slipping, and she was obviously using drugs and alcohol 
on weekends. Her attitude at home was truculent and dis­
respectful. Joyce was eventually suspended from school for 
smoking and possessing marijuana. These and other events 
created a cauldron of concern around which Mr. and Mrs. M 
focused attention and worry.

alization, increasing expectations for social and institutional 
solutions to family dilemmas, and the availability of insurance 
coverage, such a family with a secondary child-focus may 
come in contact not only with mental health clinics, but with 
courts, detention centers, special schools and psychiatric hos­
pitals. A percentage of beds in adolescent units of psychiatric 
hospitals are filled with teenagers hospitalized during a period 
of high anxiety or distress in a relatively well-functioning 
family. The potential effects on the developmental capacity of 
the child and upon the capacity of the family to handle nor­
mative disturbances may vary, but a particular mechanism for 
handling such distress has been reinforced as a potent pattern 
in that family. PART//

have reviewed 36 case records of families referred with a symp­
tom focus on an adolescent child, symptoms which were be­

1) parents could begin to address marital issues realisti­

significant as predictors of serious family dysfunction than are 
the particular styles of interaction. This is certainly an area

Working with an adolescent in a primary child-focused 
family in adjunctive, individual sessions depends upon the 
operating principles of the clinician and the direction of clinical 
work. The most valuable operating principle in working with 
adolescent clients is keeping a systems perspective, that is, 
maintaining a theoretical orientation as much as possible. This 
includes maintaining generational neutrality such that alliances 
and polarities between the generations are seen as part of the 
process of the family functioning -as well as potential quag­
mires for the clinician. It is only in this way that it is possible 
to hear the adolescent's realistic and unrealistic blaming of self 
or parents, his confusion, posturing, and sense of being stuck, 
without feeling sorry for him. Through focusing on process 
rather than content, the teenager may be guided to abstract 
the content and weave it back into a broadened exploration of 
the issue. It is important for the adolescent to see beyond the 
focus on himself which he is most likely helping to perpetuate. The second key operating principle is viewing the clinical 
sessions with the adolescent as adjunctive and supportive of 
the more basic work of the parents.

The second key operating principle is viewing the clinical 
sessions with the adolescent as adjunctive and supportive of 
the more basic work of the parents. This is based on the belief 
that unless the parents make some efforts in moving beyond 
the constricting patterns of the child-focus, little progress will 
be made in increasing the flexibility with which individual 
family members relate to each other and to the world. Most of the clinical work with adolescents is aimed at 
guiding the teenager in the task of sorting himself out from his 
family and moving toward more flexible, more responsible 
functioning. The overlapping objectives of the clinical sessions 
are: 
1) to reduce the anxiety sufficiently by generalizing the 
problem and by providing realistic feedback so that 
new ideas may be heard. 2) to teach the teenage client to observe himself as a 
functioning member of his family system and as a 
part of his extended system. To encourage his sense 
of membership, yet detoxify the sense of undue 
responsibility for family problems. 3) to guide the teenager in learning to observe the part 
that he or she plays in the family as well as in other 
relationship systems; e.g., friendship groups, school 
groups. 4) to focus on the teenager's functioning and to increase 
his capacity to see options for alternative ways of 
behaving and relating. Further objectives for the adolescent are: 
5) to identify personal goals and options for the future.

GEORGETOWN FAMILY SYMPOSIUM 
Murray Bowen, M.D. The Twentieth Symposium was in a class by itself for 
calm professional excellence. It was as good as some back in 
the late 1960's, but the Twentieth had a different quality. How 
does one get beyond subjectivity to evaluate such things? This 
is done within me, from having heard numerous positive and 
negative reports, and from having been present at all of them. The audience was small in comparison to the large crowds of 
former years, but the size of the audience appeared to have 
nothing to do with it. I think it may have been related to the 
overall thinking orientation of the faculty and presenters, to 
the ability of presenters to communicate simply and factually, 
the presence of Dr. Roger Payne as Distinguished Guest Expert, 
and the recognition of Dr. Paul D. MacLean at the Symposium 
Banquet. The Georgetown Family Program has been working 
toward this kind of an endpoint since 1959. Somehow it all 
began to come together at the Twentieth Symposium, and we 
did nothing to mark this as an anniversary. A brief history of the Symposium may help understand 
this evolution. The first Symposium was planned in 1964 as a 
small private meeting at which alumni could exchange papers 
and hear the Guest Expert. Family meetings were relatively 
new and the profession was just beginning to hear about fam­
ily therapy.

requests from others who wished to attend. Attendance dou­

a major problem. The Committee discontinued the private for­
mat and announced the Symposium as open to all professional 
people. The Symposium grew so rapidly it was forced out of 
the largest Georgetown auditorium and into hotel ballrooms 
with convention facilities. Attendance peaked at almost 1300 
in the early 1970's. The audience tended to bypass the impor­
tance of theory and see family systems theory as no more than 
another method of family "therapy." The people had slowly 
developed a feeling fervor similar to that in a religious revival 
or a political convention. Presentations were by graduates who 
knew the Georgetown theoretical orientation, but the audience 
saw it only as another method of "therapy." Several factors 
seemed to influence the evolution after that peak year. The Georgetown family program has always focused on 
theory. Since the 1940's I have considered a disciplined think­
ing orientation in the therapist as essential for the best in any WINTER 1984 
kind of therapy. That was designed to get beyond the shifting 
feelings in the person of the therapist. That was important in 
my move to family research.

theory based on the different premise.

the problem through disciplined research on the subhuman 
brain. His scientific writings. which include The Triune Brain, 
have made him into one of the most important behavioral 
scientists of this century. He has factual evidence that much of

the subhuman brains. The terminology from The Triune Brain 
has become common among those familiar with his work. At 
the Twentieth Symposium he was presented with a plaque, the 
content of which is being printed elsewhere in this Family 
Center Report. He did a response which was an addendum to 
his presentation a few years back when he was the guest expert 
at a former Georgetown Symposium. His recognition. and hit 
response to it, was a fitting highlight to the Twentieth Sympo­

work. Hopefully, there will be others in which he can go into 
more detail about his work. The two days of presentations fitted more closely with 
the overall theory than any Symposium before it. For some 
fortuitous or evolutionary reason, it all began to "come to­
gether "in a remarkable way. If this was evidence of what is to

forms of life. Bowen made a distinction between man's intel­

papers that spanned the two days. A final factor was an unusu­

interplay of the emotional systems of the black and white 
branches of her family with a common heritage. Loretta 
Nowakowski described the importance of understanding inter­
locking emotional systems in order to understand the function­
ing of residents in a nursing home. Gerald Schwan did a paper 
about Alzheimer's disease and its impact on the family emo­
tional system. Patricia Meyer used the historical evolution of 
medical knowledge about human reproduction to illustrate 
the way scientific understanding progresses. Progress is con­
strained not only by the limits of technology. but also by the 
human tendency to see only what has been seen already. Charles Paddack used descriptions of how various people res­
ponded to sea disasters as a basis for discussing factors that 
may influence adaptation to stress. Lilian Rosenbaum and 
Bernard Brown presented their research on the relationship of 
stress to the development of intelligence. Their statistical 
research supports the idea that the development of intelligence 
is not a fixed process, but can be influenced by environmental 
factors such as stress. Frank Giove and Donald Shoulberg each 
did papers examining the nature of science and theory. Each 
emphasized the importance of being precise about terminology 
in these areas. Bennett Tittler's paper reminded people of the 
value of a research attitude in doing clinical work.

transcended the polarizations that typically arise in discussions 
of this subject. Kathleen Kerr attempted to broaden under­
standing of the elusive concept of "self" by describing evidence 
of individuality in non-human animals. Finally. Polly Caskie 
centered her remarks on one of the more fascinating creatures 
in nature, the slime mold. She drew an analogy between signal­
ling systems in the human and signalling systems in other ani­
mals. Much of what was presented in all of these papers was in 
the realm of analogy, which as Bowen has repeatedly empha­
sized, is not an extension of theory. In addition. no one piece 
of research presented was complete. Yet all the papers taken 
together did stimulate a good deal of thinking about evolution, 
the nature of emotional systems, differentiation. and a variety 
of other important areas. The relevance of theory and of an 
evolutionary perspective to the conduct of clinical work was 
better appreciated. It was an important symposium. SYMPOSIA AND CONFERENCES

The other papers appear in the Fall 1983 issue. THE NATURE AND IMPORTANCE 
OF SCIENTIFIC THEORY 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. The ideas presented in this paper about the nature of 
science and theory drew heavily from the writings of others. Carl Sagan's book, Cosmos, was an especially important 
resource. Sagan beautifully described the evolution of man's 
thinking about the universe. He also demonstrated interrela­
tionships between the various branches of science in a way 
most people are not exposed to in their formal education. Schools, by virtue of communicating knowledge in compart­
ments, frequently fail to provide a broad overview. Students 
can miss the fascination of seeing the way things in nature fit 
together. While the words science and theory are used frequently, 
there is often little attempt to be precise about their definition. The terms can become meaningless abstractions. In his book, 
Fields of Force, William Berkson described the evolution of 
theory in physics from Faraday to Einstein. He wrote this 
about the nature of scientific theories: 
... scientific theories are often invented in an attempt 
to explain the phenomena of our experiences. Any search 
for an explanation assumes that there is something which 
is related to what we observe, but which is beyond our 
immediate observation and not yet known.

text:
Any search 
for an explanation assumes that there is something which 
is related to what we observe, but which is beyond our 
immediate observation and not yet known. Thus the search 
for scientific explanation is intimately connected with a 
sense of groping for the unknown.l 
(Italics in the original) 
Berkson's point about assuming there is something related 
to what is being observed is particularly relevant to the social 
sciences. It is so easy to get lost in the myriad of details of 
human behavior. The fact fundamental patterns and forces 
may exist underneath this seemingly choatic detail is easily 
forgotten. Scientific theories are not static. New technology and new 
ways of thinking lead to minor as well as sometimes dramatic 
revisions in theory. Berkson wrote the following about what is 
involved in the transition from existing theory to a new theory: 
Science is partly an attempt to find true explanations of 
phenomena of our experience. Because the existing theo­
ries may be false, they do not certainly delimit the range 
of possible solutions to present-day scientific problems; 
the existing theories are suggestive rather than completely 
constraining. Of course, the present theories are successful 
to a certain degree. They explain many phenomena and so 
solve problems which earlier theories failed to do.

Of course, the present theories are successful 
to a certain degree. They explain many phenomena and so 
solve problems which earlier theories failed to do. If a new 
theory is to supersede existing theories it must solve the 
old problems at least as well as existing theories.2 
(Italics in the original) 
lWilliam Berkson, Fields of Force. '.'iew York, John Wiley & 
Sons, 1974, p.4. 2Ibid, p.14. Existing theories are suggestive. A scientist must at one 
and the same time respect existing theory and be skeptical of 
it. Darwin was keenly aware of the ideas of others, but he did 
not automatically accept existing explanations of natural 
phenomena. He credited his having had only limited formal 
training in the natural sciences with enabling him to see nature 
in a new way. All of us would readily endorse the value of a 
healthy skepticism about existing explanations, but most of us 
still have limited awareness of our inability to see other than 
what we have been trained to see. Another important area is the relationship of theory to 
the" real "world. In 1938, Albert Einstein wrote the following: 
Physical concepts are free creations of the human mind, 
and are not, however it may seem, uniquely determined 
by the external world. In our effort to understand reality 
we are somewhat like a man trying to understand the 
mechanism of a closed watch. He sees the face and the 
moving hands, even hears it ticking, but he has no way of 
opening the case.

He sees the face and the 
moving hands, even hears it ticking, but he has no way of 
opening the case. If he is ingenious he may form some pic­
ture of a mechanism which could be responsible for all the 
things he observes, but he may never be quite sure his pic­
ture is the only one which could explain his observations. He will never be able to compare his picture with the real 
mechanism and he cannot even imagine the possibility of 
the meaning of such a comparison.3 
Einstein did not mean it will never be possible to view the 
world objectively. Saying all theories are "free creations of the 
human mind "does not imply they are all subjective. While sci­
entists do operate within the constraints of a" closed watch," 
theory can be objective to the extent that it is firmly grounded 
in the movement and ticking of the metaphorical watch. The 
movement and ticking are observable natural phenomena. The 
flowering of subjectively based concepts, on the other hand, is 
only minimally constrained by the movement and ticking of 
nature. Physicists have long been in search of a unified theory. This ultimate theory would be able to account for all the 
phenomena in the physical world. Biology is sufficiently de­
void of theory and comprised of so many variables, that no 
one seems to have seriously engaged the possibility of a unified 
theory in the life sciences.

Biology is sufficiently de­
void of theory and comprised of so many variables, that no 
one seems to have seriously engaged the possibility of a unified 
theory in the life sciences. Gary Zukav, writing in his popular 
book, The Dancing Wu Li Masters, summarized the thinking 
of a number of scientists on the possibility of some kind of 
super theory. In 1979 Zukav wrote: 
... we eventually will develop, in principle, a theory 
which is capable of explaining everything so well that 
there will be nothing left to explain. This does not mean, 
of course, that our explanation necessarily will reflect the 
way things actually are. We still will not be able to open 
the watch, as Einstein put it, but every occurrence in the 
real world (inside the watch) will be accounted for by a 
corresponding element of our final super theory. We will 
have, at last, a theory that is consistent within itself and 
which explains all observable phenomena. Einstein called 
this state the "ideal limit of knowledge."4

natural system, namely, the human family, has made the idea

developed about other natural systems. As these theories 
evolve, the possibility of integrating them into a broad natural 
systems theory will most certainly emerge. General systems 
theory has not been nor ever will be this integrative theory. It 
is too loosely anchored to the movement and ticking of nature. The gradual evolution of man's thinking about the solar 
system has many parallels to the process of theory develop­
ment that occurs in all fields of knowledge. Carl Sagan's, Cos­
mos, concentrated not so much on the scientific facts about 
our universe, but on the slow evolution of man's thinking 
about these facts. Cosmos is a fascinating story about human 
beings. The rest of this paper is predominantly a summary of 
what Sagan presented. It is not surprising that mankind has devoted so much 
energy to contemplating the heavens. The stars and planets 
could be easily observed with the naked eye and celestial events 
begged for interpretation. Human beings were free to project 
their hopes and fears on the night sky. Nor is it surprising that 
through much of recorded history man thought the earth to be 
at the center of it all. Things did seem to revolve around us. Ptolemy, a scholar who worked at the Library of Alexandria 
in the second century, was a major influence in perpetuating 
the worldview of an earth-centered solar system.

Ptolemy, a scholar who worked at the Library of Alexandria 
in the second century, was a major influence in perpetuating 
the worldview of an earth-centered solar system. While he 
made many important and accurate observations of the planets 
and stars, he was very wrong about the structure of the solar 
system. He and his followers believed that the planets and sun 
were each attached to a revolving sphere. The spheres were of 
different size and nested inside each other. They had, there­
fore, a common center, which was where the earth was loca­
ted. It was an interesting model, but there were quite a few 
facts about the motions of the planets with which it was 
inconsistent. It was Ptolemy who then imagined some modifi­
cations of the concentric spheres model that would account 
for some of these inconsistencies. This product of his imagina­
tion was to be accepted as accurate for over a thousand years! The major inconsistency Ptolemy had to resolve was that 
many of the planets, in the course of their orbit around the 
earth, would stop, go backwards for a time, and then resume 
their forward motion. Ptolemy constructed a mechanical 
model in which each of the nested concentric spheres had a 
small sphere attached to it. The planet rotated around itself on 
this small sphere, while its attachment to the larger sphere car­
ried it in its path around the earth.

The planet rotated around itself on 
this small sphere, while its attachment to the larger sphere car­
ried it in its path around the earth. Looking from the earth, 
the observer would then expect to see periodic backward loop­
ing motions as the planet traversed the night sky. The beauty 
of Ptolemy's model was that no one had to alter their basic 
belief that man was the center of the universe. It was fifteen 
hundred years before this idea was seriously challenged by 
Copernicus. What makes the long acceptance of Ptolemy's 
model even more intriguing is that as early as 300 B.C. a sun­
centered solar system had been proposed and generally rejec­
ted. Ptolemy and all those who believed his model were not 
stupid people. They were, no doubt, heavily influenced by 
their social environment and emotionally invested in preserv­
ing what was accepted. Ptolemy and those who followed him 
were not unlike ourselves. Nicholas Copernicus published his model of a sun-cen­
tered solar system in 1543. The earth was demoted to being 
just one of the planets, the third from the sun. Copernicus 
thought the planets moved in circular orbits around the sun. This concept provided a better explanation of the apparent Dr. Mfr·hael Kerr making presentation at the Symposium. backward looping motions of the planets. It was very simple. The apparent periodic backward motion resulted from the fact

that the earth-bound observer was also moving. The earth orbi­
ted the sun at a different rate than the other planets. There 
were times, therefore, when the other planets appeared to be 
moving backwards. Appearances were deceiving. In spite of 
this enormously important contribution of Copernicus, the 
idea of an earth centered universe died a slow death. Galileo 
got caught in the crossfire associated with the transition from 
the subjectively based model of Ptolemy to the more objective 
presentation of Copernicus. After nearly two thousand years 
of waiting, however, this dramatic change in man's conception 
of the universe began to take root. Copernicus' model was not 
perfect, however, and its fine tuning awaited the emergence of 
another great scientist, Kepler. Johannes Kepler was born twenty-eight years after the 
publication of Copernicus' work. He was an exceptional scien­
tist who many credit with igniting the modern scientific revo­
lution. In developing his ideas about the solar system, Kepler 
relied heavily on the extensive observations of planetary mo­
tion made by Tycho Brahe. Not all of Brahe's observations fit 
precisely with the circular orbits Copernicus had proposed. Kepler did not assume that those few observations that did not 
fit were erroneous. He had the scientific discipline to question 
the model and not the observations.

Kepler did not assume that those few observations that did not 
fit were erroneous. He had the scientific discipline to question 
the model and not the observations. Kepler worked diligently 
for many years and proceeded down numerous blind alleys in 
search of a model that would fit with all the observations. Fin­
ally, he figured out that the planets moved in elliptical rather 
than circular orbits around the sun. He was able to define pre­
cise mathematical laws of planetary motion that accounted for 
all the known facts about the planets. These laws are basically 
as accurate today as when they were developed. Kepler had 
developed these laws on the basis of empirical observation. They were an accurate description of what happened, but not 
an accounting for what happened. In other words, the ques­
tion of what actually drove and regulated the motions of the 
planets was left unanswered. Kepler did speculate that the sun 
might exert some magnetic force on the planets to account for 
their motion, but the world had to await Newton for the 
development of the first real scientific theory. The difference 
between Kepler and Newton is somewhat analogous to the 
difference between Don Jackson and Murray Bowen. Jackson 
provided brilliant descriptions of what went on in a family, 
but had no theory to account for the activity he observed. Bowen accounted for what he saw with the theory of emotion­
al systems. 7

the nervous system proceeds through a series of orderly

Daniel V. Papero, Ph.D., ACSW 
One generally assumes that training involves the transfer 
of information from someone who knows (faculty) to some­
one who knows less (learner or trainee). A second assumption, 
derived from the first, is that the learner changes most and 
derives the greatest benefit from the training process. The role 
of the faculty is presumed to consist primarily of helping or 
facilitating change in the learner.

facilitating change in the learner. In clinical settings it is gener­
ally assumed that the change in the learner will occur in the 
area referred to as therapeutic skill. Somehow in the course of 
training the learner will increase the quantity and quality of 
therapeutic skill at his disposal. The increase in therapeutic 
skill is generally measured in terms of the faculty's assessment 
of progress made, and more generally, on the basis of time 
spent in the training process. In a general sense, these assumptions appear to have play­
ed a role in the training programs at the Family Center. The 
very designation faculty suggests the operation of the first 
assumption. The general concern among faculty with the pro­
gress of trainees by year, e.g., first year, second year, etc., 
designates the equation of time spent with progress. In this 
manner, the Family Center training programs are similar to 
programs in any other institution. To create separate roles for faculty and learner establishes 
a dichotomy which does not necessarily exist. To be sure, 
every learner can profit from a mentor, but astute teachers 
continually learn from their students. In any learning situation 
one can accurately question who is really the teacher and who 
is the learner. In the long run, it might be more useful if facul­
ty could attempt to teach what it does not know rather than 
to focus on teaching what it knows.

major barrier to the instructor's learning is the tendency to fit 
what is being reported into a mental framework and thereafter 
operating as if that framework explained everything and were 
an accurate picture of reality. It seems axiomatic that no such 
mental framework is completely accurate. Yet, the more the 
instructor accepts his or her own construct as fact, the more 
he or she becomes unable to learn from the other. What is missing in such a process is the effort to note 
where one's construct does not fit. For a skilled clinician, 
such mental constructs often have a great degree of accuracy. It is a natural tendency to take new information and attempt 
to fit it into the construct. In the same way it is relatively easy 
to discard what does not fit. Yet, such divergent facts or pieces 
of information are more important to learning than those 
pieces which agree. They lead to an entire range of thinking 
and questions which have not previously been available to the 
instructor. Such engagement with the learner and the basic 
questions which result are a fundamental part of the instruc­
tor's effort to learn. They are also extremely important to the 
learner's effort. There has always been a responsibility for faculty to 
continue the effort to learn.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. This paper was presented at a symposium on borderline per­
sonality disorders held on November 18, 1983 at the V.A. Medical Center in Coatesville, Pennsylvania. 1 was invited to 
address the topic "The Borderline Family," and decided to 
approach the topic on as broad a theoretical level as 1 could 
manage. -M.E.K. I am pleased to participate in this symposium about 
borderline patients. I am pleased that Dr. Henry Lederer sug­
gested me as a possible participant. Henry was my first teacher 
in psychiatry back in 1962 when I was a freshman medical 
student at Georgetown. I am also pleased to be back in the 
area where I grew up. My topic is "The Borderline Family." I would like to 
consider the topic in a very broad context and to concentrate 
on the ways that families that generate a borderline personality 
are much like all families and much like your family and mine. It could be legitimately argued that human evolution began 
10-20 billion years ago with the cosmic big bang. At least this 
is the best theory we have. Our solar system took shape about 
4.5 billion years ago and the first life on earch appeared over 3 
billion years ago.

Humankind seems always to have wanted to see itself as 
other than it is. We are still much this way, although the sheer 
weight of scientific knowledge seems to be gaining on us. The 
"ultimate" understanding of the human and human behavior 
will be anchored in an understanding of the forces that govern 
all natural systems, of all systems that exist throughout the 
cosmos. Man can achieve this understanding, I believe. As early as 300-400 B.C., more than two thousand years 
ago, the Greeks proposed that man was not the center of the 
universe. A number of them believed that the Earth revolved 
around the sun and that complex life forms had evolved out of 
the primordial ooze. These thinkers were "proved" wrong and 
their ideas were buried for two thousand years or so until peo­
ple like Copernicus, Newton, and Darwin rediscovered them. What took us so long? What is at stake that the human persists 
in seeing only what he "wants" to see? It was the nature of 
man, but not all men. It still is the nature of man, but not all 
men. The people who "proved" the Greeks "wrong" were no 
different than we are -no smarter, no dumber. Isaac Newton gave us the first scientific theory. His theory 
of universal gravitation is a systems theory, at least in a general 
sense. People like Copernicus and Johannes Kepler provided a 
detailed description of the motions of the planets, but their 
work was descriptive and could not account for what was 
observed.

everything Kepler had observed and much more. Newton was 
able to deduce all the laws Kepler had worked so long to 
define. That is the value of theory. In the years since Newton, the physical sciences have 
come a long way indeed. Some physicists believe they are on 
the verge of a unified field theory. All physical phenomena 
would be explained by the interrelationship of four basic 
forces: gravity, electromagnetic force, strong force, and weak 
force. Maybe the physicists are not as close as some may think, 
but it is clear that they are very far ahead of the life sciences. We have barely begun to conceptualize a theory in the life 
sciences. Biology remains largely descriptive albeit with a 
rapidly developing sophistication in this regard. Concepts 
about human behavior are also mostly descriptive and often 
strongly laced with subjectivity. We demonstrate against war 
and we could just as easily demonstrate against schizophrenia.

come to be known as the family movement in psychiatry began 
in the late l 940's and early l 950's. It has been recognized on a 
national level since about 1957. Many of the early researchers 
focused on families with a schizophrenic member, but circum­
stances dictated that as much as anything else. Families in 
which any type of serious symptom existed could have just as 
profitably been studied. The extremes of criminal behavior, 
alcoholism, physical illness, eating disorders, and other prob­

vior with the potential of replacing or subsuming all existing 
theories of human behavior emerged from family research. This theory was eventually called family systems theory or, as 
I like to call it, the theory of family emotional systems. The 
man who has gone farthest in developing this theory is Murray 
Bowen. What most people tend to think emerged from the study 
of the family is a new treatment modality called family ther­

and the part still underwater in most people's eyes is family 
theory. Family systems theory is built on the premise that man is 
a product of evolution and remains an integral part of nature. It evolved from the study of the human family and not from 
general systems theory. It defines mental illness as a product 
of the part of man common to all other forms of life. To con­
vey the deeper phylogenetic roots of mental illness, the term 
mental illness was discarded in favor of "emotional illness." 
The term emotional, in other words, is considered appropri­
ately applied to the behavior of whales, horses, ants, and mice, 
as well as man. Emotion is not synonymous with feelings; feel­
ings are a much more recent evolutionary acquisition. In the 
development of family systems theory a most important effort 
was made to try to keep concepts consistent with ideas from 
natural systems. By keeping the theory open to new knowl­
edge from other scientific disciplines, it was anticipated that 
family systems theory could eventually be integrated with 
systems concepts developed from the study of other natural 
systems.

Prior to Freud, mental illness was generally considered to 
be the product of structural defects in the brain. Freud's pro­
posal of functional disturbances in the brain based on child­
hood experiences was a bold leap. Today, there is a great deal 
of interest in biochemical disturbances or defects that may 
"cause" mental illness. What all these viewpoints have in com­
mon is that they seek the primary cause of the problem within 
the individual. What intrigued family researchers were relationships. The 
thinking, feeling, and behavioral chain reactions that occurred 
within families became the focus of study. Like Johannes 
Kepler, most people in the family field have stayed on a des­
criptive level. In attempting to account for what they saw, 
they would fall back on individual psychodynamics or some 
other kind of motivating force which had been conceived 
from the study of individual patients. Bowen took a distinctly 
"Newtonian-like" step when he developed the concept of an 
emotional system to account for what could be observed in 
families. The human family was seen to be governed by natural 
life forces akin to those that operated throughout nature. Bowen's assertion that the human family is governed by an 
emotional system was supported by enough evidence to satisfy 
Bowen to build a theory on it.

the forces of individuality and togetherness are managed within 
the person and within a relationship system such as the family. There are differences between people and between family units

The first way has to do with the validity of viewing the family 
as an emotional unit rather than as a collection of individuals. The family is an emotional system. It operates in such a way 
that the thinking, feelings and behavior of each member of 
that family are regulated and directed by the system. Differen­
tiation refers to the fact that this regulatory process is more 
intense in some families than in others. One can think in terms 
of a continuum ranging from reasonably well differentiated 
families to very poorly differentiated or undifferentiated fami­
lies. The more the undifferentiation of a family, the more the 
emotional system regulates the very being of each member. Another element to be considered when evaluating the inten­
sity of this emotional regulatory process in a family is the level 
of chronic anxiety that prevails. The higher the level of chronic 
anxiety, the more the system is pushed toward greater degrees 
of undifferentiation. When the chronic anxiety level decreases, 
the system returns to its baseline level of differentiation. A second way to think about the individuality-togetherness 
concept has to do with the potential dilemma posed by rela­
tionships in which people have some degree of emotional 
investment in each other. Systems theory posits that people 
who marry have equivalent basic levels of differentiation.

who marry have equivalent basic levels of differentiation. The 
capacity of each person to function as an individual is the 
same, and the togetherness needs of each person are the same. Basic levels of differentiation are the same regardless of appear­
ances that sometimes seem to belie that fact. Since people's 
level of differentiation varies, marriages are not the same in 
terms of the mix of individuality and togetherness that charac­
terizes them. The more undifferentiated the marital relation­
ship, the more it is balanced toward togetherness. The greater 
the undifferentiation in a marriage, the greater the potential 
for problems. Another way of saying this is that the more un­
differentiated a marital relationship is, the less adaptive it is to 
stress. How to understand this diminished adaptiveness? What I 
have to say about that is oversimplified, but I will do it to 
make a point. The more the emotionally determined together­
ness needs of people in a marriage, the more emotionally inter­
dependent their functioning. People have strong needs for a 
sense of connection with each other and strong needs for each 
other to think, feel, and behave in ways that will satisfy the 
needs of oneself. People need each other and at the same time 
are prone to feel a pressure and threat from each other.

People need each other and at the same time 
are prone to feel a pressure and threat from each other. There­
fore, the greater the undifferentiation in a marriage the more 
potential for chronic anxiety to be generated by the basic 
nature of the relationship itself. There is the chronic threat of 
not enough involvement and the chronic threat of too much 
involvement such that one will be taken over, smothered, or 
diminished by the other. Not infrequently, people will play 
out the opposite sides of this dichotomy in a marriage. At the 
extremes, this dilemma becomes unsolvable and leads to a "you die" or "I die" situation. Relationships can be that 
powerful. Short of the extremes, what do people characteristically 
do to manage this dilemma? Family systems theory has defined 
four mechanisms that are related to the chronic anxiety gener­
ated by the dilemma just described. Most nuclear family units 
manifest some of all four of these mechanisms to be described. Many nuclear families use predominantly one or two "anxiety 
binding mechanisms." 
The most obvious mechanism and perhaps easiest to under­
stand is emotional distance. The anxiety generated by the 
undifferentiation is bound in the distance. It is a compromise. People withdraw physically or withdraw by means of psycho­
logical mechanisms, and the anxiety generated by their interac­
tion disappears. The anxiety is bound in that sense. A second 
mechanism is marital conflict.

The anxiety is bound in that sense. A second 
mechanism is marital conflict. Conflict provides a form of 
contact and distance at one and the same time. The undiffer­
entiation of each person is externalized into their patterns of 
interaction. While such externalization undermines cooperation 
and communication, it can act in the service of preserving the 
physical and emotional integrity of each person. A third mech­
anism is one spouse overriding the other. This is a complex 
mechanism and there is little time here to detail it. It is usually 
characterized by reciprocal functioning such as the following: 
overadequate-inadequate, strong-weak, decision-maker-non­
decision-maker, and overfunctioner-underfunctioner. This 
mechanism, taken toward the extremes, can contribute to 
clinical impairment in one spouse that can be manifested in 
physical illness, emotional illness, or social dysfunction. A fourth mechanism to be described is the one most 
relevant to the development of a borderline personality. The 
mechanism is not unique to that clinical entity. In this fourth 
situation, the undifferentiation of the parents is played out in 
relationship to a particular child. The child is an equal partici­
pant in the process. This most involved child will grow up with 
a level of differentiation slightly less than the parents. His life 
is more intensely regulated by his internal emotional reactions 
and the harmony of the emotional environment that surrounds 
him.

involved with the family, but the family emotional problem

clinical entities is replaced by focus on the "background" level

clinical entities are symptoms, not diseases. I do want to put in a word of caution. The family emo­
tional system is not the "cause" of any clinical problem.

I have not concentrated on therapy in this presentation, 
because therapy is so much a product of the way the therapist 
thinks about the problem. When family concepts are taught as 
primarily representing a new method of therapy, trainees tend 
to quickly bypass the fact that family is, most importantly, a 
new way of thinking. Trainees are quick to append therapeutic 
techniques onto their preexisting views of the nature of human 
problems. My main goal here today, in contrast, has been to 
present these new family ideas in a way that might make it 
easier to hear them as a new theory. Training therapists is 
dependent on defining and challenging their basic assumptions 
about human behavior and not on teaching them a set of tech­
niques. The goal is for all of us to examine the nature of the 
lens we use to view the world. For the most part, when view­
ing the human process, this lens has been fashioned far more 
out of subjectivity than objectivity. NURSING CONFERENCE

Patricia H. Meyer, A.C.S.W. The Seventh Annual Conference on Children was held 
March 5, 1984 under a new and permanent title, "The Trans­
mission of Emotional Processes." The history and development 
of this meeting is a reflection of the coordinator's efforts to 
work towards a systems view of the natural world and the 
place of the human species in it. The first year the conference 
focused on delinquency. For the next three years, the context 
was broadened to emotional, social, and physical functioning 
in children. In the fifth and sixth years of the conference, the 
focus shifted towards transmission, although the title remained 
the same. In 1984, the title was permanently and formally 
changed to The Transmission of Emotional Processes. This change represents much more than a shifting of 
words. It is, rather, a reflection of a belief that a conference on 
only one part of the system was not consistent with systems 
theory. Transmission, on the other hand, described the connec­
tedness and emotionality from generation to generation. Hence, a title which was once on children, now focuses on 
transmission between and among generations. This year·s conference began with a paper by Dr. Michael

in Washington, D.C. This presentation is a series of hypotheses about the 
relationship between emigration and the concept known as 
"cut-off" in Bowen Theory. Since, by defnition, a hypothesis 
is an unproved proposition, tentatively accepted to explain 
certain facts or to provide a basis for further investigation, this 
is only an initial foray into a very complex area. It is in that 
spirit that the results of my thinking are presented. The process of emigration has many implications for the 
next generation. Although I am using emigration to refer to 
the departure of people from their native land, some of these 
hypotheses may also apply to the process of leaving one region 
of a country to settle in another. Over this past year, I have had contact with approximately 
130 families. Most of these have had a member of their family 
hospitalized on an evaluation service of a private psychiatric 
institute where I work. During this year, two facts have emer­
ged: 1) Many of these families have their origin in countries 
other than the United States, and 2) The formal emigration 
took place within the past 100 years. Emigration times have 
varied from as recently as seven years ago to as long as 100 
years ago. Data about possible emigrations on all 130 families 
is not complete for several reasons.

Emigration times have 
varied from as recently as seven years ago to as long as 100 
years ago. Data about possible emigrations on all 130 families 
is not complete for several reasons. Initially, I restricted my 
questions to two or at most three generations. As I became 
aware of the importance of emigration, I became more expert 
at gathering relevant information from new families. Of the 
130 families, approximately 30 had a member or members of 
their family emigrate over the past I 00 years. Actually I think 
the number is greater. I just did not collect the data. In my 
private practice, over three quarters of the families I see have 
had a member or members of their family emigrate to the Uni­
ted States in the last 100 years, typically within the last two or 
three generations. As a result of my experience with these families, I have 
begun to think about the relationship between emigration and 
family process. Emigration-as a phenomenon-can be examined 
from other perspectives such as societal conditions or biologi­
cal factors. Of necessity I have had to restrict my area of focus 
for the time being. With regard to family process, I believe 
emigration can be understood in part as a function of the level 
of differentiation of the individuals who decide to leave. That 
is to say, people can emigrate in reaction to family process or 
can emigrate more thoughtfully and purposefully for reasons 
related to well-defined life principles.

That 
is to say, people can emigrate in reaction to family process or 
can emigrate more thoughtfully and purposefully for reasons 
related to well-defined life principles. Generally, I believe that 
the forces that propel individuals away from their country and 
family of origin represent a mixture of both emotionality and 
thoughtfulness. Further, I believe, these individuals and their 
"emigrations" are distributed along the differentiation of self 
scale as defined in Bowen Theory. For example, some of the 
individuals with whom I've had contact over the past year 
clearly state they left to "get away forever." Others state they 
left for reasons of schooling, vocational opportunity and the like. A careful history in these latter cases, however, often sug­
gests a combination of purposefulness and a need to distance 
from intensity. These considerations led to the development of my first 
hypothesis: The process of emigration can be understood as a 
function of the level of differentiation of the emigrating mem­
bers of a family. If emigration can be understood as a reflection 
of level of differentiation, then it can be assumed that some 
emigrations have the potential to result in better levels of 
differentiation for the generation who emigrated and their 
descendants. Other emigrations could promote an acceleration 
of dysfunction in the lives of the families who emigrated.

Other emigrations could promote an acceleration 
of dysfunction in the lives of the families who emigrated. That 
is to say, in the latter instance, that over several generations, 
individuals with lower levels of differentiation would occur 
with more frequency. Several further hypotheses emerge from 
this assumption and from my experience with emigrating fami­
lies. Hypothesis II: Those emigrations which result in an acceleration 
of dysfunction in the emigrating generation and its descendants 
reflect an emotional cut-off on the part of the emigrating indi­
vidual, pair, or segment of the family. Emotional cut-off as 
defined in Bowen Theory is a "concept that deals with the 
way people separate themselves from the past in order to start 
their lives in the present generation." It addresses the degree of 
unresolved emotional attachment people have towards their 
parents. I use the term "acceleration of dysfunction" to refer 
to increasing incidences in family members of physical illness, 
accidents, alcoholism, drug addiction, legal problems, voca­
tional instability, violent behavior, marital conflict, divorce, 
depression, psychosis and, for one reason or another, failure to 
reproduce. Hypothesis III: When emigrations are propelled by the need to 
cut off, they occur with less thought and planning and, there­
fore, result in increased anxiety and more difficult cultural 
transitions.

necessity or failure to adapt. Intermediate settlements are 
several moves between countries or within the United States 
before reaching a place of more permanent settlement. Hypothesis IV: Marriages formed in reaction to an emigration 
reflecting a cut-off will duplicate the original pattern that pro­
moted the cut-off and will be a more intense version. I have 
heard of many instances of an individual emigrating to this 
country and quickly forming a relationship with a soon-to-be 
spouse. The partners in these marriages develop what I call 
intense allergies to each other. An extreme example of this is a 
gentleman in his 40's who left home at the age of 17 and 
vowed never to contact his parents again. He has never been 
able to establish successful, long-lasting relationships with 
females. Somewhat wistfully, he explained to me that his "pair 
bonding mechanism is out of control." 
Hypothesis V: Given the combination of emotional cut-off 
and the intense anxiety associated with it and with the cultural 
transition, the family projection process may seriously impair 
many of the children in the next two generations. Two factors 
of significance in this hypothesis are that many children may 
be impaired and that the process directly influences at least 
two generations.

In March of 1979 I became aware of a dreadful insight: 
Bowen Theory was an attempt to move the understanding of 
the human phenomenon toward the biological sciences. This

This 
was one of the saddest days of my life. My entire formal aca­
demic training, which did not end until I was 38, was in the 
humanities. Although my training covered a range of disci­
plines, namely philosophy, theology, pastoral psychology, and 
communication studies, what unified them was a focus on the 
human as unique and more different than similar to all other 
phenomena. I purposely had taken as little science as possible in high 
school and college because of its connection with mathema­
tics. By July 1977, my clinical work was guided by Bowen 
Theory, but what I had read from the beginning about human 
behavior and biology did not register until March 1979. What 
frightened me was the degree of my ignorance of science and 
the insight that until I attempted to grasp something of scien­
tific knowing, I could not have a very profound understanding 
of Bowen Theory. This paper is a progress report on my current understand­
ing of science. The first part of the paper gives some working 
definitions of science, theory, and personal appropriation. The 
second part of the paper describes two criteria for judging the 
validity of a theory: (1) predictable reliability and (2) coher­
ence -the way a theory in one area of study may fit with a 
theory in another science. The example I will use is the con­
cept of self in the Bowen Theory and how it coheres with 
some basic ideas in immunology. The paper ends with some 
thoughts regarding science and other ways of knowing.

thoughts regarding science and other ways of knowing. Basic Definitions 
The basic assumption of this paper is that one is able to 
judge that his acceptance of the Bowen Theory is based on 
scientific knowledge when the theory has been personally 
appropriated. The Bowen Theory is a set of interrelated con­
cepts that describe and explain the functioning of emotional 
systems. Scientific knowledge involves the ability to describe 
a phenomenon by stating how it is experienced by observers, 
and to explain the phenomenon by stating how it came about 
and the relationships that occur between its various elements. Personal appropriation is the ability to affirm that a particular 
theory adequately explains the phenomenon in question 
because self has gone through the steps leading to the formula­
tion of the theory by personally performing the observations 
and experiments proposed to justify the adequacy of the the­
ory. It also involves a radical questioning of theories and beliefs 
previously appropriated to see what can remain and what must be discarded if one's theoretical stance is to be consistent. Although personal appropriation is by definition a unique 
achievement, it is assumed that a similar undertaking is neces­
sary for anyone who desires to know the Bowen Theory or 
any other scientific theory personally. Criteria for Judging a Theory: Predictable Reliability 
and Coherence

Criteria for Judging a Theory: Predictable Reliability 
and Coherence 
1. Predictable Reliability 
Sir Peter Medawar, a biologist who won the Nobel Prize in 
1960, has attempted to describe the work of science in numer­
ous papers (1 ). What he saw occurring in laboratories and had 
learned in discussions with other scientists regarding their inves­
tigations did not correspond to what he read of scientific 
methodology. The majority of texts on method, beginning 
with John Stuart Mill, state that science is an inductive process 
beginning with observation. Medawar claims this is not an 
accurate assumption. He believes that every scientist actually 
proceeds from a theory or a hypothesis, from a prediction 
about how things possibly are, and that this hypothesis guides 
any observations the scientist makes. Hypotheses are imagina­
tive conjectures and in that sense fictions in the way a novel or 
a poem is fiction. Where science differs from art is that once 
the guess or hypothesis is articulated, rigorous tests in the 
form of experiments describing what will occur in the world 
are critically applied to the phenomenon in question. For a 
hypothesis to be scientific, it must be able to be empirically 
tested. The work of science is therefore a circular or cybernetic 
process. Hypotheses are generated, and tests are devised to see 
how well the hypotheses hold up in the laboratory and even­
tually in nature.

Hypotheses are generated, and tests are devised to see 
how well the hypotheses hold up in the laboratory and even­
tually in nature. Nature itself ultimately provides the feedback 
necessary to affirm, deny, and most often to modify the initial 
prediction (2). Consequently the clearer the initial hypotheses 
and the tests that render them accurate or not, the easier it 
becomes to judge the accuracy of a theory. It is striking to see that Medawar's description of what 
scientists actually do is clearly articulated in Bowen's early 
papers on his research on schizophrenia (3). A hypothesis 
about the origin of schizophrenia and its continuance was 
articulated and a mode of therapy was designed to modify the 
symbiotic relationship between mother and schizophrenic off­
spring. When the hypothesis was changed to include the emo­
tional system of which the mother and schizophrenic offspring 
were a part, it became necessary to devise a different way of 
working with the problem. A hypothesis, a setting for actual 
observation, and a way to modify the phenomenon experimen­
tally through therapy was worked out. For the cybernetic 
feedback loop to be complete, it was necessary to see when 
the identified patient did well outside the hospital setting and 
what factors went into a return of the patterns of movement 
typical in families with a schizophrenic offspring.

My initial attraction to the Bowen Theory began to solidify 
when I failed in clinical work with a very gifted and explosive 
young woman. After working with me for six weeks, she re­
vealed that her lifelong depression had lifted. The intensity 
this evoked in me was so great that I abruptly referred her for 
psychoanalysis. During the difficult months following this 
event, I came to see that the Bowen Theory offered a way of 
working with gifted and explosive people that did not focus on 
the therapeutic relationship. 9 
 To test whether attempting to work from the Bowen 
Theory rather than the therapeutic relationship made a differ­
ence, I set up a year-long experiment ( 4). My basic hypothesis 
was that if the subjects could get a more solid relationship 
with their parents rather than with me, they would automati­
cally be better able to establish one-to-one heterosexual rela­
tionships and to become more clear about their professional 
goals. Although the experiment was fraught with methodolo­
gical difficulties, it did help me to see how a theory-guided 
therapy that attempted to minimize the therapeutic relation­
ship produced results far more substantial than those that I 
had previously produced with a similar group of clients. The more difficult task of attempting to modify self in 
my family of origin began formally about a year after the clin­
ical experiment began (5).

Although predictable reliability is the major criterion for 
testing a theory, in those cases where two theories can predict 
with equal reliability, another criterion-coherence-has to be 
applied (6). One demonstrates coherence by showing how a 
theory from one field of study fits with a theory from another. To move understanding of human nature towards biology, one 
would automatically turn to biology to see how the proposed 
theory fits with biological theory. One can operationalize the search for coherence through 
abductive thinking. Gregory Bateson describes abduction in 
the following way: 
We are so accustomed to the universe in which we live 
and to a puny method of thinking about it that we can 
hardly see that it is possible to describe some event or 
thing ... and then to look around the world for other 
causes to fit the same rules that we devise for our descrip­
tions. We can look at the anatomy of a frog and look 
around to find other instances of the same abstract rela­
tions recurring in other creatures including, in this case, 
ourselves. (7, p.

Differentiation as used in the Bowen Theory does seem to 
provide a coherent connection with biology and does illustrate 
an abductive way of thinking. What about the notion of self? Until this spring, I assumed 
that this was a concept that had no meaning in biology. But, 
by chance, I discovered that in 1949 F. Macfarlane Burnet 
began describing immunology as the science of self (8). In­
trigued with this discovery, I began reading in immunology (8, 
9,10,ll,12,13,14,15). The reading has led me to suggest that 
the notions of self and nonself, memory and tolerance, and 
individual learning are ideas within immunology that provide a 
useful bridge or abduction in trying to connect a discussion of 
emotional systems and biology. What is a self from a scientific point of view? According 
to Klein, "everything constituting an integral part of an indi­
vidual" is self Nonself makes up the rest of the universe (13, 
p. 5). Particular cells called lymphocytes mediate the immune 
response. These cells can distinguish between self and nonself 
because of an information exchange occurring at a molecular 
10 level. When this information is processed, the immune response 
begins and an antibody is generated through clonal selection 
(9,13).

When this information is processed, the immune response 
begins and an antibody is generated through clonal selection 
(9,13). This antibody then links up with nonself and renders it 
inactive so that it no longer threatens the bodily integrity of 
the self. Burnet (11) hypothesized that this characteristic of the 
immune response gradually developed over the lifetime of the 
individual organism. Early in development and shortly after 
birth, there is a period of tolerance when the distinction be­
tween self and nonself is not very well developed. Once a 
distinction between self and nonself can be made, nonself is 
defended against. Each time an antigen is encountered, the 
memory of its previous link with the immune system is recal­
led; consequently, the immune system can act more quickly 
and rid the nonself from the host more expeditiously. Burnet's 
hypothesis was validated experimentally by O·.nns in dealing 
with dyzogotic cattle twins (14), by Medawar's work with 
pure strains of mice (15), and by Burnet's own experimental 
work with chick embryos (11). Later developments showed 
how tolerance could be induced in adults by suppressing the 
immune response, a discovery that enabled transplant surgery 
to become successful (8,13). The similarities between Burnet and Bowen do not end 
with their commitment to theory and the distinction between 
self and nonself, which is as central to the science of immuno­
logy as it is crucial in understanding emotional systems.

Burnet 
could only come to a profound understanding of the immune 
system when he saw it from an evolutionary point of view; and 
Bowen, in viewing the human phenomenon from that perspec­
tive, enables a major connection to be made between homo 
sapiens and the natural world. The idea of evolution makes 
sense of the diversity of all living forms and brings order to the 
study of biology (15). But evolution always involves genetic 
changes in populations (16) -a very unconsoling thought for 
one who would like to attempt to modify self within one life­
time. A possible way out of this dilemma is to realize the 
immune system does learn and therefore is able to survive 
because of this individual learning. Given the many potential antigens that may be encoun­
tered in a single lifetime, waiting for the population to evolve 
in order to handle these antigens would prove fatal. Conse­
quently, vertebrates through the immune system gain informa­
tion by interacting with their environment. This specific 
information regarding how to respond to newly encountered 
antigens is not inherited, although the general response mech­
anism is genetically transmitted. Every "self' has to build up a 
history of encounters with "nonself' in its own lifetime in 
order to continue in existence. Cunningham describes this 
phenomenon in the following quotation: 
An immune system is like a symbiotic population of uni­
cellular organisms (lymphocytes) inside its vertebrate host.

phenomenon in the following quotation: 
An immune system is like a symbiotic population of uni­
cellular organisms (lymphocytes) inside its vertebrate host. A great variety of different types (specificities) evolves 
with this population, some of them being encouraged by 
antigens to proliferate, secrete their specific products, and 
to provide protection for· their host. Immune adaptation 
to entirely new antigens thus appear to depend ultimately 
on a classical evolutionary mechanism of individual (lym­
phocyte) variation and selection (9, p.234). When one applies this to emotional systems, it becomes 
clear that no matter how well or poorly the population has 
 done, each human self within his or her own lifetime must 
learn to deal with oneself in a way that is adaptive. This kind 
of adaptive capacity is not inherited. Although our beginnings 
are radically influenced by the past generations, without fur­
ther individual learning in interacting with the environment-a 
learning that is analogous to both "memory" and "tolerance" 
within an individual immune system-one's survival is at stake. What does the focus on predictable reliability and coher­
ence do to my previous way of knowing? At this point, I have 
more questions than answers.

What does the focus on predictable reliability and coher­
ence do to my previous way of knowing? At this point, I have 
more questions than answers. Factually, I could not make a 
serious effort to work at understanding science until I wrote 
and presented a paper documenting my effort to modify an 
emotionally cut-off position with those who most influenced 
my earlier attempts at understanding the human phenomenon 
( 16). Once personal contact was re-established with past men­
tors, I could begin to learn the basic grammar of scientific 
knowing. My current opinion is that even though science can 
generate theories that are more predictably reliable and coher­
ent, other ways of knowing are necessary for human under­
standing to be comprehensive. Reality, I believe, is more than 
what can be tested empirically through feedback with nature. What is compelling to me about science is the attempt to 
become more and more objective. I am beginning to realize 
that those thinkers who helped me most in the past were all 
engaged in a quest for objectivity that was at the same time 
deeply personal. The search for objective knowlege that can be 
personally validated may be an underlying connection between 
my past way of knowing and my desire to be scientific. REFERENCES

BIOFEEDBACK FOR DIABETES * 
Lilian Rosenbaum, LCSW, Ph.D. My initial interest and work on the question of how to 
measure and how to understand change in family psycho­
therapy led to an interest in biofeedback and to its powerful 
potential for producing as well as measuring change. Since 
biofeedback focuses on regulation of one's own physiology, it 
conceptually fits with family systems theory which focuses on 
change of self. In becoming more knowledgeable about biofeedback in 
the 1970's and more active in the national society (Biofeedback 
Society of America), I became aware that diabetes mellitus 
was considered a condition for which biofeedback was poten­
tially dangerous. An early case study by another investigator 
reported that biofeedback was helpful in decreasing required 
insulin, but produced severe and unexpected hypoglycemia. That biofeedback could produce such a powerful effect as to 
be contraindicated for diabetes further piqued my curiosity. I have been working in this area for almost ten years now. Conceptualizing and providing biofeedback treatment in the 
context of Bowen Theory helped to avert such complications.

I have been training diabetic patients with biofeedback. When 
I began treating diabetic patients with biofeedback* in 1976 
(usually for reasons other than diabetes) it was considered 
risky to train diabetic persons because of potential complica­
tions (2, 5), including insulin reactions. The integration of family therapy (1) with biofeedback 
helped to prevent such complications. Patient education and 
the advent of Hemoglobin Ale and home blood glucose moni­
toring have further reduced this risk. However, it is still essen­
tial that biofeedback be done in close collaboration with the 
attending physician. Currently, most of my work with diabetics 
takes place in the context of a team that includes a diabetolo­
gist, a dietician and a nurse educator.** 
The role of stress in metabolic decompensation in diabetes 
has been recognized for at least three centuries. Insulin defi­
ciency alone is not thought to be sufficient to induce metabolic 
decompensation. The pancreatic insuli,1 cells are directly con­
tacted by the sympathetic nervous system which suppresses 
insulin secretion and the parasympathetic nervous system 
which stimulates it. Environmental and emotional factors such 
as family processes can elevate blood glucose through sympa­
thetic nervous system hormones.

as family processes can elevate blood glucose through sympa­
thetic nervous system hormones. Thus, there is a mechanism 
whereby modulation of stress hormone excess may prevent 
metabolic decompensation. Stress is a complex psychological and biological process 
which is generally initiated by a situation perceived to be 
potentially harmful or dangerous. Cannon called it the "fight­
or flight" response. Humans, like other animals, react in a 
predictable way to acutely and chronically stressful situations 
which trigger an automatic response that has been part of our 
physiological make-up for millions of years. This reaction has 
survival value, but when real or imagined stressors persist, 
repeated "fight-or-flight" response results in chronic imbalance 
of the finely tuned systems of the body. Inability to return to 
homeostatic balance leads to the breakdown of one or more 
systems in the organism such as those that regulate blood 
glucose. The literature on stress management in clinical practice, 
especially biofeedback, clearly indicates its rapid and highly 
successful development. Biofeedback training provides imme­
diate and continuous information (through auditory or visual 
signals) of physiological responses of which the individual is
