ordinarily unaware. This information facilitates self-regulation. Biofeedback is now a major resource for the medical and psy­
chological treatment of various conditions including pain 
management, asthma, hypertension and headaches. The Biofeedback Program at the Georgetown University 
Family Center uses biofeedback in conjunction with other 
self-regulation approaches. The usual biofeedback procedure 
includes intake, baseline measurements and a minimum of 
eight hour-long weekly sessions followed by monthly or semi­
annual sessions as appropriate. The person is hooked up to 
equipment which monitors indicators of stress including 
muscle tension, skin temperature, skin conductance, blood 
pressure and heart rate, and the person learns to self-regulate 
by attending to auditory or visual signals emitted by the equip­
ment. The task, for instance, is to decrease the frequency and 
intensity of the intermittent sounds by relaxing muscle tension 
or by increasing digital skin temperature. The sound (feedback) 
facilitates achieving the task and optimizing homeostatic bal­
ance. Gradually the person learns to generalize control to daily 
life activities. In addition, such self-regulation techniques as 
diaphragmatic breathing and progressive relaxation are taught, 
and the individual practkes at home with audio cassettes. This program has pioneered the integration of family 
therapy with biofeedback.

This program has pioneered the integration of family 
therapy with biofeedback. It interprets family processes and 
life events as potential stressors. Family theory is basically a 
way of thinking for both the "coach" (therapist) and the di~­
betic individual which helps the individual to self-regulate m 
the context of family stressors. The treatment is usually done 
with one individual because the way of thinking about life and 
family process is the essential focus, not how many relatives 
are in the session. This focus is to (1) observe and define pat­
terns of behavior in self and family, (2) reduce anxiety in self 
and family by reducing one's own over-reactivity to stress­
related processes that derive from and are transmitted by the 
family system, and (3) increase one's own degree of integration 
or autonomy. In the initial clinical study(3) on the long-term impact of 
biofeedback training on six insulin treated diabetics (four 
Type I and two Type II), I found that all showed improved 
stress-coping skills and ability to control physical indicators of 
stress. Two-thirds showed a decrease in blood glucose levels, 
two-thirds reduced insulin dosages and two-thirds had lowered 
incidence of glycemic fluctuations. All improved on at least 
one of these indicators of diabetic control except one person 
who started in adequate control. 2 These people represented a wide range of life situations 
and problems.

to a country in which no medical care was available was able 
to control tachycardia, headaches, and herpes, to discontinue 
drug abuse, and to keep blood glucose values stable for five 
years. As the clinical work progresses, we are finding ways to 
improve its effectiveness. Patient care is closely coordinated 
between the biofeedback-family therapist and the diabetolo­
gist, nutritionist and nurse educator. Patients are taught to 
attend to home glucose monitoring as a stress-related biofeed­
back signal. We ( 4) recently found that blood glucose decreases 
during a single biofeedback session. When initial blood glucose 
was below 250 mg/dl at the start of the session, 93% of the 
patients showed a decrease which averaged 8% at the end of 
the session.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. It is difficult to discuss any specific symptom or clinical 
entity such as cancer without losing perspective on how that 
particular problem fits into a larger picture that pertains to all 
symptoms. The human is prone to getting lost in detail and to 
compartmentalizing bits and pieces of knowledge. The develop­
ment of theory depends on an ability to see the interrelation­
ships between these various compartments. This is never an 
easy task. The guiding assumption in my attempts to understand 
cancer has been that man is a product of evolution and that 
part of his evolutionary heritage is an emotional system go­
verned by principles that govern all life. I believe that our 
ultimate understanding of cancer will be rooted in this context. The idea of an evolutionary based emotional system was 
developed by Murray Bowen in the 1950's. For the most part 
people have had little comprehension of it. Cancer has taught 
me a great deal about my own limited understanding of the 
nature of emotional systems. One day there will be a unified theory of cancer and other 
clinical syndromes.

Cancer has taught 
me a great deal about my own limited understanding of the 
nature of emotional systems. One day there will be a unified theory of cancer and other 
clinical syndromes. This theory will be some type of systems 
theory capable of incorporating all the facts about cancer 
defined by cell research, genetics, immunology, endocrinology, 
psychology, family relationships and other fields known to 
play a role in the development and clinical course of cancer. I am convinced that the emotional aspects of family 
relationships can play a role in a particular family member 
developing cancer. This does not imply that the characteristics 
of family relationships cause cancer. I am also convinced that 
emotional factors within a person and their mechanism for 
dealing with emotion have an influence on the development 
and course of cancer. Again, this by no means implies that psy­
chological factors cause cancer. It is beyond question that

People who focus on emotional 
factors and the role of stress in cancer have as much problem 
with _this as anyone else. But with a unified theory of cancer 
we will one day see that cancer is not genes, not the immune 
system, not psychology, not family relationships, but all these 
things. The influence of any one factor will likely be shown to 
vary from case to case, with no one factor ever being shown to 
be sufficient by itself. When I began interviewing cancer patients and members 
of their families seven years ago, I thought I had a fairly good 
understanding of family systems theory. With theory as a lens, 
I wanted to learn about the nature of the emotional processes 
I believed to be important in cancer. The project led me in 
directions I had not anticipated. What I examined the most 
was my lens. Dr. Bowen had written about the nature of the emotional 
processes in the nuclear and multigenerational family that, he 
theorized, contributed to the development of all symptoms: 
physical, emotional, and social. He had written that the "de­
selfed" spouse was the one, during periods of sustained high 
anxiety, most prone to develop symptoms. So I found myself 
confronted with a patient who had cancer and pondered the 
evidence that this indeed was the more de-selfed spouse. I was 
confronted with my own simplistic understanding of what this 
concept was about. It was a fascinating experience. I had a 
new way to learn.

An unexpected dividend of the cancer research is the 
impact it has had on my approach to psychotherapy. I had no 
funding for my work with cancer patients and saw them on 
my own time at no charge. I related to them as a resource for 
my learning and the only contract I had with them was that I 
would lend a hand in any way I could if they would inform me 
about the problem to the best of their ability. In the beginning I was looking for the family that would 
give me the ultimate answer. Of course, I never found such a 
family. So I concentrated on learning whatever I could from 
each situation. To my amazement, interview sessions were 
loose and low key, even though the problems were quite ser­
ious. I was asking what I would call honest questions. I was 
genuinely trying to learn, and was not attempting to influence 
the_ family. Bowen likes to define a therapist as a person trying 
to mfluence somebody else. I was working hard not to be a 
therapist. Actually it was not work because I became fascinated 
by what I was learning and forgot all about being a therapist. 3 
 Meanwhile, I was continuing my private practice where I 
was treating a wide range of clinical problems. Gradually, I 
began to notice that the cancer families seemed to be getting 
a better therapeutic result than the families in my practice! Until that point I had not fully appreciated how much subtle 
pressure I could put on myself to provide answers to the fami­
lies I saw.

they were important enough to change my conception of the 
basis for effective therapy. Some might counter what I am saying with the view that 
one may focus on good questions and not try to influence 
people when doing research, but that is not an appropriate 
posture for people who seek therapy. I am now convinced that 
when people's thinking gets polarized into research versus ther­
apy, they have lost a systems perspective. Systems thinking 
brings theory, research and therapy into an inseparable whole. I recently conducted a two-day conference on family 
systems in upstate New York. It was a great experience. For 
the most part the people attending asked thoughtful questions 
and harnessed any preconceived notions about what I should 
be doing for them or how I should be enlightening them. A 
presenter faces the same problem with an audience that a ther­

cancer a few years ago I defined four categories of variables 
which are the same ones that Bowen has previously defined 
with other clinical problems. (2,3) The four interrelated areas 
are: differentiation of self, level of chronic anxiety, anxiety­
binding mechanisms, and emotional cut-off. An entire book 
could be written about each area. Differentiation of self is probably the least understood 
area and ironically one of the most important variables. All 
people who get cancer are not the same and all situations in 
which cancer emerges are not the same. An important way in 
which people and family situations differ is related to the level 
of differentiation. Differentiation, defined in its most basic 
sense, describes the adaptiveness of people and family systems. Over the course of generations systems can gradually lose or

This kind

juvenile diabetes, for example. Some families and patients 
adapt beautifully and the problem is managed on a thoughtful 
and realistic level. Other families are thrown into chaos that 
lasts for years. Some cancers occur when there has been a rapid 
buildup of situational factors, factors that can be remedied. Other cancers occur in emotional situations that are more 
chronic in nature. There is less flexibility and fewer options. The level of chronic anxiety is a product of the multigen­
erational past, coupled with real or anticipated events in the 
present. Events are important to the extent that they have an 
impact on the balance of emotional forces in a relationship 
system and trigger an increase in the level of chronic anxiety. Relationship systems clearly adapt more successfully when 
chronic anxiety is low. Chronic anxiety is more basic than 
what is conveyed by the statement, "I feel anxious." Some 
form of it seems to be a part of all natural systems. It is inti­
mately connected with man's evolutionary past and is influ­
enced by the social environment. Anxiety-binding mechanisms describe the way anxiety is 
managed in a relationship system and account for the fact that 
the system's anxiety can come to rest disproportionately in a 
particular person. Where the anxiety most comes to rest is a 
by-product of the way everyone in the system functions in 
relationship to everyone else.

Where the anxiety most comes to rest is a 
by-product of the way everyone in the system functions in 
relationship to everyone else. It is inaccurate to think of this as 
one person causing another to be sick. It is an emotionally 
driven, literally mindless process that nobody wants or needs. It is just a fact that when the level of chronic anxiety increases, 
people take on characteristics of functioning that they do not 
have when the system is calmer. These anxiety-driven changes 
in the way people deal with one another can leave one person 
in a more compromised position than the others and conse­
quently vulnerable to developing symptoms. The fundamental 
emotional forces are the same regardless of the type of symp­
tom that emerges. People offer all kinds of explanations for 
why people do the things they do to each other, but I believe 
a complete understanding of this will rest in a better under­
standing of all natural systems and the forces that shape evolu­
tion. Emotional cut-off describes the way people manage their 
relationships with extended family. A high percentage of 
people seek relief from problematic relationships with their 
original families by avoidance and by keeping what contacts 
do occur emotionally sterile. Others may stay in physical con­
tact, but cut-off through internal mechanisms. When people do 
this they lose the most enduring emotional support system 
they can possibly ever have.

tact, but cut-off through internal mechanisms. When people do 
this they lose the most enduring emotional support system 
they can possibly ever have. Viable emotional contact with 
extended family can be a valuable resource for cushioning the 
impact of stress in a nuclear family. Without that connection, 
people are operating with a handicap. This is not to say that 
one can automatically assume that increasing contact with the 
extended family, particularly at a time of crisis, is going to 
automatically help things. It can make the situation worse, 
particularly when people do not manage the contacts properly. But with some help toward being more objective, reduction of 
emotional cut-off can do much to ameliorate the problems of 
a given nuclear family. None of these variables taken individually or collectively 
directly causes cancer or any other clinical problem. But taken 
together they do define an important background emotional 
process to be considered in understanding the development 
and course of clinical symptoms. One day the concepts from 
family emotional systems theory will be integrated with sys­
tems concepts that emerge from other levels of investigation to 
form a unified theory in medicine. REFERENCES

literature. As with many services to the deaf, these applications

heart rate, and blood pressure that reflects the actual physio-

The title I chose, The Importance 
of Theory to Nursing Practice, gave me a lot of room to roam. I could appropriately give this same paper to a gathering of 
social workers by simply changing the title to The Importance 
of Theory to Social Work Practice. I do not view the nursing 
profession, in other words, as one that would uniquely benefit 
from hearing attempts at a broader theoretical understanding 
of the human phenomenon. The past ten to twelve months have been especially 
important in terms of achieving a little better theoretical 
understanding of human behavior. I have experienced two 
other periods like this. One was during 1970 and 1971 when 
theory was taking on new importance as I grappled to under­
stand my own family. The other was between 1977 and 1979 
when I was initially trying to make sense of the relationship of 
cancer to the emotional impact people have on one another in 
a family. The primary stimulus toward theoretical thinking in the 
past year has been writing. I have written more in these past 
twelve months than during any previous period of my profes­
sional life. Writing professional papers is always an arduous 
task, but I had made the commitment to complete certain 
book chapters and articles, and the editors were serious about 
deadlines. The problem I encounter in writing is being confronted 
with the lack of clarity of my thinking. Writing is an attempt 
to discover what I really think.

The problem I encounter in writing is being confronted 
with the lack of clarity of my thinking. Writing is an attempt 
to discover what I really think. It can be frustrating however, 
that even after third and fourth rewrites I am still discovering 
I do not know what I think. There is still something in my 
head that I have not pulled together adequately enough to get 
on paper. The end result is that I usually get a little clearer 
about the distinction between what I know and what I do not 
know. Making this distinction then helps set a more reasoned 
direction for further thinking. This process repeats and repeats. In spite of what I believe I gain, it still is almost as easy to 
put off writing as it was five or ten years ago. I especially re­
member a comment Murray Bowen made about four years ago 
after a particularly intense period of trying to clarify his think­
ing on a variety of points: "How much can I stand to learn?" 
I think I am beginning to understand what he meant. Imitating others and memorizing facts have a place and do 
require some energy, but the amount of energy expended in 
those activities is small in comparison to that expended in 
really trying to think. People tend to give a lot of automatic 
responses to many issues, responses that are strongly influ­
enced by feelings or simply what they have picked up from the 
social environment.

When I am in the middle of a writing project, I believe 
that I am also doing better psychotherapy. I think the therapy 
is improved because I am more emotionally detached from the 
clinical problem and its myriad details. At the same time, I am 
probably in better contact with people and their problems 
during these periods of greater detachment. What a paradox! Detachment promotes contact and contact promotes detach­
ment. There has been more misunderstanding about this parti­
cular point than almost any other in systems theory and that 
misunderstanding completely confuses people's ideas about 
the concept of differentiation of self. How can you be more 
separate and in better contact simultaneously? Differentiation 
permits such a seeming paradox to be a reality. Now I am not suggesting that everyone "should" be writ­
ing. Writing is an illustration of the nature of what I am trying 
to describe. It is not the writing that is so important, but the 
addressing of the thinking process that is important. If every­
one were making a serious effort to examine the nature of his 
or her mental filter and the role it played in the problems they 
see around them, I believe it would be a different world. There 
might be less war, less divorce and even less schizophrenia. I am keenly aware of how much work it takes for me to 
attempt this. It is easy to put off examining my filter and even 
easier to fail to recognize the need for such examination.

mental filter is something every individual with the motivation 
can work on and make some progress with. All that is required

about is the value and importance of looking at self. This is the 
antithesis of blaming others, focusing on others, tunnel vision, 
and reductionistic thinking. The helping professions, steeped 
as they are in the subjectivity that permeates society, promote 
a great deal of the very problems they are charged by society 
to treat. For the most part, helping professionals do this unwit­
tingly and with the best of intentions. We do it with our own

in Boston and stopped by my office to talk about his impres­
sions of the trip. Among the points he made was that he had 
realized again the difficulty people have making the distinction

Center we call a "think tank." I found this particular session 
quite thought-provoking. Dan Papero had abstracted a dozen 
articles from Scientific American that described some fascina­
ting aspects of living systems. He described, for example, the 
orderly fashion in which certain herbivorous dinosaurs nested 
their eggs. Then he described how certain carnivorous dino­
saurs had evolved to place their eggs in proximity to the eggs 
of the herbivores. When the young carnivores broke out of 
their shells, they just eased over and feasted on the herbivore 
eggs. I think what fascinated Dan was the orderly nature of 
this evolutionary arrangement. If you can see the distinction 
between content and process in the human family, and I mean 
really see it, then what becomes clear is that there is little in 
the human family that cannot be observed in the rest of nature 
and perhaps nothing in the rest of nature that cannot also be 
observed in the human family. I am not talking about the 
human family being analogous to other aspects of nature.

I am not talking about the 
human family being analogous to other aspects of nature. I am 
talking about the fact that the human family is nature and 
nature is the human family. This type of "closure" that takes 
one beyond simply making analogies between man and the rest 
of nature is automatic when homo sapiens can look at himself 
and see process as well as content. This kind of "closure" is 
not possible when one's mental filter is not able to make this 
distinction between content and process. If the observer sees 
only content, he is so overwhelmed with detail that natural 
systems can never provide more than interesting analogies to 
human activity. I was listening to a mental health professional present a 
series of clinical cases a few weeks ago. This particular thera­
pist had read a great deal about family systems theory and had 
attended many of our Family Center conferences over the 
years. But this was my first chance to really listen to how he 
thought about what he observed in clinical families. It was a 
fascinating experience to listen for what he had "heard" and 
"not heard" in terms of theory in the years of exposure. He 
had not heard numerous things that had probably been said 
hundreds of times in hundreds of different ways over the 
years. He had also heard a great deal and seemed to be a pretty 
good therapist. What intrigued me, of course, was what he had not heard. I had the challenge, as his supervisor, of addressing myself to 
those areas.

What intrigued me, of course, was what he had not heard. I had the challenge, as his supervisor, of addressing myself to 
those areas. My goal was not to change his thinking, but to 
define my own as clearly as I could to present a contrast. As 
we talked even then, I am sure that what I said and what he 
heard me say were quite different. I was also keenly aware of 
the emotional tension that could be set off in each of us based 
on my effort to stay focused on differences. It is still impres­
sive to me how the undifferentiation between people can be 
reflected in this incredible intolerance of differences and the 
push for sameness. There is a strong tendency in me, unlike a 
rebel, to obliterate differences and to bask in the comfort that 
comes from seeming agreement. It is simply easier for me to 
do it that way. A rebel will, of course, exaggerate differences 
and find some kind of comfort in that position. Automatic 
compliance or rebellion are both emotionally determined posi­
tions rooted in people's undifferentiation. What I was striving 
toward in this supervisory situation was to provide a thought­
fully determined contrast to the other person's viewpoint. This 
is not to say that I was "right" and he was "wrong," but simply 
there were differences. Dr. Bowen has provided this kind of contrast for me and 
many, many others over the years. I believe this contrast pro­
vides the potential for learning. I cannot say that Bowen 
"taught" me family theory.

heard and to say that is not what he said. Many people may already have in mind some distinction 
between content and process. I am guessing that the distinc­
tions are not particularly consistent with the distinction defin­
ed by family systems theory. If I presume that I can explain 
the distinction systems theory makes between content and 
process, I would likely be doing a disservice to your efforts to 
learn. So I will not do it. All that I will say is that I know there 
is a way to see past all the details of family interaction and 
past the myriad of reductionistic explanations that people wil­
lingly provide for why people do the things they do. When it is 
possible to see past these, it becomes possible to observe the 
more fundamental "forces" or "patterns" at work. When 
people achieve even a tiny bit more clarity in this regard, it 
automatically promotes more neutrality about the human 
process. It is this emotional neutrality that allows increased

As Carl Sagan points 
out: 
" ... from eight billion light years away we are hard pressed 
to find even the cluster in which our Milky Way galaxy is 
imbedded, much less the Sun or the Earth. The only pla­
net we are sure is inhabited is a tiny speck of rock and 
metal shining feebly by reflected sunlight, and at this 
distance utterly lost." 
At the Family Center we now have a "picture" of the Milky 
Way galaxy hanging in the waiting room. There is an arrow 
pointing toward one tiny star in the galaxy and this star is our 
own Sun. The words next to the arrow say, "You are here." 
When people see that picture, it seems to have some kind of 
calming effect on them. At least, that is the gist of the remarks 
I hear people make about it. I do believe that a broader per­
spective, the kind generated by such a picture, has that kind of 
impact on people. This is what systems thinking is basically 
about -an attempt to get away from tunnel vision and move 
toward a larger view. I would like to leave you with one last thought which 
pertains to the galaxy we have been discussing. Our galaxy is 
continually moving. We probably only know a limited amount 
about the ways in which it is moving, but we do know that it 
rotates. It takes approximately a quarter of a billion years for 
our galaxy to rotate once. It has rotated about eighteen times 
since our particular solar system began to take shape.

It takes approximately a quarter of a billion years for 
our galaxy to rotate once. It has rotated about eighteen times 
since our particular solar system began to take shape. We all 
know that the Earth goes around the Sun once a year and so 
on June 11, 1983, we were in exactly the same position in 
relationship to the Sun that we are in right now. With just a 
little difficulty you might be able to remember where you 
were and what you were doing when the Earth was in this 
same spot a year ago. Exactly eighteen orbits around the sun 
ago, I was getting married. But none of you remember what 
you were doing on even the most recent of the galaxy's last 
rotations, 250,000,000 years ago. You do not remember 
because you did not exist and homo sapiens did not exist. It 
took the Earth nearly eighteen trips around the galaxy to pro­
duce a human. Exactly one galactic rotation ago, the fishes 
were evolving rapidly, and the first dry-land plants and animals 
were emerging. Just one galactic rotation ago, the dinosaurs 
were still a distant gleam in some tiny reptile's eye. Just think 
about what it will be like the next time we pass this way again. And we still have about twenty more rotations of our galaxy 
before our little sun burns out. A lot can happen in that time.

Michael E. Kerr, M.D. The past year at the Family Center has been one of renewed 
emphasis on basic theoretical concepts, and the Twenty-Second 
Annual Family Symposium reflected that emphasis. It was an 
important meeting by virtue of its clearly defining George­
town's present direction. The Symposium was held October 19 and 20, 1985 at 
Stouffer's Hotel in Crystal City, Virginia and was attended by 
about two hundred people. The format was similar to past 
years, featuring major presentations by the Distinguished Guest 
lecturer, Dr. Stephen J. Suomi, and by Dr. Murray Bowen, and 
including fourteen other papers. The banquet on Saturday 
night again featured a "special" videotape made by Drs. Bowen 
and Kerr. The major focus of this year's meeting was the emotional 
system and differentiation of self. The emphasis was on the 
emotional system as a natural system with deep evolutionary 
roots and on differentiation as more than a psychological 
process. Dr. Stephen Suomi presented for more than two hours on 
his research with rhesus monkeys and contributed significantly 
to people's gaining more understanding of the theoretical bases 
of family systems theory. Dr. Suomi had worked under Harry 
Harlow at Wisconsin for many years, and now conducts his 
studies at the N.I.M.H.

Suomi cautioned people about making such assumptions, but 
his presentation had been so full of information and so effec­

close the barn door long after the horse had escaped the barn! Suomi's research with monkeys supports the basic assump­

duct of that part of man he has in common with the lower 
animals. The conclusion that the human process is guided by 
emotional forces similar to those that guide the other primates 
is inescapable when Suomi's findings are compared with the 
findings of human family research. Murray Bowen presented a historical perspective on the 
family movement in an effort to define the origins of the 
Georgetown Family Program, the program's current place in WINTER 1986 
the field, and its direction for the future. The goal remains to 
work toward a science of human behavior.

the concepts of family systems theory. Socio biological thinking

to specific genes. Family systems assumes the existence of an 
emotional system that is universally present in nature and 
anchored at a level more basic than genes. Dr. Papero's paper, 
Functional States, D.O. Hebb and Differentiation of Self, 
emphasized the relevance of Hebb's concepts about functional 
states in the brain to the concepts of family systems theory. Among the many areas Dr. Papero explored was the interrela­
tionship of mental activity and emotional reactivity.

about the relationship of these changes to level of differentia­

ideas from systems theory with knowledge emerging from bio­
logical psychiatry. Dr. Rosenbaum's paper, Diabetic Biological 
Markers, Biofeedback, and Family Therapy, picked up fascina­
ting new pieces of information from medicine and related 
them to family ideas. The thickness of the capillary basement 
membrane can be used to determine a person's vulnerability to 
developing diabetes. She suggested that if an understanding of 
multigenerational emotional process was combined with knowl­
edge of this biological marker, it might enhance our under­
standing of clinical diabetes. One observation that emerges from reviewing these papers 
is that people knowledgeable about family systems ideas tend 
to reach toward other sciences in an effort to further their 
understanding. Most of this still amounts to drawing analogies 
between bodies of knowledge but, as each year passes, people 
move a bit further toward transcending analogy and extending 
theory.

AND EMOTIONAL SYSTEMS * 
Edward W. Beal, M.D. Efforts have been made at Georgetown symposia over the 
years to determine what man has in common with lower forms 
of life and to use these evolutionary guidelines to develop a 
biologically based view of emotional systems. After watching 
the television series, "Cosmos," it occurred to me that the 
science of physics and mathematics might provide information 
about emotional systems that predates biology. The beginning of life might be conceptualized as the juxta­
posing of certain chemicals in the proper spatial relationship. Certainly, physical chemistry and mathematics could provide 
information about this process. This paper focuses on the con­
cepts of physical space, absolute time, the speed of light and 
the idea of relativity.

cepts of physical space, absolute time, the speed of light and 
the idea of relativity. After giving concrete examples that illus­
trate these theoretical principles related to the physical world, 
I will apply these principles derived from the observation of 
physical space to observations about emotional space. One 
purpose of the paper is to determine whether one can concep­
tualize physical and emotional space in similar patterns of 
organization. Isaac Newton lived from the mid-seventeenth until the 
early eighteenth century. In 1687, he developed a mathemati­
cal interpretation of natural phenomena in accordance with 
well defined physical principles and called it the law of univer­
sal gravitation. This was the first great systemization of knowl­
edge in the physical sciences. His formulation served as the 
groundwork from which the sciences of astronomy and mech­

This paper 
presents a single case study characteristic of this process. This woman, referred to as Mrs. K, began therapy at a 
point of general dissatisfaction in her life and the beginning of 
an effort to define a new direction for her energies. Mrs. K's 
mother is an older sister with one sister. She was married at 
age 30 and discontinued her active career as a teacher. She 
resumed her teaching only when financial need dictated, and 
only when children were school age. She was geographically 
and emotionally distant from her own family. Mrs. K's maternal grandmother was a housewife with many 
homemaking skills. Her maternal grandfather was a grocer and 
emotionally distant from the family. Their marriage was stable 
but unsatisfactory to both of them for most of their adult lives. Mrs. K's father is a youngest brother of several sisters and 
brothers. He was married at age 27 and had a career as a school 
administrator and science teacher. His father died when he was 
only 4, and his mother never remarried. She never had a formal 
career, although she attended a "normal school" before she 
married. She did not work after her husband's death except to 
"take in boarders," but she continued her education formally 
and informally all her life. Mrs. K grew up with one younger brother. She left home 
to attend college at age 16 and received her undergraduate 
degree at age 21.

Mrs. K grew up with one younger brother. She left home 
to attend college at age 16 and received her undergraduate 
degree at age 21. She married immediately and set aside all 
interest in career in favor of raising a family, something that 
was expected of her and that she expected of herself. It was 
not until the youngest of four children reached school age and 
she was clear that there would be no more children that she 
thought about a career. Without the energy absorbed in raising 
small children, she was becoming overinvolved with her hus­
band and worried over the children. Her exploration of career goals led her to graduate school 
and eventually to a position in a community mental health cen­
ter. Both graduate school and the new job put new demands on her and the family. After about two years she gave up this 
challenging, satisfying job for a teaching position that she 
believed would better satisfy perceived family needs. Her work 
satisfaction decreased, and the job became very stressful for 
her and for the family. At this point she began to explore, in 
therapy, the emotional issues that were present for her family 
through the generations. Several family themes were evident to her from the begin­
ning of therapy, but they seemed, at first, to have very little to 
do with her. She knew that she was no carbon copy of the past, 
so she did not have an appreciation for the way in which those 
themes were active in her.

past generation, the following themes from the past began to 
emerge and their connection to Mrs. K's own life began to be 
recognized: the family (i.e., children) is the most important 
aspect of life; hope resides in the next generation; anything 
can be sacrificed for the family (i.e., children) including career, 
health, life, goals, marital happiness; work or personal interests 
should never interfere with perceived family needs; don't 
expect too much from marriage during the years of raising 
children, but don't jeopardize the marriage -that is, adapt to 
the perceived needs of your spouse to maintain the bond; 
when children become distant (as each generation did with 
their parents) you will need each other; personal concerns are 
better kept quiet if they would disturb the bond. The list continued to grow as the connection between 
those past generations and her own life began to be recognized. As therapy progressed, she realized that these themes had 
operated as unstated assumptions most of her adult life. Once 
stated, it became possible to begin to examine them as satis­
factory or unsatisfactory beliefs for her own life. At the first reasonable opportunity, Mrs. K moved into 
career directions that were becoming clearer each year and 
that were more consistent with her abilities and goals.

career directions that were becoming clearer each year and 
that were more consistent with her abilities and goals. There 
were predictable reactions from family members, particularly 
her mother, when the career took on an importance equal to 
that of children and husband. During this period, despite her 
mother's reaction to the new importance of work in her life, 
she was able to know the source of many issues that had been 
"differences" between them. Her mother became a more acces­
sible person to her when she could see the way in which her 
mother had also been influenced by the beliefs and assump­
tions of the past. The responses of Mrs. K were also predictable. She found 
it emotionally upsetting to go against the part of her that was 
solidly programmed to act in accordance with the themes of 
the past. However, there was an equally strong pull toward the 
personal satisfaction that came from meaningful work. The 
results were equally positive for her husband and children, 
who did not have to carry the burden of her previous over­
involvement with them. In the past several years Mrs. K's career course has become 
more consistent with personal abilities and interests. This has 
been parallel to her gradual ability to know the important life 
 issues that were shaped by the undefined assumptions and 
beliefs that had influenced the family for several generations.

in their lives as a whole. Five have not been successful connecting their lives to the 
broader picture of themes and people from the past. They 
remain focused only on their immediate concerns in the nuclear 
family, particularly children. They have relief from their major 
symptoms, but their efforts have not been accompanied by 
broader changes in the family or in their career. Clinical practice produces many examples of women

whose lives are out of balance in the areas of work, family, and 
marriage. Knowledge of multigenerational themes provides one 
tool for increasing flexibility and self-awareness. Bowen theory 
can provide a framework for thinking about those issues so 
that it becomes more than an exercise in genealogy or family 
history. To accomplish solid change, the issues of the past must be 
more than history. A woman must know them as her own 
issues that connect to those important people in her past and 
influence the way she relates to them as well. Her ability to 
know emotionally the issues that come from the past is related 
to her ability to know the people of her past. When this know­
ing is effective, change takes place at many levels -knowledge, 
awareness, emotions and relationships-before it becomes inte­
grated into broader life changes described briefly in this paper. THE IMPACT OF EXTENDED FAMILY

mother and worker. The difficulty is finding the most appro­
priate balance among the roles each woman chooses to play. That balance, as reflected in the amount of time, energy, com­
mitment and humor invested in each area, is determined by a 
number of factors.

the most important factors influencing the balance worked out 
by each woman is the multigenerational balance worked out

prompted an attempt to observe whether there was a relation­

in operating the family grocery store. The maternal grand­

her spouse is transferred or promoted. This allows traditional 
family themes defining the role of wife and mother to converge 
abruptly with contemporary family values involving career. The first generation woman in a family to choose to make a 
transition from more traditional female roles to career, when 
in the midst of personal and professional conflict, confronts 
powerful emotional forces exerted by long held traditional 
family values. Such women may receive multiple emotionally 
charged messages from the generations above them: from overt 
hostility, to puzzlement, to benign acceptance, to the mandate 
to succeed fully in areas where past generations of women 
were unable to aspire. Progress is sought without the benefit or 
guidance of female family role models. The decisions made by 
transitional generation women to cope with these forces will 
pave the way for their own daughters and granddaughters 
potentially to make more personally autonomous decisions. This subject's career decision remains a paradox. Personal 
insight was gained only through her willingness to take the risk 
and leave her career. The emotional price paid for her willing­
ness to risk her career by leaving it was offset by the personal 
insight which she does not believe she would have gained by 
staying home.

What were the work and identity principles that guided a 
German and an Irish grandmother? How did their beliefs and 
mores affect a mother's decision in the working world? And 
what role did these generations of attitudes and actions play in 
an individual's decision to embark on a career and to begin a 
private practice? The pivotal step in finding a self involved seeing and under­
~tanding how the behavior and attitudes of past generations of 
a family shaped behaviors and attitudes of the present genera­
tion. One is never truly free of the past until one can see it 
clearly; until one can lift self out of the tangle of the past. As 
Dr. Bowen has remarked, "Freedom is not in the Constitution, 
it's in one's own life." 
The question was: How do women in a family find freedom 
in their own life around the issue of work in paid employment? To answer the question, family records were searched and the 
subject was discussed with family members to glean memories 
and attitudes. Historical and sociological background was 
researched to put the family's portrait in context. From the 17th century, the maternal family descended 
from German tradespeople and farmers, a middle-class group 
that immigrated to the U. S. to seek "a better life economic­
ally." For generations women had worked to help out the 
family while essentially adhering to the German shibboleth, 
Kindern, Kirche, Kuche, children, church and kitchen, which 
both defined and limited their sphere of activities.

primarily in government circles. She insisted on an active 
intellectual life, and her children read and reread the classics 
from their earliest years.

cation "makes a lady out of a woman." It makes her "a credit 
to her husband." Women were viewed as reflectors of their 
husbands. So, how does a person define a self in a family where tradi­
tionally the role of female has been to "help out" her spouse 
or to "reflect on him well economically and socially?" Cau­
tiously! Each person is an integral part of his family emotional 
system. Genetically for sure, and emotionally, how could it be 
otherwise? Even today family patterns are not fully clear and 
may not be for years to come. With feet rooted in a traditional 
past, from a family bearing strong definitions of what are and 
what are not acceptable female role definitions, the task of 
becoming a person in one's own right is a long and seemingly 
endless process.

THOUGHTS ON TRAINING 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. Probably one of the most important tasks of any training 
program is continually to provide a stimulus for people to 
learn. This task is continual since family systems theory is not 
a body of knowledge that can be adequately learned in just a 
few months or even a year or two of training. Experience has 
shown that trainees achieve a reasonable understanding of the 
theory and therapy over a period of many years. Trainees who have gone through the program at George­
town are on a continuum in terms of the way they have 
approached the concepts. At one extreme are people who have 
regarded family ideas as a fixed body of knowledge. Trainees 
at this end of the spectrum have tended not to stay in the 
program very long and, while in the program, have usually 
appended bits and pieces of a few of the concepts onto their 
preexisting ways of thinking. They have usually left the train­
ing program believing that they had achieved more understand­
ing of family theory than was actually the case. At the other 
extreme are trainees who became aware that family systems 
theory did not "fit" with most of their preexisting ideas about 
human behavior. These trainees were conscious of the limits of 
their knowledge and were highly motivated to work toward 
their potential for theoretical thinking. Obviously, trainees 
have existed at all gradations between these extremes.

Obviously, trainees

approached learning the theory, the faculty has also had its 
problems in teaching it. Being aware of some of these teaching 
problems, the faculty has tried to evaluate continually the 
program's effectiveness for helping people achieve their poten­
tial for theoretical thinking. It is clear that we can do a better 
job than we have done. One of the program's obvious weaknesses is that a large 
number of trainees may spend several years in the program and 
continue to harbor significant misconceptions about the con­
cept of differentiation of self. The obstacles to learning this 
important concept are not just within the heads of the trainees. The faculty's own misconceptions about differentiation also 
create obstacles for trainees. Perhaps the faculty is analogous 
to a family in that it simultaneously may be a source of 
strength and weakness for people's efforts to learn. Trainees 
need contact with a faculty that is more knowledgeable about 
theory than they are, but that very contact may also put them 
at risk for getting bogged down in the theoretical misconcep­
tions of their teachers. Our training programs still need much improvement, but I 
am pleased with the progress we have made. Perhaps the biggest 
lesson we have learned is that trainees can learn family systems 
theory provided that the faculty does not try too hard to 
teach it!

of the lectern and it is the primary force that undermines the 
effectiveness of the program. This togetherness push obliter­
ates individual differences between trainees, between faculty 
members and also between faculty and trainees. Recognizing 
and staying "on top" of this emotional process in the program 
appears to be more important to the program's effectiveness 
than the actual content of what is taught. In other words, the 
better the level of differentiation of the faculty, the better the 
learning opportunities for the trainees. There always seem to have been trainees who could rise 
above the situation and do well no matter how well the pro­
gram functioned. These trainees just seem to gravitate toward 
whatever opportunities the program provided that offered the 
most useful contrast to their existing mind set. There have also 
always been trainees who dismiss what they have heard out-of­
hand, and we probably cannot bring our program to a high 
enough level to alter that quick dismissal.

speed of light is relative, then the speed of a moving object 
emitting the light would be added to the measured speed of

with Newton's ideas. He imagined that he was traveling on a 
beam of light and was holding a mirror in front of his face 
which would reflect that light from his face. If he and the 
mirror were traveling at the speed of light, he questioned 
whether a stationary observer on the ground would see the 
light leave his face at twice the speed of light, consistent with 
Newton's laws, or would he catch up to his reflected image at 
that speed so that his image would then disappear? He rea­
soned that neither of these answers made any sense. Neither 
should his image disappear nor should the speed of light be 
different for the moving observer and the stationary observer. Nevertheless, he was troubled by the obvious conclusion that 
if the speed of light could not be added to itself, then it must 
be a constant, so that it would be the same for both the mov­
ing observer (himself) and the stationary observer (the 
audience). To continue his research Einstein needed to convince 
himself that his reflected image would be normal even if mov­
ing at the speed of light.

To continue his research Einstein needed to convince 
himself that his reflected image would be normal even if mov­
ing at the speed of light. He resorted to Galileo's (1564-1642) 
general principle of relativity: all steady motion is relative and 
cannot be detected without reference to an outside point. In 
other words, you can't tell from any effects on the ship or 
train whether it is moving smoothly or standing still. You can 
only tell if you and the ship are moving smoothly by looking 
at an outside reference point. While traveling smoothly at the 
speed of light, one's image should remain in the mirror. If the 
image were to disappear, then you could tell you were moving 
at the speed of light without reference to an outside source, 
thereby violating Galileo's general principle of relativity. Nevertheless, Einstein was troubled by the other conclu­
sion that he could see the light move away from his face at the 
speed of light relative to him while at the same time the sta­
tionary observer would see the light leave his face at the same 
speed of light relative to them. Einstein resorted to the equation: speed equals distance 
divided by time. He realized that if the speed of light were to 
be the same for both the moving observer and the stationary 
observer (that it was a constant), then distance and time would 
be different for each observer.

Einstein took Galileo's general 
principle of the relativity of motion as a starting point and was 
led to re-think the concepts of space and time to resolve this 
apparent paradox. Through a series of ingenious experiments 
and mathematical equations he showed that the speed of light 
is constant and absolute and that space and time are relative. He replaced Newton's metaphysical absolutes, the mental con­
cepts of absolute space and time, with the material absolute 
which is that there are no instantaneous interactions in nature. Einstein referred to this dilemma as the "simultaneity 
paradox." All judgments of simultaneity involve judgments of 
time. If the speed of light is constant for all observers, the 
ratio of distance and time (not the actual distance and time) 
must be the same. Einstein called this the relativity of simul­
taneity. Since the velocity of light is the same for everyone, 
events will appear to occur at the same time as long as the 
distance/time ratio remains the same; but, in fact, events do 
not occur simultaneously for the stationary observer and the 
moving observer. The sequence of events or the process of 
events remains in the same order so that harmony and balance 
are maintained in the universe. Understanding the simultaneity paradox is critical to 
understanding systems thinking. The ability to separate the 
occurrence of an event from a judgment about an event is 
what enables us to see simultaneity as a process.

The Earth's great oceans, atmosphere, and land 
have always formed an interactive whole. The planet 
is believed to be about 4000 million years old. When 
life emerged to become a fourth major component is 
not certain, but modern research has pushed the date 
backwards to a moment at least 3000 million years 
ago. The biosphere, that flexible amalgam of all living 
things and their environment, is flexible and fluid. Its 
components shift and move, adapting, adjusting, and 
responding to one another. The earth is never at rest, 
and the biosphere is never static. The atmosphere 
moves and swirls. Its component gases shift and blend 
in ever new and mostly consistent and stable ways. The land and the waters display similar fluctuations, 
again mostly within a stable and consistent range. Liv­
ing things, too, are mostly consistent and stable. From this perspective Earth is a system. A shift in 
any element produces a response in others. The shift­
response cycle can be minimal, affecting only a few 
things within a small area. It can also be global, alter­
ing the nature of the biosphere itself. As a result, the 
modern planet is different from the swirling amalgam 
of gas and molten metal which emerged from the for­
mation of the solar system four or five billion years 
ago.

As a result, the 
modern planet is different from the swirling amalgam 
of gas and molten metal which emerged from the for­
mation of the solar system four or five billion years 
ago. It is different, too, from the planet which pro­
duced living things three to four billion years ago. Living things have always had the capacity to 
influence their environment. The earliest atmosphere 
had little oxygen, which was toxic to the microbial 
life which occupied earth's niches (Margulis and Sa­
gan). These living forms, essentially cells without 
nuclei, developed mechanisms to harness light and 
elements in the air and water to produce nutrients for 
themselves. In the process, these prokaryotic cells, as 
modern scientists classify them, released waste pro­
ducts. Other microbes developed the ability to utilize 
these wastes. Clearly the interdependence of living 
things was established early in life's development. SUMMER 1987 
Microbes remain today the most abundant of liv­
ing things. They occur in all environments known on 
the Earth and are essential for the proper functioning 
of other living creatures. They live independently and 
in conjunction with other forms of life. Such cohabi­
tation is sometimes peaceful and sometimes deadly. Between one and one half and two billion years ago 
life took a second turn. A new kind of creature emer­
ged which was radically different from the microbe. This new creature was the nucleated cell, or eukaryote.

A new kind of creature emer­
ged which was radically different from the microbe. This new creature was the nucleated cell, or eukaryote. So great is the gulf between prokaryotic and eu­
karyotic cells that some have called it the most impor­
tant evolutionary development of all time (Margulis 
and Sagan). No one knows for sure how this develop­
ment came about. One line of thinking suggests that 
the nucleated cell was produced when predator and 
prey prokaryotic cells formed a cooperative relation­
ship. Instead of destroying the prey, the predator be­
came incorporated into it. The enemies merged and 
became interdependent. Each maintained some of its 
original capabilities and assumed a function necessary 
for the other. Such thought suggests that cooperation 
was at least as important as competition in the pro­
cess of evolution. The nucleated cell is the basis of all 
more complex organisms. All living things other than 
the microbes are formed from arrangements of nucle­
ated cells cooperating with one another. The eukaryotic cell is a naturally occurring sys­
tem. Like the biosphere of which it is a part, the cell 
is flexibly fluid. Its parts are functionally interdepen­
dent. Without each part of the cell fulfilling its func­
tion, the survival of the cell is jeopardized. A shift in 
the functioning of one part produces shifts in the 
functioning of other parts.

the functioning of one part produces shifts in the 
functioning of other parts. Each element of the living 
cell has the capacity to influence the whole and to re­
spond to the influence of elements outside itself. The shifting fluidity of the cell's interior results in 
certain processes or behaviors which are recognizable 
when one focuses on the cell as a whole. For example, 
food is imported, and by-products exported from the 
cell. A free-standing cell may move, altering its shape 
and its position relative to other parts of its environ­
ment. Reproduction occurs, replacing one cell with 
two identical ones. Although the cell is shifting in response to a myr­
iad of internal and external cues, its components have 
a particular interactional configuration or condition 
at any given moment. This condition can be thought 
of as the functional state of the cell. The cell's capa­
bilities for maintenance and for behavior are deter­
mined by its functional state. The notion of health is 
really one functional state. A healthy cell has certain 
capabilities and options for behavior open to it which 
differ from those of a less healthy cell. A healthy cell 
behaves differently from an unhealthy one. The func­
tional state of a cell may remain relatively stable over 
time, it may change slowly, or it may be altered rapid­
ly.

the environment. In fact it is difficult if not impossible 
to separate these processes. Organisms are composed of innumerable nucleated 
cells which have become specialized over time to cre­
ate organs and perform specific functions within the 
system of cells. Like the cell, the organism is fluid 
and shifting. The notion of the functional state is ap­
plicable to the organism as well as to the cell. Proces­
ses operate continually, and the state of the organism 
is subject to continual variation. The component sys­
tems of the organism are also functionally interdepen­
dent. Each must perform in a specified way to allow 
the organism to maintain its health. Any variation 
affects the functional state of the organism and the 
well-being of any component element. Each cell and each organism operates in accor­
dance with a built-in guidance mechanism. For exam­
ple, in the developing embryo, all cells begin alike but 
ultimately differentiate to become highly specialized. An animal moving along a forest runway changes gait, 
profile and even direction in accordance with the 
capabilities of its guidance system. A sunflower in a 
field orients its blossom regularly toward the sun.

field orients its blossom regularly toward the sun. Clearly some sort of interplay between environment 
and the living unit triggers processes within the indivi­
dual which lead to specific behaviors and choices. Out 
of the scope of all possible behaviors, only a few ap­
pear at any given time. Furthermore, not all living 
things are capable of the same behaviors. For example, 
plant behavior differs in significant ways from animal 
behavior. Among animals some are more flexible than 
others. They are able to survive and even thrive under 
a range of environmental conditions. The guidance system of the cell is basically bio­
chemical. Chemical reactions are facilitated within 
and between the cell and its environment. Such reac­
tions may alter the functional state of the cell. Some 
reactions occur regularly and repeatedly, forming the 
normal condition of the cell. Others occur rarely and 
represent basic shifts in the state or condition of the 
cell. The interaction between cells is also based in the 
biochemistry of each cell but also involves the beha­
vior of cells as entire units. How a cell behaves influ­
ences the cells with which it comes into contact. For 
2 example, the T-cells of the human immune system 
regularly patrol the body, alert to the presence of in­
vading microbes. They identify cells as self or non-self 
basically by means of chemical processes. When a for­
eign presence is located, the T-cell moves aggressively 
upon the invader.

ence -the retained effects of the interaction of the 
developing organism with its environment- also plays 
a part. In terms of the construction analogy, experi­
ence could be compared to the various craftsmen 
whose work renders a basic structure operational. The 
master electrician, trim carpenter, plumber and so on 
all leave their mark on the finished house. The evolutionary pathway leading to Homo sapi­
ens produced a brain, a spinal column and related per­
ipheral nerve systems. There is a tendency to think of 
the central and peripheral nervous system~ as the guid­
ance system for the human. In a limited sense this is 
the case. The great neuronal net serves as a central co­
ordinating and processing unit. Here signals of varying 
intensity from all over the organism are collected and 
processed. Some signals, such as the spinal reflex, un­
dergo little processing while others follow complicated 
routes where they are modified in innumerable ways 
before a signal returns to a remote region of the body. These great nerve networks are themselves a system 
with interdependent functioning. The central nervous 
system (CNS) is always active and shifting. Biochemi­
cal balances ebb and flow as hormones, neurotrans­
mitters, and other molecules are released, taken up and 
held, or destroyed. Electrical activity shifts as nerve 
"circuits" become active or dormant.

"circuits" become active or dormant. If each biochem­
ical could be imagined to have a brilliant color, and 
the electical activity of the CNS could be likened to a 
network of lights, then the CNS would seem a work 
of abstract modern art with fascinating blends of ever 
changing color and winking lights of varying intensity. The CNS, with its central coordinating role, must 
clearly be considered an influential component in the 
guidance system of the individual. But each cell and 
each organ system also contribute. Like the medieval 
English monarchs who served as primus inter pares, 
the CNS may be first among equals. But its ascendan­
cy is shaky, dependent upon the functioning of the 
other component elements of the organism. Cells and organisms are fairly easily seen as units. They are, after all, self-contained within a boundary 
(the plasma membrane of the cell and the skin of the 
organism). Units larger than the individual organism, 
where such a clear delineation is lacking, are somewhat 
more difficult to comprehend. Nevertheless, such mul­
ti-individual units are the rule among the colonial in­
vertebrates and the social insects (Wilson). Creatures 
like the Portuguese man-of-war, a colonial invertebrate 
well-known to ocean bathers of the eastern United 
States, are colonies of individual organisms which 
have evolved together to function as a unit. Such col-onies frequently display functional interdependence.

Such col-onies frequently display functional interdependence. The social insects form colonies as well. Ants and ter­
mites live in large groups of individuals which appear 
to have the behavior of a unit. Individuals assume 
functional tasks for the colony (queen, soldier, wor­
ker), and the individual has little capacity to survive 
outside the colonial structure. Such colonies appear to be guided by a system of 
interactions among the individuals which comprise 
the colony. Each individual plays a part. The idea of 
the functional state applies to the aggregate as well 
as to the individual. For example, ant colonies rest, 
march, fight and construct nests. Each activity could 
be seen as representing a functional state of the unit. That condition is shaped by the functioning of each 
individual and the clusters of individuals within the 
whole. Each organism contributes to the state of the 
unit and is influenced by that condition. Such functioning can be observed among many 
mammalian species as well. The behavior of each ani­
mal plays a part in the functional state of the group, 
and the behavior of the group influences the well-being 
of each individual. Functioning as a unit is particularly 
evident in the defensive and hunting aggregates of 
many species. Many mammals live in groups which are based 
loosely on kinship. At the core of such groupings is 
the reproductive female.

Many mammals live in groups which are based 
loosely on kinship. At the core of such groupings is 
the reproductive female. The group may be comprised 
of several such females and their appendages (mates 
and offspring). Within the group various processes are 
evident which influence the overall condition of the 
assemblage and the behavior of each individual within 
it. For example, many primate groups display hierar­
chies. The males in the group occupy different social 
rankings determined to a large degree by the effect of 
individual differences on group interaction. Similar 
processes are evident among females as well and affect 
the well-being of each individual both immediately 
and over time. The human family displays the characteristics of a 
living system. The unit is flexible and fluid. For the 
family, the question is not whether individuals respond 
to one another but how they respond. A shift in the 
functional state of the family is reflected in the state 
or condition of each individual organism. The shifts 
can be reflected behaviorally, or they may be contain­
ed within the body walls of the affected individuals. The implications of such a view are far-reaching. Not 
only can behavior be seen as a product of relationship, 
but the health of each family member may be directly 
related to the functional state of the family unit. Margulis, L., Sagan, D., MicroCosmos. New York: 
Summit Books, 1986. Wilson, E.O., Sociobiology.

 EMOTIONAL ASPECTS OF CANCER 
Michael E. Kerr, M.D. On June 5 and 6, 1987 a conference entitled "Can­
cer and Emotions: A Blending of Theory and Practice" 
was held in Syracuse, New York. The meeting was The 
Third Annual Margaret York Memorial Conference. Until her death of cancer in 1984, Margaret York had 
been a pivotal person in teaching family systems ideas 
in the Syracuse area. The two presenters at the conference were Law­
rence LeShan, Ph.D. and Michael Kerr, M.D. Dr. Kerr 
presented his understanding of the interplay between 
cancer and the family emotional system -placing par­
ticular emphasis on the multigenerational family-and 
Dr. LeShan presented the principles that guide his 
psychotherapy with cancer patients and his results. After the formal presentations, Dr. LeShan and Dr. Kerr participated in a panel discussion. Since Dr. Le­
Shan 's ideas are unfamiliar to most people interested 
in family systems theory, this article will focus on his 
presentation at the Syracuse meeting. Lawrence LeShan is a research psychologist who 
received a Ph.D. in Human Development from the 
University of Chicago in 1954. Most of his professional 
life has been spent in New York City. He has been 
interested in the emotional aspects of cancer for thir­
ty-five years and has specialized in that area since the 
early 1960's.

He has been 
interested in the emotional aspects of cancer for thir­
ty-five years and has specialized in that area since the 
early 1960's. His book, You Can Fight for Your Life, 
is one of the most important in the field of cancer 
and emotions. He is the author of many other books 
and journal articles and is a particularly articulate 
spokesman for holistic medicine. LeShan's early training was in psychoanalysis. He 
eventually decided that there was too much about 
human functioning and behavior that psychoanalytic 
theory could not explain to merit giving its precepts 
exclusive allegiance. So while retaining some basic 
psychoanalytic ideas, LeShan incorporated concepts 
and approaches from other theories and shifted to a 
psychotherapeutic approach that was much more ac­
tive. A turning point for him was the recognition that 
some analytic patients developed serious illnesses such 
as cancer while they were still in or about to complete 
psychoanalysis. If the therapy was effective, how could 
this happen? The cancer patients treated by LeShan are consi­
dered "medically hopeless." They have been treated 
with the range of medical and surgical procedures. available for their type of cancer and have not respon­
ded. The cancer is considered "out of control." Fifty 
percent of these "hopeless" patients recover. It is an 
incredible statistic that merits the attention of all of us.

The cancer is considered "out of control." Fifty 
percent of these "hopeless" patients recover. It is an 
incredible statistic that merits the attention of all of us. Most people are familiar with what Norman Cou­
sins did to reverse the course of his serious illness. The 
ability to do this seems "built-in" to certain people. People have spontaneous remissions of widely metas­
tatic cancer and some of these remissions appear to 
be related to "psychological" variables. Many people 
walk around with cancer which is never diagnosed. 4 They live long lives and die of unrelated causes. People 
exert some control over their diseases. There is more 
to this process than "the will to live" because many 
people want to live -and will fight to live -but die 
of cancer in spite of a fierce determination to survive. What is remarkable about the approach LeShan has 
developed is that it shows people can sometimes be 
helped to do what is built-in to certain other people 
who recover. The cancer itself is not hopeless; the 
patient and the people around him become hopeless 
and that makes the cancer hopeless. This does not 
imply that reversing a cancer is a simple process that 
all patients "should" be able to accomplish. It only 
implies that at times it is possible to cure a cancer 
with a psychological approach and that is important 
to recognize and to understand. LeShan has the courage and ability to get very 
involved with his patients.

LeShan has the courage and ability to get very 
involved with his patients. The nature of his relation­
ship with them seems to be the most critical element 
in the success of his therapy. He is cognizant of the 
patient's family, but treats the individual. He is the 
patient's very strong advocate. While the details of the 
therapy are complex, the basic principles that guide it 
are straightforward. He assumes that the fundamental 
loss that can trigger a cancer is a "loss of one's way." 
People are experiencing despair and hopelessness 
about ever being able "to sing their own song." LeShan 
has little interest in what is "wrong" with people; only 
in what is "right" with people. What can they do that 
will enable them "to live under their own name." He 
goes to great lengths to help people find out what 
their song is and, once defined, to help them find ways 
in which they can define a self. He is often dealing 
with people who are feeling defeated, and his ability 
to make effective contact with these people, to con­
vince them they can find a way, and to help them see 
what is involved in finding their way, is the "art" of 
his therapy. He is a master. The patient's treatment, according to LeShan, 
must include attention to the physiological, psycholo­
gical, and spiritual levels. He defines spiritual as the 
deep and basic need to have a meaningful framework 
for existence. It is also critically important that each 
patient be regarded as unique.

He defines spiritual as the 
deep and basic need to have a meaningful framework 
for existence. It is also critically important that each 
patient be regarded as unique. It is very easy for a 
patient to be thrown into a sea of homogeneity and 
anonymity in the medical setting. Patients who might 
otherwise have lived can die in such an environment. LeShan adds that not only must each patient be view­
ed as unique, but they must be an active member of 
the decision-making team. If all of these principles are 
honored, the patient's self-healing abilities will not be 
undermined. If given the opportunity, patients can 
assume considerable control over their destinies, con­
trol that can make the difference between life and 
death. While many individual physicians, nurses, and 
others already operate from these principles, such 
thinking is not yet built in to the mainstream of med­
icine. A meeting involving Lawrence LeShan is one well 
worth attending. He is a "mover and shaker" and any 
 therapist, regardless of his or her theoretical persua­
sion, can learn much from him. He seems never to 
have accepted the notion that "it can't be done." At 
the same time, he reminds audiences that "systems 
limp along." Persistence must always be tempered by 
patience. His results are undeniable and challenge any­
one interested in a natural systems understanding of 
the human process to make sense out of what he is 
able to do.

While 
others were evaluating psychological characteristics, 
intellectual capacity and psychiatric status, Dr. Pincus 
evaluated the medical differences between these two 
groups. Ninety-seven boys, up to the age of 16 were divi­
ded into four groups based upon their behavior: 1) no 
arson or offense against person; 2) potential for vio­
lence but not yet arrested; 3) documented repeated 
events of personal violence; 4) "especial" cruelty in­
cluding extreme, repetitive, and bizarre violent acts. For purposes of this study, those boys were then com­
pared in two groups: the "less" violent included cate­
gories (1) and (2); the"more"violent included (3) and 
(4). Four factors correlated with violence in this study: 
a) neurological abnormalities 
b) mental status 
c) psychiatric symptoms 
d) exposure to violence 
During the neurological examination, a statistically 
significant number of those in the more violent cate­
gory had abnormal EEGs. Psychomotor symptoms 
such as lapses of conscious contact, impaired memory, 
blackouts, deja vu experiences, lapses in auditory com­
prehension and fainting spells were more common in 
the more violent group.

Major neurological abnormal­
ities were more evident in those with more violent be­
havior: grand mal seizures, larger or smaller head cir-circumference than standard, Babinski signs which 
signal cortical spinal track involvement, choreiform 
movements or the uncontrolled movements which 
occur in some people when arms are held to the front 
for a period of time, and an inability to skip. To illus­
trate more graphically the correlation of behavior and 
EEG activity, Dr. Pincus showed a short video. An 
interaction between a female nurse and a boy spitting 
at her appeared on one side of the television screen. On the other side was the boy's EEG. During this in­
terchange the EEG activity demonstrated what Dr. Pincus called a "psychomotor seizure." 
Those boys who were more violent had a slightly 
lower IQ. Although not regarded as globally retarded, 
these boys did selectively demonstrate a lower read­
ing level, lower arithmatic skills, an inability to calcu­
late and symptoms of dyslexia. All are characteristics 
of organic brain dysfunction. Within a traditional psychiatric framework, the 
boys who were more violent were described as para­
noid. These boys had a history of not getting along 
with peers, teachers, police and parents. These boys 
demonstrated loose and rambling thought processes 
in conversation. Exposure to violence at home was the most signi­
ficant variable that correlated to violence.

SELF-DIFFERENTIATION IN CHEMISTRY 
AND IN PROCESS PHILOSOPHY 
Joseph Earley, Ph.D. Reviewed by Daniel V Papero 
On June 18, 1987, Joseph Earley, Ph.D., Chairman 
of the Department of Chemistry at Georgetown Uni­
versity, was the featured speaker of the Family Cen­
ter's Third Thursday Series. In a presentation entitled, 
"Self-Differentiation in Chemistry and in Process Phil­
osophy," Dr. Earley drew on his knowledge of systems 
in basic science, particularly chemistry, to challenge 
and entertain the audience. Using cartoons, slides, 
chemical demonstrations and stick models to illustrate 
his points, Dr. Earley moved from the second law of 
thermodynamics through current thinking about 
chemical systems to modern philosophy in a thour­
oughly enjoyable and stimulating manner. Recalling 
Walker Percy's observation that Freud's ideas reflect 
the basic science thinking of his day about thermody­
namics, Dr. Earley suggested that the new ideas now 
developing in physics and chemistry may lead to sim­
ilar influences on current and future thinking about 
the nature of human development and behavior. The second law of thermodynamics states that 
with every spontaneous change the total entropy (or 
disorder) of the universe increases. How then does one 
account for examples of evolving complexity against 
the backdrop of the second law? The answer, accord­
ing to Dr. Earley, is that the second law is correct but 
not complete.

How then does one 
account for examples of evolving complexity against 
the backdrop of the second law? The answer, accord­
ing to Dr. Earley, is that the second law is correct but 
not complete. Chemical affinity or bonding is influ­
enced by two factors: 1) disorder is more probable 
than order (second law) but 2) strong bonds overcome 
entropy except at very high temperatures. The forma­
tion of strong chemical bonds creates structures and 
forms the basis for evolving complexity. Bonding 
always has something to do with structure. A chemi­
cal structure is said to be stable when any distortion 
of the structure generates a counter restorative force 
to bring the structure back to its original state or con­
figuration. The chemical bonds within a structure are 
sufficiently strong to overcome the tendency toward 
disorder except at very high temperatures. In addition to these well-known aspects of classi­
cal thermodynamics, new ideas are developing. A cen­
tral idea is that of autocatalysis. For example, in the 
atom bomb an atom is struck by a neutron. The resu­
ting interaction releases three neutrons which in turn

Dr. Earley then demonstrated two different sorts 
of autocatalytic systems. In the first, he sketched out a 
system of foxes and squirrels. The squirrels eat and re­
produce, becoming fox food. The foxes eat the squir­
rels and reproduce. As the fox population grows, the 
squirrel population decreases, leading to a reversal of 
the cycle (i.e. fox population drops, squirrel popula­
tion rises.) This is described analytically by the Lotka­
Volterra equation. In the second, Dr. Earley recreated 
in a petri dish the Belousov Zhabotinski reaction (B-Z 
reaction) in which an initially homogeneous chemical 
solution via autocatalysis begins to oscillate from red 
to blue and blue to red. The system defined by the Lotka-Volterra equa­
tion (foxes-squirrels) is not a structure, because an in­
finite number of cycles is possible. Any disruption 
leads to another, different sort of cycle. In the B-Z 
system, on the other hand, a single trajectory is crea­
ted which is followed repeatedly. Any deviation pro­
duces forces which bring the reaction back to the ori­
ginal trajectory (a structure, therefore, by definition). This is called a limit cycle, a unique single trajectory 
in x-y space which is eventually reached from all star­
ting values. It is a structure, not of things but of pro­
cesses or interrelationships. This is a dissipative struc­
ture, using up the chemical energy of the chemical 
components.
