In the effort to move toward an understanding of 
human behavior that is based in the sciences, Bowen 
made an extensive study of philosophical as well as of 
scientific disciplines. He was particularly interested in 
understanding how the various disciplines dealt with 
the distinction between feelings and facts. These stu­
dies helped Bowen gain more clarity about the differ­
ences between the sciences and the philosophies. He 
noticed that for every philosophy there was almost 
always an "antiphilosophy." The existence of polar 
opposite philosophies, of point and counterpoint, 
highlighted the subjective nature of philosophy. Phi­
losophy deals with "eternal truths," not facts. It is a 
product of man's thinking. In contrast, science per­
tains not to subjectivity (a product of the brain), but 
to the earth, the tides, the sun, the solar system. The 
realm of science, in other words, is not created, chan­
ged, or constrained by human subjectivity. Bowen be­
came convinced that human behavior belonged in the 
realm of science, not in the realm of philosophy. He 
made this decision for himself and developed his the­
ory accordingly. He attempted to keep subjectivity 
out of the theoretical concepts as much as possible. By the early l 950's, Bowen had decided to replace 
Freudian concepts with concepts consistent with evo­
lution and natural systems.

By the early l 950's, Bowen had decided to replace 
Freudian concepts with concepts consistent with evo­
lution and natural systems. (This did not mean that 
important facts about human behavior discovered by 
Freud would not be included in a new theory.) Evolu­
tionary theory attempts to define what the world is, 
not what man imagines it to be. General system the­
ory was a derivative of mathematics and manmade 
machines and so Bowen did not consider it to be a 
suitable base for conceptualizing the human family 
system. He made a distinction between natural sys­
tems such as baboon troops and manmade systems 
such as radar devices. While some similarity exists be­
tween manmade and living systems, they are not the 
same. DIRECTOR

However, Bowen persisted in the notion that if a the­
ory was worth anything it should be useful in relation­
ship to the people who are most important in one's 
personal life. He was convinced it was possible to get 
through what he called "the emotional curtain" of 
one's own family, but for many years an essential the­
oretical piece eluded him. The theoretical breakthrough came with the un­
derstanding of triangles. Triangles provided a path 
through the emotional curtain. After a dozen years of 
thought and effort, Bowen made a trip home in Feb­
ruary 1967 that resulted in the breakthrough: he was 
involved with his family, but relatively outside of it 
emotionally. That aspect of the long odyssey was 
over. In March 1967, he presented what he had done 
with his family to a national meeting of family thera­
pists in Philadelphia. In making such a presentation, 
he did with the "family of family therapists" the same 
thing he had done with his own family: he defined a 
self. Bowen says, however, that most of the family 
therapists at the meeting misperceived the purpose of 
his presentation (Bowen's family and his efforts in it) 
rather than on the process that surrounded the presen­
tation (Bowen's effort to define a self in the family of 
family therapists). Whether recognized or not, the 
field of family therapists did react emotionally to the 
process. These reactions still reverberate in the family 
movement.

delivered the April Third Thursday presentation enti­
tled, "Thinking and Science." The talk represented his 
most recent attempt to address the interplay of scien­
tific endeavor and human mental activity. Dr. Papero began with a series of definitions. He 
began with a definition of nature as "everything that 
exists." Science, therefore, is organized knowledge of 
the facts of nature. Scientific endeavor, the effort to 
reach science through the study of nature, is aided by 
theory, a network of thought or ideas connecting a 
set of facts in a manner which outlines the potential 
relationship among the facts. In Papero's opinion, 
theory is both a tool and a structure. He compared 
theory to a navigational tool, for example a sextant, 
which allows one to plot a course into the unknown.

Dr. Papero introduced the term mindset to refer 
to the state or condition of the organism and the cen­
tral nervous system which forms the basis of percep­
tion. He made a distinction between the basic condi­
tion of the organism which governs perception, which 
he called chronic, and transitory conditions which 
temporarily affect perception, which he called acute. Chronic mindset, he proposed, is based in neural cir­
cuitry which is established through heredity and early 
life experience. It may also involve basic biochemistry 
in terms of the variety and location of neurochemical 
receptors in the central nervous system. Acute condi­
tions occur on the foundation of the chronic mindset 
and represent shifting balances of biochemistry and 
partial activation of existing neural circuitry in re­
sponse to momentary conditions. From this point, Dr. Papero went on to suggest 
that the fixedness of chronic mindset may vary among 
individuals. In some it may be so firmly established or 
3 
 fixed that it is immutable. For such people it may be 
essentially impossible to alter perception of a phenom­
enon. In others, basic mindset may be flexible enough 
to be shifted with effort. From this point of view, the 
concept of mindset comes close to that represented by 
differentiation of self in Bowen family systems theory. Dr. Papero concluded with some thoughts about 
how chronic mindset might be altered.

Dr. Papero concluded with some thoughts about 
how chronic mindset might be altered. He was careful 
to note that these are only ideas and not tested proce­
dures for attempting a difficult task. He remarked in 
passing that mindset can be altered through intensity 
of experience, citing as examples the story of Paul on 
the road to Damascus and the phenomenon called 
post-traumatic stress disorder. But an intentional ef­
fort to alter mindset is a different matter. Beginning 
with the assumption that the individual mindset has 
some flexibility, a disciplined effort to change mind­
set might be assisted by the following: 1) a carefully 
defined question or problem which cannot be answer­
ed without a shift in mindset. 2) a series of repeated 
attempts to solve the problem or question and 3) an 
effort to communicate the nature of the problem and 
the individual effort to "see" it differently. Dr. Papero's presentation addressed an interesting 
and important area, representing his latest effort to­
ward making a clear, precise theoretical statement. RECENT ADVANCES IN BRAIN IMAGING

important research in his specialized field. Dr. Mori­
hisa described the basic technologies used in brain re­
search and some of the important studies done using 
those technologies. Topographic mapping of the brain's electrical ac­
tivity is an important tool in psychiatric research. The 
mapping is done using electrode placements identical 
to those of the standard electroencephalogram. The 
strength of evoked potentials recorded by the elec­
trodes differs over parts of the head. The differences, 
which range incrementally from greatest to least, are 
used to create the topographic map. 4 Many studies have been done comparing the elec­
trical activity of the brains of schizophrenic patients 
and of matched controls. One study compared 11 nor­
mal controls (matched for age, sex, and handedness, 
and with negative neuropsychiatric histories) to 11 un­
medicated (for at least four weeks) schizophrenic pa­
tients and 14 medicated schizophrenic patients.

Reviewed by Priscilla!. Friesen 
The Biofeedback Programs sponsored the fourth 
"Physiology and Relationships" meeting on Thursday, 
June 16, 1988, to discuss ideas bridging biofeedback 
and family systems theory. The format included group­
ings of two or three presentations followed by a desig­
nated respondent, then discussion. In his presentation "Medical, Legal, and Educa­
tional Reactivity: Asthma," Dr. Edward Beal presented 
a single case study of a child with asthma. He described 
a level of reactivity within a family that manifests it­
self not only as physical symptoms in one or more 
people in a family but in numerous other institutions. In this case, numerous professionals and social agen­
cies were involved in complicated, adversarial positions 
emanating from the anxious, reactive emotional core, 
the family. How one gains functioning at the expense of ano­
ther was the focus of Louise Rauseo's talk on "Bor­
rowed Self: A Systems Phenomena." Ms. Rauseo des­
cribed this phenomenon, questioning the mechanism 
by which it occurs and how it can be studied scienti­
fically. Extending the concept of "borrowed self' to 
the societal level, Ms. Rauseo asked whether society 
"borrows self' from groups such as Native Americans. She used her consultation with members of a small 
tribe to demonstrate "borrowed self' at the tribal lev­
el.

self-centered the person; the more flexible the mindset 
the more objective and capable a person is of a broad­
er view. Biofeedback is a way of studying subjectivity

way to bridge the "psycho" and the "soma tic," and 
to learn how anxiety is manifested. Lilian Rosenbaum's presentation, "Reactivity and 
Biofeedback Frontiers," made use of slides of coral,

FAMILY CENTER 
REPORT Department of Psychiatry 
Georgetown University School of Medicine 
VOL.9, NO.4 
SOME ASPECTS OF SYSTEMS THINKING 
Michael E. Kerr 
Presentation made at the Clinical Conference Series 
May 21, 1988 
The ideas I would like to present were stimulated, 
in part, by a recent reading of the book, A Feeling for 
the Organism, by Evelyn Fox Keller. The book is a 
biography of Barbara McClintock that places particu­
lar emphasis on her professional life. Several years ago, 
Dr. McClintock was awarded the Nobel Prize for her 
pioneering work in genetics. A part of the book I found especially interesting 
was a description of the difficulty most of McClintock's 
scientific colleagues had accepting her radically new 
ideas. This resulted in her most important research 
findings being discounted for over twenty years. Were 
other scientists unable to accept McClintock's ideas 
because she could not communicate them clearly or 
was it because they were unable to listen? Indeed, her 
work is complex, requiring considerable intellectual 
discipline to follow the painstaking steps of her re­
search, but its complexity was probably not the main 
obstacle to its being understood and accepted. Almost 
certainly, the main obstacle was the tacit assumptions 
of her colleagues about the nature of genes. The facts 
about genetics revealed by McClintock's study of maize 
contradicted widely held beliefs about how genes func­
tioned.

The facts 
about genetics revealed by McClintock's study of maize 
contradicted widely held beliefs about how genes func­
tioned. Historically, when newly discovered facts have 
contradicted accepted beliefs about the natural world, 
the beliefs have yielded their grasp on human thinking 
very slowly. The resistence that McClintock encoun­
tered is similar to that experienced by other scientific 
pioneers. After reading about McClintock's difficulty being 
"heard," I began to wonder about how effective I have 
been at communicating my understanding of families. When I listen to family members and watch them in­
teract, I see an orderly, predictable, and fairly uncom­
plicated process. I think elements that are basic to the 
patterns of emotional functioning in human families 
are easily observed in subhuman species. Do others see FALL 1988 
what I see? Have I been able to describe clearly what 
I see? Rather than discuss specific concepts in systems 
theory, I will concentrate on some important, overall 
aspects of systems thinking. I hope my presentation 
will stimulate you to make some of your assumptions 
about the nature of human emotional functioning and 
behavior more explicit. Failure to define one's assump­
tions adequately is an important obstacle to changing 
from an individual, cause-and-effect model to a sys­
tems model in reference to human behavior. It is difficult to think "systems" consistently.

It is difficult to think "systems" consistently. An 
ever present "emotional undertow" undermines peo­
ple's ability to see a self-reinforcing relationship pro­
cess that transcends blame. On the contrary, emotion­
ality inclines people to ascribe cause to one or a few 
elements in that process. People can learn to think 
"systems"more consistently, but it requires more than 
an intellectual effort. An emotional change is needed. Whether an emotional change occurs depends on a 
person's willingness to engage the important people 
and issues that he would rather avoid. The alternative 
to engagement is cutoff. Emotional cutoff can provide 
comfort, but it forecloses the chance to learn about 
emotional systems and the factors that govern one's 
vulnerability to them. In addition, emotional cutoff 
often provides comfort in the short run, but not in 
the long run. I will begin the discussion of aspects of systems 
thinking by defining some terms. Several years ago, 
Bowen defined science, theory, and subjectivity. As a 
consequence, these became watchwords at the Family 
Center. However, these terms have frequently been 
used by many of us without precise definition. I think 
it is important for me to define these terms more care­
fully, particularly since I have helped make them 
watchwords at Georgetown. I hope my effort to be 
more precise will stimulate your thinking about these 
areas. I will begin with science.

text:
I hope my effort to be 
more precise will stimulate your thinking about these 
areas. I will begin with science. The definition of science 
I will present is taken from a book, The Scale of Na­
ture, by Dr. John Tyler Bonner, Professor of Biology 
at Princeton University, and Distinguished Guest Lec­
turer for this year's Family Symposium. The definition 
is as follows: 
 Science is about things. It is about rocks, 
stars, atoms, and living beings. It is about 
all those things which surround us and which 
used to be called Nature with a capital N 
Furthermore, it is about the relation of things. Science is concerned with order. Bonner's description of science is similar to one 
presented by Bowen at the 1982 Family Symposium. Bowen distinguished between that which is a produc­
tion of the human brain and that which exists inde­
pendent of the brain. The latter is the realm of science, 
a realm that is not constrained or defined by what we 
think or say about it. Man and his brain are part of 
science, but the brain's productions are not. If man 
becomes extinct, the realm of science will be changed 
little by that extinction. Defining science is important 
because family systems theory assumes that it will be 
possible to develop a science of human behavior, along 
with astronomy, biology, chemistry, geology, and 
physics. Science is distinct from the scientific method.

text:
Science is distinct from the scientific method. Pro-
fessor Bonner makes this distinction as follows: 
The pursuit of science is a human undertaking 
entirely delineated by the mind of man .... The formal approach to science is founded 
upon a scientific method which is a set of 
rules that comply with common sense. This 
has become the province of philosophy, and 
the philosophers have devised a grammar of 
scientific usage which, in its pure form, is a 
scientific method. This is sometimes called 
the philosophy of science, and various ap­
proaches have specific names, such as logic, 
logical positivism, symbolic logic, and others. But ... these approaches are no more science 
than the English language or mathematics. The scientific method is used to gain knowledge 
about science. Its application, however, is not the on­
ly path to knowledge about science. Other paths exist 
for knowing about the factual world. Nor does the 
application of the scientific method guarantee contact 
with the realm of science. Bowen has made this point 
by saying, "One cannot chi-square a feeling and get a 
fact." Rigorous statistical evaluation of subjective da­
ta, in other words, does not produce an objective con­
clusion. When sufficient facts have been defined about a 
segment of the natural world, it is then possible to 
construct a scientific theory. Theory is a generaliza­
tion that attempts to define an order to what has been 
described factually.

Theory is a generaliza­
tion that attempts to define an order to what has been 
described factually. Relationships are theorized to ex­
ist between events. Theory is not science, and if it is 
not equated with science, it is open to change. New 
facts can modify it. If theory is equated with science, 
however, it becomes dogma. Supporters of dogma ig­
nore facts that contradict it, which precludes any pos­
sibility for change. A scientist attempts not to ignore any fact about 
the natural world that is inconsistent with accepted 
2 theory. He modifies his theory rather than dismiss a 
newly discovered, errant fact. Barbara McClintock is a 
"true" scientist whose mental discipline permitted her 
to see beyond conventional theory's conception of the 
genome. Scientists are not confined to research labor­
atories. In a sense, anyone who is aware of the distinc­
tions between fact, dogma, and theory, and who is gui­
ded accordingly might be considered a scientist. By this 
definition, family therapists can be scientists. Although 
mental health professionals are steeped in truth and 
dogma, which makes it difficult for them to distin­
guish between knowledge and belief, they can learn 
to make these distinctions more consistently. Family systems theory was designed to be consis­
tent with known facts about natural systems. Bowen 
has not claimed complete success, but the develop­
ment of a theory that is consistent with the facts has 
been his goal.

been his goal. He has written extensively about what 
is involved in attempting to move towards science. Like all theories, family systems theory is not science, 
but a creation of the human brain. It conceptualizes 
a relationship between the known facts about human 
emotional functioning and behavior. The degree to 
which the theoretical concepts are linked to these facts 
is the degree to which it is a scientific theory. The terms subjectivity and objectivity are also im­
portant to define. Some argue that all knowledge about 
the natural world is subjective because all sensory stim­
uli are processed through the nervous system. As a 
consequence, the world is neither seen nor heard as it 
is, but only as the nervous system records it to be. This 
is a broad definition of subjectivity. Subjectivity can 
be more narrowly defined as that which arises from 
"conditions" within the brain and sense organs and 
not directly caused by external stimuli. The important 
point to recognize is that the "conditions" within the 
brain and sense organs can vary in the following ways: 
( 1) differences exist among individuals in the "condi­
tions" that are average for their brains over time, and 
(2) "conditions" in the same brain may fluctuate wide­
ly.

belief. To move toward the realm of science, however, 
beliefs must be replaced by factual knowledge. As far as we know, Homo sapiens is the only spe­
cies that can distinguish between objectivity and sub­
jectivity. This ability is a function of the intellectual 
system. Bowen termed the ability to be relatively ob­
jective about emotionality, emotional objectivity. Hu­
man beings can be actively involved in an emotional 
system and, at the same time, recognize the nature of 
that involvement, both in its effects on themselves 
and on others.

Hu­
man beings can be actively involved in an emotional 
system and, at the same time, recognize the nature of 
that involvement, both in its effects on themselves 
and on others. Distinguishing between objectivity and 
subjectivity is a prerequisite for modifying one's basic 
level of differentiation of self. This is because subjec­
tivity is so strongly influenced by the relationship sys­
tem. People cannot change in relationship to others 
(become better defined selfs) without becoming clear­
er about the subjective nature of their assumptions 
about themselves and others. The difference between cause-and-effect thinking 
and systems thinking is another important area. Sys­
tems thinking is concerned with how, what, when. and 
where events occur. It is not concerned with why they 
occur. Focus on why an event occurs automatically 
converts thinking from a systems to a cause-and-effect 
mode. A simple example will illustrate this. A husband 
says to his wife, "I react to what I perceive as your 
disapproving look." This statement can be consistent 
with systems thinking. In contrast, if the husband says, 
"I react because of your disapproving look;' it reflects cause-and-effect thinking. The distinction is fairly ob­
vious. The first statement describes what happens with­
out assigning blame to either spouse. The second state­
ment asserts why something happens ("because of") 
and, in this case, blames the wife.

mission process-were formulated directly b y B o w e n . The  sixth concept, sibling posi-
tion, fell into place with the publication o f Toman's (1961) book, Family Constellation:

The  effort o f systems thinking is  t o see  a broader picture o f human functioning than that
d e ﬁ n e d b y the  various perspectives o n individual functioning. T o h e l p broaden the  focus
o f research observers t o see beyond conventional psychiatry, Bowen (1977) formulated a
series  o f underlying assumptions: ( a ) that  emotional illness is  directly related t o human
biology , (b) that emotional illness is  a multigenerational process, a n d ( c ) that there is  great
variance  between what  humans  d o a n d what  they s a y t h e y d o . I n addition, B o w e n worked
t o deﬁne difﬁcult concepts into functional facts. A n example o f this effort can b e found in
the  deﬁnition o f love as  a relationship fact. H e wrote, * 1 am  not  able  t o accurately deﬁne
l o v e , but  it  is  a fact that statements t o another important person about the presence or
absence  o f love  i n self, o r i n the  other, predictably results i n a n emotional reaction i n the
relationship"' (Bowen, 1977, p . 187). Systems thinking has b e e n characterized b y a n effort t o avoid cause and effect
thinking. The  effort t o assign a single cause t o a n effect is  inherent i n human thinking. In
v e r y narrow limits there is  sume  accuracy t o this perspective. I n terms o f human eno-
tonal functioning it  surfaces i n the  efforts t o ﬁ x blame f o r misfortune o r t o see the
"cause"' o f a problem i n a single  person's behavior .

I n terms o f human eno-
tonal functioning it  surfaces i n the  efforts t o ﬁ x blame f o r misfortune o r t o see the
"cause"' o f a problem i n a single  person's behavior . The  systems viewpoint altempts to
understand human behavior as  t h e product o f a balance o f forces i n the  family . All
systems  theories operate w i t h a notion o f forces that oppose one  another t o create a
d y n a m i c balance o r homeostasis. From  this  perspective change occurs as  a result o f a
disruption o f homeostasis w h e n the  system is  stressed. All  biological systems appear 10
have  mechanisms that are activated t o restore balance t o the stressed system. Symptoms
m a y emerge when these adaptive mechanisms are overloaded, a n d the symptom that
appears  frequently c a n be  a n exaggeration o f the  restorative mechanism itself (Kerr,
1 9 8 1 ) . The  important idea, therefore, is  that symptoms emerge during periods o f system
imbalance and often represent the overloading o f a normal restorative mechanism. Bowen (1972) describes t w o major forces continually i n operation within the family. The  ﬁrst is  the  togetherness force, seen as  rooted i n the  instinctual, patterned behavior of
the  species a n d a product o f the  emotional system within each individual. The  together-
ness  force deﬁnes all family members as  alike i n terms o f their basic perspectives,
principles, a n d feelings.

a lifetime. The individuation force is  manifested i n the degree t o which a person assumes
responsibility f o r his  o r h e r o w n happiness a n d direction i n life a n d avoids the blaming of
others f o r personal malaise o r failure. The force toward individuation allows a person to
experience genuine caring f o r another without the  need t o possess o r function f o r the  other
person. The individuation force operates i n the thinking center o f the person. The  center o f human emotional functioning is  thought t o be  the  limbic system,
comprised o f the limbic cortex a n d its connections t o the  brain stem. Ancestral, patterned,
repetitive behaviors as well as  the deep-seated, instinctual emotions that become visible in
the  aggressive, defensive, a n d m a t i n g behaviors  o f humans  are  b e l i e v e d t o be  largely
controlled b y the limbic system (MacLean, 1 9 7 3 ) . The  thinking center is  thought lo
consist largely o f the  neocortex a n d t o deal primarily with perception a n d mental process-
i n g . W h e n the  t w o centers are  not  clearly a n d recognizably distinct t o a person, t h e y are
referred t o as  fused. I n a fused state t h e emotional system tends t o override the  thinking
system.

I n a fused state t h e emotional system tends t o override the  thinking
system. The  result is  the  initiation o f a semiautomatic pattem o f behavior, the  roots of
w h i c h lie  i n the personal past o f the  individual a n d the  evolutionary past o f the species. Where there is  less fusion o f the thinking a n d emotional systems, the person is  referred to
as  more differentiated. The  more highly differentiated person is  able t o maintain the
objectivity a n d careful thought o f the  thinking system f o r longer periods o f time  i n spite of
the emotional center's arousal and tendency toward automatic patterned response. E a r l y (1957) i n his  NIMH  research, B o w e n (1978a) n o t e d that anxiety was  easily
transferred among members i n a family. A n increase i n anxiety i n a mother would produce
a predictable psychotic reaction i n a daughter. The emotional system is  believed t o be
acutely sensitive t o anxiety i n s e l f o r another . The  greater the  degree o f fusion between the
emotional a n d thinking systems, the  more  the  person responds i n a n emotionally pro-
gramed manner t o the presence o f anxiety i n another, particularly i n a close network such
as  the  family . The  term fusion i s extended i n this  sense t o reciprocal emotional reactivity
o f one person to another i n the presence o f anxiety. The  idea of "emotional reactiveness" is  basic a n d important.

The  idea of "emotional reactiveness" is  basic a n d important. I n 1974, Bowen
(1978b) compared the family system t o a n electronic circuit i n which each member is
connected t o every other member. Each person becomes a nodal point o r a n electronic
center, receiving and transmitting impulses from and to the other points i n the system or
circuit. I f the major impulses sent through the  system are considered t o be  emotional,
representing the operation o f the togetherness f o r c e , t h e n the  reaction o f a n y m e m b e r upon
receipt o f a n emotional impulse a n d the  further impulse(s) he  o r she transmits i n response
can be  accurately described as  emotional reactions. The more the impulses are anxiety
based, the greater anxious reaction they provoke. Bowen (1978b) also used the term
"emotional reﬂex" t o refer t o the  same  phenomenon. This  term  conveys t h e automatic
quality of the reaction occurring out of awareness of the  person. As  is  the case with
physical reﬂexes, the  emotional reﬂex c a n be  brought within limited observation and
limited conscious control.It  is  o n this deep level that the  togetherness force i n humans appears t o operate. T o a
greater o r lesser degree fusion is  characteristic o f all people a n d o f all families. Where i t is
active, persons remain focused o n others i n a reactive manner, losing sight o f personal
beliefs a n d goals.

#closeness i n a highly fused f a m i l y automatically produces i n some  members a reactive

equilibrium c a n f a v o r either togetherness o r individuation but  not  both, a n d the  ratio
becomes  the  norm  f o r the  f a m i l y i n that  particular homeostatic conﬁguration. W h e n theequilibrium is  threatened b y a surge o f either force  the  other force  moves  t o offset thes u r g e i n the  opposite direction.

Individual thories are akin t o the description o f the carburetor. They c a n be
descriptively accurate but  have  n o w a y t o account f o r the  function o f the  person i n the
relationship system.Systems thinking permits a broad view  o f the  relationship m a t r i x a n d the  functioning
position o f each person. There are  people i n families w h o provide the  energy o r drive to
assure that things get  done. Family members automatically t u r n t o these doers i n times of
trouble a n d these resourceful people generally pull  the  family through the emotional
quagmire. Others appear continually t o be  the  focal  point  o f f a m i l y c o n c e r n . The  p e r s o n in
this position frequently develops a chronic dysfunction that worsens during periods of
family stress. Yet  others i n the  family appear t o function independently o f it  a n d t o be

origin (Bowen, 1974). Therefore a major g o a l o f therapy is  t o assist a person's movement
toward greater differentiation o f self. The foruitous realization that quicker progress
could be  made working direcily i n the family o f origin rather than i n the nuclear family

teaching the basic concepts o f family systems theory, and the individual is  encouraged to

initial goals is  the effort t o regain contact with the family o f origin where such contact has

not  increase the level of differentiation i n the family. The  effort t o establish notional contact with the family o f origin is  important in

The  Germanneurologist Gerald Heuther looks at  stress v e r y differently . He  describes stress, not  i n the  context of- disease, but  as  the  quintessential pre-requisite f o r b o t h physical  a n d psychological d e v e l o p m e n t . Thestress response is  elicited w h e n the  individual's physical o r mental constitution is  not  yet  ﬁt  t o meet  an-environmental demand, a n d the  stress response is  the  organism's attempt t o ready itself f o r s u c h a
 5d e m a n d . The  target o f the stress response is  the  associative cortex - the  part o f the  brain that recognizesa n d interprets the  stressor, decides o n a behavior t o manage  the  stressor, a n d stores the  experience inmemory . Heuther makes a n important distinction between the  stress response i n the lower vertebratesa n d the  stress response i n h u m a n s . I n the  l o w e r vertebrates, the  stress response is  a ﬁght  o r ﬂightresponse c o m i n g out  o f the  o l d brain. It  is  a n inﬂexible, genetically determined response, w h i c h doesnot vary with repeated exposure t o the same stressor over time. A snake is  wired t o strike or ﬂee andw i l l always strike o r ﬂee  w h e n stressed. I n contrast, the  associative cortex, the  target o f the  stressresponse i n humans, is  the  most  plastic a n d the  least  genetically determined part o f the  brain, a n d iscapable  o f a wide  repertoire o f response  t o a stressor .

Heuther makes a n important distinction between the  stress response i n the lower vertebratesa n d the  stress response i n h u m a n s . It  is  a n inﬂexible, genetically determined response, w h i c h doesnot vary with repeated exposure t o the same stressor over time. D.Family therapists are using the ideas o f language o f movement to describethe  m a n y complex, interwoven patterns a n d reactions that exist i n all families.I n this language, people h a v e three options: ( 1 ) standing still, ( 2 ) distancing from,or ( 3 ) m o v i n g closer t o one  another. Standing still represents the  helpless positiona n d therapists have  spent  l o n g , frustrating hours  trying t o get  helpless people  tomake a move toward or away from others.The more the the rapist tries, the lessthe "patient" moves.Is that a problem in the therapist, the "patient", or both?DistanceGaining distance i n a family is  equally clear and difﬁcult. It  is not easy forthe overconcerned mother to retreat from her child.It is equally difﬁcult for ahusband, obsessed with his wife a n d fearful o f losing her, t o give her room t o deﬁneherself.It  i s difﬁcult for the child, struggling with both uncertainty and a desirefor independence a t the same time, t o leave home without emotionally cutting offfrom his parents.In all of these situations, the move that has to be made is clearand thereis the advantage of having physical forms of distance available. One canturn on TV, take a walk, read a newspaper, or go shopping to avoid being i n thepresence o f the other person. Distancing does not have to be done gracefully.

The  expression o f negative feelingsfrom the distant position will n o t neutralize the effectiveness o f the move.ClosenessMovement toward closeness is another story. Closeness results when twopeople move toward each other and get as close as possible without fusing. Toavoid fusing into a oneness, there must always be  some space so that each o n e cank n o w where he  begins a n d ends, what is  inside him  a n d inside the  other person,where his own boundaries end and where the other's begin.It  requires a keensense o f self-identity a n d self-differentiation. T o the  extent that either or b o t h ofthese elements is  lacking, a blending o f one  self into the  other will occur.Fusionultimately results i n distance, however, since people must wrench themselvesapart i n order t o re-deﬁne themselves.I n contrast to distancing, the feelingsinside a person a n d between people are critically important i n developing closenessa n d preventing fusion.168! text: Closeness and StructureA great deal is known about the structure involved in the development of apersonal relationship. In a close relationship each person must assume respon-sibility for his o w n feelings, not tell others what to do, avoid triangles, and stopmind reading. These  s t r u c t u r a l notions are  conducive to c l o s e n e s s . They arenecessary and allow it t o happen. But, b y themselves, structural concepts willnot create closeness. Nor is closeness a natural phenomenon. The desire forit is universal but one will never attain it b y "doing what comes naturally." Norcan it be forced. To force it is to kill it.Unlike distancing from another person,closeness must be accomplished gracefully. I n the long run, closeness can onlybe  accomplished b y two people who want it, who want both the beauty of such arelationship and the emotional price that must be paid for it.It is at this point inthe development of a personal relationship that so many families fail. They havelearned a great deal, try valiantly t o follow the structural rules they have beentaught, but emotional sensitivities continue t o intrude and the sense of feelingclose remains elusive. Relationships become more functional but gracefully ﬂow-ing emotionality and connectedness between people is  absent. Openness remainslimited. Unmet expectations are controlled but will frequently manifest themselvesdirectly or indirectly and the emptiness i n the relationship will become increasinglyapparent.

The stimulus is any agent,action or condition that will elicit emotional upset i n the family or inside a person.It  can be  a thought, a feeling, a tone o f voice, a n assumption, a n implication, a ques-tion, a memory. I n any emotional problem the ﬁrst reaction t o this stimulus is afeeling o f emptiness inside followed b y hurt. This can be  a wave o f pain, suffering,injury or distress. The hurt is followed b y the emotional upset or anger and thenthe reaction.

text: W h y the W o r d Emptiness?Talking about emptiness is not a new  or different idea. M a n y people havewritten about it  for many years under different labels. "Emptiness" is a spatialterm consistent with the language o f position, movement, closeness, distance,direction o f movement toward or away , rhythm, speed, amplitude o f movement,triangles and time. The word is general enough t o encompass all the descriptivefeelings that people  report w h e n they have emotional problems. Finally, it is asimple word that is heard and recognized b y people. It is easy to identify the word"emptiness," People readily acknowledge that they have been i n that state at oneo r at many points i n their life. The word "emptiness" is also a word that has im-plications. It  is not purely descriptive but also carries implications and directionsand questions. What is missing? How  can one ﬁll it? W ith what? Was  somethinglost and, if so, where?One  might ask, " W h y call it  emptiness when it is so full o f feelings?" Thereis  the  part o f emptiness that everyone feels. There is  another part that comes fromnot  k n o w i n g a n d u s i n g one's  o w n self. The  t h i r d part  is  the  emptiness  that comesfrom relationships that d o not  work. W h e n self a n d relationships are confused,emptiness ensues.  I have called the emptiness that is i n everyone the "ﬁfth dimension" of self.The other four dimensions are the depth dimension (everything that is in a personbut without any movement), the object dimension (movement toward objects), thepersonal dimension (movement toward people), and time. text: The ﬁfth dimensionrefers to the natural incompleteness o f self and systems. N o matter how hard orlong one tries, he will never be  complete. He  cannot be  complete as a n individualnor can he  be  complete b y marrying or having children. A system does not makea complete whole.The sum of its parts does not add u p to a whole. Consequently,everyone is a t least a little lonely, and feels that he  is inadequate, a failure--in aword, empty. It  is  important t o realize a n d acknowledge this natural incomplete-ness.The myth that completeness exists and the desperate search for it leadspeople to attempt the impossible.If one  learns  t o accept  i n c o m p l e t e n e s s , t o de-ﬁne the ﬁfth dimension o f self, then he  will engage i n the possible. One  cannothave complete emotional tranquility, d o everything intellectually. I f one tries toﬁll the ﬁfth dimension o f self, h e can have only the unfulﬁlled expectation bywishful thinking and fantasy. W h e n not  acknowledged, people ﬁll the emptiness bydruge, sex, alcohol, money, attempts to accumulate self from others, conﬂict,helplessness, mysticism, causes, power seeking, phony types o f religion, andactivities. It  leads to a n unreal picture of life governed b y what should be  fairness,righteousness, what people ought to do, doing good--a dream.There  is  a confu-sion between ideals and reality. The way to handle the ﬁfth dimension is to acknowl-edge and accept it.

Acceptance is not dishonest. Itunderstands that self and others are not perfect--that it is all right not to be right--t o be  imperfect. This does wonders for the emotional climate between people, andfosters  closeness.M a n y people grew u p i n their extended family believing that if one does nothave high expectations o f others, others will deliver very little. With closerobservations, this principle comes into serious question. Such a principle isbasically pessimistic and negative. Actually, with a high level o f expectation, afamily system tends to become very sensitive and very reactive, and human failuresbecome less tolerable. Each person tends to become too important to the other,and one person, especially a child, tends to become a fused extension of the other.The forces o f interdependency, togetherness and fusion become s o strong that a let-down i n any sector has ramiﬁcations throughout the system. The emotional climatebetween people becomes very explosive.Such a high level of expectation makes theactions of other people stand out and puts the focus on the production of the otherperson. The personhood of others is ignored and one turns away from his own selfand a continuous evaluation of his own expectations.182
 I f one can lower his expectations o f others, he will have more time to devotet o his  o w n self.

Where expectations are ordinarily met, there is n o problem and one doesnot have to work i n that area. These are not reversals. Hesays nothing that even verges o n a n expectation, order or demand.This is especially difﬁcult to maintain when the other begins to live u p to thevery expectations that one has given up. Every ﬁber in one's body will pressureone to raise his level of expectation again at  that point. At  that moment, one muststrain t o make every effort t o keep the expectation at zero. People often say, "Buti f I don't expect anything, nothing will be  done." That is true. One  either does ithimself o r it is not done. Lowering expectations allows for personal re-evaluationof misperceptions from the past. text: Medicinemay always b e separated into specialties based o n clinicalskills, but i f a process is  common t o all  diseases (a  "uni-disease"), then more enlightened coordination amongspecialists i n t h e application o f their skills is  indicatedDiseased organs and tissues are too often thought aboutand treated as if they were isolated from the rest of thepatient's body; patients too often are thought aboutand treated as i f their functioning was insulated fromtheir relationships w i t h doctors, nurses, f a m i l y members,friends, a n d others. M a n y clinicians, patients, a n d fam-ilies have long been aware of the probleins stemmingfrom treatment approaches based on a narrow perspec-tive, but no integrative theory has been available to man-date and orchestrate treatment based on a broader per-spective. The Bowen theory may be an important steptoward the development o f an integrative theory.Another important implication of linking clinical dys-functions t o the emotional system is  that the emotionalsystem presumably creates a range o f adaptive function-i n g i n species other than h u m a n b e i n g s . These  otherspecies predictably spawn a percentage o f members thatare unusually vulnerable to the more extreme degrees ofdysfunction. I f a range  of adaptive functioning i s a facto f m a n y o r a l l species, it  implies that the  creation o f apercentage o f poorly adaptive people i n human society isprobably unchangeable.

RosenthalUniversity o f lowaThis article describes a procedure for training family therapists i n the  clinicalapplication o f circular questioning as  developed and implemented at the  Mar-riage and Family Therapy Clinic at the University o f Iowa. A pragmatic tax-onomy of circular questions is  presented; instructional handouts designed tofacilitate the use of these questions within the trainee's initial interviews areincluded.The concept of circularity has been widely discussed in family therapy literaturesince Bateson's (1972, 1979) elaboration o f the cybernetic epistemology o f family systems(c f, Hoffman, 1981; Keeney , 1983, 1985;  Papp, 1983; Penn, 1982; Palazzoli Selvini,Boscolo, Cecchin, & Prata, 1978a, 1980; T omm, 1984a, 1 9 8 4 b ) . The  Milan Associatesintroduced the circular interview as  a means for conducting a systemic investigation ofthe changes and differences i n family relationships which recursively support dysfunc-tional interactions or symptoms i n the family (Palazzoli Selvini et al., 1980). I n additiont o being a useful tool  f o r gathering information suited t o the generation o f hypothesesand interventions, circular questions provide the family with an opportunity t o viewitself systemically.

 INTRODUCING THE CIRCULAR INTERVIEWCircularity is  a term which bewilders many neophytes t o the ﬁeld o f family therapy.T o describe punctuated interactional sequences as a n overlay o f inﬁnite, evolving circles,loops, o r circuits, may only increase the confusion. Metaphors and images are useful;however, the essence o f circularity is  not its shape but its implication-behaviors andbeliefs do not occur in isolation. Individuals are best understood within their interre-lational contexts. A comprehensive systemic view o f the family focuses o n the evolvingrelationships of the family members within their environmental, historical, develop-mental, and ideological contexts. A circular perspective emphasizes cyclical sequencesof interactions which interconnect with family beliefs; these patterns of relating andbelieving may recursively serve t o perpetuate dysfunctional behaviors and cognitions( c f . Papp, 1983; Palazzoli Selvini et al., 1978a, 1980).The  circular interview  investigates the  recurring contextual patterns o f relatingwhich constitute a family system.

A circular viewof the problem is  obtained when the full cycle o f repeated interactions is  clear. Achronological "arc" (Penn, 1 9 8 2 ) appears b y tracing the development o f the symptomover time: the events and relational contexts which occurred prior to, and during, therecalled onset o f the symptom, the current contextual view o f the symptom, and futureexpectations f o r what may happen. P a p p , 1983;  W atzlawick, W eakland, &Fisch, 1974).Relationships, beliefs, values, myths, thoughts and feelings are explored throughquestions from the third category, Comparison and Classiﬁcation. Members are requestedt o describe the behaviors and beliefs o f the others i n the family and t o deﬁne intermemberrelationships over time. Interventive Circular Questioning, the fourth category, differsfrom the others i n intent: once the family's interactions and belief systems become clear(Papp, 1983), and hypotheses have been tentatively conﬁrmed, interventive questionsmay be  used t o challenge the family's patterns o f interacting.

K u h n , Ph.D.Papers o f this  genre  w o u l d best  b e g i n w i t h deﬁnitions o f the  terms that comprisethe  m a i n thoughts, i . e . "Triangles" a n d "Differentiation". M a n y o f y o u a r e quitefamiliar w i t h these  terms but bear w i t h m e . T h e y warrant repeating o v e r a n d overa n d o v e r . "The Triangle  is  the smallest stable relationship system. A two-personsystem is  a n unstable system that immediately forms a series o f interlockingtriangles. The  triangle has  deﬁnite relationship patterns that predictably repeat inperiods  o f s t r e s s a n d calm."  A d e s c r i p t i o n o f how  the  triangle  works  follows  thisdeﬁnition."In periods o f calm, the triangle is  made u p o f a comfortably closetwosome and a less comfortable outsider. The twosome works t o preserve thetogetherness, lest one become uncomfortable and form  a better togethernesselsewhere. The outsider seeks t o form a togetherness with one  o f the others, andthere are numerous well-known moves  t o accomplish t h i s . The  emotional forceswithin the triangle are constantly i n motion from  moment t o moment, e v e n inperiods o f calm. Moderate tension states i n the twosome are characteristically feltb y one  w h i l e the  other is  oblivious.

family systems therapy, focusing on their contrasting treatment of transference phenomena. Transference is defined as the automatic reactions, expectations, and assumptions one has toward
others, particularly evident in psychotherapy relationships and based on experiences in the primary
parental triangle. In contrast, "ference" is Murray Bowen's term for the active, lifelong process of
engaging unresolved emotional attachments to the primary parental triangle by developing
progressively more defined adult relationships with family of origin members. The fundamental distinction lies in therapeutic focus: psychodynamic therapy cultivates and analyzes
the transference relationship between patient and therapist, while family systems therapy deliberately
minimizes transference to focus on the client's relationship with their actual family system. These
theoretical differences manifest in contrasting clinical methodologies across multiple dimensions. Psychodynamic therapy employs frequent sessions (2-3 times weekly), emphasizes feelings and their
expression toward the therapist, maintains the therapist as a "blank screen," interprets unconscious
conflicts rooted in oedipal and electra complexes, and conceptualizes clients as patients with illness
requiring treatment during sessions.

flexibility to see family members separately or jointly. Diagnosis serves primarily insurance

text: Apoptosis is  considered a n "orderly" m a n n e r o f cellde a t h f o r a number o f reasons — it  usually o n l y involves a single cell, thecells shrink rather than explode, the integrity o f the membrane is  maintained,a n d the  cell's remains are  consumed o r "handled" b y its neighboring cells,rather than b y agents associated with a n inﬂammatory response. It  is  oftenreferred t o as  "orderly" cell death.The  emphasis o n "orderliness" i n apoptosis reminds me  o f t h e movie "MyLife"  s t a r r i n g Michael  K e a t o n a n d Nichole  K i d m a n . K e a t o n plays  a husbandd i a g n o s e d w i t h terminal  c a n c e r t o a n e xpe c t i ng wife  p l a y e d b y K i d m a n . Inresponse t o his diagnosis, he  decides t o carefully document his remainingdays through video s o that his  unborn s o n has  the  beneﬁt o f his wisdom,values, and presence throughout his life. Fluctuations i n functioning o f people w i t h a higher basic l e v e l ofdifferentiation are less pronounced; ﬂuctuations i n functioning f o r people at  l o w e r basiclevels o f differentiation are more pronounced. The  goal  is  t o evaluate each person a n d each family againstthemselves o v e r time, not  t o compare them t o each other . I f one is seeking more effective connectedness with others, thenone must step back and examine one's separateness--one's emotional reactivity, one'sbeliefs, one's principles. A n d the challenge o f clarifying one's separateness comes tofruition only through more active participation i n relationships. Through this paradoxicaldialectic, this movement back a n d forth between the  seemingly opposite poles ofseparateness and connectedness, differentiation o f self occurs. But what exactly is  this"self" that has become differentiated?More  broadly , L i f e , too, brings forth a sense o f paradox. The  magniﬁcentﬂowering of our existence o n Planet Earth is  destined t o end, later i f not  sooner. Butw h y , as Ernest Becker (1974) wondered some years ago i n his book, The  Denial ofDeath, should the concept o f inﬁnity reside i n a ﬁnite brain? What cruel paradox, that lifeshouldend i n death. A n d so we  seek t o avoid the recognition o f the Buddha that ourtrue nature holds f o r us  the  inevitability o f aging, sickness and death.

Scale o f Differentiation o f Self The  scale o f differentiation o f self refers toa theoretical scale that separates people along a continuum o f zero t o one hundred according totheir ability t o adapt t o life. Better differentiated people d o well i n most areas. Lessdifferentiated people d o less w e l l . This  difference i n functioning has t o d o w i t h how  they functioni n relationships, an outgrowth o f their years i n their families o f origin, the formative relationshipsystem. This  "level"  c a n be  estimated r o u g h l y but  never accurately measured, since that  wouldinvolve observing over a n entire lifetime. Indicators o f adaptation include physical health,vocational success, education, relationship history , and longevity i n the individual as well  as  inthe individuals that make u p his o r her nuclear family . N o one o f these indicators alone tells thewhole story but taken together, they form  a picture o f a life.How  we  function i n relationships directly affects the brain and its ability t o managethinking and emotions. People a t the higher end o f the scale have a greater ability t o choosebetween the intellectual system a n d the emotional/feeling system. At  the lower e n d o f the  scale,there is  little o r n o choice between the t w o systems.

text: It  is  notsurprising then that the highest level o f all  i n the classic hierarchy, that o f ultimatereality , would be  impossible t o comprehend. I f there is  a n ultimate level o f reality thatgives meaning o r purpose t o the universe, therefore, it  would comprehend us, but wecould not comprehend it.According t o most religious traditions, a "purposeful" universe m u s t have a t leastsome kind o f hierarchical arrangement. I n order t o b e the carrier o f a meaning the booko f nature has t o consist o f various levels o r dimensions, the lower able t o be informed"from  above" b y higher levels o f meaning. F o r this reason traditional religion andphilosophy almost unanimously resisted modernist attempts t o ﬂatten the hierarchydown to a single, desacralized dimension.One great advantage o f the hierarchical scheme is  that it  embeds our own brieflives and, indeed, the entire cosmos within the larger context o f an eternal realityimmune t o transience and death. Participation i n the imperishable permanence o f Godrescues the ﬂ u x o f transitory cosmic and human events from the oblivion ofnothingness. The  challenge that the new evolutionary cosmic story poses t o religion,therefore, consists i n great measure o f its  "horizontalizing" a n d "atomizing" the  sacredvertical hierarchy o f traditional religions.

text: B y ﬂattening and decomposing into atoms thehierarchy i n which the sense o f a purposeful universe has for ages been located, thenew science and cosmology seem t o have destroyed the spinal column o n which asense o f cosmic meaning had been entwined f o r thousands o f years.I cannot exaggerate the sense o f anxiety that the evolutionary scientiﬁc world-view  has thus brought about. text: The "begats" o f the bible aren't simplyanachronisms. The  New  Testament  itself, f a r from  being simply a moral compass forindividuals, i n large part was assembled as a way t o bequeath t o the next generation thewitness of an earlier generation.A crucial focus o f human evolution is  survival i n the service o f succession. A n overarchingquestion is:  How  shall life  function s o as  t o optimize survival a n d t h r i v i n g f o r one's children, forone's f a m i l y , o r c l a n o r people? But  what  might  activate (orsuppress) genetic potential?Bowen Theory focuses o n the family emotional system. A n d the l i n k between the emotionalsystem o f a family o r community and the history o f that family's o r community's evolution is  it'snarrative. This  is  one purpose, and perhaps a k e y purpose, o f language, ideas, stories, art,music, dance, drama. The  synaptic a n d neuronal activity o f the  brain functions i n the  service ofm e m o r y and narrative a n d states o f mind, both w i t h i n individuals a n d between them.

text: Even though its "aimtoward beauty" m a y not always have been successfully realized i n every episode orregion, it  is  not rash t o suspect that from its beginning the cosmos has had at  least a"loose" kind o f teleology o r purposiveness. But this does notwarrant the modern extrapolating from local disorder to the pessimistic claim that theuniverse is  pointless overall. The  judgment that the universe is  ultimately pointless isoften made o n the basis o f a purely materialist reading o f the Darwinian picture o f life.W i t h Whitehead and our ancient religious traditions, however, I suggest that we  l o o k fora "wider vision," without having t o overlook what  D a r w i n has said.The  "aesthetic" understanding o f the cosmos that I am  proposing here cautionsu s that our human vantage point is  inevitably limited, even i f it  seems t o enjoy theapparent support o f science. The  great religious and metaphysical traditions almostuniversally instruct us  that there is  always a more  expansive perspective o n the  cosmosthan a n y individual human being, o r any particular culture, o r historical epoch canlegitimately claim t o have, a n d that o u r o w n impressions are o n l y ﬂeeting glimpses ofan immeasurable and still unfolding panorama.

text: T o get life there havet o be  planets w i t h the  right chemical composition, including especially carbon, but  alsoother heavy elements. B u t where does the carbon come from? The existence ofmassive stars was required t o "cook" the lighter elements (hydrogen and helium) intocarbon and other heavy elements. But  the existence o f the massive stars, some ofwhich explode as supernovae, cannot be taken f o r granted either .
